1.title: Apollo 11 Stones
1.artist: Unknown artist(s); found in the Apollo 11 Cave, Namibia
1.plain: Seven small slabs of stone from a rock shelter in southern Namibia, with animals drawn on them in charcoal and other pigments roughly 27,500 years ago. They are among the oldest figurative art (pictures of recognizable things) ever found in Africa and the oldest work on the AP list. They matter because they prove people were making symbolic images long before farming, cities or writing.
1.spot: A flat, grayish-brown stone slab with one animal drawn in dark outline in side view, floating on bare stone with no background. The famous one has a cat-like body with odd back legs that may look human.
1.remember: Found in 1969, the year Apollo 11 landed on the Moon, so the oldest art on the list is named after the newest technology. One small step for art: Namibia, c. 25,500–25,300 B.C.E.
compare: No. 2 (§2.2), Great Hall of the Bulls: Both show animals in profile with no ground line, but Lascaux is fixed and huge while Apollo 11 is small and portable.
No. 4 (§2.4), Running horned woman: Both are African prehistoric images, but the Running Horned Woman is much later, centers a human figure and is painted on a fixed rock wall.
No. 3 (§2.3), Camelid sacrum in the shape of a canine: Another very early small object from a different continent where the animal identity is debated and the date range is wide.
1.vocab: mobiliary art, therianthrope, profile, radiocarbon dating, stratigraphy, figurative, ground line.

form: Small, flat, hand-sized slabs of quartzite (a hard, grainy stone). They are portable objects, not paintings on a cave wall.
Each animal is drawn in profile (side view), the angle that shows the most identifying features at once: legs, back line, head shape and tail.
Pigments include charcoal for black, with ochre and white on some pieces. The College Board simply lists the medium as charcoal on stone.
There is no ground line (a line for figures to stand on), no landscape and no scene. Each animal sits alone on the stone surface.
The best-known slab shows a feline body whose hind legs may be human, a possible therianthrope (part-human, part-animal being). Scholars disagree about how human those legs really are.
Outlines are simple and confident, with little interior detail, so the shape of the animal does almost all the work.
function: Nobody knows the original purpose, because the makers left no writing and the slabs were found loose in the shelter’s deposits rather than in a shrine.
Because they are portable, they count as mobiliary art (art that can be carried). They could have been held, shown, traded, used in ritual or left as offerings.

Some scholars compare them with much later San rock art of southern Africa, which ethnographers link to healers entering trance and taking on animal power. That analogy spans thousands of years, so treat it as a possibility.
content: The animals have been read as a feline, a rhinoceros and zebra- or antelope-like creatures. Identifications are uncertain because the drawings are simple and partly worn.
If the hybrid figure is a therianthrope, it suggests early ideas about spiritual transformation between humans and animals.
Choosing animals rather than people or landscape matches Paleolithic art elsewhere, such as Lascaux in France (No. 2), even though the two had no contact.
context: Apollo 11 Cave is a rock shelter in the Huns Mountains of southwestern Namibia. German archaeologist Wolfgang Erich Wendt excavated it starting in 1969 and named it after the Moon landing he heard about on the radio.

The slabs were dated by radiocarbon dating of charcoal from the same soil layer. That dates the layer, not the paint itself, so the date is indirect and relies on stratigraphy (the order of buried layers).
Some later studies suggest the layer could be a few thousand years older, near 30,000 years. Either way, these are among the oldest figurative images in Africa.
Africa has even older symbolic marks, such as the engraved ochre from Blombos Cave in South Africa, about 75,000 years old, but those are abstract patterns, not pictures of animals.
The makers were hunter-gatherers who moved through the landscape seasonally and used the shelter repeatedly over a very long time. On the exam.
If asked for the oldest work on the list → Apollo 11 Stones, Namibia, c. 25,500–25,300 B.C.E.
If asked how they were dated → radiocarbon dating of charcoal in the same layer, an indirect method based on stratigraphy.
If asked to contrast with Lascaux → Apollo 11 is portable (mobiliary) while Lascaux is fixed to a cave wall; both show animals in profile with no ground line.
Trap: the name has nothing to do with the art itself. It only marks the year of excavation, 1969.
Trap: these are not cave-wall paintings and not from Europe. They are loose slabs from a rock shelter in southern Africa.
Attribution clue: a single animal in profile on a small stone, with no setting, points to prehistoric art.

2.title: Great Hall of the Bulls
2.plain: The first large chamber of Lascaux Cave in the Dordogne region of southwestern France, its walls and ceiling covered with huge painted wild bulls, horses and deer. They were made roughly 17,000 years ago by Ice Age hunter-gatherers. They are the most famous prehistoric paintings anywhere and show that Paleolithic people were sharp observers and organized, skilled painters.
2.spot: Huge black-outlined bulls and smaller red-brown horses overlap across a pale, creamwhite rock ceiling. The bulls’ bodies are in side view but their horns curve out as if seen from the front.
2.remember: Lascaux sounds like ‘last cows’: giant Ice Age bulls in France, 15,000–13,000 B.C.E. Found by four teenagers in 1940, closed in 1963 because visitors’ breath was damaging it.
compare: No. 1 (§2.1), Apollo 11 Stones: Both show animals in profile, but Apollo 11 is small, portable and much older, while Lascaux is huge and fixed to the cave.
No. 4 (§2.4), Running horned woman: Lascaux focuses on still, overlapping animals deep in a cave; the Saharan painting centers a moving human figure in an open rock shelter.
No. 3 (§2.3), Camelid sacrum in the shape of a canine: Both makers worked with a natural shape already present, the rock bulges at Lascaux and the bone form of the camelid sacrum.
2.vocab: twisted perspective, aurochs, ochre, pigment, Paleolithic, superimposition, ground line.

form: The main animals are aurochs (huge wild cattle, now extinct), along with horses, deer, a partly hidden bear and an odd spotted creature nicknamed the ‘unicorn’. The biggest bull is about 5.2 meters (17 feet) long.
Animals use twisted perspective (body in profile but horns turned to face the viewer), so you see the most typical view of each part at once.

Black came from charcoal and manganese oxide; reds, yellows and browns from ochre (ironrich earth). Powdered pigment was mixed with water and applied by fingers, pads, brushes or blown through hollow bones or reeds.
Painters used natural bulges and ridges in the rock to suggest the swelling bellies, shoulders and heads of animals, so the cave surface itself helps create volume.
The wall is limestone coated with a thin layer of white calcite, which gave a bright ground for the color.
Animals overlap and face different directions with no ground line and no setting. Some were painted over older ones (superimposition), probably over a long period.
function: People did not live in the decorated chambers. Light came from stone lamps burning animal fat (one carved sandstone lamp was found in the cave), so painting here was a special, deliberate trip into darkness.
Proposed purposes include hunting magic (painting animals to ensure a good hunt), shamanic ritual, initiation of young people, seasonal record keeping and storytelling. None can be proven.
Reindeer bones dominate the food remains found at Lascaux, yet reindeer barely appear on the walls, so the paintings were not simply a menu of what people ate.
Today the original is sealed. Visitors see precise replicas instead: Lascaux II (opened 1983) and Lascaux IV (opened 2016).
content: The subjects are almost entirely animals. The only human figure in the whole cave is a stick-like, bird-headed man in a separate part called the Shaft, not in the Hall of the Bulls.
Abstract signs such as dots, lines and grid-like shapes appear among the animals. Their meaning is unknown.
The chosen animals are large, powerful and dangerous, which may point to ideas of strength, spirit power or fertility rather than daily diet.
context: Discovered on 12 September 1940 by four teenagers near the town of Montignac. It opened to the public in 1948.

Crowds of up to more than a thousand visitors a day brought breath, body heat, humidity and lighting that fed green algae and mineral crusts. The cave was closed in 1963; later fungus outbreaks still require careful monitoring.
It belongs to the Upper Paleolithic (late Old Stone Age), Magdalenian culture. Radiocarbon dates on charcoal found in the cave put the painting around 17,000 years ago.
Evidence elsewhere in the cave, such as sockets cut into the walls of the Axial Gallery, suggests painters built scaffolding to reach high surfaces.
Lascaux is part of a UNESCO World Heritage site (Vézère Valley, 1979). It is the classic example of the conflict between preservation and public access. On the exam.
If asked about twisted perspective → Lascaux: profile bodies with horns shown frontally.
If asked how prehistoric painters worked in the dark → animal-fat stone lamps, blown and daubed pigment, scaffolding.
If asked about function → give several theories, and cite the reindeer bones as evidence against a simple hunting-menu reading.
If asked about preservation → discovered 1940, closed 1963, replicas Lascaux II and IV.
Trap: Lascaux has almost no humans. The prehistoric work centered on a human figure is the Running Horned Woman (No. 4).
Materials: mineral pigments on limestone; dated 15,000–13,000 B.C.E. on the College Board list.
Attribution clue: large overlapping animals in profile, no ground line, natural rock contours used for form → Paleolithic cave art.

3.title: Camelid sacrum in the shape of a canine
3.plain: A fossilized bone from the base of the spine of an extinct llama-like animal, worked so that it looks like the head of a dog or coyote. It is often called the earliest known work of art from the Americas. It is interesting because the maker spotted an animal face in a natural object and then improved it, which makes art as much about seeing as making.
3.spot: A small, brownish, roughly triangular bone shaped like an animal’s head, with a pointed snout at the narrow end and holes that read as nostrils and eyes.
3.remember: Sacrum means ‘sacred bone’ in Latin, so think ‘a sacred dog made from a dead camel’. Tequixquiac, central Mexico, 14,000–7000 B.C.E.: a huge date range means huge uncertainty.
compare: No. 2 (§2.2), Great Hall of the Bulls: Both makers used a natural shape already present, rock bulges at Lascaux and bone form here, to create an animal image.
No. 9 (§2.9), The Ambum Stone: Both are small zoomorphic objects whose original function is unknown and whose animal identity is debated.
No. 1 (§2.1), Apollo 11 Stones: Both are among the earliest image-making on their continents, but Apollo 11 is drawn on stone while the sacrum is a carved found object.
3.vocab: sacrum, camelid, found object, zoomorphic, incising.

form: It is the sacrum (the triangular bone at the base of the spine, joined to the pelvis) of an extinct camelid, a relative of llamas and camels that lived in the Americas during the last Ice Age.
The bone is fossilized, meaning minerals gradually replaced its original material, making it heavy and stone-like.
Someone cut, ground and incised (scratched lines into) the bone and enlarged openings at the narrow end so they read as nostrils on a snout.
It is small enough to hold in one hand, a few inches across.
It is a found object that was modified: the key artistic act was recognizing a shape and making only small changes. Scholars disagree about how much is human work and how much is natural.
function: Its original use is unknown. It may have been a ritual object, an amulet or a personal treasure.
It shows a very human habit, seeing faces and animals in natural forms, and choosing to sharpen that likeness.
Later Mesoamerican cultures linked the pelvic region with fertility and rebirth, but those ideas come thousands of years later and cannot be assumed for this maker.
content: The head is usually identified as a canine: dog, coyote or wolf. Dogs later carried strong meaning in Mesoamerica, such as guiding souls of the dead, but that is a much later belief.
The work involves transformation: one animal’s bone becomes the image of a different animal.
The word sacrum is a European, Latin anatomical name. It tells us nothing about what the original maker believed, which is a common exam trap.
context: It was found in 1870 at Tequixquiac, north of Mexico City, during digging for drainage works in the Valley of Mexico.
The find came before modern excavation methods, so its exact layer was not recorded carefully. That is why the date range, 14,000–7000 B.C.E., is so wide.

A further problem: the bone could be much older than the carving, since someone could have worked an old fossil long after the animal died. The date of the bone and the date of the art are not necessarily the same.
It is kept in the Museo Nacional de Antropología in Mexico City.
Humans had reached the Americas by at least about 15,000 years ago, so the work belongs to the early period of human settlement there. On the exam.
If asked for the earliest Americas work on the list → the camelid sacrum, Tequixquiac, central Mexico, 14,000–7000 B.C.E.
If asked about materials → fossilized bone, a found object modified by carving and incising.
If asked why the date range is huge → poorly recorded 1870 discovery and uncertain archaeological context.
Trap: it is not a dog’s bone. It is a camelid bone made to look like a canine.
Trap: do not claim the maker thought it was ‘sacred’ because of its Latin name; that link is modern.
Big idea: the line between found form and made art is blurry, just as Lascaux painters used bulges in the rock.

4.title: Running horned woman
4.plain: A painted figure of a running or dancing woman wearing horns, on a rock shelter wall in the Tassili n’Ajjer mountains of the Algerian Sahara. It was made when the Sahara was green grassland with lakes and animals. It is one of the few prehistoric works on the list centered on a human, and the site as a whole records a lost climate and way of life.
4.spot: A tall, slim figure in mid-stride with a horned headdress, its body covered in white and red dots, with fringes streaming from the arms, waist and knees, painted on reddish rock with smaller faint figures around it.
4.remember: Tassili is the Sahara’s picture gallery: a horned woman running out of a green Sahara, 6000–4000 B.C.E. Lascaux’s bulls stand still; she runs.
compare: No. 2 (§2.2), Great Hall of the Bulls: Lascaux shows still animals with almost no humans; this painting puts a moving human figure at the center.
No. 10 (§2.10), Tlatilco female figurine: Both focus on the female body and probable ritual or fertility meanings in early societies.
No. 1 (§2.1), Apollo 11 Stones: Both are African prehistoric images, but Apollo 11 is portable and far older, while this is painted on a fixed rock wall.
4.vocab: rock shelter, ochre, pigment, superimposition, scarification, pastoralism.

form: Painted with natural pigments, red and yellow ochre and white clay, on the wall of an open rock shelter, not deep inside a cave.
The figure is in a dynamic striding pose, legs wide apart, which gives a strong sense of motion rare in prehistoric art.
Her body is covered with dots and lines, probably body paint, scarification (decorative scars) or a costume.
Fringes hang from her arms, waist and legs, perhaps raﬀia or fiber attachments worn in ritual dance.
A horned headdress tops the head; a cloud of dots near the horns is sometimes read as falling grain.
Smaller, fainter figures surround and overlap her. Superimposition (painting over older images) is common at the site because the shelters were used for thousands of years.
function: Probably ritual. She may be a goddess, a priestess or a dancer in a ceremony; the costume details suggest a real performance someone saw.
The horns might link her to cattle, fertility or supernatural power, or simply be part of a ceremonial headdress.
Today the paintings are part of a national park and UNESCO World Heritage site (1982) and a destination for researchers and tourists.
content: A female figure in motion suggests dance, ritual performance or a spiritual journey.
If the dots are falling grain, the image may relate to fertility and abundance. This reading is a guess, not a fact.
Horns can mark a being as more than human, a common way to show supernatural status in many cultures.
context: Tassili n’Ajjer, a sandstone plateau in southeastern Algeria, holds more than 15,000 paintings and engravings, one of the largest rock art collections in the world.
Between about 9000 and 3500 B.C.E. the Sahara was much wetter, with grassland, lakes, giraffes, elephants and hippos. The paintings record life in that green Sahara.

This figure is usually assigned to the early ‘Round Head’ style. Later layers at Tassili show herds of cattle, then horses, then camels, tracking the shift from hunting to herding and finally to desert.

French explorer Henri Lhote copied the paintings in 1956–57. His team splashed water on the rock to brighten the colors, which damaged them, an example of research harming the thing studied. On the exam.
If asked about climate change in prehistoric art → Tassili n’Ajjer: the Sahara was once fertile, and the paintings track hunting, herding and desertification.
If asked for a prehistoric human figure in motion → the Running Horned Woman, Tassili n’Ajjer, Algeria, 6000–4000 B.C.E.
Rock painting in an open shelter, not a deep cave like Lascaux (No. 2).
Horns, body markings and fringes = probable ritual costume.
Trap: it is from the Sahara in Algeria, not Egypt and not Namibia (Apollo 11, No. 1).
Preservation point: Lhote’s 1950s team wet the paintings and damaged them.

5.title: Beaker with ibex motifs
5.plain: A tall, thin painted clay cup from a cemetery at Susa in southwestern Iran, decorated with a mountain goat (ibex) whose horns curl into a giant circle, plus bands of dogs and birds. It shows early potters turning real animals into elegant geometry. Its fine craftsmanship points to specialist craftspeople in an early settled society.
5.spot: A tall, slightly flaring cream-colored beaker painted in dark brown with horizontal bands: tiny vertical strokes at the top, a stripe of stretched-out running dogs, and a large geometric goat whose horns sweep into a huge circle.
5.remember: The Susa ibex’s horns make a giant zero: zero chance of confusing it with anything else. Iran, 4200–3500 B.C.E., buried with the dead.
compare: No. 11 (§2.11), Terra cotta fragment: Both are early decorated pottery, but Susa paints its designs while Lapita presses them into the clay with toothed stamps.
No. 2 (§2.2), Great Hall of the Bulls: Lascaux’s animals are naturalistic and loose; the Susa animals are tightly stylized into geometric pattern.
No. 13 (§3.2), Palette of King Narmer: Both organize images in horizontal registers, a habit that runs through ancient Near Eastern and Egyptian art.
No. 19 (§3.8), The Code of Hammurabi: Both were found at Susa by French excavators and are now in the Louvre.
5.vocab: register, stylized, terracotta, necropolis, grave good, abstract.

form: Made of terra cotta (fired clay) with very thin walls, about 29 cm (11 inches) tall. It may have been shaped on a slow turntable; sources differ on how much a wheel was used.
Painted in dark brown, iron-based paint on pale buff clay, before firing.
Decoration is arranged in horizontal registers (bands). At the top, long-necked wading birds are reduced to vertical lines; below, running dogs are stretched into thin streaks.
The main panel holds an ibex whose body is two triangles and whose huge horns form a near circle around a central motif, often read as a plant or geometric design.
Strong stylization (simplifying nature into pattern), symmetry and geometric abstraction. The design is planned to fit the curve of the vessel.
Framing lines divide bands and panels, giving the whole a careful, measured order.
function: A grave good (object buried with the dead) from a large necropolis (cemetery) at Susa with about 2,000 graves.
It may have held food or drink for the dead person or signaled their status. The thin, fragile walls suggest it may not have been for rough daily use, though this is uncertain.
Today it is displayed in the Louvre as a key example of early Iranian painted pottery.
content: The ibex is a wild mountain goat of the nearby Zagros Mountains. It may have stood for fertility, abundance or the natural cycle; the exact meaning is not known.
Dogs may refer to hunting, and wading birds to the marshes and rivers around Susa.
One reading sees the bands as a small world: birds of the water, dogs of the plain and goats of the mountains. It is an interpretation, not a proven fact.
context: Susa, in the Khuzestan region of Iran, was settled around 4200 B.C.E. It later became the capital of Elam and then a royal capital of the Persian Empire.
This beaker belongs to the period archaeologists call Susa I, in the Chalcolithic (copper and stone age), when villages were growing into towns.
French archaeologists led by Jacques de Morgan excavated Susa in the early 1900s, and many finds were taken to Paris. The beaker is now in the Louvre.
The skill shows a specialist potter, a sign of social complexity: some people could spend their time on a craft instead of farming.
Fun link: the Code of Hammurabi (No. 19) was also found at Susa, carried there as war booty much later. On the exam.
If asked to identify → Beaker with ibex motifs, Susa, Iran, 4200–3500 B.C.E., painted terra cotta.
If asked about form → registers, stylized animals, horns turned into a circle, symmetry.
If asked about function → funerary, found in a large cemetery.
Trap: it is a vessel, not a sculpture, and it is painted, not glazed.
If asked what it shows about society → specialist craftsmen and settled life.
Attribution clue: geometric animal bands on a thin, pale pot → ancient Near Eastern painted pottery.

6.title: Anthropomorphic stele
6.artist: Unknown maker; Arabian Peninsula (near Ha’il, Saudi Arabia)
6.plain: A slab of sandstone about 3 feet tall carved into a flat, simplified human figure, found near Ha’il in northern Saudi Arabia. It is one of the earliest monumental images of a person from the Arabian Peninsula. It tells you who someone was through what he wore and carried, not through what his face looked like.
6.spot: An upright, tombstone-like slab with a small trapezoid-shaped head set right on square shoulders, a tiny simplified face, two cords crossing the chest, and a wide belt holding a doublebladed dagger.
6.remember: A stele is a standing stone that carries a message. Ha’il, Arabia, fourth millennium B.C.E.: a man you know by his dagger and belt, like an ID badge in stone.
compare: No. 171 (§7.5), Ndop: The Kuba ndop also identifies a specific person through attributes rather than a realistic likeness.
No. 36 (§3.25), Grave stele of Hegeso: Both are stone grave markers commemorating a person, but the Greek stele uses naturalistic figures and a domestic scene.
No. 214 (§10.2), Moai on platform: Both are simplified, frontal stone figures that likely stood for important ancestors or leaders.
6.vocab: stele, anthropomorphic, low relief, frontal, attribute, monument.

form: Carved from sandstone, about 90 cm to 1 meter (roughly 3 feet) tall.
Carved in low relief (shapes slightly raised from the surface) on both faces, with the front, especially face, chest and waist, given the most attention.
A trapezoidal head sits directly on squared shoulders with no neck. The face is outlined, with two close-set eyes and a flattened nose.
He wears a robe and a necklace from which two cords cross diagonally over the torso, with an awl (a small pointed tool) attached.
A wide belt, continuing around the back, holds a double-bladed dagger at the waist.
The figure is frontal, flat and symmetrical, simplified into geometric shapes.
function: Most likely a grave marker or memorial, possibly set up in an open-air sanctuary connected to burial or religious ritual.
It may have stood for an ancestor, a deity or an important individual and been visited in ceremonies.
Being upright and outdoors, it was a monument: meant to be seen, to last and to mark a place.
content: Identity comes from attributes (objects that identify someone): the dagger suggests authority or warrior status, while the belt, robe, cords and awl mark rank or role.
The figure is generally read as a high-status man, though that is an interpretation.
The absence of an individual likeness suggests that a person’s role and status mattered more than their physical appearance.
context: It is one of three stelae found in the Ha’il region. Rock carvings near Tabuk, a broken stele from Riqseh in Jordan and stelae from Rawk in Yemen show similar details, pointing to a tradition shared across Arabia.
In the fourth millennium B.C.E. Arabia was moving out of a wetter climatic phase; herding communities moved across the region along routes that later became trade roads.
It is contemporary with the rise of the first cities in Mesopotamia, such as Uruk (No. 12), which shows that monumental human imagery was developing in several places at once.
It is kept in the National Museum in Riyadh. The maker is unknown, and the precise date within the fourth millennium is uncertain. On the exam.
If asked how identity is shown → through attributes (dagger, belt, cords, robe), not through realistic likeness.
If asked to identify → Anthropomorphic stele, Arabian Peninsula (Ha’il region, Saudi Arabia), fourth millennium B.C.E., sandstone.
Form keywords: frontal, flat, symmetrical, low relief, trapezoidal head.
Function: probably funerary or commemorative.
Trap: it is from Arabia, not Mesopotamia, and it is not a law stele like Hammurabi’s (No. 19).
Big idea: an early example of a monument commemorating an individual through status markers.

7.title: Jade cong
7.plain: A jade tube, square on the outside and round on the inside, made by the Liangzhu culture near the mouth of the Yangzi River in China some 4,000 to 5,000 years ago. Jade is so hard that each cong took enormous labor, so owning one, and being buried with it, signaled power. It is an early root of the Chinese love of jade that lasts to this day.
7.spot: A greenish or mottled stone block shaped like a squared tube with a round hole through the middle, its corners carved with small stacked faces made of circles for eyes and bars for mouths.
7.remember: Cong = square peg, round hole: square outside, circle inside. Liangzhu, China, 3300–2200 B.C.E. Jade means ‘you paid’, in months of labor.
compare: No. 196 (§9.5), Gold and jade crown: The Silla crown also uses jade and gold to mark royal status, and it too was found in an elite burial.
No. 193 (§9.2), Terra cotta warriors: Another Chinese burial that uses enormous labor and rich objects to secure status in the afterlife.
No. 8 (§2.8), Stonehenge: Both use circle-based geometry that may relate to the sky and the cosmos.
7.vocab: jade, nephrite, abrasion, cong, bi, taotie, grave good.

form: Carved from nephrite, one of the two minerals called jade. Colors range from green to brown to milky white, often altered by burial.
A square outer form around a circular bore (the hole through the middle). Taller cong are divided into stacked tiers.
Each corner carries a masklike face: large round eyes and a bar for the mouth or nose. Some examples show a fuller figure of a human in a feathered headdress over a monster face.
Jade is too hard to carve with a knife. It was shaped by abrasion: grinding with wet sand, using tools of bamboo, bone, stone or string, and drilling from both ends. One piece could take months.
Surfaces are polished, and incised lines can be extremely fine, sometimes less than a millimeter apart.
function: Found in elite burials, arranged around the body together with bi (flat jade discs with central holes) and ceremonial jade axes, at sites such as Fanshan and Yaoshan.
Probably ritual objects for communicating with spirits, ancestors or gods, though no texts explain their use.
They were status displays: the labor and rare material showed the wealth and power of the person buried with them.
Much later, Chinese collectors, including the Qianlong emperor in the 1700s, prized ancient cong as antiques.
content: Chinese texts written some 2,000 years later link the circle with heaven and the square with earth, so the cong may join the two realms. Use this carefully: it is a later idea projected back.
The faces may be a god, an ancestor or a spirit-animal. Some scholars see them as an ancestor of the taotie (monster-face motif) later found on Shang bronzes.
The geometry itself, square around circle, suggests order, structure and links between worlds.
context: The Liangzhu culture (late Neolithic) lived around Lake Tai in the Yangzi River delta, near modern Hangzhou and Shanghai.
Its main city had walls and large dams for water management. The Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2019.
Graves show a stratified society: some burials are packed with jade, while others have almost nothing.
Jade stayed China’s most valued material for millennia, linked to virtue in Confucian thought and used in later royal burials such as Han dynasty jade suits. On the exam.
If asked to identify → Jade cong, Liangzhu culture, China, 3300–2200 B.C.E., carved jade.
Form: square outside, round inside, with face motifs at the corners.
If asked about technique → jade cannot be cut, only abraded with sand and water and drilled, which means huge labor.
If asked about function → elite burials with bi discs; ritual and status.
Trap: the heaven-and-earth reading comes from much later texts; say so if you use it.
Trap: a bi is the flat disc and a cong is the square tube. Do not mix them up.
Big idea: labor-intensive material equals status and a stratified society.

8.title: Stonehenge
8.plain: A ring of huge standing stones on Salisbury Plain in southern England, built and rebuilt in stages over about 1,500 years. Its main axis lines up with the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset, and people were buried there, so it was probably a ceremonial site tied to the sun, the seasons and the dead. The real achievement is organization: moving and fitting stones weighing many tons without metal tools or wheels.
8.spot: Massive gray upright stones topped by horizontal slabs, arranged in a circle on open grassland, some fallen, with an inner horseshoe of taller three-stone gateways.
8.remember: Stone-HENGE: the henge is the ditch and bank around it. Wiltshire, c. 2500– 1600 B.C.E. It is built like a wooden barn, with carpentry joints, but in stone.
compare: No. 156 (§6.4), Great Serpent Mound: The Great Serpent Mound is also a monumental landscape work that may be aligned with the summer solstice.
No. 213 (§10.1), Nan Madol: Nan Madol is another megalithic site built by organized labor moving enormous stones.
No. 167 (§7.1), Conical tower and circular wall of Great Zimb…: Great Zimbabwe also shows monumental stone construction requiring large-scale coordination.
No. 17 (§3.6), Great Pyramids: The Giza pyramids are a roughly contemporary display of organized labor and alignment, but with a centralized state and a known king.
8.vocab: megalith, henge, trilithon, post-and-lintel, mortise-and-tenon joint, cromlech, sarsen.

form: A henge (circular ditch with a bank) came first, around 3000 B.C.E. Unusually, the bank is inside the ditch.
The sarsen (a hard sandstone) circle originally had 30 uprights capped by 30 lintels in a continuous ring, using post-and-lintel construction (two uprights supporting a horizontal beam).
Inside stands a horseshoe of five trilithons (two uprights plus one lintel), rising in height toward the center; the largest stones weigh over 30 tons.
Smaller bluestones form an inner circle and horseshoe. They are mostly volcanic rocks such as dolerite and rhyolite, not sandstone.
Joints copy woodworking: mortise-and-tenon (a knob on the upright fits a hole in the lintel) and tongue-and-groove (lintels slot into each other). The lintels are curved to follow the circle.
Stones were shaped by pounding with stone hammers. The Heel Stone stands outside along the processional Avenue.
function: Its axis aligns with the summer solstice sunrise and the winter solstice sunset, so it likely marked the year’s turning points for ceremonies.
Many archaeologists think midwinter mattered most: pig bones from nearby Durrington Walls show feasts held in winter.
It was also a cemetery: cremated remains of perhaps around 150 people were buried there, especially in the early phases.
Other theories include a place of healing or a monument for ancestors, with stone standing for the permanence of the dead.
Today it is a heavily visited heritage site, and crowds gather there at the solstices.
content: There are no images. Meaning comes from arrangement, alignment with the sun and movement along the Avenue toward the stones.
The circle may model the sky or the cycle of the year, and the durable stone may stand for ancestors and permanence.
context: Built in phases: the ditch and bank about 3000 B.C.E., the great sarsens and bluestones about 2500 B.C.E., and rearrangements until about 1600 B.C.E.

Most sarsens came from West Woods, about 25 km (15 miles) north. The bluestones were brought about 240 km (150 miles) from the Preseli Hills in Wales; in 2024 the Altar Stone was traced to northeastern Scotland.
Movement probably used sledges, ropes, timber tracks and hundreds of people. The work implies leadership, planning and shared belief across a wide region.

It became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1986, together with nearby Avebury. Debates over traﬀic and a planned road tunnel show the tension between modern needs and protecting ancient landscapes. On the exam.
If asked about construction → post-and-lintel, trilithons, mortise-and-tenon and tongueand-groove joints borrowed from carpentry.
If asked about function → solstice alignment, ceremony and burial.
If asked about labor → bluestones hauled about 240 km from Wales without wheels or metal tools.
Built in phases; the College Board date is c. 2500–1600 B.C.E., though the earthwork is older.
Trap: the Druids did not build it. They lived some 2,000 years later.
Trap: the College Board lists the medium as sandstone, which is true of the sarsens, but most bluestones are volcanic rock.
Vocabulary: megalith (large stone), cromlech (circle of megaliths), henge.

9.title: The Ambum Stone
9.artist: Unknown maker; Ambum Valley, Enga Province, Papua New Guinea
9.plain: A small polished stone carving, about 20 cm tall, from the highlands of Papua New Guinea, probably made around 3,500 years ago. It is usually identified as a long-snouted animal such as an echidna, possibly shown as an embryo. It is among the oldest known sculptures in Oceania, and it is also known for its second life as a sacred Enga object and for a long fight over who should own it.
9.spot: A dark, smooth stone figure with a long trunk-like snout curving down, a bent neck, a rounded belly-like body and little limbs tucked in, looking like an anteater or a curled-up animal embryo.
9.remember: Ambum sounds like ‘a bump’, as in a baby echidna in its mother’s bump. Papua New Guinea, c. 1500 B.C.E., greywacke.
compare: No. 3 (§2.3), Camelid sacrum in the shape of a canine: Both are small zoomorphic prehistoric objects whose animal identity and original use are debated.
No. 10 (§2.10), Tlatilco female figurine: Both may relate to fertility and both were valued in later ritual settings.
No. 222 (§10.10), Malagan display and mask: Malagan objects from Papua New Guinea also raise questions about ritual purpose versus museum display.

form: Carved from greywacke, a hard, dark gray sedimentary stone with natural fracture lines.
About 20 × 7.5 × 14 cm (roughly 8 inches tall), small enough to hold in two hands.
Shaped by grinding and polishing rather than chiseling, giving a very smooth surface.
Zoomorphic (animal-shaped) and possibly embryonic: a long snout, head bent forward, limbs tucked against a rounded body.
The shape would suit a pestle (a pounding tool), with the animal forming the handle and top.
It balances simplification with natural observation, so the form reads clearly from every side.
function: Its original use is unknown. It may have been a pestle for pounding food or a ritual object; many prehistoric New Guinea stone pestles have animal or bird heads.

Much later, Enga people who found it treated it as a sacred object, one of the ‘bones of the ancestors’. Such stones were buried on ancestral land and fed with pig sacrifices to protect the group and promote fertility.
Today it is a museum object in Canberra, studied and displayed as one of the oldest sculptures from the Pacific.
content: The animal is usually read as an echidna (spiny anteater), a valued food. Others suggest a bird, a fruit bat or an extinct giant marsupial; scholars disagree.
If the body is a fetus or embryo, the work may relate to birth, growth and fertility.
Its meaning changed over time: unknown to its makers, ancestral power to the Enga, and ‘oldest sculpture’ to museums.
context: It comes from the Ambum Valley in Enga Province. The New Guinea highlands were one of the world’s independent centers of early farming, at sites like Kuk Swamp.
Outsiders learned of it in the early 1960s. It was sold by local boys to a trade-store owner in Wabag, passed to a London dealer, and bought by the National Gallery of Australia in 1977.
Papua New Guinea had laws restricting the export of antiquities, and whether this export was legal is still disputed. That makes it a case study in repatriation and cultural ownership.
In 2000, while on loan to a museum in Marseille, France, it was dropped and broke into three main pieces. It was repaired, and the accident renewed the ownership debate.
The date of about 1500 B.C.E. is approximate. On the exam.
If asked to identify → The Ambum Stone, Ambum Valley, Enga Province, Papua New Guinea, c. 1500 B.C.E., greywacke.
If asked about technique → ground and polished hard stone, not chiseled.
If asked about function → possibly a pestle; later reused as an Enga ritual object.
If asked about later history → bought by the National Gallery of Australia in 1977, broken in 2000, and the subject of ownership and repatriation debates.
Trap: it is from Papua New Guinea, not Aboriginal Australia, even though it is in Canberra.
Big idea: an object’s meaning changes as different communities use it.

10.title: Tlatilco female figurine
10.artist: Unknown maker; central Mexico, site of Tlatilco
10.plain: A small hand-modeled clay figure of a woman with two faces sharing one head, from a village cemetery at Tlatilco, near today’s Mexico City. Hundreds of such figurines were buried with the dead. It shows an early interest in fertility and in duality, ideas that remain central to later Mesoamerican cultures.
10.spot: A tiny tan clay woman with a pinched waist, huge rounded thighs, stubby arms, legs that taper without feet, and a head with two faces side by side sharing three eyes.
10.remember: Two-faced Tlatilco, with a T for twins. Central Mexico, 1200–900 B.C.E., buried with the dead.
compare: No. 4 (§2.4), Running horned woman: Both focus on the female body and probable ritual meaning, one painted on rock and the other modeled in clay.
No. 217 (§10.5), Female deity: The Nukuoro female deity also abstracts the female body, but into smooth geometric planes rather than swelling curves.
No. 9 (§2.9), The Ambum Stone: Both are small objects possibly linked to fertility, from very different regions.
10.vocab: figurine, hand-modeled, duality, appliqué, ceramic, Formative period.

form: Hand-modeled ceramic (shaped by hand, not in a mold) and fired at a low temperature.
Only a few inches tall, small enough to hold in one hand.
The body has a tiny waist, very full hips and thighs, small breasts and short, stubby arms. The legs taper to points, so many such figurines cannot stand up.
Details are added with appliqué (small pieces of clay pressed on) for hair and ornaments and punched holes or incised lines for eyes and mouths. Traces of red, white or yellow paint survive on many.
The head shows two overlapping faces: three eyes, two noses and two mouths.
function: Hundreds were found in burials of men, women and children, so they were part of funeral practice.
Some turn up in household trash, so they may have been used in home rituals before being buried or thrown away.
Proposed meanings include fertility, protection, healing, ancestors or status. Scholars disagree.
content: The doubled face suggests duality: life and death, human and supernatural, twins, or transformation. Duality became a core idea in later Mesoamerican religion, such as the Aztec dual creator Ometeotl.
Exaggerated hips and thighs likely express fertility, abundance or an ideal of beauty.
Elaborate hairstyles may mark identity, age or status.
Most Tlatilco figurines are female. Male figures more often appear in costumes, such as ballplayers or ritual performers.
context: Tlatilco was a farming village on the western shore of Lake Texcoco, in the Valley of Mexico, now inside the Mexico City metropolitan area.

Brickmakers digging for clay discovered the site in the 1930s. Excavations from the 1940s to 1960s uncovered hundreds of burials, and artist-archaeologist Miguel Covarrubias helped make the figurines famous.
Some burials contain Olmec-style ceramics, evidence of contact and trade with the Olmec heartland on the Gulf Coast.
It belongs to the Formative (Preclassic) period. The nickname ‘pretty ladies’ is a modern one and says more about modern viewers than about the makers. On the exam.
If asked to identify → Tlatilco female figurine, central Mexico, 1200–900 B.C.E., ceramic.
If asked about the two faces → duality, a lasting Mesoamerican theme.
If asked about function → found in burials, probably linked to fertility or ritual.
Trap: Tlatilco is not Olmec; it is a village culture influenced by Olmec contact.
Form keywords: hand-modeled, small, exaggerated hips and thighs, tiny waist, no feet.
Big idea: early art often centers on the female body and the continuation of life.

11.title: Terra cotta fragment
11.artist: Lapita culture; Solomon Islands, Reef Islands
11.plain: A broken piece of a clay pot made by the Lapita people, seafarers who were the first humans to settle the remote islands of the Pacific. It is pressed with tiny teeth-like stamps into patterns that form a stylized face. Lapita pottery is how archaeologists trace that voyage, and its designs live on in Polynesian tattoo and barkcloth.
11.spot: A curved, reddish-brown pottery fragment covered in rows of tiny dotted lines, like stitching, sometimes filled with white, forming bands and a stylized face with eyes and a nose.
11.remember: Lapita patterns look like tiny teeth marks: the dotted breadcrumb trail across the Pacific. Reef Islands, Solomon Islands, c. 1000 B.C.E.
compare: No. 219 (§10.7), Hiapo: The Niuean hiapo continues the geometric design tradition that began on Lapita pottery, now on barkcloth.
No. 5 (§2.5), Beaker with ibex motifs: Both are early decorated pottery; Susa paints its designs while Lapita stamps them into the clay.
No. 221 (§10.9), Navigation chart: The Marshall Islands navigation chart reflects the same Pacific voyaging knowledge that let Lapita people settle the islands.
11.vocab: dentate stamping, sherd, terracotta, earthenware, tapa, Austronesian. 3 Ancient Mediterranean Content area 2 · 3500 B.C.E.–300 C.E. · works 12–47 · about 15% of the multiple-choice section. Egypt, the Near East, Greece, the Etruscans and Rome. This is the unit where most art-history vocabulary comes from (columns, temples, contrapposto, idealized versus realistic portraits). The recurring story is power: kings and emperors using statues, buildings and carved stories to say they were chosen by the gods, and Greek and Roman artists slowly working out how to make bodies look natural and alive.

form: Made of terra cotta (low-fired earthenware) mixed with sand or crushed shell, and hand-built rather than thrown on a wheel.
The main technique is dentate stamping: pressing a tool with a toothed edge into soft clay to make lines of tiny dots. Some lines are incised, which is why the College Board lists it as incised.
White lime was sometimes rubbed into the impressions so the pattern stood out against the reddish clay.
Designs form horizontal bands of zigzags, arcs and interlocking shapes that combine into stylized human faces.
Full Lapita vessels include flat dishes, cylinder stands and pots with sharp shoulders.
function: Plain Lapita pots were used for cooking and storage. The elaborately stamped wares were probably for ceremonies, feasting, display or exchange.
Some decorated pots appear in burial contexts, so they may also have had a role in honoring the dead.
Today the sherds serve as evidence: their designs and clay help archaeologists map migration and trade routes.
content: The faces may represent ancestors or deities watching over the community.
Repeated patterns acted like a shared visual language, marking a common identity across islands thousands of kilometers apart.
The geometric motifs may be connected to tattoo designs on the body, a link many scholars accept.
context: Lapita is named after a site in New Caledonia excavated in 1952. The Lapita people spoke Austronesian languages; their ancestors came from Taiwan through Island Southeast Asia.

Lapita culture appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago around 1350–1300 B.C.E. and spread by outrigger canoe to the Reef and Santa Cruz Islands, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa by about 800 B.C.E.
The Reef Islands, in the eastern Solomon Islands, were one of the first steps into Remote Oceania, islands never before reached by humans.
They carried pigs, dogs, chickens and food plants with them.
Pottery making later stopped in western Polynesia, but the designs survived in tattoo and tapa (barkcloth). On the exam.
If asked to identify → Terra cotta fragment, Lapita, Reef Islands, Solomon Islands, c. 1000 B.C.E.
If asked about technique → dentate stamping, sometimes with lime infill.
If asked about significance → Lapita pottery traces the first settlement of Remote Oceania; the Lapita are ancestors of the Polynesians.
If asked about continuity → Lapita designs survive in later tattoo and tapa, such as the Hiapo (No. 219).
Trap: it is not wheel-made, and it is not from Australia or New Guinea’s highlands.
Attribution clue: rows of tiny stamped dots forming geometric faces → Lapita.

12.title: White Temple and its ziggurat
12.plain: A small whitewashed temple set on a tall mud-brick platform in Uruk, one of the world’s first cities, in what is now southern Iraq. The platform is an early ziggurat, a humanmade mountain on a flat plain. It shows how early cities used architecture to connect gods, priests and political power.
12.spot: A massive, sloping mud-brick mound with a stair and ramp climbing up at an angle, topped by a small rectangular white building with buttressed walls.
12.remember: Uruk rocks: they literally built a mountain out of mud. The White Temple sits on top, close to Anu, the sky god. Sumerian, c. 3500–3000 B.C.E.
compare: No. 17 (§3.6), Great Pyramids: Both are artificial mountains, but the pyramids are sealed tombs for dead kings while the ziggurat is a stage for a living god’s temple.
No. 157 (§6.5), Templo Mayor: The Templo Mayor is also a raised, layered temple platform symbolizing a sacred mountain, rebuilt over older versions.
No. 20 (§3.9), Temple of Amun-Re and Hypostyle Hall: Both control access to the god: a bent climb at Uruk, a sequence of darker, restricted halls at Karnak.
12.vocab: ziggurat, cella, bent-axis approach, mud brick, buttress, battered wall.

form: A ziggurat (stepped or sloped temple platform) about 12 meters (40 feet) high, made of mud brick (sun-dried clay bricks).
The sides are battered (sloped inward), with recesses and buttresses (projections that strengthen a wall), helping the mass stand and shed rainwater.
On top stands a rectangular temple about 17.5 by 22.3 meters, coated in white gypsum plaster so it gleamed in the sun.
A bent-axis approach: stairs and ramps climb at an angle, so worshippers turned corners before reaching the door rather than walking straight in.
Inside, a long central room, the cella (main sanctuary), held an altar and offering table, with smaller rooms on each side. The temple’s corners point to the cardinal directions.
The platform grew in layers: older shrines were buried inside as new ones were built on top.
function: A temple usually attributed to Anu (An), the sky god, treated as the god’s house.
Priests performed rituals and offerings there. Ordinary people probably did not enter the sanctuary itself.
Temples were also economic centers that managed farmland, herds and surplus grain. The world’s earliest writing, at Uruk, was mostly for this accounting.
Visible from far across the plain, it was a symbol of the city.
content: Height brought the god’s house closer to the heavens; mountains were sacred places in Mesopotamian belief.
The winding climb turned the approach into a ritual journey.
The gleaming white surface made the temple stand out and probably suggested purity, though that is an interpretation.
context: Uruk, in Sumer in southern Mesopotamia, was one of the first true cities, with perhaps 40,000 people by about 3000 B.C.E. It was the legendary home of the hero Gilgamesh.
Proto-cuneiform tablets from Uruk, around 3300–3100 B.C.E., are among the oldest writing in the world.
Mesopotamia had little stone or timber, so builders relied on mud brick, which wears away and needs constant repair.
German archaeologists excavated Uruk in the 1900s. This is an early or ‘proto’ ziggurat; fully stepped ziggurats, such as the one at Ur, came about 1,000 years later.
Iraqi heritage sites have faced damage and looting during recent wars, which raises questions about protecting ancient sites. On the exam.
If asked to identify → White Temple and its ziggurat, Uruk (modern Warka, Iraq), Sumerian, c. 3500–3000 B.C.E., mud brick.
Key terms: ziggurat, bent-axis approach, cella, mud brick.
If asked why so high → closeness to the gods and visibility as a sign of priestly and civic power.
Trap: the ziggurat is the platform; the temple is the white building on top.
Trap: it is a temple, not a tomb, unlike the pyramids of Giza (No. 17).
If asked about materials → mud brick, because southern Mesopotamia lacked stone and timber.

13.title: Palette of King Narmer
13.plain: A shield-shaped slab of dark stone about 2 feet tall, carved on both sides to celebrate King Narmer, often credited with uniting Upper and Lower Egypt around 3000 B.C.E. It is shaped like a makeup palette but is far too big and elaborate for daily use. Almost every rule Egyptian art then followed for 3,000 years appears here for the first time.
13.spot: A gray-green shield-shaped slab with cow-headed faces at both top corners. One side shows a large king raising a mace over a kneeling enemy; the other shows two long-necked beasts whose necks wrap around a round dish.
13.remember: Narmer is spelled with a catfish (‘nar’) and a chisel (‘mer’) in the name box at the top. One king, two crowns: White Crown (Upper Egypt) on the smiting side, Red Crown (Lower Egypt) on the parade side. c. 3000–2920 B.C.E.
compare: No. 16 (§3.5), Standard of Ur, from the Royal Tombs at Ur: The Standard of Ur also uses registers and hierarchic scale to tell a story of royal war and power.
No. 19 (§3.8), The Code of Hammurabi: Both present a ruler supported by divine power; Narmer celebrates conquest while Hammurabi presents justice.
No. 169 (§7.3), Wall plaque, from Oba’s palace: The Benin plaque also uses hierarchic scale and frontality to show a ruler’s dominance.
13.vocab: palette, low relief, register, hierarchical scale, composite view, ground line, serekh, serpopard.

form: Carved from greywacke (a dark, fine-grained stone), about 64 cm (25 inches) tall, in low relief on both sides.
Organized in registers (horizontal bands), each with a ground line for figures to stand on.
Hierarchic scale: Narmer is the largest figure because he is the most important.
Composite view: head and legs in profile, but eye and shoulders frontal, so each part is shown in its clearest view.
At the top, two cow heads flank the serekh (a rectangular frame for the king’s name), which holds the hieroglyphs of a catfish and a chisel.
On one side, two serpopards (imaginary leopards with snake necks) are held by leashes, their necks curving around the circular grinding area.
function: Ordinary palettes were used to grind minerals for eye paint, which protected against the sun’s glare and infection.
This oversized one is ceremonial. It was found in a temple deposit at Hierakonpolis (ancient Nekhen) by James Quibell and Frederick Green in 1897–98, probably as an offering to the god.
It may have been used to grind pigment for decorating a cult statue, but that is a hypothesis.
It is also political imagery: a public statement of royal victory and order.
content: Smiting side: Narmer wears the White Crown of Upper Egypt and raises a mace over an enemy he holds by the hair. A sandal-bearer stands behind him.
On the same side, a falcon (Horus, the god linked to the king) perches on papyrus plants and holds a rope tied to a human head, a symbol of conquered Lower Egypt, since papyrus grows in the Delta.
Other side: Narmer wears the Red Crown of Lower Egypt and marches with standardbearers to inspect two rows of beheaded enemies, their heads placed between their feet.
At the bottom, a bull, a symbol of the king’s strength, breaks down a city wall and tramples an enemy. The entwined serpopards may suggest union.
The cow heads are usually called Hathor, though some scholars identify them as the earlier cow goddess Bat.
context: It dates to the very start of Egyptian kingship (late Predynastic or early First Dynasty). Narmer is often linked with Menes, the legendary first king, but that link is debated.
It is among the earliest objects with hieroglyphic writing.
Scholars debate whether it records a real war of unification or presents an ideal of kingship: the king imposing order on chaos.
It is now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. On the exam.
If asked about unification → two crowns: White = Upper Egypt (south), Red = Lower Egypt (north, the Delta).
Trap: Upper Egypt is in the south because the Nile flows north.
Conventions that last 3,000 years: registers, ground lines, hierarchic scale, composite view, the smiting pose.
If asked about function → ceremonial palette, a temple offering found at Hierakonpolis.
Horus the falcon = the king’s divine protector.
Attribution clue: composite view and hierarchic scale in registers → ancient Egypt.

14.title: Statues of votive figures, from the Square Temple at Eshnunna
14.medium: Gypsum inlaid with shell and black limestone
14.plain: A group of twelve stone statues of worshippers with huge staring eyes and clasped hands, found buried together under the floor of a temple at Eshnunna (modern Tell Asmar, Iraq). Each one was a stand-in for a real person, praying nonstop on his or her behalf. They are a classic example of early Mesopotamian religious sculpture.
14.spot: A crowd of standing figures of different heights with tube-like bodies, fringed skirts, long rippled beards on the men, enormous black-and-white inlaid eyes and hands clasped at the chest.
14.remember: Eshnunna’s eyes say, ‘Don’t worry, I’m still praying for you.’ Sumerian, c. 2700 B.C.E., twelve stand-ins buried under the floor of the Square Temple.
compare: No. 15 (§3.4), Seated scribe: Both are non-royal stand-in bodies, but the scribe is naturalistic and made for a tomb while the votives are stylized and made for a temple.
No. 28 (§3.17), Peplos Kore from the Acropolis: The Peplos Kore was also a votive offering left in a sanctuary and later buried, on the Athenian Acropolis.
No. 214 (§10.2), Moai on platform: The moai are also stylized figures defined by their gaze and set up in a sacred context.
14.vocab: votive, cache, inlay, bitumen, gypsum, frontal.

form: Carved mainly from gypsum, a soft stone that is easy to carve. The eyes are inlaid (set in) with shell and black limestone, and bitumen (natural tar) colored some hair, beards and brows.
They range from small figures to about 72 cm (roughly 2.5 feet) tall.
Bodies are built from cylinders and cones, with very little anatomy: simple geometric forms.
Men wear fringed skirts and have long hair and beards in neat ripples; women wear dresses draped over one shoulder.
Hands are clasped at the chest, and several hold small cups.
They are frontal and symmetrical, standing on solid bases.
function: They are votive figures (offerings to a god): worshippers placed them in the temple to pray on their behalf permanently.
Elsewhere in Sumer, some votive statues carry inscriptions naming the donor and asking the god for long life.
When the temple was remodeled, the figures were buried together in a cache (a hidden deposit) rather than thrown away, because sacred objects could not simply be discarded.
content: Huge eyes express attention and awe, staying fixed on the god at all times.
Clasped hands and cups suggest prayer and offering.
Size probably reflects the donor’s wealth or status rather than importance in the scene.
The excavator first thought the two largest figures were the god Abu and a mother goddess. Most scholars now see all of them as worshippers.
context: They date to the Early Dynastic period of Sumer, when city-states competed and temples were at the center of city life.
They were excavated in 1933–34 by the University of Chicago’s Oriental Institute (now the Institute for the Study of Ancient Cultures), led by Henri Frankfort.
The group was divided among the Iraq Museum in Baghdad, the museum in Chicago and the Metropolitan Museum in New York.
The Square Temple was probably dedicated to Abu, possibly a god of vegetation. This is an early example of proxy worship in Mesopotamia. On the exam.
If asked to identify → Statues of votive figures, Square Temple at Eshnunna (modern Tell Asmar, Iraq), Sumerian, c. 2700 B.C.E., gypsum inlaid with shell and black limestone.
If asked about function → votive stand-ins that pray to the god on the donor’s behalf.
Key visual clues: huge inlaid eyes, clasped hands, cylindrical bodies, fringed skirts.
Trap: these were temple objects, not tomb statues. Contrast the Egyptian ka statues, such as the Seated scribe (No. 15).
If asked where they were found → a buried cache under the temple floor.
Attribution clue: geometric bodies with enormous staring eyes → Sumerian votive sculpture.

15.title: Seated scribe
15.artist: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty; Saqqara, Egypt
15.plain: A painted limestone statue of an oﬀicial sitting cross-legged with a papyrus scroll on his lap, ready to write. It comes from a tomb at Saqqara, Egypt. It is famous for its lifelike crystal eyes and soft, middle-aged body, very different from idealized kings, and it reminds us that in ancient Egypt writing meant power.
15.spot: A reddish-brown man sitting cross-legged on the ground, his white kilt stretched tight like a desk, an open scroll on his lap, with a fleshy chest and belly and alert, glittering eyes.
15.remember: Scribe as in ‘describe’: he waits to write down the pharaoh’s business forever. Saqqara, Old Kingdom, c. 2620–2500 B.C.E., Louvre.
compare: No. 18 (§3.7), King Menkaura and queen: Menkaura’s idealized, rigid royal body contrasts with the scribe’s realistic, soft, non-royal one.
No. 14 (§3.3), Statues of votive figures, from the Square Te…: Both are stand-in bodies, but the votives pray in a temple while the scribe’s ka lives on in a tomb.
No. 42 (§3.31), Head of a Roman patrician: The Roman patrician’s head also uses unflattering realism to signal dignity and status.
No. 205 (§9.14), Portrait of Sin Sukju: The Korean portrait of Sin Sukju also honors an oﬀicial whose status came from service to the state.
15.vocab: ka, naturalism, idealization, inlay, serdab, limestone.

form: Painted limestone, about 54 cm (21 inches) tall. The skin is reddish brown, the usual Egyptian color for men.
The eyes are inlaid: white magnesite, polished rock crystal for the iris and copper outlines, which makes the gaze startlingly alive. The nipples are small pieces of wood.
The body is naturalistic (true to life): a sagging chest, a roll of fat at the belly, a lean face with high cheekbones and thin lips.
He sits cross-legged in a compact, stable, pyramid-like shape. His right hand once held a brush, now lost.
Arms are carved free of the body, possible because limestone is softer and easier to work than the hard stone used for royal statues.
function: A tomb statue meant to house the ka (life force or spirit double), so the man’s spirit had a body to return to and could receive offerings.
It probably stood in the tomb chapel or a serdab (a sealed statue room), allowing the oﬀicial to keep his status and role in the afterlife.
Today it is one of the most famous Egyptian objects in the Louvre in Paris.
content: Being shown seated, alert and ready to write was the honor: literacy itself was the claim to status.
The soft body signals success: a well-fed man with a desk job, not a laborer. Egyptians would not have seen it as unflattering.
The lively eyes suggest the presence of the ka, keeping him permanently ‘on duty’.
context: Found in 1850 by French archaeologist Auguste Mariette at Saqqara, the great cemetery of the city of Memphis.
His name is unknown because the base with the inscription is lost. Scholars have proposed names, but none is certain.
The date is debated: the College Board says Fourth Dynasty, but the Louvre allows Fourth or Fifth Dynasty.
Only a tiny fraction of Egyptians could read and write. Scribes ran the state’s records, taxes and building projects.
Egyptian art reserved strict idealization (a perfected body) for kings and gods; oﬀicials could be shown more realistically. On the exam.
If asked to identify → Seated scribe, Saqqara, Egypt, Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, c. 2620–2500 B.C.E., painted limestone.
If asked about function → ka statue in a tomb.
If asked about style → naturalism for non-royal people, idealization for royalty.
Key detail: inlaid rock-crystal eyes.
Trap: he is not a pharaoh, and this is not a temple votive figure.
Big idea: literacy equals status in the Old Kingdom.

16.title: Standard of Ur, from the Royal Tombs at Ur
16.medium: Wood inlaid with shell, lapis lazuli, and red limestone
16.plain: A hollow wooden box about 8 by 19.5 inches, covered in a mosaic-like inlay of shell, blue lapis lazuli and red limestone, found in a royal tomb at Ur in Sumer. One side shows war and the other peace, with a banquet. Together they read like a comic strip of what a Sumerian king was supposed to do: win battles and provide plenty.
16.spot: A bright blue background with small white shell figures in three rows. One side shows donkey-drawn chariots and naked prisoners; the other shows animals being led and men drinking at a banquet with a lyre player.
16.remember: Ur’s ‘standard’ is the standard king job: War on one side, Peace and a party on the other. Read from bottom to top, climbing toward the king. Sumerian, c. 2600–2400 B.C.E.
compare: No. 13 (§3.2), Palette of King Narmer: The Narmer Palette also uses registers and hierarchic scale to tell royal narrative.
No. 59 (§4.12), Bayeux Tapestry: The Bayeux Tapestry is another long narrative of conquest told in a continuous band.
No. 45 (§3.34), Forum of Trajan: Trajan’s Column in his forum tells a war story to glorify a ruler, spiraling upward instead of in stacked registers.
16.vocab: register, inlay, lapis lazuli, hierarchical scale, bitumen, composite view.

form: A wooden box (the wood has decayed and was restored) about 21.6 by 49.5 cm, with two long sides and two triangular ends.
Inlay (pieces set into a surface) of white shell figures, a lapis lazuli (deep blue stone) background and red limestone, all set in bitumen.
Each long side has three registers read from bottom to top, each with a ground line.
Hierarchic scale: the king is the tallest figure, and on the War side his head breaks through the top border.
Figures use composite view, much like Egyptian art. Repetition of similar figures creates rhythm.
Its present shape is a modern reconstruction, so the original form is not certain.
function: The original use is unknown. Excavator Leonard Woolley guessed it was carried on a pole as a battle standard, which gave it its name.
Other ideas: the sound box of a musical instrument or a container for valuables.
It was buried in a royal tomb, so it also served to show royal power and wealth in death.
content: War side, bottom: four-wheeled chariots pulled by donkey-like animals trample enemies. These are among the earliest images of wheeled vehicles.
War side, middle and top: helmeted soldiers in cloaks lead naked, bound captives, who are presented to the king, who has stepped down from his chariot.
Peace side, bottom and middle: men carry goods and lead cattle, goats and sheep, perhaps tribute or harvest.
Peace side, top: the king, seated and larger than the rest, drinks with nobles while a musician plays a lyre and a singer performs.
Message: the king is both military leader and provider of prosperity.
context: Ur was a powerful Sumerian city-state. Its Royal Cemetery was excavated in 1922–34 by Leonard Woolley for the British Museum and the University of Pennsylvania.
It was found in tomb PG 779, lying near the shoulder of a man. Some royal tombs at Ur held dozens of attendants buried with their rulers.
The lapis lazuli came from Afghanistan, over 2,000 km away, and shell came from the Persian Gulf, evidence of long-distance trade.
It is now in the British Museum in London; other Ur finds are divided between Philadelphia and Baghdad. On the exam.
If asked to identify → Standard of Ur, from the Royal Tombs at Ur (modern Tell el-Muqayyar, Iraq), Sumerian, c. 2600–2400 B.C.E.
If asked how to read it → bottom to top, in registers.
If asked about trade → lapis lazuli from Afghanistan.
Trap: nobody knows it was actually a standard; the name is Woolley’s guess.
Hierarchic scale: the king breaks the border on the War side.
If asked about kingship → the king as warrior and as provider.

17.title: Great Pyramids (Menkaura, Khafre, Khufu) and Great Sphinx
17.artist: Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty; Giza, Egypt
17.plain: Three huge pyramids at Giza, near Cairo, built as tombs for the pharaohs Khufu, Khafre and Menkaura around 2550–2490 B.C.E., guarded by the Great Sphinx. Khufu’s pyramid was the tallest human-made structure on Earth for nearly 4,000 years. They show the power of the Old Kingdom state to organize labor, materials and belief.
17.spot: Three big smooth-sided pyramids in the desert with small pyramids nearby, and in front a lion-bodied figure with a human head wearing a striped headcloth. The middle pyramid still has a cap of smooth casing at the top.
17.remember: Khufu, Khafre, Menkaura: grandfather, son, grandson, biggest to smallest. Kings Keep Making smaller pyramids. Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, c. 2550–2490 B.C.E.
compare: No. 12 (§3.1), White Temple and its ziggurat: Both are artificial mountains, but the ziggurat raises a living god’s temple while the pyramid seals a dead king.
No. 209 (§9.18), Taj Mahal: The Taj Mahal is another royal tomb meant to impress for eternity, set within a carefully planned landscape.
No. 193 (§9.2), Terra cotta warriors: The tomb of the first Qin emperor also used massive state labor to secure a ruler’s afterlife.
No. 8 (§2.8), Stonehenge: Both required huge organized labor and astronomical alignment around the same era.
17.vocab: mastaba, pyramid, ka, mortuary temple, valley temple, causeway, sphinx.

form: True pyramids (smooth sides) developed from the earlier mastaba (flat-topped tomb) and Djoser’s step pyramid.
Khufu’s pyramid was originally about 146.6 meters (481 feet) tall, built of about 2.3 million blocks averaging around 2.5 tons each.
The core is local limestone. The casing was fine white Tura limestone, polished to shine; granite from Aswan lines the king’s burial chamber, and Menkaura’s lower courses were cased in red granite.
Khafre’s pyramid looks tallest because it sits on higher ground and keeps some casing at its peak.
Each pyramid had a mortuary temple on its east side, a causeway and a valley temple at the edge of the Nile floodplain. Menkaura’s pair statue (No. 18) was found in his valley temple.
The Great Sphinx was carved from the bedrock: a lion’s body about 73 meters long with a pharaoh’s head in a nemes headcloth, probably Khafre.
function: Tombs protecting the king’s mummified body and his ka, along with goods for the afterlife.
Funerary cults, with priests paid by royal estates, kept up offerings long after the king’s death.
The Sphinx guarded Khafre’s complex. Much later, in the New Kingdom, it was worshipped as a form of the sun god, and Thutmose IV set up a stele between its paws.
The tombs were robbed in antiquity, and in medieval times much of the casing was stripped for buildings in Cairo.
content: The pyramid shape may recall the primordial mound of creation (the benben) or the rays of the sun god Ra, a path for the king to join the sky.
They sit on the west bank of the Nile, where the sun sets, the land of the dead.
The Sphinx joins a lion’s strength to a king’s intelligence.
context: Built under the Fourth Dynasty, when the Old Kingdom state was highly centralized. They are precisely aligned to the cardinal directions.
Builders were permanent skilled crews plus rotating teams of conscripted laborers, housed and fed in a workers’ town; their tombs have been excavated. They were not slaves.
Papyri found in 2013 at Wadi al-Jarf, the ‘Diary of Merer’, record boat crews hauling Tura limestone to Giza for Khufu’s pyramid.
The Sphinx’s nose was gone long before Napoleon’s army arrived; the cannonball story is a myth.
The Great Pyramid is the only surviving Wonder of the Ancient World. Giza became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1979. On the exam.
If asked to identify → Great Pyramids (Menkaura, Khafre, Khufu) and Great Sphinx, Giza, Egypt, Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, c. 2550–2490 B.C.E., cut limestone.
Order: Khufu (largest, first), Khafre (his son, with the Sphinx), Menkaura (grandson, smallest).
If asked about placement → west bank (land of the dead) and cardinal alignment.
Parts of the complex: pyramid, mortuary temple, causeway, valley temple.
Trap: built by organized, fed laborers, not slaves.
Trap: pyramids are tombs; ziggurats (No. 12) are temple platforms.

18.title: King Menkaura and queen
18.plain: A statue, slightly less than life-size, of the pharaoh Menkaura and a queen standing side by side, carved from a single block of hard greywacke, from his valley temple at Giza. It is the textbook example of Old Kingdom royal sculpture: frontal, idealized and built to last forever. Greek sculptors later borrowed its stance (No. 27).
18.spot: A dark stone pair attached to a back slab: a man in a striped headcloth, false beard and short kilt, fists clenched and left foot forward; a woman in a tight sheath dress and heavy wig with her arm around his waist.
18.remember: Men-KA-ura: his ka needs a body. Left foot forward means ‘left for eternity’. Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, c. 2490–2472 B.C.E.
compare: No. 27 (§3.16), Anavysos Kouros: The Greek kouros adopts the Egyptian stance but removes the back slab and shows the body nude.
No. 15 (§3.4), Seated scribe: The scribe’s soft, realistic body contrasts with the idealized royal body of Menkaura.
No. 22 (§3.11), Akhenaton, Nefertiti, and three daughters: The Amarna stele breaks this rigid canon with curving bodies and an intimate family scene.
No. 43 (§3.32), Augustus of Prima Porta: Augustus of Prima Porta is another idealized, ageless ruler image meant to project eternal authority.
18.vocab: ka, frontal, idealization, nemes, canon, greywacke, back slab.

form: Carved from greywacke (a very hard, fine-grained dark stone), about 142 cm (4 feet 8 inches) tall.
Frontal (facing straight ahead) and symmetrical, still joined to a back slab, with stone left between the limbs and body so nothing projects or breaks.
The king has broad shoulders, a narrow waist and a muscular, youthful body. He wears the nemes (striped royal headcloth), a false beard and a kilt, and his fists are clenched.
His left foot steps forward, but his weight stays evenly on both legs, so he does not truly move.
The queen wears a clinging sheath dress and a heavy wig; her left foot is slightly forward too. She stands almost as tall as he does.
It is unfinished: the lower part was never fully polished and there is no inscription. Traces of red paint remain on his face and black on her wig.
function: A ka statue, giving the king’s spirit a permanent body to inhabit and receive offerings.
It stood in Menkaura’s valley temple, part of his pyramid complex at Giza (No. 17).
It was excavated in 1910 by George Reisner for Harvard University and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, where it is now displayed.
content: The queen’s embrace, one arm around his waist and a hand on his arm, expresses support and legitimacy; royal women helped carry the dynasty forward.
She is probably his queen Khamerernebty II, but with no inscription her identity is uncertain; some suggest his mother.
Idealization presents the king as eternal and godlike rather than as a real, aging man.
Her near-equal height may signal her importance.
context: Menkaura built the third and smallest pyramid at Giza.
Egyptian royal sculpture valued permanence: hard stone, compact forms and no projecting limbs. Artists followed a canon (set system of proportions).
The rigid royal style contrasts with the realism allowed for oﬀicials, such as the Seated scribe (No. 15).
Greeks trading in Egypt in the 600s B.C.E. borrowed the frontal, left-foot-forward pose for the kouros but freed the figure from the slab. On the exam.
If asked to identify → King Menkaura and queen, Old Kingdom, Fourth Dynasty, c. 2490– 2472 B.C.E., greywacke.
If asked about function → ka statue from the valley temple at Giza.
Form keywords: frontality, back slab, left foot forward, idealized bodies, symmetry.
If asked about Greek influence → the Anavysos Kouros (No. 27) borrows the stance but is freestanding and nude.
Trap: the queen’s identity is not certain.
Trap: the statue is unfinished, so its lower half is unpolished.

19.title: The Code of Hammurabi
19.artist: Susian; Babylon (found at Susa, modern Iran)
19.plain: A black stone pillar more than 7 feet tall carved with about 282 laws of the Babylonian king Hammurabi, topped by a relief showing him receiving authority from the sun god Shamash. It is one of the most complete early law collections. It is also an early example of using an image to sell a text: the picture tells you the laws come from a god.
19.spot: A tall, finger-shaped black stone covered in dense wedge-shaped writing. At the top, a standing figure with one hand raised to his face faces a seated god in a horned crown with rays rising from his shoulders.
19.remember: Hammurabi hammers out the law: ‘an eye for an eye’. Shamash is the sun, who sees everything, so he is the god of justice. Babylon, c. 1792–1750 B.C.E., found at Susa.
compare: No. 13 (§3.2), Palette of King Narmer: Both show a ruler backed by a god; Narmer celebrates conquest while Hammurabi presents justice.
No. 25 (§3.14), Lamassu from the citadel of Sargon II, Dur Sh…: The Assyrian lamassu also use stone imagery to project Mesopotamian royal power and divine protection.
No. 5 (§2.5), Beaker with ibex motifs: Both were found at Susa by French archaeologists and are now in the Louvre.
19.vocab: stele, cuneiform, relief, composite view, lex talionis, horned crown.

form: Carved from basalt (a dark, hard volcanic stone), about 2.25 meters (7.4 feet) tall. Older books call it diorite, but the Louvre lists basalt.
At the top, a relief shows Hammurabi standing with his right hand raised to his mouth, a gesture of respect or prayer.
Shamash sits on a throne shaped like a temple front, his feet on a mountain pattern, wearing a horned crown (the sign of a god) with rays rising from his shoulders.
Composite view: Shamash’s shoulders are frontal and his head is in profile, but his crown is shown from the front.
Below, columns of cuneiform (wedge-shaped writing pressed or carved into a surface) in the Akkadian language record a prologue, the laws and an epilogue.
Several columns near the bottom were erased in antiquity, probably to make room for a new inscription that was never added.
function: A public monument, probably first set up in a temple, perhaps at Sippar. The epilogue invites a wronged man to have the stele read to him to learn his rights.
It is as much a statement of the king’s justice and legitimacy as a working rulebook; scholars note that court records rarely cite it.
Later it became a war trophy, carried off to Susa.
content: Shamash hands Hammurabi a rod and ring, symbols of authority and just rule. The image makes the laws look divinely granted.
The laws cover trade, wages, property, marriage, inheritance and injury, and include lex talionis (‘an eye for an eye’).
Penalties depend on social class: free men, commoners and slaves were treated differently.
The figures are close in size, suggesting how near the king stands to the god.
context: Hammurabi was the sixth king of the First Dynasty of Babylon and united much of Mesopotamia; his reign is usually dated c. 1792–1750 B.C.E.
It is not the first law code. Ur-Nammu’s laws, around 2100 B.C.E., are older.
Around 1158 B.C.E. the Elamite king Shutruk-Nahhunte carried it off as booty to Susa, in modern Iran.
A French expedition under Jacques de Morgan found it at Susa in 1901–02. It is now in the Louvre.
The College Board labels it ‘Susian’ because of where it was found, but it is a Babylonian work. On the exam.
If asked to identify → The Code of Hammurabi, Babylon, found at Susa (modern Iran), c. 1792–1750 B.C.E., basalt.
If asked how the laws gain authority → the relief shows Shamash, god of justice, granting Hammurabi power.
Key facts: about 282 laws, cuneiform, lex talionis, penalties vary by class.
Trap: Shamash is the sun god, not a moon god or a storm god.
Trap: it is Babylonian, even though it was found in Susa and the College Board calls it Susian.
Trap: it is not the oldest law code, just one of the most complete.

20.title: Temple of Amun-Re and Hypostyle Hall
20.artist: New Kingdom, 18th and 19th Dynasties; Karnak, near Luxor, Egypt
20.date: Temple c. 1550 B.C.E.; hall c. 1250 B.C.E.
20.plain: The giant temple complex of the god Amun-Re at Karnak, in ancient Thebes (modern Luxor), the largest religious site of ancient Egypt, enlarged by pharaoh after pharaoh for some 2,000 years. Its highlight is the hypostyle hall, a forest of 134 huge columns. It shows how architecture could control who got close to a god.
