20.spot: A dense forest of enormous carved columns, some with open flower-shaped tops and others with closed bud tops, covered in carved figures and hieroglyphs, with a raised center aisle and stone window grilles above.
20.remember: Hypostyle means ‘under columns’: a parking lot packed with 134 of them. AmunRe, New Kingdom; the hall c. 1250 B.C.E. under Seti I and Ramesses II.
compare: No. 21 (§3.10), Mortuary temple of Hatshepsut: Both are New Kingdom temples near Thebes linked by festival processions, but one serves a god and the other a ruler’s funerary cult.
No. 56 (§4.9), Great Mosque: The Great Mosque of Córdoba also creates a forest of columns, though for open communal prayer rather than restricted access.
No. 30 (§3.19), Audience Hall: The Persian apadana is another vast columned hall built to awe visitors with royal and divine power.
No. 60 (§4.13), Chartres Cathedral: Chartres also uses a clerestory to bring symbolic light into a sacred space.
20.vocab: hypostyle hall, clerestory, pylon, capital, axial plan, sunken relief, obelisk.

form: An axial plan: a series of pylons (massive sloping gateway towers), open courtyards and halls leading to the sanctuary. Floors rose and ceilings dropped as you went in, so spaces grew darker and smaller.
The hypostyle hall (a hall whose roof rests on rows of columns) covers about 5,000 square meters, with 134 columns in 16 rows.
The 12 central columns are about 21 meters (70 feet) tall with open papyrus-flower capitals (column tops); the other 122 are shorter, with closed papyrus-bud capitals.
The raised center creates a clerestory (a row of high windows above lower roofs); stone grilles let light fall onto the central processional path.
Columns are built from stacked sandstone drums and covered in painted relief. Seti I’s work inside is in raised relief; Ramesses II often used sunken relief.
Materials: sandstone from Gebel el-Silsila for the temple, mud brick for enclosure walls and construction ramps. Obelisks, including one of Hatshepsut’s, still stand.
function: The house of Amun-Re, king of the gods, whose cult statue lived in the sanctuary and was washed, dressed and fed daily by priests.
Access was restricted: ordinary people stayed in outer areas, while only priests and the pharaoh entered the inner rooms.
In festivals such as Opet, the god’s statue traveled in a portable boat-shrine to Luxor Temple; in the Beautiful Festival of the Valley it crossed to the west bank (No. 21).
The temple owned land and workers, making the priests of Amun rich and powerful.
content: Papyrus columns recall the marsh at the creation of the world; the temple models the cosmos, with the floor as earth and the ceiling as sky.
Reliefs show the pharaoh making offerings to the gods, while the outer walls show his battles, presenting him as both pious and victorious.
Light from the clerestory falling on the central aisle marked the god’s processional route.
context: Building began in the Middle Kingdom and continued into Ptolemaic and Roman times, but the New Kingdom (18th and 19th Dynasties) added the most.
The hypostyle hall was begun under Seti I and finished under Ramesses II, both of the 19th Dynasty.
Amun-Re combined Amun (the hidden one) with Re (the sun) and became the state god of the New Kingdom.
Akhenaton (No. 22) turned against Amun’s cult; after his reign, the old religion and Karnak were restored.
Today it is part of the UNESCO site of Ancient Thebes (1979). Recent cleaning has revealed original painted colors. On the exam.
If asked to identify → Temple of Amun-Re and Hypostyle Hall, Karnak, near Luxor, Egypt, New Kingdom, temple c. 1550 B.C.E., hall c. 1250 B.C.E.
Key terms: hypostyle hall, clerestory, pylon, axial plan, papyrus capitals.
If asked how architecture controls access → darker, lower, more restricted spaces toward the sanctuary.
Built over centuries by many pharaohs, including Hatshepsut, Seti I and Ramesses II.
Trap: it is a cult temple for a god, not a mortuary temple for a king like Hatshepsut’s (No. 21).
Comparisons: a forest of columns like Córdoba (No. 56); a clerestory like Chartres (No. 60).

21.title: Mortuary temple of Hatshepsut
21.artist: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty; near Luxor, Egypt
21.medium: Sandstone, partially carved into a rock cliff, and red granite
21.plain: A temple built for Hatshepsut, one of the few women to rule Egypt as pharaoh, at Deir el-Bahri on the west bank of the Nile across from Luxor. Three wide colonnaded terraces step up against a sheer cliff. It was also propaganda: its carvings argue that she was chosen by the gods to rule.
21.spot: Three broad horizontal terraces lined with rows of square pillars and joined by long central ramps, set right against towering tan cliffs.
21.remember: Hatshepsut wears the false beard to prove she’s the boss. Three terraces = three levels of ‘I’m legit’. New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1473–1458 B.C.E.
compare: No. 17 (§3.6), Great Pyramids: Old Kingdom pyramids put tomb and temple together on flat desert; Hatshepsut’s New Kingdom temple stands apart from her hidden tomb and merges with a cliff.
No. 20 (§3.9), Temple of Amun-Re and Hypostyle Hall: Karnak and Deir el-Bahri were linked by the same festival procession of Amun.
No. 161 (§6.9), City of Machu Picchu: Machu Picchu also uses terraces to fit architecture into dramatic natural terrain.
No. 139 (§5.41), Fallingwater: Fallingwater is a modern building that, like this temple, echoes the horizontal layers of its rocky setting.
21.vocab: mortuary temple, colonnade, terrace, pier, proto-doric, regalia.

form: Three terraces linked by central ramps, each fronted by a colonnade (a row of columns or pillars).
Square piers and some 16-sided fluted columns, often called proto-Doric because they resemble later Greek Doric columns.
Strong horizontal and vertical lines echo the cliffs behind, so the building seems to grow out of the landscape.
The upper terrace has a courtyard with statues of Hatshepsut as the god Osiris and a sanctuary for Amun cut into the rock. Chapels to Hathor and Anubis sit on the middle level.
Built mostly of local limestone, with sandstone and red granite for some doorways and statues. The College Board medium lists sandstone and red granite.
Terraces once held gardens, including incense trees brought from Punt; their root pits survive. It sits next to and borrows ideas from the older terraced temple of Mentuhotep II.
function: A mortuary temple: a place for her funerary cult and for the worship of Amun. Her actual tomb was separate, in the Valley of the Kings behind the cliff.
It was the destination of the Beautiful Festival of the Valley, when Amun’s statue crossed the Nile from Karnak (No. 20).
It also honored her father Thutmose I, linking her to the previous king.
content: Reliefs show her divine birth: the god Amun visits her mother, and the god Khnum shapes her on a potter’s wheel. The message is that Amun is her true father.
Reliefs record a trade expedition to Punt (probably in East Africa), with ships, incense trees and exotic animals, showing prosperity under her rule.
Statues often show her with male regalia (royal symbols): the false beard, the nemes headcloth and a male body, as in the red granite kneeling statue offering jars to the gods.
She was also shown as a sphinx, combining royal power with a lion’s body.
context: Daughter of Thutmose I and wife of Thutmose II, she served as regent for her young stepson Thutmose III, then declared herself king around 1473 B.C.E. and ruled until 1458.
The architect is traditionally named as Senenmut, her steward, though the evidence is not certain.
About 20 years after her death, Thutmose III had her name and images removed and her statues smashed and dumped. This was probably political, to secure his son’s succession, not personal revenge.
The Metropolitan Museum’s excavations in the 1920s recovered and reassembled many statue fragments, now in New York and Cairo. A Polish-Egyptian team has restored the temple since 1961. On the exam.
If asked to identify → Mortuary temple of Hatshepsut, near Luxor, Egypt, New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1473–1458 B.C.E.
If asked how a female pharaoh claimed legitimacy → divine birth reliefs, Punt reliefs and male royal regalia.
Form keywords: terraces, colonnades, ramps, cliff setting, harmony with landscape.
If asked what happened later → Thutmose III erased her images.
Trap: a mortuary temple is not a tomb. She was buried in the Valley of the Kings.
Trap: the building is mostly limestone, though the College Board medium lists sandstone and red granite.

22.title: Akhenaton, Nefertiti, and three daughters
22.plain: A small limestone slab carved in sunken relief showing the pharaoh Akhenaton, Queen Nefertiti and three of their daughters relaxing under the sun disk, the Aten. It was a private altar in an elite home in Amarna, Akhenaton’s new capital. It breaks sharply with tradition: soft, curving bodies and family tenderness replace a royal style that had been rigid for over 1,000 years.
22.spot: Two seated figures with long heads, thin necks and round bellies face each other holding small children, beneath a sun disk whose rays end in tiny hands.
22.remember: Akhenaton only knows the Aten: sun rays with hands give the royal family a high-five of life. Amarna, 18th Dynasty, c. 1353–1335 B.C.E.
compare: No. 18 (§3.7), King Menkaura and queen: Menkaura’s rigid, idealized pair shows the traditional canon that the Amarna stele rejects.
No. 23 (§3.12), Tutankhamun’s tomb, innermost coﬀin: Tutankhamun’s coﬀin marks the return to traditional style and religion after Amarna.
No. 20 (§3.9), Temple of Amun-Re and Hypostyle Hall: Karnak represents the powerful cult of Amun that Akhenaton tried to displace.
No. 13 (§3.2), Palette of King Narmer: The Narmer Palette set the conventions, such as composite view and hierarchy, that Amarna art bends but does not fully abandon.
22.vocab: sunken relief, Amarna, Aten, ankh, monotheism, canon, house altar.

form: Limestone, about 32.5 cm (roughly 1 foot) tall, with traces of paint.
Carved in sunken relief: outlines are cut into the surface so figures sit below it, creating crisp shadows in strong light.
Amarna style: elongated skulls, long necks, narrow shoulders, thin arms, rounded bellies and wide hips and thighs, drawn with flowing curves.
The couple sit on cushioned stools facing each other, arranged symmetrically on either side of the central sun disk.
Some old conventions remain, such as profile heads with frontal shoulders, but the poses are relaxed and informal.
function: A house altar: an object of private devotion in a wealthy oﬀicial’s home in Amarna.
People worshipped the royal family as the link to the Aten, since only the king and queen could worship the god directly.
It was excavated at Amarna by a German team in the early 1900s and is now in the Egyptian Museum in Berlin.
content: The Aten (the sun disk) sends rays ending in small hands; some hold ankhs (the hieroglyph for life) to the faces of the king and queen only.
Akhenaton kisses his eldest daughter Meritaten; Nefertiti holds Meketaten on her lap and Ankhesenpaaten on her shoulder, who plays with her mother’s earring.
The tender family scene expresses the life-giving love of the Aten flowing through the royal family.
Nefertiti is shown at nearly the same scale as the king, a sign of her unusual status.
context: Akhenaton was born Amenhotep IV and changed his name around the fifth year of his reign. He promoted worship of the Aten above all other gods, close to monotheism (belief in one god).
He built a new capital, Akhetaten (modern Amarna), and cut the power of the wealthy priests of Amun at Karnak (No. 20).

Why the bodies look this way is debated: a medical condition (not supported by clear evidence), a religious idea of the Aten as both mother and father, or simply a new style the king required. His sculptor Bek wrote that the king himself instructed him.

After his death the old religion returned. The daughter on Nefertiti’s shoulder became Ankhesenamun, wife of Tutankhamun (No. 23), whose reign restored tradition; Akhenaton’s name was later left off king lists. On the exam.
If asked to identify → Akhenaton, Nefertiti and three daughters, New Kingdom (Amarna), 18th Dynasty, c. 1353–1335 B.C.E., limestone.
If asked about style → Amarna style: elongated, curving bodies and informal, intimate poses.
If asked about religion → the Aten sun disk; rays with hands offering ankhs.
Technique: sunken relief, not low relief.
Function: a private house altar.
Trap: the Aten is not Amun-Re. Akhenaton turned away from Amun.
If asked about change and continuity → a break from the Old Kingdom canon (No. 18), then a return to tradition under Tutankhamun (No. 23).

23.title: Tutankhamun’s tomb, innermost coﬀin
23.medium: Gold with inlay of enamel and semiprecious stones
23.plain: The innermost of three nested coﬀins that held the mummy of Tutankhamun, a teenage pharaoh of Egypt who died around 1323 B.C.E. The two outer coﬀins are gilded wood, but this one is solid gold, about 110 kg (roughly 243 pounds). It matters because his tomb is the only Egyptian royal tomb ever found nearly intact, so it shows what a king’s burial actually held.
23.spot: A mummy-shaped gold coﬀin with a calm young face, a striped royal headcloth, a braided false beard, and arms crossed on the chest holding a hooked crook and a flail. The body is covered in a feather pattern of colored inlaid wings.
23.remember: Work No. 23, date c. 1323: Tut’s numbers end the same way. Think ‘Tut = Total Untouched Treasure’, the one royal tomb the robbers mostly missed.
compare: No. 22 (§3.11), Akhenaton, Nefertiti, and three daughters: The Amarna relief shows the relaxed style Tutankhamun’s reign abandoned for traditional idealized forms.
No. 17 (§3.6), Great Pyramids: Both are royal burials meant to preserve the king’s body forever, but the pyramids were robbed and KV62 was not.
No. 170 (§7.4), Sika dwa kofi: Gold used as a sacred material that embodies divine and royal power in Asante culture.
No. 193 (§9.2), Terra cotta warriors: Another ruler buried with lavish goods to equip him for the afterlife, in Qin dynasty China.
23.vocab: sarcophagus, cloisonné, nemes, crook and flail, ka, inlay.

form: Made of hammered sheet gold 2.5 to 3.5 mm thick, about 1.88 m (6 feet 2 inches) long.

Decorated with cloisonné (small cells of gold wire filled with colored material): semiprecious stones such as lapis lazuli, turquoise and carnelian, plus colored glass. The oﬀicial label says ‘enamel’, but the colored inlay is really glass paste.
The king is shaped like a mummy, only his face and hands showing. This is the pose of Osiris (god of the dead, always shown wrapped like a mummy).
He wears the nemes (striped linen royal headcloth) and a curled, braided divine beard. A vulture head and a rearing cobra sit on his brow.
The inlaid wings wrapped around his upper body belong to the vulture goddess Nekhbet and the cobra goddess Wadjet. Lower on the lid, Isis and Nephthys spread engraved wings over his legs.
Strictly symmetrical, frontal and idealized, following centuries-old royal conventions.
Nested like Russian dolls inside two gilded wooden coﬀins, a stone sarcophagus and four gilded shrines. The gold mask is a separate object that lay on the mummy inside.
function: Held and protected the mummy, the home of the king’s ka (life force) in the afterlife. If the body was destroyed, the ka had nowhere to return.
Turned the king into Osiris. Shown as the god who died and was reborn, the dead king would be reborn too.
Gold was believed to be the flesh of the gods because it never tarnishes, so encasing the king in gold made his body imperishable and divine.
Today it is a museum object in Cairo. Tutankhamun’s tomb contents have been gathered at the Grand Egyptian Museum near Giza, which fully opened in November 2025.
content: Crook and flail: the crook (shepherd’s staff) means the king guides his people; the flail (a tool for threshing grain) means he provides food and enforces order. Both belong to Osiris.
Crossed arms are the standard pose of Osiris and of the mummified dead.
Vulture and cobra stand for Upper and Lower Egypt. With both goddesses guarding him, he rules a united Egypt even in death.
The feather-covered body, called the rishi pattern (from the Arabic for ‘feathered’), shows the king sheltered under divine wings, like a bird protecting its young.
context: Tutankhamun (born Tutankhaten) became king as a boy around 1336 B.C.E. and died at about 18 or 19 after roughly ten years on the throne. Exact dates differ by a few years between scholars.
He reversed Akhenaton’s religious revolution (No. 22): he restored the old gods, especially Amun, changed his name from ‘-aten’ to ‘-amun’ and moved the court away from Amarna.

His tomb, KV62 in the Valley of the Kings, was small and hastily fitted out, probably because he died unexpectedly. Robbers broke in soon after the burial but took little, and later debris hid the entrance.
British archaeologist Howard Carter, funded by Lord Carnarvon, found the tomb in November 1922. This coﬀin was not opened until 1925, after years of clearing the outer rooms.
Egypt kept the entire find instead of splitting it with the excavators, a turning point in who owns excavated heritage.
If a minor king got this much gold, the looted tombs of great pharaohs like Ramesses II probably held far more. On the exam.
If asked about material → solid gold with inlaid semiprecious stones and colored glass; the innermost of three nested coﬀins.
If asked why he holds the crook and flail → he is shown as Osiris, god of the afterlife, which guarantees his rebirth.
If asked for period → New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1323 B.C.E., the same dynasty as Hatshepsut (No. 21) and Akhenaton (No. 22).
Trap: the colored inlaid wings belong to Nekhbet and Wadjet; Isis and Nephthys are engraved lower down. Also, do not confuse this coﬀin with the gold death mask, a separate object.
If asked about style → a return to rigid, idealized traditional royal style after the curving, unusual figures of the Amarna period.
Attribution clues → mummy form, nemes, false beard, crook and flail, frontal symmetry: Egyptian royal funerary art.

24.title: Last judgment of Hu-Nefer, from his tomb (page from the Book of the Dead)
24.plain: A painted page from a papyrus scroll buried with Hunefer, a royal scribe, around 1275 B.C.E. Like a comic strip, it shows the moment Egyptians most feared: their heart weighed in front of the gods to decide whether they deserved eternal life. Hunefer passes, of course, because he paid for the scroll and the picture was meant to make the good outcome happen.
24.spot: A long horizontal strip on yellowish papyrus: a jackal-headed god at a balance scale, an ibis-headed god writing, a crocodile-headed monster waiting, and a green-skinned god seated in a shrine at the right. A row of small seated gods runs across the top.
24.remember: Hu-Nefer ‘Who Never Failed’ the heart test: a 19th Dynasty scribe’s cheat sheet for the afterlife exam, c. 1275 B.C.E.
compare: No. 58 (§4.11), Church of Sainte-Foy: A Christian Last Judgment in which souls are weighed and sorted between heaven and hell.
No. 75 (§4.28), Sistine Chapel ceiling and altar wall frescoes: Michelangelo’s Last Judgment is a later, monumental vision of the same idea of judgment after death.
No. 23 (§3.12), Tutankhamun’s tomb, innermost coﬀin: Same goal of eternal life, but for a king in solid gold rather than a scribe on papyrus.
24.vocab: papyrus, register, composite view, continuous narrative, hieroglyph, Book of the Dead.

form: Ink and mineral pigments on papyrus (a paper-like sheet made from thin strips of the papyrus reed, pressed and dried). This sheet is about 40 cm (16 inches) tall, part of a much longer scroll.
Organized in registers (horizontal bands) and read left to right as a continuous narrative (one character shown several times as the story unfolds).
Figures use composite view (head and legs in profile, eye and shoulders seen from the front). Gods have human bodies with animal heads.
Columns of hieroglyphs (Egyptian picture-writing) caption the scene with spells and the names of gods and of Hunefer.
Flat colors, crisp outlines, no shading or depth. Osiris’s canopied shrine at the far right stops the eye and marks the goal.
A high-quality custom copy. Many Books of the Dead were made in workshops, sometimes with blanks left for the buyer’s name.
function: A Book of the Dead: a collection of nearly 200 spells (Egyptians called it the ‘Spells for Coming Forth by Day’) to guide the dead safely through the underworld.
Placed in the tomb with the mummy. Showing a successful judgment was meant to make it true by magic: the picture guaranteed the verdict.
Hunefer was a scribe and steward under King Seti I, wealthy enough to commission a topquality scroll that also announced his status.
Now in the British Museum, London, which acquired it in 1852.
content: At left, jackal-headed Anubis (god of embalming) leads Hunefer in by the hand, then adjusts the scale where Hunefer’s heart, in a small jar, is weighed against a feather.
The feather of Ma’at stands for truth, justice and cosmic order. A heart heavy with wrongdoing would sink; a balanced scale means a truthful life.
Ammit, the ‘Devourer of the Dead’, with a crocodile head, lion front and hippo hindquarters, waits to eat a failing heart, which meant a permanent second death.
Ibis-headed Thoth, god of writing, records the verdict, a fitting witness for a dead scribe.

At right, falcon-headed Horus presents Hunefer to green-skinned Osiris (green for rebirth and vegetation), with Isis and Nephthys behind him. At the top, Hunefer kneels before a panel of judging gods.
context: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, from Hunefer’s tomb at Thebes, around 1275 B.C.E.

In the Old Kingdom, elaborate afterlife texts were mostly reserved for kings (the Pyramid Texts). By the New Kingdom, wealthy non-royals could buy funerary texts, so the afterlife was opened to a wider elite.
Ethics mattered. In the related Spell 125, the dead person recites a list of sins he did not commit, such as stealing or lying, a speech scholars call the ‘negative confession’.
Scribes were a small literate elite in a society where few people could read, so the scroll was a status object as well as a religious one. On the exam.
If asked to identify the scene → the weighing of the heart against the feather of Ma’at, from a Book of the Dead.
If asked who is who → Anubis (jackal, embalming and the scale), Thoth (ibis, scribe), Ammit (hybrid monster), Horus (falcon), Osiris (green-skinned, enthroned judge).
If asked about function → a funerary text placed in the tomb as a magical guarantee of a good verdict.
If asked about change over time → by the New Kingdom, the afterlife was open to non-royal elites who could pay for texts.
Medium trap: it is painted papyrus, not a wall painting or a carved relief.
Reading trap: left to right, continuous narrative, with Hunefer appearing several times.
If asked to compare judgment scenes → the Sainte-Foy tympanum (No. 58) and Michelangelo’s Last Judgment (No. 75); weighing of souls also appears in Christian art.

25.title: Lamassu from the citadel of Sargon II, Dur Sharrukin
25.plain: Giant stone guardian spirits with a man’s head, a bull’s body and eagle’s wings that stood in pairs at the gates of the new capital of the Assyrian king Sargon II, around 720–705 B.C.E. Examples stand about 4.2 to 4.9 m (14 to 16 feet) tall and weigh many tons. They were built to scare off evil spirits and to intimidate human visitors into respecting the king.
25.spot: A colossal winged bull with a bearded human face and a tall cylindrical cap ringed with horns, carved from a single slab, with five legs and lines of wedge-shaped writing between them.
25.remember: Lamassu: ‘Lam-a-SUE you if you enter uninvited.’ Five legs for two views. Sargon II, Neo-Assyrian, c. 720–705 B.C.E.
compare: No. 17 (§3.6), Great Pyramids: The Great Sphinx is another colossal human-animal hybrid that guards a royal site.
No. 30 (§3.19), Audience Hall: Persian Persepolis later borrowed Assyrian ideas such as bull imagery and gate guardians for its own palaces.
No. 153 (§6.1), Chavín de Huántar: The Lanzón at Chavín is a composite sacred being placed to awe people entering a sacred space.
No. 19 (§3.8), The Code of Hammurabi: Another Mesopotamian royal monument that pairs imagery with cuneiform text to assert a king’s authority.
25.vocab: apotropaic, high relief, in the round, cuneiform, citadel.

form: Carved from huge single blocks of gypsum alabaster (a soft, fine-grained stone that is easy to carve), probably roughed out at the quarry and finished in place.
A blend of high relief (carving that projects strongly from a background) and sculpture in the round: the front is nearly freestanding, while the side is relief attached to the gate wall.
Five legs: from the front, two legs stand still; from the side, four legs stride forward. A viewer sees one complete animal from either angle and never notices the fifth leg.
Decorative, patterned detail: tightly curled beard and hair, neat rows of feathers, ringlets of fur along the belly and flanks.
The face is idealized, calm and stern, not a portrait of a specific person.
Lines of cuneiform (wedge-shaped writing pressed or carved into clay or stone) run between and behind the legs.
function: Apotropaic (meant to turn away evil): pairs flanked gateways and doorways, where Mesopotamians believed demons and chaos could slip in.
Political theater: ambassadors and subject peoples passed these towering hybrids before they ever reached the throne room, a reminder of the king’s power.
Part of the architecture itself: they formed the side walls of the gate passages, framing the arched entrance.
Examples from Khorsabad are now in the Louvre (Paris), the British Museum (London) and the ISAC Museum, formerly the Oriental Institute, in Chicago.
content: The hybrid combines the best of three creatures: human intelligence, a bull’s strength and an eagle’s speed and command of the sky.
The horned crown (here with several pairs of horns) is the Mesopotamian sign of divinity: these are protective divine beings, not monsters.
The cuneiform text praises Sargon II, lists his titles, building works and conquests, and calls on the gods to protect the palace.
Assyrian texts used ‘lamassu’ and ‘shedu’ for related protective spirits; art historians generally call these figures lamassu.
context: Sargon II (ruled 721–705 B.C.E.) of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, centered in northern Iraq, built a brand-new capital called Dur Sharrukin (‘Fortress of Sargon’), modern Khorsabad, from about 717 B.C.E.
The city was barely finished when Sargon was killed in battle in 705 B.C.E. His son Sennacherib abandoned it and moved the capital to Nineveh.
French diplomat Paul-Émile Botta began digging at Khorsabad in 1843, one of the first major excavations in Mesopotamia. A later shipment of finds sank in the Tigris in 1855.
The Chicago lamassu was excavated by the Oriental Institute around 1929 and cut into pieces to ship it.
Assyrian palaces were lined with relief slabs of royal lion hunts and military campaigns, an art designed to intimidate.
In 2015 the militant group ISIS filmed itself smashing lamassu at Nineveh and destroyed much of Nimrud, renewing debate over heritage destruction and the role of foreign museums. On the exam.
If asked how the five legs work → designed for two viewpoints: standing still from the front, striding from the side.
If asked about function → apotropaic gate guardians and a display of royal power to visitors.
If asked about culture → Neo-Assyrian; king Sargon II; Dur Sharrukin (Khorsabad, Iraq); c. 720–705 B.C.E.
Trap: do not confuse Sargon II with Sargon of Akkad (about 2300 B.C.E.), or Assyria with Hammurabi’s Babylon (No. 19).
If asked about technique → high relief merged with sculpture in the round; alabaster; cuneiform inscription.
Attribution clues → curled, patterned beard, horned cylindrical cap, rows of feathers, wedgeshaped writing: Assyrian.
If asked for cross-cultural guardians → the Great Sphinx (No. 17) and the Chavín Lanzón (No. 153), both human-animal hybrids.

26.title: Athenian agora
26.artist: Archaic through Hellenistic Greek; Athens, Greece
26.plain: The agora was the big open square at the center of ancient Athens: market, town hall, courthouse and hangout all in one. It is studied as a site plan, not a single building, because it grew piece by piece over about 750 years. This is where Athenian democracy actually happened day to day.
26.spot: A site plan (map) of an irregular open square crossed by a diagonal road, lined with long rectangular colonnaded buildings, a round building, and a temple on a low hill to the west.
26.remember: Agora = where you GO to ARGUE. A plan, not a building, used from 600 B.C.E. to 150 C.E.
compare: No. 35 (§3.24), Acropolis: The sacred Acropolis rises directly above the civic agora; together they show the two sides of Athenian public life.
No. 45 (§3.34), Forum of Trajan: The Roman Forum of Trajan is a civic center planned in one go to glorify an emperor, unlike the agora’s gradual growth.
No. 159 (§6.7), City of Cusco: Inka Cusco is another city organized around a central public plaza for ritual and political life.
26.vocab: agora, stoa, bouleuterion, tholos, colonnade, post-and-lintel.

form: An open, irregular square, not a rigid grid, bounded by public buildings added over centuries.

Stoas (long roofed colonnades open on one side): the Royal Stoa, the Painted Stoa, the Middle and South Stoas, and the two-story Stoa of Attalos, a gift from King Attalos II of Pergamon around 150 B.C.E.
The bouleuterion (council house where the 500-member Council met) and the round tholos, where a rotating group of council members ate and slept so someone was always on duty.
The Hephaisteion (Temple of Hephaistos), a marble Doric temple on a low hill to the west, is one of the best-preserved Greek temples anywhere.
The Panathenaic Way, the main processional road, cuts diagonally across the square on its way up to the Acropolis.
Built of local limestone and marble using post-and-lintel construction (upright posts or columns carrying horizontal beams), with Doric and Ionic columns.
function: Civic: council meetings, magistrates’ oﬀices, law courts, public archives, oﬀicial weights and measures, and a mint.
Commercial: market stalls and shops selling everything from food to pottery.
Intellectual and social: Socrates questioned people here, and Zeno taught in the Painted Stoa, which is why his philosophy is called Stoicism.
Religious: altars and temples stood around the square, and the Panathenaic procession for Athena passed through it.
content: The plan shows architecture designed for citizens to take part: shaded stoas made room for daily conversation, business and politics.
The Monument of the Eponymous Heroes served as a public notice board for proposed laws and lawsuits.
Ostracism votes (exiling an over-powerful politician for ten years by scratching his name on pottery shards) were held in the agora.
context: Athens developed democracy after the reforms of Kleisthenes in 508 B.C.E. Only adult male citizens could vote; women, enslaved people and foreigners were excluded.
The agora was in use from the Archaic period through Roman rule. The Romans added buildings such as the Odeion (concert hall) of Agrippa, around 15 B.C.E.
It was sacked by the Persians in 480 B.C.E. and wrecked again by the Herulians, a raiding people, in 267 C.E.
The American School of Classical Studies has excavated it since 1931. The Stoa of Attalos was rebuilt in the 1950s and now serves as the site museum.
Contrast: the agora below was the civic heart of the city; the Acropolis above it (No. 35) was the sacred heart. On the exam.
If asked about function → the civic, commercial and political center of democratic Athens.
If asked to name structures → stoa, bouleuterion, tholos, Hephaisteion, Panathenaic Way.
Trap: the agora is a plan of an urban space, not one building, and its date range (600 B.C.E.–150 C.E.) runs from Archaic Greece to Roman times.
If asked how architecture supported democracy → open, accessible space, shaded meeting places, and council buildings next to the market.
If asked to compare civic centers → the Forum of Trajan (No. 45) is planned, axial and imperial; the agora grew organically for a democracy.
If asked sacred versus civic → Acropolis (No. 35) versus agora.

27.title: Anavysos Kouros
27.plain: A life-size marble statue of a nude young man that marked the grave of Kroisos, a soldier killed in battle around 530 B.C.E. It is a kouros (Greek for ‘youth’), a type that copied the stiff Egyptian standing pose but stripped the figure naked and freed it from the stone. It is a checkpoint on the Greek road from rigid patterns toward realistic bodies.
27.spot: A naked, muscular young man standing straight and facing forward, left foot slightly ahead, arms at his sides with clenched fists, beaded hair falling down his back, and a slight closed-lip smile.
27.remember: Kroisos Kouros, two K’s: the ‘Kouros Killed’ in battle. Archaic, c. 530 B.C.E., the smiling soldier of Anavysos.
compare: No. 18 (§3.7), King Menkaura and queen: The Egyptian royal pose the kouros borrowed, but Menkaura stays attached to its stone slab.
No. 28 (§3.17), Peplos Kore from the Acropolis: The clothed female counterpart from the same decade, used as a votive rather than a grave marker.
No. 34 (§3.23), Doryphoros: The Classical solution to the kouros’s stiffness: contrapposto and a body at ease.
No. 41 (§3.30), Seated boxer: A Hellenistic body that shows age and injury instead of the kouros’s untouched ideal.
27.vocab: kouros, archaic smile, frontal, freestanding, polychromy, idealization.

form: Marble, about 1.94 m (6 feet 4 inches) tall, slightly larger than life.
Frontal, symmetrical pose with the left foot forward and weight spread evenly, so he looks as if he is stepping but goes nowhere.
Freed from the block: open space between arms and body and between the legs. Egyptian statues keep a stone back slab and fill those gaps.
Rounder, more naturalistic anatomy than earlier kouroi such as the boxy New York Kouros of about 600 B.C.E.: swelling thighs and a fuller chest, though knees and abdomen are still somewhat patterned.
The Archaic smile (a set, slight smile on Archaic Greek statues) signals that the figure is alive, not that he is happy.
Stylized hair in beaded strands. Traces of paint survive, a reminder that Greek statues were colored.
function: A grave marker standing over Kroisos’s tomb in the countryside of Attica, the region around Athens.
The inscribed base reads: ‘Stop and mourn at the tomb of dead Kroisos, whom raging Ares destroyed one day as he fought in the front ranks.’
It advertised the family’s wealth and rank; a marble statue this size was an expensive aristocratic commission.
Other kouroi served as votive offerings in sanctuaries, especially of Apollo.
content: Not a portrait: an idealized type standing in for Kroisos and showing the excellence he had in life.
Ares is the Greek god of war; the inscription treats Kroisos as a hero who fell in the front line.
Nudity marks him as heroic and ideal. The male nude embodied arete (excellence, virtue) for the Greeks; it does not mean he fought naked.
context: Archaic period (about 600–480 B.C.E.). Greek traders and mercenaries in Egypt saw Egyptian stone statues, and kouroi borrow the pose and perhaps a similar proportional grid.
Dug up illegally at Anavysos, near Athens, in the 1930s and recovered by Greek authorities; the inscribed base was later matched to it.
Now in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens.
Within about 50 years, Greek sculptors abandoned this pose for contrapposto (weight on one leg), as in the Doryphoros (No. 34). On the exam.
If asked about Egyptian influence → frontal pose, left foot forward, arms at sides, clenched fists, as in King Menkaura (No. 18).
If asked what is new and Greek → nude, freestanding with open spaces, no back slab, more naturalistic anatomy.
If asked about the smile → the Archaic smile is a convention that signals life, not an emotion.
Function trap: a funerary marker, not a portrait and not a cult statue.
If asked about change over time → kouros (Archaic, stiff) → Doryphoros (Classical, contrapposto) → Seated boxer (Hellenistic realism).
If asked for the female counterpart → the kore (No. 28), always clothed.

28.title: Peplos Kore from the Acropolis
28.plain: A marble statue of a young woman, about 1.2 m (4 feet) tall, dedicated on the Athenian Acropolis around 530 B.C.E. She is a kore (Greek for ‘maiden’), the clothed female counterpart to the nude kouros. She is famous for the paint that survives on her, proof that Greek sculpture was brightly colored, and for the debate over whether she is a girl or a goddess.
28.spot: A stiff, frontal young woman in a heavy, column-like belted garment, long hair in wavy locks over her shoulders, an Archaic smile, the right arm straight down ending in a fist, and the left forearm missing.
28.remember: Peplos Kore: Clothed, Colored, and Covered up after the Persians. Same date as the Anavysos Kouros, c. 530 B.C.E.
compare: No. 27 (§3.16), Anavysos Kouros: The nude male counterpart from the same decade, used as a grave marker.
No. 36 (§3.25), Grave stele of Hegeso: A Classical woman whose drapery reveals the body, showing how much Greek carving changed in 120 years.
No. 14 (§3.3), Statues of votive figures, from the Square Te…: Sumerian votive figures also stood in a sanctuary on behalf of worshippers.
28.vocab: kore, votive, peplos, polychromy, archaic smile, frontal.

form: Marble with painted details. Traces of color survive on her hair, eyes and lips, and patterns once ran down her dress.
Frontal and symmetrical, feet together, the body block-like under heavy cloth: typical Archaic style.
Her left forearm was carved separately and fitted into a socket; it is lost. Her right fist has a hole that held a metal object.
Long wavy locks fall over each shoulder, and she wears the Archaic smile.
Holes in her head probably held a metal crown and a spike to stop birds from perching on her.
Named for the peplos (a heavy wool tube of cloth, belted and pinned at the shoulders). Many scholars now think she wears a decorated over-garment on top of a chiton, not a plain peplos.
Painted reconstructions, such as Vinzenz Brinkmann’s ‘Gods in Color’ project, show her dress covered in bands of animals and patterns.
function: A votive offering (a gift to a god) set up in Athena’s sanctuary on the Acropolis, probably by a wealthy family.
If she represents a mortal maiden, she served the goddess forever in stone; if she represents a goddess, she was a divine image given to Athena’s sanctuary.
Her extended forearm once held out an object toward worshippers, making the statue interact with them.
content: The hole in her fist and her elaborate dress suggest a goddess, possibly Artemis holding a bow and arrows, or Athena. Scholars disagree.
If she is a maiden, she stands for the ideal young Athenian woman: modest, clothed and decorative.
Clothing is the key contrast with the kouros: Greek ideals placed male excellence in the nude body and female virtue in modest dress.
context: The Persians sacked the Acropolis in 480 B.C.E. and smashed its statues. Athenians buried the broken korai as fill while rebuilding, which accidentally protected her paint.
Excavated in 1886, she is now in the Acropolis Museum in Athens.
Some scholars attribute her to the ‘Rampin Master’, the anonymous sculptor of the Rampin Rider, also from the Acropolis.
Dozens of korai were dedicated on the Acropolis in the later 6th century B.C.E., many by aristocratic families during the rule of the tyrant Peisistratos and his sons. On the exam.
If asked kore versus kouros → a kore is female, clothed, usually a votive; a kouros is male, nude, a votive or grave marker.
If asked about polychromy (painting sculpture in many colors) → she is the key example that Greek marble sculpture was painted.
If asked why her paint survives → she was buried after the Persian sack of 480 B.C.E.
Identity trap: she may be a goddess (Artemis or Athena) rather than a mortal girl, and her dress may not be a peplos at all.
If asked for Archaic traits → frontality, Archaic smile, stylized hair, block-like body.
Date: c. 530 B.C.E., the same as the Anavysos Kouros (No. 27).

29.title: Sarcophagus of the Spouses
29.plain: A life-size terra cotta container shaped like a banquet couch, with a husband and wife reclining together on top, made by the Etruscans of central Italy around 520 B.C.E. It is famous because it shows a married couple as near-equals at a party, something Greek art of the time would never show. Despite the name ‘sarcophagus’, it probably held cremated ashes.
29.spot: A smiling couple lying side by side on a cushioned couch, propped on their elbows, the woman in front and the man’s arm at her shoulder, both with almond eyes, long braids and gesturing hands, their lower bodies flat and stiff.
29.remember: Spouses on a Sofa, Etruscan, c. 520 B.C.E.: couch potatoes for eternity.
compare: No. 32 (§3.21), Tomb of the Triclinium: Another Etruscan tomb image of men and women banqueting together forever.
No. 31 (§3.20), Temple of Minerva and sculpture of Apollo: The Apollo of Veii shows the same Etruscan skill in large-scale terra cotta sculpture.
No. 47 (§3.36), Ludovisi Battle Sarcophagus: A later Roman marble sarcophagus, made when burial had replaced cremation, with war instead of a feast.
29.vocab: terracotta, sarcophagus, cinerary urn, kline, archaic smile, necropolis.

form: Terra cotta (fired clay), about 1.14 m tall and 1.9 m long, roughly life-size. It was made in four pieces, fired separately and joined, because something this large could not be fired whole.
Modeled rather than carved: soft clay was built up and shaped by hand, which allowed lively gestures and details.
Upper bodies are lively and rounded with expressive hands; the legs flatten into the couch. Etruscan artists cared more about faces and gestures than consistent anatomy.
Archaic features shared with Greek art: almond eyes, the Archaic smile, stylized braided hair.
Etruscan fashion details: the woman’s soft cap and both figures’ pointed shoes.
The couch is a kline (banquet couch) with a cushion, possibly shaped like a wineskin. Originally painted in bright colors, of which traces remain.
function: A funerary container from the Banditaccia necropolis (city of the dead) at Cerveteri, ancient Caere, where tombs were cut and built to look like houses.
It probably held cremated remains rather than bodies; the Etruscans practiced both cremation and burial.
Placed in a family tomb, it showed the couple enjoying forever the banquet that was part of Etruscan funerals and of their hopes for the afterlife.
content: Their hands once held small objects, now lost. Suggestions include a perfume flask (she may be pouring perfume into his palm), an egg as a symbol of rebirth, or drinking cups.
The banquet stands for social status, pleasure and an afterlife imagined as a continuing feast.
The man’s arm around his wife shows affection and partnership.
context: The Etruscans lived in central Italy (Etruria, roughly modern Tuscany and northern Lazio) before Rome took over. They traded heavily with Greeks and absorbed their style while keeping their own customs.
Etruscan women attended banquets with men and often appear in inscriptions under their own names. Greek writers such as Theopompus found this scandalous.
Etruscan sculptors were specialists in large terra cotta figures, since good marble was not yet exploited in central Italy.
Found in fragments at Cerveteri in 1881; now in the National Etruscan Museum (Villa Giulia), Rome. A very similar couple sarcophagus is in the Louvre.
Most of what we know about the Etruscans comes from tombs, because their cities lie under later Roman and Italian towns. On the exam.
If asked about gender → Etruscan women’s higher social status; a respectable Greek wife would never recline at a banquet.
If asked about material → terra cotta, modeled by hand, fired in four sections and painted.
If asked about culture → Etruscan, from Cerveteri, c. 520 B.C.E.
Trap: called a sarcophagus, but it probably held ashes.
If asked about style → Archaic smile and almond eyes from Greek art, but an Etruscan focus on gesture and flattened lower bodies.
If asked about the afterlife → banquet and sociability, as in the Tomb of the Triclinium (No. 32).

30.title: Audience Hall (apadana) of Darius and Xerxes
30.plain: The apadana was the giant audience hall at Persepolis, the ceremonial capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire, at the time the largest empire the world had seen. Darius I began it around 520 B.C.E. and his son Xerxes finished it. Its stair reliefs show people from across the empire bringing gifts to the king, an advertisement for orderly, peaceful power.
30.spot: Tall, thin columns standing on a ruined stone platform; capitals carved as two bulls back to back; staircases lined with long rows of figures in profile, in different national costumes, carrying gifts and leading animals.
30.remember: APADana: ‘A Party Attended by Delegations’, 23 nations visiting Darius and Xerxes. Burned by Alexander in 330 B.C.E.
compare: No. 20 (§3.9), Temple of Amun-Re and Hypostyle Hall: Another hypostyle hall, but Karnak’s columns are massive and crowded and it served a god rather than a king.
No. 25 (§3.14), Lamassu from the citadel of Sargon II, Dur Sh…: Assyrian royal imagery of bulls and guardians that Persian art inherited and softened.
No. 35 (§3.24), Acropolis: The Acropolis was rebuilt after Xerxes’s army burned it; both are imperial building programs on raised rock.
No. 206 (§9.15), Forbidden City: The Forbidden City also stages a ruler’s audiences with approach, hierarchy and scale.
30.vocab: hypostyle hall, protome capital, capital, terrace, register, low relief.

form: A hypostyle hall (a roof held up by many columns): 36 columns in a 6-by-6 grid in the main hall plus 12 in each of three porches, 72 in all. Only about 13 still stand.
Columns are very slender and about 20 m (65 feet) tall, so the hall felt open and airy, unlike the crowded columns of Karnak’s hypostyle hall (No. 20).
Protome capitals (carved front halves of animals): two bulls back to back, with a saddle between them that held huge cedar roof beams.
Built of gray limestone on a raised terrace (artificial stone platform), reached by monumental double staircases with low, shallow steps.
Stair reliefs in low relief, arranged in long horizontal registers, figures in profile, rhythmic and repetitive, with crisp detail. They were originally painted.
A deliberate mix of styles: Persian builders drew on Assyrian, Egyptian, Greek and other traditions, and inscriptions name workers from across the empire.
function: A reception hall where the king received oﬀicials and foreign delegations, perhaps during festivals such as Nowruz, the Persian New Year (an old theory, still debated).
Displayed the empire’s reach and harmony to everyone who climbed the stairs.
Persepolis was a ceremonial and administrative center; the empire was also governed from Susa, Babylon and Ecbatana.
content: Twenty-three delegations, among them Ethiopians, Indians, Lydians and Bactrians, bring tribute such as gold, textiles, vessels and animals, each group identified by clothing and hairstyle.
Each delegation is led by the hand by a Persian or Median usher: the image is of willing cooperation, not slaughter.
Guards alternate between Persians in fluted hats and Medes in rounded caps, the two founding peoples of the empire.
A lion attacking a bull appears at the corners. It may symbolize royal power, or the turning of the seasons at the new year.
context: The Achaemenid Empire stretched from Egypt and Anatolia to the Indus River. Darius I (ruled 522–486 B.C.E.) began Persepolis around 518 B.C.E.; Xerxes I (ruled 486–465 B.C.E.) completed the Apadana.
Persian rule generally tolerated local religions and customs as long as subjects paid tribute, and the reliefs present that ideal.
Xerxes invaded Greece and burned the Athenian Acropolis in 480 B.C.E. In 330 B.C.E. Alexander the Great burned Persepolis, as revenge according to ancient writers.
The fire and collapsing mud brick buried the stair reliefs, which preserved their crisp carving.
Persepolis, in southern Iran near Shiraz, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. On the exam.
If asked about function → an audience hall for receiving delegations and displaying imperial power.
If asked about the stair reliefs → 23 subject nations bring tribute peacefully, stressing unity and order.
If asked about architecture → hypostyle hall, tall slender columns, double-bull protome capitals, raised terrace.
If asked who built it → Achaemenid Persia: begun by Darius I, completed by Xerxes I.
Event trap: Alexander the Great destroyed it in 330 B.C.E. Xerxes is the king who burned Athens, which led to the rebuilding of the Acropolis (No. 35).
Number trap: 36 columns in the main hall, 72 counting the three porches.
If asked to compare hypostyle halls → Karnak (No. 20): dense, massive columns versus Persepolis’s tall, widely spaced ones.

31.title: Temple of Minerva and sculpture of Apollo
31.artist: Master sculptor Vulca; Veii, near Rome, Italy
31.medium: Original temple of wood, mud brick, or tufa; terra cotta sculpture
31.plain: An Etruscan temple at Veii, about 16 km (10 miles) north of Rome, and the life-size painted terra cotta statue of Apollo that stood on its roof, around 510–500 B.C.E. The temple was built of wood and mud brick, so only its stone foundations survive; we reconstruct it from those and from the Roman writer Vitruvius. Its design became the model for Roman temples.
31.spot: Temple: a reconstruction model on a tall base with steps only at the front, a deep porch of widely spaced plain columns, a low wide roof with statues along the top ridge. Apollo: a striding clay figure with an Archaic smile, long ringlets and curving patterned folds on his cloak, with a decorated support between his legs.
31.remember: Veii’s ‘Very frontal’ temple: steps in front, statues on top. Vulca’s Apollo walks the roof, c. 510–500 B.C.E.
compare: No. 35 (§3.24), Acropolis: The Parthenon shows the Greek alternative: marble, columns on all sides, sculpture in the pediments.
No. 46 (§3.35), Pantheon: The Pantheon’s porch keeps the Etruscan frontal approach that Roman temples inherited.
No. 29 (§3.18), Sarcophagus of the Spouses: Another Etruscan masterwork in terra cotta, from the same decades.
No. 27 (§3.16), Anavysos Kouros: A Greek Archaic figure that shares the smile but stands still, while Apollo strides.
31.vocab: podium, portico, cella, Tuscan order, terracotta, tufa.

form: The temple stands on a high podium (raised platform) with steps only at the front, so it faces one way and directs visitors straight in.
A deep portico (front porch) of widely spaced Tuscan columns (similar to Doric but with a base and a smooth, unfluted shaft).
Inside, a cella (inner room for a cult statue) divided into three rooms, or, as some scholars read the remains, one room flanked by two side wings.
Stone foundations, walls of mud brick or tufa (soft volcanic stone) on a timber frame, a wide wooden roof with deep eaves, and painted terra cotta plaques protecting the wood.
Statues stood on the ridgepole (the top beam of the roof) instead of in a pediment, outlined against the sky.
Apollo is terra cotta, about 1.8 m (6 feet) tall and painted. A decorative scroll-shaped support between his legs keeps the heavy clay from collapsing.
His style: a vigorous forward stride, a rounded body under clinging drapery with patterned folds, almond eyes and the Archaic smile.
function: A sanctuary temple: the cella held cult statues, and worship and sacrifice took place at an altar in front.
The roof statues worked like a billboard, telling a myth to people approaching from a distance.
Votive inscriptions found at the site suggest the temple honored Menrva, the Etruscan Minerva; other gods may also have been worshipped there.
content: The roof group told the myth of Apollo and Herakles fighting over a sacred deer, the goldenhorned hind. Other figures included the goddess Leto holding baby Apollo, and Hermes.
Apollo strides forward to confront Herakles: a frozen moment of conflict, staged for a public audience.
Greek gods and myths in Etruscan form show the Etruscans absorbing Greek religion and adapting it to their own buildings and taste.
context: Veii was a rich Etruscan city that Rome conquered in 396 B.C.E. after a long war.
The Roman writer Pliny the Elder says Vulca of Veii was called to Rome to make the terra cotta statue of Jupiter for the Capitoline temple. He is one of the very few Etruscan artists known by name.
The Apollo is traditionally attributed to Vulca or his workshop, but that is an educated guess based on time and place, not a signature.
The Apollo was found in 1916 at the Portonaccio sanctuary and is now in the National Etruscan Museum (Villa Giulia), Rome.
Vitruvius, a Roman architect writing around 25 B.C.E., described this ‘Tuscan’ temple type. Roman temples kept its podium, front stairs and deep porch. On the exam.
If asked Etruscan versus Greek temple → Etruscan: podium, front steps only, deep porch, wood and mud brick, roof statues. Greek: low stepped base, columns all around, marble, pediment sculpture.
If asked about materials → perishable wood, mud brick and tufa for the building; terra cotta for the sculpture.
If asked who made the sculpture → Vulca of Veii, a rare named Etruscan artist; the attribution is traditional, not proven.
If asked about legacy → Roman temples, including the Pantheon’s porch (No. 46), keep the podium and frontal approach.
Name trap: the statue is Apollo, but the building is called the Temple of Minerva.
If asked about movement → Apollo’s energetic stride contrasts with the static Greek kouros (No. 27).

32.title: Tomb of the Triclinium
32.plain: An Etruscan underground tomb at Tarquinia, cut into soft rock around 480– 470 B.C.E., with walls painted with dancers, musicians and a banquet. It is named for the triclinium, the set of three dining couches shown on the back wall. Its cheerful party scenes show how the Etruscans imagined death: as a celebration, not only a loss.
32.spot: Wall paintings of slim dancers in profile, men with dark reddish skin and women pale, in thin fluttering robes, separated by slender trees with birds; a lyre player and a double-flute player; a checkerboard pattern on the ceiling.
32.remember: TRI-clinium = THREE couches. Tarquinia tomb: dance till you’re dead, c. 480–470 B.C.E.
compare: No. 29 (§3.18), Sarcophagus of the Spouses: The same Etruscan theme of couples banqueting in the afterlife, in terra cotta sculpture instead of paint.
No. 39 (§3.28), House of the Vettii: Roman fresco in a house for the living, using painting to display wealth and culture.
No. 48 (§4.1), Catacomb of Priscilla: Early Christian paintings in an underground burial space express hope for the afterlife in a different faith.
No. 194 (§9.3), Funeral banner of Lady Dai: A Han Chinese funerary image that also imagines the dead enjoying a comfortable afterlife.
32.vocab: fresco, tufa, necropolis, triclinium, chamber tomb, profile.

form: A single rectangular chamber cut into tufa (soft volcanic rock), reached by a sloping passage, in the Monterozzi necropolis (city of the dead) at Tarquinia.
Fresco (painting on wet plaster): pigments were brushed onto a thin layer of fresh plaster spread on the rock and bound into it as it dried.
Side walls: dancers and musicians move in profile among slender trees and birds, as if the party were outdoors.
Back wall, badly damaged: couples reclining on couches attended by servants, with animals such as a cat beneath the couches.
Flat, bright colors and strong outlines, no shading. Fluttering drapery and swinging limbs give the figures energy.
Color convention for gender: men are painted reddish-brown, women pale, as in Egyptian and Greek painting.
The ceiling is painted with a checkerboard pattern, perhaps imitating a tent or fabric canopy.
function: A family tomb: the dead, or their ashes, were laid here with goods for the afterlife.
The paintings re-created the funeral banquet, music and dancing held in honor of the dead, keeping the celebration going forever.
Like many Etruscan tombs, it worked as a house for the dead, furnished in paint.
content: Music, dance, wine and food signal pleasure, abundance and high status in the afterlife.
Men and women appear together, as on the Sarcophagus of the Spouses (No. 29), reflecting Etruscan social customs.
Trees and birds may suggest a sacred grove or the open-air setting of funeral games.
The mood later changes: after about 400 B.C.E., Etruscan tomb paintings turn darker, with underworld demons such as Charun.
context: Discovered in 1830.
To save them from damp and decay, the paintings were detached from the walls in 1949 and moved to the National Archaeological Museum in Tarquinia.
The Etruscan cemeteries of Tarquinia and Cerveteri together form a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Greek influence is strong: the profile figures recall Greek vase painting, and Etruscans imported Greek pottery in huge quantities.
Almost all Greek wall painting is lost, so Etruscan tombs are among our best evidence for large-scale painting in the Mediterranean before Rome. On the exam.
If asked about medium → fresco on the tufa walls of a rock-cut chamber tomb.
If asked about function → tomb decoration showing a funeral banquet and celebration for the dead.
If asked about culture → Etruscan, Tarquinia, c. 480–470 B.C.E.
If asked about the name → triclinium means a set of three dining couches.
If asked about themes → banquet, music, dance, men and women together, afterlife as a celebration.
If asked to compare painted burial spaces → Catacomb of Priscilla (No. 48), and Lady Dai’s funeral banner (No. 194).

33.title: Niobides Krater
33.artist: Niobid Painter (anonymous vase painter of Classical Greece)
33.plain: A big Athenian painted vase, a calyx krater for mixing wine and water at drinking parties, made around 460–450 B.C.E. by a painter scholars call the Niobid Painter, after this very pot. One side shows the gods Apollo and Artemis shooting the children of Niobe; the other shows a gathering of heroes. It matters because it shows Greek painters trying to show depth by placing figures up and down a hillside, probably copying famous lost wall paintings.
33.spot: A wide-mouthed vase with orange figures on a black background; figures scattered at different heights on wavy ground lines; a nude archer god and a goddess shooting arrows at falling, dying youths.
33.remember: Niobe: ‘Knee-OH-bee, no brag, no kids.’ Red-figure, c. 460–450 B.C.E., the vase that tries to go 3D.
compare: No. 40 (§3.29), Alexander Mosaic, from the House of the Faun,…: Another work that preserves the look of lost Greek painting, in a Roman mosaic copy.
No. 34 (§3.23), Doryphoros: Classical naturalism in sculpture from the same decade as the krater’s naturalism in drawing.
No. 27 (§3.16), Anavysos Kouros: The Archaic stiffness that the Niobid Painter’s twisting, foreshortened bodies leave behind.
33.vocab: krater, red-figure, black-figure, slip, symposium, foreshortening, ground line.

form: A calyx krater (a wide bowl shaped like the calyx, the cup of leaves under a flower), about 54 cm (21 inches) tall.
Red-figure technique: figures are left in the orange color of the clay while the background is painted black, and details are drawn with a fine brush, allowing more naturalistic anatomy.
The black comes from slip (liquid clay), which turns glossy black during a three-stage firing that alternates oxygen-rich and smoky conditions.
Figures stand on multiple ground lines at different heights across a rocky landscape, a new way to suggest that some are farther away.
Bodies in three-quarter view and foreshortening (a shortened view of a body seen at an angle), such as a fallen son sprawled on the ground.
Touches of added white for highlights.
function: Used at the symposium, an all-male aristocratic drinking party. Greeks diluted their wine with water in a krater before serving it.
The myths gave drinkers something to talk about, including moral lessons and displays of education.
Exported: it was found in an Etruscan tomb at Orvieto, Italy, evidence of the trade in Athenian pottery. It is now in the Louvre.
content: Side A: Niobe boasted that she had more children (seven sons and seven daughters in most versions) than the goddess Leto, who had only Apollo and Artemis. The twins avenge their mother by shooting Niobe’s children.
The moral is about hubris (arrogant pride that challenges the gods), which always brings punishment.
The calm, idealized gods contrast with the suffering mortal children: divine power versus human vulnerability.
Side B: Herakles with Athena among a group of warriors. Scholars debate the subject; suggestions include the Argonauts and Athenian heroes before the battle of Marathon.
context: Early Classical period, just after the Persian Wars (490–479 B.C.E.), when Greek art was moving from Archaic patterns toward naturalism.
Red-figure was invented in Athens about 530 B.C.E. and gradually replaced black-figure (black silhouettes on orange clay with scratched-in details).
The hillside arrangement probably imitates lost wall paintings by Polygnotos of Thasos, which ancient writers describe as placing figures up and down slopes.
Large-scale Greek painting is almost entirely lost, so painted vases are among our best evidence for it.
The painter’s real name is unknown; scholars group other vases with this one by style and name him after it. On the exam.
If asked about technique → red-figure: figures in the clay color, background black, details painted with a brush.
If asked about function → mixing wine and water at a symposium.
If asked about subject → Apollo and Artemis kill Niobe’s children as punishment for her hubris.
If asked what is new → multiple ground lines and foreshortening suggest space, probably borrowed from lost wall painting.
Trap: ‘Niobid Painter’ is a nickname taken from this vase, not a known person’s name.
If asked about evidence for lost Greek painting → this krater and the Alexander Mosaic (No. 40).

34.title: Doryphoros (Spear Bearer)
34.plain: A statue of a nude young man who once held a spear, designed by the Greek sculptor Polykleitos around 450–440 B.C.E. to demonstrate his rules for the perfect body. The original was bronze and is lost; we know it from Roman marble copies, the best one from Pompeii. It is the textbook example of contrapposto, the relaxed standing pose Western art has used ever since.
34.spot: A nude, muscular young man with a squared-off ideal body, weight on his right leg and left heel lifted, head turned slightly to his right, left arm bent as if holding a spear, with a tree-trunk support beside his right leg.
34.remember: Doryphoros: ‘Door-for-us’, Polykleitos opens the door to contrapposto. His Canon is the rulebook, 450–440 B.C.E.
compare: No. 27 (§3.16), Anavysos Kouros: The Archaic kouros shows the stiff, frontal pose that contrapposto replaced.
No. 43 (§3.32), Augustus of Prima Porta: Augustus of Prima Porta borrows the Doryphoros’s stance and proportions for imperial propaganda.
No. 69 (§4.22), David: Donatello’s David revives contrapposto and the freestanding nude in Renaissance Florence.
No. 41 (§3.30), Seated boxer: The Seated boxer replaces Classical perfection with Hellenistic realism and suffering.
34.vocab: contrapposto, chiasmus, canon, idealization, lost-wax casting, Roman copy.

form: Classical contrapposto (weight on one leg, so the hips and shoulders tilt in opposite directions): weight on the right leg, left leg bent with the heel raised.
Chiastic balance (crosswise, from the Greek letter chi, X): the tense right leg pairs with the relaxed right arm, and the relaxed left leg with the bent left arm that held the spear.
The body is idealized: broad shoulders, clearly divided chest and abdomen, a strong ridge above the hips. It is a perfect type, not a real individual.
Head turned slightly aside, calm face, short cap-like hair: no emotion, complete control.
The best-known copy, about 2.1 m (6 feet 11 inches) tall, was found in an exercise ground at Pompeii and is now in the National Archaeological Museum, Naples.
The tree stump and the strut at the hip were added by Roman copyists, because marble cannot support a pose that bronze can hold on its own.
The original was cast in bronze by the lost-wax process (a wax model is coated in clay, the wax melted out, and molten bronze poured into the gap).
function: Polykleitos wrote a treatise called the Canon (‘rule’ or ‘measure’) defining ideal proportions as ratios between body parts. The statue was its physical demonstration.
The Canon is lost. Later writers such as the physician Galen report that it related every part to every other: finger to finger, finger to hand, hand to forearm, and so on.
The original setting is unknown; the figure may represent Achilles, the hero of the Trojan War, or an idealized athlete.
Romans used marble copies to decorate exercise grounds, villas and baths, showing off their taste for Greek culture.
content: A model of the ideal male citizen-athlete: harmony, balance, discipline and self-control.
The balance of opposites (tense and relaxed, moving and still) reflects Greek interest in harmony and number, also seen in Pythagorean philosophy.
Nudity still means the heroic ideal, as with the kouros, but now the body seems capable of real movement.
context: High Classical period. Polykleitos worked mainly in Argos and was active in the same years as the Parthenon (No. 35).
It solves the problem of the Archaic kouros (No. 27): the figure finally looks relaxed and able to move.
Romans admired Greek masterpieces and ordered many copies; most Greek bronze originals were later melted down for their metal.
Augustus of Prima Porta (No. 43) borrows its pose, and Renaissance artists such as Donatello (No. 69) and Michelangelo revived contrapposto. On the exam.
If asked to define contrapposto → weight on one leg, hips and shoulders tilting in opposite directions, a natural relaxed stance.
If asked about the Canon → Polykleitos’s treatise on ideal proportion; the Doryphoros illustrates it.
Material trap: the original was bronze; what survives are Roman marble copies, hence the tree-trunk support.
If asked about period → Classical Greek, 450–440 B.C.E., idealized naturalism.
If asked about change over time → kouros (No. 27) rigid → Doryphoros balanced → Seated boxer (No. 41) realistic and emotional.
If asked about legacy → Augustus of Prima Porta (No. 43) and Donatello’s David (No. 69).

35.title: Acropolis
35.plain: The Acropolis is the rocky hill above Athens crowned with marble temples, rebuilt under the statesman Pericles after the Persians burned the old ones in 480 B.C.E. Its centerpiece, the Parthenon, was designed by the architects Iktinos and Kallikrates, with sculpture supervised by Phidias. It was a temple to Athena and a giant statement of Athenian pride, paid for partly with money from Athens’s allies.
35.spot: A rocky plateau with a large rectangular marble temple ringed by thick fluted Doric columns (8 across the front), a monumental gateway, and a smaller temple with a porch of female statues holding up its roof.
35.remember: PARThenon: ‘Pericles’ Athens Rebuilt Then.’ Iktinos and Kallikrates build it, Phidias decorates it, c. 447–410 B.C.E.
compare: No. 26 (§3.15), Athenian agora: The civic agora below versus the sacred Acropolis above: two halves of Athenian public life.
No. 46 (§3.35), Pantheon: The Pantheon keeps the Greek temple porch but adds a Roman concrete dome.
No. 38 (§3.27), Great Altar of Zeus and Athena at Pergamon: The Pergamon Altar quotes the Parthenon’s sculpture to present Pergamon as a new Athens.
No. 169 (§7.3), Wall plaque, from Oba’s palace: Benin plaques taken by the British in 1897 are another case at the center of repatriation debates.
35.vocab: Doric order, Ionic order, entasis, frieze, metope, pediment, caryatid, wet drapery.

form: Built of Pentelic marble from Mount Pentelikon near Athens, in post-and-lintel construction (columns carrying horizontal beams) with metal clamps and no mortar.
The Parthenon (447–432 B.C.E.) is a Doric temple, 8 by 17 columns, with Ionic touches such as a continuous frieze and four Ionic columns in the back room.

Optical refinements: the floor bulges up in the middle, columns swell slightly (entasis) and lean inward, and the corner columns are thicker, so the building looks straight and solid rather than sagging.
Sculpture everywhere: 92 metopes (square relief panels), two pediments (triangular gables) full of statues, and an Ionic frieze about 160 m (524 feet) long.
The Propylaia (monumental gateway, by Mnesikles), the Erechtheion (an Ionic temple with a porch of caryatids, female figures used as columns) and the small Ionic Temple of Athena Nike.
Victory Adjusting Her Sandal (about 410 B.C.E., from the Nike temple’s parapet) shows wet drapery: thin cloth clinging to the body as if wet, revealing the form beneath.
function: Religious center for Athena, the city’s patron goddess. The Parthenon housed Phidias’s gold-and-ivory statue of Athena Parthenos, nearly 12 m (about 38 feet) tall, now lost.
The Parthenon also worked as a treasury, storing the city’s wealth and the allies’ tribute.
Every year the Panathenaic procession climbed the hill, and every four years, at the Great Panathenaia, it presented Athena with a new woven peplos (robe).
Later uses: a Christian church, a mosque, and an Ottoman gunpowder store that exploded when Venetian forces shelled it in 1687.
content: East pediment: the birth of Athena from Zeus’s head. At the corner, the sun god Helios’s horses rise from the sea next to a reclining nude god, usually identified as Dionysus, possibly Herakles.
West pediment: Athena and Poseidon compete to become the patron of Athens.
Metopes: Greeks fighting centaurs, Amazons, giants and Trojans. Order defeating chaos stands in for the Greek victory over Persia.
The Panathenaic frieze shows the procession itself. The Plaque of the Ergastines shows young women who wove Athena’s peplos walking in calm, rhythmic order.
Putting ordinary Athenians on a temple was unusual: the city celebrated itself next to its gods.
context: After beating Persia, Athens led the Delian League, an alliance of Greek states paying into a shared fund. The treasury moved from Delos to Athens in 454 B.C.E., and Pericles used it for the building program.
Ancient critics, as reported by Plutarch, accused Pericles of misusing allied money to dress up Athens.
Built during the height of Athenian democracy and power, which ended with defeat by Sparta in the Peloponnesian War (431–404 B.C.E.).
Lord Elgin, British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire, removed about half the surviving sculpture between 1801 and 1812; the British Museum bought it in 1816. Greece keeps asking for its return.
The Acropolis Museum (opened 2009) displays the frieze with gaps left for the pieces in London. The Plaque of the Ergastines is in the Louvre. On the exam.
If asked about architects → Iktinos and Kallikrates (Parthenon); Phidias supervised the sculpture; Pericles was the political force behind it.
If asked about refinements → entasis, curved floor, inward-leaning columns, thicker corner columns.
If asked about funding and politics → Delian League money; a victory monument after the Persian Wars.
If asked about wet drapery → Victory Adjusting Her Sandal: cloth that reveals the body underneath.
If asked about repatriation → the Elgin Marbles in the British Museum; Greece requests their return.
Trap: the Parthenon is Doric with Ionic elements; the Erechtheion and the Nike temple are Ionic.
Date: c. 447–410 B.C.E. covers the whole program, not only the Parthenon (447–432 B.C.E.).

36.title: Grave stele of Hegeso
36.plain: A marble grave marker from the Kerameikos cemetery of Athens, around 410 B.C.E., carved in relief with a seated woman named Hegeso picking a piece of jewelry from a box held by her servant. It turns a quiet, everyday moment into a memorial. It is attributed, without certainty, to the sculptor Kallimachos.
36.spot: A tall relief panel framed like a tiny temple front with a triangular top: a seated, veiled woman with her feet on a footstool, looking at something in her raised hand, while a standing girl in a cap holds an open box toward her.
36.remember: Hegeso: ‘Hey, gimme so-and-so’s necklace.’ Seated lady, standing servant, c. 410 B.C.E.: the quiet Classical goodbye.
compare: No. 27 (§3.16), Anavysos Kouros: An earlier Greek grave marker that presents the dead as an idealized nude youth instead of a domestic scene.
No. 28 (§3.17), Peplos Kore from the Acropolis: An Archaic female figure whose stiff garment contrasts with Hegeso’s clinging Classical drapery.
No. 35 (§3.24), Acropolis: The Nike temple parapet on the Acropolis shares the wet-drapery style that supports the Kallimachos attribution.
36.vocab: stele, relief, isocephaly, chiton, pyxis, wet drapery.

form: A stele (upright stone slab used as a marker) of Pentelic marble, about 1.58 m (5 feet 2 inches) tall, carved in relief (figures projecting from a flat background).
Framed like a small temple front: two flat pilasters and a pediment, turning the grave into a little sacred building.
Both heads sit at nearly the same height even though one woman sits and the other stands, a Classical convention called isocephaly (heads aligned on one level).
Graceful drapery: Hegeso’s thin chiton (light linen tunic) clings to her body, while her heavier cloak and veil fall in deeper folds.
The jewelry was painted on, not carved, so today she seems to hold nothing.
Calm, idealized faces with no visible grief: typical Classical restraint.
function: A grave marker in the Kerameikos, the main cemetery of Athens, lined along roads outside the city walls where passersby could see the monuments.
The inscription above reads ‘Hegeso, daughter of Proxenos’, identifying her through her father, as Athenian custom did.
It displayed the family’s wealth and respectability to the public.
content: The jewelry box (a pyxis, a small lidded container) and the jewelry suggest wealth and possibly her dowry, the property a bride brought into marriage.
The servant’s long-sleeved dress and hair net mark her lower status; she was probably enslaved.
Choosing jewelry is a private, domestic moment: the ideal Athenian woman lived her life inside the home, not in public.
Hegeso’s downward gaze suggests quiet reflection. Classical grave reliefs often show the dead in an ordinary moment with a hint of farewell.
context: Late 5th century B.C.E., the end of the High Classical period, during the Peloponnesian War, when Athens was suffering heavy losses. (It is sometimes loosely called ‘Late Classical’, a label usually kept for the 4th century.)
Athenian women could not vote and were legally represented by male relatives, so the memorial frames her through family and household.
The attribution to Kallimachos, a sculptor known for elegant drapery, rests on style, especially its resemblance to the Nike temple parapet. It is not documented.
Found in 1870 in the Kerameikos; the original is in the National Archaeological Museum, Athens, and a copy stands at the site.
Carved grave stelai like this became popular again in Athens in the later 5th century, after a period without lavish grave monuments. On the exam.
If asked about function → a grave marker commemorating a wealthy Athenian woman.
If asked about gender roles → a private, domestic scene; jewelry and a servant show status; she is named as ‘daughter of Proxenos’.
If asked about style → Classical: calm, idealized, restrained emotion, naturalistic drapery, isocephaly.
If asked about a missing detail → the jewelry was painted, not carved.
Attribution trap: Kallimachos is a stylistic attribution, not a certainty.
If asked to compare grave markers → the Anavysos Kouros (No. 27) shows the dead as a heroic nude type; Hegeso shows a domestic moment.

37.title: Winged Victory of Samothrace
37.plain: A larger-than-life marble statue of Nike, the Greek goddess of victory, landing on the prow of a warship, made around 190 B.C.E. for a sanctuary on the island of Samothrace in the northern Aegean. Her head and arms are missing, but the wind-blown drapery and twisting pose make her a defining example of Hellenistic drama. She now stands at the top of a grand staircase in the Louvre.
37.spot: A headless, armless winged woman striding forward on the bow of a ship, wings swept back, thin drapery plastered against her body and whipping out behind her legs.
37.remember: Nike on the ship: ‘Just do it’, land and win. Hellenistic, c. 190 B.C.E., from Samothrace to the Louvre stairs.
compare: No. 35 (§3.24), Acropolis: The Classical Nike from the Athena Nike temple parapet shows calm wet drapery; this Nike shows the same idea in a storm.
No. 38 (§3.27), Great Altar of Zeus and Athena at Pergamon: The Pergamon Altar shares Hellenistic drama, deep carving and figures that invade the viewer’s space.
No. 89 (§4.42), Ecstasy of Saint Teresa: Bernini’s Saint Teresa uses swirling drapery and a staged setting for theatrical effect, as Hellenistic sculptors did.
37.vocab: Hellenistic, wet drapery, undercutting, personification, mystery cult.

form: The figure, of white Parian marble, is about 2.75 m (9 feet) tall with her wings. The ship’s prow base is gray marble from Rhodes; the whole monument stands about 5.5 m (18 feet).
Carved in several blocks fitted together, including separately carved wings.
Wet drapery taken to an extreme: wind presses cloth against her stomach and legs and swirls it into deep folds behind her, revealing the body and suggesting motion at once.
Deep undercutting (carving behind and beneath folds) creates strong contrasts of light and shadow.
A strong twisting, diagonal pose: she leans into the wind as if she has just touched down.
Finished more carefully on her left side, because she was meant to be seen from the front left; the right side is rougher.
Her right hand was found in 1950 and is displayed separately. It was probably raised, perhaps in greeting or a victory gesture.
function: A victory monument dedicated in the Sanctuary of the Great Gods on Samothrace, almost certainly for a naval victory.
The gray Rhodian marble suggests that Rhodes dedicated it, perhaps after sea battles against the Seleucid king Antiochus III around 190 B.C.E. Scholars still debate this.
It stood in a niche on a hillside above the sanctuary, possibly with water nearby, so she seemed to land on the sea.
The sanctuary was the center of a mystery cult (secret rituals for initiates) believed to protect sailors.
content: Nike is a personification (an idea, here victory, shown as a person). Her landing on a ship announces that the gods granted victory at sea.
She seems to enter the viewer’s space, as if descending among us: theater in stone.
Her lost raised arm may have held a wreath or a trumpet, or simply greeted; the exact gesture is unknown.
context: Hellenistic period (323–31 B.C.E., from Alexander’s death to Rome’s conquest of Egypt): kingdoms ruled by his successors, and art that favored drama, emotion, movement and realism.
Found in 1863 by Charles Champoiseau, a French consul, who sent her to Paris. The prow pieces were found later and shipped in 1879.
