Displayed at the top of the Louvre’s Daru staircase since 1884, and cleaned and restored in 2013–2014.
The date is debated, with proposals from about 220 to 180 B.C.E.; c. 190 B.C.E. is the AP date. On the exam.
If asked about style → Hellenistic: dramatic movement, wind-whipped drapery, theatrical setting.
If asked about function → a victory monument, probably for a naval battle, set up in a sanctuary.
If asked to compare with Classical → Victory Adjusting Her Sandal (No. 35) is calm and graceful; the Samothrace Nike is dynamic and theatrical.
If asked about viewpoint → designed for a three-quarter view from the front left.
Trap: she is Nike, goddess of victory, not Athena or an angel, and the ship’s prow is part of the original monument.
If asked about location → Sanctuary of the Great Gods, Samothrace; now in the Louvre, Paris.

38.title: Great Altar of Zeus and Athena at Pergamon
38.plain: A huge altar built around 175 B.C.E. on the acropolis of Pergamon, a Greek kingdom in what is now western Turkey. Its base is wrapped in a frieze about 113 m (370 feet) long showing the gods defeating the giants, carved in deep relief with extreme emotion and movement. German excavators shipped it to Berlin in the late 1800s, where it is reassembled in the Pergamon Museum.
38.spot: A wide flight of marble stairs rising between two projecting wings, with an Ionic colonnade on top; around the base a crowded relief of muscular giants (some with snake legs) battling gods, with bodies spilling onto the steps.
38.remember: Pergamon’s ‘Giant Problem’: gods versus giants, the Gigantomachy. Hellenistic, c. 175 B.C.E., now in Berlin.
compare: No. 35 (§3.24), Acropolis: The Parthenon is the Classical model the altar quotes, but with calm control instead of frenzy.
No. 37 (§3.26), Winged Victory of Samothrace: Another Hellenistic victory monument built on drama, movement and deep carving.
No. 47 (§3.36), Ludovisi Battle Sarcophagus: The Ludovisi sarcophagus also packs a battle of civilized victors and ‘barbarians’ into crowded high relief.
38.vocab: frieze, high relief, Gigantomachy, pathos, undercutting, colonnade, allegory.

form: A U-shaped structure on a high podium, roughly 36 by 34 m, with a broad stairway cut into the west front leading up to a courtyard that held the altar itself.
Topped by an Ionic colonnade (row of columns) running around three sides.
The base carries a frieze about 2.3 m (7.5 feet) tall in very high relief: figures project almost fully in the round and are deeply undercut.
Figures burst out of the frame and crawl onto the stair steps, so sculpture and architecture invade the visitor’s path.
Writhing bodies, flying drapery, wild hair and faces twisted in pain: Hellenistic pathos (emotion designed to make viewers feel pity or fear).
A smaller inner frieze in the courtyard tells the life of Telephos, mythical founder of Pergamon, as a continuous narrative.
function: An altar for burnt sacrifices, traditionally dedicated to Zeus and Athena, though its exact dedication is debated.
A royal monument: the Attalid kings, probably Eumenes II (ruled 197–159 B.C.E.), built it to display their power, piety and culture.
The battle of gods and giants celebrated Pergamon’s victories over the Galatians, Celtic invaders (Gauls) who had settled in Asia Minor.
content: Gigantomachy: the Olympian gods fight the giants, children of Gaia (Earth), who tried to overthrow them. Order and Greek civilization defeat chaos and ‘barbarism’.
Famous scene: Athena grabs the winged giant Alkyoneus by the hair while her snake bites him; his mother Gaia rises from the ground pleading, and Nike flies in to crown Athena.
Zeus fights three giants at once, including their leader Porphyrion.
The Athena group deliberately echoes the Parthenon’s west pediment, presenting Pergamon as a new Athens.
context: Pergamon, one of the kingdoms that formed after Alexander’s empire split, made itself a cultural capital with a great library. The word ‘parchment’ comes from the city’s name.
The Dying Gaul, known from a Roman marble copy, comes from Pergamon’s earlier victory monuments against the Gauls.
The German engineer Carl Humann excavated the altar from 1878 and shipped it to Berlin under an agreement with the Ottoman government.
Turkey has asked for its return. The museum’s altar hall closed for renovation in 2023 and is expected to reopen around 2027.
In the Bible, Revelation 2:13 calls Pergamon the place ‘where Satan’s throne is’, which some readers connect to this altar. On the exam.
If asked about subject → the Gigantomachy, gods versus giants, as an allegory of Pergamon’s victory over the Gauls.
If asked about style → Hellenistic: high relief, dramatic movement, emotion, figures spilling into the viewer’s space.
If asked to compare with Classical → Parthenon sculpture is calm and contained; Pergamon is agitated and bursts its frame.
If asked about location and controversy → Pergamon Museum, Berlin; Turkey has requested repatriation.
Key scene → Athena seizing Alkyoneus while Gaia pleads.
Trap: it is an altar, not a temple; there was no cella with a cult statue.

39.title: House of the Vettii
39.date: c. second century B.C.E.; rebuilt c. 62–79 C.E.
39.plain: A large townhouse in Pompeii owned by two brothers, Aulus Vettius Conviva and Aulus Vettius Restitutus, freedmen (former slaves) who got rich in trade. Its walls were repainted in the latest fashion after an earthquake in 62 C.E., then buried by Vesuvius in 79 C.E. It is the standard example of a Roman house, of Fourth Style wall painting, and of new money using art to claim status.
39.spot: Red and black painted walls divided into panels, with framed mythological pictures and painted architecture that seems to open into fantasy spaces; a garden courtyard surrounded by columns, with statues and fountains.
39.remember: Vettii: ‘Very wealthy ex-slaves.’ Pompeii, Fourth Style, rebuilt after 62 C.E., buried in 79 C.E.
compare: No. 40 (§3.29), Alexander Mosaic, from the House of the Faun,…: Another wealthy Pompeii house that used Greek-inspired art to display the owner’s culture.
No. 32 (§3.21), Tomb of the Triclinium: Etruscan fresco in a house for the dead, versus Roman fresco in a house for the living.
No. 102 (§5.4), Monticello: Jefferson’s Monticello is another house designed to present its owner’s status and classical learning.
39.vocab: domus, atrium, impluvium, peristyle, fresco, lararium.

form: A domus (private Roman townhouse): visitors enter through a narrow entrance passage into the atrium (central hall with an opening in the roof and a basin below, the impluvium, to catch rain).
Unusually, it has no tablinum, the owner’s oﬀice normally placed between atrium and garden, so the view runs straight from the front door to the peristyle (garden courtyard ringed by columns).
The peristyle held marble and bronze statues that spouted water into basins through lead pipes.
Walls of cut stone, rubble and concrete, coated in plaster and painted.
Fourth Style wall painting (the last Pompeian fashion, about 62–79 C.E.): flat colored panels, framed ‘pictures’ of myths and fantastic architecture, combining all the earlier styles.
Painted in fresco (pigment on wet plaster), with intense red and black grounds; a frieze of cupids at work runs around one reception room.
function: Home and business space: Roman patrons received their clients in the morning, so the front rooms were semi-public.
Two strongboxes on display in the atrium advertised the owners’ wealth to every visitor.
Dining rooms (triclinia) hosted guests among mythological paintings meant to spark conversation and display learning.
A painted household shrine (lararium) shows the household gods and a protective snake.
content: Entrance fresco: Priapus, a fertility god, weighs his huge phallus against a bag of money, a symbol of prosperity and a charm against the evil eye.
Myth panels show the power of the gods: King Pentheus torn apart for rejecting Dionysus, Ixion bound to a wheel, and the baby Hercules strangling snakes.
The cupid frieze shows cupids as goldsmiths, perfume makers and wine sellers, perhaps a nod to the trades that made such owners rich.
Choosing Greek myths let former slaves claim the cultural polish of the elite.
context: Pompeii was a prosperous Roman town near Naples. The house dates back to the 2nd century B.C.E. and was redecorated after a major earthquake of 62 C.E. (some sources say 63).
Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 C.E. and buried Pompeii under volcanic ash, preserving buildings and paintings.
Freedmen could become rich citizens but were barred from the highest oﬀices; display was one way to assert success.
Excavated in 1894–95. After about 20 years of restoration, it reopened to visitors in January 2023.
The four ‘Pompeian styles’ of wall painting were defined by the German scholar August Mau in 1882. On the exam.
If asked about parts of a domus → entrance passage, atrium with impluvium, peristyle garden, triclinium.
If asked about painting → Fourth Style fresco: mythological panels framed by illusionistic architecture.
If asked about patrons → wealthy freedmen, the Vettius brothers: evidence of social mobility in Rome.
If asked about preservation → buried by Vesuvius in 79 C.E.
Date trap: the original house is 2nd century B.C.E.; what we see was rebuilt and repainted about 62–79 C.E.
If asked for another Pompeii house → the House of the Faun, source of the Alexander Mosaic (No. 40).

40.title: Alexander Mosaic, from the House of the Faun, Pompeii
40.plain: A huge floor mosaic, about 5.8 by 3.1 m (19 by 10 feet), from the House of the Faun in Pompeii, made around 100 B.C.E. It shows Alexander the Great charging at the Persian king Darius III, who turns to flee. It is almost certainly a copy of a famous lost Greek painting, so it is our best evidence of what great Greek painting looked like.
40.spot: A crowded battle in earthy browns, reds and blacks: a bareheaded rider charging from the left, a king in a tall chariot at the right turning back in alarm, a forest of long spears slanting against a pale sky, a horse seen from behind, and a bare tree.
40.remember: ‘Alex attacks, Darius dashes.’ Pompeii’s House of the Faun, c. 100 B.C.E., copied from a Greek painting.
compare: No. 203 (§9.12), Night Attack on the Sanjô Palace: A Japanese handscroll battle that also uses crowds, horses and chaos, but unrolls as a continuous narrative.
No. 33 (§3.22), Niobides Krater: The Niobides Krater is another surviving clue to how lost Greek wall paintings looked.
No. 30 (§3.19), Audience Hall: The Persian Empire shown at its peak, whose defeat the mosaic celebrates.
No. 59 (§4.12), Bayeux Tapestry: The Bayeux Tapestry is another battle narrative in a medium other than paint, celebrating a conqueror.
40.vocab: mosaic, tesserae, opus vermiculatum, foreshortening, exedra.

form: A mosaic of tesserae (small cut cubes of stone and glass), well over a million of them; estimates range from about 1.5 million to 4 million.
Opus vermiculatum (Latin for ‘worm-like work’): tiny tesserae laid in curving rows that follow the contours of forms, allowing fine, painterly detail.
A limited palette of white, black, red and yellow and their mixtures, the four-color scheme ancient writers credited to famous Greek painters.
Painterly effects: modeling (shading to create volume), cast shadows, and foreshortening, such as the horse seen from behind at the center.
A dying Persian sees his own face reflected in a polished shield, a detail that shows off interest in light and optics.
Crowded, overlapping figures in a shallow space; the slanting spears and the bare tree organize the chaos.
A large damaged area at the left has lost much of Alexander’s army.
function: Floor decoration in an exedra (open reception room) between the two peristyle gardens of the House of the Faun, the largest house in Pompeii.
It showed the owner’s wealth and his taste for Greek culture and history.
Moved in 1843 to the National Archaeological Museum in Naples; a copy now lies on the original floor in Pompeii.
content: Alexander (left, bareheaded, wide-eyed) charges and spears a Persian noble who has thrown himself between Alexander and Darius.
Darius III (right, in a tall chariot) stretches out an arm toward his dying men while his charioteer whips the horses to flee.
The battle is probably Issus (333 B.C.E.) or Gaugamela (331 B.C.E.), both decisive victories over Persia.
The moment shown is the turning point when Darius gives up, celebrating Alexander’s destiny while showing sympathy for the defeated king.
context: The original painting was probably made around 310 B.C.E., soon after Alexander’s death. Pliny mentions Philoxenos of Eretria painting Alexander’s battle against Darius for King Cassander; the link is likely but unproven.
Rome conquered the Greek world in the 2nd century B.C.E. and eagerly imported Greek art and artists, so many Roman works copy Greek originals.
Discovered in 1831. A major conservation project began in 2021.
The House of the Faun is named for a small bronze statue of a dancing faun found in its atrium.
Republican Rome: the mosaic predates the emperors, when wealthy Romans competed through houses, art and learning. On the exam.
If asked about medium → floor mosaic of tesserae in opus vermiculatum.
If asked why it matters → a Roman copy of a lost Greek painting, our best evidence of Greek painting.
If asked about subject → Alexander the Great versus Darius III at Issus (or Gaugamela).
If asked about techniques → foreshortening, modeling, cast shadows, overlapping figures.
Period trap: Republican Roman, c. 100 B.C.E., from Pompeii; the subject is Greek and Macedonian history from the 330s B.C.E.
If asked for a comparison essay pair → Night Attack on the Sanjô Palace (No. 203): two chaotic battle scenes from very different cultures.

41.title: Seated boxer
41.plain: A life-size bronze statue of a battered boxer sitting down after a fight, made by a Greek sculptor around 100 B.C.E. (the date is debated). His broken nose, swollen ears and bleeding cuts are shown without flattery. It is one of the few original Greek bronzes to survive, and it shows how Hellenistic art turned to pain, age and exhaustion instead of perfect heroes.
41.spot: A nude, heavily muscled bronze man seated on a rock, forearms resting on his knees, hands wrapped in leather boxing straps, head twisted up and to his right, with a broken nose, scarred face, swollen ears and a beard.
41.remember: ‘Boxer, boxed out.’ A Hellenistic bronze, c. 100 B.C.E., now in Rome’s Palazzo Massimo.
compare: No. 34 (§3.23), Doryphoros: Classical idealization of the athlete’s body versus Hellenistic realism and exhaustion.
No. 42 (§3.31), Head of a Roman patrician: Roman verism also shows age and wear, but to signal civic virtue rather than suffering.
No. 27 (§3.16), Anavysos Kouros: The Archaic kouros presents an untouched, idealized youth; the boxer shows a body marked by life.
41.vocab: bronze, lost-wax casting, inlay, Realism, pathos, Hellenistic.

form: Hollow bronze, cast in sections by the lost-wax process and joined; about 1.28 m (4 feet 2 inches) tall as he sits.
Inlay (pieces of another material set into the surface): copper marks blood and cuts on his face, shoulder, arm and thigh; the eyes, now empty, were once inlaid too.
A realistic, non-idealized face: broken nose, swollen ‘cauliflower’ ears, cuts, and an open mouth as if breathing hard.
A powerful, mature body, still athletic but slumped with exhaustion.
The sharply turned head implies someone just out of view, drawing the viewer into the story.
His hands are wrapped in Greek boxing gear: long leather thongs bound over fleece-lined bands.
function: The original setting is unknown. It may have been a public monument, a dedication in a sanctuary, or a work for a private collector.
It could represent a famous champion, a mythical boxer or a generic veteran fighter; no inscription survives.
In Rome, where boxing and gladiatorial combat were popular, it was clearly valued, and someone took care to bury it.
content: Endurance and its cost: win or lose, his body bears the price of the fight.
Pathos (emotion that makes the viewer feel pity): we sympathize with his exhaustion and pain.
His upward glance may suggest he is listening to a verdict, hearing a crowd, or being called back for another round.
context: Hellenistic art (323–31 B.C.E.) widened its subjects to include the old, the young, the defeated and ordinary workers, not just gods and heroes.
Found in 1885 on the Quirinal Hill in Rome, apparently buried carefully in antiquity, perhaps to protect it.
Most Greek bronzes were melted down for metal, so this original is rare.
Now in the National Museum of Rome (Palazzo Massimo). It was lent to the Metropolitan Museum in New York in 2013.
Proposed dates range from the late 4th to the 1st century B.C.E.; c. 100 B.C.E. is the AP date. On the exam.
If asked about material → bronze, cast by lost-wax, with copper inlay for blood and wounds.
If asked about style → Hellenistic realism and pathos; a non-idealized subject.
If asked to compare → the Doryphoros (No. 34) is Classical, idealized and calm; the Seated boxer is realistic, battered and emotional.
If asked why it matters → a rare surviving Greek bronze original, not a Roman marble copy.
If asked about the viewer → the turned head implies another figure outside the sculpture.
Trap: it is Hellenistic Greek, not Roman, even though it was found in Rome.

42.title: Head of a Roman patrician
42.plain: A life-size marble portrait head of an old Roman aristocrat, made around 75– 50 B.C.E. Every wrinkle, sagging cheek and sharp bone is shown on purpose. In Republican Rome, an aged, weathered face advertised experience, seriousness and service to the state, the values that justified a man’s power.
42.spot: An old man’s head with very short hair, a deeply lined forehead, sunken cheeks, thin tight lips, heavy bags under the eyes and loose skin on the neck.
42.remember: VERy old, VERism: ‘Wrinkles win elections’ in the Roman Republic, c. 75–50 B.C.E.
compare: No. 43 (§3.32), Augustus of Prima Porta: Imperial idealization replaces Republican verism to present Augustus as ageless and divine.
No. 41 (§3.30), Seated boxer: Hellenistic realism shows wear and age for emotional effect rather than civic virtue.
No. 205 (§9.14), Portrait of Sin Sukju: A Korean portrait of a scholar-oﬀicial also uses a sober likeness to express rank and public virtue.
42.vocab: verism, patrician, bust, gravitas, imagines, portrait.

form: Marble, roughly life-size; probably once part of a full statue or bust.
Verism (extreme ‘warts-and-all’ realism): deep forehead creases, crow’s feet, sagging jowls, loose skin and a sunken, possibly toothless mouth.
The features may be deliberately exaggerated to stress age and toughness; this is a style, not a photograph.
Stern, set expression with no idealizing softness.
Many such portraits were probably carved by Greek or Greek-trained sculptors, adapting Hellenistic realism to Roman values.
function: A commemorative portrait of a patrician (member of Rome’s old hereditary aristocracy), shown in a home, tomb or public space.
It advertised the family’s lineage and its claim to political oﬀice.
It is linked to the custom of imagines: wax masks of ancestors kept in the atrium and worn by actors in family funeral processions, as the Greek historian Polybius described.
content: Age equals wisdom, experience and gravitas (seriousness and dignity), core Roman virtues.
The face says: I have worked hard for the Republic and earned respect. Character matters more than beauty.
It is a deliberate rejection of the Greek ideal of youthful perfection.
context: Late Roman Republic: a state run by elected magistrates and a Senate of aristocrats, not yet an empire, and torn by civil wars (Sulla, then Caesar against Pompey).
Aristocratic families competed fiercely for oﬀice and prestige, and portraits helped them advertise their ancestry.
Usually said to come from Otricoli, north of Rome; it belongs to the Torlonia collection in Rome.
Under Augustus (No. 43), oﬀicial portraits switched to ageless, idealized faces. On the exam.
If asked to define verism → extreme realism showing age and flaws, valued in Republican Rome.
If asked why → age signaled wisdom, experience, gravitas and public service.
If asked about origins → ancestral wax masks (imagines) displayed at home and in funerals.
If asked to contrast → Augustus of Prima Porta (No. 43): an idealized, youthful imperial image.
Period trap: Republican, not Imperial; c. 75–50 B.C.E.
If asked about realism across cultures → Greek realism in the Seated boxer (No. 41) invites pity; Roman verism commands respect.

43.title: Augustus of Prima Porta
43.plain: A larger-than-life marble statue of Augustus, Rome’s first emperor, found at his wife Livia’s villa at Prima Porta just outside Rome. He stands like a Greek athlete, raises his arm to address his troops, and wears a breastplate covered with political messages. It is state propaganda that presents him as general, peacemaker and descendant of the gods.
43.spot: A marble emperor in a decorated breastplate with a cloak wrapped around his hips, right arm raised, weight on his right leg, barefoot, with a small cupid riding a dolphin beside his right leg.
43.remember: Augustus brings ‘All Good Under Stable Times’ (the Pax Romana); Cupid on a dolphin shows his Venus family tree. Early 1st century C.E.
compare: No. 34 (§3.23), Doryphoros: The Greek source of Augustus’s contrapposto and ideal proportions.
No. 42 (§3.31), Head of a Roman patrician: Republican verism shows age to signal virtue; Augustus is ageless and idealized.
No. 104 (§5.6), George Washington: Houdon’s George Washington is another leader’s statue built on classical references to project virtue and authority.
No. 212 (§9.21), Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan: Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan is modern state propaganda that idealizes a leader for mass display.
43.vocab: contrapposto, adlocutio, cuirass, propaganda, idealization, iconography.

form: Marble, about 2 m (6 feet 8 inches) tall, slightly larger than life; probably a copy of a bronze original made around 20 B.C.E.
Contrapposto and proportions borrowed from Polykleitos’s Doryphoros (No. 34).
Adlocutio pose (an arm raised to address an army) presents him as speaker and commander.
A cuirass (breastplate) carved with a detailed scene in low relief, and a general’s cloak draped around his hips and over his left arm.
An idealized, youthful face with his trademark forked locks of hair over the forehead. His portraits never aged, though he lived to 75.
Originally painted: traces of color found on the statue have led to painted reconstructions.
The cupid and dolphin also serve as a support for the marble leg, like the tree stump on copies of the Doryphoros.
function: Propaganda: approved images of Augustus spread across the empire to present one oﬀicial image of the ruler.
This version was found in 1863 at the villa of Livia. It may have been made after his death in 14 C.E. to honor him as a god; the dating is debated.
Now in the Vatican Museums.
content: Center of the cuirass: a Parthian hands back Roman military standards lost by the general Crassus in 53 B.C.E., a diplomatic win Augustus achieved in 20 B.C.E. without a battle.
The figure receiving the standards may be Tiberius, the god Mars, or a symbolic Roman soldier; scholars disagree.

Around them: the sky god spreading the heavens, the sun in his chariot, Mother Earth with a cornucopia at the bottom, and mourning conquered provinces at the sides. The whole cosmos is at peace under Augustus.
Cupid on a dolphin: Cupid is the son of Venus, who was born from the sea, and Augustus’s Julian family claimed descent from Venus through her son Aeneas.
Bare feet: gods and heroes were shown barefoot, hinting that Augustus is more than human.
context: Augustus, born Octavian and adopted heir of Julius Caesar, defeated Antony and Cleopatra in 31 B.C.E., took the name Augustus in 27 B.C.E. and ruled until 14 C.E.
He claimed to have restored the Republic while holding sole power, and art was central to that message.
His reign began the Pax Romana (about 200 years of relative peace inside the empire).
Choosing Classical Greek style linked his rule to Athens’s golden age and to order and stability, unlike Republican verism. On the exam.
If asked about the source of the pose → the Doryphoros (No. 34): contrapposto and ideal proportions.
If asked about iconography → returned Parthian standards on the cuirass; Cupid on a dolphin for divine ancestry; bare feet for divinity.
If asked about function → imperial propaganda presenting Augustus as general, peacemaker and favored by the gods.
If asked about style contrast → idealized youth versus Republican verism (No. 42).
Trap: the event on the cuirass was diplomacy in 20 B.C.E., not a battle.
Date: early 1st century C.E., probably a marble copy of a bronze original; Imperial Roman.

44.title: Colosseum (Flavian Amphitheater)
44.plain: The Colosseum is the giant oval arena in the center of Rome, built 70–80 C.E. by the Flavian emperors Vespasian and Titus, where around 50,000 people watched gladiator fights and animal hunts for free. It shows off Roman engineering: concrete, arches and vaults that let a huge crowd get in and out quickly. It was also a political move, built on land the hated emperor Nero had taken for his private palace.
44.spot: A huge oval ruin with four stories: three levels of arches framed by attached columns (plain at the bottom, scrolled in the middle, leafy at the top) and a solid top story with flat pilasters; inside, the arena floor is gone, exposing underground passages.
44.remember: ‘Flavian means fun for all’: Vespasian starts it, Titus opens it in 80 C.E. The orders climb ‘Tough, Ionic, Curly’: Tuscan, Ionic, Corinthian.
compare: No. 46 (§3.35), Pantheon: The Pantheon shows Roman concrete used for a sacred interior instead of a public arena.
No. 70 (§4.23), Palazzo Rucellai: Palazzo Rucellai borrows the Colosseum’s stacked orders for a Renaissance family palace.
No. 45 (§3.34), Forum of Trajan: Another imperial building program, paid for by conquest and offered to the public to win goodwill.
44.vocab: amphitheater, concrete, barrel vault, groin vault, engaged column, pilaster, hypogeum.

form: An amphitheater (oval arena with seating all around; the word means ‘double theater’), about 189 by 156 m (620 by 513 feet) and 48 m (about 157 feet) high.
Built of concrete (Roman mix of lime, volcanic ash and rubble), travertine, tufa and brick; iron clamps held the travertine blocks together.
Barrel vaults (tunnel-shaped curved ceilings) and groin vaults (two barrel vaults crossing at right angles) carry the sloping seats, corridors and stairs.

The facade has three levels of arches framed by engaged columns (half-columns attached to the wall): Tuscan at the bottom, Ionic in the middle, Corinthian at the top, then a solid attic story with flat Corinthian pilasters.
Brackets and holes in the top story held masts for the velarium, a huge canvas awning worked by sailors to shade the crowd.
The hypogeum (underground level) beneath the wooden arena floor held tunnels, cages and lifts that raised animals and scenery; it was added under Domitian.
Eighty entrances, 76 of them numbered for the public, and passages called vomitoria let crowds enter and leave quickly.
function: Free public entertainment: gladiator fights, wild animal hunts, executions and staged reenactments.
Titus opened it in 80 C.E. with 100 days of games.
Seating was ordered by social rank: senators nearest the arena, ordinary citizens higher up, women and the poorest at the top.
‘Bread and circuses’, the poet Juvenal’s phrase: food and spectacle kept the city’s population content.
content: Building on the drained lake of Nero’s Golden House handed private imperial land back to the people, a direct political message after Nero’s unpopular rule.
A dedication inscription, reconstructed by scholars from holes left by its bronze letters, suggests it was paid for with spoils from the Jewish War, including the sack of Jerusalem in 70 C.E.
The stacked Greek orders ‘dress’ a concrete structure, signaling order, hierarchy and culture.
context: Built by the Flavian dynasty (Vespasian, Titus, Domitian), which took power after the civil war of 69 C.E. that followed Nero’s death.
The name ‘Colosseum’ appears in the Middle Ages, probably from the nearby Colossus of Nero, a giant bronze statue.
Gladiator fights ended in the 5th century C.E. Earthquakes damaged the building, and later Romans quarried its stone for other buildings.
The Catholic Church later honored it as a site of Christian martyrdom, though historians find little evidence that Christians were executed there.
Its arch-and-order facade inspired Renaissance architects, including Alberti’s Palazzo Rucellai (No. 70). On the exam.
If asked about function → mass public entertainment and political goodwill.
If asked about materials and technique → concrete, travertine, barrel and groin vaults, arches.
If asked about the facade → engaged columns in the order Tuscan, Ionic, Corinthian, with Corinthian pilasters on top.
If asked about patrons → the Flavian emperors, building on the site of Nero’s private lake.
Date: 70–80 C.E., Imperial Roman.
Trap: an amphitheater (oval, freestanding) is not a Greek theater (a half-circle set into a hillside).
If asked about Renaissance borrowing → Palazzo Rucellai (No. 70) stacks the orders the same way.

45.title: Forum of Trajan
45.date: Forum and markets 106–112 C.E.; column completed 113 C.E.
45.plain: The last and largest of Rome’s imperial forums, built 106–112 C.E. for the emperor Trajan and designed by his architect Apollodorus of Damascus, paid for with the riches of his conquest of Dacia (modern Romania). It combined a huge plaza, a basilica, two libraries, a multi-level market complex and the Column of Trajan, which carries a carved war story spiraling up its shaft. It shows how Roman emperors turned military victories into public monuments.
45.spot: A site plan of a large rectangular plaza with a long hall with rounded ends across it, and a small court with a column between two libraries; or a tall marble column wrapped in a spiral band of tiny carved soldiers, topped by a statue of Saint Peter; or curved brick terraces of shops.
45.remember: Trajan’s Column: ‘the spiral story of Dacia.’ Apollodorus of Damascus designs, 106–113 C.E., and Trajan’s ashes rest in the base.
compare: No. 26 (§3.15), Athenian agora: The Athenian agora grew gradually for a democracy; Trajan’s forum was planned at once to glorify an emperor.
No. 49 (§4.2), Santa Sabina: Santa Sabina adapts the basilica plan of the Basilica Ulpia for Christian worship.
No. 59 (§4.12), Bayeux Tapestry: The Bayeux Tapestry is another long continuous narrative celebrating a military conquest.
No. 44 (§3.33), Colosseum: Another imperial building paid for with war spoils and offered to the Roman public.
45.vocab: forum, basilica, apse, continuous narrative, relief, equestrian.

form: A vast open plaza enclosed by colonnades, with a bronze equestrian statue of Trajan in the center.
Basilica Ulpia: a huge basilica (a long hall with a central nave, side aisles and an apse, a semicircular end) with a timber roof, the largest in Rome at the time.
Two libraries, one for Greek and one for Latin texts, flank the column. Hadrian later added a temple to the deified Trajan; its exact location is debated.
The Markets of Trajan: a terraced complex of brick-faced concrete cut into the Quirinal hillside, with about 150 shops and oﬀices on several levels and a groin-vaulted hall.

The Column of Trajan: a marble shaft 100 Roman feet tall (about 30 m), rising to about 38 m (125 feet) with its pedestal and statue. It is built of about 20 huge drums, with a spiral staircase inside.
Its relief band is about 190 m (625 feet) long, winds 23 times around the shaft and shows more than 2,500 figures in low relief.
The upper scenes are hard to see from the ground; viewers could see more from the libraries’ upper floors.
function: Civic center: law courts and business in the basilica, public speeches and imperial ceremonies in the plaza.
Commercial: shops and oﬀices in the market complex.
Commemoration and burial: the column celebrated the Dacian Wars and became Trajan’s tomb, with his ashes, and later those of his wife Plotina, placed in a golden urn in its base.
Cultural: the libraries held books and public records.
content: The relief tells the story of the two Dacian Wars (101–102 and 105–106 C.E.) as a continuous narrative: marches, camp building, river crossings, battles and the suicide of the Dacian king Decebalus.
Trajan appears about 60 times, usually addressing troops, sacrificing or supervising, as a careful, involved commander rather than a lone warrior.
The focus on engineering and discipline says Rome wins through organization.
At the start, a river god (the Danube) watches the army cross, a classical touch in a documentary-style story.
context: Trajan (ruled 98–117 C.E.), born in Spain, was the first emperor from outside Italy and expanded the empire to its largest size.
Dacian gold paid for the forum: a monument literally built from conquered wealth.
Apollodorus of Damascus also built Trajan’s bridge over the Danube; the markets are usually, but not certainly, credited to him.
In 1587 Pope Sixtus V replaced Trajan’s lost statue on top of the column with a bronze Saint Peter.
The basilica plan became the model for early Christian churches such as Santa Sabina (No. 49).
Plaster casts of the column, made in the 1860s, are displayed at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London. On the exam.
If asked about the architect → Apollodorus of Damascus.
If asked about funding → spoils of the Dacian conquest.
If asked about the column → a continuous spiral relief of the Dacian Wars; Trajan’s ashes in the base.
If asked about the basilica → the Basilica Ulpia, a model for early Christian churches.
If asked about materials → brick and concrete for the forum and markets, marble for the column.
Dates: forum and markets 106–112 C.E.; column completed 113 C.E.
Measurement trap: the shaft is 100 Roman feet; textbook figures of 125 to 128 feet include the pedestal and statue.
Trap: the statue on top today is Saint Peter, not Trajan.

46.title: Pantheon
46.plain: The Pantheon in Rome is a temple ‘to all the gods’ built under Emperor Hadrian around 118–125 C.E.: a classical columned porch attached to a round hall with a gigantic concrete dome. The dome is 43.3 m (142 feet) across and the interior is just as tall, so a perfect sphere would fit inside. Almost 1,900 years later it is still standing and is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome in the world.
46.spot: A porch of tall granite columns and a triangular pediment with a Latin inscription, attached to a massive round brick drum; inside, a huge dome with square recessed panels and a round hole at the top letting in a disk of sunlight.
46.remember: Pan-theon = ‘all gods.’ 142 feet wide and 142 feet high. ‘Agrippa’s name, Hadrian’s game’, 118–125 C.E.
compare: No. 52 (§4.5), Hagia Sophia: Hagia Sophia raises a huge dome on pendentives over a square base, solving the same problem of covering vast space.
No. 102 (§5.4), Monticello: Jefferson’s Monticello borrows the Pantheon’s portico-and-dome formula for an American house.
No. 67 (§4.20), Pazzi Chapel: Brunelleschi’s Pazzi Chapel revives the Roman centralized dome and geometric harmony in the Renaissance.
No. 31 (§3.20), Temple of Minerva and sculpture of Apollo: The Pantheon’s deep frontal porch on a raised base descends from the Etruscan temple plan.
46.vocab: portico, rotunda, dome, coffer, oculus, concrete, pediment.

form: A portico (porch) of 16 single-piece Corinthian columns of Egyptian granite, each about 12 m (39 feet) tall, under a triangular pediment.
A rectangular block joins the porch to the rotunda (round building), an awkward junction that suggests the design changed during construction.
The concrete dome is lined with coffers (recessed square panels), five rings of 28, which reduce weight and add rhythm.
The concrete gets lighter as it rises: heavy travertine and brick rubble low down, light volcanic pumice near the top. The walls are about 6 m (20 feet) thick.
The oculus (round opening) at the top, roughly 8 to 9 m (27 to 29 feet) across depending on the source, is the only light source. Rain falls in and drains through holes in the gently sloping floor.
Interior geometry: the diameter equals the height, and the floor and walls play circles against squares in colored marble.
The brick-faced exterior was once covered with marble and stucco, and the dome with gilded bronze tiles, later removed.
function: A temple to the gods of Rome. Scholars debate whether it served as a regular temple, a shrine to the emperor’s family and patron gods, or a hall where Hadrian held court.
In 609 C.E. the Byzantine emperor Phocas gave it to Pope Boniface IV, who consecrated it as the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres. Continuous use saved it.
It is also a burial place: the painter Raphael and two kings of Italy are buried inside.
Since 2023 visitors pay a small entry fee that funds its upkeep.
content: The dome stands for the dome of the heavens. The disk of light from the oculus moves across the interior through the day, like a sundial.
All gods under one roof suggested the empire as the center of the world.

The inscription reads, in Latin, ‘Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, consul for the third time, made this’. It honors Agrippa, who built an earlier temple here around 27–25 B.C.E.; Hadrian kept the original builder’s name.
context: Agrippa’s temple burned in 80 C.E., was rebuilt by Domitian and burned again around 110 C.E. Brick stamps suggest the present building was begun late in Trajan’s reign and completed under Hadrian.
The architect is unknown. Apollodorus of Damascus and Hadrian himself have both been suggested, without proof.
Roman concrete (lime, volcanic ash called pozzolana, water and stone or brick rubble) allowed huge curved interiors, unlike the post-and-lintel boxes of Greek temples.

It remained the largest dome in the world until Brunelleschi’s dome for Florence Cathedral (completed 1436), and it inspired Renaissance and Neoclassical domes, including Jefferson’s Monticello (No. 102).
Pope Urban VIII, of the Barberini family, stripped bronze from the porch ceiling in the 1620s, prompting the saying ‘What the barbarians did not do, the Barberini did.’ On the exam.
If asked about materials → concrete faced with brick and stone (marble and granite); lighter aggregate higher up.
If asked how the dome stays up → thick walls, lighter concrete toward the top, thinning toward the crown, coffers to cut weight, and a ring around the oculus that works in compression.
If asked about geometry → 142 feet wide and 142 feet high; a perfect sphere fits inside.
If asked why it survived → it became a church in 609 C.E.
Trap: the inscription names Agrippa, but Hadrian built the present building.
If asked about plan → a traditional rectangular temple porch joined to a centralized rotunda.
If asked about later domes → Hagia Sophia (No. 52) sets its dome on pendentives; Monticello (No. 102) copies the Pantheon idea in brick and wood.

47.title: Ludovisi Battle Sarcophagus
47.plain: A marble coﬀin carved around 250 C.E. with a chaotic battle between Romans and barbarians, probably Goths, packed so tightly that there is almost no empty stone. A calm, bareheaded Roman general rides at the top center above the chaos. It shows how Roman art changed during the 3rd-century crisis: crowded, anxious and less interested in classical balance.
47.spot: A rectangular coﬀin front crammed with horses, soldiers and dying bearded men in trousers, stacked from top to bottom with no background; one young bareheaded rider at the top center stretches out his open right hand.
47.remember: Ludovisi: a ‘LOUD VISIon’ of chaos. Romans on top, Goths on the bottom, c. 250 C.E., during the Crisis of the Third Century.
compare: No. 38 (§3.27), Great Altar of Zeus and Athena at Pergamon: Another crowded battle in high relief that sets ‘civilized’ victors against defeated enemies.
No. 40 (§3.29), Alexander Mosaic, from the House of the Faun,…: The Alexander Mosaic also centers a heroic leader in a chaotic battle, but with real depth and space.
No. 29 (§3.18), Sarcophagus of the Spouses: An earlier Etruscan funerary container with a peaceful banquet instead of war, made for ashes rather than a body.
47.vocab: sarcophagus, high relief, horror vacui, drill, pathos, inhumation. 4 Early Europe and Colonial Americas Content area 3 · 200–1750 C.E. · works 48–98 · about 21% of the multiple-choice section. Roughly the fall of Rome to the 1700s: early Christian churches, Byzantine mosaics, medieval manuscripts, Gothic cathedrals, the Renaissance in Italy and the North, the Baroque, and art made in the Spanish colonies in the Americas. Most works are religious, so the exam leans on Christian stories and symbols. It also asks how artists rediscovered ancient Greek and Roman ideas, how patrons like the Medici and the Church paid for art, and how printing changed who could own images.

form: A marble sarcophagus (stone coﬀin) about 1.5 m (5 feet) tall. A lid fragment in Mainz, Germany, may belong to it.
Extremely high relief, with figures projecting almost fully from the block thanks to deep undercutting.
Horror vacui (Latin for ‘fear of empty space’): every surface is filled with bodies, with no landscape or sky.
No single ground line and no consistent depth: figures are stacked from top to bottom, with the Romans higher than their enemies.
Anti-classical proportions: some bodies are twisted or awkward and heads are relatively large.
Romans are armored and orderly; the barbarians are bearded, wear trousers, and fall, plead or die in agony.
A drill was used heavily to cut deep pockets of shadow in hair, eyes and folds.
function: A coﬀin for a wealthy and probably military Roman, and a monument to his virtues.
Possibly made for Hostilian, son of Emperor Decius, who died of plague in 251 C.E.; his brother Herennius Etruscus is another candidate. The identification is uncertain.
Found in 1621 in Rome and named for the Ludovisi family, who collected it; now in the Palazzo Altemps, part of the National Museum of Rome.
content: The general’s calm face and open gesture show confident victory, perhaps also triumph over death.
A mark on his forehead, carved as an X or cross, may indicate initiation into the cult of Mithras, popular with soldiers. It is not usually read as a Christian symbol.
Romans above and barbarians below: a hierarchy of order over chaos.
The barbarians’ anguished faces carry Hellenistic-style pathos, giving the defeated a certain dignity.
context: Crisis of the Third Century (235–284 C.E.): dozens of emperors and claimants in about 50 years, along with invasions, plague and economic collapse.
Burial of the body (inhumation) replaced cremation among wealthy Romans from the 2nd century C.E., creating demand for carved sarcophagi.
Goths and other peoples pressed on the Danube frontier; Decius himself died fighting the Goths at Abritus in 251 C.E.
Its style points toward late antique and medieval art, which preferred hierarchy and symbolism to naturalistic space. On the exam.
If asked about style → horror vacui, no ground line, stacked figures, deep relief: anti-classical.
If asked about context → the Crisis of the Third Century and wars with the Goths.
If asked about function → a sarcophagus for a high-ranking Roman, made when burial had replaced cremation.
If asked about the central figure → a calm, bareheaded general, possibly Hostilian, with a forehead mark possibly linked to Mithras.
If asked to compare battle reliefs → the Pergamon Altar (No. 38): Hellenistic gods versus giants.
If asked about change over time → classical balance (the Parthenon, No. 35) gives way to crowded, symbolic late Roman style.

48.title: Catacomb of Priscilla
48.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
48.plain: The Catacomb of Priscilla is an underground cemetery cut into the soft rock beneath the Via Salaria, just outside the walls of ancient Rome, used for burials from about 200 to 400 C.E. Its painted burial rooms hold some of the oldest Christian pictures anywhere: a shepherd carrying a lamb, a woman praying with her arms raised, and what may be the earliest known image of the Virgin and Child. It shows Christian art being born by borrowing ordinary Roman pictures and giving them new meanings.
48.spot: Dim, rough rock tunnels and small rooms with quick, sketchy paintings in reddishbrown and green lines on pale plaster. Look for a young beardless shepherd with a sheep across his shoulders, or a veiled woman standing frontally with both arms raised.
48.remember: Priscilla’s basement is Christianity’s first picture book: Good Shepherd on the ceiling, praying lady on the wall, painted in the 200s and 300s C.E., starting while Christianity was still illegal. Think ‘burial plots, not hideouts.’
compare: No. 49 (§4.2), Santa Sabina: Before and after legalization: hidden, small-scale funerary painting underground versus a large, public church built for crowds in daylight.
No. 32 (§3.21), Tomb of the Triclinium: Both are painted underground tombs with banquet imagery, but the Etruscan tomb celebrates earthly feasting while the catacomb scenes promise salvation.
No. 39 (§3.28), House of the Vettii: The catacomb painters used the same Roman fresco methods and panel divisions as wall painting in Roman houses like the House of the Vettii.

No. 47 (§3.36), Ludovisi Battle Sarcophagus: Both are Roman burial art of the 200s C.E.: the Ludovisi sarcophagus shows pagan military glory in crowded marble relief, while the catacombs use small, symbolic Christian paintings.
48.vocab: catacomb, tufa, loculus, cubiculum, arcosolium, orant, fresco, Good Shepherd.

form: The catacomb was dug, not built. Workers carved corridors and rooms out of tufa (a soft volcanic rock that is easy to cut and hardens on exposure to air), expanding outward and downward as more graves were needed.
Corridor walls are lined with stacked loculi (shelf-like slots cut for one body each, sealed with tiles or a marble slab). It looks like a filing cabinet for the dead.
Families who could pay more had cubicula (small private burial rooms) and arcosolia (arched niches over a tomb cut into the wall). These are the spaces that were painted.

The paintings are fresco (pigment brushed onto wet plaster so it bonds into the wall). Painters worked fast in the dark by lamplight, using thin red and green lines to divide walls and ceilings into panels like a Roman house.
Figures are small, sketchy and simplified, done with a few quick strokes. The painters cared about making the message clear, not about realistic bodies or deep space.
The Greek Chapel, named for its Greek inscriptions, has walls painted in Pompeian red with Old Testament scenes and a banquet scene nicknamed the Fractio Panis (‘breaking of the bread’).
function: Above all it was a cemetery. Roman law banned burial inside the city walls, so catacombs sit outside them along the main roads.
Christians believed the body would rise again at the end of time, so they preferred burial to cremation, which was common among Romans. Catacombs gave them cheap space for thousands of bodies.
Families came to hold funeral meals and anniversary gatherings for the dead, a Roman custom (the refrigerium) that the banquet scenes may reflect.
Myth trap: catacombs were not secret hiding places or ordinary churches. Authorities knew where they were. After persecution ended, they became pilgrimage sites honoring the martyrs buried in them.
content: The Good Shepherd stands for Christ, who calls himself the good shepherd in the Gospel of John. The image itself is borrowed from pagan art: the Greek ram-bearer figure and Roman country scenes of shepherds.

The orant (a figure praying with arms raised and palms open) in the room called the Velatio stands for the dead woman’s soul praying, or for salvation. Side scenes may show her marriage and her motherhood, though scholars debate them.

The Greek Chapel’s Old Testament rescue stories, such as Daniel in the lions’ den, Noah’s ark and three young Hebrews saved from a furnace, plus the raising of Lazarus, all say the same thing: God saves the faithful from death.
A painting of a woman holding a child next to a man pointing at a star is often called the earliest known Virgin and Child, probably third century. The man is probably a prophet, Balaam or Isaiah.
The banquet scene may show a funeral meal or the Eucharist (the Christian ritual meal of bread and wine). Scholars disagree.
context: Early Christians were a small, sometimes persecuted minority. Emperor Constantine legalized Christianity with the Edict of Milan in 313, so the catacomb’s use runs from before legalization to after it.
Tradition says the land belonged to a noblewoman named Priscilla, linked to the senatorial family of the Acilii, who allowed Christians to bury their dead there.
Several early popes and many martyrs were buried here, which earned it the nickname ‘queen of the catacombs.’
Burials stopped in the early 400s. The catacombs were gradually forgotten, then rediscovered and explored from the late 1500s on.
Jewish and pagan Romans also used catacombs, so the burial method was not uniquely Christian. What is new is the Christian meaning of the pictures.
The Vatican’s Pontifical Commission for Sacred Archaeology looks after it today. A 2013 laser cleaning removed grime and revealed much clearer details of the paintings. On the exam.
If asked about function → burial and remembrance of the dead, not hiding and not regular Sunday worship.

If asked about artistic traditions → Christian meanings poured into pagan Roman forms: the Good Shepherd comes from the ram-bearer, the orant from Roman figures of piety, the painting style from Roman houses like No. 39.
If asked why the paintings are so simple → small private patrons, cramped dark rooms and quick painters. The message mattered more than realism.
Date trap: c. 200–400 C.E. begins before the Edict of Milan (313). The big public churches like Santa Sabina (No. 49) come after it.
Vocabulary trio: loculi (wall slots), cubicula (family rooms), arcosolia (arched wall tombs). Material: tufa plus fresco.
Why burial and not cremation → belief in the resurrection of the body.

49.title: Santa Sabina
49.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
49.plain: Santa Sabina is one of the oldest churches in Rome that still looks much as it did when it was built, on the Aventine Hill in about 422–432 C.E., roughly a century after Christianity became legal. It shows the building type Christians chose for worship: not a pagan temple but a Roman basilica, a long meeting hall that could hold a crowd. Almost every large church in Western Europe descends from this plan.
49.spot: Inside: a long, bright nave lined with two rows of matching fluted white Corinthian columns carrying round arches, big windows high up, a flat wooden ceiling and a rounded apse at the far end. Outside: plain brown brick with no decoration.
49.remember: Santa Sabina is ‘simple outside, shiny inside’: a plain brick box with a light-filled colonnade. 420s C.E., 24 recycled columns, and a plan copied from a Roman courthouse (basilica), not a temple.
compare: No. 45 (§3.34), Forum of Trajan: The Basilica Ulpia in Trajan’s Forum is the kind of Roman civic hall that Christians adapted into the church plan.
No. 51 (§4.4), San Vitale: Longitudinal basilica versus central plan: two early Christian solutions to the shape of a church.
No. 60 (§4.13), Chartres Cathedral: Chartres keeps the basilica’s nave, aisles, clerestory and apse but replaces the wooden roof with stone rib vaults and the walls with stained glass.
No. 35 (§3.24), Acropolis: The Parthenon was designed to be seen from outside by a crowd standing around it, while Santa Sabina hides its splendor inside for the worshippers.
49.vocab: basilica, nave, aisle, apse, clerestory, spolia, narthex, opus sectile.

form: The plan is a basilica (a long rectangular hall with a tall central aisle, lower side aisles and a rounded end).
The tall central aisle is the nave (the main space where the congregation stands), and the rounded end is the apse (a semicircular recess), where the altar and clergy were.
Twenty-four fluted Corinthian marble columns are spolia (building parts reused from older structures), probably taken from a nearby pagan temple. Unusually for reused columns, they match.

Above the arcade is a clerestory (a row of windows in the upper wall). Its large arched windows flood the nave with even light. Their panes of thin selenite (a see-through mineral) are modern restorations of the original idea.
The roof is a simple wooden truss (a triangular frame of beams), light enough for thin walls. There is no stone vault.

The triangles between the arches carry opus sectile (designs made of cut colored marble pieces), and above the entrance a gold-on-blue mosaic inscription is flanked by two women representing the Church.
The main doors are carved cypress wood panels from the 400s with Bible scenes. Eighteen of the original 28 panels survive, including one of the earliest known images of the Crucifixion.
function: It is a church for congregational worship: the whole community gathers inside, and the long axis pulls everyone’s attention and processions from the door toward the altar.
This is the opposite of a Greek or Roman temple, where the public stayed outside and only priests entered the god’s room.

Since 1222 it has been the home church of the Dominican order, given to Saint Dominic by Pope Honorius III. It is still in use, and popes traditionally hold the Ash Wednesday service here to begin Lent.
content: The contrast of a plain outside and a glowing inside is often read as a metaphor: the real riches of the Church, and of the soul, are spiritual and hidden within.
Walking down the nave toward the apse acts out the Christian journey toward God and salvation.

The two women in the entrance mosaic personify the Church of converts from Judaism (Ecclesia ex circumcisione) and the Church of converts from the pagan world (Ecclesia ex gentibus): one united Church.
Saint Sabina was a Roman woman martyr. Tradition says the church stands over her house, but that is not proven.
context: The mosaic inscription names the founder, Peter of Illyria, a priest from the Balkans, building during the papacy of Celestine I (422–432).

After Constantine legalized Christianity in 313, Christians avoided the temple form, tied to pagan sacrifice, and adapted the Roman civic basilica, a hall for law courts and business like the Basilica Ulpia in the Forum of Trajan (No. 45).
In a Roman basilica the apse held the magistrate or the emperor’s statue. In the Christian version that place of authority passed to the bishop and the altar.
It was built less than a generation after the Visigoths sacked Rome in 410, when the Church was becoming the city’s most powerful institution.

Restorations in 1914–1919 and 1936–1937 by Antonio Muñoz removed later Baroque additions and returned it to an early Christian look, so part of what you see is a careful 20th-century reconstruction. On the exam.
If asked why a basilica and not a temple → it held a large congregation inside and carried no pagan religious associations.
Parts to label: narthex (entrance porch), nave, side aisles, arcade, clerestory, apse.
If asked about materials → spolia columns show both practical recycling and a claim to continue Roman grandeur.
Trap: Santa Sabina has a flat wooden roof, not a stone vault. Stone vaults come later, in Romanesque (No. 58) and Gothic (No. 60) churches.
Plan comparison: longitudinal basilica (Santa Sabina) versus central plan (San Vitale, No. 51) versus a mix of both (Hagia Sophia, No. 52).
If asked about the viewer’s experience → plain exterior, then a bright, rhythmic interior that leads the eye to the altar; the reverse of a Greek temple (No. 35) meant to be seen from outside.

50.title: Rebecca and Eliezer at the Well and Jacob Wrestling the Angel,
50.medium: Illuminated manuscript (tempera, gold, and silver on purple vellum)
50.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
50.plain: These are two painted pages from the Vienna Genesis, one of the oldest surviving illustrated Bibles, a luxury copy of the Book of Genesis made in the early 500s C.E. on parchment dyed purple and written in silver ink. Each picture tells its story like a comic strip, with the same people appearing several times in one frame. The book mixes Roman picture habits, like a nature spirit lounging by a spring, with Christian scripture.
50.spot: A dark purple page with lines of silver Greek letters across the top and small, brightly colored figures moving across the bottom half. The same people repeat along a winding road or bridge, and in one scene a half-nude woman reclines beside a stream.
50.remember: Vienna Genesis: purple page, silver ink, 500s, and it lives in Vienna. Rebecca passes the ‘water test’ for a husband; Jacob wins a wrestling match with an angel.
compare: No. 55 (§4.8), Lindisfarne Gospels: Both are sacred manuscripts, but the Vienna Genesis tells stories in lively figures while the Lindisfarne Gospels turns its pages into dense abstract ornament.
No. 59 (§4.12), Bayeux Tapestry: Both tell a story through continuous narrative, one in a small luxury book and one in a 230-foot embroidered strip.
No. 64 (§4.17), Golden Haggadah: Another illustrated narrative of the Hebrew Bible, made 800 years later for a Jewish family in Gothic style.
No. 45 (§3.34), Forum of Trajan: Trajan’s column also uses continuous narrative, repeating the emperor scene after scene, showing the Roman roots of the technique.
50.vocab: vellum, codex, illuminated manuscript, continuous narrative, personification, tempera.

form: Made of vellum (fine parchment from calfskin), dyed purple, a color linked to emperors. The text is in silver ink, now darkened by tarnish.
It is a codex (a book of bound pages), the format that was replacing the scroll in the late Roman world. Only 24 leaves survive, a fraction of the original book.
Pictures are painted in tempera (pigment mixed with a binder such as egg) with touches of gold, set in the lower half of each page under the Greek text.
Both pages use continuous narrative (several moments of a story shown in one picture, so the same character appears more than once).
Figures are small and lively, with quick highlights. They stand on a simple ground line with almost no background. A curving road or a bridge suggests space rather than true perspective.

In the Rebecca scene, a semi-nude woman leaning on an overturned water jar is a personification (a figure standing for an idea or a place), here the spring itself, borrowed straight from classical art.
Several painters seem to have worked on the book, since the style changes from page to page.
function: It is an illustrated copy of Genesis in Greek, from the Septuagint translation, made for a very rich owner, probably imperial or aristocratic.
The pictures helped readers follow and remember the stories, while the costly purple and silver made the book a treasure that displayed its owner’s wealth and piety.
It eventually reached the Habsburg imperial library in Vienna, which gave it its name. Today it is in the Austrian National Library.
content: Rebecca and Eliezer at the Well (Genesis 24): Abraham sends his servant Eliezer to find a wife for his son Isaac. Eliezer prays that the right woman will offer water to him and his camels, and Rebecca does exactly that.

In the picture, Rebecca leaves the walled city of Nahor with a jug on her shoulder, walks down a curving road to the spring, and then gives Eliezer a drink while his camels wait to drink. The reclining nymph marks the spring.

Jacob Wrestling the Angel (Genesis 32): Jacob sends his family across the river Jabbok, wrestles all night with a mysterious figure, shown as an angel, and receives a blessing and the new name Israel.
Jacob appears several times on one page: crossing a bridge with his family and flocks, wrestling the angel, and being blessed, laid out in two rows.
Christian readers often treated Old Testament stories as foreshadowing the New Testament, so both scenes about choosing and blessing could carry extra Christian meaning.
context: It is Early Byzantine, probably made in Syria (perhaps Antioch) or in Constantinople. Scholars are not sure where.
Imperial purple dye came from murex sea snails and was enormously expensive, though cheaper dyes may have been used on parchment. Either way, purple books were a top luxury.
It belongs to a small group of purple manuscripts from the 500s, such as the Rossano Gospels in southern Italy.
The mix of a pagan water nymph and Roman-style figures with Bible stories shows Christian artists still working inside the classical tradition.
The switch from scroll to codex suited Christians, whose scriptures were collected into books that could be opened to any page. On the exam.
If shown purple pages with silver writing → Vienna Genesis, Early Byzantine, early sixth century C.E.
If asked about narrative technique → continuous narrative: the same figure repeated within one frame, like Trajan’s column (No. 45) and the Bayeux Tapestry (No. 59).
Trap: it is Old Testament (Genesis), not a Gospel book, and its text is Greek, not Latin.
If asked about continuity with classical art → the reclining nymph who personifies the spring.
If asked about materials → purple-dyed vellum, silver ink, tempera and gold in a codex.
If asked about function → a luxury book for an elite patron, signaling wealth, status and devotion.

51.title: San Vitale
51.medium: Brick, marble, and stone veneer; mosaic
51.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
51.plain: San Vitale is an eight-sided church in Ravenna, Italy, finished around 547 C.E., whose apse is covered with gold mosaics of the Byzantine emperor Justinian and empress Theodora bringing gifts to the altar. It is the best place to see how Byzantine art turned rulers into holy, floating figures and fused church and state. Neither ruler ever visited Ravenna, so the mosaics stand in for them.
51.spot: Two mosaics facing each other on a gold ground: a row of stiff, frontal men with a haloed Justinian in purple at the center holding a gold bowl, and a row of women with Theodora in a towering jeweled crown holding a gold cup. Feet seem to float. The building is a squat brick octagon.
51.remember: Justinian and Theodora ‘phone in’ to Ravenna by mosaic: they never visited. San Vitale has eight sides, like a stop sign: stop and look at the gold. About 547 C.E.
compare: No. 52 (§4.5), Hagia Sophia: Both were built under Justinian in the 530s and 540s, one a central-plan octagon and one a domed basilica in the capital.
No. 49 (§4.2), Santa Sabina: Central plan versus longitudinal basilica: two early Christian church shapes with very different paths for the worshipper.
No. 185 (§8.5), Dome of the Rock: The Dome of the Rock also uses an octagonal central plan with an ambulatory and gold-ground mosaics, in an Islamic shrine.

No. 43 (§3.32), Augustus of Prima Porta: Both are imperial images meant to stand in for an absent ruler and project power, but Augustus is classical and lifelike while Justinian is flat and otherworldly.
51.vocab: central plan, ambulatory, mosaic, tesserae, exedra, impost block, martyrium, apse.

form: It has a central plan (a building organized around a central point rather than a long axis): an inner octagon of eight piers under a dome, wrapped by an ambulatory (a walkway circling the center) with a gallery above.
Between the piers, two-story exedrae (semicircular niches) bulge outward, so the space ripples. Only the chancel and apse on the east side break the circle.

The outside is plain brick. Inside, walls are veneered in colored marble and the chancel is covered in mosaic (pictures made of small cubes of glass or stone called tesserae), many backed with gold leaf.
Capitals are carved like deeply drilled lacy baskets and topped by impost blocks (wedgeshaped blocks that carry the weight of the arches down onto the columns).
The dome is light, built partly with interlocking hollow clay tubes, so the walls did not need heavy buttresses.
The figures are frontal, tall and slim, with almond eyes and tiny feet that overlap or point downward as if hovering. Robes are flat pattern with little sense of a body underneath.
Gold backgrounds remove any sense of a real place. The figures stand in a timeless, heavenly space.
function: It is a church dedicated to Saint Vitalis, an early martyr. Central plans were traditional for a martyrium (a building honoring a martyr’s tomb or relics).
The mosaics show the imperial couple joining the procession that brings bread and wine for the Eucharist, as if they were forever donating to this church.
Politically, it advertised Byzantine control of Ravenna, which Justinian’s army took from the Ostrogoths in 540 and which became the center of Byzantine rule in Italy.
content: Justinian panel: the haloed emperor in purple holds a gold paten (bowl) for the Eucharistic bread. Bishop Maximianus, the only figure named in the mosaic, stands to his left holding a jeweled cross.
Clergy stand on one side of Justinian and soldiers and oﬀicials on the other, so he appears as head of both church and state. A soldier’s shield carries the Chi-Rho, the monogram of Christ’s name.
Theodora panel: the empress holds a gold chalice (cup) for the Eucharistic wine. The hem of her robe shows the Three Magi bringing gifts to the infant Christ, linking her gift to theirs.
In Theodora’s panel an attendant lifts a curtain and a fountain plays, suggesting she is at a doorway about to enter. Her ladies’ patterned silks display court luxury.
Halos mark the rulers’ sacred authority, not sainthood. In the apse above, a young Christ seated on a globe hands a crown to Saint Vitalis, while Bishop Ecclesius offers a model of the church.
context: Building began around 526 under Bishop Ecclesius, while Ravenna was still ruled by the Ostrogoths. A wealthy banker, Julius Argentarius, paid for it, and Maximianus consecrated it around 547.
Justinian I (reigned 527–565) tried to win back the western Roman Empire. His general Belisarius captured Ravenna in 540, and the mosaics celebrate that new rule.
Theodora, a former actress who became a powerful empress and political partner, died in 548, very soon after the mosaics were finished.
Byzantine style turns away from classical realism toward flat, spiritual forms meant to suggest heaven rather than the physical world.
About 250 years later, Charlemagne admired San Vitale and modeled his Palatine Chapel at Aachen, in Germany, on its octagonal plan. On the exam.
If shown gold mosaics of an emperor and empress with attendants → San Vitale, Ravenna, Justinian and Theodora, c. 547 C.E.
If asked about church and state → Justinian holds the Eucharistic bread and stands between clergy and soldiers.
Attribution clues for Byzantine style: frontal, weightless, elongated figures, gold ground, almond eyes, the ruler at the center.
Trap: San Vitale is in Ravenna, not Constantinople, and the rulers never went there.
Plan comparison: central plan (San Vitale) versus basilica (No. 49) versus a combination (Hagia Sophia, No. 52).
Iconography trap: Theodora holds the chalice (wine) and Justinian the paten (bread), and the Magi on her robe signal royal gift-giving.

52.title: Hagia Sophia
52.artist: Anthemius of Tralles and Isidorus of Miletus; Constantinople (Istanbul)
52.medium: Brick and ceramic elements with stone and mosaic veneer
52.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
52.plain: Hagia Sophia is the enormous church of Holy Wisdom that Emperor Justinian built in Constantinople (now Istanbul) in about five years, 532–537 C.E. Its giant dome seems to float on a ring of light, an engineering feat that set the standard for domes for a thousand years. It has been a cathedral, a mosque, a museum and, since 2020, a mosque again, so one building carries the history of two religions.
52.spot: A massive shallow dome surrounded by cascading half-domes, with four slender pencilshaped minarets at the corners outside. Inside: a vast space, a ring of windows at the dome’s base, huge round green-and-gold discs with Arabic calligraphy, and arches resting on curved triangular supports.
52.remember: Hagia Sophia means ‘Holy Wisdom,’ and it took wise men to build it: two mathematicians, Anthemius and Isidorus, 532–537 C.E. Its dome floats on 40 windows and four pendentives.
compare: No. 46 (§3.35), Pantheon: Two record-setting domes: the Pantheon’s concrete dome sits on a round drum, while Hagia Sophia’s brick dome rides on pendentives over a square.
No. 84 (§4.37), Mosque of Selim II : Sinan’s Mosque of Selim II answers Hagia Sophia, using a dome on an octagon of piers to create a single open space.
No. 51 (§4.4), San Vitale: Both are Justinian projects of the same decades, a domed basilica in the capital and a central-plan octagon in Ravenna.
No. 185 (§8.5), Dome of the Rock: Both are domed sacred buildings tied to rival claims on a city, and both mix Byzantine techniques with Islamic use.
52.vocab: pendentive, dome, central plan, basilica, buttress, minaret, mihrab, exedra.

form: It combines a basilica (a long hall for processions, here running east to west) with a central plan (a huge dome over the middle).

The main dome is about 31 meters (roughly 102 feet) across and about 55 meters (180 feet) above the floor. It rests on four pendentives (curved triangles that turn a square base into a circle to hold the dome).
Forty windows ring the base of the dome. Light between the ribs makes the dome look detached, and the writer Procopius said it seemed hung from heaven on a golden chain.
Half-domes to the east and west and smaller exedrae (semicircular niches) step the weight down and stretch the space lengthwise. Huge buttress piers outside do the real structural work.
It is built of brick and mortar with thick mortar joints. Walls are sheathed in colored marble, and the vaults were once covered in gold mosaic.
Capitals are carved with drilled, lace-like leaves and the monograms of Justinian and Theodora.

Ottoman additions include four minarets (towers for the call to prayer), a mihrab (a niche showing the direction of Mecca) set slightly off the church’s axis, a pulpit, and giant calligraphy roundels.
function: It was built as the cathedral of Constantinople and the stage for imperial ceremonies, where the emperor and the patriarch (the city’s chief bishop) appeared together.
After the Ottoman conquest in 1453, Sultan Mehmed II made it the city’s main mosque. Figural mosaics were plastered over or hidden, not all destroyed.
In 1934 the secular Turkish Republic under Atatürk turned it into a museum. A court ruling and presidential decree made it a mosque again in 2020, though it stays open to visitors.
content: The name means Holy Wisdom, which in Christian theology refers to Christ as the Word of God. It is not named after a saint called Sophia.
Light is the main symbol: the dome stands for heaven, and light pouring in from above stands for God’s presence.
Surviving mosaics are mostly later, from the 800s to the 1200s, including the Virgin and Child in the apse and the Deësis, Christ between Mary and John the Baptist.
The eight calligraphy roundels name God, the Prophet Muhammad, the first four caliphs and Muhammad’s grandsons Hasan and Husayn.
context: Justinian rebuilt it after the Nika riots of 532 burned the previous church. He hired Anthemius of Tralles and Isidorus of Miletus, experts in geometry and mechanics rather than traditional builders.
Work began in February 532 and the church was dedicated in December 537. A later legend says Justinian exclaimed, ‘Solomon, I have outdone you.’
Earthquakes weakened the first, flatter dome, which collapsed in 558. Isidore the Younger rebuilt it about 6 meters (20 feet) higher by 562.
During Iconoclasm (726–843), when Byzantine emperors banned religious images, figural images were removed, which is why most surviving mosaics date after it.
The calligraphy roundels were added in the 1840s and 1850s, during a restoration by the Swiss Fossati brothers, not at the 1453 conversion. The minarets were added at various dates after 1453.
Ottoman architects studied it for a century. Sinan’s Mosque of Selim II (No. 84) set out to match and beat its dome. On the exam.
If asked how a round dome sits on a square base → pendentives. The Pantheon’s dome (No. 46) sits on a round drum instead.
If asked about the visual effect → the ring of 40 windows makes the dome seem to float, and light stands for the divine.
Patron: Justinian. Architects: Anthemius of Tralles and Isidorus of Miletus. Date: 532–537 C.E.
Plan: a longitudinal basilica merged with a central dome.
Change over time: church → mosque in 1453 (minarets, mihrab, later roundels) → museum in 1934 → mosque in 2020.
Trap: the minarets and calligraphy roundels are Ottoman additions, not original Byzantine features.

53.title: Merovingian looped fibulae
53.medium: Silver gilt worked in filigree, with inlays of garnets and other stones
53.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
53.plain: These are a matching pair of fancy cloak pins, each about 10 cm (4 inches) long, made by the Merovingian Franks in the mid-500s C.E. from gilded silver set with red garnets. They were worn as jewelry that showed off status and were buried with their owner, which is why they survived. They represent the art of the so-called Migration Period, when wealth and art had to be small enough to carry.
53.spot: A mirror-image pair of small metal brooches shaped like an ornate safety pin: a semicircular head edged with little knobs, a short arched bow and a long tapering foot, studded with flat red garnets set in gold cells, with hooked bird beaks curling from the edges.
53.remember: Fibula = fancy safety pin. The Franks were on the move, so their art moved with them: small, shiny and portable. Mid-500s, the same century as Justinian’s mosaics.
compare: No. 55 (§4.8), Lindisfarne Gospels: The Lindisfarne Gospels translates the same kind of metalwork interlace and animal ornament onto the painted page.
No. 196 (§9.5), Gold and jade crown: The Silla gold and jade crown is another dazzling precious-metal status object found in an elite burial.
No. 23 (§3.12), Tutankhamun’s tomb, innermost coﬀin: Tutankhamun’s coﬀin also uses gold and inlaid stones in cells, showing the ancient link between precious burial goods and status.
53.vocab: fibula, cloisonné, filigree, gilding, grave good, animal style, Migration Period.

form: Made of silver covered with a thin layer of gold, called silver gilt, so they look like solid gold for far less metal.
Filigree (fine twisted or beaded wire soldered onto the surface) creates the rope-like borders.
Red garnets and other stones are set in cloisonné (little cells made from thin metal strips, each holding a cut stone), so the stones form flat, glittering patterns.
Each brooch has a semicircular head ringed with loops or knobs, an arched bow, and a long flat foot. On the back, a pin and catch work like a modern safety pin.
Animals are built into the design: heads of eagles or other birds of prey with hooked beaks curve from the edges, and fish shapes run down the center of the foot.
Strict symmetry and dense surface pattern dominate. There is no interest in realistic space, and the pair are mirror images of each other.
function: They fastened clothing. Frankish women often wore such brooches in pairs, on the upper body or at the waist, as grave finds show.
They displayed wealth and rank: precious metal and imported garnets were visible signs of family status.
They were buried with their owner as grave goods (objects placed in a tomb with the dead), which is why they survive in such good condition.
They were portable wealth: they could be handed down, given as gifts or traded.
content: Birds of prey and fish may carry Christian meaning, since the fish was an early symbol of Christ and the Franks converted after King Clovis’s baptism around 500. They may also be traditional power animals from pre-Christian art. Scholars disagree.
The main message is not a story but wealth, skill and identity. The wearer’s status is literally pinned to her clothes.
The tight, interlocking animal forms are an early example of the animal style (ornament built from stylized, intertwined animal shapes) of early medieval northern Europe.
context: The Merovingians were the first royal dynasty of the Franks, a Germanic people who ruled much of what is now France, Belgium and western Germany from the late 400s to 751.
In the Migration Period (roughly 300–700 C.E.), peoples such as the Franks, Goths and Lombards moved into former Roman lands. Portable art made sense for groups whose wealth traveled with them.
Scientific tests suggest the garnets in Merovingian jewelry of this era came from as far away as India and Sri Lanka, evidence of long-distance trade.
The same garnet cloisonné style appears across Europe, from Frankish graves to the AngloSaxon ship burial at Sutton Hoo in England.
They are now in the National Archaeological Museum (Musée d’Archéologie nationale) at Saint-Germain-en-Laye, near Paris. On the exam.
If shown small jeweled metalwork with garnets set in cells → Migration Period, Merovingian Franks, mid-sixth century C.E.
If asked about materials and technique → silver gilt, filigree and cloisonné garnets.
If asked about function → clothing fastener and status symbol, later buried as grave goods.
If asked about artistic traditions → the animal style and dense pattern continue in Insular manuscripts like the Lindisfarne Gospels (No. 55).
Vocabulary trap: here a fibula is a brooch, not the leg bone.
If asked about mobile societies → they favor small, precious, portable objects over monumental buildings.

54.title: Virgin (Theotokos) and Child between Saints Theodore and George
54.date: Sixth or early seventh century C.E.
54.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
54.plain: This wooden panel, about 68.5 by 49.7 cm (27 by 19.5 inches), shows Mary holding the Christ Child on a throne, flanked by two soldier saints, with two angels behind. It is one of the few Byzantine icons to survive from before Iconoclasm, when emperors had religious images destroyed, because it was kept at a remote monastery in the Sinai desert. It shows how Byzantines used images as windows to the holy, and how they mixed lifelike and abstract styles in one picture.
54.spot: A small wooden panel: Mary seated on a jeweled throne with the Christ Child on her lap, her eyes glancing to the side; two stiff saints in long cloaks on either side, one bearded and one young; two angels behind looking up at a hand reaching down in a beam of light.
54.remember: Theotokos = ‘Theo’ (God) + ‘tokos’ (birth): God-bearer. Two soldier saints, Theodore (bearded) and George (young), guard her like bodyguards. Sinai saved it from the imagesmashers.
compare: No. 71 (§4.24), Madonna and Child with Two Angels: Lippi’s Renaissance Madonna and Child turns Mary into a real young woman in a window frame, the opposite of the Sinai icon’s formality.
No. 95 (§4.48), The Virgin of Guadalupe: Another Marian image believed to have special holy power, painted for devotion in colonial Mexico.
