No. 184 (§8.4), Jowo Rinpoche, enshrined in the Jokhang Temple: Jowo Rinpoche is also a holy image treated as a living presence and visited by pilgrims, in Tibetan Buddhism.
No. 51 (§4.4), San Vitale: San Vitale’s mosaics share the frontal, hieratic Byzantine style, but on a monumental church wall rather than a portable panel.
54.vocab: icon, encaustic, Theotokos, iconoclasm, hieratic, intercessor.

form: It is painted in encaustic (pigment mixed with hot wax, applied while warm), the same technique used for Roman-era mummy portraits in Egypt. Wax allows soft modeling of faces.
The picture uses different styles in three zones. The angels in back are loose and lifelike, turning their heads. Mary is gently shaded but formal. The saints are rigid, frontal and flattened.
The arrangement is hieratic (formal, rigid and sacred-looking): symmetrical, with Mary and Christ at the center and the most important figures largest.
Mary wears dark purple-blue robes and looks off to the side, not at the viewer. The saints stare straight out at us.
Each saint holds a small cross, a sign of martyrdom. Behind the angels is an architectural setting, and a beam of light from the hand of God falls toward Mary.
The panel is small enough to carry or to set up for prayer in a monastery chapel.
function: It is an icon (a sacred image of holy figures used in prayer). Byzantines believed an icon made the holy figures present and carried prayers to them.
Monks and pilgrims kissed icons, bowed before them and lit candles. Byzantine teaching held that the honor passed to the person shown, so the panel itself was venerated, not worshipped.
Mary acts as an intercessor (someone who pleads with God on your behalf), presenting Christ to the viewer, while the saints serve as protectors and models of faith.
content: Theotokos (Greek for ‘God-bearer’) is Mary’s title, made oﬀicial at the Council of Ephesus in 431: she gave birth to God made human.
The hand of God and the beam of light from above show divine approval of the Incarnation, God becoming human through Mary.
Saints Theodore and George were warrior martyrs. They guard the throne like palace guards, showing heaven organized like the Byzantine imperial court.
One common reading sees three levels of reality: airy, lifelike angels (heaven), Mary and Christ (the bridge between heaven and earth), and solid, stiff saints (holy humans on earth).
context: It is kept at Saint Catherine’s Monastery at the foot of Mount Sinai in Egypt, founded under Justinian in the mid-500s. It may have been painted in Constantinople and sent there.

During Iconoclasm (726–787 and 814–843), Byzantine emperors banned and destroyed religious images, fearing idolatry. Sinai had been under Muslim rule since the 630s, outside Byzantine control, so its icons survived.
When images were restored in 843, the Orthodox Church celebrated it as the ‘Triumph of Orthodoxy,’ still a feast day today.
The monastery holds about 2,000 icons, including some of the oldest in the world.
Encaustic links it to Roman painting. Later Byzantine icons mostly switched to egg tempera. On the exam.
If asked why it survived → it was in a remote monastery at Sinai, outside the emperor’s reach during Iconoclasm.
If asked about technique → encaustic on wood, continuing Roman portrait painting.
If asked about style → naturalistic angels and hieratic saints in one image, a Byzantine mix of classical and abstract.
Iconography: Theotokos = God-bearer. Theodore and George = soldier saints. Hand of God above.
If asked about function → an icon for devotion and intercession, not decoration.
Trap: it is not a mosaic (No. 51) or a fresco. It is portable wax paint on a wooden panel.

55.title: Lindisfarne Gospels: St. Matthew, cross-carpet page; St. Luke
55.medium: Illuminated manuscript (ink, pigments, and gold on vellum)
55.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
55.plain: The Lindisfarne Gospels is a hand-made book of the four Gospels created around 700 C.E. at the monastery on Lindisfarne, a small tidal island off the northeast coast of England. Its pages swarm with knotted bands, coiling animals and swelling letters, merging the patterns of Celtic and Anglo-Saxon metalwork with Mediterranean Christian book painting. It is the classic example of Insular (Hiberno-Saxon) art.
55.spot: A page packed edge to edge with tiny knots and twisting birds and dog-like animals around a cross; or a first word whose giant letters are outlined in thousands of red dots; or a seated evangelist with a halo and a winged animal overhead.
55.remember: Carpet page = a rug with a cross woven in. Luke’s giant first letter is outlined in over 10,000 red dots. Around 700 C.E., on an island, by Bishop Eadfrith.
compare: No. 53 (§4.6), Merovingian looped fibulae: The Merovingian fibulae show the metalwork interlace and animal style that the Lindisfarne artist transferred to the page.
No. 187 (§8.7), Folio from a Qur’an: Both treat sacred text as art, but the Qur’an folio relies on calligraphy alone while Lindisfarne adds figures and animal ornament.
No. 50 (§4.3), Rebecca and Eliezer at the Well and Jacob Wre…: Both are early sacred manuscripts, but the Vienna Genesis is a narrative picture book and Lindisfarne is mostly abstract ornament.
55.vocab: illuminated manuscript, vellum, carpet page, incipit page, interlace, Insular art, evangelist, colophon.

form: It is written and painted on vellum (calfskin parchment) with ink, pigments and a little gold. It has 259 leaves.

The cross-carpet page (a full page of ornament like a rug, built around a cross) that opens Matthew’s Gospel shows a cross filled and surrounded by interlace (woven, knotted bands), with birds and dog-like creatures biting one another.
The patterns were planned with compasses, rulers and grids. The backs of pages show prick marks and ruled lines, and the artist made early use of a lead point, an ancestor of the pencil.

The incipit page (the decorated opening words of a book) for Luke begins Quoniam quidem multi. A huge Q and other letters are filled with spirals and animals and outlined in thousands of tiny red dots.

The evangelist portrait (a picture of a Gospel author) of Saint Luke shows him seated, writing, with his symbol, a winged calf, overhead. It follows a Mediterranean model but flattens the figure into pattern.
Most pigments were probably made from local plant and mineral sources, such as indigo or woad for blue, rather than imported lapis lazuli.
The text is in Latin. In the 900s a word-by-word Old English translation was squeezed between the lines, the oldest surviving English version of the Gospels.
function: It is a Gospel book, used in the liturgy on the altar, especially on feast days, and kept as a sacred treasure honoring God and Saint Cuthbert, whose shrine was at Lindisfarne.
Making it was itself a form of prayer: years of copying and drawing were an act of devotion.
The hidden cross and endless knots reward slow, meditative looking, like a visual prayer.
content: The cross on the carpet page shows Christ’s victory, emerging out of a tangle of interlace, often read as order emerging from chaos.
Each Gospel has its evangelist symbol: Matthew a man or angel, Mark a lion, Luke an ox or calf, John an eagle.
Labels such as ‘O Agios Lucas’ (Saint Luke) use Greek words in Latin letters, showing the monks’ links to the wider Christian world.
Animal ornament inherited from pre-Christian metalwork now serves Christian scripture: old visual traditions converted along with the people.
context: The monastery was founded in 635 by Aidan, an Irish monk from Iona. Saint Cuthbert (died 687) became its most famous bishop, and pilgrims came to his shrine.

A colophon (a note at the end of a book about who made it), added in the 900s by the priest Aldred, says Eadfrith, Bishop of Lindisfarne (698–721), wrote it. Most scholars accept Eadfrith as the main scribe and artist.
Hiberno-Saxon or Insular art means the blend of Irish (Hiberno) and Anglo-Saxon styles made in the British Isles from about 600 to 900.
Vikings raided Lindisfarne in 793. The monks later left the island in 875, carrying Cuthbert’s body and their treasures, and eventually settled at Durham.
Its jeweled metal cover is lost. After Henry VIII closed the monasteries it passed to the collector Robert Cotton, and it is now in the British Library, London.
Some people in northeast England have long called for it to return there. It has been lent back for exhibitions in Durham and Newcastle. On the exam.
If shown dense interlace, knotted animals and red-dot outlines → Insular (Hiberno-Saxon), Lindisfarne Gospels, c. 700 C.E.
Know the three page types: carpet page, evangelist portrait, incipit page.
Maker: Eadfrith, Bishop of Lindisfarne, known through a later colophon by Aldred.
If asked about artistic traditions → Celtic and Anglo-Saxon metalwork patterns (like No. 53) merged with Mediterranean figure painting.
Trap: it is a Gospel book (New Testament), not Genesis (No. 50) or a moralized Bible (No. 61).
If asked about function → liturgy and devotion; the labor of making it was itself an offering to God.

56.title: Great Mosque
56.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
56.plain: The Great Mosque of Córdoba, in southern Spain, was begun in 785–786 C.E. by the Umayyad ruler Abd al-Rahman I and expanded over two centuries into a forest of more than 800 columns topped by striped double arches. It was the main mosque of Muslim Spain (al-Andalus). After the Christian conquest a cathedral was built right in its middle, so today it is both at once.
56.spot: Rows upon rows of short columns carrying two tiers of arches striped in red brick and cream stone, receding like a forest; or a small, jewel-like niche framed by a horseshoe arch covered in gold mosaic, under a dome of crisscrossing ribs.
56.remember: Córdoba has candy-cane arches: red and white stripes, stacked two high. 785, Abd al-Rahman I, the Umayyad prince who escaped to Spain.
compare: No. 20 (§3.9), Temple of Amun-Re and Hypostyle Hall: Both are hypostyle halls, but Karnak’s massive columns make a dark, exclusive temple while Córdoba’s slender ones make an open space for the whole community.
No. 168 (§7.2), Great Mosque of Djenné: The Great Mosque of Djenné is another congregational mosque, built of mud brick and adapted to a very different climate and building tradition.
No. 159 (§6.7), City of Cusco: At Cusco the Spanish built a church on top of the Inka Qorikancha, as Christians inserted a cathedral into Córdoba’s mosque: conquest written into architecture.
No. 185 (§8.5), Dome of the Rock: Both are Umayyad monuments using Byzantine-style gold mosaic and calligraphy to make the dynasty’s claims visible.
56.vocab: hypostyle hall, horseshoe arch, voussoir, spolia, mihrab, qibla, maqsura, kufic.

form: It is a hypostyle hall (a roof held up by many columns). There is no central focus, just repeating aisles that seem endless in every direction.
Many columns are spolia (reused parts) from Roman and Visigothic buildings. Because they were short and uneven, builders stacked a second tier of arches on top to gain height and light.

The lower arches are horseshoe arches (arches that curve inward before meeting their supports, a form also used by the Visigoths), and the upper ones are round. Both alternate red brick and white stone voussoirs (wedge-shaped blocks forming an arch).
In the 960s, al-Hakam II added a maqsura (a screened area for the ruler near the mihrab) with lobed, interlacing arches and domes on crisscrossing ribs.

The mihrab (a niche in the wall facing Mecca) is a small octagonal room behind a horseshoe arch covered in gold and colored glass mosaic and Qur’anic inscriptions in Kufic (an angular style of Arabic script). Its scalloped dome is carved marble.
A courtyard of orange trees with fountains for washing before prayer leads to the prayer hall. The old minaret is now encased inside the cathedral’s bell tower.
function: It was a congregational (Friday) mosque for the whole community. The open plan lets long rows of worshippers line up facing the qibla wall (the wall that faces Mecca).
Oddly, the qibla wall faces south rather than southeast toward Mecca, perhaps following the orientation of the Great Mosque of Damascus. Scholars debate why.
Since 1236, when King Ferdinand III of Castile captured Córdoba, it has been a Catholic cathedral. From 1523 a tall Renaissance cathedral nave and choir were built into its center.
Today it is a working cathedral and a major tourist site. Muslim prayer is not permitted there, which remains controversial.
content: The endless repetition of columns suggests infinity and makes every worshipper part of an equal community, without a single focus on a priest or altar.
The religious space avoids images of people and animals, a practice called aniconism. Decoration is geometry, plant patterns and calligraphy.
The striped arches may recall Roman aqueducts in Spain and the Umayyad mosque in Damascus, a visual claim to the dynasty’s homeland and heritage.

The mihrab’s mosaics were made with help from a craftsman and materials sent by the Byzantine emperor, linking Córdoba’s caliphs to imperial luxury and to earlier Umayyad mosaics like those of the Dome of the Rock (No. 185).
context: Abd al-Rahman I escaped when the Abbasids massacred his Umayyad family in 750. He fled to Spain and founded an independent emirate there in 756.

According to tradition the site held a Visigothic church of Saint Vincent. The mosque started small and grew in major expansions under Abd al-Rahman II, al-Hakam II and the minister al-Mansur in the 900s.
In 929 Abd al-Rahman III declared himself caliph, and Córdoba became one of the largest and most learned cities in Europe.
Emperor Charles V supposedly complained, on seeing the new cathedral, that they had destroyed something unique to build something found everywhere. The story may be legend.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984. The Church’s 2006 registration of the building as its property has been disputed by some activists and oﬀicials. On the exam.
If shown red-and-white striped double arches → Great Mosque of Córdoba, Umayyad Spain, begun 785–786 C.E.
If asked about plan → hypostyle: flexible, expandable and egalitarian prayer space.
If asked about engineering → spolia columns plus a second tier of arches to gain height.
If asked about the mihrab → marks the qibla (direction of prayer), decorated with Byzantinestyle mosaic and Kufic calligraphy.
Change over time: mosque → cathedral after 1236, with a cathedral nave inserted from 1523.
Trap: Umayyad Córdoba (700s–900s) is not the Nasrid Alhambra in Granada (No. 65), which is about 600 years later.

57.title: Pyxis of al-Mughira
57.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
57.plain: The Pyxis of al-Mughira is a small round ivory box with a domed lid, carved in 968 C.E. in the caliph’s workshops near Córdoba for al-Mughira, a young prince of the Umayyad family. Its deep carvings show court life, animal fights and men stealing eggs from birds’ nests. It proves that Islamic art was often full of people and animals when it was not made for a mosque, and it may carry a hidden political message.
57.spot: A small cylinder of creamy ivory with a domed lid, carved all over in deep relief: four eight-lobed medallions holding figures (seated men with a lute player, lions attacking bulls), a dense background of vines with birds and animals, and an Arabic inscription around the lid.
57.remember: Pyxis sounds like ‘pick-sis’: a lidded box. 968, a teen prince’s gift box that may hide a warning, and he was killed in 976 when he became a threat.
compare: No. 188 (§8.8), Basin: The Baptistère de St. Louis is another courtly Islamic luxury object crowded with human and animal figures.
No. 56 (§4.9), Great Mosque: Same city and dynasty: the mosque avoids figures in its religious space, while this palace object is full of them.
No. 53 (§4.6), Merovingian looped fibulae: Both are small, portable luxury objects whose main job was to signal the owner’s rank.
57.vocab: pyxis, ivory, relief, undercutting, kufic, secular, medallion.

form: It was carved from a section of elephant tusk into a hollow cylinder about 15 cm (6 inches) tall, with a domed lid.
The carving is deep relief (figures that project from a background), heavily undercut (cut behind the forms) so the figures stand out against dark shadows.
Four eight-lobed medallions divide the body. Between and around them, a dense background of vines, leaves, birds and small animals fills every gap.
An Arabic inscription in Kufic (an angular style of Arabic script) runs around the base of the lid.
Figures are compact and patterned rather than lifelike, and the design loves symmetry: paired animals, mirrored riders and balanced vines.
function: A pyxis (a small lidded cylindrical box) like this held luxury goods such as perfumes, musk, camphor or ambergris.
It was a gift to al-Mughira, probably to mark his coming of age at about 18.
Boxes like this were prestige gifts within the ruling family and court, showing off the skill of the caliph’s own workshops.
content: The inscription says, roughly, ‘God’s blessing, favors, joy and delight to al-Mughira, son of the Commander of the Faithful, may God have mercy on him, in the year 357’ (968 C.E.). The blessing for the dead shows his father, the caliph, had died.
One medallion shows a court scene: a seated figure holding a flask and a flower, a lute player and an attendant. It is a picture of princely pleasure and authority.
Lions attacking bulls are an ancient Near Eastern symbol of royal power and victory.

Other scenes show men picking dates and young men climbing to rob eagles’ or falcons’ nests. Some scholars read these as allegories of stealing legitimacy, a hint that al-Mughira was a rival for the throne. Others see ordinary princely pastimes.
context: The Umayyad caliphate of Córdoba (929–1031) was founded when Abd al-Rahman III declared himself caliph. His son al-Hakam II ruled from 961 to 976.
Al-Mughira was a younger son of Abd al-Rahman III and the younger brother of the reigning caliph al-Hakam II, not the son of the ruling caliph.
When al-Hakam II died in 976 and his young son Hisham II took the throne, court oﬀicials had al-Mughira killed to remove a rival claimant.
Ivory came by trade from sub-Saharan Africa. Workshops at the palace city of Madinat al-Zahra, outside Córdoba, carved many such boxes for the court.
It is now in the Louvre, Paris. Several Córdoban ivory boxes later ended up in Christian church treasuries, reused as containers for relics. On the exam.
If shown a carved ivory cylinder with an Arabic inscription and figures → Pyxis of al-Mughira, Umayyad Córdoba, 968 C.E.
Trap: Islamic art is not always free of figures. Figural imagery is common in secular (nonreligious) objects; aniconism applies mainly to religious spaces.
If asked about materials → ivory, a luxury import from Africa, carved in deep, undercut relief.
If asked about function → a container for perfume or cosmetics, given to mark coming of age.
If asked about content → courtly life, animal combat and a possible political allegory about succession, which scholars debate.
If asked about context → dynastic rivalry, ending with al-Mughira’s murder in 976.

58.title: Church of Sainte-Foy
58.date: Church c. 1050–1130 C.E.; reliquary ninth century C.E. with later additions
58.medium: Stone (architecture and tympanum); gold, silver, gemstones, and enamel over
58.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
58.plain: Sainte-Foy is a Romanesque abbey church in Conques, a hill village in southern France, built about 1050–1130 C.E. as a stop for pilgrims heading to Santiago de Compostela in Spain. Its doorway carries a Last Judgment carving that warned every visitor about heaven and hell, and its treasury holds a gold, gem-crusted statue containing relics of a girl martyr, Saint Foy (Saint Faith). Relics drew pilgrims, and pilgrims brought money.
58.spot: A stone church with a half-moon carving over the door, crowded with small figures: Christ in the center raising one hand and lowering the other, orderly heaven on the left and chaotic hell full of devils on the right. Or a stiff seated gold figure with a large, staring face, covered in gems.
58.remember: Foy means ‘Faith.’ Romanesque roads to Santiago, around 1100: barrel vaults, round arches, and a gold girl with a borrowed Roman head.
compare: No. 24 (§3.13), Last judgment of Hu-Nefer, from his tomb: Two judgment scenes 2,300 years apart: the Egyptian weighing of Hu-Nefer’s heart and the Christian weighing of souls both decide the afterlife.
No. 60 (§4.13), Chartres Cathedral: Romanesque versus Gothic: thick walls and barrel vaults at Conques versus rib vaults, flying buttresses and glass at Chartres.
No. 179 (§7.13), Reliquary figure: The Fang byeri is also a sculpted guardian tied to the bones of the honored dead, a different culture’s way of making relics powerful.
No. 184 (§8.4), Jowo Rinpoche, enshrined in the Jokhang Temple: Jowo Rinpoche is also a jeweled sacred image that draws pilgrims from far away.
58.vocab: Romanesque, tympanum, barrel vault, ambulatory, radiating chapels, reliquary, mandorla, pilgrimage church.

form: The Romanesque style (a Roman-like style of about 1000–1200) uses thick stone walls, small windows, round arches and a stone barrel vault (a half-cylinder ceiling) over the tall nave, which also reduced fire risk.

The pilgrimage plan is a cross-shaped basilica with a transept (the arm that crosses the nave), plus an ambulatory (a walkway curving around the apse) lined with radiating chapels, so crowds could pass the relics without disturbing services.
Galleries over the side aisles help hold up the vault and gave pilgrims extra space.

The west tympanum (the half-moon space above a doorway) shows the Last Judgment in stone relief with about 124 figures in horizontal bands with Latin inscriptions. It was originally painted, and traces of color remain.
The reliquary statue has a carved wooden core covered in gold and silver sheet, studded with gems, cameos and enamel added by donors over centuries. It is about 85 cm (33 inches) tall.
Its gold head is older than the body and may be a reused late Roman head, perhaps of a boy or an emperor, with a wide-eyed, fixed stare.
function: It was a monastery church that sheltered Saint Foy’s relics and served pilgrims on the route through France to the shrine of Saint James at Santiago de Compostela.
The statue is a reliquary (a container for holy remains). It holds part of the saint’s skull. Pilgrims believed she worked miracles, especially curing blindness and freeing prisoners.
Freed prisoners were said to leave their chains as thank-you offerings, and tradition says they were reforged into the iron grilles around the choir.
The tympanum taught a mostly illiterate public as they entered: repent, behave and give. Pilgrims on the Way of Saint James still stop here today.
content: Christ sits as judge inside a mandorla (an almond-shaped frame of light), raising his right hand toward the saved and lowering his left toward the damned.

On Christ’s right (our left), heaven is calm and orderly, with Abraham, Mary and saints. On his left (our right), devils torture sinners for specific sins such as greed and pride, shown with grim humor.
In a small scene, the archangel Michael and a devil compete over the scales that weigh souls.
Saint Foy herself bows before the hand of God, with prisoners’ chains hanging nearby, showing she can plead with God for pilgrims.
The gold and gems on the reliquary say her remains are more precious than any treasure, and each added jewel recorded a donor’s devotion.
context: Saint Foy was a young girl traditionally said to have been martyred around 303 at Agen, in southwest France, for refusing to sacrifice to pagan gods.
In the late 800s a monk from Conques stole her relics from Agen. Such ‘holy thefts’ (furta sacra) were justified as the saint’s own wish to move.
A pilgrimage economy drove building: relics attracted pilgrims, pilgrims brought donations, and donations paid for bigger churches. Churches competed for famous relics.
The reliquary’s core probably dates to the late ninth or tenth century, with additions continuing for centuries. Scholars debate its exact dates.
During the French Revolution, villagers hid the treasury to protect it from confiscation, which is why it survives. On the exam.
If shown a semicircular door carving of judgment with devils → Romanesque tympanum, Sainte-Foy, Conques.
If asked how the plan serves pilgrims → ambulatory, radiating chapels and transept let crowds circulate around relics.
Romanesque markers: barrel vaults, thick walls, small windows, round arches. Contrast Gothic Chartres (No. 60).
Reliquary of Sainte-Foy: gold, silver, gemstones and enamel over wood, possibly with a reused Roman head, holding a skull relic.
If asked about the tympanum’s function → a warning and lesson for pilgrims at the threshold of the church.
Trap: Conques is a stop on the way to Santiago, not Santiago itself.

59.title: Bayeux Tapestry
59.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
59.plain: The Bayeux Tapestry is a strip of linen about 70 meters (230 feet) long and 50 cm (20 inches) tall, embroidered in wool to tell the story of the Norman Conquest of England in 1066. It runs like a comic strip with Latin captions, from the English earl Harold’s oath to William of Normandy through the Battle of Hastings. It is propaganda for the winners and also the best picture we have of 11th-century life.
59.spot: A long horizontal band of stitched figures in a few earthy colors (tan, blue-green, red, yellow) on plain off-white linen: soldiers in chain mail, horses, ships with dragon heads, Latin words above, and narrow borders of animals and fables above and below.
59.remember: The ‘Tapestry’ is a fib: it’s embroidery. 1066: Harold swears, breaks his oath and loses at Hastings. Bishop Odo ordered it, English needles stitched it.
compare: No. 45 (§3.34), Forum of Trajan: Trajan’s column and the Bayeux Tapestry both tell a war of conquest in continuous narrative to glorify the winner.
No. 203 (§9.12), Night Attack on the Sanjô Palace: Night Attack on the Sanjô Palace is another long horizontal narrative of war, unrolled as a handscroll in Japan.
No. 16 (§3.5), Standard of Ur, from the Royal Tombs at Ur: The Standard of Ur also arranges war and feasting in horizontal bands to celebrate a ruler’s victory.
59.vocab: embroidery, tapestry, continuous narrative, couching, stem stitch, propaganda, register.

form: It is embroidery (designs stitched onto a finished cloth), not a tapestry (designs woven into the cloth on a loom).

Wool yarn in about ten colors is stitched onto nine joined linen panels, mostly with stem stitch for outlines and laid-and-couched work (long threads laid flat, then tacked down with small stitches) to fill shapes.
It uses continuous narrative (one scene flowing into the next) reading left to right, with trees or buildings dividing about 58 scenes.
Figures are flat and outlined, with no deep space. Horses come in odd colors, such as blue, so overlapping legs can be told apart.
Borders above and below hold animals and Aesop’s fables. During the battle they fill with dead soldiers being stripped of their chain mail.
The end is missing. It may once have shown William’s coronation.
function: It was probably commissioned by Bishop Odo of Bayeux, William’s half-brother, who appears prominently. It may have been made for the dedication of Bayeux Cathedral in 1077.
Hung around a large hall or a church nave, it told the story to viewers walking alongside it: captions for the literate, pictures for everyone.
It justifies William’s claim. In Norman eyes Harold broke a sacred oath, so the conquest was lawful and approved by God.
A 1476 inventory of Bayeux Cathedral records it being hung around the nave every year for a feast.
content: It opens with King Edward the Confessor sending Harold to Normandy, where Harold swears on holy relics to support William’s claim to the English throne.
When Edward dies in January 1066, Harold is crowned. Halley’s comet appears as an omen, and William builds a fleet and invades.
The First Meal after landing shows Odo blessing food at a curved table, echoing the Last Supper and giving the bishop a holy role.

The cavalry attack at the Battle of Hastings (October 14, 1066) shows Norman knights charging English foot soldiers. Harold dies, possibly the figure with an arrow in his eye, a detail that 19th-century restoration may have changed.
Odo appears in the battle holding a club, rallying young soldiers. Clergy were not supposed to shed blood with a blade.
context: The Norman Conquest transformed England: a French-speaking ruling class, new stone castles and cathedrals, and many French words entering English.
It was probably stitched in England, likely around Canterbury, by skilled Anglo-Saxon embroiderers. English embroidery was famous across Europe.
Napoleon displayed it in Paris in 1803–1804 to drum up support for his own planned invasion of England. In World War II, Nazi researchers studied it as Germanic heritage.
It is also a valuable record of 11th-century armor, ships, cooking and building.

It has been shown in a dedicated museum in Bayeux since 1983. A loan to the British Museum in London was announced for 2026–2027, which would be its first return to England in over 900 years, despite worries about its fragility. On the exam.
Technique trap: embroidery on linen, not a woven tapestry.
Dates: the conquest is 1066; the work was made c. 1066–1080.
Patron: Bishop Odo of Bayeux. Makers: probably English embroiderers.
If asked about message → Norman propaganda: Harold as oath-breaker, William as rightful king.
If asked about format → continuous narrative read left to right, like Trajan’s column (No. 45).
Key scenes to know: the cavalry attack and the First Meal (a Last Supper echo).

60.title: Chartres Cathedral
60.date: Original construction c. 1145–1155 C.E.; reconstructed c. 1194–1220 C.E.
60.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
60.plain: Chartres Cathedral, the cathedral of Our Lady in Chartres, France, was mostly rebuilt in about 1194–1220 C.E. after a fire and is the textbook example of High Gothic architecture. Pointed arches, ribbed stone vaults and flying buttresses let its walls turn into huge windows of colored glass, so the inside glows deep blue and red. It was built to house a famous relic, a tunic said to have belonged to the Virgin Mary.
60.spot: A west front with three doors and two mismatched spires: a plain one on the right and a taller, lacy one on the left. Tall, stiff column-statues of kings and queens stand beside the doors. Inside, a tall nave of pointed arches and walls of deep blue stained glass; outside, arched flying buttresses line the sides.
60.remember: Chartres charted the Gothic rules: pointed arch, rib vault, flying buttress, stained glass. The 1194 fire spared Mary’s tunic, taken as a sign to rebuild bigger.
compare: No. 58 (§4.11), Church of Sainte-Foy: Romanesque versus Gothic: the dark, heavy barrelvaulted pilgrimage church versus the tall, glass-filled cathedral.
No. 112 (§5.14), Palace of Westminster: The Palace of Westminster revives Gothic pointed arches and tracery in the 1800s as a symbol of English national identity.
No. 20 (§3.9), Temple of Amun-Re and Hypostyle Hall: Both use a clerestory to bring light high into a sacred space, at Karnak through stone grilles and at Chartres through stained glass.
No. 61 (§4.14), Dedication Page with Blanche of Castile and K…: The Bible moralisée’s stacked roundels imitate the medallion layout of Gothic windows like those at Chartres.
60.vocab: Gothic, pointed arch, rib vault, flying buttress, stained glass, triforium, jamb figure, rose window.

form: Two Gothic tools shape the inside: pointed arches (which send weight more steeply downward than round arches) and rib vaults (stone ceilings framed by crossing ribs).
A third works outside: flying buttresses (arched supports standing away from the wall) brace the walls against the outward push of the vaults.

Because the buttresses carry the load, the walls could open into stained glass (pieces of colored glass held together by lead strips). Chartres keeps more than 150 windows, most with their original 13th-century glass.

The nave wall has three levels: an arcade, a narrow triforium (a passage in the wall above the arcade), and a tall clerestory of paired pointed windows topped by small round windows. The vault rises about 37 meters (121 feet).

The Royal Portal on the west facade (c. 1145–1155) survived the fire. Its jamb figures (statues attached to the columns beside a doorway) of Old Testament kings, queens and prophets are tall, stiff and column-like.
Huge rose windows (round windows with petal-like stone tracery) fill the west front and both transept ends.
The Notre Dame de la Belle Verrière window places a 12th-century Virgin and Child, saved from the fire, inside 13th-century glass with angels.
function: It is a cathedral (the main church of a bishop) dedicated to the Virgin Mary and a pilgrimage center for the Sancta Camisa, a tunic believed to be Mary’s, given to Chartres in 876 by King Charles the Bald.
Fairs held on the feasts of the Virgin brought crowds and money to the town, tying the economy to the relic.
The windows taught Bible stories and saints’ lives to viewers who could not read. It is still an active cathedral.
content: Colored light was understood as divine light, the lux nova (‘new light’) associated with Abbot Suger, who rebuilt the abbey church of Saint-Denis near Paris in the 1140s.
In the Belle Verrière, Mary is Queen of Heaven and the ‘Throne of Wisdom’ holding Christ on her lap, with the dove of the Holy Spirit above.
The Old Testament figures on the Royal Portal literally hold up the church, a way of saying the Old Testament supports the New.
Above the Royal Portal’s central door, Christ in Majesty sits among the symbols of the four evangelists, with the Virgin and Child over the right door and the Ascension over the left.
Donor scenes at the bottom of many windows show the guilds who paid for them, such as bakers, butchers and wine merchants, at work.
context: A fire in June 1194 destroyed most of the earlier cathedral. The tunic survived in the crypt, and the clergy presented this as Mary’s wish for a grander church.
Money came from the clergy, nobles, the French crown and town guilds. The main rebuilding took only about 25 years, so the style is unusually unified.
The plan is a Latin cross with an ambulatory and radiating chapels, inherited from Romanesque pilgrimage churches like Sainte-Foy (No. 58).
Gothic began around Paris in the 1140s, at Saint-Denis. Chartres is called High Gothic, the mature phase.
The south spire (right) dates to the 1100s. The taller, more ornate north spire (left) was built in 1507–1513, which is why they do not match.

A restoration begun in 2009 repainted the interior a pale cream to match its 13th-century appearance, and some critics called it a disfigurement. It has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979. On the exam.
Gothic trio: pointed arches, rib vaults and flying buttresses → thinner walls and far more glass.
If asked about change over time → the stiff Royal Portal jamb figures (c. 1145–1155) versus freer, more lifelike figures on the later transept portals.
Dates: original construction c. 1145–1155; rebuilt c. 1194–1220 C.E.
Relic: the Sancta Camisa. Dedication: the Virgin Mary.
If asked about the meaning of the glass → light as a sign of the divine (lux nova).
Trap: Chartres is Gothic. Sainte-Foy (No. 58) is Romanesque, with barrel vaults and thick walls.

61.title: Dedication Page with Blanche of Castile and King Louis IX of
61.medium: Illuminated manuscript (ink, tempera, and gold leaf on vellum)
61.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
61.plain: These are pages from a luxury picture Bible made in Paris about 1225–1245 C.E. for the French royal family. One page shows the queen mother, Blanche of Castile, and her son, the young King Louis IX, with a cleric and an artist below making the very book. The other pages pair Bible scenes with moral lessons in rows of circles that look like stained-glass windows.
61.spot: A gold-ground page divided into four compartments under small arches: a crowned woman and a young crowned king seated at the top, a cleric and a scribe working on a page of circles below. Or a page of eight small circles in two columns with narrow strips of text beside them, like a stained-glass window.
61.remember: Mom Blanche teaches Louis IX (the future Saint Louis) with a ‘moralized’ Bible: Bible scene plus moral lesson. Paris, 1220s–40s, gold leaf and roundels.
compare: No. 60 (§4.13), Chartres Cathedral: The roundels and deep blues imitate Chartres-style stained-glass windows, bringing the cathedral’s look onto the page.
No. 64 (§4.17), Golden Haggadah: Both are Gothic illuminated manuscripts with gold grounds, one for a Christian king and one for a Jewish family’s Passover.
No. 55 (§4.8), Lindisfarne Gospels: Both are sacred books made by teams of skilled makers, but the Lindisfarne Gospels is monastic and abstract while the Bible moralisée is courtly and narrative.
61.vocab: illuminated manuscript, roundel, gold leaf, trefoil, regent, Gothic.

form: Ink, tempera (pigment in egg binder) and gold leaf on vellum. The gold backgrounds are burnished (rubbed smooth) so they shine.
The dedication page sets four figures in four compartments under trefoil (three-lobed) arches topped by little towers and rooftops, like a miniature Gothic building.
The text pages hold eight roundels (circular picture frames) in two columns, each paired with a short text. The layout imitates stained-glass windows like those at Chartres (No. 60).
Figures are slender and elegant, with small heads, slight swaying poses and crisp folds of drapery, the refined Gothic court style of Paris.
Deep blue and red dominate, again echoing stained glass.
Each moralized Bible needed teams of professional artists. Paris was becoming Europe’s center of commercial book production, with workshops run by lay craftsmen as well as clergy.
function: A Bible moralisée (‘moralized Bible’) pairs a Bible scene with a second scene that explains its moral or Christian meaning.
It was made to educate and guide the young king in Christian kingship, a royal luxury book for the family’s private use.
Complete moralized Bibles held thousands of roundels, making them among the most expensive and labor-intensive books of their time.
content: Top: Blanche of Castile, regent and queen mother, gestures toward Louis IX, enthroned with a scepter. She instructs him, and the picture gives her authority equal to his.
Bottom left: a cleric, probably a monk or theologian, explains the text. Bottom right: a lay illuminator (a painter of manuscripts) works on a page laid out in paired roundels, the book in progress.
The page mirrors medieval society: royals on top, the religious adviser and the craftsman below.
The Apocalypse pages illustrate visions from the Book of Revelation, such as angels, the Lamb and the end of the world, each with a moral lesson about sin and salvation.
context: Louis IX became king in 1226 at age 12. Blanche ruled as regent (someone governing for a child ruler) until about 1234 and remained powerful afterward.
Blanche, a princess of Castile in Spain and granddaughter of Eleanor of Aquitaine, was one of the most powerful women in medieval Europe and oversaw Louis’s strict religious education.
Louis grew famously pious. He built the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris (1240s) to house the Crown of Thorns, led two crusades, died on crusade in 1270, and was made a saint in 1297.
The dedication page is now in the Morgan Library and Museum in New York, part of a fragment of a moralized Bible whose other parts are elsewhere.
The image of a cleric and an artist at work is a rare medieval picture of how a book was made, giving visible status to the craft. On the exam.
If shown a page of stacked roundels on gold → Gothic Bible moralisée, Paris, c. 1225–1245 C.E.
Dedication page: Blanche of Castile and Louis IX above; a cleric and a scribe-illuminator below.
If asked about function → teach a young king moral lessons by pairing Bible scenes with their interpretations.
If asked about links to architecture → the roundels resemble stained glass and the arches resemble cathedral architecture.
If asked about patronage → royal, and a striking example of a powerful female patron and regent.
Trap: this is a Christian French royal manuscript. The Golden Haggadah (No. 64) is a Jewish manuscript from Catalonia in a similar Gothic style.

62.title: Röttgen Pietà
62.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
62.plain: The Röttgen Pietà is a painted wooden sculpture, about 88 cm (34.5 inches) tall, made in Germany about 1300–1325 C.E., of the Virgin Mary holding her dead son across her lap. It is deliberately ugly: Christ is a stiff, starved figure with huge, bloody wounds, and Mary’s face is twisted with grief. It was made for private prayer, to make viewers feel pain and pity rather than admire a beautiful body.
62.spot: A small painted wooden group: a heavy, grieving Mary seated with a thin, rigid, shrunken Christ across her knees, his head tipped back, ribs showing, and wounds bulging out in red, grapelike clusters.
62.remember: Röttgen sounds like ‘rotten’: a raw, ruined body on purpose. Pietà means ‘pity.’ German, early 1300s, painted wood. Feel the pain.
compare: No. 63 (§4.16), Arena: Giotto’s Lamentation shows the same mourning over Christ’s body, but with calm, weighty naturalism and a crowd of mourners.
No. 77 (§4.30), Isenheim altarpiece: The Isenheim altarpiece also shows a horribly wounded Christ to help viewers who were suffering identify with him.
No. 78 (§4.31), Entombment of Christ: Pontormo’s Entombment treats the dead Christ with grace and elegance, the opposite emotional strategy.

form: It is carved from wood and painted, or polychrome (in several colors), with red blood standing out against pale skin.

A Pietà (Italian for ‘pity’) is a sculpture of Mary holding the dead Christ. In German it is a Vesperbild (‘vespers image’), tied to the evening prayers of Good Friday, when Christ was taken down from the cross.
Christ is shrunken, almost child-sized next to Mary, as if he were a baby on her lap. His body is stiff and angular, with ribs and veins standing out.
The wounds in his side, hands and feet are carved as raised, grape-like clusters of blood.
Mary’s face is contorted with sorrow. Her body is bulky and block-like under heavy drapery.
It is expressive rather than naturalistic or idealized: the anatomy is wrong on purpose to show emotion.
function: It is an Andachtsbild (German for ‘devotional image’): an image for private, emotional prayer that focuses on a single moment for the viewer to meditate on.
It was probably used in a convent or by devout lay people. The viewer was meant to put themselves in Mary’s place, feel her grief, and be moved to repentance.
Its modest size invites close, personal viewing rather than display to a crowd.
content: Mary holding the dead Christ echoes Mary holding the baby Jesus, joining his birth and his death in one image.
The grape-like clusters of blood may refer to the Eucharist, Christ’s blood shared as wine.
The exaggerated suffering shows how much Christ endured for humanity’s sins, so the viewer feels guilt, gratitude and compassion.
Mary appears as the Mater Dolorosa (Mother of Sorrows), a model for the viewer’s own grief.
context: It was made in the Rhineland region of Germany. It is named after a later owner, the collector Ludwig Röttgen, and is now in the Rheinisches Landesmuseum in Bonn.
It belongs to late medieval mysticism and emotional devotion, strong among nuns and lay religious women, which encouraged people to identify personally with Christ’s suffering.
Times were hard: the Great Famine of 1315–1317 struck northern Europe. The Black Death came later, in 1347–1351, so the Pietà predates the plague.
The German Pietà type spread across Europe. Michelangelo’s marble Pietà in Rome (1498– 1499) reverses the approach with a calm, beautiful, idealized Christ.
Painted wood was lighter and cheaper than stone, suitable for small chapels and convents. On the exam.
If shown a painted wooden Pietà with a gaunt, bloody Christ → Röttgen Pietà, German, c. 1300–1325 C.E.
If asked about function → an Andachtsbild for private devotion, meant to stir emotion, not tell a story.
If asked about style → expressive distortion: emotion over beauty or accuracy.
Trap: it predates the Black Death (1347), so do not say it responds to the plague.
If asked about artistic traditions → it rejects the idealized classical body seen in works like the Doryphoros (No. 34).
Material: painted (polychrome) wood.

63.title: Arena (Scrovegni) Chapel, including Lamentation
63.artist: Giotto di Bondone (artist); unknown architect; Padua, Italy
63.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
63.plain: The Arena Chapel is a plain brick chapel in Padua, Italy, whose inside walls Giotto covered with frescoes around 1305, telling the stories of the Virgin Mary and Christ in tidy rows. Its most famous scene, the Lamentation, shows Christ’s followers mourning over his body with real weight and real grief. Giotto’s solid, emotional figures are why he is often called the starting point of Renaissance painting.
63.spot: A fresco with a bright blue sky, a sharp rocky ridge running diagonally down to the left with a bare tree on top, Mary cradling Christ’s head at the lower left, two hooded mourners seen from behind in the foreground, and small angels wailing in the sky.
63.remember: Giotto’s ‘Arena’ stands on the site of a real Roman arena. A Padua chapel paid for to clean up Daddy Scrovegni’s moneylending. Blue vault, painted c. 1305.
compare: No. 62 (§4.15), Röttgen Pietà: Both mourn the dead Christ, but the Röttgen Pietà distorts the body for shock while Giotto uses believable weight and gesture.

No. 75 (§4.28), Sistine Chapel ceiling and altar wall frescoes: Another chapel transformed by a single painter’s fresco cycle, from Giotto’s narrative tiers to Michelangelo’s ceiling and Last Judgment.
No. 78 (§4.31), Entombment of Christ: Pontormo’s Entombment shows Christ’s body mourned two centuries later, trading Giotto’s solid weight for Mannerist weightlessness.
No. 51 (§4.4), San Vitale: The flat, frontal, gold-ground Byzantine figures of San Vitale are the tradition Giotto moved away from.
63.vocab: fresco, buon fresco, giornata, grisaille, barrel vault, Lamentation, usury.

form: The building is a simple rectangular brick box with a barrel vault (a half-cylinder ceiling) painted deep blue with gold stars. The outside is plain.

The walls are painted in buon fresco (pigment applied to wet plaster, so the color binds into the wall) in sections called giornate (each a ‘day’s work’ of fresh plaster). Some details added on dry plaster have flaked away.
Three tiers of narrative scenes wrap the walls: the story of Mary’s parents, Joachim and Anna, the Life of the Virgin, and the Life and Passion of Christ, read in order.
At the bottom, grisaille (painting in shades of gray to imitate stone sculpture) figures of seven Virtues face seven Vices across the room.
A huge Last Judgment covers the entrance wall. In it, Enrico Scrovegni kneels and offers a model of the chapel to the Virgin.
In the Lamentation, a diagonal rock leads the eye down to the faces of Mary and Christ. Figures are bulky and three-dimensional, overlapping in a shallow, stage-like space.
Mourners seen from behind block part of our view, which pulls us into the scene as if we were in the crowd.
function: It was a private chapel next to the Scrovegni family palace, dedicated to the Virgin of Charity (Santa Maria della Carità) and consecrated on March 25, 1305, the feast of the Annunciation.
It was probably meant partly as atonement for usury (lending money at interest), which the Church condemned and by which the family had grown rich.
It also displayed the family’s wealth and status in Padua. Nearby Augustinian friars complained in 1305 that it was too grand for a private chapel.
content: In the Lamentation, Mary holds Christ’s head, Mary Magdalene holds his feet, and John the Evangelist flings his arms back in grief.
The bare tree on the ridge may refer to the Tree of Knowledge, which legend said withered after Adam’s sin and supplied the wood for the cross. Christ’s death promises new life.
Angels twist and wail in the sky: grief reaches even heaven.
The Virtues line the wall on Christ’s right in the Last Judgment, the side of heaven, and the Vices the wall on his left, the side of hell.
context: Enrico’s father, Reginaldo Scrovegni, was a notorious moneylender whom the poet Dante placed among the usurers in hell in his Inferno.
The chapel stands on the site of an ancient Roman arena, which gave it its name. The architect is unknown.
Giotto di Bondone (about 1267–1337) came from Florence. Dante wrote that Giotto’s fame had eclipsed his teacher Cimabue’s.
Giotto broke with the flat Byzantine ‘Greek manner’ by giving figures weight, natural settings and readable emotions.

Since 2000, visitors pass through a climate-controlled airlock and stay only about 15 minutes to protect the paintings. It joined UNESCO’s list with Padua’s other 14th-century fresco cycles in 2021. On the exam.
Artist: Giotto. Patron: Enrico Scrovegni. Dates: chapel c. 1303, frescoes c. 1305. Place: Padua.
If asked about technique → buon fresco painted in giornate.
If asked about the Lamentation → diagonal rock, figures seen from behind, weight and emotion, wailing angels.
If asked about artistic traditions → a break from Byzantine flatness (compare No. 51) toward Renaissance naturalism and emotion.
If asked about motive → atonement for usury, with the Dante connection.
Trap: Giotto is the painter. The architect is unknown.

64.title: Golden Haggadah (The Plagues of Egypt, Scenes of Liberation, and Preparation for Passover)
64.medium: Illuminated manuscript (pigments and gold leaf on vellum)
64.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
64.plain: The Golden Haggadah is a Jewish book for the Passover meal, made in Catalonia, Spain, probably near Barcelona, around 1320 C.E., with full-page pictures painted on shining gold backgrounds. The pictures tell stories from Genesis and Exodus and show a Jewish household preparing for Passover. It shows Jewish patrons using the fashionable Gothic style of Christian manuscripts for their own sacred text.
64.spot: A page divided into four small scenes on gold backgrounds stamped with tiny patterns, with slender Gothic figures in medieval Spanish clothing; the scenes are read starting at the top right.
64.remember: Golden Haggadah: gold for the Seder. Catalonia, around 1320, Gothic look, Jewish text, read right to left.
compare: No. 61 (§4.14), Dedication Page with Blanche of Castile and K…: Both are Gothic manuscripts with gold grounds and slender swaying figures, made for a Christian king and a Jewish family respectively.
No. 50 (§4.3), Rebecca and Eliezer at the Well and Jacob Wre…: Both illustrate stories of the Hebrew Bible in luxury books, 800 years apart.
No. 187 (§8.7), Folio from a Qur’an: Both are sacred books of a religious community, but the Qur’an folio relies on calligraphy alone while the Haggadah adds narrative pictures.
64.vocab: Haggadah, seder, illuminated manuscript, gold leaf, tooling, Sephardi, miniature.

form: Pigments and gold leaf on vellum. The gold grounds are tooled (pressed with small punches to make patterns), so they glitter.
It has fourteen full-page miniatures, each split into four framed panels, for 56 scenes in all, placed before the Hebrew text.
The scenes read right to left, like Hebrew: top right, top left, bottom right, bottom left.
Figures are slim, elegant and swaying, in the French Gothic court style, with small heads and bright robes. Settings are minimal: a building, a tree, a band of waves.
Scholars distinguish two main artists by their different styles.
function: A Haggadah (Hebrew for ‘telling’) is the text read at the Seder, the ritual Passover meal that retells the Exodus from Egypt and explains its customs.
This was a luxury book for a wealthy Jewish family’s home Seder. The pictures helped engage children, who are supposed to ask questions during the meal.
An inscription records that a later owner in Italy gave it as a wedding gift in 1602.
It is used at home, not in a synagogue.
content: The Plagues of Egypt: God’s ten plagues, such as frogs, lice and hail, punish Pharaoh for refusing to free the Israelites.
Scenes of Liberation: the Israelites leave Egypt and Pharaoh’s army drowns in the Red Sea. The cycle includes Miriam and other women celebrating with music and dance.

Preparation for Passover: scenes include the head of the household handing out matzah (unleavened bread) and haroset (a sweet fruit paste) and the house and dishes being cleaned of leaven for the holiday.
Biblical figures wear 14th-century Spanish clothes, linking the ancient liberation to the family’s own lives.
God is not shown in human form, in keeping with Jewish tradition.
context: It was made in Catalonia, under Christian kings, where Jews were a protected but restricted minority. Coexistence was real but fragile.
The artists are unknown. They may have been Christian or Jewish, but either way they worked in the same Gothic style as Christian manuscripts.
Violence grew: the anti-Jewish riots of 1391 devastated Spain’s Jewish communities, and in 1492 Ferdinand and Isabella expelled all Jews who refused to convert.
The book probably left Spain with exiles. It was in Italy by 1602 and is now in the British Library, London.
Its name comes from its gold backgrounds. Sephardic (Spanish Jewish) families produced several luxury Haggadot in this period. On the exam.
If shown a Gothic-style manuscript with gold grounds and Hebrew → Golden Haggadah, Catalonia, c. 1320 C.E.
If asked about function → read at the Passover Seder in the home.
If asked how to read it → right to left, like Hebrew.
If asked about style → Gothic, like Christian manuscripts (No. 61), showing cultural exchange between communities.
If asked about context → Sephardic Jews in Christian Spain, before the 1391 riots and the 1492 expulsion.
Trap: it is a bound book (codex) for home ritual, not a Torah scroll.

65.title: Alhambra
65.medium: Whitewashed adobe stucco, wood, tile, paint, and gilding
65.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
65.plain: The Alhambra is a hilltop palace-fortress in Granada, southern Spain, built mostly in the 1300s by the Nasrids, the last Muslim dynasty to rule in Spain. The required parts, the Court of the Lions and the Hall of the Sisters, were built in 1354–1391 under Sultan Muhammad V. Their rooms are covered in lacy carved plaster, tile and poetry, arranged around water and gardens to suggest paradise.
65.spot: An arcaded courtyard of thin white columns, single and paired, carrying lace-like carved arches, with a fountain on twelve stone lions at the center; or a domed ceiling that looks like a honeycomb or hanging stalactites made of thousands of small cells.
65.remember: Alhambra = ‘al-Hamra,’ the Red One. Nasrid, 1354–1391, under Muhammad V. Lions in the court, Sisters under the honeycomb.
compare: No. 56 (§4.9), Great Mosque: Two Islamic monuments in Spain six centuries apart: an Umayyad congregational mosque and a Nasrid palace.
No. 209 (§9.18), Taj Mahal: The Taj Mahal also uses a four-part paradise garden with water channels to evoke the gardens of paradise.
No. 186 (§8.6), Great Mosque: The Great Mosque of Isfahan uses muqarnas too, there on a monumental scale in its iwans.
No. 93 (§4.46), The Palace at Versailles: Versailles is another royal palace built to display power, but through vast axial gardens and gold rather than intimate courtyards.
65.vocab: muqarnas, stucco, arabesque, calligraphy, charbagh, courtyard.

form: Outside are plain reddish fortress walls and towers. Inside are delicate, light-filled courtyards, the opposite of the exterior.
Cheap materials are made precious: stucco (carved or molded plaster) over brick and rammed earth, whitewashed and once painted, plus carved wooden ceilings and glazed tile along the lower walls.
The Court of the Lions is a rectangular courtyard ringed by 124 slender marble columns, with a fountain on twelve stone lions in the center and four water channels dividing the court into quarters.
The Hall of the Sisters, named for two large marble slabs in its floor, is topped by an octagonal dome of muqarnas (small nested, honeycomb-like cells that break up a vault), some 5,000 of them.
Windows at the dome’s base let shifting light play across the cells, so the ceiling seems to dissolve and turn.
Walls carry dense arabesque (endless curling plant patterns), geometric star patterns and calligraphy (artistic writing).
function: It was the royal palace, government center and fortified city of the Nasrid sultans. The Palace of the Lions was a private, ceremonial residence.
Halls opening onto courtyards were used for receptions, poetry, music and leisure.
After 1492, Christian kings used it as a royal residence. Emperor Charles V began a Renaissance palace inside the grounds in 1527.
content: The four-part court with four water channels recalls the chahar bagh (a four-part paradise garden), echoing the four rivers of paradise in the Qur’an.
The muqarnas dome stands for the dome of heaven. A poem by Ibn Zamrak on the walls of the Hall of the Sisters compares the room to the heavens and boasts that the stars envy it.
The Nasrid motto, wa la ghalib illa Allah (‘there is no victor but God’), is repeated across the walls.
Lions carrying the fountain symbolize power. Their origin is debated: some scholars once thought they were reused from an 11th-century palace, but most now date them to the 1300s.
Water, light and pattern together suggest an earthly paradise and the ruler’s abundance.
context: The Nasrids ruled the Emirate of Granada from the 1230s to 1492, often paying tribute to the Christian kingdom of Castile to survive.
Granada surrendered to Ferdinand and Isabella on January 2, 1492, ending Muslim rule in Spain.
Ibn Zamrak (1333–1393) was a court poet and minister. His verses on the walls let the building ‘speak’ about itself.
Washington Irving’s Tales of the Alhambra (1832) made it famous with Romantic travelers. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1984 and is one of Spain’s most visited sites.
Its tile and plaster patterns inspired the Dutch artist M. C. Escher after his visits in 1922 and 1936. On the exam.
If shown a honeycomb ceiling with Arabic script and slender columns → Alhambra, Nasrid, Granada, 1354–1391 C.E.
Key terms: muqarnas, stucco, arabesque, calligraphy, chahar bagh.
If asked about function → a palace (secular), not a mosque, with poetry that describes the architecture itself.
If asked about meaning → paradise imagery built from water, gardens and light.
If asked about form → plain exterior versus richly decorated interior.
Trap: Nasrid Granada (1300s) is not Umayyad Córdoba (No. 56, 700s–900s).

66.title: Annunciation Triptych (Merode Altarpiece)
66.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
66.plain: The Annunciation Triptych is a small three-panel oil painting from Flanders (now Belgium), made about 1427–1432 C.E. in the workshop of Robert Campin. It sets the Annunciation, when the angel Gabriel tells Mary she will bear Christ, in an ordinary middle-class living room, where almost every household object doubles as a religious symbol. It was a private altarpiece for a family’s home, and it shows the new power of oil paint to capture small, real details.
66.spot: Three hinged panels: on the left, a kneeling couple outside an open door in a garden; in the center, Mary reading on the floor beside a bench while an angel kneels, with lilies in a jug and a brass pot hanging in a niche; on the right, Joseph the carpenter at work, with mousetraps on his bench and in his shop window.
66.remember: Merode: Mary’s room, oil details everywhere. Campin’s workshop, around 1430. Joseph builds mousetraps to catch the devil.
compare: No. 68 (§4.21), The Arnolfini Portrait: Both are Flemish oil paintings of domestic rooms packed with symbolic objects and precise detail.
No. 92 (§4.45), Woman Holding a Balance: Vermeer’s Woman Holding a Balance also sets a quiet spiritual message inside an ordinary Dutch room.
No. 71 (§4.24), Madonna and Child with Two Angels: Lippi’s Madonna also brings holy figures into a contemporary, human setting, but in the Italian style with a landscape view.
66.vocab: triptych, altarpiece, oil paint, disguised symbolism, Annunciation, donor.

form: It is a triptych (a picture in three hinged panels), small enough for a home. The center panel is roughly 64 cm (25 inches) square.
It uses oil paint in thin glazes (transparent layers of color), which allow rich, glowing color and tiny details: wood grain, gleaming brass, the folds of Mary’s robe.
The perspective is steep and inconsistent. The floor and table tilt up toward us as if the room were sliding forward. It is based on observation, not mathematical one-point perspective.
Light comes from several directions, with careful shadows cast by objects.
Drapery falls in crisp, angular folds, and figures are heavy and sculptural.
Through Joseph’s window and the garden gate on the left, we glimpse a busy Flemish town.
function: It is a private devotional altarpiece (a painting set on or behind an altar) for a home rather than a church, letting a merchant family pray at home.
The donors kneel in the left wing. Coats of arms in the window suggest the Inghelbrecht family of Mechelen. The wife may have been added later, perhaps after a marriage.
It later belonged to the Belgian noble Merode family, hence the name. The Metropolitan Museum bought it in 1956 for The Cloisters in New York.
content: In the center, a tiny Christ child carrying a cross flies toward Mary on rays of light through the round window: the moment of the Incarnation, God becoming human.
Lilies stand for Mary’s purity, the hanging basin and towel for cleansing, and the just-snuffed candle perhaps for divine light replacing earthly light. Scholars debate the candle.
Mary sits on the floor as a sign of humility, reading, as she traditionally was when Gabriel arrived.
Joseph makes mousetraps: Saint Augustine called the cross the devil’s mousetrap, with Christ’s human body as the bait.
Hiding holy meanings in everyday objects is called disguised symbolism, a term coined by the art historian Erwin Panofsky.
context: It belongs to the Northern Renaissance in the Burgundian Netherlands, where rich trading cities like Tournai, Bruges and Mechelen created demand for private paintings.
Robert Campin (about 1375–1444) was the leading painter of Tournai and is often identified with the ‘Master of Flémalle.’ Rogier van der Weyden probably trained in his workshop.
Oil paint was not invented here, but Flemish painters like Campin and Jan van Eyck developed its glazing techniques to a new level.
A movement called the devotio moderna encouraged personal, everyday religion, which suited private altarpieces like this.
The setting reflects new middle-class patrons who wanted to see their own homes in sacred stories. On the exam.
If shown a Flemish room full of objects with an angel and Mary → Merode Altarpiece, workshop of Robert Campin, 1427–1432 C.E.
Medium: oil on wood, built up in glazes for detail.
Disguised symbolism: lilies, candle, basin and towel, mousetraps.
If asked about function → private devotion in a home, with donors in the left wing.
If asked about space → intuitive, tilted perspective, not Italian one-point perspective.
Attribution trap: ‘workshop of Robert Campin,’ not Jan van Eyck.

67.title: Pazzi Chapel
67.artist: Filippo Brunelleschi (architect); Santa Croce, Florence, Italy
67.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
67.plain: The Pazzi Chapel is a small chapter house, a meeting room for friars, in the cloister of the church of Santa Croce in Florence, designed by Filippo Brunelleschi and built in about 1429–1461 C.E. Gray stone lines on white walls make its simple geometry as easy to read as a diagram. It is a model of Early Renaissance architecture: classical forms, mathematical proportion and calm order.
67.spot: Inside: white plaster walls marked out by dark gray stone pilasters, arches and moldings, a ribbed dome over a ring of round windows, and blue-and-white glazed terracotta roundels. Outside: a porch of six Corinthian columns with an attic level above.
67.remember: Pazzi = perfect proportions by Brunelleschi: gray lines on white like graph paper. c. 1429–1461, Florence.
compare: No. 46 (§3.35), Pantheon: The Pantheon’s dome, oculus and classical orders were the Roman models Brunelleschi studied and revived.
No. 70 (§4.23), Palazzo Rucellai: Both are Early Renaissance Florentine buildings for wealthy families, one a chapel by Brunelleschi and one a house by Alberti.
No. 52 (§4.5), Hagia Sophia: Both set a dome on pendentives, but Hagia Sophia aims for overwhelming mystery while the Pazzi Chapel aims for clarity.
No. 88 (§4.41), San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane: Borromini’s San Carlo turns Renaissance clarity into Baroque movement, with undulating walls and complex geometry.
67.vocab: pietra serena, pilaster, pendentive, module, chapter house, lantern, entablature.

form: It is a rectangular hall with a central dome on pendentives (curved triangles that turn a square into a circle for the dome), flanked by short barrel-vaulted arms, plus a small square altar chapel with its own dome.
Pietra serena (a gray Tuscan sandstone) forms the pilasters (flat columns attached to a wall), arches and moldings against white plaster, as if drawing the geometry on the walls.
The design uses a module (a basic unit of measurement repeated throughout) and simple ratios, so all the parts relate to one another.
The vocabulary is classical: Corinthian pilasters, round arches and an entablature (the horizontal band above columns), all revived from Roman architecture.
The ribbed dome has small round windows at its base and a lantern (a small open structure on top of a dome that lets in light).
Glazed terracotta roundels of the Twelve Apostles are by Luca della Robbia. The four Evangelists in the pendentives are colorful too, but whose design they are is debated.
Stone benches line the walls, where the friars sat.
function: It is a chapter house (a room where friars met each day to hear a chapter of their rule, discuss business and confess faults) for the Franciscan friars of Santa Croce.
It was also a family chapel and burial place for the Pazzi, earning the banking family prestige and prayers for their souls.
It is dedicated to Saint Andrew, the patron saint of Andrea de’ Pazzi, and a della Robbia roundel of Saint Andrew hangs over the door.
content: The geometry stands for divine order. Renaissance thinkers believed that perfect proportions reflected the harmony of God’s creation.
Apostles and Evangelists, the founders of the Church and the authors of the Gospels, surround the friars as they meet.
Classical forms connected Christian Florence with ancient Rome, presenting the city as Rome’s cultural heir.
context: Filippo Brunelleschi (1377–1446) designed the dome of Florence Cathedral and demonstrated linear perspective. He died in 1446, long before the chapel was finished.
The patron, Andrea de’ Pazzi, headed a banking family that rivaled the Medici.

In the Pazzi Conspiracy of 1478, Pazzi family members murdered Giuliano de’ Medici in the cathedral during Mass and wounded Lorenzo. The plot failed, the family was crushed, and parts of the chapel may have been left unfinished as a result.
Humanism, the revival of classical learning and confidence in human reason, drove architects to study Roman ruins and the ancient writer Vitruvius.
Documents are sparse, so scholars debate how much of the final building, especially the porch and dome, follows Brunelleschi’s own design. On the exam.
If shown gray stone lines on white walls → Brunelleschi, Early Renaissance Florence.
Key terms: pietra serena, pilaster, pendentive, module, Corinthian order.
If asked about function → chapter house for Franciscan friars, and a Pazzi family chapel.
If asked about artistic traditions → revival of Roman forms (compare the Pantheon, No. 46).
If asked about the Renaissance ideal → rational, mathematical proportion as a reflection of divine harmony.
Trap: like Hagia Sophia (No. 52) it uses pendentives, but at a small scale and with a clear, legible system.

68.title: The Arnolfini Portrait
68.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
68.plain: The Arnolfini Portrait is a small oil painting of 1434 by Jan van Eyck showing a wealthy Italian merchant and a woman, usually called his wife, standing in their room in Bruges. Its detail is almost microscopic, and a round mirror on the back wall reflects two more people in the doorway. Nobody agrees exactly what it records: a marriage, an engagement, a memorial, or simply a status portrait.
68.spot: A couple holding hands in a bedroom: the man in a huge black hat and a fur-trimmed purple tunic, the woman in a full green dress lifted in front; a brass chandelier with one lit candle, a round convex mirror on the back wall, a small dog at their feet and wooden clogs on the floor.
68.remember: ‘Jan van Eyck was here, 1434,’ he wrote over the mirror like graﬀiti. Arnolfini = a rich Italian merchant in Bruges. Oil, 1434, one candle, one dog, one mirror.
compare: No. 66 (§4.19), Annunciation Triptych: Both are Flemish oil paintings of interiors packed with symbolic objects and painstaking detail.
No. 91 (§4.44), Las Meninas: Both use a mirror on the back wall to reflect figures outside the picture and insert the artist into the scene.
No. 80 (§4.33), Venus of Urbino: Titian’s Venus of Urbino is another domestic interior with a dog and possible marriage symbolism, in Venetian oil painting.
68.vocab: oil paint, convex mirror, Northern Renaissance, panel, Symbolism.

form: It is oil on an oak panel, about 82 by 60 cm (32 by 24 inches), built up in thin glazes (transparent layers of oil paint) that give glowing color and touchable textures.
The detail is extreme: individual dog hairs, fur linings, reflections on the brass chandelier and the beads of a rosary hanging on the wall.
Light from the window on the left gently models the faces and fabrics and casts soft shadows.
The convex mirror (a mirror that bulges outward) on the back wall reflects the room in reverse and two figures in the doorway. Its frame holds ten tiny scenes of Christ’s Passion.
The perspective is worked out by eye, with several vanishing points, so the floor tilts slightly.
Above the mirror, an elegant Latin signature, like a legal document, reads Johannes de eyck fuit hic 1434 (‘Jan van Eyck was here 1434’).
function: It records the couple’s status and wealth. It may also commemorate a marriage or betrothal, or, in one theory, memorialize a wife who had died.
It was a luxury object for a private home. Later it belonged to Habsburg rulers, first Margaret of Austria and later the Spanish royal collection.
It reached Britain in the early 1800s, and the National Gallery in London bought it in 1842.
content: The single burning candle in daylight may signal God’s presence, a marriage candle, or a candle lit for someone who has died. Scholars disagree.
The dog suggests fidelity and also wealth, since lap dogs were costly. The removed shoes may mark holy ground, as with Moses at the burning bush, or simply a domestic custom.
Oranges on the windowsill were expensive imports, signs of wealth and perhaps of innocence before the Fall.
The woman’s held-up green dress is fashion, and she is probably not pregnant. A carved saint on the bedpost may be Saint Margaret, patron of childbirth.
context: Jan van Eyck (about 1390–1441) was court painter to Duke Philip the Good of Burgundy. He did not invent oil paint, as a later legend claimed, but he mastered its glazes.

The sitters were long identified as Giovanni di Arrigo Arnolfini and Giovanna Cenami, but they married in 1447, after van Eyck’s death. Most scholars now favor Giovanni di Nicolao Arnolfini, a merchant from Lucca.
Giovanni di Nicolao’s first wife, Costanza Trenta, may already have died by 1434, which supports the memorial theory.
Bruges was a hub of international trade where Italian merchants and bankers lived, and the painting advertises cosmopolitan wealth.
In 1934 Erwin Panofsky argued that it was a kind of marriage certificate, with van Eyck as witness. Many scholars now reject that reading. On the exam.
Artist, date and medium: Jan van Eyck, 1434, oil on wood.
Northern Renaissance hallmarks: oil glazes, minute detail, symbolism in everyday objects.
If asked about the mirror → it shows two figures in the doorway, one probably the artist (compare Las Meninas, No. 91).
If asked about the signature → ‘Johannes de eyck fuit hic 1434,’ possibly a witness’s statement.
Trap: the woman is probably not pregnant; the full skirt is fashion.
Trap: van Eyck did not invent oil painting.

69.title: David
69.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
69.plain: Donatello’s David is a bronze statue of the young biblical hero David standing on the severed head of the giant Goliath, made sometime around 1440–1460 C.E. for the Medici family palace in Florence. It is usually called the first freestanding nude male statue made in Europe since ancient times. It was also political: little David beating a giant was Florence’s favorite image of itself.
69.spot: A slim, soft-bodied nude boy in bronze, wearing only a brimmed hat wreathed with laurel and knee-high boots, one hand on his hip and the other holding a large sword, with one foot on a bearded severed head whose helmet wing runs up his leg.
69.remember: Donatello’s David is the first freestanding bronze nude since Rome. Medici courtyard, 1440s–60s. Little David = little Florence, and the giants are Milan and anyone else.
compare: No. 34 (§3.23), Doryphoros: The Doryphoros is the classical model of contrapposto and the idealized nude that Donatello revived.
No. 43 (§3.32), Augustus of Prima Porta: Both use an idealized body to carry political meaning, the Augustus for imperial Rome and the David for republican Florence.
No. 74 (§4.27), Adam and Eve: Dürer’s Adam and Eve also revives classical ideal bodies in the Renaissance, in Northern Europe and in print.
69.vocab: contrapposto, lost-wax casting, bronze, in the round, nude, humanism.

form: It was cast in bronze by the lost-wax method (a wax model is covered in clay, the wax is melted out, and molten metal is poured into the gap), then finished by hand. It stands about 158 cm (5 feet 2 inches) tall.
David stands in contrapposto (weight on one leg, so the hips and shoulders tilt in opposite directions), borrowed from Greek and Roman statues like the Doryphoros (No. 34).
His body is adolescent, smooth and slender rather than muscular. His head is bowed under the shadow of the hat, as if thinking rather than celebrating.
He wears only a pointed shepherd’s hat topped with a laurel wreath and ornate boots, and holds a stone in his left hand.
Goliath’s head lies under David’s foot, and a long wing from Goliath’s helmet rises up David’s inner leg. The helmet’s visor shows a small relief of winged children pulling a triumphal chariot.
It was meant to be seen in the round (from all sides), on a column in a courtyard.
function: It was made for the courtyard of the Palazzo Medici in Florence, where it stood on a column by 1469 and greeted guests as they entered.
It presented the Medici as protectors of Florence and as patrons of classical culture.
After the Medici were expelled in 1494, the city moved it to the Palazzo della Signoria, the town hall, as a civic symbol. It is now in the Bargello Museum in Florence.
content: In the story (1 Samuel 17), the shepherd boy David kills the giant Philistine Goliath with a stone from his sling, then cuts off his head with Goliath’s own sword.
David = Florence: a small republic defeating bigger tyrants, especially the dukes of Milan.
A lost inscription on the base reportedly urged citizens to defend their homeland, noting that even a boy can overcome a great tyrant.
The laurel stands for victory and possibly puns on the name of Lorenzo de’ Medici (‘laurel’ is lauro in Italian).
The sensual body and the feather running up the leg have led some scholars to see homoerotic meaning. Others read it as a classical ideal of youthful beauty. The debate continues.
context: Donatello (about 1386–1466) was a Florentine sculptor who studied Roman ruins with Brunelleschi and led Early Renaissance sculpture.
No document dates it. Guesses run from the 1430s to the 1460s, which is why the oﬀicial date is a wide range.
The patron was probably Cosimo de’ Medici, the banker who effectively ran Florence.
It revived the classical nude after roughly a thousand years in which nude figures in art were mostly limited to Adam and Eve or the damned.
Florence collected Davids: Donatello’s earlier marble David (1408–1409), Verrocchio’s bronze (1470s) and Michelangelo’s marble giant (1501–1504). On the exam.
Artist, date and medium: Donatello, c. 1440–1460 C.E., bronze.
If asked why it matters → usually called the first freestanding nude male sculpture since antiquity.
If asked about style → contrapposto and the revival of the classical nude.
Patron and location: the Medici, for the courtyard of their palace.
If asked about political meaning → David = Florence, the small republic beating bigger enemies.
Trap: this is not Michelangelo’s marble David (1501–1504), which is not on the required list.

70.title: Palazzo Rucellai
70.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
70.plain: The Palazzo Rucellai is the town house of the rich Florentine merchant Giovanni Rucellai, whose front was designed around 1450 by the humanist architect and writer Leon Battista Alberti. Alberti covered the facade with a grid of flat classical pilasters stacked in three stories, an idea taken from the Colosseum. It is probably the first Renaissance house front to wear the stacked orders of ancient Rome.
70.spot: A flat, three-story stone facade divided into a neat grid by thin flat pilasters and horizontal bands, with paired arched windows in each bay, a heavy projecting cornice on top, and diamond-pattern stonework behind a stone bench at street level.
70.remember: Alberti put the Colosseum on a house: stacked orders like a layered cake. Rucellai = rich merchant, c. 1450.
compare: No. 44 (§3.33), Colosseum: The Colosseum’s stacked Tuscan, Ionic and Corinthian orders are the direct source of Alberti’s three-story grid.
No. 67 (§4.20), Pazzi Chapel: Both are Early Renaissance Florence: Brunelleschi’s interior geometry in gray stone and Alberti’s classical street facade.
No. 102 (§5.4), Monticello: Jefferson’s Monticello also dresses a private home in classical architecture to present its owner as learned and virtuous.
70.vocab: pilaster, superimposed orders, entablature, rustication, ashlar masonry, cornice, opus reticulatum, palazzo.

form: Three stories are separated by horizontal entablatures (bands of beam-like moldings) and divided vertically by flat pilasters (flat columns attached to a wall), making a grid of bays.
