It uses superimposed orders (different column types stacked story by story): a Tuscanstyle order at the bottom, a variant order Alberti invented in the middle, and Corinthian at the top, following the Colosseum (No. 44).

The walls are smooth ashlar (squared stone) with lightly cut joint lines. This shallow, even rustication (stonework with emphasized joints) is far flatter than the rough blocks of the nearby Palazzo Medici.
Some joint lines are cut for visual effect and do not match the real edges of the stones, so the ‘blocks’ are partly an illusion.
The upper floors have paired arched windows divided by a small column, set under round arches.
The ground floor has small square windows set high up and a stone bench along the base, backed by diamond-patterned stonework imitating ancient Roman opus reticulatum (netpattern masonry).
The right edge is ragged and unfinished, because the family never acquired the neighboring property needed to extend it.
function: It was the home and business headquarters of the Rucellai family, who were wool-cloth merchants and bankers.
The facade advertised the family’s wealth, learning and classical taste to everyone on the street.

The street-level bench offered a public seat for visitors and clients, linking the family to its neighborhood. The family loggia (an open arcade) across the little square hosted weddings and celebrations.
content: Classical orders signal learning and civic virtue: the merchant presents himself as a modern Roman.

The frieze shows the Rucellai emblem, a billowing sail of Fortune, and the Medici emblem, a diamond ring with feathers, celebrating the 1466 marriage of Giovanni’s son Bernardo to Nannina de’ Medici, Lorenzo the Magnificent’s sister.
The grid of proportions expresses order and rational control, key Renaissance values.
context: Leon Battista Alberti (1404–1472) was a humanist, architect and theorist who wrote On Painting (1435) and On the Art of Building (about 1452), based on the Roman writer Vitruvius.
Alberti probably designed the facade, and the builder was probably Bernardo Rossellino. Work began around 1450 and continued for years, and some scholars debate how much is Alberti’s own.
Giovanni Rucellai also hired Alberti for the marble facade of the church of Santa Maria Novella.

The nearby Palazzo Medici by Michelozzo (begun 1444) uses rustication that changes from rough to smooth as it rises, with no classical orders. Alberti’s facade is more intellectual and less fortress-like.
The design became a model for later Renaissance palaces in Italy and beyond. On the exam.
Architect, date and place: Leon Battista Alberti, c. 1450 C.E., Florence.
If asked about sources → superimposed orders taken from the Colosseum (No. 44) and applied to a private house.
If asked about structure → the pilasters are decoration, not support: the classical system is a skin over a conventional Florentine house.
If asked about humanism → the architect as intellectual and author, reviving Vitruvius.
Patron: Giovanni Rucellai, merchant-banker. The frieze records a marriage alliance with the Medici.
Trap: Brunelleschi designed the Pazzi Chapel (No. 67); Alberti designed the Palazzo Rucellai.

71.title: Madonna and Child with Two Angels
71.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
71.plain: A small panel painting of Mary praying while two angels hold up the baby Jesus, made in Florence around 1465 by the friar-painter Fra Filippo Lippi. It matters because it makes the holy family look like real, fashionable Florentines: Mary could be a young woman from a wealthy local household, and one angel grins at you like a kid caught misbehaving. It shows the Early Renaissance pulling religious art down to earth.
71.spot: Mary in near-profile with hands pressed together in prayer, wearing a pearl headdress and see-through veil, seated in front of a window that frames a rocky landscape with water. At lower right, two angels lift a chubby baby toward her, and one of them smirks straight out at the viewer.
71.remember: Lippi’s ‘lippy’ angel: the cheeky one grinning at you is the signature touch of Filippo Lippi, the friar who ran off with a nun and painted this about ten years later, c. 1465.
compare: No. 54 (§4.7), Virgin: Both show Mary and the Christ child, but the Byzantine icon is flat, frontal and otherworldly while Lippi’s Mary is a believable Florentine woman.
No. 72 (§4.25), Birth of Venus: Botticelli, Lippi’s pupil, carried the same graceful line and pale idealized beauty into a secular mythological subject.
No. 66 (§4.19), Annunciation Triptych: Both bring sacred figures into a domestic setting with a view or window, one Flemish in oil and one Florentine in tempera.
71.vocab: tempera, atmospheric perspective, Andachtsbild, Madonna, humanism, line.

form: Tempera (pigment mixed with egg yolk, which dries fast and matte) on a wooden panel, about 95 by 63 cm, so colors are clear and pale and built up in fine strokes rather than blended.
Lippi is known for delicate line: the transparent veil, the pearls braided into Mary’s hair and the crisp edge of her profile. His pupil Botticelli (No. 72) inherited this linear grace.
The window acts like a picture within the picture. The landscape uses atmospheric perspective (distant things paler, bluer and hazier) as rocks and water fade into the distance.
The painted window frame and the angels overlapping its edge set up a shallow, believable space very close to the viewer, like a scene happening just behind a ledge.
Figures are rounded with soft shading, but nothing is dramatic. The mood is calm, sweet and intimate rather than solemn.
function: A private devotional image (a picture you pray in front of), sized for a home rather than a church altar.
The original owner is not documented. It belonged to Florentine collections and is now in the Uﬀizi Gallery, Florence.
Its human warmth invited personal, emotional prayer: you relate to Mary as a mother before you remember she is the Queen of Heaven.
content: Mary prays to her own child, recognizing him as God, while the baby reaches toward her. Tender family moment and theology in one image.
Only thin, transparent golden halos mark the figures as holy. Without them, this could pass for a portrait of a rich Florentine mother.
Pearls were a traditional symbol of Mary’s purity, but here they also read as fashionable jewelry, mixing sacred and worldly beauty.
The grinning angel acts as a go-between, breaking the fourth wall and inviting the viewer into the scene.
context: Fra Filippo Lippi (c. 1406 to 1469) was a Carmelite friar and one of Florence’s leading painters, supported by the Medici family.
Around 1456, while working in Prato, he ran off with Lucrezia Buti, a young nun. Their son Filippino Lippi also became a painter. Tradition says she modeled for his Madonnas, but that is unproven.
Lippi taught Sandro Botticelli, who later trained Filippino. That makes this panel the start of a teacher-to-student chain worth knowing.
Early Renaissance humanism showed the sacred through the beautiful and everyday. The window landscape also reflects Florentine interest in Flemish painting (compare No. 66 and No. 68). On the exam.
If asked to attribute: delicate line, a pretty, fashionable Madonna and a window landscape point to Fra Filippo Lippi, Florence, c. 1465.
Medium trap: it is tempera on wood, not oil on canvas.
If asked to compare with the Byzantine icon (No. 54): the icon’s Mary is frontal, gold-backed and otherworldly; Lippi’s is a real woman in a room with a view.
If asked about humanism: the sacred figures are idealized but believable people, a key Early Renaissance shift.
Lineage fact: Lippi taught Botticelli; Lippi’s son Filippino later worked with Botticelli.
The angel looking out at the viewer is a classic ‘engagement’ device to mention in visual analysis.

72.title: Birth of Venus
72.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
72.plain: Botticelli’s large painting of Venus, goddess of love, arriving at the shore on a scallop shell, painted in Florence around 1484 to 1486. It is one of the first large European paintings since ancient times to make a nude pagan goddess the main subject, which shows how deeply the Medici circle loved Greek and Roman culture. It cares more about graceful line and ideal beauty than about believable bodies.
72.spot: A pale nude woman with long reddish-gold hair stands on a giant scallop shell, covering herself with her hand and hair. Winged wind gods blow from the left, roses float in the air, a woman on the right holds out a flowered cloak, and the sea is flat with little V-shaped waves.
72.remember: ‘Botti-SHELL-i’: the shell ride belongs to Botticelli, Florence, mid-1480s. She’s on the half shell because she’s half covered.
compare: No. 80 (§4.33), Venus of Urbino: Two Renaissance Venuses: Botticelli’s linear, standing, heavenly goddess versus Titian’s colorful, reclining, very earthly woman.
No. 71 (§4.24), Madonna and Child with Two Angels: Botticelli learned his delicate line and pale idealized faces from his teacher Lippi.
No. 107 (§5.9), La Grande Odalisque: Ingres’s elongated nude shows the same choice to stretch anatomy for elegance, centuries later.
72.vocab: tempera, Venus pudica, Neoplatonism, contour line, nude, mythological painting.

form: Tempera on canvas, about 1.7 by 2.8 m. Canvas was unusual for a big Florentine painting then; most important works were on wooden panels.
Line rules: crisp contours wrap every figure, with very little shading. Botticelli also added touches of gold to highlight the hair and trees.
Venus is elongated, with a long neck, sloping shoulders and an awkwardly attached left arm. Her weight could not really balance on the shell’s edge. Grace beats anatomy.
The pose is the ancient Venus pudica (‘modest Venus’: one hand over the breasts, one over the groin), borrowed from classical statues like the Medici Venus.
Space is shallow and the sea is a flat decorative pattern, so the figures read like a frieze across the surface.
function: A secular, mythological painting for a private villa, not a church.
The patron is not documented. It has long been linked to Lorenzo di Pierfrancesco de’ Medici, cousin of Lorenzo the Magnificent, but scholars debate this.
Vasari saw it in the mid-1500s at the Medici villa at Castello. It is now in the Uﬀizi, Florence.
content: Greek myth says Venus was born from sea foam and blown ashore. Botticelli shows the arrival, not the birth itself.
On the left, Zephyr (the west wind) blows, wrapped around a female companion usually identified as Aura (a breeze) or Chloris (a nymph). Falling roses were said to appear at Venus’s birth.
On the right, a Hora (one of the goddesses of the seasons, probably Spring) rushes to cover Venus with a cloak embroidered with flowers.
In Neoplatonism (a Renaissance philosophy based on Plato), physical beauty reflects divine beauty, so this Venus could stand for heavenly love lifting the soul toward God.
context: Sandro Botticelli (c. 1445 to 1510) trained with Fra Filippo Lippi (No. 71) and worked for the Medici. In 1481 to 1482 he painted wall frescoes in the Sistine Chapel, decades before Michelangelo’s ceiling.
The Medici circle included philosopher Marsilio Ficino and poet Angelo Poliziano, whose verses describe Venus’s birth and may be a literary source.
Medieval art showed nudity mainly as shame (Adam and Eve). A monumental nude goddess for a private patron was a bold revival of antiquity.
Vasari says Botticelli later followed the preacher Savonarola; stories that he burned his own paintings in the 1497 ‘bonfire of the vanities’ are uncertain.
Forgotten for centuries, it was rediscovered in the 1800s and is now one of the most reproduced images in Western art. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: linear, pale, elongated, decorative and mythological point to Botticelli, Florence, 1480s.
Medium trap: tempera on canvas, not oil and not fresco.
If asked about classical borrowing: the Venus pudica pose comes from ancient sculpture.
If asked about meaning: Neoplatonism in the Medici circle turned a pagan nude into an image of divine love.
If asked to compare with Titian (No. 80): linear Florentine disegno and a standing heavenly goddess versus Venetian color and a reclining earthly woman.
Know the cast: Zephyr and companion on the left, a Hora on the right, Venus on a scallop shell.

73.title: Last Supper
73.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
73.plain: Leonardo da Vinci’s huge painting of Jesus’s final meal with his twelve apostles, on the end wall of a monastery dining hall in Milan, made around 1494 to 1498. It freezes the moment after Jesus says one of them will betray him, and every perspective line in the room runs to his head. It is also a famous technical failure: Leonardo’s experimental paint began flaking within about twenty years.
73.spot: A long table parallel to the picture plane with Jesus at the center, arms spread in a triangle shape, framed by a bright window. Six apostles on each side, bunched in groups of three, under a coffered ceiling with wall hangings receding toward him. The surface looks faded and patchy.
73.remember: ‘Leonardo’s Last Supper lasted least’: experimental paint, Milan, 1490s, and the vanishing point sits in Jesus’s head.
compare: No. 76 (§4.29), School of Athens: Both High Renaissance works use one-point perspective that converges on the central figures.
No. 63 (§4.16), Arena: Giotto’s earlier frescoes tell sacred stories with emotional gesture, but in true fresco and simpler space.
No. 85 (§4.38), Calling of Saint Matthew: Caravaggio also stages a split-second Gospel reaction, but with tenebrist lighting and contemporary clothes.
73.vocab: one-point perspective, vanishing point, refectory, fresco, fresco secco, High Renaissance, Eucharist.

form: Painted on a dry plaster wall in an experimental mix of oil and tempera, not true fresco (paint applied into wet plaster so it bonds chemically). Leonardo wanted time to rework; the paint never bonded and began peeling.
One-point linear perspective (all receding lines meet at a single vanishing point): they converge at Christ’s right temple, where a small hole may mark the nail used to snap the guide strings.
Christ forms a stable triangle, isolated by open space. The window behind him, topped by a curved pediment, works as a natural halo.
The apostles form four groups of three, rippling outward like waves of shock from the center.
About 4.6 by 8.8 m. The painted room seems to continue the real dining hall, and it is lit from the left like the real windows.
function: Decoration for the refectory (dining hall) of the Dominican friary of Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan. Monks ate in silence while Christ’s table seemed to sit at the head of their room.
Patron: Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan, who planned the church as his family’s burial place; Sforza coats of arms appear in the lunettes above.
Bread and wine on the table recall the Eucharist (the Mass’s bread and wine), so the monks’ daily meal echoed Christ’s.
content: The moment just after ‘One of you will betray me’, combined with the institution of the Eucharist: two Gospel moments in one image.
Judas recoils into shadow, clutching a money bag and knocking over salt. Unusually, he sits on the same side of the table as everyone else.
Peter leans in holding a knife (foreshadowing his attack in Gethsemane); young John sways away; Thomas raises a finger.
Leonardo wanted gestures to show ‘the motions of the mind’, so each apostle’s body language reveals a different emotion.
context: Leonardo (1452 to 1519), trained in Florence, worked in Milan for Ludovico Sforza from about 1482 to 1499.
The painting defines the High Renaissance: balance, idealized figures, clear geometry and psychological drama.
Damage piled up: a door cut through the bottom in 1652 removed Jesus’s feet; an Allied bomb in 1943 wrecked the refectory, but the sandbagged wall survived.
A restoration from 1978 to 1999 stripped centuries of overpaint. Much of the original paint is lost, and visitors now enter in small, timed groups. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: one-point perspective converging on Christ, apostles in groups of three, Judas in shadow point to Leonardo, Milan, 1490s.
Trap: it is not a true fresco; the experimental oil and tempera on dry plaster explains the deterioration.
If asked about function: a refectory painting for monks, tied to the Eucharist.
Judas is on the same side of the table, singled out by shadow and his recoiling pose.
If asked to compare with School of Athens (No. 76): both put the vanishing point at the key figures and use architecture to frame them.
Patron: Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan.

74.title: Adam and Eve
74.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
74.plain: Albrecht Dürer’s small 1504 print of Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden, just before the first sin. It is a showpiece: a German artist from Nuremberg proving he could draw Italian-style ideal nudes built on ancient proportions, using a technique that could be printed many times and sold across Europe.
74.spot: Two pale, idealized nudes standing in mirror-image poses against a nearly black forest. Eve takes a fruit from the serpent’s mouth, Adam holds a branch, small animals (cat, mouse, rabbit, elk, ox, parrot, goat on a cliff) fill the scene, and a little sign hangs from a branch with a Latin inscription and 1504.
74.remember: ‘Dürer’s Duo, 1504’: the cat, rabbit, elk and ox are the four humors, all in balance until Eve bites.
compare: No. 79 (§4.32), Allegory of Law and Grace: Another German print, but a woodcut used to spread Lutheran doctrine rather than to show off ideal anatomy.
No. 87 (§4.40), Self-Portrait with Saskia: Rembrandt’s etching is looser and freer, showing how a different intaglio method changes the line.
No. 34 (§3.23), Doryphoros: Polykleitos’s statue is the ancient model of ideal proportion and contrapposto that Dürer was chasing.
74.vocab: engraving, burin, intaglio, cross-hatching, contrapposto, four humors, cartellino.

form: Engraving (lines cut into a copper plate with a sharp tool called a burin; the plate is inked and pressed onto paper), about 25 by 19 cm.
Fine curving lines and cross-hatching (crisscrossed lines that build up shadow) model the bodies. Dürer was a goldsmith’s son, trained in precise metalwork.
Both figures stand in contrapposto (weight on one leg, so the hips and shoulders tilt). Adam recalls the ancient Apollo Belvedere; Eve recalls classical Venus statues.
Proportions follow Vitruvius’s ancient ratios and Dürer’s own years of measuring studies.
Pale bodies glow against a dark forest like sculpture. Surviving trial proofs show he finished the background before completing the figures.
function: Sold to collectors and connoisseurs across Europe, and it worked as an advertisement of Dürer’s skill.
Prints were portable and multiple, so his reputation could travel far faster than any single painting.
Artists in Italy and the north studied and copied it as a model of ideal anatomy.
content: Genesis: Eve takes the forbidden fruit from the serpent and Adam reaches for it, the instant before the Fall.
The animals stand for the four humors (body fluids thought to control temperament): cat is choleric, rabbit sanguine, elk melancholic, ox phlegmatic. Before the Fall they were in balance.
The cat about to pounce on the mouse, and the goat on the cliff edge, signal the danger about to break loose.
The parrot on Adam’s branch is often read as a good, wise counterpart to the serpent across the scene.
The tablet reads, in Latin, ‘Albrecht Dürer of Nuremberg made this, 1504’, with his AD monogram.
context: Albrecht Dürer (1471 to 1528) of Nuremberg visited Italy in about 1494 to 1495 and again in 1505 to 1507, bringing Italian Renaissance ideas north.
Nuremberg was a printing center; his godfather Anton Koberger was a major publisher.
Dürer ran his prints as a business, and his wife Agnes sold them at fairs. His AD monogram became a kind of trademark.
The print fuses Northern Renaissance detail (bark, fur, leaves) with Italian ideal anatomy. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: German print, ideal nudes plus tiny detailed animals and a signed tablet point to Dürer, 1504.
Medium trap: engraving cuts lines into metal (intaglio); a woodcut (No. 79) is a relief print; an etching (No. 87) uses acid.
Know the four humors: cat choleric, rabbit sanguine, elk melancholic, ox phlegmatic.
If asked about self-promotion: the Latin tablet and monogram advertise the artist across Europe.
If asked about cross-cultural exchange within Europe: Northern detail meets Italian classical proportion.
If asked to compare with Doryphoros (No. 34): both treat the human body as a system of ideal measurements.

75.title: Sistine Chapel ceiling and altar wall frescoes
75.date: Ceiling c. 1508–1512 C.E.; altar c. 1536–1541 C.E.
75.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
75.plain: Michelangelo’s two giant fresco projects in the pope’s private chapel at the Vatican: the ceiling (1508 to 1512), with nine stories from Genesis including the Creation of Adam, and, more than twenty years later, the Last Judgment on the altar wall (1536 to 1541). He saw himself as a sculptor, and it shows: the figures are massive and muscular and look carved. Cardinals still lock themselves in this room to elect a new pope.
75.spot: Ceiling: a grid of painted architecture with rectangular Genesis scenes down the center, muscular nude youths at the corners and giant seated prophets and sibyls in thrones along the sides. Altar wall: a swirl of hundreds of nude bodies on a blue sky around a powerful, beardless Christ with a raised arm.
75.remember: ‘Ceiling = Creation (1508 to 1512, Julius II); Wall = Wrath (1536 to 1541, Paul III).’
compare: No. 76 (§4.29), School of Athens: Raphael’s fresco was painted a few rooms away at the same time, with calm balance instead of Michelangelo’s muscular energy.
No. 63 (§4.16), Arena: Giotto’s Arena Chapel is an earlier full-room fresco cycle that also ends with a Last Judgment.
No. 58 (§4.11), Church of Sainte-Foy: The Last Judgment tympanum at Sainte-Foy shows the same subject in Romanesque sculpture, ordered and diagrammatic.
No. 24 (§3.13), Last judgment of Hu-Nefer, from his tomb: The Egyptian Hu-Nefer papyrus shows a judgment of the dead in a very different religious system.
75.vocab: fresco, giornata, ignudo, sibyl, foreshortening, conclave, Counter-Reformation.

form: Fresco (water-based pigment brushed into wet plaster so it becomes part of the wall), painted in patches called giornate (one day’s worth of fresh plaster).
The chapel is about 40 by 13 m with the vault around 20 m up. Michelangelo painted standing on a scaffold he designed, head bent back, not lying down.
Painted architecture divides the vault into nine Genesis panels framed by prophets, sibyls and ignudi (nude male youths), with Christ’s ancestors in the lunettes.
Bodies twist and are sharply foreshortened (shortened to look as if they project toward or away from you), the habits of a sculptor.
The Last Judgment is one unframed field of more than 300 figures against lapis-blue sky. A 1980 to 1994 cleaning removed candle soot and revealed startlingly bright color.
function: Built 1473 to 1481 for Pope Sixtus IV (hence ‘Sistine’) as the main papal chapel for major ceremonies.
It hosts the conclave, the closed meeting where cardinals elect a new pope.
The Last Judgment fills the wall behind the altar, a reminder of final judgment aimed at the pope and cardinals themselves.
content: The ceiling runs in three groups of three: the Creation of the world, Adam and Eve, and Noah (including the Flood). Read from the altar, it goes in story order.
In the Creation of Adam, a rushing God, wrapped in a cloak full of figures, reaches toward a limp Adam; the gap between fingers is the moment before life passes.
Hebrew prophets and pagan sibyls (prophetesses of the ancient world, like the Delphic Sibyl) were believed to foretell Christ, uniting Jewish, classical and Christian traditions.

In the Last Judgment, St. Bartholomew holds his own flayed skin, its sagging face usually read as Michelangelo’s self-portrait. Minos in hell carries the face of a papal oﬀicial who complained about the nudity.
context: Pope Julius II forced Michelangelo off his sculpted tomb project to paint the ceiling; Michelangelo protested he was not a painter.
The walls already held frescoes from the 1480s by Botticelli, Perugino, Ghirlandaio and others.
The Last Judgment was commissioned under Clement VII and carried out for Paul III, after the 1527 Sack of Rome and amid the Reformation, which helps explain its darker mood.

After the Council of Trent demanded decency in sacred art, Daniele da Volterra painted cloth over genitals in 1565, the year after Michelangelo died, earning the nickname ‘the breechesmaker’. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: muscular, sculptural, twisting nudes point to Michelangelo.
Know the dates and popes: ceiling 1508 to 1512 for Julius II; Last Judgment 1536 to 1541 for Paul III.
Medium: fresco, true buon fresco on plaster.
If asked about Counter-Reformation reception: the nudes were criticized and partly covered after Trent.
Self-portrait: the flayed skin of St. Bartholomew.
Same years, same building complex: Raphael’s School of Athens (No. 76), where Michelangelo appears as Heraclitus.
Trap: he did not paint lying on his back.

76.title: School of Athens
76.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
76.plain: Raphael’s fresco in a Vatican room for Pope Julius II, painted 1509 to 1511, gathering the great thinkers of ancient Greece in a grand classical hall. Plato and Aristotle stand at the center, exactly where the perspective lines meet. It is the poster image of the High Renaissance: calm, balanced and devoted to classical learning, painted while Michelangelo was working on the Sistine ceiling nearby.
76.spot: A huge barrel-vaulted hall receding through arches, with two philosophers at the center: an old white-bearded man pointing up and a younger man holding his palm flat toward the ground. Crowds on wide steps, a man sprawled on the stairs, statues in wall niches and groups bent over slates in the foreground.
76.remember: Plato points to the sky (ideas), Aristotle to the earth (observation). ‘Raphael Reasons, 1509 to 1511.’
compare: No. 73 (§4.26), Last Supper: Leonardo’s perspective converges on Christ just as Raphael’s converges between Plato and Aristotle.
No. 75 (§4.28), Sistine Chapel ceiling and altar wall frescoes: Michelangelo’s ceiling was painted nearby at the same time, and Michelangelo appears in this fresco as Heraclitus.
No. 26 (§3.15), Athenian agora: The Athenian agora was the real public space where Greek philosophers like Socrates actually argued.
76.vocab: fresco, one-point perspective, vanishing point, lunette, barrel vault, coffer, humanism.

form: Fresco about 5 by 7.7 m, filling a lunette-shaped wall (with an arched top) in the Stanza della Segnatura.
One-point perspective: floor tiles and coffered vaults converge between Plato and Aristotle, so the geometry points at the heart of the debate.
The architecture of coffered barrel vaults and a dome was likely inspired by Bramante’s plans for the new St. Peter’s. Statues of Apollo and Athena stand in niches.
More than fifty figures are arranged in balanced groups left and right, with varied poses but a calm overall symmetry.
Even light, clear color and idealized bodies give the classic High Renaissance feel of harmony.
function: Painted for Pope Julius II. The room was probably his private library and later housed a papal court called the Segnatura, which gave the room its name.
The four walls represent Philosophy (this fresco), Theology (the Disputà, opposite), Poetry and Law.
The scheme shows the pope as patron of all learning, with reason and faith in harmony.
content: Plato holds his Timaeus and points up toward the ideal world of Forms; Aristotle holds his Ethics and gestures toward the earthly world we can observe.
Left side leans toward abstract and moral thought (Socrates arguing on his fingers, Pythagoras writing); right side toward science (Euclid with compass, Ptolemy with a globe).
Heraclitus, brooding alone on a block in front, was probably added later and given Michelangelo’s features after Raphael saw the Sistine ceiling.
Raphael includes himself at the far right edge in a dark cap, looking out at us.
context: Raphael (1483 to 1520), from Urbino, trained with Perugino and came to Rome around 1508 in his mid-twenties.
Julius II, the ‘warrior pope’, was rebuilding Rome: new St. Peter’s by Bramante, Michelangelo’s ceiling and these rooms all date from his reign.
Renaissance humanism held that classical philosophy and Christian theology fit together.
Contemporary faces stand in for ancients: tradition says Leonardo for Plato (not proven), Bramante for Euclid, Michelangelo for Heraclitus. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: balanced, classical architecture, deep perspective and idealized figures point to Raphael, High Renaissance.
Plato points up; Aristotle gestures down.
Location: Stanza della Segnatura, Vatican, for Julius II, facing the Disputà (theology).
Trap: Raphael did not paint the Sistine ceiling, and this is fresco, not oil.
If asked about humanism: contemporary artists as ancient philosophers plus a self-portrait raise the artist’s status.
If asked to compare with Last Supper (No. 73): both use converging perspective to frame the central figures.

77.title: Isenheim altarpiece
77.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
77.plain: A giant folding altarpiece made c. 1512 to 1516 for a monastery hospital at Isenheim, in Alsace (now France), that cared for people with ergotism, called ‘St. Anthony’s Fire’. Closed, it shows the most gruesome Crucifixion in European art, with Jesus covered in sores like the patients. Opened, it turns joyful and ends in a glowing Resurrection. The paintings are by Matthias Grünewald; the carved shrine inside is by Niclaus of Haguenau.
77.spot: Closed view: a black sky, an enormous greenish Christ on a rough cross, body pocked with sores and thorns, fingers clawing upward. Mary in white faints into John’s arms at left; John the Baptist points with a huge finger at right, a lamb at his feet.
77.remember: ‘Grim Grünewald, green Jesus’, c. 1512 to 1516: Isenheim was a hospital for the ill.
compare: No. 62 (§4.15), Röttgen Pietà: Both German devotional works exaggerate Christ’s wounds so viewers feel his suffering.
No. 66 (§4.19), Annunciation Triptych: Another Northern hinged altarpiece, but domestic and calm, packed with hidden symbols.
No. 78 (§4.31), Entombment of Christ: Pontormo’s dead Christ is a pale, elegant body made for the Eucharist, the opposite of Grünewald’s ravaged one.
77.vocab: polyptych, altarpiece, predella, hierarchical scale, Eucharist, Northern Renaissance.

form: A polyptych (an altarpiece of many hinged panels) whose wings open in stages to show three different views. Paintings are oil on wood; the innermost shrine is carved and gilded wood.
The closed Crucifixion panel alone is roughly 2.7 by 3.1 m. Christ is far larger than the people around him, a form of hierarchical scale (size shows importance).
Expressive distortion: gray-green skin, splinters, crushed feet and hands twisting like claws against a dark, empty background.
Closed, St. Sebastian and St. Anthony flank the Crucifixion, and a Lamentation fills the predella (the strip at the base).
Second view: Annunciation, a concert of angels, Nativity and a Resurrection in which Christ rises inside a huge halo of yellow, red and blue light, his skin now flawless.
function: High altarpiece of the hospital monastery of the Antonites (Order of St. Anthony), which specialized in treating ergotism.
Ergotism came from a fungus on rye bread: burning pain, convulsions, hallucinations and gangrene that could require amputation.
Patients were brought before the altar to see Christ suffering as they did, with the promise of healing or resurrection.
The wings were opened according to the church calendar, so different views appeared on feast days.
content: John the Baptist was already dead at the time of the Crucifixion, so his presence is symbolic. Latin words beside him say ‘He must increase, but I must decrease’.
The Lamb of God bleeds into a chalice, a symbol of Christ’s sacrifice and the Eucharist.
St. Sebastian and St. Anthony were protectors against plague and ergotism, the diseases patients feared most.

In the third view, carved figures of St. Anthony enthroned between Augustine and Jerome are flanked by painted scenes, including a Temptation of St. Anthony with a sore-covered demon often read as an ergotism victim.
context: Grünewald’s real name was probably Mathis Gothart Nithart; the name ‘Grünewald’ came from a 17th-century writer. Little else is known about him.
The painted wings were commissioned under preceptor Guido Guersi, whose coat of arms appears on them; the carved shrine was made earlier.
Painted at the same time as Raphael’s and Michelangelo’s Vatican work, it rejects idealized bodies for raw, expressive suffering.
Now in the Unterlinden Museum, Colmar, France, displayed taken apart so all views can be seen at once. On the exam.
If asked about function: an altarpiece for a hospital treating ergotism (St. Anthony’s Fire), run by Antonite monks.
If asked about form and function together: the closed view mirrors patients’ suffering; the open views offer hope.
If asked to attribute: harsh, expressive, Northern and gruesome rather than idealized point to Grünewald.
Trap: the carved sculpture is by Niclaus of Haguenau, not Grünewald.
Visual analysis hooks: hierarchical scale, distorted hands, the anachronistic John the Baptist.
If asked to compare with the Röttgen Pietà (No. 62): both stress Christ’s wounded body to provoke empathy.

78.title: Entombment of Christ
78.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
78.plain: Pontormo’s tall altarpiece, painted 1525 to 1528 for a small family chapel in Florence, showing mourners carrying the dead Christ. It is the textbook example of Mannerism, a style that came right after the High Renaissance and deliberately broke Raphael-style balance: candy colors, stretched weightless bodies, no ground underfoot and nowhere obvious to go.
78.spot: Pastel pink, baby blue and orange figures stacked in a rising spiral. Two crouching youths, one balanced on tiptoe, hold Christ’s pale, limp body at lower left; Mary faints at right; the center is an empty gap; there is no cross, no tomb and only one small cloud.
78.remember: ‘Pontormo’s Pastel Pile’, Florence, 1525 to 1528. Mannerism means ‘mannered’: weird on purpose.
compare: No. 76 (§4.29), School of Athens: Raphael’s calm, symmetrical High Renaissance order is exactly what Pontormo rejects.
No. 63 (§4.16), Arena: Giotto’s Lamentation shows a similar grieving group, but grounded and solid in clear space.
No. 77 (§4.30), Isenheim altarpiece: Both present Christ’s dead body for devotion, but Grünewald’s is ravaged while Pontormo’s is pale and elegant.
78.vocab: Mannerism, cangiante, altarpiece, Eucharist, elongation, High Renaissance.

form: Oil on wood panel, about 3.1 m tall and 1.9 m wide.
Mannerism (a style of about 1520 to 1600 that prizes elegance, artifice and tension over natural balance): long limbs, small heads, twisting poses.
Acid, unnatural colors, including cangiante (shot color, where a fabric shifts from one hue to another in light instead of just getting lighter or darker).
No ground line: the crouching youth balances on his toes and everyone seems to float. The setting is just a sliver of sky and a single cloud.
The figures swirl around an empty center, the opposite of the stable triangle used by Leonardo and Raphael. Many faces look out at us with wide, anxious eyes.
function: Altarpiece for the Capponi Chapel in the church of Santa Felicita, Florence, bought in 1525 by banker Ludovico Capponi as his family burial chapel.
Above the altar, the priest raised the Eucharist (bread believed to become Christ’s body) beneath an image of Christ’s real body being offered down toward the viewer.
Pontormo also painted an Annunciation fresco on the chapel’s side wall, so the whole small room works as one scheme.
content: The subject is debated: Entombment, Deposition or Lamentation. With no cross and no tomb, it reads more as a devotional display of Christ’s body than a single story moment.
Christ’s hanging arm and limp body echo Michelangelo’s marble Pietà in St. Peter’s (1498 to 1499).
Mary, reaching toward her son as she collapses, is the emotional center; the mourners’ grief is shown through gesture rather than story.
The bearded man at the far right edge is usually identified as Pontormo’s self-portrait.
context: Jacopo da Pontormo (1494 to 1557), Florentine, trained with Andrea del Sarto and was famously eccentric and reclusive; his diary records his meals and health.
The 1520s were a crisis decade: plague, the Medici thrown out of Florence, the Reformation and the Sack of Rome in 1527. How directly this shaped Mannerism is debated.
Mannerists learned from late Michelangelo and Raphael but pushed toward ‘maniera’, a stylish, self-conscious artifice that educated viewers admired.
The painting is still in Santa Felicita and was cleaned in a 2016 to 2017 restoration. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: elongated floating figures, acid colors and ambiguous space point to Mannerism and Pontormo, Florence, 1520s.
If asked about continuity and change: compare to School of Athens (No. 76), stable balance versus deliberate instability.
If asked about function: Capponi family chapel altarpiece tied to the Eucharist below it.
Visual clue: no cross, no tomb, empty center.
Self-portrait at the right edge.
Trap: Mannerism is not Baroque; it falls between the High Renaissance and the Baroque.

79.title: Allegory of Law and Grace
79.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
79.plain: A single-sheet print from about 1530 that explains Martin Luther’s central idea in one picture: you are saved by God’s grace through faith, not by following rules or doing good works. A tree splits it down the middle into Law and Grace. Cranach was Luther’s friend in Wittenberg, and prints like this were the Reformation’s social media: cheap, copyable and captioned with Bible verses in German.
79.spot: A black-and-white print divided by a central tree, bare on the left and leafy on the right. On the left a skeleton and a devil chase a naked man toward flames; on the right a man is shown the crucified Christ, whose blood streams onto him. Blocks of printed text run along the bottom.
79.remember: ‘Left is Law and Lost; right is Grace and Rescued.’ Cranach plus Luther equals Lutheran, c. 1530.
compare: No. 74 (§4.27), Adam and Eve: Both are German prints, but Dürer’s engraving shows off artistic skill while Cranach’s woodcut teaches doctrine.
No. 82 (§4.35), Il Gesù, including Triumph of the Name of Jes…: The Jesuit church is the Catholic Counter-Reformation answer, using spectacle rather than text-heavy teaching.
No. 85 (§4.38), Calling of Saint Matthew: Caravaggio also shows divine grace calling a sinner, but from a Catholic viewpoint and through dramatic light.
79.vocab: woodcut, relief print, letterpress, allegory, Reformation, iconoclasm.

form: Woodcut (a relief print: the artist cuts away everything that should be white and inks the raised lines left standing), about 27 by 32 cm.
Letterpress text (printed with movable type) beneath the image gives German Bible passages, so the picture and its scriptural proof travel together.
A near-symmetrical split, like a diptych: dead branches over Law, living branches over Grace, readable at a glance.
Bold, simple lines suited cheap mass printing. Clarity matters more than beauty here.
Many small scenes are packed into each half, like a diagram to be studied piece by piece.
function: A teaching tool for Lutheran doctrine. Cranach’s workshop also made painted versions of the same design.
Cheap enough to buy, pin up at home or bind into books, it reached people who never saw a church altarpiece.
It works as propaganda against the Catholic emphasis on good works, saints and indulgences.
content: Left (Law): Moses holds the Ten Commandments while Death and the Devil drive a naked man toward hell. Adam and Eve’s sin and a Last Judgment appear behind. The Law shows sin but cannot save.
Right (Grace): John the Baptist points the same man toward the crucified Christ, whose blood streams onto him. The risen Christ tramples Death and the Devil.
Background details tie the Old Testament to the New, such as Moses’s bronze serpent prefiguring the Crucifixion.
The message is sola fide (by faith alone) and sola gratia (by grace alone): the same sinner appears on both sides, and only what he trusts changes.
context: Lucas Cranach the Elder (1472 to 1553) was court painter to the Electors of Saxony in Wittenberg. He also ran a print shop and a pharmacy and served as the town’s mayor.
He was a close friend of Martin Luther: a witness at Luther’s 1525 wedding and godfather to his son. His portraits of Luther spread the reformer’s face across Europe.
Luther’s 95 Theses (1517) started in Wittenberg, and printing let his ideas spread faster than the Church could stop them.
Some Protestants smashed religious images (iconoclasm); Lutherans kept teaching images like this, as instruction rather than objects of worship. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: a divided woodcut with German text and Law versus Grace points to Cranach the Elder, Lutheran Reformation, c. 1530.
Medium trap: woodcut is a relief print; Dürer’s engraving (No. 74) and Rembrandt’s etching (No. 87) are intaglio.
Core doctrine: salvation by faith and grace, not good works.
If asked about function: mass-produced, inexpensive teaching and propaganda.
If asked to compare with Il Gesù (No. 82): the Protestant print teaches with words and diagrams; the Catholic church overwhelms the senses.
The tree’s dead and living branches are the quickest visual clue.

80.title: Venus of Urbino
80.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
80.plain: Titian’s oil painting of a nude woman lying on a bed in a contemporary Venetian palace room, looking straight at the viewer, bought in 1538. It is called Venus, but nothing about her is a goddess: no shell, no Cupid. That is why scholars still argue whether it is a marriage picture, an erotic picture or both. It set the template for the reclining nude for 300 years, including Manet’s Olympia.
80.spot: A nude woman reclines left to right on white sheets, head at left, gazing at us, holding roses, her left hand over her groin. A small dog sleeps at her feet, a dark green curtain splits the background, and two maids dig in a chest in a tiled room behind.
80.remember: ‘Titian’s tease from Urbino, 1538: the dog is asleep, but she isn’t.’
compare: No. 72 (§4.25), Birth of Venus: Botticelli’s linear, standing goddess versus Titian’s colorful, reclining, very human Venus.
No. 115 (§5.17), Olympia: Manet directly quotes Titian’s pose and gaze to expose modern prostitution behind the ‘goddess’ label.
No. 107 (§5.9), La Grande Odalisque: Ingres reworks the reclining nude as an exotic harem fantasy.
80.vocab: colorito, disegno, cassone, reclining nude, iconography, oil paint.

form: Oil on canvas, about 1.2 by 1.65 m. Oil on canvas suited humid Venice better than fresco.
Venetian colorito (building form through color and soft, blended brushwork) instead of Florentine disegno (form built on drawing and line).
Warm, glowing flesh against white sheets and a dark curtain whose edge lands right at her hand, splitting the picture into an intimate front and a deep room behind.
The tiled floor recedes in perspective toward a window, where a potted plant (myrtle) sits on the sill.
The pose comes from Giorgione’s Sleeping Venus, which Titian probably finished; Titian wakes her up and moves her indoors.
function: Bought in 1538 by Guidobaldo della Rovere, soon to be Duke of Urbino. His letters simply call it ‘the nude woman’.
Possibly connected to his 1534 marriage to a very young bride, as an image of marital love, but that is debated.
Made for private viewing. It came to Florence through a Medici marriage in 1631 and is now in the Uﬀizi.
content: Marriage symbols: roses (Venus’s flower), myrtle (an evergreen meaning constancy), the cassone (a chest for a bride’s trousseau) and a sleeping dog (fidelity).
Another reading: she is a courtesan, and the title ‘Venus’ is a respectable cover for an erotic picture. Scholars disagree.
Her direct gaze involves the original male owner: she knows she is being looked at.
The hand echoes the ancient Venus pudica pose but reads as more knowing than modest.
context: Titian (Tiziano Vecellio, c. 1488/90 to 1576) was Venice’s leading painter and worked for emperors and dukes across Europe.
Venice was a rich trading city famous for color-based painting and for its courtesans.
Mark Twain in 1880 called it the ‘foulest, the vilest, the obscenest picture the world possesses’, a reminder that reception changes.
Manet’s Olympia (No. 115, 1863) copies the pose and swaps the dog for a black cat and Venus for a Parisian sex worker. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: rich Venetian color, soft flesh, a reclining nude in a domestic interior point to Titian, Venice, 1538.
Know colorito versus disegno; Botticelli (No. 72) is the linear Florentine contrast.
Iconography: dog equals fidelity; roses, myrtle and cassone suggest love and marriage.
Patron: Guidobaldo della Rovere of Urbino, which gives the title.
Influence: Manet’s Olympia (No. 115) parodies it; Ingres’s Grande Odalisque (No. 107) continues the type.
Visual analysis hook: the direct gaze.

81.title: Frontispiece of the Codex Mendoza
81.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
81.plain: The opening picture-page of a book made by Indigenous (Nahua) painters in Mexico City around 1541 to 1542, about twenty years after the Spanish conquest, for the Spanish king. It shows the founding of Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, as an eagle landing on a cactus, the same image on Mexico’s flag today. The book mixes Aztec picture-writing with Spanish notes so Europeans could read Aztec history, tribute and daily life.
81.spot: A square page with a border of blue year signs; inside, a blue X of canals divides a square into four triangles, with an eagle perched on a cactus on a rock at the center. Seated men in white cloaks with name signs surround it, two small battle scenes run along the bottom, and Spanish handwriting labels everything.
81.remember: ‘Mendoza Maps Mexico’: eagle plus cactus equals Tenochtitlan, made for Charles V, c. 1541 to 1542.
compare: No. 157 (§6.5), Templo Mayor: The Templo Mayor stood at the sacred heart of the city whose founding this page records.
No. 158 (§6.6), Ruler’s feather headdress: The feather headdress is another Aztec object that ended up in Europe after the conquest.
No. 97 (§4.50), Spaniard and Indian Produce a Mestizo: A casta painting is another colonial image from New Spain made to explain the colony to Europeans.
81.vocab: codex, frontispiece, glyph, pictograph, gloss, folio.

form: Ink and color on European paper, in a bound codex (a book of bound pages), about 32 by 22 cm.
Aztec pictographs and glyphs (pictures and signs standing for names, places and dates): flat color, firm outlines, no shading, no perspective.
The border holds 51 blue year signs, counting the years of the founder Tenoch’s rule on the Aztec calendar.
Spanish glosses (handwritten explanations) were added afterward to label names and places.
Figures are shown in profile, seated men wrapped in white cloaks, sized by meaning rather than realism.
function: Made in the colonial capital, traditionally for the first viceroy, Antonio de Mendoza, to inform Emperor Charles V about the Aztec state.
Three sections: Mexica rulers and their conquests, a tribute list of goods owed by each province, and daily life from birth to old age.
Practical information for ruling and taxing the new colony.
French privateers captured it on the way to Spain. It passed through French and English hands and has been in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, since 1659.
content: The eagle on a prickly pear cactus growing from a rock is the city’s name glyph: Tenochtitlan means roughly ‘place of the prickly pear cactus on the rock’.
Legend says the god Huitzilopochtli told the wandering Mexica to settle where they saw this sign.
Ten founders sit around it. Tenoch, the leader, has a speech scroll and sits on a reed mat, a sign of authority. A skull rack and a shield with arrows signal sacrifice and war.
At the bottom, Mexica warriors conquer the towns of Colhuacan and Tenayuca, the first victories of a growing empire.
context: Tenochtitlan was founded around 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco. Hernán Cortés and his Indigenous allies took it in 1521, and Mexico City was built on top.
The painters were Indigenous tlacuiloque (painter-scribes) trained in pre-conquest tradition, working for a colonial government.
Spanish clergy destroyed most pre-conquest manuscripts as idolatrous, so post-conquest codices like this are key sources for Aztec history.
It is a hybrid: Mexica pride in their imperial past, packaged for the conqueror’s needs. On the exam.
If asked for content: the founding of Tenochtitlan, eagle on cactus, city divided into four quarters by canals.
If asked who made it and for whom: Indigenous scribes for the Spanish crown, c. 1541 to 1542.
If asked about cultural hybridity: Aztec pictographs plus Spanish alphabetic glosses, on European paper in a bound book.
Trap: unlike the modern Mexican flag, the eagle here holds no snake.
If asked to compare with the Templo Mayor (No. 157): the Codex records the founding story the great temple stood for.
Today it is in the Bodleian Library, Oxford, not in Mexico or Spain.

82.title: Il Gesù, including Triumph of the Name of Jesus ceiling fresco
82.artist: Giacomo da Vignola (plan); Giacomo della Porta (facade); Giovanni Battista
82.date: Church 16th century C.E.; facade 1568–1584 C.E.; fresco and stucco 1676–1679
82.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
82.plain: The mother church of the Jesuits in Rome, designed from 1568 as a preaching machine for the Catholic Counter-Reformation: one huge open nave so everyone could see the altar and hear the sermon. About a century later, in 1676 to 1679, Gaulli painted the nave ceiling so it seems to burst open into heaven, with figures spilling over the frame. The church became a model for Catholic churches worldwide.
82.spot: Facade: two stories, a temple-front top with a triangular pediment, paired flat pilasters and big S-shaped scrolls linking the narrow upper story to the wider lower one. Ceiling: a glowing golden IHS monogram in a burst of light, with clouds and bodies tumbling over a gilded frame on the vault.
82.remember: ‘Jesuits’ Gesù: Vignola plans it, della Porta fronts it, Gaulli floats it.’ Gesù is Italian for Jesus.
compare: No. 79 (§4.32), Allegory of Law and Grace: The Lutheran print teaches through text and diagram; the Jesuit church persuades through overwhelming sensory experience.
No. 89 (§4.42), Ecstasy of Saint Teresa: Bernini’s Cornaro Chapel also fuses painting, sculpture and architecture into Counter-Reformation theater.
No. 88 (§4.41), San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane: Borromini’s facade takes the stacked twostory church front and makes it ripple.
No. 75 (§4.28), Sistine Chapel ceiling and altar wall frescoes: Michelangelo’s ceiling frames scenes in painted architecture; Gaulli’s breaks the frame open into heaven.
82.vocab: Latin cross plan, nave, barrel vault, volute, di sotto in sù, stucco, CounterReformation.

form: Latin-cross plan (a long nave crossed by shorter arms, like a Christian cross) with one wide nave (main hall), no side aisles and side chapels instead, plus a dome over the crossing.
A broad barrel vault covers the nave, leaving the space open and unobstructed.
Della Porta’s facade: two stories joined by volutes (big S-shaped scrolls), with paired pilasters that step forward toward the central door, focusing attention on the entrance.
Gaulli’s ceiling uses di sotto in sù (‘seen from below’: figures foreshortened as if overhead in real space). Painted clouds and figures overlap the gilded frame and cast painted shadows.
Fresco plus stucco (plaster sculpture): Antonio Raggi’s stucco angels blur the line between painted and three-dimensional figures. The structure is brick faced with marble and stucco.
function: Mother church of the Society of Jesus, built for preaching and the Mass. The single nave gave everyone a clear view of the altar and good acoustics.
Side chapels served private devotion and patron families; St. Ignatius of Loyola is buried in a lavish chapel in the left transept.
Jesuit missionaries carried the plan across Europe, Latin America and Asia.
content: IHS is the first three letters of Jesus’s name in Greek and the Jesuits’ emblem.
On the ceiling, the saved rise toward the radiant name while the damned, often read as heretics and vices, tumble down as if falling into the church.
The message is Catholic triumph: heaven made visible and emotional to the ordinary worshiper.
The volute facade links a tall center to wide sides, an idea borrowed from Alberti’s Santa Maria Novella and copied by countless Baroque churches.
context: The Jesuits were founded by Ignatius of Loyola and approved in 1540. They focused on education, missions and fighting Protestantism.
The Council of Trent (1545 to 1563) wanted art to be clear, moving and instructive.
Cardinal Alessandro Farnese paid for the building; his name is on the facade. Vignola designed the plan, and Giacomo della Porta designed the facade and finished the dome after Vignola died in 1573.
Giovanni Battista Gaulli, nicknamed Baciccio, was a protégé of Bernini, who probably helped him win the ceiling commission. On the exam.
If asked about function: Counter-Reformation preaching church; the single nave lets everyone see and hear.
Who did what: Vignola plan, della Porta facade, Gaulli ceiling with Raggi stucco, 1676 to 1679.
The volute facade is the model for later Baroque church fronts.
Ceiling illusion: figures break the frame and blur painted and real space.
Trap: the ceiling is about a century later than the church.
If asked to compare with Cranach (No. 79): Protestant print as instruction versus Catholic spectacle as persuasion.

83.title: Hunters in the Snow
83.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
83.plain: Pieter Bruegel the Elder’s 1565 winter landscape, part of a series about the seasons painted for a rich Antwerp merchant. Three tired hunters trudge home with a poor catch while the village below goes about winter life: skating, cooking, hauling wood. It is one of the first great European paintings where landscape and ordinary people, not saints or kings, are the whole point.
83.spot: A snowy hilltop at lower left with dark hunters and dogs seen from behind, a row of bare trees with black birds and a steep diagonal down to the right. Below, gray-green frozen ponds full of tiny skaters stretch toward jagged mountains under a pale green-gray sky.
83.remember: ‘Bruegel’s brrr’, 1565: one sad fox for a whole day’s hunt.
compare: No. 201 (§9.10), Travelers among Mountains and Streams: Both dwarf people in vast landscapes, one for Daoist and Confucian contemplation, one for a merchant’s seasonal cycle.
No. 109 (§5.11), The Oxbow: Cole’s Oxbow is a later landscape that also carries meaning about people, land and change.
No. 211 (§9.20), Under the Wave off Kanagawa: Hokusai’s print also sets ordinary working people against overwhelming nature.
83.vocab: genre scene, landscape, bird’s-eye view, atmospheric perspective, labors of the months.

form: Oil on wood panel, about 1.2 by 1.6 m.
A high, bird’s-eye view (seen from above) and a strong diagonal from the hunters at upper left down into the valley pull the eye deep into space.
Cold, limited palette of white, gray-green, brown and black. Hunters, dogs, trees and birds read as dark silhouettes against the snow.
Atmospheric perspective (distant forms paler and bluer) softens the far mountains.
The jagged peaks are invented: Flanders is flat. Bruegel had crossed the Alps on a trip to Italy in the early 1550s.
function: One of six panels on the times of the year commissioned by Nicolaes Jonghelinck for his house in Antwerp. Five survive; this one covers roughly December and January.
Decoration for a wealthy collector, continuing the medieval ‘labors of the months’ tradition in a modern, secular form.
In 1566 the series was pledged against a debt and passed to the city of Antwerp, later entering the Habsburg collection. It is now in the Kunsthistorisches Museum, Vienna.
content: The labors of the months (scenes of seasonal work, common in medieval prayer books) here become one full-scale landscape.
The hunters’ single fox and the drooping dogs suggest hardship. At left, villagers singe a pig over a fire, a winter slaughter task.
The inn sign hangs from one hinge; it shows St. Eustace, patron saint of hunters, an ironic note on the hunt’s failure.
People are part of nature’s cycle, shown without a moral lesson or mockery.
context: Pieter Bruegel the Elder (c. 1525/30 to 1569) worked in Antwerp and Brussels. Nicknamed ‘Peasant Bruegel’, he was actually an educated city artist with humanist clients.
Antwerp was northern Europe’s richest trading city, with an open market for secular subjects like genre (everyday life) and landscape.
Protestant ideas reduced demand for religious images, and the Spanish-ruled Netherlands was heading toward religious riots and revolt.
Europe was in the Little Ice Age, and the winter of 1564 to 1565 was especially harsh. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: high viewpoint, peasants, invented mountains and a wintry palette point to Bruegel the Elder, Flemish, 1565.
Function: a seasons series for merchant patron Jonghelinck.
If asked about change: landscape and genre become independent subjects in Northern art.
Context hook: the Little Ice Age.
Trap: oil on wood, not canvas; and Bruegel the Elder, not his sons.
If asked to compare with Fan Kuan (No. 201): both make humans tiny in nature, but the Chinese scroll is spiritual and monumental while Bruegel’s is social and seasonal.

84.title: Mosque of Selim II
84.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
84.plain: The imperial mosque the Ottoman architect Sinan built for Sultan Selim II in Edirne, the former Ottoman capital, in 1568 to 1575. One enormous dome, about 31 m (102 feet) across, rests on eight piers, so the prayer hall is a single open space you can take in at a glance. Sinan, then in his eighties, called it his masterpiece and claimed it beat the dome of Hagia Sophia.
84.spot: Outside: a big central dome surrounded by smaller half-domes and buttress turrets, with four very tall, needle-thin minarets at the corners of the prayer hall. Inside: a vast, bright dome on eight piers, a raised marble platform under the center and red, blue and turquoise tiles.
84.remember: ‘Selim’s Sinan sits on eight’: eight piers, Edirne, 1568 to 1575. Sinan’s apprentice, journeyman and master works end here.
compare: No. 52 (§4.5), Hagia Sophia: Hagia Sophia was the model and rival that Sinan set out to surpass.
No. 56 (§4.9), Great Mosque: The Great Mosque of Córdoba uses a hypostyle forest of columns, the opposite of Sinan’s single open dome.
No. 186 (§8.6), Great Mosque: The Great Mosque of Isfahan shows a different Islamic plan built around courtyard and iwans.
84.vocab: dome, pier, minaret, mihrab, külliye, Iznik tile, aniconism, congregational mosque.

form: Cut stone and brick, with lead-covered domes. The main dome is about 31 m across and sits on an octagon of eight massive piers.
Small half-domes fill the four corners, turning a square hall into an octagon under the dome. Buttresses are pushed to the outside, leaving the interior open.
Walls are pierced by many windows, so the space is flooded with even light.
Four minarets (towers from which the call to prayer is given), each about 70 m tall with three balconies, are among the tallest the Ottomans built.
Inside: Iznik tiles (bright glazed ceramic tiles from Iznik, famous for tomato red and cobalt blue), especially in the mihrab area and the sultan’s private loge, plus large calligraphy.
function: An imperial Friday mosque (congregational mosque for the weekly Friday prayer) built for the sultan’s prestige and the city’s worship.
The center of a külliye (a complex of buildings around a mosque), with schools and a covered market whose rents funded upkeep.
A raised platform for the prayer callers sits right under the dome’s center, and the mihrab (niche facing Mecca) sits in a bright recess visible from everywhere.
content: No figurative images: in keeping with Islamic aniconism (avoiding images of living beings in religious spaces), meaning comes from space, light, pattern and calligraphy.
The single, unified space is often read as expressing the oneness of God and the equality of worshipers praying shoulder to shoulder.
Four minarets announced imperial status; ordinary mosques had one.
Calligraphy gives Qur’an verses and the names of God, Muhammad and the first caliphs.
context: Sinan (c. 1490 to 1588) was chief architect of the Ottoman court for about fifty years and designed hundreds of buildings. He began as a military engineer in the Janissary corps.
In his memoirs he called the Şehzade Mosque his apprentice work, the Süleymaniye in Istanbul his journeyman work and the Selimiye his masterpiece.

Ottoman architects measured themselves against Hagia Sophia (No. 52), converted to a mosque in 1453. Sinan claimed a wider dome; in fact the two are about the same width, and Hagia Sophia’s is much higher.
Selim II died in 1574 before it was finished. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: one huge dome on eight piers, four pencil minarets and Iznik tile point to Sinan, Ottoman, 1568 to 1575.
Location trap: Edirne, not Istanbul. The Süleymaniye is the Istanbul one.
Function: Friday mosque within a külliye complex.
If asked to compare with Hagia Sophia: the Byzantine church stretches along an axis; Sinan’s octagonal support creates one centralized open space.
If asked about rivalry and emulation: Sinan openly set out to outdo Hagia Sophia’s dome.
Contrast with Córdoba (No. 56): a forest of columns versus one unified dome.

85.title: Calling of Saint Matthew
85.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
85.plain: Caravaggio’s painting of Jesus walking into a dim room of tax collectors and pointing at Matthew, who will drop everything to become an apostle. A hard beam of light follows Jesus’s gesture across the dark wall, and the men wear the clothing of Rome around 1600, so it looks like a scene from a gambling den down the street. It made Caravaggio famous almost overnight and launched a dramatic dark-and-light style copied all over Europe.
85.spot: A dark room crossed by a diagonal beam of light from the upper right, above a shuttered window. At left, men in feathered caps and slashed sleeves sit around a table with coins; at right, two barefoot robed figures stand, one (Christ, with a faint halo) pointing with a relaxed hand.
85.remember: ‘Christ points, the light follows.’ Caravaggio, Contarelli Chapel, Calling, c. 1600: lots of C’s.
compare: No. 73 (§4.26), Last Supper: Both freeze a split-second Gospel reaction, but Leonardo uses calm perspective and Caravaggio uses theatrical light.
No. 89 (§4.42), Ecstasy of Saint Teresa: Bernini also uses directed light as a sign of divine grace in a Counter-Reformation chapel.
No. 75 (§4.28), Sistine Chapel ceiling and altar wall frescoes: Caravaggio quotes Michelangelo’s Adam in Christ’s pointing hand.
85.vocab: tenebrism, chiaroscuro, naturalism, Baroque, caravaggisti, Counter-Reformation.

form: Oil on canvas, about 3.2 by 3.4 m, with life-size figures.
Tenebrism (extreme contrast between deep darkness and a harsh spotlight), a more intense version of chiaroscuro (modeling forms with light and shadow).
The light enters on a diagonal from the upper right, matching the direction of the chapel’s real window, and runs parallel to Christ’s arm.
The picture splits in two: men in flashy contemporary clothes at the table, and Christ and Peter in timeless robes and bare feet.
Christ’s hand quotes Adam’s limp hand from Michelangelo’s Creation of Adam (No. 75), presenting Christ as the ‘new Adam’.
Ordinary faces, no idealizing and a bare background. Caravaggio worked from live models and apparently painted straight onto the canvas with few or no drawings.
function: One of three paintings of St. Matthew for the Contarelli Chapel in San Luigi dei Francesi, the French national church in Rome; the others show his Inspiration (above the altar) and Martyrdom (opposite wall).
Funded from the estate of the French Cardinal Mathieu Cointrel (Italianized as Contarelli), named for his patron saint. Installed in 1600.
Caravaggio’s first major public commission, reportedly arranged through his patron Cardinal Francesco Maria del Monte.
content: From Matthew’s Gospel: Jesus saw Matthew at his tax booth and said ‘Follow me’. Tax collectors were despised as greedy collaborators.
Which man is Matthew is debated: the bearded man pointing to himself (‘Me?’) or the young man hunched over the coins at the end of the table. Scholars disagree.
Light stands for divine grace breaking into a sinful world and calling for a response, a Catholic emphasis on free will.
Peter, standing partly in front of Christ, can be read as the Church acting as go-between. X-rays suggest Caravaggio added him during painting.
context: Caravaggio (Michelangelo Merisi, 1571 to 1610) came from Lombardy and lived violently: brawls, arrests and a killing in 1606 that forced him to flee Rome. He died in 1610.
Counter-Reformation leaders wanted art that ordinary people could understand and feel. Caravaggio’s realism fit, though some clergy rejected other works of his as vulgar.
Followers called Caravaggisti spread his style to Naples, Spain, the Netherlands and beyond. Artemisia Gentileschi, Ribera and the Utrecht painters all drew on it.
Its influence reached Rembrandt and Velázquez, making him one of the founders of Baroque painting. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: tenebrism, contemporary dress and ordinary people point to Caravaggio, Rome, c. 1600.
Light as grace, aligned with the chapel’s real window.
Location: Contarelli Chapel, San Luigi dei Francesi, Rome.
If asked about borrowing: Christ’s hand echoes Michelangelo’s Adam.
If asked about Counter-Reformation goals: direct, emotional, accessible storytelling.
Debate to mention: which figure is Matthew.
Trap: tenebrism is the extreme form of chiaroscuro; do not use them as exact synonyms.

86.title: Henri IV Receives the Portrait of Marie de’ Medici, from the
86.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
86.plain: One of 24 huge canvases Peter Paul Rubens painted in 1621 to 1625 for Marie de’ Medici, widow of King Henri IV of France, to turn her not-very-glorious life into an epic. This one shows Henri falling in love with her portrait before they ever met, while Jupiter and Juno bless the match from the clouds. It is political spin in paint: an arranged marriage for money and alliances recast as a love story approved by the gods.
86.spot: An armored king at right gazes at a framed portrait of a woman held up by two winged boys. A helmeted woman in a blue cloak covered with gold fleurs-de-lis leans on his shoulder, gods with an eagle and peacocks sit on clouds above, and chubby babies play with his helmet and shield at the bottom.
86.remember: ‘Rubens’s romance: Henri falls for a picture.’ Marie de’ Medici cycle, 1621 to 1625.
compare: No. 93 (§4.46), The Palace at Versailles: Versailles stages French royal power at the scale of architecture and landscape.
No. 43 (§3.32), Augustus of Prima Porta: Augustus uses gods and symbols, like Cupid on a dolphin, to legitimize political power.
No. 91 (§4.44), Las Meninas: Velázquez also builds a painting around royal images and the power of looking at a picture.
86.vocab: allegory, personification, Baroque, putto, oil sketch, propaganda.

form: Oil on canvas, about 3.9 m tall and 3 m wide, one of 24 in the cycle.
Baroque style (17th-century art of motion, drama, rich color and strong diagonals): a diagonal sweeps from the gods at upper left down to Henri at right.
Loose, energetic brushwork and warm, glowing flesh show Rubens’s study of Titian and Venetian color.
Real people and mythological figures share the same space with no visual break between them.
Rubens planned the cycle with small oil sketches; assistants in his large workshop helped, but he painted key passages himself.
function: Commissioned in 1621 by Marie de’ Medici for a long gallery in the Luxembourg Palace, her new Paris residence.
Political: to restore her reputation after a bitter feud with her son, King Louis XIII, and present her as essential to France.
A second cycle about Henri IV was planned but never finished. The Marie cycle is now in the Louvre.
content: Henri IV, in armor as a soldier-king, is captivated by the portrait. France, personified as a helmeted woman in a fleur-de-lis cloak, leans in to advise him.
Cupid and Hymen (god of marriage) present the portrait, making the match about love.
Above, Jupiter (with his eagle) and Juno (with her peacocks), king and queen of the gods, model the ideal royal marriage.
Putti (chubby winged babies) play with Henri’s helmet and shield: war set aside for love and peace. A portrait inside a painting also reminds us how powerful images can be.
context: Marie de’ Medici (1575 to 1642) of Florence married Henri IV in 1600; her huge dowry helped offset French debts to the Medici bank.
Henri was assassinated in 1610. Marie ruled as regent until Louis XIII seized power in 1617 and exiled her to Blois; they reconciled around the time of this commission.
Later, in 1631, she was exiled again and died in Cologne in 1642.

Peter Paul Rubens (1577 to 1640) of Antwerp trained in Italy, ran Europe’s busiest studio and worked as a diplomat, knighted by both the Spanish and English kings. With so little heroic material, he leaned on allegory. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: fleshy figures, sweeping diagonals and gods mixed with real rulers point to Rubens, Flemish Baroque.
Function: political propaganda for Marie de’ Medici, made for the Luxembourg Palace.
Key device: allegory and personification (France, Cupid, Hymen, Jupiter and Juno).
A portrait within a painting: images can win hearts and power.
If asked to compare with Augustus of Prima Porta (No. 43): both use divine imagery to legitimize a ruler.
If asked to compare with Versailles (No. 93): French royal image-making, from one canvas to a whole palace.

87.title: Self-Portrait with Saskia
87.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
87.plain: A tiny 1636 etching of Rembrandt, then about 30 and newly successful in Amsterdam, sitting at a table with his wife Saskia behind him. It is a working portrait: he holds a drawing tool, and it was printed and sold, spreading his face and skill widely. Rembrandt made more self-portraits than almost any artist before him, by most counts around 80 in paintings, prints and drawings.
87.spot: A small print in quick, sketchy lines: a man in a floppy beret with a feather sits in the left foreground, turned toward us, holding a drawing tool at a table. A woman in a headdress sits behind him at right, smaller, also looking out.
87.remember: ‘Rem-ETCH, 1636’: Rembrandt plus Saskia, etched in the happy early years.
compare: No. 91 (§4.44), Las Meninas: Velázquez also portrays himself at work, but inside a royal court rather than the open market.
No. 74 (§4.27), Adam and Eve: Dürer’s engraving is also an intaglio print, but its precise carved lines contrast with Rembrandt’s free etched ones.
No. 105 (§5.7), Self-Portrait: Vigée Le Brun’s self-portrait also presents the artist at work to build a reputation.
87.vocab: etching, intaglio, cross-hatching, self-portrait, plate, impression.

form: Etching (the artist draws through a waxy, acid-resistant coating on a copper plate; acid ‘bites’ the exposed lines; the plate is then inked and printed).
An intaglio print (ink sits in grooves below the plate’s surface and is pressed onto damp paper), the same family as engraving.
Because drawing through wax is easy, the line is free and sketchy, unlike the controlled, carved lines of engraving.
Tiny: about 10 by 9 cm, palm-sized.
Cross-hatching builds the darks; bare paper gives the lights. Rembrandt often reworked his plates, so different impressions vary.
function: Printed and sold on the open market, an affordable way for collectors to own a Rembrandt.
Self-promotion: his own face became a recognizable brand.
A study in character and expression, and perhaps a celebration of his 1634 marriage.
content: Rembrandt presents himself as a working artist, drawing tool in hand and brow furrowed, wearing a plumed, old-fashioned beret: he loved costumes.
Saskia is wife and model, and she also signals social standing: she came from a well-off Frisian family, and her cousin Hendrick van Uylenburgh was Rembrandt’s art dealer.
A double portrait of artist and wife, with the artist at work, is more intimate and informal than a standard marriage portrait.
Both look out at us, which makes the viewer part of the moment.
context: Rembrandt van Rijn (1606 to 1669), born in Leiden, moved to Amsterdam in the early 1630s, during the Dutch Golden Age.
The Dutch Republic was Protestant and commercial: few church commissions, so artists sold portraits, prints, landscapes and genre scenes to merchants.
Saskia van Uylenburgh married him in 1634. Three of their children died in infancy; son Titus, born 1641, survived. Saskia died in 1642, about age 29.
Rembrandt went bankrupt in 1656. His self-portraits track his whole life, from confident youth to worn old age. On the exam.
If asked about medium: etching (acid, intaglio) versus engraving (burin, intaglio, No. 74) versus woodcut (relief, No. 79).
If asked about the artist’s identity: Rembrandt made self-portraiture a lifelong subject.
Context: the Dutch open art market without church or court patrons.
If asked to compare with Las Meninas (No. 91): both show the artist at work, but Velázquez for a king and Rembrandt for buyers.
Date: 1636, early career, before Saskia’s death and his money troubles.
Visual clue: tiny size and loose, scribbly line.

88.title: San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane
88.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
88.plain: A tiny Baroque church in Rome designed by Francesco Borromini for a poor Spanish religious order, squeezed onto a cramped street corner. Instead of flat walls and straight lines, the walls ripple in and out, and the oval dome is covered in a honeycomb of crosses, octagons and hexagons that shrink as they rise. The interior dates to 1638 to 1646; the rippling facade came later, in the 1660s.
88.spot: Facade: two stories of wavy walls, curving in, out and in, with columns, statues in niches and an oval medallion held by angels at the top; a fountain is set into the corner. Interior: all white, with an oval dome of deep crosses, octagons and hexagons rising to a lantern.
88.remember: ‘Borromini bends’: San Carlino curves. Interior 1638 to 1646; facade 1665 to 1667.
compare: No. 46 (§3.35), Pantheon: Both domes use coffers, but the Pantheon’s are regular squares while Borromini’s are shrinking, interlocking shapes.
No. 82 (§4.35), Il Gesù, including Triumph of the Name of Jes…: Il Gesù’s flat two-story facade is the model that Borromini makes ripple and move.
No. 89 (§4.42), Ecstasy of Saint Teresa: Bernini, Borromini’s rival, also uses hidden light sources for a heavenly effect.
No. 240 (§11.17), Guggenheim Museum Bilbao: Gehry’s Guggenheim Bilbao is a modern building that also rejects straight walls for curving, dynamic form.
88.vocab: coffer, oval dome, lantern, stucco, undulating facade, cornice, Baroque.

form: Stone and stucco (plaster that hardens smooth, cheaper than marble). The interior is almost entirely white, which suited a tight budget and shows off form.
The plan grows from geometry: scholars describe it in different ways, but it starts from triangles and ovals, with walls that swell and recede around them.
The oval dome is lined with coffers (sunken panels) shaped as interlocking crosses, octagons and hexagons. They shrink toward the top, faking extra height.
Windows hidden at the base of the dome and in the lantern flood it with light, so it seems to float.
The facade, built 1665 to 1667 and finished after Borromini’s death, has a lower story that curves in, out and in, with a continuous bending cornice.
function: Church and monastery for the Discalced (barefoot) Trinitarians, a Spanish order devoted to ransoming Christians held captive, especially in North Africa.
Dedicated to San Carlo Borromeo (St. Charles Borromeo), a Counter-Reformation saint canonized in 1610.
Borromini also designed the small cloister and monastery buildings; it was his first independent commission.
content: Triangles in the plan and a dove (the Holy Spirit) in the lantern are often read as references to the Trinity, fitting a Trinitarian order.
Crosses in the coffers echo the order’s cross badge and Christian devotion generally.
Light pouring down from above stands for heaven; the rising, shrinking coffers make the dome feel like it is lifting away.
context: Francesco Borromini (1599 to 1667) trained as a stonemason, worked under Carlo Maderno and alongside Bernini at St. Peter’s, then became Bernini’s bitter rival. He died by suicide in 1667.
Baroque architecture (17th-century style that favors movement, curves and drama) replaced Renaissance regularity. Borromini was the most radical, treating walls as if flexible.
The name ‘Quattro Fontane’ comes from the four fountains on the corners of the intersection.

Critics in his day called his work bizarre; later Central European Baroque architects and even modern architects admired it. It is often said the whole church would fit inside one of St. Peter’s dome piers. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: an undulating facade and an oval dome with geometric coffers point to Borromini, Roman Baroque.
Date trap: the interior is 1638 to 1646; the facade is 1665 to 1667.
Function: a small church for the Discalced Trinitarians on a cramped corner site.
If asked to compare with the Pantheon (No. 46): regular square coffers versus shrinking, interlocking geometric coffers.
If asked to compare with Il Gesù (No. 82): a flat stacked facade versus a rippling one.
Context hook: the Bernini versus Borromini rivalry.

89.title: Ecstasy of Saint Teresa
89.artist: Gian Lorenzo Bernini; Cornaro Chapel, Santa Maria della Vittoria, Rome
89.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
89.plain: Gian Lorenzo Bernini’s marble sculpture of the Spanish nun Teresa of Ávila swooning as an angel prepares to pierce her heart with a golden arrow, made c. 1647 to 1652. It sits like a stage scene in a chapel Bernini designed for the Cornaro family in Rome, combining sculpture, colored marble, hidden light and a painted ceiling into one experience. It is the best-known example of Baroque theater put to Catholic use.
89.spot: A white marble nun collapsing backward on a cloud, eyes half closed and mouth open, one bare foot hanging, with a smiling angel holding a golden arrow. Gilded bronze rays stream down behind them inside a colored-marble frame, and on the side walls marble men lean out of balcony boxes.
