89.remember: ‘Teresa’s theater, Bernini’s box seats’, 1647 to 1652. Cornaro sounds like ‘corner’, and the family watches from the corner boxes.
compare: No. 85 (§4.38), Calling of Saint Matthew: Caravaggio also uses directed light to show divine grace, in paint instead of real light.
No. 82 (§4.35), Il Gesù, including Triumph of the Name of Jes…: The Il Gesù ceiling similarly breaks the frame and merges painting, stucco and architecture.
No. 37 (§3.26), Winged Victory of Samothrace: The Winged Victory is an ancient example of sculpture staged theatrically, with wind-whipped drapery and a dramatic setting.
89.vocab: bel composto, aedicula, gilding, transept, Baroque, Counter-Reformation.

form: Marble group about 3.5 m tall including the cloud, with gilded bronze rays (thin gold layer over bronze) behind.
Bernini makes marble imitate many textures: heavy, rumpled robes, soft flesh, fluffy cloud and the angel’s thin, clinging drapery.
Light comes from a window of yellow glass hidden above the sculpture, so it glows as if lit from heaven.
The group sits in an aedicula (a shrine-like frame of columns and pediment) that bows forward like a stage.
On the side walls, marble Cornaro men sit in theater boxes, chatting, reading and looking. The ceiling fresco by Guidobaldo Abbatini shows heaven with clouds spilling over the frame.
function: Funerary chapel of the Venetian Cardinal Federico Cornaro, in the left transept of Santa Maria della Vittoria, a church of the Discalced Carmelites, the order Teresa herself reformed.
Built to inspire devotion: worshipers witness a mystical experience as if it were happening in front of them.
It also glorifies the family: Federico, his father (a Doge of Venice) and other Cornaro cardinals appear as witnesses. Marble floor inlays show skeletons, a reminder of death and resurrection.
content: In her autobiography, Teresa described an angel piercing her heart with a golden spear tipped with fire, leaving her ‘on fire with a great love of God’, a pain so intense she moaned, yet sweet.
Bernini makes that vision visible. Her ecstasy is deliberately ambiguous between spiritual and physical; an 18th-century French visitor famously joked about it in earthly terms.
The golden rays and real light from above mean divine grace descending.
The Cornaro witnesses mirror us, the viewers: everyone is an audience to a miracle.
context: Bernini (1598 to 1680) was Rome’s leading Baroque sculptor and architect, designer of St. Peter’s baldacchino and colonnade.
He took this private commission while out of favor with Pope Innocent X, after a bell tower he built at St. Peter’s had to be torn down.
Teresa of Ávila (1515 to 1582), mystic and reformer, was canonized in 1622. Mystical experience and saints were exactly what Protestants rejected and the Counter-Reformation promoted.
Bernini also wrote and staged plays, which helps explain the theatrical design. He reportedly called it the least bad thing he ever made. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: marble that looks soft, theatrical staging and hidden light point to Bernini, Roman Baroque.
Key term: bel composto (‘beautiful whole’), Bernini’s fusion of architecture, sculpture, painting and light into one work.
Hidden yellow window plus gilt bronze rays equal divine light.
The Cornaro family in theater boxes on the side walls.
If asked about Counter-Reformation goals: an emotional, personal religious experience that also honors a recently canonized saint.
Location trap: Santa Maria della Vittoria, Rome, not St. Peter’s.

90.title: Angel with Arquebus, Asiel Timor Dei
90.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
90.plain: A painting made in the Andes (in present-day Bolivia), probably in the late 1600s, showing an angel dressed like a Spanish nobleman, loading a gun called an arquebus. It belongs to a series of angels painted for the church of Calamarca, near La Paz, by an unnamed artist called the Master of Calamarca. Armed angels became a specialty of colonial Andean art, mixing European military fashion, Catholic angel lore and possibly older Andean ideas about sky beings.
90.spot: A single elegant, youthful figure with small wings against a plain dark background, wearing a wide hat with plumes, lace collar and cuffs and a gold-patterned coat, holding a long gun in a precise loading pose. A Latin name is written at the bottom.
90.remember: ‘Asiel aims’: angel plus arquebus equals Andes. Asiel Timor Dei means ‘Asiel, Fear of God’.
compare: No. 95 (§4.48), The Virgin of Guadalupe: Another colonial religious image that adapts European Catholic imagery for American viewers.
No. 159 (§6.7), City of Cusco: Colonial Cusco shows the same Spanish layering over Andean culture, in architecture.
No. 94 (§4.47), Screen with the Siege of Belgrade and hunting…: The biombo’s battle scene also borrows from European prints to show military glory in the colonies.
90.vocab: syncretism, brocateado, iconography, viceroyalty, print source, archangel.

form: Oil on canvas, flat and decorative, with little depth: the figure stands on a strip of ground before a plain backdrop.
Lavish Spanish court and military fashion of the time: broad-brimmed hat with ostrich plumes, lace, brocade and puffed breeches. Pattern matters more than volume.
The gold-patterned clothing recalls the brocateado (gold applied over paint in patterns) typical of Andean painting schools.
The pose comes from a European printed drill manual. Scholars have traced it to Jacob de Gheyn’s Exercise of Arms (1607), which showed each step of handling a gun.
The face is soft and androgynous, idealized rather than a portrait.
function: One of a series of named angels lining the nave of the church of Calamarca, seen by largely Indigenous (Aymara-speaking) congregations.
Teaching Catholic ideas: angels as God’s army, protecting the faithful and the Church against evil.
It also displayed Spanish colonial power, presenting the colonizer’s elite soldier as holy.
content: Asiel is an angel named in apocryphal texts outside the standard Bible. ‘Timor Dei’ is Latin for ‘Fear of God’.
The arquebus (an early matchlock gun) was the most powerful weapon the Spanish brought. It turns the angel into a soldier of God.

Scholars suggest armed angels may have absorbed Andean associations with sky and weather beings, since gunfire was linked to thunder and lightning. This syncretism (blending of religious traditions) is debated.
Aristocratic dress made heavenly order look like the Spanish social order.
context: Calamarca lay in the Viceroyalty of Peru (Spain’s colonial government in South America), on the high plateau between La Paz and Oruro.
Cuzco and La Paz had busy painting workshops, many staffed by Indigenous and mestizo artists who worked from imported European prints.
Church authorities were uneasy about naming angels beyond Michael, Gabriel and Raphael, yet Andean series of named angels flourished.
‘Master of Calamarca’ is a name invented by scholars for an anonymous painter or workshop; proposed identifications are not certain.
Armed angels like this are unique to the colonial Andes, with no real equivalent in Europe. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: an elegant angel in Spanish clothes holding a gun, in a flat decorative style, points to the colonial Andes (La Paz school), late 1600s.
Key idea: syncretism, Catholic imagery meeting Andean beliefs.
If asked about sources: the pose comes from a European military drill print, showing how colonial artists adapted imported prints.
Function: devotion and conversion in the Calamarca church series.
Trap: it is not a European painting and not a portrait of a real soldier.
If asked to compare with the Virgin of Guadalupe (No. 95): both adapt Catholic images to colonial American audiences.

91.title: Las Meninas
91.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
91.plain: Diego Velázquez’s enormous group portrait of the Spanish royal court from about 1656, centered on the five-year-old Princess Margarita and her maids of honor (‘meninas’), with Velázquez himself painting a huge canvas at the left. The king and queen appear only as a blurry reflection in a mirror at the back, standing, it seems, exactly where you are. It is endlessly debated because the painting keeps asking who the subject is, who is watching and what is being painted.
91.spot: A tall, dark room with a high ceiling and paintings on the walls. A small blonde girl in a wide silver-white dress stands at center while a kneeling maid offers her a red cup; a painter with a palette stands at left by the back of a huge canvas; two dwarfs and a sleepy dog are at right; a man stands in a glowing doorway; a small mirror holds two faces.
91.remember: ‘Las Meninas, the mirror mystery’: Velázquez, 1656. Meninas means maids of honor.
compare: No. 68 (§4.21), The Arnolfini Portrait: Van Eyck’s back-wall mirror, which Velázquez probably saw in the royal collection, also reveals figures standing where the viewer stands.
No. 87 (§4.40), Self-Portrait with Saskia: Both show the artist at work, one serving a king, one selling to the open market.
No. 86 (§4.39), Henri IV Receives the Portrait of Marie de’ M…: Rubens also builds a royal painting around a picture within the picture.
91.vocab: group portrait, self-portrait, naturalism, focal point, brushwork.

form: Oil on canvas, about 3.2 by 2.8 m, with life-size figures.
Loose, visible brushwork: up close the princess’s dress dissolves into dabs, but from a distance it resolves. Manet and the Impressionists admired this.
Deep space and naturalistic light: windows at right light the figures, the upper room sinks into shadow and a bright back doorway pulls the eye deep.
Multiple focal points compete: princess, painter, mirror and the man in the doorway.
The mirror recalls the Arnolfini Portrait (No. 68), which was then in the Spanish royal collection, so Velázquez likely knew it.
function: Painted for Philip IV and hung in his private summer oﬀice in the Alcázar palace, Madrid: a picture for the king’s own eyes.
Rescued from the 1734 fire that destroyed the Alcázar; now in the Prado, Madrid.
Its old title was The Family of Philip IV ; it was called Las Meninas in a Prado catalogue in 1843.
content: Cast: Infanta Margarita Teresa; maids María Agustina Sarmiento (kneeling with a red clay cup of water) and Isabel de Velasco; dwarfs Mari Bárbola and Nicolasito Pertusato (foot on the dog); a chaperone and guard; the queen’s chamberlain in the doorway.
The mirror shows King Philip IV and Queen Mariana. Perhaps they are posing where we stand, and Velázquez is painting them; scholars disagree.
Velázquez wears the red cross of the Order of Santiago, a knighthood he received in 1659, so it was added after the painting was finished.
The paintings on the back wall have been identified as copies after Rubens of myths about divine artistic contests, a hint about art’s status.
context: Diego Velázquez (1599 to 1660) of Seville was court painter to Philip IV from 1623 and also held palace oﬀices; the key at his belt marks his post.
In Spain painting counted as a manual craft, and knighthood required proof you did not work with your hands for money. The painting argues painting is an intellectual, noble art.
Spain’s Habsburg monarchy was in decline; Margarita later married the Holy Roman Emperor Leopold I.
Picasso painted 58 variations on it in 1957, and philosopher Michel Foucault opened his book The Order of Things (1966) with an essay on it. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: loose brushwork, a deep dark room, court figures and the painter at an easel point to Velázquez, Spanish Baroque, c. 1656.
The mirror reflects Philip IV and Queen Mariana.
Self-portrait with the Santiago cross: the status of painting and the painter.
If asked about the viewer: we may stand in the king and queen’s place.
Count carefully: there are two dwarfs, not one.
If asked to compare with the Arnolfini Portrait (No. 68): both use a back-wall mirror to reveal figures outside the picture.
If asked to compare with Rembrandt (No. 87): both show the artist at work.

92.title: Woman Holding a Balance
92.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
92.plain: A small, quiet painting by Johannes Vermeer of Delft, from about 1664, showing a woman in a blue fur-trimmed jacket holding up an empty set of scales by a window. Behind her hangs a painting of the Last Judgment, when Christians believe God weighs souls. It looks like an everyday moment but works as a calm meditation on judgment, balance and life choices, and it shows off Vermeer’s famous soft light.
92.spot: A small, dim interior: a woman in a blue jacket with white fur trim and a white head covering stands at a table, eyes lowered, holding a tiny balance. Soft light falls from a window at upper left behind an orange-yellow curtain; pearls and gold sit on the table; a dark Last Judgment painting hangs behind her and a mirror hangs at left.
92.remember: ‘Vermeer’s very still scales’, c. 1664: the balance is empty, and the Judgment hangs behind.
compare: No. 24 (§3.13), Last judgment of Hu-Nefer, from his tomb: The Egyptian papyrus shows the heart weighed against a feather; scales stand for judgment of the soul in both.
No. 68 (§4.21), The Arnolfini Portrait: Both are Northern domestic interiors whose everyday objects carry moral or religious meaning.
No. 96 (§4.49), Fruit and Insects: Ruysch’s still life also uses beautiful, costly things to hint at life’s fragility.
92.vocab: genre scene, camera obscura, ultramarine, vanitas, vanishing point.

form: Oil on canvas, only about 40 by 36 cm.
Soft, diffused window light from the upper left glints off pearls and gold as tiny dots of light.
Calm geometry: horizontal table, vertical picture frames. The perspective lines converge near her hand holding the scales, putting the balance at the structural center.
A restrained palette of blues (including costly ultramarine, a pigment ground from lapis lazuli), yellows and browns.
Vermeer may have used a camera obscura (a dark box with a lens that projects an image) to study light effects; scholars disagree.
function: A genre painting (a scene of everyday life) for the Dutch open market and private contemplation in a well-off home.
It may have belonged to Vermeer’s Delft patron Pieter van Ruijven; a painting matching it was listed in a 1696 Amsterdam sale as a young lady weighing gold.
Now in the National Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C.
content: Close study shows the pans are empty: she is not weighing pearls or gold. The act is about balance and judgment, not money.
The Last Judgment painting, with Christ judging souls, sits right behind her, linking her small act of weighing to the final weighing of the soul against earthly treasure.
The mirror can suggest vanity or self-knowledge. Whether she is pregnant or simply wearing the fashionable puffed jacket of the time is debated.
Vermeer married into a Catholic family and probably converted, so some scholars read a Catholic message about free will and moderation; this is not certain.
context: Johannes Vermeer (1632 to 1675) of Delft worked slowly; only about 35 paintings survive. He died in debt, leaving a wife and many children.
Dutch Golden Age: a prosperous, mostly Protestant merchant republic buying genre scenes, still lifes and landscapes.
Pearls and gold reflect the wealth of Dutch global trade, including the Dutch East India Company.
Vermeer was largely forgotten for almost two centuries until a French critic rediscovered him in the 1860s. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: soft light from a left window, a quiet interior and a woman absorbed in a task point to Vermeer, Delft, 1660s.
Empty balance plus the Last Judgment equals spiritual weighing and moderation.
Function: genre painting for the open market.
If asked to compare across cultures: Hu-Nefer (No. 24) shows an Egyptian heart weighed against a feather; scales mean judgment in both.
If asked to compare with the Arnolfini Portrait (No. 68): a domestic interior full of symbolic objects.
Trap: it is small (about 40 cm), and Vermeer, not Rembrandt.

93.title: The Palace at Versailles
93.artist: Louis Le Vau and Jules Hardouin-Mansart (architects); Versailles, France
93.medium: Masonry, stone, wood, iron, and gold leaf (architecture); marble and bronze
93.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
93.plain: The enormous palace and gardens that Louis XIV, the ‘Sun King’, built outside Paris by expanding his father’s hunting lodge, with major building beginning in 1669. He moved his court and government there in 1682 and made the nobility live under his eye, turning daily life into ceremony with himself at the center. Every part, from the symmetrical facades to the Hall of Mirrors and the geometric gardens, was designed to show absolute royal power, even over nature.
93.spot: A very long, low, symmetrical classical facade with rows of arched windows and a flat roofline lined with a balustrade and statues. Vast geometric gardens with straight paths, fountains, pools and a long canal spread along a central axis. Inside, a gilded gallery lined with arched mirrors and chandeliers.
93.remember: ‘17 windows, 17 mirrors, 1 Sun King’: Louis XIV, building begun 1669, court moved in 1682.
compare: No. 206 (§9.15), Forbidden City: The Forbidden City also uses a strict central axis and layers of controlled access to display imperial power.
No. 86 (§4.39), Henri IV Receives the Portrait of Marie de’ M…: Rubens’s Medici cycle is French royal propaganda on canvas, a generation earlier.
No. 30 (§3.19), Audience Hall: The Persian apadana also staged a ruler’s power through a vast ceremonial hall.
93.vocab: axial plan, symmetry, parterre, gallery, absolutism, Baroque, gilding.

form: Stone, brick, wood, iron and gold leaf, with marble and bronze sculpture and water-filled gardens.

The garden facade is long, horizontal and three-storied, with a rusticated ground floor, a main floor with tall arched windows and a balustraded top. It is a restrained, classical take on the Baroque.

The Hall of Mirrors (1678 to 1684, by Hardouin-Mansart), about 73 m long, sets 17 arched windows opposite 17 arches filled with 357 mirrors. Large mirrors were hugely expensive, and these were made in France to rival Venice.
Charles Le Brun painted the hall’s ceiling with Louis’s military and political victories.
André Le Nôtre’s gardens use axial symmetry (mirror-image halves along a central line), parterres (flat, geometric planting beds), fountains and a Grand Canal over 1.5 km long.
function: Royal residence and seat of government from 1682 until the French Revolution in 1789.
A political tool: nobles had to live at court, spending fortunes on fashion and gambling while competing for royal favor, which kept them from rebelling.
The king’s rising and going to bed were public ceremonies, and simply being present was a privilege.
Later uses: a museum from the 1830s; the German Empire was proclaimed in the Hall of Mirrors in 1871, and the Treaty of Versailles was signed there in 1919.
content: Louis cast himself as Apollo, the sun god. Sun motifs are everywhere, and the Apollo Fountain sits on the main garden axis.
Roads from Paris converge on the palace and the gardens radiate out from it: the king as the center of the state and the universe.
Geometric control of nature stands for control of France.
Mirrors meant wealth, light and self-display, and they advertised French industry under the minister Colbert.
context: Louis XIV reigned 1643 to 1715. Riots of his childhood, the Fronde (1648 to 1653), taught him to distrust Paris and the nobility.
The team: Louis Le Vau (architect), Jules Hardouin-Mansart (architect after 1678), Charles Le Brun (painting and decoration) and André Le Nôtre (gardens).
The same team had built the chateau of Vaux-le-Vicomte for finance minister Nicolas Fouquet. Louis had Fouquet arrested in 1661 and hired his designers.
The palace cost staggering sums and huge labor, from draining marshes to pumping water for the fountains, and it became the model for palaces across Europe. On the exam.
If asked about function: absolutism, controlling the nobility, seat of government from 1682.
Hall of Mirrors: 17 windows facing 17 mirrored arches, with Le Brun’s victory ceiling.
Le Nôtre’s gardens mean control of nature through geometry.
Names: Le Vau, Hardouin-Mansart, Le Brun, Le Nôtre.
Later history: German Empire proclaimed in 1871; treaty ending World War I signed in 1919.
If asked to compare with the Forbidden City (No. 206): both use a central axis and controlled access to express a ruler’s power.
Trap: begun 1669 but built in phases; the Hall of Mirrors is 1678 to 1684.

94.title: Screen with the Siege of Belgrade and hunting scene
94.medium: Tempera and resin on wood, shell inlay
94.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
94.plain: A large folding screen made in Mexico City around 1697 to 1701, painted on both sides. One side shows the 1688 Siege of Belgrade, when Habsburg armies captured the city from the Ottoman Turks; the other shows elegant aristocrats hunting. The screen form came from Japan and the shimmering shell inlay recalls Asian lacquer, while the subjects came from Europe, so one object maps the global trade network running through New Spain.
94.spot: A wide, multi-panel screen. One side is a bird’s-eye panorama of a walled city under siege, with tiny soldiers, cannon smoke, tents and rivers, glittering with bits of shell, inside a wide flowered border. The other side shows horsemen and hunters in a landscape.
94.remember: ‘Byōbu to biombo’: Japan to Mexico on the galleon, with Belgrade’s battle on the front, c. 1697 to 1701.
compare: No. 210 (§9.19), White and Red Plum Blossoms: Korin’s Japanese folding screen represents the byōbu tradition that biombos copied.
No. 95 (§4.48), The Virgin of Guadalupe: The same González workshop circle used enconchado for this shimmering devotional image.
No. 90 (§4.43), Angel with Arquebus, Asiel Timor Dei: Another colonial painting that adapts European military prints for American viewers.
94.vocab: biombo, byōbu, enconchado, mother-of-pearl, bird’s-eye view.

form: A biombo (Spanish word from the Japanese byōbu, ‘wind wall’, a folding screen) with ten hinged panels, about 2.3 m tall and 2.76 m wide.
Enconchado (a Mexican technique of setting slivers of mother-of-pearl shell into the surface and painting thin, see-through layers over them so the shell shimmers through).
The College Board lists tempera and resin on wood with shell inlay; the Brooklyn Museum describes it as oil on wood with mother-of-pearl. Sources differ.
The battle side is a high, bird’s-eye view (seen from above) that runs continuously across the panels, ignoring the folds, crowded with tiny figures.
A wide border of flowers and scrolls frames the scene, much like lacquer and textile borders.
function: Luxury furniture for an elite home in New Spain (colonial Mexico): it divided rooms, blocked drafts and showed off wealth and taste.
Painted on both sides so it could be seen from either room. Scholars suggest the battle faced the more public reception space and the hunt faced a private one.
Some scholars connect it to Viceroy José Sarmiento de Valladares (in oﬀice 1696 to 1701), which would explain the dates, but this is not certain. It is now in the Brooklyn Museum.
content: In 1688, during the Great Turkish War, Habsburg imperial forces led by the Elector of Bavaria took Belgrade from the Ottomans, five years after the failed Ottoman siege of Vienna. Europeans celebrated it as a Christian victory.
Spain’s king, Charles II, was also a Habsburg, so colonial elites identified with the victory and with Catholic Europe.
The hunt shows aristocratic leisure and skill, the peaceful side of noble identity, while the battle shows its military side.
The battle scene was probably adapted from European prints, as colonial artists often did.
context: The Manila galleons (1565 to 1815) carried Chinese silk and porcelain and Japanese screens and lacquer from the Philippines to Acapulco, paid for with Mexican silver.
Japanese screens also arrived as diplomatic gifts; a Japanese embassy passed through Mexico in 1614. Mexican workshops were making biombos for local buyers by the early 1600s.
The González family (including Miguel and Juan) were leading enconchado specialists in Mexico City (see No. 95).
The object combines Asian form, European subject and an American workshop: a textbook case of early global exchange. On the exam.
If asked about global exchange: Japanese form, European subject, Mexican workshop and shell inlay.
Know the terms: biombo (from byōbu) and enconchado (shell inlay).
Content: Siege of Belgrade (1688) on one side, a hunting scene on the other.
Function: a domestic room divider and status object for colonial elites.
If asked to compare with White and Red Plum Blossoms (No. 210): the Japanese folding screen is the source of the form.
Trap: made in Mexico, not Japan or Spain.

95.title: The Virgin of Guadalupe (Virgen de Guadalupe)
95.medium: Oil on canvas on wood, inlaid with mother-of-pearl
95.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
95.plain: A copy of Mexico’s most sacred image, the Virgin of Guadalupe, made by Miguel González in Mexico City around 1698 using enconchado: pieces of mother-of-pearl set under the paint so it glows. The original image, kept at Tepeyac outside Mexico City, is said to have appeared miraculously on the cloak of an Indigenous man, Juan Diego, in 1531. Copies like this spread her image as a symbol of Mexican Catholic identity, and later of Mexico itself.
95.spot: A standing Mary with joined hands and tilted head, in a blue-green star-covered mantle over a rose-colored dress, framed by an almond-shaped burst of golden rays. She stands on a dark crescent moon held up by a small angel, with four small scenes in the corners, a shimmering surface and an ornate border.
95.remember: ‘Guadalupe glows’: González, c. 1698, mother-of-pearl. The legend is 1531; the painting is 1698.
compare: No. 54 (§4.7), Virgin: Both are Marian images in traditions that treated certain images as miraculous or holy in themselves.
No. 94 (§4.47), Screen with the Siege of Belgrade and hunting…: The same enconchado shellinlay technique, used for a secular screen.
No. 90 (§4.43), Angel with Arquebus, Asiel Timor Dei: Another colonial devotional image adapting Catholic subjects for American audiences.
95.vocab: enconchado, mandorla, vignette, iconography, syncretism, criollo.

form: Oil on canvas mounted on wood, with enconchado (mother-of-pearl inlay under thin, seethrough paint layers).
A frontal, symmetrical figure that faithfully copies the original image. Exact copying mattered because the original was believed not to be made by human hands.
A mandorla (an almond-shaped frame of light around a holy figure) of golden rays surrounds Mary.
Four corner vignettes (small inset scenes) tell the apparition story.
The shell shows through in the garments, rays and border, giving a glittering effect that recalls Asian lacquer.
function: A devotional image, a stand-in for the original at the shrine of Guadalupe for worship at home or in church.
Enconchado works were expensive luxury objects, and some were shipped to Spain.
It spread a devotion that tied New Spain’s identity to a miracle that happened there. Now at LACMA (Los Angeles County Museum of Art).
content: Mary appears as the Woman of the Apocalypse from the Book of Revelation, ‘clothed with the sun’ with the moon under her feet, imagery also used for the Immaculate Conception.
Stars on the mantle, sun rays and the moon present her as a cosmic queen; for Nahua viewers, sun and moon imagery may have carried their own meanings.
The corners show her appearances to Juan Diego and the miracle: roses blooming in December, and her image appearing on his tilma (cloak) before Bishop Juan de Zumárraga.
Her darker complexion led many to see her as identifying with Indigenous and mestizo Mexicans; she is affectionately called ‘La Morenita’.
context: Legend: in December 1531 Mary spoke in Nahuatl to Juan Diego on the hill of Tepeyac and asked for a church. The full story was first published in 1648 to 1649, and historians debate its early history.
Tepeyac had been a shrine to Tonantzin (‘Our Revered Mother’), an Aztec mother goddess; some scholars see continuity, others disagree.
Criollos (American-born Spaniards) embraced her as proof that God favored New Spain. In 1754 the pope confirmed her as patroness of New Spain.
In 1810 Father Miguel Hidalgo carried her banner at the start of the war for independence. Juan Diego was canonized in 2002.
Miguel González and his relatives were the leading enconchado makers in Mexico City. On the exam.
Content: Juan Diego, Tepeyac, the tilma and 1531; the corner scenes tell the story.
Technique: enconchado, influenced by Asian lacquer and shell work arriving via the Manila galleons.
Iconography: rays, crescent moon, star-covered mantle, angel below.
Context: criollo identity and later a national symbol of Mexico.
Syncretism with Tonantzin is a common argument but debated; say so.
Trap: the legend is 1531, but this painting is c. 1698.
If asked to compare with the Theotokos icon (No. 54): both come from traditions of revered images believed to carry holy power.

96.title: Fruit and Insects
96.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
96.plain: A 1711 still life by Rachel Ruysch, the most famous and best-paid Dutch still-life painter of her day, showing fruit, grain and a bird’s nest heaped on a forest floor, with insects and a lizard crawling through it. The detail is scientific, since her father was a celebrated anatomist and botanist, but the scene is impossible: fruits from different seasons ripen together. Beauty, abundance and decay share the same panel.
96.spot: A dark background with a spill of glowing peaches, grapes, grain stalks and a bird’s nest with eggs across a mossy forest floor. Butterflies, other insects and a small lizard creep among them, all sharply lit and finely detailed.
96.remember: ‘Rachel Ruysch: ripe, rotting, realistic’, 1711. Ruysch’s bugs are there to bug you about death.
compare: No. 92 (§4.45), Woman Holding a Balance: Vermeer also uses a quiet arrangement of precious things to point toward judgment and transience.
No. 110 (§5.12), Still Life in Studio: Daguerre’s early photograph is a still life arranged in the studio, carrying the tradition into a new medium.
No. 66 (§4.19), Annunciation Triptych: The Merode Altarpiece shows the older Netherlandish habit of hiding meaning in carefully painted objects.

form: Oil on wood panel, about 89 by 69 cm, built up in thin glazes (transparent layers of oil paint) with almost invisible brushstrokes.
Still life (a painting of arranged objects such as fruit, flowers and food).
Strong light against a dark background makes forms pop forward like a spotlit stage.
An asymmetrical, cascading arrangement keeps the eye moving across the pile.
Botanical accuracy: individual species can be identified, and insects are painted with a naturalist’s precision.
function: A luxury collectible for wealthy buyers and princes, and a display of skill.
Painted while Ruysch was court painter to Johann Wilhelm, Elector Palatine, in Düsseldorf (1708 to 1716). His wife was a Medici, which probably explains how it reached Florence. Now in the Uﬀizi.
It also appealed to collectors’ interest in natural history, the same impulse behind cabinets of specimens.
content: Vanitas (an image reminding you that life, beauty and wealth are short-lived): ripe fruit begins to spoil while insects nibble.
Life cycle: the nest with eggs suggests birth, ripe fruit maturity, decay death.
Fruits from different seasons appear together, so this is a composite built from separate studies, an invented abundance rather than one observed moment.
The richness can also be read as praise of God’s creation, seen through careful scientific looking.
context: Rachel Ruysch (1664 to 1750) of Amsterdam was the daughter of Frederik Ruysch, a professor of anatomy and botany famous for his preserved specimens, which gave her access to plants and insects.
She trained from about age 15 with still-life painter Willem van Aelst, married painter Juriaen Pool in 1693, had ten children and painted into her eighties.
She joined the painters’ guild in The Hague in 1701, one of the first women to do so. Her paintings reportedly sold for more than Rembrandt usually received.
Women were barred from training with nude models, so still life, which could be done at home, was a field where they could excel. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: a dark background with precise fruit, nests and insects points to Rachel Ruysch, Dutch, 1711.
Meaning: vanitas, abundance with decay.
Context: a successful woman artist, a court painter with very high prices.
Science and art: her father’s anatomy and botany collections.
Trap: oil on wood, and 1711, at the late end of the Dutch still-life tradition, not the mid1600s.
If asked to compare with Vermeer (No. 92): Dutch paintings that use beautiful objects to make moral points.

97.title: Spaniard and Indian Produce a Mestizo
97.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
97.plain: A painting from one of the earliest casta series, made in Mexico City around 1715 and attributed to Juan Rodríguez Juárez. Each canvas in a series shows a family whose parents come from different racial groups, labeled with the name given to their child; here a Spanish father and an Indigenous mother produce a ‘mestizo’. The paintings look like warm family portraits, but they promoted a colonial ranking system with Spaniards at the top.
97.spot: A small family group close to the picture plane: a man in a European suit and powdered wig, a woman in an embroidered Indigenous tunic with fine fabric, and their small child. A painted caption names the mixture.
97.remember: ‘Casta equals caste chart’: Spaniard plus Indian gives Mestizo, c. 1715, Rodríguez Juárez.
compare: No. 81 (§4.34), Frontispiece of the Codex Mendoza: Another New Spain image that packages colonial knowledge for European eyes.
No. 99 (§5.1), Portrait of Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz: Cabrera’s portrait of Sor Juana comes from the same 18th-century Mexico City painting world and its criollo elite.
No. 95 (§4.48), The Virgin of Guadalupe: The Virgin of Guadalupe shows how criollos built a positive colonial identity, while casta paintings sorted and ranked people.
97.vocab: casta painting, mestizo, criollo, huipil, limpieza de sangre.

form: Oil on canvas, painted with the polish of a leading Mexico City portraitist.
The figures are carefully individualized, with highly detailed textiles: lace, embroidery and tailoring all signal status and ethnicity.
The woman wears a huipil (a traditional embroidered Indigenous tunic), while the man wears fashionable European dress.
A painted caption names the combination, roughly ‘From Spaniard and Indian, Mestizo is produced’.
It is one canvas in a numbered series, usually sixteen, read in order like a chart.
function: Casta series classified the mixed population of New Spain. Many were bought by Spanish oﬀicials and sent to Spain as records or souvenirs of the colony.
They presented colonial society as orderly, prosperous and classifiable, a kind of propaganda of control.
This one is now at Breamore House, a country house in Hampshire, England.
content: The Spanish father and Indigenous mother appear dignified; the child is labeled mestizo, the first and highest-ranked mixture in most series.
In the system, the less Spanish ancestry a person had, the lower their rank. Mixtures had names like castizo, mulato, morisco and lobo.
Key asymmetry: in most series Indigenous ancestry could be ‘cleaned’ back to Spanish over generations, but African ancestry was presented as permanent.
The idea grew from the Spanish concept of limpieza de sangre (‘purity of blood’), first used against people of Jewish or Muslim descent in Spain.
context: By the 1700s New Spain had a large mixed population. Labels affected taxes (Indigenous people paid tribute) and access to guilds, the priesthood and universities.
Real life was more fluid than the paintings: a person’s label could shift with wealth, clothing and paperwork. The paintings fixed what was actually unstable.
Casta painting flourished from about 1711 to the 1790s, and more than 100 series survive. This series, c. 1715, is among the earliest.
Juan Rodríguez Juárez (1675 to 1728) came from a Mexico City family of painters. ‘Attributed to’ means the identification rests on style, not a signature. On the exam.
If asked about function: to classify and rank the mixed population, largely for European and elite audiences.
Content: Spaniard plus Indian equals mestizo; part of a numbered series.
Context terms: casta system, limpieza de sangre, colonial hierarchy.
Attribution: attributed to Juan Rodríguez Juárez, c. 1715.
Trap: these are types, not portraits of a specific real family.
If asked to compare with the Codex Mendoza (No. 81): both are made in New Spain to explain the colony to Europeans.

98.title: The Tête à Tête, from Marriage à la Mode
98.content: CA3, Early Europe and Colonial Americas
98.plain: The second of six paintings in William Hogarth’s comic-tragic series Marriage A-la-Mode, c. 1743, about a loveless marriage arranged between a broke earl’s son and a rich merchant’s daughter. In this scene, soon after the wedding, both spouses are wrecked after separate late nights, the house is a mess and the steward gives up on their unpaid bills. Hogarth packed every object with clues, then sold engraved copies to a wide middle-class public.
98.spot: An elegant drawing room in disarray. A young man slumps in a chair at center, hat on and hands in pockets, while a small dog sniffs a woman’s cap sticking out of his coat. A young woman stretches at left near an overturned chair and playing cards; an older man in a dark coat walks off with a fistful of bills; an arched room with paintings and a clock lies behind.
98.remember: ‘Hogarth’s hangover’: The Tête à Tête, c. 1743, episode 2 of 6. The clock says it’s past noon.
compare: No. 101 (§5.3), The Swing: Fragonard’s Rococo painting enjoys aristocratic flirtation that Hogarth satirizes.
No. 59 (§4.12), Bayeux Tapestry: The Bayeux Tapestry also tells a story in sequential scenes full of readable detail.
No. 79 (§4.32), Allegory of Law and Grace: Cranach’s woodcut also used inexpensive prints to spread a moral message widely.
98.vocab: satire, narrative series, engraving, Rococo, genre scene, modern moral subject. 5 Later Europe and Americas Content area 4 · 1750–1980 C.E. · works 99–152 · about 21% of the multiple-choice section. From the 1750s to about 1980 in Europe and the Americas: Rococo, Neoclassicism, Romanticism, Realism, Impressionism and all the “-isms” of modern art, plus photography and new architecture made of iron, steel and glass. The big theme is artists breaking rules: leaving the oﬀicial Academy, painting ordinary life instead of heroes, and finally questioning what counts as art at all.

form: Oil on canvas, about 70 by 91 cm, painted as models for engravings.
Staged like a play: characters spread across a shallow stage-like space facing us, with exaggerated faces and body language.
A crowded interior where every object tells part of the story.
Fussy ornaments mock fashionable Rococo taste (the light, curvy, ornamental 18th-century style that came from France).
One painting in a narrative series read in sequence, like panels of a comic strip.
function: A moralizing satire (mocking vice and folly to correct behavior), aimed at aristocratic marriages for money and at middle-class social climbing.
Engravings of the series were published in 1745 and sold by subscription; Hogarth earned his money from prints, not paintings.
Hogarth had lobbied for the 1735 Engravers’ Copyright Act, often called ‘Hogarth’s Act’, to stop pirated copies.
The paintings were auctioned in 1751 and are now in the National Gallery, London.
content: The husband, Viscount Squanderfield, is exhausted after a night out. The dog pulls a woman’s lace cap from his pocket, evidence of an affair, and his sword lies broken on the floor.
The wife has stayed up hosting a card party: cards, an overturned chair, music and a book about the card game whist lie scattered.
The steward holds unpaid bills, with only one receipt, and a Methodist tract in his pocket; he raises his hand in despair.

The clock reads past noon. Religious paintings hang beside a curtained one with only a bare foot showing, a hint of hidden erotic art and hypocrisy. Over the mantel, a painting of Cupid amid ruins means love in ruins.
context: William Hogarth (1697 to 1764) of London trained as an engraver on silver and invented ‘modern moral subjects’: A Harlot’s Progress (1732), A Rake’s Progress (1735), then this series.

Plot: 1, the fathers negotiate money for a title; 2, this scene; 3, a quack doctor visit; 4, the wife’s morning party with her lawyer-lover Silvertongue; 5, Silvertongue kills the husband; 6, the wife poisons herself.
Britain’s rising merchant class wanted aristocratic rank, and indebted aristocrats needed merchant cash; marriage was the deal.
Hogarth disliked imported French and Italian taste and promoted English art. The French title, meaning ‘fashionable marriage’, is itself a jab. On the exam.
If asked to attribute: a crowded, satirical, story-packed English interior points to Hogarth, c. 1743.
Function: moral satire, spread through engravings to a mass market.
Content clues: dog with cap, broken sword, steward with bills, clock past noon, cards.
Context: arranged marriages of money and rank in 18th-century England.
If asked to compare with The Swing (No. 101): Fragonard celebrates aristocratic frivolity; Hogarth mocks it.
Trap: this is scene 2 of 6, and the series was best known through its engravings.

99.title: Portrait of Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz
99.plain: A large oil portrait of Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz, a nun in Mexico City who was also the most famous poet and scholar of colonial Latin America. Miguel Cabrera painted it around 1750, roughly 55 years after she died, so it is a tribute, not a sitting. Instead of showing her as a saint in a vision, it shows her as an intellectual surrounded by books, which makes it one of the clearest images of a learned woman from the colonial Americas.
99.spot: A nun in a white habit and black veil sits at a writing desk in front of tall shelves packed with books. A large round painted medallion is pinned on her chest, one hand rests on the pages of an open book, and the other holds a rosary.
99.remember: Sor Juana would rather read than anything, so Cabrera parked her in a library. Think ‘Cabrera’s camera, 1750’: a posthumous snapshot of the Tenth Muse of New Spain.
compare: No. 97 (§4.50), Spaniard and Indian Produce a Mestizo: Also from New Spain in the 1700s; a casta painting about race and social rank versus a portrait celebrating one woman’s intellect.
No. 105 (§5.7), Self-Portrait: Another woman shown as a working professional, with the tools of her craft in hand.
No. 95 (§4.48), The Virgin of Guadalupe: Colonial Mexican religious art; Cabrera himself studied and copied the Virgin of Guadalupe image.
99.vocab: posthumous portrait, escudo de monja, attribute, cartouche, criollo, New Spain, casta painting.

form: Oil on canvas (pigment mixed with oil, painted on stretched cloth), close to life-size, in the polished European portrait style that wealthy patrons in New Spain (colonial Mexico) expected.
She sits in a high-backed chair at a cloth-covered table holding an inkwell, quill pens and papers: the working tools of a writer.
The background is a wall of leather-bound books. Cabrera painted the spines carefully, and scholars have tried to match them to real authors in theology, science and classical literature.
On her chest is an escudo de monja (nun’s shield: a large painted medallion worn by nuns in New Spain) showing the Annunciation, the angel telling Mary she will bear Christ.
A painted text panel, or cartouche (decorative frame holding an inscription), records her biography, a standard feature of colonial portraits of notable people.
Because she was long dead, Cabrera worked from an earlier image, probably the portrait by Juan de Miranda from about 1713. His version is softer, richer in color and more elegant.
function: A posthumous (made after death) commemorative portrait honoring a famous member of the Hieronymite convent of San Jerónimo in Mexico City. Exactly who ordered it is not documented; it may have been made for the convent itself.
It held up a model of devout but learned womanhood for nuns, clergy and the educated criollo (American-born Spanish) elite.
Today it hangs in the National Museum of History in Chapultepec Castle, Mexico City, and it is the standard image of Sor Juana reproduced on stamps, book covers and banknotes.
content: Books, inkwell and quills are her attributes (objects that identify a person), the same props used for scholar saints. Fittingly, her order was named after Saint Jerome, the patron saint of scholars and translators.
The habit, the rosary and the Annunciation badge insist that her learning sits inside religious devotion, not against it.
The open book under her hand shows her in the middle of study: a mind at work rather than a passive pious figure.
The overflowing library is a claim about range. She wrote love poems, plays, theology and essays, and owned scientific and musical instruments as well as books.
context: Juana Inés de Asbaje was born around 1648 near Mexico City, was a child prodigy at the viceroy’s court, and in 1669 entered the convent largely because it let her study and write instead of marry.
Her poems were published in Spain from 1689, where admirers called her the Tenth Muse. Her 1691 letter, the Respuesta a Sor Filotea, defends women’s right to learn.

Church superiors, including the Bishop of Puebla and the archbishop of Mexico, pressured her. Around 1693 to 1694 she gave up her library and instruments and renewed her vows. She died in 1695 nursing sisters during an epidemic.
Miguel Cabrera (1695 to 1768), born in Oaxaca, was the leading painter of his day in New Spain. His ancestry is uncertain; he may have been of Zapotec or mixed descent.
Cabrera also painted casta paintings, examined the original Virgin of Guadalupe image in 1751 with other painters, and helped found an early painters’ academy in Mexico City in 1754.
By the 1750s criollos were proud of local achievements, and Sor Juana was a hero of that pride. Today she appears on Mexico’s 100-peso note. On the exam.
If asked to attribute it → New Spain, mid-1700s: European portrait conventions, a nun’s escudo badge and a biographical cartouche.
Trap: it is not a self-portrait and not painted from life. Cabrera painted it about 55 years after her death.
Painter: Miguel Cabrera, not Manuel de Arellano (No. 95) or Juan Rodríguez Juárez (No. 97).
Key theme: women and learning. She is shown as a scholar, not as a mystic or a saint in a vision.
If asked about context → Church authorities pressured her to stop writing; she defended women’s education in the 1691 Respuesta.
Function → a posthumous commemorative portrait for a colonial elite audience proud of a local genius.
Visual evidence for a scholar: books, desk, quills, inkwell, hand on an open book.

100.title: A Philosopher Giving a Lecture on the Orrery
100.plain: A big night scene in which a lecturer shows a group of people a mechanical model of the solar system, lit by a single hidden lamp that stands in for the sun. Joseph Wright of Derby painted it in England in the 1760s. The point is that science itself is treated with the drama and glowing light that earlier painters used for religious miracles, which makes it a picture of the Enlightenment.
100.spot: A dark room, a ring of glowing faces around a brass machine of hoops and little balls, and a boy in black silhouette in the foreground blocking the light source. A man in a red robe on the right leads the demonstration, and a man on the left takes notes.
100.remember: Wright got it right: the lamp is the sun, the faces are the planets. Orrery = ‘or very science-y’. Joseph Wright of Derby, 1760s, England’s Enlightenment.
compare: No. 85 (§4.38), Calling of Saint Matthew: Same tenebrist lighting, but Caravaggio uses it for a divine calling and Wright uses it for a science lesson.
No. 76 (§4.29), School of Athens: Both gather thinkers around ideas; Raphael idealizes ancient philosophers, Wright shows ordinary modern people learning.
No. 101 (§5.3), The Swing: Painted in the same decade: Enlightenment seriousness versus Rococo pleasure.
100.vocab: orrery, tenebrism, chiaroscuro, Enlightenment, heliocentric, history painting, genre scene.

form: Oil on canvas, about 147 by 203 centimeters (roughly 5 by 7 feet), a large size usually saved for history painting.
Lit by one hidden lamp at the center of the orrery, so faces glow against deep darkness: tenebrism (extreme dark and light contrast) or strong chiaroscuro (light and shadow modeling).
Wright learned this candlelight effect from Caravaggio’s followers, especially Dutch painters such as Gerrit van Honthorst. He became famous for these ‘candlelight pictures’.
The figures form a circle around the machine, so the composition itself orbits the light, the way planets circle the sun.
Faces range from children leaning eagerly on the rail to a man lost in thought and a note-taker. Each reacts differently, a study in human attention.
Polished brass hoops and tiny planets are painted with sharp, almost photographic precision.
function: Painted for exhibition and sale. It was shown at the Society of Artists in London in 1766 and bought by Washington Shirley, the 5th Earl Ferrers, an amateur astronomer who owned an orrery himself.
It records a real social activity of the time: paying audiences, including families and women, attending lectures in which traveling teachers demonstrated science with models.
Today it is the star of the Derby Museum and Art Gallery in Derby, England.
content: An orrery is a clockwork model of the solar system, named after Charles Boyle, Earl of Orrery, who owned an early one. Here it demonstrates an eclipse, with the shadow falling across a planet.
The lamp-sun shows the heliocentric (sun-centered) model, a symbol of reason and observation replacing older beliefs.
Light means knowledge: the people literally become ‘enlightened’. The arrangement recalls a Nativity, where faces glow around the Christ child, now replaced by science.
The lecturer, sometimes compared to Isaac Newton, plays the role a saint or prophet would have played in a religious painting. The note-taker is probably Wright’s friend Peter Perez Burdett.
context: The Enlightenment (about 1680 to 1800) promoted reason, experiment and education, and science became popular entertainment for the middle and upper classes.
Joseph Wright of Derby (1734 to 1797) worked in the English Midlands, the heart of the early Industrial Revolution, not in fashionable London.
His friends included scientists and industrialists in the circle that became the Lunar Society, such as Erasmus Darwin and Josiah Wedgwood.
Critics did not know how to classify it: modern people doing something ordinary, painted at a scale and seriousness meant for gods and heroes.
He followed it with An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump (1768), not on the required list, another candlelit science scene. On the exam.
If asked how it reflects the Enlightenment → science as the subject, light as a metaphor for knowledge, and a mixed audience learning together.
Technique → hidden single light source and tenebrism borrowed from Caravaggio-style painting (compare No. 85).
Trap: it is not a religious painting, but it borrows religious lighting and the Nativity’s circle of glowing faces.
Artist and place: Joseph Wright of Derby, England, about 1763 to 1765.
Scale matters: a contemporary, everyday scene painted at history-painting size was new.
Contrast with The Swing (No. 101), painted at almost the same moment: reason and instruction versus aristocratic flirtation.

101.title: The Swing
101.plain: A small, frothy painting of a young woman in a pink dress flying high on a swing while her lover hides in the bushes below to look up her skirt. Jean-Honoré Fragonard painted it in 1767 for a private patron who wanted a naughty picture of his mistress. It is the textbook example of Rococo: aristocratic, playful, flirtatious and full of hidden jokes.
101.spot: A woman in a billowing pink silk dress on a swing in a lush, overgrown garden, one shoe flying off her foot. A young man reclines in the roses at lower left looking up, and an older man in the shadows at right pulls the swing’s ropes.
101.remember: Fragonard = ‘Frag-on-guard’: the husband is NOT on guard while the lover peeks. Swing, 1767, pink, Rococo.
compare: No. 244 (§11.21), The Swing: A 2001 sculptural remake that critiques the colonial wealth and class privilege behind Rococo leisure.
No. 103 (§5.5), The Oath of the Horatii: The Neoclassical reaction: stern civic virtue and hard lines replacing pleasure and pastel curves.
No. 98 (§4.51), The Tête à Tête, from Marriage à la Mode: Hogarth satirizes aristocratic morals for a moral lesson, while Fragonard indulges them for fun.
No. 100 (§5.2), A Philosopher Giving a Lecture on the Orrery: Same decade: Enlightenment science versus Rococo flirtation.
101.vocab: Rococo, fête galante, iconography, patron, pastel, commission.

form: Oil on canvas, only about 81 by 64 centimeters: a private picture for a small room, not a public statement.
Rococo style (from French rocaille, shell-work decoration): pastel pinks and greens, curving lines, feathery brushwork and a light, airy mood.
A spotlight of sun falls on the woman, while the edges of the garden are dark and dense. She is the bright center of a triangle formed with the two men.
Fluffy trees, clouds and foliage surround the figures like a stage set, which recalls the fête galante (elegant outdoor party) paintings of Antoine Watteau.
Quick, loose strokes in the leaves contrast with careful detail in her silk dress and lace.
The composition runs on diagonals: the rope, her body and the flying shoe all move upward and outward.
function: A private commission for a wealthy patron’s own enjoyment, meant to be shared with friends who got the joke.
According to a memoir by the playwright Charles Collé, a gentleman first asked the painter Gabriel-François Doyen, who refused and passed it to Fragonard.
Today it hangs in the Wallace Collection in London.
content: The patron reportedly asked that his mistress be pushed by a bishop while he sat where he could see her legs. Fragonard replaced the bishop with an older layman, often read as her husband.
The statue of Cupid at left holds a finger to his lips: keep the secret. It is based on ÉtienneMaurice Falconet’s Menacing Cupid (1757).
Her flying slipper is a traditional symbol of lost innocence. The lover holds out his hat, which many read as a sexual joke.
A small dog, a common symbol of fidelity, barks near the older man, who is unaware of what is happening.
The wild, overgrown garden suggests nature, fertility and desire running out of control.
context: The patron is traditionally named as the Baron de Saint-Julien, a tax oﬀicial for the French clergy, which would make the bishop joke sharper. The identification rests on gossip and is not certain.
Jean-Honoré Fragonard (1732 to 1806) trained with Chardin and Boucher and won the Prix de Rome. He became the favorite painter of private aristocratic pleasure.
Enlightenment critics such as Denis Diderot attacked Rococo art as immoral and trivial and called for art that taught virtue.
After the French Revolution of 1789 his aristocratic clients vanished. Jacques-Louis David helped him get a museum post, but he died largely forgotten.
Later viewers treat the painting as a symbol of the careless luxury of the nobility just before the Revolution. On the exam.
Style ID → Rococo: pastel colors, curving forms, lush gardens, flirtatious upper-class subject.
Trap: the person pushing the swing is not a bishop. The patron asked for one, but Fragonard painted an older layman.
Iconography → Cupid hushing, flying shoe, lover in the bushes, unaware older man, barking dog.
Function → a private commission for a small room, not a public or religious work.
Context → painted in 1767, about twenty years before the Revolution; Neoclassicism (No. 103) rose partly in reaction against this style.
Yinka Shonibare’s The Swing (after Fragonard) (No. 244) beheads the woman and dresses her in African wax-print fabric to comment on the wealth behind such leisure.

102.title: Monticello
102.plain: Monticello is Thomas Jefferson’s house on a hilltop near Charlottesville, Virginia, which he designed himself and kept rebuilding for about forty years. It uses Roman and Renaissance forms such as a columned porch and a dome to link the new American republic with ancient Rome. It was also the center of a plantation run on the labor of enslaved people, a contradiction that is now central to how the site is explained.
102.spot: A red-brick house with white trim, a white columned porch topped by a triangular gable, and a low octagonal dome behind it. It looks like a single-story villa, though it actually has three floors.
102.remember: Monticello means ‘little mountain’ in Italian; Jefferson put a mini-Pantheon on it. It is the building on the back of the US nickel.
compare: No. 46 (§3.35), Pantheon: The Roman source for the dome and portico combination.
No. 104 (§5.6), George Washington: Same circle and moment: Neoclassicism used to give the young United States Roman civic virtue.
No. 70 (§4.23), Palazzo Rucellai: Both revive classical forms for a private residence; Alberti in Renaissance Florence, Jefferson in republican Virginia.
No. 93 (§4.46), The Palace at Versailles: Both are a powerful man’s estate as a statement of ideas, but Versailles glorifies a king while Monticello claims republican simplicity.
102.vocab: Neoclassicism, portico, pediment, dome, Palladian, symmetry.

form: Materials: brick made on the site by enslaved workers, white-painted wood trim, stone, and imported glass.
Neoclassical style (reviving ancient Greek and Roman forms): a symmetrical block with a columned portico (porch) at front and back.
Each portico carries a triangular pediment (gable), and a low dome sits on an octagonal base over the garden front.
The first version (begun 1768) followed Andrea Palladio, the Italian Renaissance architect, with two stacked porticoes.

After living in Paris, Jefferson rebuilt it (1796 to 1809): he doubled its size, added the dome, often called the first on an American house, and disguised three floors as one with windows aligned in a single band.
Inside are his inventions and gadgets: a two-faced Great Clock with cannonball weights, dumbwaiters hidden in the dining-room fireplace, and a revolving serving door.
Service spaces (kitchen, stables, storerooms) are tucked under long terraces on either side, so the work of enslaved people was kept out of sight of guests.
function: The home of Thomas Jefferson and the headquarters of a working plantation of about 5,000 acres.
A showcase of his taste and ideas for the many visitors he received, and a working laboratory for his architectural experiments.
Today it is a museum run by the Thomas Jefferson Foundation, owner since 1923, and a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with the University of Virginia.
content: Jefferson treated classical architecture as a political style: Rome’s republic and Greece’s democracy were models for the United States.
The dome and portico echo the Pantheon (No. 46); he later based the University of Virginia’s Rotunda directly on it.
The careful symmetry and order express Enlightenment ideals of reason and balance.
The hidden service wings say the opposite of the ideals on the facade: freedom for some depended on the unseen labor of others.
context: Jefferson (1743 to 1826), author of the Declaration of Independence and third president, was a self-taught architect who studied Palladio’s Four Books of Architecture.
As American minister to France (1784 to 1789) he admired the Hôtel de Salm in Paris and the Roman temple called the Maison Carrée in Nîmes.
He modeled the Virginia State Capitol on the Maison Carrée; Houdon’s statue of Washington (No. 104) stands inside it.
Jefferson enslaved more than 600 people over his lifetime, including Sally Hemings, with whom he fathered children. The site now interprets their lives, including those along Mulberry Row.
He died deeply in debt; the house and the enslaved people were sold. Uriah Levy bought the house in 1834 and his family preserved it until the Foundation took over. On the exam.
Style → Neoclassical/Palladian: portico, pediment, dome, symmetry.
Sources → Palladio, the Pantheon (No. 46), and French Neoclassical buildings he saw in Paris.
If asked about meaning → classical forms tie the new republic to ancient Roman and Greek civic ideals.
Contradiction → built and run by enslaved people while its owner wrote that all men are created equal.
Date span 1768 to 1809: a house designed and redesigned over a lifetime, not built at once.
Trap: the dome does not crown a grand central hall like the Pantheon’s; it covers a small top-floor room that was rarely used.

103.title: The Oath of the Horatii
103.plain: A huge, severe painting of three Roman brothers swearing to fight to the death for Rome while their father holds up their swords and the women of the family collapse in grief. Jacques-Louis David painted it in 1784 for King Louis XVI. With its hard edges, frozen poses and message of self-sacrifice for the state, it became the defining picture of Neoclassicism and was later read as a rallying cry for the French Revolution.
103.spot: Three men on the left thrust their arms out in a stiff salute toward three swords held up by an older man in red at center. On the right, women droop and weep with small children, all in front of three round Roman arches.
103.remember: Three arches, three brothers, three swords, three groups: David’s ‘rule of three’ oath, 1784. David beats Goliath-sized frivolity of the Rococo.
compare: No. 101 (§5.3), The Swing: Rococo versus Neoclassicism: pastel flirtation in a garden versus stern duty in a Roman hall.
No. 108 (§5.10), Liberty Leading the People: Both images of revolutionary commitment, but David’s cool, linear Neoclassicism contrasts with Delacroix’s heated Romanticism.
No. 106 (§5.8), Y no hai remedio: David glorifies dying for the state; Goya shows death in war as pointless and anonymous.
103.vocab: Neoclassicism, history painting, Salon, frieze, civic virtue, focal point.

form: Oil on canvas, enormous: about 3.3 by 4.25 meters (roughly 11 by 14 feet).
Neoclassical style: smooth, nearly invisible brushwork, crisp outlines, sculptural bodies and a restrained palette punctuated by reds.
A shallow, stage-like space in front of three arches on plain Doric columns, like a frieze (a horizontal band of relief sculpture).
The picture divides into three groups, each framed by an arch: the brothers, the father, and the women and children.
Men are built from straight lines and braced legs; women are made of soft, collapsing curves. The contrast is the whole design.
The swords meet at the exact center, the focal point where all the gestures converge.
function: Commissioned for the French Crown through the Comte d’Angiviller, director of the King’s Buildings, as part of a program of morally uplifting history paintings.

David painted it in Rome to be near ancient models, showed it to crowds in his Roman studio, then exhibited it at the Paris Salon (the oﬀicial public art exhibition) of 1785, where it was a sensation.
Today it hangs in the Louvre, Paris.
content: In the 600s B.C.E., Rome and the city of Alba Longa settled a war by a fight between three Roman brothers, the Horatii, and three Alban brothers, the Curiatii.

The families were intertwined: the Horatii’s sister Camilla was engaged to one Curiatius, and Sabina, a Curiatii sister, was married to one of the Horatii. The women know they will lose someone either way.
The oath scene is not in the ancient historian Livy. David invented it, possibly inspired by Corneille’s play Horace (1640).
Only one Horatius survives; he later kills Camilla for mourning her dead fiancé. The painting’s message: the state comes before family and feeling.
context: Jacques-Louis David (1748 to 1825) reacted against the Rococo of Boucher and Fragonard and looked to ancient sculpture and to Nicolas Poussin.
Enlightenment critics wanted art that taught civic virtue (putting the public good first), and David delivered it.
Although made for the king, it was soon read as revolutionary. David became a Jacobin, voted in 1793 for Louis XVI’s execution, and painted The Death of Marat.
He later served as Napoleon’s chief painter and died in exile in Brussels after the monarchy returned.
The rigid separation of heroic men and emotional women reflects 18th-century ideas, voiced by Rousseau, about separate male public and female private roles. On the exam.
Style ID → Neoclassical: clear line, shallow space, Roman setting, moral subject, sculptural figures.
Patron → the French king, Louis XVI, yet later embraced by revolutionaries. Do not say it was commissioned by the Revolution.
Function → a moralizing history painting about civic duty and self-sacrifice.
Composition → three groups under three arches; men straight lines, women curves.
Contrast pair → The Swing (No. 101): private pleasure versus public duty, curves versus straight lines.
Date: completed 1784, shown at the Salon of 1785.
Romantic contrast → Liberty Leading the People (No. 108) uses loose paint and emotion for a revolution.

104.title: George Washington
104.plain: A life-size marble statue of George Washington by the French sculptor JeanAntoine Houdon, made for the Virginia State Capitol in Richmond. Houdon traveled to Mount Vernon to cast Washington’s face, so it is the most accurate likeness we have of him. It mixes a real modern uniform with Roman symbols, presenting Washington as a citizen-soldier who gave up power and went home to farm.
104.spot: A standing marble man in an 18th-century military coat, knee breeches and boots, with his left hand resting on a bundle of rods that has a sword hanging from it. A plow stands behind him and he holds a walking cane in his right hand.
104.remember: Houdon came to ‘house-don’ Washington’s face at Mount Vernon. Fasces of 13 rods = 13 states; plow = Cincinnatus. 1788 to 1792, Richmond.
compare: No. 43 (§3.32), Augustus of Prima Porta: Both are portrait statues of leaders in contrapposto, but Augustus claims divine power while Washington gives power away.
No. 34 (§3.23), Doryphoros: The ancient Greek source for the contrapposto stance.
No. 102 (§5.4), Monticello: Jefferson’s Neoclassicism; Jefferson recommended Houdon and designed the building this statue stands in.
No. 119 (§5.21), The Burghers of Calais: Public civic monuments to self-sacrifice: one calm and idealized, the other anguished and anti-heroic.
104.vocab: contrapposto, life mask, fasces, Neoclassicism, marble, civic virtue.

form: White marble, life-size: about 6 feet 2 inches, said to match Washington’s own height.
The pose is classical contrapposto (weight on one leg, so hips and shoulders tilt), borrowed from ancient statues like the Doryphoros (No. 34).
Highly realistic face based on a life mask (a plaster cast taken directly from the living face) and careful measurements Houdon took at Mount Vernon in 1785.
He wears his actual uniform as commander of the Continental Army, not a Roman toga, with every button, fold and buckle carved precisely.
His left hand rests on a fasces (a bundle of rods, the ancient Roman symbol of authority), with his cloak and sword hung on it. His right hand holds a walking cane.
Signed and dated 1788, finished around 1792, and installed in the Capitol rotunda in 1796.
function: Commissioned in 1784 by the Virginia General Assembly to honor Washington for winning the Revolutionary War.
It stands in the rotunda of the Virginia State Capitol, which Jefferson designed after the Roman Maison Carrée. The inscription on the pedestal is credited to James Madison.
A public civic monument: a role model of republican virtue placed in the seat of state government.
content: Washington is cast as Cincinnatus, the Roman leader who was called from his farm to save Rome, then gave up power and went back to plowing.
Washington really did this in 1783, resigning his command and returning to Mount Vernon. The plow behind him is the farm he went home to.
The fasces has 13 rods for the 13 states: unity and lawful civic power.
Sword hung up, cane in hand: a general turned private citizen. The figure is relaxed and civilian rather than triumphant.
context: Jean-Antoine Houdon (1741 to 1828) was the leading portrait sculptor of Enlightenment Europe, known for busts of Voltaire, Benjamin Franklin and Jefferson.
Jefferson and Franklin, then in Paris, recommended him. He sailed to America and stayed at Mount Vernon for about two weeks in October 1785.
There was debate about classical versus modern dress. Washington reportedly preferred modern clothes, and the result blends contemporary realism with classical symbols.
Compare Horatio Greenough’s 1840 seated Washington (not on the list), shown half-naked like a Greek god, which the public mocked.
Washington also headed the Society of the Cincinnati, a group of former oﬀicers named after the same Roman hero. On the exam.
If asked about iconography → fasces with 13 rods (unity and authority), plow (Cincinnatus, return to farming), sword hung up (giving up power).
Material and method → marble, life mask taken from life at Mount Vernon.
Patron → Virginia General Assembly; location → Virginia State Capitol, Richmond.
Style → Neoclassical: classical contrapposto and Roman symbols, combined with realistic modern dress.
Trap: he does not wear a toga; he wears his Continental Army uniform.
Compare a ruler as god-like commander (Augustus, No. 43) with a ruler who gives power back.

105.title: Self-Portrait
105.plain: A self-portrait of Élisabeth Louise Vigée Le Brun, the most successful woman painter of 18th-century France and Marie Antoinette’s portrait painter, showing herself at work at her easel. She painted it in Rome in 1790 after fleeing the French Revolution, for the famous collection of artists’ self-portraits in the Uﬀizi in Florence. It presents her as both a charming woman and a serious professional.
105.spot: A young woman with loose, curly unpowdered hair, a black dress, a red sash and a frilly white collar turns toward us with a slight smile, holding a palette and brush. On the easel behind her is a faint sketch of another woman, Marie Antoinette.
105.remember: ‘Vigée’ sounds like ‘vigor’: she keeps painting even in exile. 1790, a year after she fled 1789’s Revolution, for the Uﬀizi.
compare: No. 91 (§4.44), Las Meninas: Both show the painter at work with brush in hand, connected to royalty; Velázquez claims nobility for painting, Vigée Le Brun claims professional status for a woman.
No. 96 (§4.49), Fruit and Insects: Rachel Ruysch was another highly successful woman painter of the period, working in still life.
No. 87 (§4.40), Self-Portrait with Saskia: Another artist’s self-presentation; Rembrandt shows himself as a prosperous husband, she shows herself as a working painter.
No. 99 (§5.1), Portrait of Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz: Two images of women defined by their intellectual or professional work in the 1700s.
105.vocab: self-portrait, attribute, Royal Academy, Rococo, Neoclassicism, palette.

form: Oil on canvas, about 100 by 81 centimeters, with smooth, soft brushwork and fresh, luminous skin tones.
A three-quarter-length figure turned at an angle, glancing over her shoulder: lively and informal, as if we interrupted her.
A limited, elegant palette: black dress, white lace collar, a red sash as the only strong accent.
Her unpowdered, natural curls follow a newer fashion for simplicity, linked to Rousseau’s ideas of nature, rather than the towering powdered wigs of court.
The canvas on the easel shows a chalk-like sketch in light lines, a painting within a painting.
Style sits between Rococo grace and Neoclassical clarity: charming and soft, but calm and clearly drawn.
function: Painted for the Uﬀizi Gallery in Florence, whose collection of artists’ self-portraits was begun by Cardinal Leopoldo de’ Medici in the 1600s. Being invited was an honor.
It advertised her skill to new clients across Europe during her exile, when she needed work.
It is also a statement about her identity: a professional painter first.
content: Palette and brushes are her attributes: she shows herself as the maker of images, not just a pretty subject of one.
The sketch on the easel is usually identified as Marie Antoinette, her most important patron, a reminder of her royal connections even as the monarchy fell.
Her friendly smile and direct glance make her approachable, softening the boldness of a woman claiming professional status.
context: Vigée Le Brun (1755 to 1842), daughter of a pastel portraitist, was largely self-trained and supporting herself by painting portraits as a teenager.
She painted Marie Antoinette more than 30 times, including Marie Antoinette with Her Children (1787), meant to improve the queen’s unpopular image.
In 1783, with the queen’s support, she was admitted to the French Royal Academy, which limited women members to four. Adélaïde Labille-Guiard was admitted the same day.
Rumors claimed a male painter did her work, a common attack on successful women artists.
In October 1789 she fled with her daughter. She worked in Italy, Vienna and Saint Petersburg, returned to France in 1802, and later wrote popular memoirs. On the exam.
If asked about women artists → a woman asserting professional status through the self-portrait at the easel.
Function → made for the Uﬀizi’s collection of artists’ self-portraits.
Context → painted in exile in Rome in 1790 after fleeing the French Revolution because of her royal ties.
Iconography → palette and brushes; Marie Antoinette sketched on the canvas.
Trap: the sitter is the artist herself, not Marie Antoinette, who appears only as a sketch on the easel.
Academy link → one of very few women in the French Royal Academy (admitted 1783).

106.title: Y no hai remedio (And There’s Nothing to Be Done), from Los
106.plain: A small black-and-white print by Francisco de Goya showing a blindfolded man tied to a post a moment before a firing squad shoots him. It belongs to Goya’s series of more than 80 prints about the brutal war in Spain against Napoleon’s armies from 1808 to 1814. There are no heroes and no glory here, just anonymous killing, which makes it one of the first modern anti-war images. It was so dangerous that it was published only in 1863, 35 years after Goya died.
106.spot: A small, gritty black-and-white print with lots of empty background. A blindfolded man with bound hands is tied to a post at the center, rifle barrels poke in from the right edge, and a dead body lies at his feet.
106.remember: ‘No hay remedio’ = no remedy: there is no cure for war. Goya’s Disasters, plate 15, published long after his death (1863).
compare: No. 108 (§5.10), Liberty Leading the People: Delacroix makes revolutionary violence heroic and allegorical; Goya makes violence anonymous and pointless.
No. 134 (§5.36), Memorial Sheet for Karl Liebknecht: Both are prints used to protest political violence and mourn its victims.
No. 103 (§5.5), The Oath of the Horatii: David glorifies dying for the state; Goya shows death in war stripped of glory.
106.vocab: etching, drypoint, burin, burnishing, series, guerrilla.

form: An etching (lines scratched through a wax coating on a copper plate, then bitten into the metal with acid) about 14 by 17 centimeters, smaller than a sheet of notebook paper.
Goya added drypoint (scratching directly into the copper, which leaves a soft, fuzzy line) to strengthen some lines.
He also used the burin (an engraving tool that cuts crisp grooves) and burnishing (polishing areas smooth so they print lighter).
Harsh, scratchy lines, stark black and white, and a mostly blank background make the scene feel bare and exposed.
The executioners are cropped off: only their rifles show. The killers are faceless, and so is the victim behind his blindfold.
Behind him, other prisoners are tied to posts, waiting their turn.
function: A personal record and protest of what Goya witnessed or heard about, not a commission.
He printed a few proof sets for himself and friends, titled Fatal Consequences of Spain’s Bloody War with Bonaparte, and Other Emphatic Caprices.
The Royal Academy of San Fernando in Madrid first published the series in 1863, giving it the title Los Desastres de la Guerra.
content: The title, in Goya’s old spelling, means ‘And there’s nothing to be done’: despair, not heroism.
The anonymous executioners and victim turn a specific event into a universal statement about state violence.
Other plates show atrocities by both French soldiers and Spanish fighters, the famine of 1811 to 1812, and attacks on the restored repressive monarchy and Church.
Goya’s caption technique, a short bitter title under each image, works like a modern photojournalist’s caption.
context: Peninsular War (1808 to 1814): Napoleon occupied Spain and put his brother Joseph on the throne. Spanish guerrilla (Spanish for ‘little war’) fighters resisted, and reprisals were savage.
Francisco de Goya (1746 to 1828) was First Painter to the Spanish king and, deaf after an illness in 1793, increasingly made private, dark work.
He kept his court position under Joseph Bonaparte, then under the restored Ferdinand VII, whose repression made publishing these prints impossible.
He moved to Bordeaux, France, in 1824 and died there in 1828.
His painting The Third of May 1808 (1814, not on the list) shows a similar execution, but with a lit, Christ-like victim. On the exam.
Medium → etching with drypoint, burin and burnishing: a print, made in multiples.
If asked about context → Napoleon’s occupation of Spain, the Peninsular War, 1808 to 1814.
Date trap → made 1810 to 1823 but published 1863, after Goya’s death, because it was too politically dangerous.
Function → anti-war protest and witness; it refuses to glorify either side.
Composition → faceless soldiers cropped at the edge, blindfolded victim, empty background.
Contrast with heroic war images such as Delacroix’s Liberty (No. 108) or David’s Oath (No. 103).

107.title: La Grande Odalisque
107.plain: A reclining nude woman, imagined as a harem concubine, painted by JeanAuguste-Dominique Ingres in 1814. Her back and arm are stretched far longer than any real body so that her outline makes one long, elegant curve. It is a key example of Orientalism, the European habit of fantasizing about the Middle East as exotic and sensual, and it mixes Neoclassical technique with a Romantic subject.
107.spot: A pale nude woman lying on blue silk with her back to us, looking over her shoulder, wearing a turban and holding a peacock-feather fan. Her back looks impossibly long, and there is a hookah pipe and incense burner at the right.
107.remember: Ingres made her ‘in-grossly’ long: extra vertebrae for an extra-long curve. Odalisque, 1814, Orientalism.
compare: No. 80 (§4.33), Venus of Urbino: The Renaissance reclining nude that Ingres and Manet both respond to.
No. 115 (§5.17), Olympia: Manet’s Olympia rejects the exotic fantasy and shows a modern Parisian sex worker.
