No. 235 (§11.12), Rebellious Silence, from the Women of Allah s…: Shirin Neshat answers Western Orientalist fantasies with a veiled Iranian woman holding a rifle.
No. 123 (§5.25), Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are…: Gauguin’s Tahiti is another European fantasy of an exotic, sensual ‘elsewhere’.
107.vocab: odalisque, Orientalism, Neoclassicism, Romanticism, elongation, line.

form: Oil on canvas, about 91 by 162 centimeters, with enamel-smooth surfaces and no visible brushstrokes, a hallmark of Neoclassical finish.
Her anatomy is deliberately distorted: the back is stretched by the length of a few vertebrae, the right arm is boneless and long, and the left leg twists impossibly.
Ingres valued line over color: the clean outline matters more than anatomical truth. This recalls Mannerist elongation, like Parmigianino’s Madonna with the Long Neck.
Cool, pale skin against rich blue silk, with soft, even lighting rather than dramatic shadows.
Carefully rendered luxurious textures: silk, fur, pearls, feathers and metal.
function: Commissioned in 1813 by Caroline Murat, Napoleon’s sister and Queen of Naples. The Murats lost power in 1815, so it was never delivered.
Ingres exhibited it at the Paris Salon of 1819, where critics mocked it; one complained she had too many vertebrae.
Today it hangs in the Louvre, Paris.
content: An odalisque (from Turkish for a chamber servant) is a woman of a harem, in European fantasy a concubine.
Props such as the turban, peacock fan, hookah and incense burner signal an imagined ‘East’ of luxury and idleness.
Her cool glance over her shoulder is detached rather than inviting, making her both on display and distant.
Setting the nude in a faraway harem let a French artist paint a sensual nude as ‘exotic’ rather than as a scandalous Frenchwoman.
context: Orientalism (a term later defined critically by Edward Said in 1978) is the Western depiction of North Africa and the Middle East as exotic, sensual and backward, which supported colonial attitudes.
Interest grew after Napoleon’s invasion of Egypt (1798 to 1801). Ingres never traveled there; he relied on books and travelers’ accounts.
Jean-Auguste-Dominique Ingres (1780 to 1867) was a pupil of David and defended line and drawing against Delacroix’s emphasis on color.
Critics at first saw it as too strange; later artists and critics admired its abstraction of form.
In 1989 the Guerrilla Girls used this body, with a gorilla head, on a poster protesting how few women artists were in museums while female nudes were everywhere. On the exam.
Visual ID → elongated back, cool smooth finish, turban, peacock fan, hookah: Ingres.
Key concept → Orientalism; be ready to explain the colonial fantasy behind it.
Style → Neoclassical technique (line, polish) applied to a Romantic exotic subject.
Patron → Caroline Murat, Queen of Naples, Napoleon’s sister; never delivered.
Trap: the distortions are deliberate choices for line, not mistakes from lack of skill.
Tradition → the reclining nude from Titian (No. 80) through Manet’s parody (No. 115).

108.title: Liberty Leading the People
108.plain: A huge, smoky, chaotic painting of a bare-breasted woman personifying Liberty, carrying the French flag over a barricade piled with bodies while armed Parisians of different classes charge behind her. Eugène Delacroix painted it in 1830 to celebrate the July Revolution, three days of street fighting that toppled King Charles X. It is the classic example of French Romanticism: emotion, color and movement instead of calm and order.
108.spot: A woman in a red Phrygian cap holds up the red, white and blue flag and a bayonet musket, striding forward over corpses. A man in a top hat with a musket is at her right and a boy waving two pistols is at her left, with Notre-Dame’s towers faint in the smoke.
108.remember: Liberty Leading, 1830: ‘Dela-CROWD’ leads the crowd. Tricolor flag, Phrygian cap, top hat, pistol boy.
compare: No. 103 (§5.5), The Oath of the Horatii: Both rally people to fight for the nation, but David uses Neoclassical restraint and Delacroix uses Romantic energy.
No. 106 (§5.8), Y no hai remedio: Heroic, idealized struggle versus Goya’s anonymous, pointless death.
No. 111 (§5.13), Slave Ship: Turner and Delacroix both use loose paint and color for emotional, Romantic effect.
108.vocab: Romanticism, allegory, Phrygian cap, pyramidal composition, Salon.

form: Oil on canvas, about 2.6 by 3.25 meters: life-size figures, a scale normally used for great historical or religious scenes.
Romantic style: loose, energetic brushwork, swirling smoke, dramatic light and strong color, the opposite of David’s crisp line.
A pyramidal composition (figures arranged in a triangle) with the flag at the peak and dead bodies forming the base.
Red, white and blue are repeated throughout the picture, for example in the clothes of the wounded man at Liberty’s feet, tying the crowd to the flag.
The figures push toward the viewer, as if about to step out of the canvas.
A half-naked corpse at lower left recalls Géricault’s Raft of the Medusa (1819), which Delacroix had posed for.
function: Commemorates the July Revolution of 27 to 29 July 1830, which replaced Charles X with the ‘citizen king’ Louis-Philippe.
Shown at the Salon of 1831; the new government bought it, displayed it briefly, then returned it to Delacroix because it seemed too likely to stir up more rebellion.
It went on show again in 1855 and entered the Louvre in 1874. A recent cleaning at the Louvre brought back much brighter colors.
content: Liberty is an allegory (an idea shown as a person). Her Phrygian cap was worn by freed slaves in ancient Rome and became a symbol of the 1789 Revolution.
She is both ideal and real: classical profile and bare breasts like an ancient Victory statue, but with dirty feet and armpit hair.
Different classes unite: a worker with a saber, a man in a top hat (often said to be Delacroix, which is unproven) and a street boy with pistols.
The boy is often said to have inspired Gavroche in Victor Hugo’s Les Misérables (1862).
Notre-Dame in the background, with a tiny flag on its tower, firmly places the fight in Paris.
context: Charles X had tried to censor the press and dissolve the elected chamber, which set off barricade fighting in Paris.
Eugène Delacroix (1798 to 1863) did not fight. He wrote to his brother that if he had not fought for his country, at least he would paint for her.
Romanticism valued emotion, imagination and freedom over the rules and restraint of Neoclassicism; Delacroix and Ingres were seen as rivals for color versus line.
The image became a national symbol, printed on the French 100-franc banknote from 1978 to 1995 and endlessly copied in protests and pop culture. On the exam.
Style → Romanticism: loose brushwork, rich color, emotion, dramatic diagonals and a pyramid composition.
Event → July Revolution of 1830, not the French Revolution of 1789.
Iconography → Phrygian cap, tricolor flag, classes united behind an allegorical woman.
Reception → bought by the state, then hidden away as too dangerous.
Comparison → Neoclassical David (No. 103) versus Romantic Delacroix; heroic Delacroix versus bleak Goya (No. 106).
Trap: Liberty is an allegory, not a real historical woman.

109.title: The Oxbow (View from Mount Holyoke, Northampton, Massachusetts, after a Thunderstorm)
109.plain: A big landscape by Thomas Cole showing the view from Mount Holyoke in Massachusetts over a loop in the Connecticut River just after a thunderstorm. The left side is wild, dark wilderness; the right side is sunny, cleared farmland. The painting is an argument about America itself: is the spread of farms and towns progress, or the loss of something sacred?
109.spot: A landscape split by a diagonal: dark storm clouds and a broken tree on a wooded hilltop at left, and a bright valley with a river curving in a U-shape through neat fields at right. A tiny painter at an easel peeks out from the bottom center.
109.remember: Cole’s ‘Ox-bow’ = a river bent like the U-shaped collar on an ox. Cole paints coal-dark storm left, sunny farms right. 1836, Hudson River School.
compare: No. 118 (§5.20), The Valley of Mexico from the Hillside of San…: Both are national landscapes that build identity from land, one American and one Mexican.
No. 201 (§9.10), Travelers among Mountains and Streams: Fan Kuan’s monumental landscape also uses nature to express a worldview, with humans tiny before it.
No. 151 (§5.53), Spiral Jetty: Smithson makes the land itself the artwork, rather than a painting of it.
No. 111 (§5.13), Slave Ship: Turner’s sublime storm also carries a moral and political message.
109.vocab: Hudson River School, sublime, picturesque, panoramic, atmospheric perspective, landscape.

form: Oil on canvas, about 1.3 by 1.9 meters, large and showy, made to stand out at an exhibition.
A strong diagonal divides the picture: dark, stormy, untamed forest on the left; calm, sunlit farmland on the right.
Wilderness details include a blasted, broken tree and rain still falling. Civilization includes tidy fields, boats on the river and smoke from settlers clearing land.
A high viewpoint gives a sweeping panorama (a wide view) with atmospheric perspective: distant hills fade to pale blue-gray.
Cole painted himself, very small, at the bottom center with his easel and umbrella, turning to look at us.
function: Exhibited at the National Academy of Design in New York in 1836.
Cole told his patron Luman Reed that he painted it as an eye-catching exhibition picture, partly to boost his reputation and sales.
Today it hangs in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
content: Wilderness versus civilization: the choice facing a young nation pushing west.
The storm moving away to the left may suggest that cultivation is the future, or that wild nature is being driven out.
The scholar Matthew Baigell proposed that the cleared patches on the far hill, read upside down, form Hebrew letters for ‘Noah’ or ‘the Almighty’: God’s signature on the land. This idea is debated.
Cole’s self-portrait reminds us that the artist chooses how to frame America, and possibly that he stands with the wild side.
context: Thomas Cole (1801 to 1848) was born in England and came to the United States in 1818. He is considered the founder of the Hudson River School, a group of American landscape painters.
The same year he published his Essay on American Scenery, praising wilderness as America’s special glory and regretting its destruction by ‘the axe of civilization’.
He was also painting The Course of Empire (1833 to 1836), a five-picture series about a civilization rising and collapsing, which shows his doubts about progress.
The sublime (awe mixed with fear before vast nature) and the picturesque (pleasant, varied scenery) were key ideas of the time.
The phrase Manifest Destiny, the belief that the United States was meant to expand west, was coined in 1845, nine years after this painting, but the idea was already in the air. On the exam.
Artist and school → Thomas Cole, Hudson River School, 1836.
Composition → diagonal split between wild and cultivated land.
Theme → American national identity, expansion and the cost of ‘progress’.
Concepts → sublime versus picturesque; Romantic landscape.
Trap: ‘Manifest Destiny’ was coined in 1845; use it as a related idea, not a slogan Cole was illustrating.
Detail → the artist’s tiny self-portrait at the bottom.

110.title: Still Life in Studio
110.plain: One of the earliest surviving photographs, made by Louis-Jacques-Mandé Daguerre in 1837 to show off his new process. It shows a still-life corner of plaster casts, a bottle and a framed picture, arranged like a traditional painting. Photography would change how people recorded the world and push painters to rethink their role, and this plate is one of its first steps.
110.spot: A small, mirror-like silvery-gray photo of a cluttered corner: white plaster heads of chubby cherubs, a carved relief, a wicker-covered bottle, a framed print and draped cloth, lit from a window at one side.
110.remember: Daguerre made a dagger-sharp image in 1837: still things for a still camera, since early exposures took minutes.
compare: No. 114 (§5.16), Nadar Raising Photography to the Height of Art: Daumier satirizes the debate over whether photography could be art.
No. 117 (§5.19), The Horse in Motion: Long, still exposures here versus split-second exposures capturing motion 40 years later.
No. 96 (§4.49), Fruit and Insects: A painted still life; Daguerre borrows the same genre for the camera.
110.vocab: daguerreotype, still life, exposure, negative, vanitas, photography.

form: A daguerreotype: a one-of-a-kind photograph on a polished, silver-coated copper plate, about 16 by 21 centimeters.
Process: the plate was made light-sensitive with iodine fumes, exposed in a camera for several minutes, developed over heated mercury fumes, then fixed with a salt solution.
There is no negative, so it cannot be copied; the image is also reversed left to right, like a mirror.
The surface is like a mirror, so the picture only appears clearly when held at the right angle. Daguerreotypes were usually kept under glass in cases.
Extremely fine detail and a soft range of grays; light falls across the objects from one side, emphasizing texture.
function: A demonstration piece to prove what Daguerre’s invention could do, made two years before the process was made public.
The objects were chosen partly because they stayed still during the long exposure.
Today it belongs to the Société française de photographie in Paris.
content: A still life (an arrangement of objects) of plaster casts of classical sculpture, a relief, a wicker-covered bottle and a framed print.
Choosing a painting genre claimed artistic respectability for the new medium.
Plaster casts of ancient art were standard tools in art schools, so the subject links photography to the traditions of art training.
Some see a hint of vanitas (reminders that time passes and things decay) in the arrangement, though this reading is debated.
context: Louis-Jacques-Mandé Daguerre (1787 to 1851) was a stage-set painter who invented the Diorama, a theater of giant illuminated paintings.
He partnered with Joseph Nicéphore Niépce, who made the earliest surviving camera photograph around 1826 to 1827. Niépce died in 1833 and Daguerre perfected the process.
The process was announced in January 1839 and fully revealed in August 1839. The French state bought the rights and released it freely, though it was patented in England.
The painter Paul Delaroche is reported to have said, ‘From today, painting is dead.’
In England, William Henry Fox Talbot developed a paper negative-and-positive process that could make many copies, the ancestor of later photography. On the exam.
Medium → daguerreotype: silvered copper plate, unique image, no negative, long exposure.
Date trap → made in 1837, but the process was announced to the public in 1839.
Subject → a still life chosen because objects do not move during long exposures and because it borrows painting’s prestige.
Impact → challenged painting’s role in recording reality; later pushed painters toward personal expression.
Related works → Daumier’s Nadar cartoon (No. 114) about photography as art; Muybridge (No. 117) on fast exposures.

111.title: Slave Ship (Slavers Throwing Overboard the Dead and Dying, Typhoon Coming On)
111.plain: A blazing seascape by J. M. W. Turner in which a ship sails into a storm while, in the foreground, chained enslaved people who have been thrown overboard drown among fish and birds. It refers to a real atrocity, the Zong massacre of 1781, and was shown in London in 1840 during a major campaign to end slavery worldwide. Turner’s paint is so loose and fiery that the horror only becomes clear the longer you look.
111.spot: A swirling, almost abstract storm of orange, red and yellow sky over a churning sea, with a dark sailing ship at left. At lower right a shackled leg sticks out of the waves, surrounded by fish, gulls and chains.
111.remember: Turner turns the sea blood-orange in 1840: the Zong ship threw people overboard for insurance money.
compare: No. 109 (§5.11), The Oxbow: Both are Romantic landscapes with storms that carry a moral argument.
No. 243 (§11.20), Darkytown Rebellion: Kara Walker also confronts the history of slavery, using silhouettes instead of a stormy sea.
No. 108 (§5.10), Liberty Leading the People: Romantic painting tied to current politics, with loose, emotional brushwork.

form: Oil on canvas, about 91 by 123 centimeters.
Forms dissolve into color and light: thick, swirling paint, scraping and thin glazes (transparent layers of paint), close to abstraction decades before abstract art.
A blood-red sunset fills the center; the sea is a mix of red, brown and green, as if stained.
The ship at left leans into a typhoon, small against overwhelming nature.
Lower right: a leg in shackles, hands reaching from the water, and fish and birds attacking. The detail is easy to miss at first.
function: Exhibited at the Royal Academy in London in 1840, with lines from Turner’s own unfinished poem Fallacies of Hope ending ‘Where is thy market now?’
That summer London hosted the World Anti-Slavery Convention, so the painting entered a live public debate.
The critic John Ruskin owned it, praised it, then sold it because he found it too painful to live with. It is now in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
content: In 1781 the captain of the slave ship Zong threw more than 130 sick Africans overboard, claiming insurance for lost ‘cargo’, since deaths from illness aboard were not covered.

The incident became famous through the court case that followed and through abolitionists such as Olaudah Equiano and Granville Sharp, and in Thomas Clarkson’s history of abolition, which Turner probably knew.
The approaching typhoon reads as nature’s judgment on human greed.
The poem’s last line, ‘Where is thy market now?’, attacks the economics of slavery: people treated as goods.
context: J. M. W. Turner (1775 to 1851), son of a London barber, entered the Royal Academy schools at 14 and became Britain’s great painter of light, weather and the sea.
Romanticism and the sublime (awe and terror before overwhelming nature) shape the picture.
Britain abolished the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in most of its empire by an act of 1833, but slavery continued in the United States, Brazil and Cuba.
Research has shown that the young Turner had invested in a Jamaican plantation scheme that relied on enslaved labor, which complicates the story.
Not everyone understood it: Mark Twain mocked it as looking like a tortoise-shell cat having a fit in a platter of tomatoes. On the exam.
Artist and date → Turner, 1840, exhibited at the Royal Academy.
Subject → the Zong massacre of 1781; abolitionist context of 1840.
Style → Romantic sublime, nearly abstract color and brushwork.
If asked about function → a moral and political protest against slavery shown to a public audience.
Trap: Britain had already abolished slavery in its empire; the painting targets the ongoing international slave trade and the moral memory of it.
Compare modern artists confronting slavery’s history, such as Kara Walker (No. 243).

112.title: Palace of Westminster (Houses of Parliament)
112.artist: Charles Barry and Augustus W. N. Pugin (architects); London
112.plain: The Palace of Westminster is the home of the British Parliament in London, rebuilt after a fire destroyed most of the old palace in 1834. Charles Barry designed the overall plan and Augustus W. N. Pugin designed its Gothic decoration, inside and out. They chose a medieval Gothic style on purpose, to present Britain’s government as old, Christian and English rather than copying the classical style of revolutionary France and America.
112.spot: A long, pale stone building along the River Thames covered in pointed arches, pinnacles and vertical stone ribs. A tall square clock tower (Big Ben) stands at one end and an even bigger square tower (Victoria Tower) at the other.
112.remember: Barry built the body, Pugin pinned on the Gothic: ‘Barry plus Pugin, Parliament reborn’ after the 1834 fire. Big Ben is technically the bell.
compare: No. 60 (§4.13), Chartres Cathedral: Real medieval Gothic, the source the Victorians were reviving.
No. 102 (§5.4), Monticello: Opposite national style choice: Jefferson used classical forms to signal a republic.
No. 124 (§5.26), Carson, Pirie, Scott and Company Building: Both use modern iron technology but wrap it in decoration, Gothic here and organic ornament in Chicago.
112.vocab: Gothic Revival, Perpendicular Gothic, tracery, pinnacle, picturesque, pointed arch.

form: Gothic Revival style (a 19th-century return to medieval Gothic forms): pointed arches, pinnacles, turrets and carved stone everywhere.
Specifically English Perpendicular Gothic, with strong vertical lines and panel-like tracery (stone ornament in openings and on walls).
Materials: limestone masonry and glass over a structure that used iron, including cast-iron roof plates for fire safety.
Barry’s plan is regular and symmetrical along the river front, nearly 270 meters long, a classical way of organizing space.
Asymmetrical towers create a picturesque skyline: the Victoria Tower (royal entrance) and the clock tower, completed 1859 and renamed the Elizabeth Tower in 2012.
Pugin designed everything down to tiles, wallpaper, stained glass, furniture, inkstands and the clock dial.
function: The seat of the UK Parliament: the House of Lords and the House of Commons, joined by the Central Lobby.
Ceremonial center of government, including the monarch’s State Opening of Parliament through the Victoria Tower.
It incorporates surviving medieval parts, especially Westminster Hall (built 1097, with a huge timber roof from the 1390s).
content: Gothic signaled tradition, Christianity and continuity with England’s medieval past and its long-standing institutions.
Classical styles had become linked with revolutionary France and the American republic, which the British establishment wanted to avoid.
The 1835 design competition required a Gothic or Elizabethan style; the choice was deliberate national branding.
The style matches Westminster Abbey and Henry VII’s Lady Chapel across the road, making a unified medieval-looking district.
context: A fire on 16 October 1834 destroyed most of the old palace. Charles Barry (1795 to 1860) won the competition in 1836, and the foundation stone was laid in 1840.
Augustus W. N. Pugin (1812 to 1852), a Catholic convert, argued in Contrasts (1836) that Gothic was the only truly Christian architecture.
Pugin reportedly summed it up as ‘all Grecian, sir; Tudor details on a classic body’.
Pugin died in 1852 and Barry in 1860; Barry’s son E. M. Barry completed the work around 1870.
It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and now needs a massive, very expensive restoration. On the exam.
Style → Gothic Revival (Perpendicular Gothic) on a symmetrical, classically ordered plan.
Architects → Charles Barry (plan) and Augustus W. N. Pugin (Gothic details and interiors).
Why Gothic → national identity, medieval tradition and Christianity, not classical republicanism.
Date → 1840 to 1870, after the fire of 1834.
Trap: Big Ben is the bell, not the tower; the tower is the Elizabeth Tower.
Compare with real medieval Gothic (No. 60) and with American Neoclassicism (No. 102).

113.title: The Stone Breakers
113.plain: A life-size painting by Gustave Courbet of two road workers, an old man and a boy, breaking rocks by hand at the side of a road. It was a manifesto for Realism: ordinary poor laborers painted at a scale previously reserved for kings, saints and heroes. The original was destroyed during the Second World War in 1945, so we know it today only from photographs.
113.spot: Two figures in ragged, earth-colored clothes, faces turned away or hidden: an old man kneeling with a raised hammer at right, a boy carrying a heavy basket of stones at left. A dark hillside fills the background, with only a sliver of sky.
113.remember: Courbet = ‘curb’ workers: men who build the road curb. Stones, 1849, Realism, bombed 1945.
compare: No. 83 (§4.36), Hunters in the Snow: Bruegel also shows peasants at work, but within a wide, ordered seasonal landscape rather than up close and life-size.
No. 115 (§5.17), Olympia: Manet extends Realism’s challenge to Salon conventions with a modern subject.
No. 141 (§5.43), The Migration of the Negro, Panel no. 49: Jacob Lawrence also depicts working-class lives and social conditions.
113.vocab: Realism, Salon, history painting, picture plane, genre scene.

form: Oil on canvas, about 1.65 by 2.57 meters, so the figures are life-size.
Dull, earthy browns and grays, heavy paint and solid, unidealized bodies.
Neither face is clearly visible, so the workers are anonymous types rather than individuals.
The figures are pressed close to the front of the picture, with a hillside blocking deep space: no escape, no distant view.
Ragged details: a torn shirt, a worn vest, patched socks in clogs, a pot and bread for a poor lunch.
No moral lesson or story is stated: Courbet just shows the work.
function: Exhibited at the Paris Salon of 1850 to 1851 alongside his huge A Burial at Ornans, which also shocked critics.
A deliberate provocation: putting ordinary labor on the scale of a history painting.
It later belonged to the Dresden painting gallery in Germany and was destroyed in February 1945 during the Allied bombing of Dresden.
content: The old man and the boy suggest that poverty and hard labor stretch from youth to old age with no way out.
Breaking stones for road building was among the lowest-paid, most exhausting jobs.
Courbet wrote that it was rare to meet such a complete expression of poverty; he had seen two real men on a road near his hometown, Ornans, and had them pose.
The anarchist thinker Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, Courbet’s friend, praised it as a social and political image.
context: Gustave Courbet (1819 to 1877) founded Realism: paint only what you can see in your own time. The line ‘Show me an angel and I will paint one’ is popularly attributed to him.
After the Revolution of 1848, the poor and working class were a hot political issue; conservatives read paintings like this as socialist.
In 1855 Courbet set up his own ‘Pavilion of Realism’ and published a Realist manifesto when the oﬀicial exhibition rejected key works.
During the Paris Commune of 1871 he supported toppling the Vendôme Column, was jailed and fined, and died in exile in Switzerland. On the exam.
Style → Realism: everyday working-class subject, life-size scale, no idealization.
Artist → Gustave Courbet, 1849.
Status → destroyed in 1945; known from photographs.
If asked why controversial → a humble subject painted at the grand scale of history painting.
Faces turned away → anonymity; they represent a whole class.
Link → Realism leads to Manet’s modern-life subjects (No. 115).

114.title: Nadar Raising Photography to the Height of Art
114.plain: A cartoon by Honoré Daumier showing the famous photographer Nadar leaning out of a hot-air balloon over Paris, camera pointed down, with his top hat flying off. Every building below has a sign reading ‘Photographie’. It pokes fun at the photography craze and at the hot debate over whether a camera could make real art, and it was printed cheaply for a mass newspaper audience.
114.spot: A black-and-white sketchy drawing of a man in a balloon basket, coattails flapping and hat flying, aiming a big box camera down at a city of rooftops. Signs on the buildings say ‘PHOTOGRAPHIE’.
114.remember: Daumier’s ‘Nadar-in-the-air’: a pun on height. 1862, lithograph, photography raised (literally) to the height of art.
compare: No. 110 (§5.12), Still Life in Studio: The early photograph whose status as art Daumier’s cartoon questions.
No. 98 (§4.51), The Tête à Tête, from Marriage à la Mode: Another satirical image reproduced for a broad public; Hogarth’s engraved series mocked high society.
No. 117 (§5.19), The Horse in Motion: Photography used as a scientific tool rather than as an art claim.
114.vocab: lithograph, caricature, satire, mass media, printmaking, photography.

form: A lithograph: the artist draws with a greasy crayon on a flat stone; water is wiped on, ink sticks only to the greasy drawing, and many prints can be pulled.
Lithography was invented by Alois Senefelder in Bavaria in the 1790s and made fast, cheap mass printing of images possible.
Loose, quick, sketchy lines and expressive exaggeration typical of caricature (a drawing that exaggerates features to mock).
Strong contrast between the dark, busy balloon figure and the lighter, receding city below.
function: Published on 25 May 1862 in the satirical newspaper Le Boulevard.
Satire for a broad audience: fast, funny commentary on current events and culture.
It could reach thousands of readers, far more than any painting in a gallery.
content: The title puns on ‘height’: Nadar raises photography to a great altitude, but has he raised it to the level of fine art?
The sea of ‘Photographie’ signs mocks the explosion of portrait studios in Paris.
Nadar’s hat flying off and his precarious lean make him look slightly ridiculous but also daring.
The joke may be affectionate: Daumier and Nadar were both caricaturists and knew each other’s world.
context: Nadar was the pseudonym of Gaspard-Félix Tournachon (1820 to 1910), a caricaturist turned photographer who made portraits of Baudelaire, Sarah Bernhardt and many others.
He took the first aerial photographs from a balloon in 1858 and later built a giant balloon, Le Géant. In 1874 his former studio hosted the first Impressionist exhibition.
Debate raged: in 1859 the poet Charles Baudelaire attacked photography as a refuge for failed painters. In 1862 a French court case considered whether photographs could be protected as works of art.
Honoré Daumier (1808 to 1879) made about 4,000 lithographs and was jailed for six months in 1832 for a caricature of King Louis-Philippe. On the exam.
Medium → lithograph, printed in a popular newspaper.
Function → satire for a mass audience; mass media.
Subject → Nadar, a photographer, in a balloon; aerial photography; photography’s claim to be art.
Artist → Honoré Daumier, 1862.
Trap: Nadar is the subject, not the artist; Daumier drew it.
Link → early photography (No. 110) and its later uses (No. 117).

115.title: Olympia
115.plain: A reclining nude painted by Édouard Manet in 1863: a Parisian sex worker who looks straight at the viewer while her Black maid brings her flowers from a client. Manet copied the pose from Titian’s famous Venus of Urbino, but replaced the goddess with a real modern woman and painted her with flat, harsh light. It caused a scandal at the Salon of 1865 and is a starting point of modern art.
115.spot: A pale nude woman lies on white sheets, staring directly at you, hand pressed on her thigh, wearing a black ribbon at her neck and an orchid in her hair. A Black woman in pink holds a big bouquet behind her and a black cat arches its back at the foot of the bed.
115.remember: Olympia = O-LOOK-at-me: she stares back. Manet, 1863, black ribbon, black cat, flowers from a client.
compare: No. 80 (§4.33), Venus of Urbino: The direct source: Titian’s goddess with a sleeping dog becomes Manet’s modern courtesan with a cat.
No. 107 (§5.9), La Grande Odalisque: Ingres puts the nude in an exotic fantasy; Manet puts her in a real Parisian bedroom.
No. 126 (§5.28), Les Demoiselles d’Avignon: Picasso’s prostitutes also stare out and push modern art further toward flatness.
115.vocab: Salon, Realism, modernism, reclining nude, gaze.

form: Oil on canvas, about 1.3 by 1.9 meters.
Flat, harsh frontal light, like a camera flash, with very little modeling (shading to show roundness). Critics thought she looked like a cutout.
Sharp contrasts: pale body and white sheets against a dark background and the dark skin and pink dress of the maid.
Visible brushwork and simplified forms, influenced by Spanish painters such as Velázquez and Goya.
Shallow space: a dark green curtain and wall push everything to the front.
function: Painted in 1863 but shown only at the Salon of 1865, after the scandal of his Luncheon on the Grass at the Salon des Refusés in 1863.
Public outrage was so strong that guards were posted and the painting was rehung high, out of reach of canes and umbrellas.
In 1890 Claude Monet organized a public subscription to buy it for France; it entered the Louvre in 1907 and is now in the Musée d’Orsay.
content: ‘Olympia’ was a name linked with Parisian courtesans; her jewelry, slipper and orchid mark her as a sex worker.
Her hand covers her body in a firm, controlling way, not shyly, and her gaze is direct: she sets the terms.
Titian’s sleeping dog (fidelity) becomes an alert black cat, linked with sexuality and independence.
The flowers are from a client, implying a male viewer who arrives as a customer and puts us in his place.
The maid was modeled by Laure, a Black woman living in Paris; recent scholarship examines how she is shown and often overlooked.
context: Édouard Manet (1832 to 1883) painted modern Paris and is often called the first modernist painter.
The model for Olympia was Victorine Meurent, who later became a painter and exhibited at the Salon herself.
Manet had copied Titian’s Venus of Urbino (No. 80) in Florence; Olympia updates it as a contemporary scene.
Critics attacked both the subject and the style: the flatness seemed unfinished and the body ‘dirty’.
Manet admired Courbet’s Realism and inspired the Impressionists, though he never exhibited with them. On the exam.
Source → a deliberate modern reworking of Titian’s Venus of Urbino (No. 80).
If asked why scandalous → a real prostitute instead of a goddess, a confrontational gaze, and flat, ‘unfinished’ painting.
Iconography → black ribbon, orchid, slipper, flowers from a client, black cat.
Date trap → painted 1863, exhibited 1865.
Modernity → flatness and emphasis on the painted surface lead toward modern art.
Race and representation → the figure of Laure is now a key discussion point.

116.title: The Saint-Lazare Station
116.plain: A painting by Claude Monet of the inside of a Paris train station full of locomotives, steam and smoke under a huge iron-and-glass roof. Monet painted around a dozen views of the station in 1877, capturing changing light and atmosphere rather than describing the trains in detail. It shows Impressionism turning a modern, industrial place into a subject worthy of art.
116.spot: A triangular iron-and-glass station roof frames clouds of blue-white steam. A dark locomotive comes toward you, people and tracks are only suggested with dabs of paint, and buildings are visible through the haze at the far end.
116.remember: Monet’s money shot: steam at Saint-Lazare, 1877. Impressionists loved trains because trains took them to paint in the countryside.
compare: No. 124 (§5.26), Carson, Pirie, Scott and Company Building: Iron, steel and glass: new industrial materials shaping modern architecture.
No. 120 (§5.22), The Starry Night: Van Gogh pushes visible brushwork from recording light to expressing emotion.
No. 118 (§5.20), The Valley of Mexico from the Hillside of San…: Modern transportation and progress within a national landscape.
116.vocab: Impressionism, broken color, en plein air, series, modernity.

form: Oil on canvas, about 75 by 104 centimeters (the Musée d’Orsay version).
Impressionism: quick, broken brushstrokes, unmixed color placed side by side, and soft, blurred forms.
Steam and smoke dissolve the scene into blues, violets and grays, with sunlight filtering through the glass roof.
The pitched roof forms a strong triangle that frames the scene, contrasting solid iron structure with shifting vapor.
Figures and machines are suggested, not detailed: Monet paints atmosphere and light, not objects.
function: One of about a dozen canvases of the station; several were shown at the third Impressionist exhibition in April 1877.
Painted for sale and exhibition outside the oﬀicial Salon system.
Today the version usually shown for the AP course is in the Musée d’Orsay, Paris.
content: The Gare Saint-Lazare, Paris’s oldest station, served Normandy and western suburbs such as Argenteuil, where Monet had lived and painted.
Trains symbolize modern speed, industry and the new rhythms of city life.
The writer Émile Zola praised the series and urged painters to find poetry in railway stations as earlier artists had in landscapes.
context: Claude Monet (1840 to 1926) gave Impressionism its name: a critic mocked his painting Impression, Sunrise at the 1874 exhibition.
He rented a small studio nearby; according to Renoir, he talked the station director into holding trains and stoking up extra steam for him.
Paris was being remade by Baron Haussmann’s boulevards; iron-and-glass buildings like this train shed, designed by Eugène Flachat, were new symbols of engineering.
Monet had seen J. M. W. Turner’s paintings, including a famous train in the rain, while in London in 1870 to 1871.
The series method, painting the same motif in different conditions, became central to Monet’s later work, such as haystacks and Rouen Cathedral. On the exam.
Style → Impressionism: broken brushwork, light and atmosphere, modern-life subject.
Artist and date → Claude Monet, 1877.
Subject → modern industrial Paris; iron-and-glass architecture and steam trains.
Function → part of a series shown at the Impressionist exhibition of 1877.
Trap: Monet is not interested in mechanical detail; he paints the effect of steam and light.
Iron and glass link → Carson, Pirie, Scott (No. 124) and the industrial age.

117.title: The Horse in Motion
117.plain: A grid of small photographs taken in quick succession by Eadweard Muybridge in 1878, showing a racehorse galloping across a track. It proved that a galloping horse has all four hooves off the ground at one moment, something no human eye could see. Paid for by the railroad tycoon Leland Stanford, it changed how artists drew horses and was a direct ancestor of motion pictures.
117.spot: A grid of about a dozen small brown-toned photos of the same dark horse and rider, each slightly further along in the stride. The horse is a silhouette against a pale background marked with vertical numbered lines.
117.remember: ‘Muy-bridge’ built a bridge from photos to movies. 1878, Stanford’s horse, all four hooves up.
compare: No. 110 (§5.12), Still Life in Studio: Minutes-long exposures of still objects in 1837 versus split-second exposures of motion in 1878.
No. 238 (§11.15), Electronic Superhighway: Nam June Paik’s wall of moving video images descends from Muybridge’s sequential pictures.
No. 114 (§5.16), Nadar Raising Photography to the Height of Art: Another view of photography’s expanding role, satirized by Daumier.
117.vocab: albumen print, chronophotography, exposure, zoopraxiscope, negative, photography.

form: Albumen prints: paper coated with egg white and salt, made light-sensitive with silver nitrate, then printed in contact with glass negatives. This gives the warm brown tone.
A sequence of images arranged in a grid, read like a comic strip, each frozen in a split second.
Twelve cameras lined up beside the track; the galloping horse broke threads stretched across its path, firing each shutter in turn.
A white backdrop with vertical lines and numbers let viewers measure the horse’s position in each frame.
The horse appears almost as a silhouette: detail was sacrificed for speed, since exposures were a tiny fraction of a second.
function: Commissioned by Leland Stanford, railroad magnate and former governor of California, to settle whether a trotting or galloping horse ever has all four feet off the ground.
Stanford bred horses and wanted to improve their training scientifically. The often-repeated story of a 25,000-dollar bet is probably a legend.
Photographed in June 1878 at Stanford’s Palo Alto Stock Farm, the land that later became Stanford University. The results were sold as cards and reproduced in Scientific American that October.
content: The answer: yes, all four hooves leave the ground, but when the legs are gathered under the body, not stretched out front and back.
Painters had long shown the ‘flying gallop’ with legs outstretched, as in Géricault’s Derby at Epsom (1821). The photos proved this was wrong.
The work shows photography revealing what the eye cannot see, making it a tool of science, not just of portraits.
context: Eadweard Muybridge (1830 to 1904), born Edward Muggeridge in England, first became known for photographs of Yosemite and San Francisco.
Earlier attempts in 1872 to 1873 were blurry. In between, he was tried for shooting his wife’s lover in 1874 and acquitted.

In 1879 he invented the zoopraxiscope, which projected sequences as moving images; later, at the University of Pennsylvania, he published Animal Locomotion (1887) with hundreds of plates of people and animals moving.
Painters such as Edgar Degas, Ernest Meissonier and Thomas Eakins studied his photographs.
Stanford later published a book on the study that barely credited Muybridge; Muybridge sued and lost. On the exam.
Medium → albumen prints from a sequence of cameras triggered by threads.
Patron → Leland Stanford; place → his Palo Alto farm; date → 1878.
Finding → all four hooves off the ground when gathered under the horse.
Impact → science of motion, changes in art, and a precursor of motion pictures.
Trap: it is many separate photos in sequence, not a single long exposure or a film.
Contrast early long exposures of still objects (No. 110) with this split-second capture.

118.title: The Valley of Mexico from the Hillside of Santa Isabel
118.plain: A wide, bright landscape by the Mexican painter José María Velasco looking out over the Valley of Mexico, with Mexico City, Lake Texcoco and two snow-capped volcanoes in the distance. Velasco was trained in science as well as art, so the geology, plants and light are very accurate. He used the land itself to build a sense of Mexican national identity after independence, linking the Aztec past to the modern nation.
118.spot: A huge sweeping view from a high, reddish-brown hillside down across a flat valley with a shining lake and a distant city. Two volcanoes sit on the far horizon under a big sky with clouds, with tiny human figures in the foreground.
118.remember: Velasco’s ‘Valley’ is very-vast-co: a giant panorama of Mexico, 1882, painted by a scientist-painter.
compare: No. 109 (§5.11), The Oxbow: Both are national landscapes that use panoramic views to build identity and debate progress.
No. 81 (§4.34), Frontispiece of the Codex Mendoza: The Codex Mendoza frontispiece shows the same founding legend of the eagle on the cactus.
No. 157 (§6.5), Templo Mayor: The Templo Mayor stood at the heart of Tenochtitlan, the Aztec city in this very valley.
118.vocab: panoramic, atmospheric perspective, Academic art, landscape, national identity.

form: Oil on canvas, a broad horizontal panorama (a wide, sweeping view) seen from a high vantage point.
Extremely detailed, scientifically accurate rendering of rocks, plants and soil in the foreground.
Clear light and atmospheric perspective (distant things look paler and bluer) create enormous depth.
A raised horizon gives more space to the land than the sky, emphasizing the valley itself.
Tiny human figures in the foreground give scale and make the landscape feel vast.
Academic realism: smooth finish and careful drawing, rejecting the loose brushwork of the Impressionists.
function: Velasco painted this view many times (versions date from the 1870s onward), and versions were sent to international exhibitions to present Mexico to the world.
His valley paintings won medals abroad, including at the 1876 Philadelphia Centennial Exhibition and the 1889 Paris Exposition Universelle.
They served the government’s aim of showing Mexico as modern, scientific and rich in natural resources.
content: The view looks south from the Cerro de Santa Isabel, a hill in the Sierra de Guadalupe north of the city, toward the volcanoes Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl.
In Velasco’s versions of this view, an eagle recalls the founding legend of Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, where the Mexica saw an eagle on a cactus (see No. 81).
Study guides often point to a rail line or train in the valley, a symbol of modernization; Velasco did paint railways in other works, such as his views of the Metlac bridge.
Lake Texcoco, the lake on which Tenochtitlan was built, connects the modern city to its Aztec origins. Most of it has since been drained.
context: José María Velasco (1840 to 1912) trained at the Academy of San Carlos in Mexico City under the Italian landscape painter Eugenio Landesio, then taught there; one of his students was Diego Rivera.
He also studied botany, zoology and geology, illustrated scientific publications, and belonged to Mexico’s natural history society.
His career coincided with the rule of Porfirio Díaz (1876 to 1911), which promoted railways, science and foreign investment.
After independence from Spain (1821), artists searched for subjects that were distinctly Mexican; the valley, with its Aztec history, was ideal.
In 2025 London’s National Gallery gave him a solo exhibition, its first for a Latin American artist. On the exam.
Artist and nationality → José María Velasco, Mexican, 1882.
Theme → national identity built through landscape; past (Aztec legend) and present (modernization).
Style → academic realism, panoramic view, atmospheric perspective, scientific accuracy.
Function → shown at world fairs to present Mexico internationally.
Compare → Cole’s Oxbow (No. 109) as another national landscape.
Trap: not a pre-Columbian or colonial work; it is 19th-century, after Mexican independence.

119.title: The Burghers of Calais
119.plain: A bronze group of six men by Auguste Rodin, commissioned by the French city of Calais to honor citizens who, in 1347, offered their lives to the English king to save their starving town. Instead of a heroic monument, Rodin showed six separate men in dread and despair, ropes around their necks. He wanted them close to the ground so viewers could walk among them as equals, which made it a turning point for public sculpture.
119.spot: Six gaunt, slightly larger-than-life bronze men in rough sack-like robes, each in a different anguished pose, with nooses around their necks. They have big, heavy hands and feet, one holds a huge key, and they stand loosely grouped rather than in a neat pyramid.
119.remember: Six burghers of Calais facing their ‘calamity’: Rodin, 1884 to 1895. Remember the key, the nooses and the six.
compare: No. 225 (§11.2), Vietnam Veterans Memorial: Another memorial that rejects triumphal heroism and invites viewers into a personal encounter.
No. 104 (§5.6), George Washington: Houdon’s calm, idealized civic hero versus Rodin’s six frightened, ordinary men.
No. 41 (§3.30), Seated boxer: Both bronzes show physical and emotional exhaustion rather than ideal beauty.
119.vocab: bronze, lost-wax casting, public art, pedestal, psychological realism, texture.

form: Bronze, cast from Rodin’s clay and plaster models; the group is about 2 meters tall.
Rough, lumpy, textured surfaces catch light and shadow, increasing emotional intensity.
Oversized hands and feet exaggerate gesture and weight: anguish expressed through the body.
The figures form a loose cluster with no single front view; viewers must walk around to understand the group.
Rodin first modeled each figure nude to get the body right, then draped it in heavy sackcloth.
There is no clear leader at the top of a pyramid: each man is isolated in his own feelings.
function: A public monument commissioned in 1884 by the city council of Calais and unveiled in June 1895.
The city wanted a single heroic figure of the leader, Eustache de Saint-Pierre; Rodin gave them six suffering men instead.

Rodin discussed either a very high pedestal or setting the group at ground level. In 1895 it was placed on a raised pedestal with railings; in 1924, after his death, it was moved and set on a low base.
content: During the Hundred Years’ War, King Edward III of England besieged Calais for about a year (1346 to 1347). He offered to spare the town if six leading citizens surrendered to be executed.
They came out in plain shirts with ropes around their necks, carrying the keys of the city; Jean d’Aire holds the giant key.
Edward’s queen, Philippa of Hainault, pleaded for them and they were spared, but the sculpture shows the moment before anyone knew that.
The story comes from the medieval chronicler Jean Froissart.
context: Auguste Rodin (1840 to 1917) was rejected three times by the École des Beaux-Arts and was once accused of casting a figure from a live model because it looked so real.
He stressed emotion, surface and fragmentation, opening the way to modern sculpture; The Thinker and The Gates of Hell date from the same years.
Calais oﬀicials complained that the figures looked defeated rather than heroic.

Twelve authorized casts exist worldwide. One stands in Victoria Tower Gardens in London, right beside the Houses of Parliament (No. 112); others are in Paris, Philadelphia, Washington and elsewhere. On the exam.
Artist and material → Auguste Rodin, bronze, 1884 to 1895.
Subject → six citizens of Calais, Hundred Years’ War, 1347; self-sacrifice.
Approach → psychological realism and individual anguish instead of heroic idealization.
Display → Rodin wanted it at viewer level so we meet the burghers as equals.
Patron → the city of Calais, which was disappointed by the lack of heroism.
Compare → anti-heroic memorial (No. 225) versus idealized hero (No. 104).

120.title: The Starry Night
120.plain: Vincent van Gogh’s painting of a swirling night sky over a sleeping village, made in 1889 while he was a patient at an asylum in southern France. He painted it partly from memory and imagination, using thick, rhythmic brushstrokes and intense blues and yellows to express feeling rather than record what he saw. It is a key work of Post-Impressionism and one of the most reproduced images in the world.
120.spot: A deep blue sky full of glowing yellow stars and a crescent moon, with a giant spiral swirl across the middle. A dark, flame-shaped cypress tree rises at the left, and a small village with a pointed church steeple sits below.
120.remember: Van Gogh went ‘van go’ into the stars: swirling sky, flame cypress, 1889, SaintRémy asylum.
compare: No. 116 (§5.18), The Saint-Lazare Station: Impressionist broken brushwork records light; van Gogh’s strokes express feeling.
No. 122 (§5.24), The Scream: Both turn landscape and sky into vehicles for intense inner emotion.
No. 125 (§5.27), Mont Sainte-Victoire: Another Post-Impressionist, but Cézanne seeks structure while van Gogh seeks expression.
120.vocab: impasto, Post-Impressionism, complementary colors, brushwork, Expressionism, cypress.

form: Oil on canvas, about 74 by 92 centimeters.
Thick impasto (paint applied so heavily it stands up from the surface), laid down in short, directional strokes you can trace.
Swirling, rhythmic lines in the sky contrast with the calm, straight lines of the village.
Complementary colors (opposites on the color wheel) of blue and yellow-orange make each other more intense.
The cypress fills the left foreground like a dark flame, linking earth and sky.
Eleven stars and a moon are surrounded by halos of light, built up in concentric strokes.
function: Painted in June 1889 at the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, where van Gogh admitted himself in May 1889 after breakdowns in Arles.
Not a commission: he painted constantly, sending work to his brother Theo, an art dealer in Paris.
Van Gogh himself considered it a failed experiment in ‘abstraction’. It has been in the Museum of Modern Art, New York, since 1941.
content: Based on the view from his east-facing window, but the village was not visible from there; he added it, and its steeple looks more Dutch than French.
He wrote to Theo that he had seen the countryside from his window before sunrise with only the morning star, probably Venus, which is likely the bright star near the cypress.
Cypresses were planted in Mediterranean cemeteries, so the tree may suggest death, but also reaching toward heaven.
He had written that just as we take a train to get to a town, we take death to reach a star: the night sky may express longing for the infinite.
context: Vincent van Gogh (1853 to 1890), Dutch, painted for only about ten years and sold very little in his lifetime.
Post-Impressionism: artists who took Impressionist color and brushwork in more personal, structured or expressive directions (van Gogh, Gauguin, Cézanne, Seurat).
He was influenced by Japanese woodblock prints, which he collected, and by Impressionist color he saw in Paris.
Because he could not paint in his bedroom, he worked in a studio room by day, partly from memory.
He died in July 1890 at Auvers-sur-Oise from a gunshot wound, generally considered a suicide. On the exam.
Artist and date → Vincent van Gogh, 1889, Saint-Rémy.
Technique → impasto, directional brushstrokes, complementary colors.
Approach → expressive color and line conveying emotion, not observation; PostImpressionism.
Iconography → cypress (death or eternity), stars (the infinite), steeple (memory of the Netherlands).
Trap: it was painted from memory and imagination, not on the spot at night.
Comparison → Monet’s light-recording brushwork (No. 116) versus van Gogh’s emotional brushwork.

121.title: The Coiffure
121.plain: A color print by the American artist Mary Cassatt showing a woman, nude to the waist, arranging her hair in front of a mirror. Cassatt made it in 1890 to 1891 after seeing a big exhibition of Japanese woodblock prints in Paris, and borrowed their flat colors, patterns and tilted views. It shows a private, everyday moment of a woman’s life, seen from a woman’s point of view.
121.spot: A seated woman seen from behind and the side, arms raised to pin up her hair, with a mirror reflecting her. The image is made of thin outlines and flat, soft pink and tan color areas, with a patterned chair and carpet.
121.remember: Cassatt’s ‘coiffure’ = hairdo, and her prints are Japanese ‘to-do’: flat color and patterns, 1890 to 1891.
compare: No. 211 (§9.20), Under the Wave off Kanagawa: A Japanese woodblock print of the kind that inspired Cassatt’s flat colors and patterns.
No. 107 (§5.9), La Grande Odalisque: A female nude made for a male viewer’s fantasy versus Cassatt’s private, unposed moment.
No. 92 (§4.45), Woman Holding a Balance: Vermeer also shows a woman alone in a quiet domestic interior, absorbed in a private task.
121.vocab: drypoint, aquatint, intaglio, Japonisme, ukiyo-e, edition.

form: A color print combining drypoint (lines scratched straight into a copper plate, giving a soft, slightly fuzzy line) and aquatint (a resin-dust technique that creates areas of tone).
Cassatt inked the plates by hand with different colors and printed them in several passes with a professional printer; each impression varies slightly.
Flat color areas, clear outlines and almost no shadow, imitating Japanese ukiyo-e woodblock prints.
A high, tilted viewpoint and cropped edges, also borrowed from Japanese prints.
Patterned surfaces (floral chair, carpet, wallpaper) set against the smooth, pale body.
function: One of a set of ten color prints, including The Bath, The Letter and The Fitting, showing women’s daily routines.
Shown in April 1891 at the Durand-Ruel gallery in Paris, her first solo exhibition.
Made in small editions of about 25, for collectors of fine prints.
content: A private, intimate act: a woman doing her hair, absorbed in herself, unaware of us.
Unlike many male artists’ bathers, she is not posed for a viewer’s pleasure; the scene feels matter-of-fact.
The mirror adds a second view of her and emphasizes self-attention and privacy.
Cassatt chose the domestic, female world that was open to her as a respectable woman in Paris.
context: Mary Cassatt (1844 to 1926), born near Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, moved to Paris and was the only American to exhibit with the Impressionists, invited by Edgar Degas.
In April 1890 she and Degas visited a huge exhibition of Japanese prints at the École des Beaux-Arts, including works by Kitagawa Utamaro of women at their toilette.
Japonisme (Western enthusiasm for Japanese art after Japan opened to trade in the 1850s) shaped Monet, van Gogh, Whistler and many others.
Cassatt also advised wealthy American collectors such as the Havemeyers to buy Impressionist paintings, many now in US museums. On the exam.
Medium → drypoint and aquatint, a color intaglio print, not a woodcut.
Influence → Japanese ukiyo-e prints: flat color, outlines, patterns, tilted space (see No. 211).
Artist → Mary Cassatt, American woman Impressionist working in Paris, 1890 to 1891.
Theme → women’s private, everyday life, seen from a woman’s perspective.
Trap: Cassatt was American, not French; and this is a print, not a painting.
Compare the male gaze in Ingres (No. 107) with Cassatt’s matter-of-fact view.

122.title: The Scream
122.plain: A painting by the Norwegian artist Edvard Munch of a skull-like figure on a bridge clutching its head under a blood-red sky. Munch based it on a moment when he felt ‘an infinite scream passing through nature’, so the scream is in the landscape as much as in the person. Made in 1893, it is a key Symbolist image and a forerunner of Expressionism, and today it is a worldwide symbol of anxiety.
122.spot: A pale, hairless, wavy figure with an open mouth holds its hands to its face on a bridge with a straight diagonal railing. The sky is swirling bands of orange and red over a dark blue fjord, and two dark figures walk behind.
122.remember: Munch makes you crunch your face: The Scream, 1893, Norway. The scream is nature’s, not just his.
compare: No. 120 (§5.22), The Starry Night: Both use swirling skies and expressive color to show inner emotion.
No. 133 (§5.35), Self-Portrait as a Soldier: German Expressionism continues Munch’s distorted forms and colors to show psychological wounds.
No. 111 (§5.13), Slave Ship: Turner’s flaming sky also carries moral horror, though Munch’s horror is personal.
122.vocab: Expressionism, Symbolism, tempera, pastel, diagonal, series.

form: Tempera (paint bound with egg or glue) and pastel or crayon on cardboard, about 91 by 74 centimeters; the cardboard shows through in places.
Wavy, flowing lines in the sky, fjord and figure contrast with the hard straight diagonal of the bridge railing rushing into depth.
Intense, unnatural colors: blood-orange and red sky, deep blue fjord.
The figure is simplified into a sexless, skull-like form that echoes the curves of the landscape, as if both are vibrating.
Quick, rough handling makes the work feel urgent and raw.
function: Part of Munch’s Frieze of Life, a series about love, anxiety and death that he exhibited together, starting in Berlin in 1893.
Munch made several versions: two in 1893 (this painting and a crayon one), a pastel in 1895, a painted one around 1910, and a lithograph in 1895 that spread the image widely.
This version is in the National Museum in Oslo; the 1895 pastel sold at auction in 2012 for about 120 million dollars.
content: Munch’s diary describes walking at sunset with two friends when the sky turned blood red; he stopped, trembling with anxiety, and ‘sensed an infinite scream passing through nature’.
The setting is the Ekeberg hill above Oslo (then called Kristiania) and its fjord.
The two figures walking away show isolation: no one else hears it.
The faint pencil words ‘Could only have been painted by a madman’ in the sky were confirmed in 2021 to be in Munch’s own handwriting.
context: Edvard Munch (1863 to 1944) lost his mother and a sister to tuberculosis in childhood, and another sister was hospitalized for mental illness; he said illness, insanity and death watched over his cradle.
Symbolism sought to show inner states and ideas rather than outer appearances, and Expressionism in Germany built on this.
Some have suggested the red skies came from volcanic ash after the 1883 Krakatoa eruption, or unusual clouds; this is speculation.
Versions were stolen in 1994 and 2004 and recovered. The image is endlessly copied in pop culture. On the exam.
Artist and date → Edvard Munch, Norwegian, 1893.
Medium → tempera and pastels on cardboard.
Theme → anxiety, inner emotion projected onto nature; Symbolism leading to Expressionism.
Form → wavy lines versus a hard diagonal railing; unnatural color.
Series → part of the Frieze of Life; multiple versions exist, including prints.
Trap: Munch said the figure hears a scream passing through nature; it may not be screaming itself.

123.title: Where Do We Come From? What Are We? Where Are We
123.plain: A huge painting by Paul Gauguin, made in Tahiti in 1897 to 1898, that shows the whole cycle of human life from birth to death across a dreamlike tropical landscape. Gauguin meant it as his final testament and tried to kill himself after finishing it. It is a key PostImpressionist work, but also an example of a European man’s colonial fantasy about a ‘primitive’ paradise.
123.spot: A very wide, frieze-like painting of Tahitian figures in a blue-green landscape, with a baby lying at the right, a figure reaching up to pick fruit at the center, and an old woman crouched at the left. A blue idol stands in the background and the title is written in a yellow corner at upper left.
123.remember: Gauguin asks three questions and reads right to left: baby to old age. Tahiti, 1897 to 1898.
compare: No. 126 (§5.28), Les Demoiselles d’Avignon: Picasso’s primitivism borrows from African and Iberian art, following Gauguin’s lead.
No. 107 (§5.9), La Grande Odalisque: Ingres’s Orientalism and Gauguin’s Tahiti are both European fantasies of an exotic, sensual ‘other’.
No. 179 (§7.13), Reliquary figure: African reliquary figures like the byeri were collected and appropriated by European modernists.
123.vocab: synthetism, primitivism, Post-Impressionism, frieze, colonialism, Symbolism.

form: Oil on canvas, about 1.4 by 3.75 meters (over 12 feet wide), painted on rough, coarse cloth.
Flat areas of strong, non-natural color (blues, greens, golds), with simplified figures outlined in dark lines.
Synthetism: combining observed forms with memory, feeling and symbols, rather than copying nature.
A frieze-like arrangement read right to left; space is dreamlike and inconsistent rather than realistic.
The upper corners are painted yellow, like old, damaged frescoes, with the title at upper left and his signature at upper right.
function: Gauguin intended it as a summary of his ideas and a testament before death.
After finishing it he attempted suicide with arsenic, around the end of 1897, and survived.
He sent it to Paris to be shown and sold; it is now in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
content: Right: a sleeping baby with three seated women (where do we come from?).
Center: a figure picking fruit, often compared to Eve, and young people living (what are we?).
Left: an old woman near death and a strange white bird holding a lizard, which Gauguin said stood for the futility of empty words (where are we going?).
A blue idol in the background stands for a spiritual world beyond; two robed figures behind discuss destiny.
The three title questions come from the catechism Gauguin learned as a boy in a Catholic school.
context: Paul Gauguin (1848 to 1903), a former stockbroker, left his wife and children to paint full time, working in Brittany and with van Gogh in Arles.
He went to Tahiti in 1891 looking for an unspoiled ‘primitive’ paradise, but Tahiti was already a French colony with missionaries and Western towns.
In 1897 he was ill, poor, and grieving after hearing of his daughter Aline’s death.

His Primitivism (Western artists idealizing cultures they saw as simpler) relied on colonial assumptions. His relationships with Tahitian girls as young as 13 are now central to critiques of his work.
He died in 1903 in the Marquesas Islands. His flat color and symbolism influenced Matisse, Picasso and the Fauves. On the exam.
Artist and place → Paul Gauguin, Tahiti, 1897 to 1898.
Reading order → right to left: birth, life, death.
Style → Post-Impressionism, Synthetism, flat color, outlines, symbolic rather than realistic.
Context → colonialism and primitivism: a European fantasy of the ‘exotic’.
Function → a personal philosophical testament.
Trap: read right to left, not left to right.

124.title: Carson, Pirie, Scott and Company Building
124.medium: Iron, steel, glass, and terra cotta
124.plain: A department store in downtown Chicago designed by Louis Sullivan and built from 1899 to 1903. Its steel skeleton lets the upper floors become a simple grid of wide windows, while the street-level entrance is wrapped in lavish, plant-like cast-iron ornament designed to lure shoppers inside. It is a landmark of the Chicago School and of early skyscraper design.
124.spot: A white, gridded commercial building with wide horizontal windows stacked in rows, and a rounded corner tower. The bottom two floors are covered in dark, lacy cast-iron ornament full of swirling leaves and vines around the corner entrance.
124.remember: Sullivan’s store: form follows function upstairs, fancy iron frosting downstairs. Chicago, 1899 to 1903.
compare: No. 146 (§5.48), Seagram Building: Mies’s Seagram Building takes the steel frame to its logical end with a glass curtain wall and almost no ornament.
No. 112 (§5.14), Palace of Westminster: Both use modern iron construction but dress it in historical or organic ornament.
No. 116 (§5.18), The Saint-Lazare Station: Iron and glass as new industrial materials of modern life.
124.vocab: steel frame, Chicago window, terracotta, cast iron, skyscraper, form follows function.

form: A steel frame (skeleton) carries the weight, so the walls do not need to be thick and can be mostly glass.
Chicago windows: a large fixed central pane flanked by two narrow windows that open, for light and ventilation.
Upper floors are clad in white glazed terra cotta (fired clay), which is fireproof and reveals the grid of the frame beneath.
The two lower floors are covered in cast-iron ornament, designed with Sullivan’s assistant George Grant Elmslie: dense, organic, plant-like swirls related to Art Nouveau.
A rounded corner tower marks the entrance at the busy intersection of State and Madison Streets.
The original top story had a recessed loggia and projecting cornice, removed in 1948.
function: Built as the Schlesinger and Mayer department store; Carson, Pirie, Scott and Company took it over in 1904.
The ornament acts like picture frames around the display windows, drawing pedestrians’ eyes to the merchandise.
Extended later by D. H. Burnham and Company (1906) and Holabird and Root (1961). The store closed in 2007; the restored building, now called the Sullivan Center, has housed a Target store since 2012.
content: Sullivan wrote in 1896 that ‘form ever follows function’: a building’s appearance should express its use and structure.
The upper grid expresses oﬀices and sales floors stacked identically; the rich base expresses the street-level job of attracting customers.
Sullivan did not see ornament as contradicting function. He believed organic ornament was natural and essential, and he gave the base the most decoration where people saw it up close.
The plant forms reflect his belief that architecture should grow like nature.
context: After the Great Chicago Fire of 1871 destroyed the city center, Chicago rebuilt with fireproof materials and new technologies such as steel frames and safety elevators.
The Chicago School of architects pioneered the commercial high-rise; William Le Baron Jenney’s Home Insurance Building (1885) is often called the first skyscraper.
Louis Sullivan (1856 to 1924) worked in partnership with Dankmar Adler and mentored Frank Lloyd Wright, the architect of Fallingwater (No. 139).
His career declined after 1900 and he died poor, but he is often called the father of the skyscraper and of modernism in architecture. On the exam.
Architect and place → Louis Sullivan, Chicago, 1899 to 1903.
Materials → iron, steel, glass and terra cotta.
Structure → steel frame allowing wide Chicago windows.
Phrase → ‘form ever follows function’.
Trap: Sullivan did not reject ornament; he concentrated it at the entrance where shoppers would see it.
Function → department store designed to attract consumers in a modern commercial city.

125.title: Mont Sainte-Victoire
125.plain: A landscape by Paul Cézanne of a limestone mountain near his hometown of Aix-en-Provence in southern France, painted from 1902 to 1904. Instead of capturing a fleeting moment of light, Cézanne built the scene out of blocky patches of color, almost like tiles, so the image feels solid and structured. He painted this mountain dozens of times, and this approach led directly to Cubism.
125.spot: A pale blue-gray mountain peak rises under a patchy blue-green sky. Below it, a valley of green, ochre and orange blocks of color stands for fields and houses, and the brushstrokes look like little flat rectangles laid side by side.
125.remember: Cézanne ‘says, Ann, cube it!’: the mountain made of color blocks, 1902 to 1904, the grandfather of Cubism.
compare: No. 130 (§5.32), The Portuguese: Braque’s Cubism develops Cézanne’s flattened planes and geometric structure.
No. 201 (§9.10), Travelers among Mountains and Streams: Fan Kuan also builds a monumental mountain image from accumulated strokes, aiming at permanence rather than a fleeting moment.
No. 109 (§5.11), The Oxbow: Both are landscapes of a specific place, but Cole tells a story about America while Cézanne explores the act of seeing.
No. 120 (§5.22), The Starry Night: Fellow Post-Impressionist van Gogh uses brushwork for emotion, Cézanne for structure.
125.vocab: Post-Impressionism, passage, modulation, Cubism, picture plane, series.

form: Oil on canvas, about 73 by 92 centimeters (Philadelphia Museum of Art version).
Built from small, flat, often parallel patches of color, sometimes called his ‘constructive stroke’.
Warm colors (orange, ochre) and cool colors (green, blue, violet) modulate form: color itself, not light and shadow, creates volume and depth.
Space is flattened: sky, mountain and fields are made of the same kinds of strokes, so near and far sit together on the surface.
Passage (edges left open so one plane slides into another) blurs the boundaries between objects.
Forms are reduced toward simple geometry: blocks, planes and wedges.
function: Made for himself, as part of a lifelong study of one motif; he painted the mountain in dozens of oils and watercolors (counts vary, often given as more than 60).
Painted from the hill of Les Lauves, where he built a studio in 1902, looking east to the mountain.
Late in life his work was sold through the dealer Ambroise Vollard, who gave him his first solo show in 1895.
content: The subject is the mountain, but the real subject is how we see: how three-dimensional nature can be rebuilt on a flat canvas.
Mont Sainte-Victoire, about 1,000 meters high, was a landmark of Cézanne’s home region and his childhood.
The repetition across many paintings shows how perception changes, and searches for something permanent beneath appearances.
context: Paul Cézanne (1839 to 1906), a banker’s son and school friend of Émile Zola, exhibited with the Impressionists in 1874 and 1877, then worked mostly alone in Aix.
He reportedly wanted to make of Impressionism something solid and lasting, like the art of museums.
In a 1904 letter to the painter Émile Bernard he advised treating nature by means of the cylinder, the sphere and the cone.
He died in 1906 after being caught in a storm while painting outdoors. A 1907 retrospective in Paris deeply influenced Picasso and Braque.
A remark calling him the father of us all is attributed to both Picasso and Matisse. On the exam.
Artist and subject → Paul Cézanne, Mont Sainte-Victoire near Aix-en-Provence, 1902 to 1904.
Technique → patches of color, warm and cool modulation, flattened space, passage.
Style → Post-Impressionism focused on structure, not fleeting light.
Legacy → a direct bridge to Cubism (No. 130).
Series → he painted this mountain many times.
Trap: Cézanne is Post-Impressionist, not Impressionist; he wanted solidity, not momentary atmosphere.

126.title: Les Demoiselles d’Avignon
126.plain: A huge, aggressive painting of five naked prostitutes that Pablo Picasso made in Paris in 1907, when he was 25. He chopped their bodies into sharp, flat planes and gave two of them faces based on African masks. It broke the 500-year-old rule that a painting should look like a window onto real space, and it opened the door to Cubism.
126.spot: Five pink and ochre nudes with angular, shard-like bodies against icy blue and white ‘curtains’. The two on the right have mask faces with striped, hatched cheeks; one squats with her back to you but her face turned toward you. A small still life of fruit pokes up at the bottom center.
126.remember: ‘Demoiselles’ means ‘young ladies’. Think ‘Picasso at 25 smashes the picture in 1907’, and ‘Africa is on the right’: the two mask faces are on the right side.
compare: No. 115 (§5.17), Olympia: Both show prostitutes who stare straight at the viewer, but Manet keeps a readable room and body while Picasso shatters both into planes.
No. 173 (§7.7), Female: A real Central African mask with its own meaning, useful for showing what Picasso’s primitivism borrowed and what it left out.
No. 130 (§5.32), The Portuguese: Braque’s The Portuguese shows where the fragmentation begun here led: fully developed Analytic Cubism four years later.
No. 142 (§5.44), The Jungle: Wifredo Lam reclaims African-derived forms from inside the African diaspora, answering Picasso’s outsider borrowing.
126.vocab: proto-cubism, Cubism, primitivism, multiple viewpoints, Iberian sculpture, memento mori.

form: Big on purpose: about 8 feet by 7 feet 8 inches (244 × 234 cm), oil on canvas, a ‘statement’ size meant to rival museum paintings. It is now in MoMA, New York.
Bodies are broken into flat, angular planes, like shards of glass, with almost no shading. The curtains behind are cut into the same shards, so figures and space melt together.
Multiple viewpoints (showing something from several angles at once): the squatting woman at lower right shows her back and her face together, and noses appear in profile on frontal faces.

Two styles collide. The three women on the left have almond eyes and simplified faces based on ancient Iberian (pre-Roman Spanish) stone heads; the two on the right have mask faces that Picasso repainted after seeing African masks.
Color is harsh: pinks and ochres against cold blue. The right side is painted more roughly and looks almost unfinished, which adds to the violence.
Debts to Cézanne (No. 125), who built forms out of planes and flattened space, and to El Greco’s stretched figures and tilted space.
function: Not a commission: Picasso painted it for himself as a manifesto, partly to outdo his rival Matisse, whose large painting Le Bonheur de vivre (1905–06) had caused a stir.
It stayed in his studio for nearly a decade, shown only to friends, critics and dealers, most of whom were shocked. Braque reportedly compared it to drinking kerosene.
It was first shown in public in 1916 at the Salon d’Antin in Paris, where the writer André Salmon gave it its polite title. MoMA bought it in 1939.
content: The women are prostitutes in a brothel on Carrer d’Avinyó (Avignon Street) in Barcelona, the city where Picasso spent his teens. The woman at left pulls back a curtain as if presenting them.
They stare straight out at you, so the viewer is cast as the client. The painting turns the male gaze back on the viewer and mixes desire with fear.
Early sketches included a sailor and a medical student holding a skull, a memento mori (a reminder of death), probably about venereal disease. Picasso cut the men out and left only the threat.
The mask faces signal danger and the ‘unknown’. Many scholars read the painting as both a fear of women’s sexuality and a fear of disease.
Fruit in a still life traditionally hints at sexuality and temptation, so even the melon slice belongs to the theme.
context: Pablo Picasso (1881–1973) was Spanish and living in Paris. This work ends his Rose Period and starts the path to Cubism, which he built with Braque (No. 130) around 1908–1912.
In 1907 Picasso visited the ethnographic museum at the Trocadéro in Paris and saw African and Oceanic objects, then repainted the two right-hand heads.
This is primitivism (European artists borrowing from African, Oceanic or folk art they imagined as raw and primal). Picasso used the forms while ignoring what the objects meant to their makers.

The Iberian heads have a scandalous source: in 1907 Picasso bought two ancient Iberian stone heads that had been stolen from the Louvre. He returned them in 1911 during the panic after the Mona Lisa theft.
Today the painting sits at the center of debates about colonialism. France ruled much of West and Central Africa, and many objects at the Trocadéro arrived through conquest. On the exam.
If asked what started Cubism → Les Demoiselles d’Avignon (1907) is usually called protoCubism. Fully developed Analytic Cubism comes with Braque and Picasso around 1909– 1912.
If asked about African influence on Modernism → the two right-hand mask faces. Pair it with a real African mask, such as the Chokwe Pwo mask (No. 173) or a Fang byeri (No. 179).
Trap: the brothel is in Barcelona, not in the French city of Avignon.
Trap: the public did not see it until 1916, so its early impact came through artists who visited Picasso’s studio.
If asked how it breaks with tradition → no single viewpoint, no deep space, no ideal nude. Compare Titian’s reclining Venus (No. 80) and Manet’s confrontational Olympia (No. 115).
Attribution clues for Picasso in 1907: shard-like planes, a mix of Iberian and African faces, a pink, ochre and blue palette, and aggressive frontal stares.

127.title: The Steerage
127.plain: A black-and-white photograph that Alfred Stieglitz took in 1907 aboard the ocean liner Kaiser Wilhelm II, looking down at the cheapest-class passengers on the decks below him. He saw the scene as a pattern of shapes: a straw hat, a stairway, a gangway, a funnel. He used it to argue that a camera could make modern art without pretending to be a painting.
127.spot: A crowded ship deck split across the middle by a bright white gangway. Men in hats crowd the upper level, women and children the lower level; a stairway slants at right, and a pale round straw hat sits near the center as the eye’s landing point.
127.remember: Steerage means ‘steer clear of first class’. Stieglitz shot it in 1907, the same year as Picasso’s Demoiselles (No. 126): two artists in one year both cutting their world into shapes.
compare: No. 117 (§5.19), The Horse in Motion: Both are 19th–20th-century photographs that changed how people saw, but Muybridge studied motion scientifically while Stieglitz composed for beauty.
No. 110 (§5.12), Still Life in Studio: Daguerre’s early still life shows photography’s beginnings; Stieglitz’s print shows it claiming a place as modern art.
No. 141 (§5.43), The Migration of the Negro, Panel no. 49: Both deal with migration and class, Stieglitz through a single photograph, Lawrence through a 60-panel painted narrative.
127.vocab: photogravure, straight photography, Pictorialism, focal point, composition.
