form: A photogravure (a photograph transferred to a copper plate, etched, and printed in ink, giving rich, velvety blacks). The negative dates from 1907; the print was published in 1911.
The picture is split into two horizontal zones by the white gangway (a walkway bridge), with strong diagonals from the stairway, the mast and the chains.
A man’s flat straw boater hat on the upper deck makes a pale circle that pulls your eye to the center.
It is straight photography (sharp focus, no soft-focus effects, no hand-retouching of the print). This breaks with Pictorialism, the earlier style that made photos look like hazy paintings.
Lights and darks are arranged almost abstractly. Stieglitz later listed what he saw: ‘a round straw hat, the funnel leaning left, the stairway leaning right, the white drawbridge’.
The crowd is captured in a split second, with laundry, suspenders and shawls, showing the camera’s ability to freeze ordinary life.
function: Published in Stieglitz’s own journal Camera Work (1911) and again in the magazine 291 (1915), both platforms for the claim that photography is a fine art.
Stieglitz told its origin story in a 1942 essay, ‘How The Steerage Happened’: he ran to his cabin for his camera and had a single glass plate left.
Today it hangs in major museums as a founding image of modernist photography, and it is also studied as a document of class and migration.
content: Steerage was the cheapest class of travel, crammed near the lower decks. Stieglitz was traveling first class with his family, looking down on these passengers both literally and socially.
The ship was sailing east, from New York to Bremen in Germany. Many passengers were probably migrants going home, some turned away or disappointed by America, not hopeful arrivals.
Stieglitz insisted it was about form, but most viewers read class division into the split decks, and the gap between the photographer and his subjects.
Steel stairs, chains and a funnel make it a picture of the machine age as well as of people.
context: Alfred Stieglitz (1864–1946), an American, founded the Photo-Secession (1902) and ran the Little Galleries of the Photo-Secession at 291 Fifth Avenue, known simply as 291.
291 showed modern European art, including Rodin, Matisse, Cézanne and Picasso (his first American show, 1911), placing photography beside painting and sculpture.
1907 was a peak year for migration: about 1.3 million immigrants entered the United States, the most of any single year until then.
Stieglitz photographed Duchamp’s Fountain (No. 144) in 1917; his photo is the only record of the lost original.
He later married the painter Georgia O’Keeffe and photographed her for decades. On the exam.
If asked how photography became accepted as art → Stieglitz, Camera Work, the 291 gallery, and straight photography replacing Pictorialism.
Trap: the ship was leaving America, not arriving at Ellis Island.
Medium trap: it is a photogravure (ink on paper), not a daguerreotype like Daguerre’s Still Life in Studio (No. 110).
Compare with Muybridge’s The Horse in Motion (No. 117): both are photographs, but Muybridge’s purpose was scientific and Stieglitz’s was aesthetic.
Form points: two tiers divided by the gangway, the straw hat as focal point, diagonals of stair and funnel.
Context point: same year as Les Demoiselles (No. 126), and Stieglitz’s gallery was among the first in America to show Picasso.

128.title: The Kiss
128.medium: Oil and gold leaf on canvas
128.plain: A square painting by Vienna’s Gustav Klimt of a couple wrapped in one glittering golden cloak, kneeling at the edge of a flowery cliff. Real gold leaf is laid onto the canvas, borrowing the look of Byzantine church mosaics. It is the high point of his ‘Golden Phase’, and the Austrian government bought it in 1908, before it had even left the exhibition.
128.spot: A square canvas with a speckled gold background. A man, face mostly hidden, bends to kiss the cheek of a woman with closed eyes. His robe has black, white and gold rectangles; hers has colorful circles and flowers. They kneel on a flower meadow that ends at a cliff edge, her toes curled over it.
128.remember: Klimt = gold. ‘Klimt’s Kiss is gold, Brancusi’s Kiss is stone’, and both date to 1907–1908.
compare: No. 129 (§5.31), The Kiss: Same subject and same years, but Brancusi reduces the lovers to a carved stone block while Klimt dissolves them in flat gold ornament.
No. 51 (§4.4), San Vitale: The gold mosaics of San Vitale, which Klimt saw in 1903, are the direct source of his shimmering gold surfaces.
No. 54 (§4.7), Virgin: Byzantine icons use flat gold backgrounds to signal holiness; Klimt applies the same device to earthly love.
128.vocab: gold leaf, Vienna Secession, Art Nouveau, Gesamtkunstwerk, pattern.

form: Oil and gold leaf on canvas (gold leaf is gold hammered thinner than paper and glued down). Klimt also used silver and platinum flecks. It is about 6 feet square (180 × 180 cm).
Flat, decorative pattern dominates: the two bodies disappear under robes that merge into one bell-shaped golden form.
Only faces, hands and feet are modeled with shading, so the realistic skin stands out sharply against the flat ornament.
Pattern signals gender: hard rectangles in black, white and gold on the man; soft circles and flowers on the woman.
The background is a shimmering gold-brown void with no horizon and no room, like the gold backgrounds of icons and mosaics.
The flowing, organic lines link it to Art Nouveau (called Jugendstil in German: a decorative style of curving lines taken from nature).
function: First shown at the 1908 Kunstschau exhibition in Vienna, where the Austrian state’s Ministry of Education bought it for 25,000 crowns, a very high price.
It has hung in the Belvedere museum in Vienna ever since and is Austria’s most reproduced image, on posters, mugs and umbrellas.
A private subject, erotic love, turned into a public, almost sacred object of luxury.
content: The kiss stands for erotic love and union: two people merging into one shape inside one cloak.
The cliff edge adds tension. The woman’s feet curl over the drop, suggesting love is both ecstatic and dangerous.
Some think Klimt and his longtime companion, the fashion designer Emilie Flöge, were the models. This is a popular guess, not proven.
Gold suggests the sacred and the timeless. Klimt borrows Byzantine holiness for a secular, sensual subject.
context: Gustav Klimt (1862–1918), son of a gold engraver, co-founded the Vienna Secession in 1897, a group that broke away from the conservative oﬀicial art academy. He and his circle left the Secession in 1905.
He visited Ravenna in 1903 and saw the gold mosaics of San Vitale (No. 51), which helped spark his gold period.
Vienna around 1900 was also the city of Sigmund Freud. Open sexuality in art was controversial: Klimt’s ceiling paintings for the University of Vienna had been attacked as pornographic.
The Secession’s motto: ‘To every age its art, to art its freedom.’
Klimt and his allies pursued the Gesamtkunstwerk (total work of art), blending painting with architecture, furniture, fashion and crafts. On the exam.
If asked about Byzantine influence on modern art → Klimt’s gold leaf, inspired by the mosaics of San Vitale (No. 51) in Ravenna.
Classic comparison: Klimt’s Kiss (flat, ornamental, gold) versus Brancusi’s Kiss (No. 129: a blocky, three-dimensional stone, nearly abstract). Same title, same years.
Trap: Klimt belongs to the Vienna Secession, not Fauvism, Cubism or German Expressionism.
Gender coding in the pattern: rectangles for him, circles and flowers for her.
Materials: real gold leaf combined with oil paint, unusual for an easel painting.
Reception: bought by the state at once, so it was an oﬀicial success, not a scandal.

129.title: The Kiss
129.plain: A small block of limestone carved by the Romanian-born sculptor Constantin Brancusi into two lovers embracing so tightly that they become one rectangular mass. He carved it himself, straight into the stone, instead of modeling in clay and having assistants copy it. It was a deliberate rejection of Rodin and an early step toward abstract sculpture.
129.spot: A squat, rectangular stone block with two figures face to face. Their eyes meet to form what looks like one shared eye, their arms wrap around the block in parallel grooves, and hair is shown as incised lines on top. Only her long hair and breasts tell the two apart.
129.remember: Brancusi’s Kiss is a ‘brick of love’. Same years as Klimt’s (1907–1908): flat gold painting versus solid stone block.
compare: No. 128 (§5.30), The Kiss: Same subject and same years: Klimt flattens the lovers into gold ornament, Brancusi compresses them into a solid stone block.
No. 119 (§5.21), The Burghers of Calais: Rodin’s modeled, cast and dramatically naturalistic bronzes are exactly what Brancusi rejected when he chose direct carving.
No. 126 (§5.28), Les Demoiselles d’Avignon: Both Picasso and Brancusi drew on African and ancient sculpture around 1907 to break with European naturalism.
129.vocab: direct carving, truth to materials, abstract, symmetry.

form: Limestone, and small: the 1907–08 original is about 11 inches (28 cm) tall. The version usually shown, made in 1916 and now in the Philadelphia Museum of Art, is about 23 inches (58 cm) tall.
Direct carving (the artist carves the final material himself, with no clay model and no pointing machine to copy it). Chisel marks and the shape of the original block remain.
The work stays a rectangular block: the figures are cut into its surface rather than freed from the stone.
Simplified and nearly symmetrical: two half-length figures mirror each other, eyes forming a single shared eye, lips pressed together, arms encircling the block.
Detail is reduced to lines and bands. The deliberately ‘primitive’ look recalls ancient and folk carving.
function: Brancusi made many versions from 1907 into the 1940s, treating the Kiss as an ongoing idea rather than a single object.

A 1909 version was placed on the grave of a young Russian woman, Tatiana Rachewskaïa, in Montparnasse Cemetery in Paris, turning the motif into a funerary monument about love beyond death. French courts have since fought over whether it may be removed and sold.
Other versions went to collectors and museums; the 1916 version entered the Philadelphia Museum of Art with the Arensberg collection.
content: Love as union: two bodies become literally one block, one eye, one mass.
Equality of the lovers: man and woman are almost identical, distinguished only by hair and breasts.
By keeping the block shape, Brancusi makes the couple feel timeless and primal, like an ancient idol rather than a dramatic moment.
context: Constantin Brancusi (1876–1957) came from a Romanian peasant family and trained as a woodcarver. According to legend, he walked much of the way from Romania to Paris, arriving in 1904.
He worked in Rodin’s workshop for about a month in 1907, then left, reportedly saying ‘Nothing grows in the shadow of great trees.’
Rodin modeled in clay and had others carve or cast his works (No. 119). Brancusi’s direct carving was a statement of truth to materials (letting stone look like stone).
Influences include Romanian folk woodcarving and the Egyptian, Cycladic and African sculpture he saw in Paris museums.
His later works became so abstract that in 1926 US customs refused to classify his Bird in Space as art. A 1928 court ruling decided it was art. On the exam.
If asked about direct carving → Brancusi’s Kiss; contrast Rodin’s modeled and cast bronzes, such as The Burghers of Calais (No. 119).
Classic pairing: Brancusi versus Klimt (No. 128). Same title and years, opposite approaches: essential block versus gold ornament.
Trap: the date 1907–1908 refers to the first version; the photo you usually see is the 1916 version.
Material: limestone, not marble or bronze.
Key idea: simplification toward essential form, a step toward abstract sculpture.
Attribution clue: a compact block with minimal, symmetrical, incised features suggests Brancusi.

130.title: The Portuguese
130.plain: A brown and gray painting by Georges Braque of a Portuguese guitar player in a bar in Marseille, broken into so many small, see-through planes that you can barely find him. It is Analytic Cubism at its most extreme. Its stenciled letters and numbers, among the first in Cubist painting, point the way to collage.
130.spot: A tall canvas of tan, ochre and gray facets arranged in a loose pyramid. Near the bottom center you can make out a guitar’s round sound hole and strings. Stenciled letters ‘D BAL’ sit near the upper right, with the numbers ‘10,40’ below them.
130.remember: Braque’s Portuguese is the ‘brown bar band’. The stencils read ‘BAL’ (a dance) and ‘10,40’ (a price), and it is dated 1911, four years after Les Demoiselles.
compare: No. 125 (§5.27), Mont Sainte-Victoire: Cézanne’s landscapes built from planes of color are the direct source for Braque’s fragmented, shallow space.
No. 126 (§5.28), Les Demoiselles d’Avignon: Picasso’s proto-Cubist painting of 1907 starts the fragmentation that Braque pushes almost to abstraction in 1911.
No. 131 (§5.33), Goldfish: Painted a year apart in France, one dissolves form into gray-brown planes while the other builds everything from bright color.
130.vocab: Analytic Cubism, Synthetic Cubism, collage, stencil, picture plane, monochrome.

form: Oil on canvas, about 46 × 32 inches (117 × 81 cm), in the Kunstmuseum Basel, Switzerland.
Analytic Cubism (breaking objects into many small planes seen from different angles, then reassembling them on a flat surface). The figure dissolves into overlapping facets.
Almost monochrome: browns, ochres and grays, so that color does not distract from the analysis of form.
Facets are partly transparent and shaded at their edges, creating a flickering, shallow space with no single light source.
Stenciled letters and numbers, painted through a cut template the way a sign painter would, sit perfectly flat on the surface.
Braque had trained as a house painter and decorator, which is where his stenciling and imitation wood-grain techniques came from.
function: An experimental easel painting for the small avant-garde market. The dealer Daniel-Henry Kahnweiler handled Braque’s and Picasso’s Cubist works.
Painted in Céret, in southern France, in summer 1911, as part of Braque’s day-to-day exchange of ideas with Picasso.
Now in a public museum and used everywhere as the textbook example of Analytic Cubism.
content: The subject is a Portuguese musician (or emigrant) playing a guitar in a bar in Marseille, a scene Braque remembered.
The letters suggest a poster for a dance (‘BAL’ means a ball or dance hall) and a price (‘10,40’), evoking the bar’s walls and advertisements.
The larger point: a painting is a flat object covered with marks, not a window. The letters remind you that you are looking at a surface.
context: Georges Braque (1882–1963), French, began as a Fauve and met Picasso around 1907. Braque later said the two were ‘like two mountaineers roped together’.
Their 1911 paintings are so similar that experts can struggle to tell them apart, and they often left the fronts unsigned.
The source is Cézanne (No. 125). When Braque showed landscapes built from simple blocks in 1908, the critic Louis Vauxcelles mocked them as ‘little cubes’, naming the movement.
Next step: in 1912 Braque and Picasso began gluing real paper and objects into their works (papier collé and collage), starting Synthetic Cubism.
World War I ended the partnership; Braque was seriously wounded in 1915. On the exam.
If asked to define Analytic Cubism → fragmentation into planes, a muted palette, shallow space and multiple viewpoints. The Portuguese is the textbook example.
If asked about the stenciled letters → they flatten the picture plane and bring popular culture (signs, posters) into fine art, pointing toward collage.
Trap: Braque, not Picasso. The date is 1911, after Les Demoiselles (No. 126, 1907).
Contrast with Matisse’s Goldfish (No. 131), made a year later: Cubism is about form and structure, Matisse about color.
Lineage to know: Cézanne (No. 125) → Les Demoiselles (No. 126) → The Portuguese (No. 130).

131.title: Goldfish
131.plain: A still life by Henri Matisse of four orange goldfish in a glass jar on a small round table, surrounded by plants and flowers. The real subject is color: hot orange against cool green, flat patterns instead of shadows. Matisse wanted paintings that calm the viewer, and goldfish, which he had watched people gaze at for hours in Morocco, became his symbol of peaceful contemplation.
131.spot: A tall canvas with a clear cylindrical glass bowl in the center holding four bright orangered fish, their reflections visible near the water’s surface. The bowl stands on a pink round tabletop tilted up toward you, surrounded by green leaves and pink and blue flowers.
131.remember: Matisse’s fish are ‘Moroccan meditation in a jar’. In 1912 Matisse paints in blazing color while Braque (No. 130) paints in browns and grays.
compare: No. 130 (§5.32), The Portuguese: Made in France a year apart, Braque’s Cubism breaks form into neutral planes while Matisse lets color carry the whole picture.
No. 125 (§5.27), Mont Sainte-Victoire: Cézanne’s tilted tabletops and multiple viewpoints lie behind Matisse’s upturned table and side-view bowl.
No. 96 (§4.49), Fruit and Insects: Ruysch’s Dutch still life uses precise detail and dark backgrounds, while Matisse’s modern still life flattens everything into bright pattern.
131.vocab: Fauvism, complementary colors, still life, flatness.

form: Oil on canvas, about 4.8 × 3.2 feet (146 × 97 cm), in the Pushkin State Museum of Fine Arts, Moscow.
Complementary colors (colors opposite each other on the color wheel, which make each other look stronger): orange fish against green leaves, pink against green.
Flat areas of color with little shading; outlines and decorative leaf patterns fill the space around the bowl.
Mixed perspective: the tabletop is tilted up as if seen from above, while the bowl and fish are seen from the side, a device Matisse learned from Cézanne (No. 125).
The fish appear twice, inside the water and again distorted near the surface, showing how glass and water bend what we see.
Warm accents (fish, table, flowers) repeat around the canvas so your eye circles back to the bowl.
function: An easel painting sold on the private market to the Moscow textile merchant Sergei Shchukin, one of Matisse’s most important patrons.
After the 1917 Russian Revolution, Shchukin’s collection was taken by the Soviet state, which is why the painting is in a Moscow museum.
Matisse said he wanted art to be ‘like a good armchair’ for a tired worker: a source of rest and balance.
content: Goldfish stand for contemplation and calm. In Morocco, Matisse saw people sit for long stretches watching goldfish in bowls.
The bowl, plants and flowers suggest a small, closed paradise, a peaceful garden world.
Goldfish were originally bred in China and were an exotic, modern domestic pleasure in Paris; Matisse painted them in several works around 1912–1913.
The fish’s double appearance hints at the difference between seeing and reality, a playful nod to how painting itself works.
context: Henri Matisse (1869–1954), French, led Fauvism (‘wild beasts’: a movement of about 1905–1907 that used intense, unnatural color), named after a critic’s insult at the 1905 Salon d’Automne.
By 1912 Fauvism had ended as a group, but Matisse kept its bold color and flatness for the rest of his career.
He traveled to Morocco in early 1912 and again in 1912–1913. North African light, textiles and decorative patterns shaped his work; Goldfish was painted in his studio near Paris between the trips.
In ‘Notes of a Painter’ (1908) Matisse called for an art of ‘balance, purity and serenity’.
Matisse and Picasso were friendly rivals: Picasso pushed form, Matisse pushed color. On the exam.
If asked about color as the main subject → Matisse; complementary orange and green.
Trap: painted after the Fauve years (1905–07), but still taught as an example of Fauvist-style color.
Function point: art as calm decoration and contemplation, the opposite of the anxious German Expressionists (No. 133).
Perspective point: multiple viewpoints like Cézanne’s, but driven by color rather than by breaking up form as Cubism does (No. 130).
Context hooks: Morocco, and the Moscow collector Shchukin.
Attribution clues for Matisse: saturated flat color, decorative pattern, tilted tabletop, a peaceful domestic subject.

132.title: Improvisation 28 (second version)
132.plain: One of the first almost completely abstract paintings in Western art, made in Munich in 1912 by the Russian painter Vassily Kandinsky. Patches of color and black lines float across the canvas like a piece of music. Hidden inside are faint images of disaster on the left and a new paradise on the right, but Kandinsky wanted you to feel the painting before you try to read it.
132.spot: A wide canvas of bright patches of yellow, blue, red and green crossed by thick black lines and squiggles. On the left, jagged shapes that may be a cannon, waves and boats; on the right, softer, rounder shapes that may be a couple, a sun and a walled city. No horizon, no clear objects.
132.remember: Improvisation means jazz on canvas. ‘Kandinsky makes color sing’, and 1912 is the year his book on spiritual art came out.
compare: No. 136 (§5.38), Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow: Both painters sought spiritual truth through abstraction, but Kandinsky’s loose, emotional shapes contrast with Mondrian’s strict grid of primaries.
No. 145 (§5.47), Woman, I : De Kooning’s gestural Abstract Expressionism inherits Kandinsky’s belief that marks and color can express inner feeling directly.
No. 149 (§5.51), The Bay: Frankenthaler’s floating color fields continue the idea that color alone can carry emotion, without depicting objects.
132.vocab: nonrepresentational, abstract, synesthesia, Theosophy, Expressionism, improvisation.

form: Oil on canvas, about 3.7 × 5.3 feet (111 × 162 cm), in the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York.
Nearly non-objective (not showing recognizable things): color patches and black lines move independently of each other.
The black lines work like a drawing laid on top, and the color areas spill past them rather than filling them in neatly.
The left side is darker and jagged, the right side brighter and rounder, setting up a visual contrast between violence and calm.
The paint looks quick and spontaneous, though Kandinsky prepared his Improvisations with studies.
There is no foreground or background; shapes float in an undefined space, much as notes float in sound.
function: Kandinsky sorted his works into three types: Impressions (from nature), Improvisations (spontaneous expressions of inner feeling) and Compositions (slowly worked out, the most complex).
Meant to affect the soul directly, the way music does, without needing a story.
Later bought by Solomon R. Guggenheim, whose collection, first shown as the Museum of Non-Objective Painting (1939), was built around art like this.
content: Kandinsky believed each color has its own emotional and spiritual effect; he described yellow as earthly and aggressive and blue as deep and spiritual.
Scholars find hidden apocalyptic imagery (relating to the end of the world): cannons, boats on stormy waves and destruction on the left; a couple, a sun and a walled city of renewal on the right.
Kandinsky expected the materialist world to end and a spiritual age to begin, an idea shaped by Theosophy (a mystical movement blending world religions).
He described synesthesia (experiencing one sense through another): he said that hearing Wagner’s opera Lohengrin made him see colors.
context: Vassily Kandinsky (1866–1944), Russian, gave up a career in law at 30 to study painting in Munich.
In 1911 he co-founded Der Blaue Reiter (The Blue Rider) with Franz Marc, a group of German Expressionists interested in spirituality, music and color.
His book Concerning the Spiritual in Art (published in December 1911, dated 1912) argued that art should come from ‘inner necessity’.
Later he taught at the Bauhaus (1922–1933), and his style became more geometric. The Nazis branded his work ‘degenerate’.

Other artists reached abstraction around the same time, including František Kupka, Robert Delaunay and the Swedish painter Hilma af Klint, who began abstract works in 1906, so ‘first abstract painter’ is debated. On the exam.
If asked about abstraction linked to music and spirit → Kandinsky: ‘Color is the keyboard, the eyes are the hammers, the soul is the piano with many strings.’
Contrast with Mondrian (No. 136): Kandinsky’s expressive, organic abstraction versus Mondrian’s geometric, ruled abstraction. Both were drawn to Theosophy.
Trap: Kandinsky was in Der Blaue Reiter (Munich); Kirchner (No. 133) was in Die Brücke (Dresden, then Berlin). Both are German Expressionism.
Content point: ‘abstract’ does not mean meaningless; there is hidden imagery of apocalypse and rebirth.
Influence: his ideas feed into Abstract Expressionism in New York (No. 145, No. 149).

133.title: Self-Portrait as a Soldier
133.plain: A self-portrait by the German Expressionist Ernst Ludwig Kirchner, showing himself in army uniform with his right hand cut off at the wrist and a bloody stump raised in front of a canvas and a naked model. He was never actually wounded. Painted in 1915 after he broke down during military training, it shows his terror that the war had destroyed him as an artist.
133.spot: A gaunt man in a dark blue military tunic and cap, a cigarette in his mouth and a vacant, mask-like stare. His raised right arm ends in a red stump. Behind him, a nude woman stands in a cramped studio with canvases against the wall, all in acid yellows, greens and blues.
133.remember: ‘Kirchner’s Cut’: soldier, stump, studio. 1915, World War I: the painter fears his painting hand is gone.
compare: No. 122 (§5.24), The Scream: Munch’s Scream pioneered the distorted color and anxious mood that Kirchner turns on his own wartime breakdown.
No. 134 (§5.36), Memorial Sheet for Karl Liebknecht: Both are German responses to the violence of 1914–1919, one a private self-portrait of trauma, the other a public print of mourning.
No. 105 (§5.7), Self-Portrait: Vigée Le Brun presents herself as a confident working artist with brush in hand, while Kirchner shows himself robbed of his painting hand.
133.vocab: Expressionism, Die Brücke, arbitrary color, self-portrait, degenerate art.

form: Oil on canvas, about 27 × 24 inches (69 × 61 cm), in the Allen Memorial Art Museum at Oberlin College, Ohio.
Harsh arbitrary color (color chosen for emotion, not realism): a yellow face, sickly greens, a bright blue uniform and blood red.
Jagged, angular shapes and rough, quick brushstrokes give the scene a nervous energy.
The space is tilted and cramped: floor and walls seem to slide, making the room feel claustrophobic, like a stage set.
His face is long and mask-like, partly influenced by the African and Oceanic carvings Kirchner studied in the ethnographic museum in Dresden.
function: A self-portrait used as a psychological record, painted in 1915 as Kirchner tried to work through his own collapse.
Not commissioned: it was made for himself and his small circle, and later entered a museum collection in the United States.
Today it is a key image for discussing artists’ trauma in World War I.
content: The severed painting hand (he was right-handed) symbolizes lost creativity. Many scholars also read it as castration or impotence: fear that he could no longer paint or love.
The nude model behind him represents the life he had lost: art, freedom and sexuality in the bohemian studio.
The uniform stands for the state and the war machine that swallowed individuals.
The cigarette and blank stare suggest nervous exhaustion, what was then called shell shock or neurasthenia.
context: Ernst Ludwig Kirchner (1880–1938) co-founded Die Brücke (The Bridge) in Dresden in 1905, the first German Expressionist group.
In 1915 he volunteered (so that he could choose his unit) as a driver in a field artillery regiment, then suffered a breakdown during training and was discharged that same year.
He spent time in sanatoriums and in 1917 moved to the mountains near Davos, Switzerland, where he lived for the rest of his life.
In 1937 the Nazis removed more than 600 of his works from German museums and showed some in the ’Degenerate Art’ exhibition. He took his own life in 1938.
Influences include Van Gogh, Munch (No. 122) and African and Oceanic sculpture. On the exam.
If asked about World War I in art → Kirchner’s psychological self-portrait (No. 133) and Kollwitz’s memorial print (No. 134).
Trap: the wound is imaginary; it is a symbol, not a record of an injury.
Movement trap: Kirchner belongs to Die Brücke, not Der Blaue Reiter (Kandinsky, No. 132).
Form: arbitrary color plus distortion to show inner feeling = German Expressionism.
Compare with Munch’s The Scream (No. 122): anxiety expressed through distorted color and form.
Context: later condemned by the Nazis as ‘degenerate’, a common theme for German modernists.

134.title: Memorial Sheet for Karl Liebknecht
134.plain: A black-and-white woodcut print by Käthe Kollwitz of grieving workers crowding around the body of Karl Liebknecht, a communist leader murdered in Berlin in January 1919. Kollwitz did not share his revolutionary politics, but she felt deeply for the working people who mourned him. The rough, gouged lines of the woodblock make the grief feel raw and direct.
134.spot: A horizontal print in stark black and white. A dead man lies stretched across the bottom on a white sheet, while a row of rough, dark mourners bends over him from above. Below runs a short carved inscription in German.
134.remember: ‘Kollwitz Carves for Karl’: K plus K plus woodcut, 1919–1920, ‘the living to the dead’.
compare: No. 63 (§4.16), Arena: Giotto’s Lamentation supplies the composition of mourners bent over a body, which Kollwitz transfers from Christ to a political martyr.
No. 106 (§5.8), Y no hai remedio: Both are prints that bear witness to political killing, Goya through etching, Kollwitz through woodcut.
No. 133 (§5.35), Self-Portrait as a Soldier: Both are German reactions to the violence of 1914–1919: Kirchner’s is private and psychological, Kollwitz’s is public and collective.
134.vocab: woodcut, relief print, Lamentation, etching, lithograph, printmaking.

form: A woodcut (a relief print: the artist cuts away the wood that should print white, inks the raised surface and presses paper onto it).
Heavy blacks and gouged white lines; the cuts of the knife and gouge are coarse and visible, giving a raw, folk-like look.
The composition is horizontal: the corpse forms a stiff line along the bottom while the mourners pile up in an arc above.
Figures are simplified, faces reduced to bold strokes, hands large and expressive.
Kollwitz tried the image first as a drawing, then as an etching and a lithograph, before choosing woodcut after seeing Ernst Barlach’s woodcuts in 1920.
function: A memorial print (Gedenkblatt means memorial sheet) honoring Liebknecht for the workingclass people who mourned him.
Liebknecht’s family invited Kollwitz to draw him in the mortuary, and the print grew out of those drawings.
Prints can be made in many copies and sold cheaply, so they reach far more people than a single painting.
content: The inscription reads ‘Die Lebenden dem Toten. Erinnerung an den 15. Januar 1919’: ‘The living to the dead. In memory of 15 January 1919.’
The grieving crowd echoes Christian Lamentation scenes (mourners over the dead Christ, as in Giotto, No. 63), turning a political martyr into an almost religious figure.
The mourners are anonymous working people, not heroes or oﬀicials: grief belongs to ordinary people as a group.
The calm, pale face of the dead man contrasts with the dark, anguished faces above him.
context: Käthe Kollwitz (1867–1945), a German printmaker and sculptor, devoted her work to the poor, to war and to mothers’ grief. Her younger son Peter was killed in World War I in October 1914.
Karl Liebknecht co-led the Spartacist uprising (a communist revolt in Berlin in January 1919). He and Rosa Luxemburg were murdered by right-wing Freikorps (paramilitary) soldiers on 15 January 1919.
Kollwitz was a socialist and later a pacifist, but she opposed violent revolution. She wrote that she could honor Liebknecht as a person without following him politically.
In 1919 she became the first woman elected to the Prussian Academy of Arts; the Nazis forced her out in 1933.
Woodcut had deep roots in German art going back to the Renaissance, and the German Expressionists of Die Brücke had revived it. On the exam.
If asked how artists responded to the politics after World War I → Kollwitz’s memorial to Liebknecht, a print for ordinary people.
Process question: woodcut is a relief print; contrast intaglio prints such as Goya’s etching (No. 106) and Dürer’s engraving (No. 74).
Composition borrowed from the Lamentation tradition (Giotto, No. 63).
Trap: Kollwitz was not a communist; she honored Liebknecht for his bond with workers.
Dates: murder in 1919, print finished in 1920 (hence 1919–1920).
Pair with Goya’s Y no hai remedio (No. 106): printmaking as witness and protest against violence.

135.title: Villa Savoye
135.plain: A white concrete weekend house outside Paris that Le Corbusier designed for the Savoye family, built from 1928 to 1931. It floats on thin columns, has strip windows running along every side and a garden on the roof. It is the clearest built example of his ‘Five Points of a New Architecture’, and it became a model for modernist houses around the world.
135.spot: A flat-roofed white box lifted on slender round columns above a recessed, curved, darkpainted ground floor. Long horizontal strip windows wrap the upper floor, and curved white screen walls rise from the roof terrace.
135.remember: Savoye: ‘save the ground, raise the house’. The Five Points spell P-P-F-W-R: Pilotis, Plan, Façade, Windows, Roof. ‘Pretty Plain, Flat White Roof.’
compare: No. 139 (§5.41), Fallingwater: Two famous modern houses of the 1930s: Le Corbusier’s white machine lifted off the ground versus Wright’s organic house anchored in rock over a waterfall.
No. 146 (§5.48), Seagram Building: Both are International Style, Le Corbusier’s for a private house and Mies’s for a corporate skyscraper, each stripped of ornament.
No. 152 (§5.54), House in New Castle County: Venturi’s Postmodern house answers the plain white box with gables, cut-out arches and playful historical ornament.
135.vocab: pilotis, free plan, ribbon windows, reinforced concrete, International Style, roof garden.

form: Reinforced concrete (concrete with steel bars inside, strong under both pushing and pulling forces) with a steel frame, plastered and painted white.
Pilotis (thin columns that lift a building off the ground) free the ground level for cars and movement.
Free plan: because columns carry the weight, interior walls can go anywhere.
Free façade: the outer walls are a skin, not structural, so windows can be placed freely. Ribbon windows (horizontal strip windows) give even light and wide views.
A roof garden with curved windscreens replaces the land the house covers. A ramp climbs from ground to roof, alongside a spiral staircase.
The curved glass wall of the ground floor follows the turning circle of a car: drive in under the house, drop off passengers, curve around into the garage.
function: A weekend country house in Poissy, about 30 km (20 miles) northwest of Paris, for Pierre and Eugénie Savoye and their son.
Designed around the automobile: a modern family drove out from Paris, and the house welcomed the car into its very shape.
It leaked badly and was hard to heat; Madame Savoye complained bitterly in the late 1930s. The family left during World War II, when the house was used by occupying German and then American troops.

Nearly demolished in the 1950s to make way for a school, it was saved, protected as a historic monument in the 1960s, and is now a museum and part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing of Le Corbusier’s works (2016).
content: ‘A house is a machine for living in’: Le Corbusier’s slogan from his book Toward an Architecture (1923). The house should be eﬀicient, hygienic and industrial.
White surfaces, sun and air signaled health and cleanliness, important in an age of tuberculosis.
The ramp creates an architectural promenade (a planned walk through changing views), so moving through the house is part of the design.
context: Le Corbusier (1887–1965) was the pen name of Charles-Édouard Jeanneret, a Swiss-born architect who worked in France. He designed the villa with his cousin Pierre Jeanneret.
He published the Five Points of a New Architecture in 1926: pilotis, free plan, free façade, ribbon windows and roof garden.
The villa belongs to the International Style, a name coined by MoMA’s 1932 architecture exhibition: flat roofs, smooth white surfaces, no ornament, emphasis on volume rather than mass.
His earlier Dom-Ino system (1914–15), a concrete frame of slabs and columns, made the Five Points possible. On the exam.
If asked to list the Five Points → pilotis, free plan, free façade, horizontal ribbon windows, roof garden.
Trap: Le Corbusier, not Mies van der Rohe (No. 146) or Frank Lloyd Wright (No. 139).
Machine versus nature: Villa Savoye stands apart from its site on pilotis; Fallingwater (No. 139) grows out of its rock and water.
Postmodern response: Venturi, Rauch and Scott Brown (No. 152) brought back gables, ornament and history.
Memorable fact: the curved ground floor follows a car’s turning circle.
Materials: steel and reinforced concrete, finished in white.

136.title: Composition with Red, Blue and Yellow
136.plain: A small square painting by the Dutch artist Piet Mondrian made of nothing but thick black lines, white rectangles and the three primary colors. It looks simple, but Mondrian adjusted every line and block by eye until the uneven parts balanced. He believed this strippeddown language could show the universal harmony hidden beneath the messy surface of the world.
136.spot: A square canvas dominated by a big red square at the upper right, with a small blue square at the lower left and a small yellow rectangle at the lower right, all divided by thick black horizontal and vertical lines on a white ground.
136.remember: Mondrian = ruler plus primaries. In 1930 ‘red rules the top right corner’, with tiny blue and yellow keeping the balance.
compare: No. 132 (§5.34), Improvisation 28: Both sought spiritual truth through abstraction, but Kandinsky’s expressive swirls oppose Mondrian’s ruled grid of primaries.
No. 146 (§5.48), Seagram Building: The Seagram Building’s regular grid of glass and bronze shows how Mondrian’s geometric order echoed in modern architecture.
No. 135 (§5.37), Villa Savoye: Le Corbusier’s white, rectilinear villa shares De Stijl’s ideal of pure, unornamented form for a new modern age.
136.vocab: De Stijl, Neoplasticism, primary colors, asymmetry, geometric abstraction, grid.

form: Oil on canvas, and small: about 18 inches (46 cm) square, in the Kunsthaus Zürich, Switzerland.
Only horizontal and vertical black lines, the three primary colors (red, blue, yellow) and the ‘non-colors’ white, gray and black.
Asymmetrical balance (unequal parts that still feel balanced): the large red square is offset by the small blue and yellow areas and the heavy black lines.
No diagonals, no curves and no illusion of depth; everything sits on the flat surface.
The surface is not machine-perfect. Up close, brushstrokes are visible and the white areas are built up in several layers, some slightly tinted.
Line thickness varies, and Mondrian adjusted lines and color areas by trial and error, using tape and repainting, not mathematical formulas.
function: A purely abstract easel painting meant to reveal a universal harmony beneath the chaos of nature.
Mondrian saw it as a model for a future society, in which art would eventually merge into architecture, design and everyday life.
Its look spread into design, architecture and fashion; Yves Saint Laurent’s 1965 ‘Mondrian’ dresses are a famous example.
content: Horizontal and vertical lines stand for opposites held in balance: male and female, spirit and matter, a pairing drawn from Theosophy.
Primary colors are the pure building blocks of all other colors, so the painting avoids personal emotion and aims at the universal.
Balancing unequal parts expresses dynamic equilibrium: a living harmony, not static mirror symmetry.
context: Piet Mondrian (1872–1944), Dutch, began as a landscape painter and abstracted trees, step by step, into grids after encountering Cubism in Paris (1911–1914).
He co-founded De Stijl (‘The Style’) in 1917 with Theo van Doesburg, and called his approach Neoplasticism (a ‘new plastic art’ reduced to its essential elements).
He joined the Theosophical Society in 1909; its mysticism shaped his search for universal order.
He broke with van Doesburg around 1924, partly because van Doesburg began using diagonals.
He moved to London in 1938 and New York in 1940, where late works like Broadway Boogie Woogie became more rhythmic. On the exam.
If asked about geometric abstraction → Mondrian, De Stijl and Neoplasticism: primaries plus black, white and gray, only horizontals and verticals.
Contrast with Kandinsky (No. 132): both spiritual and influenced by Theosophy, but Kandinsky is expressive and loose while Mondrian is strict and geometric.
Trap: the arrangement is not random; the asymmetrical balance was worked out carefully.
Connection: De Stijl ideas fed into the Bauhaus and International Style architecture (No. 135, No. 146).
Attribution clues: black grid, primary colors, white ground, no diagonals = Mondrian.

137.title: Illustration from The Results of the First Five-Year Plan
137.plain: A double-page propaganda spread that Soviet artist Varvara Stepanova designed for a 1932 book celebrating the Soviet Union’s first Five-Year Plan. A giant cut-out photograph of Lenin speaking is wired to an electric transmission tower and loudspeakers above a vast crowd. It used photomontage, a modern, machine-age technique, to sell the idea that industry and electricity were transforming the country.
137.spot: Black-and-white photographs cut out and combined with bold red graphic shapes: an oversized Lenin speaking, a red lattice transmission tower with wires, loudspeakers on a platform marked with a big ‘5’, and a dense crowd filling the bottom.
137.remember: ‘Stepanova Sells Socialism’: the 5 means the Five-Year Plan, and Lenin’s voice flows through wires to the masses. 1932.
compare: No. 212 (§9.21), Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan: Both are communist propaganda images glorifying a revolutionary leader and mass-produced for millions, one Soviet, one Chinese.
No. 108 (§5.10), Liberty Leading the People: Delacroix’s Liberty also turns politics into a rousing image, but as a single oil painting rather than a mass-printed montage.
No. 147 (§5.49), Marilyn Diptych: Warhol also builds images from reproduced photographs, but to examine celebrity and consumer culture rather than to serve a state.
137.vocab: photomontage, Constructivism, propaganda, Socialist Realism, avant-garde.

form: Photomontage (a picture made by cutting and combining photographs, often with graphics or type): cut-out photos of Lenin, crowds and technology.
Strong red accents (the tower, the number 5, a triangle) against black-and-white photographs. Red is the color of communism.
Dynamic diagonals and sudden jumps in scale: the giant Lenin dwarfs the crowd.
Wires connect Lenin to loudspeakers and to placards reading ‘СССР’ (USSR in Cyrillic letters), as if his speech is being broadcast electrically.
Designed for mass printing: a flat page layout, bold and legible, made to be reproduced by the thousands.
function: Propaganda: an illustration in a book on The Results of the First Five-Year Plan (1928–1932), Stalin’s crash program of industrialization and collectivized farming.
Aimed at a mass audience, at home and abroad, to celebrate progress and loyalty to the state.
It puts into practice the Constructivist idea that artists should be engineers of society, making useful designs rather than paintings for rich collectors.
content: Lenin, who had died in 1924, appears as the founding father whose ideas power the nation, literally through electric wires. He had declared that ‘Communism is Soviet power plus the electrification of the whole country.’
The crowd shows collective unity: the people appear as a mass, not as individuals.
The tower and loudspeakers symbolize modern technology, radio and electrification.
The big ‘5’ stands for the Five-Year Plan, which the government announced had been fulfilled early, in about four years.
context: Varvara Stepanova (1894–1958) was a leading Constructivist (a Soviet movement that treated art as production: design, typography, textiles, posters). She often designed books and magazines with her husband, Aleksandr Rodchenko.
Constructivists rejected easel painting as bourgeois; in the 1920s Stepanova designed textiles and sportswear for factory production.
The reality behind the image: forced collectivization caused the famine of 1932–1933 that killed millions, including in Ukraine (the Holodomor). Propaganda hid this.
In 1932 the regime dissolved independent art groups, and Socialist Realism became oﬀicial policy in 1934. Photomontage was one of the last avant-garde forms still in oﬀicial use.
Photomontage felt more truthful than painting because it used photographs, which made it especially persuasive as propaganda. On the exam.
If asked about art as propaganda → Stepanova’s photomontage for the Five-Year Plan; compare Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan (No. 212).
Process: photomontage means cut and combined photographs, then reproduced in print.
Movement: Constructivism, Soviet Union: art in the service of the state and industry.
Trap: Lenin is the giant central figure. Stalin launched the plan, but he is not the focus of this spread.
Context trap: the image shows triumph, but the plan brought famine and repression.
Gender point: one of the few women among the AP works of 1900–1945; the Soviet avantgarde gave women designers leading roles.

138.title: Object (Le Déjeuner en fourrure)
138.plain: A real teacup, saucer and spoon that the 22-year-old Swiss artist Meret Oppenheim covered in the fur of a Chinese gazelle in 1936. It looks soft and luxurious, but the thought of putting your lips to a hairy cup is revolting. It became the best-known Surrealist object, and New York’s Museum of Modern Art bought it the same year.
138.spot: A small teacup and saucer with a teaspoon, entirely covered in tan, speckled fur, displayed on a plinth or in a glass case.
138.remember: Oppenheim’s Object: ‘the hair of the cup’. 1936: Surrealism serves fur for breakfast.
compare: No. 144 (§5.46), Fountain: Duchamp presents a mass-produced object almost unchanged, while Oppenheim alters hers to create a disturbing new sensation.
No. 230 (§11.7), Pink Panther: Koons also turns everyday, kitsch materials into gallery objects that play on desire and taste.
No. 115 (§5.17), Olympia: The title nods to Manet, whose deliberately shocking images of women unsettled viewers just as Oppenheim’s cup does.
138.vocab: Surrealism, found object, assemblage, uncanny, readymade.

form: An assemblage of found objects (ordinary items the artist did not make): a store-bought cup about 4.3 inches (11 cm) across, a saucer about 9.4 inches (24 cm) across, and a spoon about 8 inches (20 cm) long.
The fur is from a Chinese gazelle, glued over every surface; the hair follows the curves, so the shapes still read as a cup and saucer.
Materials clash: hard, smooth china meets soft animal fur, so the sense of touch is central.
Small and domestic in scale, it is meant to be seen up close.
Not a pure readymade like Duchamp’s (No. 144): the objects are altered by hand.
function: First shown in Paris in May 1936 at the Surrealist exhibition of objects at the Galerie Charles Ratton.
Then shown in MoMA’s exhibition ‘Fantastic Art, Dada, Surrealism’ (December 1936); the museum’s director, Alfred Barr, bought it for the collection.
Made to provoke a bodily reaction and unsettle the viewer, not to be used.
content: It makes the ordinary uncanny (familiar but strangely disturbing), a key Surrealist goal.
It carries strong sexual connotations, combining fur, a cup, a spoon and the mouth; many read it as an erotic, even female, image.
It plays with gender roles: a dainty, feminine, domestic tea set turned animal and wild.
The title, given by André Breton, mixes Manet’s scandalous picnic painting Le Déjeuner sur l’herbe with the novel Venus in Furs by Leopold von Sacher-Masoch.
context: Meret Oppenheim (1913–1985) was born in Berlin, grew up partly in Switzerland, and moved to Paris at 18, where she joined the Surrealists and modeled for Man Ray’s photographs.
Origin story: at the Café de Flore, Picasso admired her fur-covered metal bracelet and said you could cover anything with fur. She answered: ‘Even this cup and saucer.’
Surrealism, founded by André Breton in 1924, tried to unlock the unconscious mind, drawing on Freud’s ideas about dreams and desire.
Instant fame weighed on her; she went through years of creative crisis and resisted being defined by one object.
Women were often cast as muses in Surrealism; Oppenheim is a woman whose object became the movement’s emblem. On the exam.
If asked about Surrealist objects → Oppenheim’s fur-covered cup (1936): the familiar made strange.
Readymade comparison: Duchamp’s Fountain (No. 144) is selected and signed; Oppenheim’s cup is altered.
Material is the meaning: touch, texture and the mouth.
Trap: Oppenheim was Swiss (born in Berlin), not French; the fur is gazelle, not rabbit.
Title links: Manet’s Déjeuner sur l’herbe and Venus in Furs; compare Manet’s Olympia (No. 115) for the same provocative spirit.
Exhibition history: Paris first, then MoMA, which bought it in 1936.

139.title: Fallingwater
139.artist: Frank Lloyd Wright; Mill Run, Pennsylvania
139.medium: Reinforced concrete, sandstone, steel, and glass
139.plain: A weekend house that Frank Lloyd Wright designed for a Pittsburgh department-store family and perched directly over a waterfall in the Pennsylvania woods. Concrete terraces shoot out over the stream while stone walls anchor the house to the rock. It is the most famous example of Wright’s ‘organic architecture’, a building that seems to grow out of its site instead of sitting on top of it.
139.spot: Cream-colored horizontal concrete balconies stacked and jutting out over a small waterfall, crossed by a tall vertical mass of rough, layered tan sandstone, with long bands of red-framed windows, all surrounded by trees.
139.remember: Fallingwater: the house that falls over the water. ‘Kaufmann wanted a view of the falls; Wright gave him a house on top of them’ (1936–1939).
compare: No. 135 (§5.37), Villa Savoye: Two landmark modern houses: Le Corbusier’s white box stands apart from its site, while Wright’s house grows out of the rocks and stream.
No. 207 (§9.16), Ryoan-ji: Both arrange stone, water and space to invite contemplation of nature, reflecting the Japanese design ideas Wright admired.
No. 124 (§5.26), Carson, Pirie, Scott and Company Building: Sullivan, Wright’s teacher, also combined new building technology with ornament drawn from nature.
139.vocab: cantilever, organic architecture, reinforced concrete, Prairie style.

form: Reinforced concrete cantilevers (horizontal slabs anchored at one end and projecting into the air) are stacked over the stream called Bear Run.
A vertical core of local sandstone, quarried on the property and laid in rough horizontal layers like the rock ledges of the site.
A boulder from the site rises through the living room floor to form the hearth (the fireplace area) at the heart of the house.
Glass meets glass at corners without posts, dissolving the idea of a closed box. Steel window frames are painted Wright’s signature ‘Cherokee red’.
A glass hatch in the living room opens onto a suspended stairway that leads straight down to the water.
Inside: low ceilings, built-in furniture and long horizontal lines that pull your eye outward to the trees.
function: A weekend retreat for Edgar J. Kaufmann Sr., his wife Liliane and their son Edgar Jr., owners of Kaufmann’s department store in Pittsburgh.
The family expected a house facing the falls; Wright put it on the falls, so they would live with the sound of water everywhere.
In 1963 Edgar Jr. gave it to the Western Pennsylvania Conservancy, and it has been open to the public as a museum ever since.
content: Organic architecture: a building should harmonize with its site, materials and inhabitants, like a plant growing from the land.
Horizontal concrete trays echo the rock ledges, and the vertical stone echoes the trees, so the house rhymes with the landscape.
Wright admired Japanese architecture’s flow between inside and outside and its respect for nature; he was a major collector of Japanese prints.
context: Frank Lloyd Wright (1867–1959), American, trained in Chicago under Louis Sullivan (see No. 124) and developed the low, horizontal Prairie Style houses.
Edgar Kaufmann Jr. had joined Wright’s apprentice program, the Taliesin Fellowship, which connected his father to the architect.
Wright was nearly 70 and many thought his best years were behind him; Fallingwater, and a 1938 Time magazine cover, revived his career.
Engineering problems: the cantilevers sagged for decades, and in 2002 they were strengthened with steel cables (post-tensioning).
Designed in 1935 and built 1936–1938, with a guest house added in 1939; the final cost was several times the original budget. On the exam.
If asked about organic architecture → Fallingwater: Wright, cantilevers over a waterfall, native stone.
Contrast with Villa Savoye (No. 135): Le Corbusier’s white machine lifted off the ground versus Wright’s house rooted in rock and water.
Function: a private weekend house, now a museum.
Materials: reinforced concrete, sandstone, steel and glass.
Japanese link: compare the harmony with nature in the Ryoan-ji rock garden (No. 207).
Trap: it is in Pennsylvania (Mill Run), not in Wright’s Midwest.

140.title: The Two Fridas
140.plain: A large double self-portrait by the Mexican painter Frida Kahlo, painted in 1939 as her marriage to the muralist Diego Rivera ended. Two Fridas sit hand in hand, one in a white European lace dress and one in traditional Mexican Tehuana clothing, their hearts exposed and joined by a single vein. It shows a divided identity and a broken heart, made literal.
140.spot: Two seated women with the same face, joined eyebrows and dark hair, holding hands on a bench before a gray, stormy sky. The left one wears a white lace dress spotted with blood; the right one wears a Tehuana skirt and blouse. Both have exposed red hearts linked by a vein.
140.remember: Two Fridas, one vein: Europe on the left bleeds, Mexico on the right holds little Diego. 1939 = the divorce year.
compare: No. 143 (§5.45), Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda Pa…: Rivera’s mural includes Frida standing protectively behind young Diego, a public view of the couple to set beside her private one.
No. 235 (§11.12), Rebellious Silence, from the Women of Allah s…: Neshat also uses her own body and clothing to explore a divided cultural identity, Iranian and Western.
No. 133 (§5.35), Self-Portrait as a Soldier: Both are self-portraits of crisis that turn inner pain into a visible wound.

form: Oil on canvas, large for Kahlo: about 5.7 feet (173.5 cm) square, in the Museo de Arte Moderno, Mexico City.
Symmetrical, frontal composition: two near-identical women, hands joined at the center.
Precise, detailed brushwork and flat, stage-like space recall Mexican retablos (small devotional paintings, often on tin) and folk art.
A dramatic, turbulent sky fills the background like an omen.
Anatomically drawn hearts: the left one is cut open, the right one whole, with a vein winding between them.
function: A personal self-portrait working through heartbreak around her divorce from Diego Rivera, final in late 1939. They remarried in December 1940.
Shown at the International Exhibition of Surrealism in Mexico City in January 1940.
Bought by Mexico’s national fine arts institute in 1947; it is now a national treasure.
content: Left Frida: European, in a Victorian-style lace dress, linked to her German-born father. Her heart is cut open and she clamps the severed vein with surgical forceps, yet blood still drips onto her white skirt.
Right Frida: Mexican, in Tehuana dress (from the Isthmus of Tehuantepec, a region known for strong, independent women), the self Diego loved. She holds a tiny oval portrait of Diego as a child.
The shared vein: the two selves keep each other alive. The bleeding suggests lost love and recalls her many surgeries.
Joined hands suggest self-reliance: after Diego, Frida has only herself for company.
context: Frida Kahlo (1907–1954), Mexican. Her father, Guillermo Kahlo, was a German-born photographer; her mother, Matilde Calderón, was of Mexican Indigenous and Spanish descent.
A 1925 bus accident shattered her spine and pelvis; she endured around 30 operations and lifelong pain.
She embraced Mexicanidad (pride in Mexico’s Indigenous heritage and folk culture), part of the national identity promoted after the Mexican Revolution.
André Breton claimed her as a Surrealist; she replied that she never painted dreams, only her own reality.
Rivera, the famous muralist (No. 143), had many affairs, including one with Frida’s sister Cristina, which strained the marriage. On the exam.
If asked about identity → The Two Fridas: European versus Mexican heritage in a double self-portrait.
Symbol checklist: exposed hearts, a linking vein, surgical forceps, blood, the miniature of Diego, Tehuana dress, a stormy sky.
Trap: the European Frida holds forceps (a clamp) to stop the bleeding, not scissors cutting the vein.
Trap: Kahlo resisted the Surrealist label even though she exhibited with the Surrealists.
Context: painted around her 1939 divorce from Rivera.
Compare with Shirin Neshat (No. 235) and Cindy Sherman (No. 231): women artists using their own image to explore identity.

141.title: The Migration of the Negro, Panel no. 49
141.plain: One of sixty small panels that Jacob Lawrence painted in 1940–41 to tell the story of the Great Migration, when African Americans left the rural South for Northern cities. Panel 49 shows a Northern restaurant where a barrier still divides Black and white diners. The message: the North had its own racism, even without the South’s written laws.
141.spot: Simplified, flat figures seated at tables, white diners on one side and Black diners on the other, split by a long dividing barrier. Bold, flat areas of brown, yellow, green and red, hard edges, a tilted, high viewpoint, and a numbered caption.
141.remember: Lawrence: 60 panels, the Migration north. Panel 49 = ‘made it North, still roped off’.
compare: No. 232 (§11.9), Dancing at the Louvre: Ringgold also pairs images with written text to tell African American stories, in a painted story quilt.
No. 127 (§5.29), The Steerage: Both deal with migration and class: Stieglitz in a single photograph of a ship’s poorest passengers, Lawrence in a 60-part history.
No. 243 (§11.20), Darkytown Rebellion: Kara Walker also confronts the history of racism in America through flat, simplified silhouettes.

form: Casein tempera on hardboard (casein: a fast-drying, matte paint made with milk protein; hardboard: a panel of compressed wood fiber). Each panel is about 12 × 18 inches.
Lawrence painted all 60 at the same time, applying one color at a time across every panel, so the color stays consistent through the series.
Flat areas of color with hard edges, simplified figures, almost no shading, and a limited palette of earthy tones with bright accents.
Influences include Cubism’s flat planes and Harlem’s visual culture: posters, comic strips and storefront signs.
Strong geometric shapes and a tilted perspective stress the separation between the two groups.
Each panel has a written caption, so the series reads like a book or a film.
function: To tell a historical story to the public, especially Black audiences, who rarely saw their own history in museums.
Shown in 1941 at Edith Halpert’s Downtown Gallery in New York, making Lawrence the first African American artist represented by a major New York gallery. Fortune magazine reproduced 26 panels.
Bought jointly: MoMA took the even-numbered panels and the Phillips Collection in Washington, D.C., the odd-numbered ones, so Panel 49 is at the Phillips.
content: Original 1941 caption: ‘They also found discrimination in the North although it was much different from that which they had known in the South.’
The barrier is a visual metaphor: Northern segregation was often informal custom (de facto) rather than law (de jure).
The series as a whole shows push factors (lynching, floods, the boll weevil, Jim Crow laws) and pull factors (factory jobs during World War I).
Faces are generalized, so the figures stand for a whole people, not specific individuals.
context: Jacob Lawrence (1917–2000) was born in Atlantic City, New Jersey, to parents who had migrated from the South, and grew up in Harlem after the peak of the Harlem Renaissance.

He trained at the Harlem Art Workshop with Charles Alston, was encouraged by the sculptor Augusta Savage, and researched the series at the 135th Street branch of the New York Public Library (now the Schomburg Center).
A Julius Rosenwald Fund fellowship paid for the project; he was 23 when he began.
The Great Migration: from about 1915 to 1940 roughly 1.5 million Black Southerners moved north, and a second wave (1940–1970) moved millions more.
In 1993 the series was retitled The Migration Series, and Lawrence rewrote the captions. On the exam.
If asked about narrative series in modern art → Lawrence’s 60 captioned panels.
Content trap: Panel 49 shows discrimination in the North, not the South.
Material: casein tempera on hardboard, painted assembly-line style for consistency.
Context: the Harlem Renaissance legacy and the Great Migration.
Compare with Faith Ringgold (No. 232): an African American artist combining text and image to tell a story.
Collection fact: split between MoMA and the Phillips (odd numbers at the Phillips).

142.title: The Jungle
142.medium: Gouache on paper mounted on canvas
142.plain: A huge painting by the Cuban artist Wifredo Lam showing four strange hybrid figures, part human, part plant, part animal, hidden among tall stalks of sugarcane. Lam used the Cubist and Surrealist ideas he had learned in Paris but turned them toward Afro-Cuban religion and the history of slavery on Cuba’s sugar plantations. It talks back to Picasso’s borrowing of African forms.
142.spot: A dense, nearly square tangle of green, blue, yellow and orange stalks and leaves. Longlimbed figures with crescent-moon or mask-like faces, rounded buttocks and oversized hands and feet stand among them; one figure at the upper right holds a pair of scissors.
142.remember: Lam’s Jungle is ‘not a jungle but a cane field’. 1943: Cuba answers Picasso.
compare: No. 126 (§5.28), Les Demoiselles d’Avignon: Picasso borrows African mask forms as an outsider; Lam, of African descent, uses them to speak about his own people’s history.
No. 233 (§11.10), Trade: Both artists use modernist styles to confront colonial exploitation of their own communities.
No. 111 (§5.13), Slave Ship: Turner’s Slave Ship also addresses the Atlantic slave trade, from a British viewpoint a century earlier.
142.vocab: gouache, biomorphic, Santería, primitivism, all-over composition.

form: Gouache on paper mounted on canvas (gouache: an opaque, water-based paint), very large: about 7.8 × 7.5 feet (239 × 230 cm), in MoMA.
An all-over composition with no clear space or horizon: figures and plants interlock edge to edge.
The figures are hybrids: legs merge with cane stalks, faces are masks, bodies sprout leaves.
Influences: Cubist fragmentation, Surrealist biomorphic (organic, body-like) forms, and the mask faces of African art.
Rhythmic vertical stalks create a pulse, like drumming or thick foliage.
function: Painted in Havana after Lam returned to Cuba in 1941, and first exhibited at the Pierre Matisse Gallery, New York, in 1944.
MoMA bought it in 1945. For years it reportedly hung near the museum’s coat check, which critics later read as a sign of how marginal Latin American modernism was treated.
Lam called his painting ‘an act of decolonization’, not physical but mental.
content: The setting is a sugarcane field, not a real jungle. Sugar was Cuba’s main export, built on enslaved African labor.
The mask-like faces and crescent shapes recall the orishas (deities) of Santería, an AfroCuban religion blending Yoruba beliefs with Catholicism.
The scissors at upper right may suggest cutting cane or cutting the ties of colonialism; scholars disagree.
The title plays on the European fantasy of a ‘primitive’ jungle; Lam reclaims that imagery from inside Afro-Caribbean culture.
context: Wifredo Lam (1902–1982), Cuban, had a Chinese immigrant father and a mother of African and Spanish descent. His godmother was a Santería priestess.
He studied in Madrid, fought for the Republic in the Spanish Civil War, and moved to Paris in 1938, where he became close to Picasso.
In 1941 he fled Nazi-occupied France by ship with André Breton and other refugees, reaching Martinique and then Cuba.
The work turns modernist primitivism around: Picasso borrowed African forms from outside (No. 126); Lam draws them from his own heritage. On the exam.
If asked about a critique of primitivism → Lam’s The Jungle versus Picasso’s Les Demoiselles d’Avignon (No. 126).
Medium trap: gouache on paper, mounted on canvas, not oil.
Content: sugarcane, slavery, Santería, hybrid figures.
Style: a fusion of Cubism, Surrealism and Afro-Cuban culture.
Compare with Jaune Quick-to-See Smith (No. 233): an artist reclaiming her culture’s imagery against colonial history.
Attribution clues: crescent mask faces, long limbs, cane stalks, all-over composition = Lam.

143.title: Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda Park
143.plain: A fresco mural about 50 feet long that Diego Rivera painted in 1947–48 for a hotel dining room in Mexico City. It imagines a Sunday stroll through Alameda Park in which four centuries of Mexican history mingle in one crowd: conquistadors, emperors, presidents, revolutionaries, street vendors and Rivera’s own childhood self. In the center stands an elegant skeleton lady, La Calavera Catrina.
143.spot: A long, crowded frieze of figures under park trees. At the center, a skeleton in a large plumed hat and a feather boa holds the hand of a chubby boy in short pants; Frida Kahlo stands behind the boy with her hand on his shoulder.
143.remember: ‘Dream of Diego’: little Diego holds Death’s hand in the Alameda. Rivera, 1947– 1948, 50 feet of Mexican history.
compare: No. 140 (§5.42), The Two Fridas: Kahlo’s private double self-portrait contrasts with Rivera’s huge public mural, yet both build Mexican identity from history and folk culture.
No. 63 (§4.16), Arena: Both are true frescoes telling a story through rows of figures, Giotto’s sacred and Rivera’s national and political.
No. 232 (§11.9), Dancing at the Louvre: Ringgold’s story quilt also gathers famous figures from history into one imagined scene.
143.vocab: fresco, mural, frieze, calavera, Mexican muralism.

form: Fresco (pigment painted into wet lime plaster so it binds into the wall), about 4.8 × 15.6 m (roughly 15 × 50 feet).
A crowded, frieze-like composition (a long horizontal band of figures) of well over a hundred people, layered like a group photo under the park’s trees.
Bright colors, solid rounded figures and clear outlines: Rivera’s style blends the Italian Renaissance fresco he studied in Italy with Mexican folk art.
Roughly arranged in time from left (the Conquest and colonial era) through the center (the 19th century and the Porfirio Díaz era) to right (the 1910 Revolution and modern times).
The central group: Catrina stands between young Diego and the printmaker José Guadalupe Posada, who invented her, with her arm linked through his.
function: Commissioned for the dining room of the new Hotel del Prado, facing Alameda Park in Mexico City.
After the 1985 earthquake wrecked the hotel, the mural, weighing many tons, was moved in one piece to a new museum nearby, the Museo Mural Diego Rivera, which opened in 1988.
Public art: the Mexican muralists wanted art that everyone could see, not only collectors.
content: La Calavera Catrina: Posada’s satirical skeleton of an upper-class lady, mocking Mexicans who copied European fashions. Death makes everyone equal.
Her feather boa is a feathered serpent, a nod to the Aztec god Quetzalcoatl and pre-Hispanic Mexico.
Historical cast includes Hernán Cortés, Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz (see No. 99), Benito Juárez, Emperor Maximilian and Empress Carlota, the dictator Porfirio Díaz, and revolutionaries.
Frida Kahlo stands behind young Diego as a protective, almost motherly figure, holding a yin-yang symbol.
Social contrasts: a policeman pushes away a poor Indigenous family while the elite promenade, reflecting Rivera’s Marxist view of class.
context: Diego Rivera (1886–1957) led Mexican Muralism with José Clemente Orozco and David Alfaro Siqueiros, a movement after the Mexican Revolution that painted national history for the people.
Rivera was a committed communist. The mural originally showed the 19th-century writer Ignacio Ramírez holding a paper reading ‘Dios no existe’ (‘God does not exist’).
Catholic protesters scratched out the words, and the mural was hidden from view for years. In 1956 Rivera replaced the phrase with a neutral reference to a lecture Ramírez gave.
Rivera and Kahlo married in 1929, divorced in 1939 and remarried in 1940. On the exam.
If asked about public murals → Rivera, Mexican Muralism, fresco, history told for the people.
Iconography checklist: Catrina, Posada, young Diego, Frida, Juárez, Díaz, Cortés.
Function change: a hotel dining room → its own museum after the 1985 earthquake.
Medium: true fresco, like Giotto’s Arena Chapel (No. 63) and Michelangelo’s Sistine Chapel (No. 75).
Controversy: the ‘Dios no existe’ inscription and its removal.
Trap: the Catrina was invented by Posada, not by Rivera.

144.title: Fountain (second version)
144.medium: Readymade glazed sanitary china with black paint
144.plain: A mass-produced porcelain urinal, turned on its back, signed ‘R. Mutt 1917’ and submitted to an exhibition as a sculpture. Marcel Duchamp’s 1917 original vanished soon afterward; the work on the AP list is a 1950 replica he approved. Its claim, that an artist’s choice and idea can make something art, is one of the most influential ideas of the 20th century.
144.spot: A white glazed porcelain urinal lying on its back on a pedestal, with a black painted signature, ‘R. MUTT 1917’, on the lower left of the rim.
144.remember: R. Mutt comes from the Mott plumbing company plus the comic strip ‘Mutt and Jeff’. Original 1917, this replica 1950: ‘Duchamp flushed old art down the drain’.
compare: No. 138 (§5.40), Object: Both turn household objects into art, but Duchamp barely alters his while Oppenheim transforms hers with fur.
No. 230 (§11.7), Pink Panther: Koons’s porcelain Pink Panther continues Duchamp’s game of placing mass-culture objects in the gallery.
No. 250 (§11.27), Kui Hua Zi: Ai Weiwei’s millions of porcelain seeds also question craft, mass production and what counts as an artwork.
144.vocab: readymade, Dada, conceptual art, found object, anti-art.

form: A readymade (an ordinary manufactured object that the artist selects and presents as art): glazed sanitary china with black paint.
Turned 90 degrees and laid on its back on a pedestal, it loses its function and gains a smooth, curving, almost figure-like shape; early supporters compared it to a seated Buddha or a Madonna.
Signed in black paint with a fake name, ‘R. Mutt 1917’. Nothing else was changed.
No craft by the artist: the art lies in selection, placement, title and signature.
The 1950 version was found in a Paris flea market by the dealer Sidney Janis and approved by Duchamp; it is now in the Philadelphia Museum of Art. An edition of eight more replicas followed in 1964.
function: Submitted in 1917 to the first exhibition of the Society of Independent Artists in New York, which promised to show any work by anyone who paid a six-dollar fee.
The board, of which Duchamp was secretly a member, refused to display it as indecent and not art; Duchamp resigned in protest.
Alfred Stieglitz (No. 127) photographed it at his 291 gallery, and the photo ran in the little magazine The Blind Man, which defended it.
Today replicas stand in major museums, the opposite of its original anti-museum point.
content: The Blind Man argued that whether Mr. Mutt made the fountain with his own hands did not matter: he CHOSE it, and created a new thought for that object.
It challenges what art is, who decides (juries, museums, critics), and whether skill matters at all.
It is also a joke: a ‘fountain’ that receives water instead of spouting it, and a bathroom fixture placed in the temple of art.
context: Marcel Duchamp (1887–1968), French, moved to New York in 1915. His Nude Descending a Staircase had already caused a scandal at the 1913 Armory Show.
Dada: an anti-art movement that began in Zurich in 1916 as a reaction to the senseless slaughter of World War I. It attacked logic, good taste and the art establishment.
His earlier readymades include a bicycle wheel mounted on a stool (1913) and a bottle rack (1914).
Some scholars argue that the Dada artist Elsa von Freytag-Loringhoven had a hand in the idea; most still credit Duchamp.
In a 2004 poll of 500 British art experts, Fountain was voted the most influential modern artwork. On the exam.
If asked what a readymade is → Fountain: a mass-produced object chosen, positioned and signed by the artist.
Date trap: the original is from 1917 and is lost; the AP version is a 1950 replica.
Movement: Dada. Influence: Conceptual art, Pop art (No. 147), Koons (No. 230), Ai Weiwei (No. 250).
Trap: there was no jury; the society’s board refused to show it even though the rules said anything could be shown.
Compare with Oppenheim (No. 138): an altered everyday object versus a merely selected one.
Key idea: idea over craftsmanship.

145.title: Woman, I
145.plain: A large, violent, smeared painting by Willem de Kooning of a giant grinning woman with huge staring eyes and bared teeth. He struggled with it for about two years, scraping it down and repainting it again and again, and nearly gave up. When it was shown in 1953, other artists were shocked that a leading abstract painter had returned to the human figure.
145.spot: A seated female figure filling the canvas, built from slashing strokes of pink, yellow, blue and red, with enormous staring eyes, a wide toothy grin, huge breasts, and a loose, scribbled background.
145.remember: De Kooning’s Woman I: ‘scary smile, two years, 1950–52’. Abstract Expressionism with a face.
compare: No. 14 (§3.3), Statues of votive figures, from the Square Te…: De Kooning said the huge staring eyes came partly from Sumerian votive statues like those from Eshnunna.
No. 149 (§5.51), The Bay: Two sides of Abstract Expressionism: de Kooning’s violent gestures versus Frankenthaler’s calm soaked-in color.
No. 147 (§5.49), Marilyn Diptych: Warhol’s mechanically printed Marilyn is a cool Pop answer to de Kooning’s hot, hand-made image of a woman.
145.vocab: Abstract Expressionism, gestural, action painting, figurative, New York School.

form: Oil on canvas, about 6.3 × 4.8 feet (193 × 147 cm), in MoMA.
Gestural brushwork (the visible record of the artist’s arm movement): aggressive slashes, drips and smears.
Built up through many layers; he scraped paint off, repainted, and pressed newspaper onto wet paint to slow drying, leaving transferred marks.
Figure and background run together, and the body is broken into planes, a legacy of Cubism.
Colors are fleshy pinks and acid yellows against blues and greens, jarring rather than pretty.
During the process he pinned on a smiling mouth cut from a magazine ad, reportedly for Camel cigarettes.
function: The first of a series of Woman paintings, shown at the Sidney Janis Gallery in New York in 1953.
MoMA bought it in 1953, making it an early museum-approved Abstract Expressionist work.
In 1952 the art historian Meyer Schapiro saw the canvas de Kooning had set aside and encouraged him to finish it.
content: It mixes ancient and modern sources: de Kooning cited Mesopotamian votive figures (No. 14) and prehistoric fertility goddesses alongside pin-ups and billboards.
Some see it as misogynistic, a monstrous, devouring woman; others see a satire of advertising’s ideal woman, or a portrait of the artist’s own anxieties.
De Kooning said ‘Flesh was the reason oil paint was invented’, and the picture is as much about paint as about a woman.
context: Willem de Kooning (1904–1997) was born in the Netherlands and came to the United States as a stowaway in 1926. He became a leader of the New York School.
Abstract Expressionism (New York painting of the 1940s–50s stressing spontaneous gesture or huge fields of color). Critic Harold Rosenberg called its gestural side action painting.
Critic Clement Greenberg championed pure abstraction, so a return to the figure looked to some like a betrayal.
After World War II, New York replaced Paris as the center of the art world, and Cold War politics promoted Abstract Expressionism as an image of American freedom.
His wife, Elaine de Kooning, was also a painter in the same circle. On the exam.
If asked about gestural Abstract Expressionism → de Kooning’s Woman I ; contrast Frankenthaler’s soak-stain Color Field (No. 149).
Trap: it is Abstract Expressionist yet figurative.
Sources: Mesopotamian votive figures (No. 14), pin-ups and advertising.
Debate: misogyny or satire, useful for contextual essays.
Process: about two years of painting, scraping and repainting.

146.title: Seagram Building
146.artist: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Philip Johnson; New York
146.medium: Steel frame with glass curtain wall and bronze
146.plain: A 38-story bronze and glass oﬀice tower in Manhattan, finished in 1958 for the Seagram whiskey company and designed by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe with Philip Johnson. It stands back from the street behind a large empty plaza, a radical use of very expensive land. Its simple, refined box became the template for corporate skyscrapers around the world.
146.spot: A dark bronze-brown rectangular tower with a regular grid of tinted glass and thin vertical bronze I-beams running its full height, set back behind a wide granite plaza with two rectangular pools on Park Avenue.
146.remember: Mies says ‘less is more’ but spends more: bronze I-beams that hold up nothing. Seagram, 1954–1958.
compare: No. 124 (§5.26), Carson, Pirie, Scott and Company Building: Sullivan’s steel-frame department store is an ancestor, but it still uses rich ornament where Mies uses almost none.
No. 152 (§5.54), House in New Castle County: Venturi’s Postmodern house mocks the ‘less is more’ ideal with flat, playful historical ornament.
No. 135 (§5.37), Villa Savoye: Both are International Style: Le Corbusier’s white villa and Mies’s bronze tower share a rejection of ornament.
