146.vocab: curtain wall, steel frame, I-beam, mullion, International Style, plaza.

form: Steel frame with a glass curtain wall (a non-load-bearing outer wall of glass hung on the frame) in tinted glass and bronze.
Bronze I-beams run vertically as mullions (the bars between window panes). They are decorative, expressing the steel structure hidden inside.
38 stories, about 515 feet (157 m) tall, a rectangular slab with lower wings at the back.
Raised on tall columns over a glass-walled lobby and set back roughly 90 feet from Park Avenue behind a granite plaza with two pools.
Uniform everywhere: Mies even specified blinds that could only be fully open, half open or closed, so the facade always looks orderly.
function: Headquarters of the Seagram distilling company: a prestige building to give a liquor business an image of refinement.
The architect Phyllis Lambert, daughter of Seagram’s head Samuel Bronfman, persuaded her father to hire Mies instead of a conventional firm.
Philip Johnson designed interiors, including the Four Seasons restaurant, which operated there until 2016.
content: ‘Less is more’: Mies’s motto for reduced, refined form, with luxury expressed through materials and proportion instead of ornament.
The bronze I-beams look like honest structure, but technically they are decoration: fire codes required the real steel to be encased in concrete.
The empty plaza is a gift of public space and a display of corporate wealth.
context: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe (1886–1969), German, was the last director of the Bauhaus design school, which closed in 1933 under Nazi pressure. He emigrated to Chicago in 1938.
International Style: the modernist architecture named by MoMA’s 1932 exhibition, which Philip Johnson co-organized.
It cost about 41 million dollars, one of the most expensive skyscrapers per square foot of its time.
Its plaza helped inspire New York’s 1961 zoning law, which allowed developers extra floors in exchange for public plazas.
It was designated a New York City landmark in 1989. On the exam.
If asked about International Style skyscrapers → the Seagram Building: glass curtain wall, steel frame, bronze, plaza.
Trap: the bronze I-beams are non-structural.
Quote pair: ‘Less is more’ (Mies) versus ‘Less is a bore’ (Venturi, No. 152).
Ancestry: Sullivan’s Carson, Pirie, Scott building (No. 124), an early steel-frame commercial building with large windows.
Influence: the model for countless corporate towers worldwide.

147.title: Marilyn Diptych
147.medium: Oil, acrylic, and silkscreen enamel on canvas
147.plain: Two big canvases by Andy Warhol, each printed 25 times with the same publicity photo of Marilyn Monroe, made in the weeks after her death in August 1962. The left panel is loud color; the right panel is black and white, smeared and fading away. It is about celebrity, mass media and death, made with a commercial printing method instead of a paintbrush.
147.spot: Two side-by-side panels, each a 5 × 5 grid of Monroe’s face. The left panel has bright yellow hair, turquoise eyeshadow and red lips on orange; the right panel has black-and-white prints that grow blotchy, dark or faded.
147.remember: Marilyn times 50: ‘Warhol multiplied Marilyn, then made her fade’. 1962, the year she died.
compare: No. 54 (§4.7), Virgin: Byzantine icons present holy figures in gold for veneration; Warhol presents a movie star as a mass-produced modern icon.
No. 145 (§5.47), Woman, I : Both depict women from popular imagery, but de Kooning paints with violent gestures while Warhol erases the hand through printing.
No. 150 (§5.52), Lipstick: Oldenburg’s giant lipstick is another Pop work built from consumer culture, turned toward protest rather than celebrity.
147.vocab: screenprint, Pop Art, diptych, repetition, icon.

form: Silkscreen (a stencil printing method in which ink is pushed through a fine mesh screen): the photo was screened onto canvas 50 times over painted color.
Oil, acrylic and silkscreen ink on canvas; about 6.7 × 9.5 feet overall (205 × 290 cm), in Tate, London.
Left panel: flat, bright, unnatural colors applied roughly and slightly out of register (misaligned), like cheap printing.
Right panel: black ink only, with uneven, smudged and fading impressions caused by too much or too little ink.
Repetition in a grid suggests products on supermarket shelves or frames of film.
function: An art-market work, shown in Warhol’s first New York solo exhibition, at the Stable Gallery in November 1962.
A response to Monroe’s death on 4–5 August 1962 (a probable suicide), which Warhol began working on within weeks.
Bought by the Tate in 1980.
content: The source is a publicity still for the 1953 film Niagara: the public mask of the star, not the private person.
A diptych (a two-panel work) recalls religious altarpieces, turning Marilyn into a modern icon, like a Byzantine saint (No. 54).
Left is the vivid celebrity image; right is fading life and death. Together they show the cost of fame.
Repetition both multiplies and empties the image, the way media saturation numbs us.
context: Andy Warhol (1928–1987), son of Carpatho-Rusyn immigrants from present-day Slovakia, grew up in Pittsburgh and first worked as a successful commercial illustrator in New York.
Pop Art (late 1950s–60s art using mass-culture imagery: ads, comics, celebrities) rejected Abstract Expressionism’s heroic personal brushwork (No. 145).
From 1963–64 his studio was known as ‘The Factory’, where assistants did much of the screening; he said ‘I want to be a machine’.
The same year he made Campbell’s Soup Cans and began his Death and Disaster paintings, linking glamour and death. On the exam.
If asked about Pop Art and celebrity → Warhol’s Marilyn Diptych: silkscreen, repetition, mass media.
Process: silkscreen, a commercial technique that removes the artist’s hand.
Form: diptych, color versus black and white, fading on the right.
Icon link: compare the Byzantine Theotokos icon (No. 54).
Contrast with de Kooning’s Woman I (No. 145): a mechanical image versus a gestural painting of a woman.
Trap: it was made after her death in 1962, not as a fan portrait.

148.title: Narcissus Garden
148.plain: An installation and performance that Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama staged at the 1966 Venice Biennale: about 1,500 mirrored plastic balls spread on a lawn, which she offered to visitors for about two dollars each. Viewers saw themselves reflected over and over. It mocked the vanity of the art world and its habit of treating art as merchandise, until oﬀicials made her stop selling.
148.spot: Hundreds of identical shiny silver spheres spread across grass or a floor or floating on water, reflecting the surroundings and the viewers. In 1966 photographs, Kusama in a gold kimono sits among them beside hand-lettered signs.
148.remember: Narcissus loved his own reflection; Kusama sold you yours for 1,200 lire. Venice, 1966, 1,500 balls.
compare: No. 144 (§5.46), Fountain: Like Duchamp, Kusama challenges the art establishment, here by turning an elite exhibition into a cheap market stall.
No. 250 (§11.27), Kui Hua Zi: Both installations multiply huge numbers of identical units, raising questions about mass production and value.
No. 224 (§11.1), The Gates: Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s The Gates is another temporary, site-based installation that reaches the public outside museum walls.
148.vocab: installation, performance art, repetition, art market, convex mirror.

form: Installation (an artwork made of objects arranged to fill a space): about 1,500 mirrored plastic spheres in 1966. Later versions use stainless steel.
Each sphere is a convex mirror that reflects the sky, the crowd and you, distorted.
Mass-produced, identical units: repetition and multiplication, constants in Kusama’s work.
The arrangement is loose and flexible, so the work changes shape at each site, from lawns to ponds to abandoned buildings.
In 1966 two signs stood on the lawn: ‘NARCISSUS GARDEN, KUSAMA’ and ‘YOUR NARCISSIUM [sic] FOR SALE’.
function: Staged at the 33rd Venice Biennale (1966) on the lawn outside the Italian Pavilion. Kusama was not oﬀicially invited, though she reportedly had permission to install the balls.
Performance: wearing a gold kimono, she sold balls for 1,200 lire (about two dollars) each until Biennale oﬀicials stopped the sales.
According to her autobiography, the Italian artist Lucio Fontana gave her moral and financial support.
It has been re-created many times since (Central Park in 2004, Rockaway Beach in New York in 2018, and elsewhere), usually in stainless steel.
content: Named after Narcissus, the youth in Greek myth who fell in love with his own reflection: viewers see only themselves.
A critique of the art market: selling art like cheap souvenirs exposed the commerce behind the prestigious Biennale.
Also self-promotion: Kusama made herself the spectacle, gaining press while criticizing celebrity.
Endless mirrored repetition suggests infinity, linked to her lifelong theme of self-obliteration.
context: Yayoi Kusama (born 1929), Japanese, moved to New York in 1958 and became a leading avant-garde figure with her Infinity Net paintings and mirror rooms.

She has described hallucinations since childhood, and repeating dots and nets is partly a way of coping. Since 1977 she has lived by choice in a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo, working in a nearby studio.
As an Asian woman in a mostly white, male art scene, she saw male artists borrow her ideas; the Venice stunt pushed back against her exclusion.
She is now one of the best-selling living artists, an irony given the work’s critique of the market. On the exam.
If asked about performance and critique of the art market → Kusama, Venice 1966, selling mirror balls.
Trap: the AP date refers to the 1966 original installation and performance; photos often show later stainless-steel versions.
Myth link: Narcissus and his reflection.
Compare with Duchamp (No. 144): both question art institutions.
Compare with Ai Weiwei’s Sunflower Seeds (No. 250): vast numbers of identical small objects.

149.title: The Bay
149.plain: A large abstract painting by Helen Frankenthaler, made by pouring thinned acrylic paint onto raw, unprimed canvas so it soaked into the fabric like dye. The result is big, soft-edged pools of blue and green with no brushstrokes at all. Her soak-stain method, which she invented in 1952, launched the style later called Color Field painting.
149.spot: A nearly square canvas dominated by a large, irregular pool of deep blue in the center, flanked by softer areas of lighter blue, green and earth tones, with raw canvas showing in places. Edges are soft and blotted, like ink spilled on cloth.
149.remember: Frankenthaler’s Bay: ‘blue soaked in, not painted on’. 1963 = acrylic and stain.
compare: No. 145 (§5.47), Woman, I : Both are Abstract Expressionists, but de Kooning attacks the canvas with gestures while Frankenthaler lets color soak quietly into it.
No. 132 (§5.34), Improvisation 28: Kandinsky’s belief that color alone can stir emotion lies behind Frankenthaler’s floating fields.
No. 234 (§11.11), Earth’s Creation: Kngwarreye’s Earth’s Creation is another large abstract painting rooted in the experience of landscape.
149.vocab: soak-stain, color field painting, acrylic paint, unprimed canvas, Abstract Expressionism.

form: Acrylic on canvas, about 6.7 × 6.8 feet (205 × 207 cm), in the Detroit Institute of Arts.
Soak-stain technique: thinned paint poured onto unprimed canvas (raw canvas without a sealing layer of gesso) laid on the floor, so color sinks into the threads.
No visible brushstrokes: paint and canvas become one surface, stressing flatness.
Organic, irregular shapes with soft, bleeding edges, made by pouring, tilting the canvas and sponging.
Areas of bare canvas act as part of the composition.
She switched from thinned oil to acrylic around 1962; acrylic stains crisply without the oily halo that can damage raw canvas.
function: An independent abstract painting for museums and collectors, now in the Detroit Institute of Arts.
Meant to be experienced as color and feeling, large enough to fill your field of vision.
Shows the possibilities of the technique a decade after her breakthrough painting Mountains and Sea (1952).
content: Mostly abstract, but the title and shapes suggest landscape: a blue bay of water.
Frankenthaler often worked from memories of landscape and the feeling of a place rather than from direct observation.
It celebrates color itself and the balance between chance (how paint spreads) and control.
context: Helen Frankenthaler (1928–2011), a New Yorker, was a second-generation Abstract Expressionist.
She was inspired by Jackson Pollock’s poured paintings made on the floor, but she thinned her paint until it stained the canvas instead of sitting on top.
In 1953 the critic Clement Greenberg brought painters Morris Louis and Kenneth Noland to her studio. Louis called her ‘a bridge between Pollock and what was possible’, and both adopted staining.
Color Field painting (abstraction built from large, flat areas of color) followed; Greenberg’s 1964 term was ‘Post-Painterly Abstraction’.
A rare woman at the top of a male-dominated movement, she represented the United States at the 1966 Venice Biennale. On the exam.
If asked about soak-stain → Frankenthaler: acrylic on unprimed canvas.
Contrast with de Kooning (No. 145): gestural action painting versus smooth, stained Color Field.
Material trap: acrylic in this work, although her earlier stains used oil.
Influence: Morris Louis and Kenneth Noland.
Fun link: she represented the US at the 1966 Venice Biennale, the same one where Kusama (No. 148) sold mirror balls uninvited.

150.title: Lipstick (Ascending) on Caterpillar Tracks
150.medium: Cor-Ten steel, steel, aluminum, and cast resin; painted with polyurethane enamel
150.plain: A giant red lipstick rising out of a tank-like base on caterpillar treads, by the Pop artist Claes Oldenburg. Yale graduate students commissioned it in 1969 and set it up, unannounced, in the middle of campus as a stage for anti-Vietnam War speeches. Its original inflatable vinyl tip drooped unless someone pumped it up; Oldenburg rebuilt it in steel and resin in 1974.
150.spot: A tall red lipstick tip on a ribbed cylinder, standing upright on a boxy, tank-like base with caterpillar treads, in a stone-walled, Gothic-style college courtyard.
150.remember: Lipstick on a tank = ‘make love, not war’. Oldenburg, Yale, 1969, rebuilt 1974.
compare: No. 147 (§5.49), Marilyn Diptych: Both are Pop Art built on consumer culture, Warhol through repeated photos and Oldenburg through a giant product.
No. 225 (§11.2), Vietnam Veterans Memorial: Both respond to the Vietnam War, Oldenburg with a mocking protest platform, Lin with a quiet, reflective memorial.
No. 230 (§11.7), Pink Panther: Koons also enlarges kitsch consumer imagery into sculpture, but without Oldenburg’s political protest.
150.vocab: Pop Art, monumental, soft sculpture, Cor-Ten steel.

form: Monumental scale: about 24 feet (7.3 m) tall.
The 1969 original had a plywood tank-tread base and a red inflatable vinyl lipstick tip that was supposed to inflate during speeches; it sagged and leaked.
The 1974 version: Cor-Ten steel (a steel that forms a stable protective rust coat), steel, aluminum and cast resin, painted with polyurethane enamel.
Pop strategy: a small everyday object enlarged to monument size, which changes its meaning.
Bright, commercial colors and smooth surfaces, like an ad or a toy.
function: Commissioned by the ‘Colossal Keepsake Corporation’, a group of Yale graduate students, mainly in architecture, who raised the money.
Installed without permission on 15 May 1969 in Beinecke Plaza, near the university’s war memorial, as a speaker’s platform for protest rallies.
Yale had not accepted it; after vandalism and decay Oldenburg took it back in 1970, rebuilt it, and in 1974 it was reinstalled in the courtyard of Morse College, where it still stands.
content: It combines a feminine consumer product (lipstick) with a military machine (tank): sex and war, desire and violence.
The lipstick is also phallic and looks like a missile or bullet; ‘ascending’ suggests both erection and launch.
‘Make love, not war’: an anti-war joke turned into a monument.
It mocks traditional heroic campus monuments, such as statues of generals.
context: Claes Oldenburg (1929–2022), a Swedish-born American Pop artist, was known for soft sculptures (giant floppy hamburgers, toilets) and, from 1976, huge outdoor works made with his wife Coosje van Bruggen.
Pop Art: art about consumer culture and mass production; Oldenburg added humor, softness and enormous scale.
1969 was a peak of Vietnam War protest and campus activism across the United States.
Since 1966 Oldenburg had drawn proposals for ‘colossal monuments’, including lipsticks rising in London’s Piccadilly Circus. On the exam.
If asked about Pop monuments and protest → Oldenburg’s Lipstick (Ascending), Yale, 1969.
Materials trap: AP lists the 1974 materials (Cor-Ten steel, steel, aluminum, cast resin, polyurethane enamel); the original was vinyl and plywood.
Function: a speaker’s platform for anti-war protests.
Iconography: lipstick plus tank = sex plus war.
Compare with Maya Lin’s Vietnam Veterans Memorial (No. 225): opposite ways of responding to the Vietnam War.

151.title: Spiral Jetty
151.medium: Earthwork: mud, precipitated salt crystals, rocks, and water coil
151.plain: A giant coil of black basalt rock and earth, about 1,500 feet long, that Robert Smithson built out into Utah’s Great Salt Lake in April 1970. It is Land art: you cannot put it in a museum, so you must travel to a remote shore to see it. It disappears under the water when the lake rises and reappears, crusted white with salt, when the lake falls.
151.spot: Aerial photos of a counterclockwise spiral path of dark rock curling out from the shore into pinkish-red or pale water, often edged with white salt crystals.
151.remember: Smithson’s spiral: ‘a salty snail in a pink lake’. 1970, Great Salt Lake, 1,500 feet.
compare: No. 156 (§6.4), Great Serpent Mound: Both are monumental earthworks in serpentine or spiral shapes, one built for ancient ritual, the other as modern art.
No. 224 (§11.1), The Gates: Both place art outdoors at landscape scale and depend on photographs and film for most of their audience.
No. 8 (§2.8), Stonehenge: Stonehenge is another huge arrangement of stone in the landscape, tied to natural cycles and requiring a journey to experience.
151.vocab: earthwork, land art, entropy, site-specific, basalt.

form: An earthwork (art made by moving and shaping the land itself): about 1,500 feet long and 15 feet wide, built from roughly 6,650 tons of basalt rock and earth.
Built with dump trucks and a front loader, not by hand; Smithson directed the crew.
A counterclockwise spiral running out from the shore at Rozel Point on the northeast arm of the Great Salt Lake.
The water there is pinkish red from salt-loving algae and bacteria, and salt crystals coat the rocks white.
Its appearance changes with the lake level: long submerged, later exposed, and recently often left on dry lakebed.
function: Land art meant to exist outside galleries and the art market; you experience it by walking the coil.
Smithson also made a film, Spiral Jetty (1970), and wrote an essay about it; for most people these documents are how they know the work.
Funded by the gallery owner Virginia Dwan; since 1999 it has belonged to the Dia Art Foundation, which leases the lakebed from the State of Utah.
content: Entropy (the tendency of all systems to break down into disorder): Smithson welcomed erosion, flooding and change as part of the work.
The spiral echoes the crystal growth of salt at the site and a local legend that the lake was connected to the Pacific by an underground channel that caused whirlpools.
Spirals also suggest time, galaxies and ancient symbols.
The site, near abandoned oil-drilling equipment, mixes industrial ruin with a prehistoriclooking landscape.
context: Robert Smithson (1938–1973), American, was a leading figure in Land art, as was his wife, Nancy Holt.
In the late 1960s many artists left the gallery to escape commercialism and the idea of art as a portable product.
Smithson died in 1973 in a plane crash while surveying the site of his Amarillo Ramp in Texas.
Rising water covered the jetty within a few years of 1970; it re-emerged around 1999–2002 and has been visible much of the time since.
There is ongoing debate about whether it should be restored or left to entropy, as Smithson might have wanted. On the exam.
If asked about Land art or earthworks → Spiral Jetty: Smithson, Great Salt Lake, 1970.
Key ideas: entropy and site-specificity (made for one place, meaningless if moved).
Compare with the Great Serpent Mound (No. 156): an ancient earthwork versus a modern one, both coiling shapes in the land.
Compare with Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s The Gates (No. 224): art placed in the landscape, temporary versus slowly eroding.
Trap: it is made of basalt rock and earth, not concrete; salt crystals form on it naturally.

152.title: House in New Castle County
152.artist: Robert Venturi, John Rauch, and Denise Scott Brown
152.plain: A family house in the countryside of northern Delaware by Robert Venturi, John Rauch and Denise Scott Brown. From a distance it looks like a big traditional farmhouse with a gabled roof, but it wears flat, cartoon-like cut-out arches and stubby columns. It is a key work of Postmodern architecture, which brought back history, symbolism and humor after decades of plain modernist boxes.
152.spot: A long, white house with a big gabled roof. On one side a huge flat arch shape floats across the gable like a sign; on the other, a broad arched screen rests on four squat, flat Doric columns over a recessed porch, like a stage set.
152.remember: Venturi’s house is ‘a farmhouse in costume’. 1978–1983: ‘less is a bore’.
compare: No. 146 (§5.48), Seagram Building: The Seagram Building’s ‘less is more’ minimalism is exactly what Venturi’s ornament and wit rebel against.
No. 135 (§5.37), Villa Savoye: Le Corbusier’s white box on pilotis is the modernist house type that Venturi’s gabled, decorated house answers.
No. 102 (§5.4), Monticello: Jefferson used classical columns and arches earnestly in an American country house; Venturi flattens them into ironic cut-outs.
152.vocab: postmodernism, applied ornament, gable, Doric order, vernacular, decorated shed. 6 Indigenous Americas Content area 5 · 1000 B.C.E.–1980 C.E. · works 153–166 · about 6% of the multiple-choice section. Art of Indigenous peoples of Mesoamerica, the Andes and North America, from about 1000 B.C.E. to the 20th century: temples, sculpture, textiles, featherwork, painted hides, pottery and masks. Much of it was made for rituals, rulers and ancestors, and much of it was damaged, taken or misunderstood after European contact. Expect questions on function, materials and how these works were used in ceremony.

form: Wood frame. AP lists ‘wood frame and stucco’, though the exterior reads mainly as whitepainted siding under a shingled roof, like a traditional Delaware farmhouse.
Entrance side: a large, flat arched screen floats in front of the gable like a billboard announcing ‘house’. Venturi claimed it had Austrian Baroque origins.
Back: a wide arched screen supported by four squat, flat Doric columns around a recessed porch. One column is split by a drainpipe, a deliberate joke.
Applied ornament: the forms are flat cut-outs, clearly decoration rather than structure.
Inside: a vaulted music room with an organ and painted cut-out arches recalling 19thcentury American Carpenter Gothic and Queen Anne woodwork.
Large windows in the breakfast area let the owners watch birds.
function: A private home for a family of three who loved music and birdwatching.
Planned around a central music room for playing and performing.
The clients are reportedly members of the du Pont family. The house won a Progressive Architecture award in 1980.
content: Plays with symbolism: the arch screen signals ‘home’ and ‘entrance’ like a sign, the opposite of modernism’s anonymous boxes.
Irony and wit: classical columns that hold almost nothing, and a grand arch flattened like a stage prop.
Mixes high and low: classical architecture, American vernacular (ordinary local building) farmhouses, and commercial signs.
It illustrates Venturi’s idea of the decorated shed: a plain, functional building with ornament and signs applied to it.
context: Robert Venturi (1925–2018), Denise Scott Brown (born 1931) and John Rauch were partners in a Philadelphia firm; Venturi and Scott Brown were also married.
Venturi’s book Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture (1966) answered Mies’s ‘less is more’ with ‘less is a bore’.
Learning from Las Vegas (1972, by Venturi, Scott Brown and Steven Izenour) praised roadside commercial signs as genuine American architecture.
When Venturi alone received the Pritzker Prize in 1991, Scott Brown was left out; a 2013 petition protesting the omission became a landmark case about women’s recognition in architecture.
Venturi’s earlier Vanna Venturi House (1964), built for his mother, is often called one of the first Postmodern buildings. On the exam.
If asked about Postmodern architecture → House in New Castle County: flat cut-out classical forms, applied ornament, irony.
Quote pair: Mies’s ‘less is more’ (No. 146) versus Venturi’s ‘less is a bore’.
Trap: three architects, including Denise Scott Brown; don’t leave her out.
Contrast with Villa Savoye (No. 135): a house as machine versus a house as symbol.
Compare with Monticello (No. 102): classical forms in an American country house, taken seriously there and played with here.

153.title: Chavín de Huántar
153.medium: Stone (architectural complex); granite (Lanzón and sculpture); hammered gold
153.plain: Chavín de Huántar is a stone temple complex in the Andes of northern Peru, used from about 900 to 200 B.C.E. as a pilgrimage center and oracle. Pilgrims were led through pitch-dark tunnels full of the roar of rushing water to face the Lanzón, a granite shaft carved with a fanged god. It matters because it is one of the earliest large religious centers in South America, and its art style spread across much of Peru.
153.spot: A tall, narrow, knife-shaped stone carved with a snarling face, fangs and snake hair, wedged into a cramped stone corridor. Or flat granite reliefs of fanged, clawed creatures whose lines turn into snakes, or a thin hammered-gold nose ornament ending in serpent heads.
153.remember: Chavín sounds like “chew-veen”: the Lanzón god has fangs for chewing. Fangs plus dark tunnels plus Peru plus very early (900 B.C.E.) means Chavín, the oldest work in the Indigenous Americas unit.
compare: No. 157 (§6.5), Templo Mayor: Both are temples built as sacred landscapes that staged myth and ritual, but the Templo Mayor’s sacrifices were public while Chavín’s rites were hidden in dark tunnels.
No. 164 (§6.12), Transformation mask: Both show a human transforming into an animal, Chavín in stone tenon heads and the Kwakwaka’wakw mask in live performance.
No. 8 (§2.8), Stonehenge: Both are ancient ritual sites where architecture and landscape were arranged to shape a religious experience.
No. 161 (§6.9), City of Machu Picchu: Both are Andean sites tied to sacred mountains and rivers, though Machu Picchu was built almost 2,000 years later.
153.vocab: contour rivalry, cruciform, tenon head, oracle, repoussé, horizon, pilgrimage.

form: The Old Temple is a U-shaped stone platform whose arms open east, toward the sunrise and the river, around a sunken circular plaza lined with carved reliefs of jaguars and costumed figures in procession.
Inside the platforms runs a maze of narrow, unlit galleries (stone tunnels) with small air vents and stone drainage channels; water rushing through them may have made the whole building seem to roar.

The Lanzón (Spanish for “lance”) is a granite shaft about 4.5 m (15 ft) tall set in a cruciform (cross-shaped) chamber where galleries meet. Its top passes through the ceiling, so it was built in place and never moved.

The Lanzón figure has fangs, claws, snakes for hair and eyebrows, and one hand up and one hand down. Its lines use contour rivalry (one line belongs to two images at once), so the image seems to shift as you look.
The later New Temple has the Black and White Portal, whose two columns pair black limestone with white granite and are carved with birds of prey (harpy eagles and hawks).
Tenon heads (stone heads with a long peg on the back, set into the outer walls) show a human face changing step by step into a snarling jaguar.
Gold objects such as the nose ornament were hammered into thin sheets, cut out, and decorated by repoussé (pushing the design out by hammering from the back).
function: A pilgrimage center: people traveled from the coast, highlands and jungle to consult the god, bringing offerings such as fine pottery and exotic shells.
An oracle (a place where a god answers questions): priests probably spoke for the Lanzón, perhaps from the gallery above, which connects to the top of the stone.
Priests likely took hallucinogens such as the San Pedro cactus, which appears in the carvings, to experience turning into jaguars, as the tenon heads suggest.
Gold ornaments were worn on the body; a nose ornament hung from the pierced nose and marked its wearer’s rank and spiritual power.
content: The animals are from the Amazon rainforest to the east: jaguars, caimans (crocodile relatives), harpy eagles and snakes. Using them signaled exotic, cosmic power and longdistance contact.
The Lanzón god blends human and animal traits. The raised and lowered hands may stand for balance between the upper and lower worlds; scholars disagree on the details.
The tenon heads show shamanic transformation: a priest becoming a jaguar through ritual and drugs.
The black-and-white portal may express duality (pairs of opposites, such as male and female), a core idea in later Andean thought.
context: Built at about 3,150 m (10,300 ft) where the Mosna and Huachecsa rivers meet, on a route linking the Pacific coast, the highlands and the Amazon basin.

The Chavín style spread so widely that archaeologists name the era after it, calling it the Early Horizon (a period when one style is shared across a large region). It predates the Inka by more than 1,500 years.
Excavators found decorated conch-shell trumpets (pututus) inside the galleries, which supports the idea that sound was part of the ritual.
Peruvian archaeologist Julio C. Tello studied the site from 1919. A flood and landslide in 1945 buried much of it. It became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1985. On the exam.
If asked about a multisensory religious experience → darkness, maze-like galleries, roaring water, conch trumpets and hallucinogens at Chavín.
If asked where the Lanzón is → still in place, in a cramped cruciform chamber deep in the Old Temple. Nobody could walk around it or see it whole.
If asked how to recognize Chavín style → fangs, claws, snake hair and contour rivalry in thin incised lines on flat stone.
Trap: Chavín is not Inka or Aztec. At 900–200 B.C.E. it is the oldest work in the Indigenous Americas unit.
If asked about trade or contact → Amazonian animals carved in the high Andes show links across the mountains.
If asked about transformation → the tenon heads move from human to jaguar; compare the Kwakwaka’wakw transformation mask (No. 164).

154.title: Mesa Verde cliff dwellings
154.plain: Mesa Verde is a group of stone villages built into shallow caves in the canyon walls of southwestern Colorado by Ancestral Puebloan people. The largest, Cliff Palace, has about 150 rooms and 23 kivas (round ceremonial rooms). The villages show how a farming people used local sandstone and the shape of the cliffs to deal with heat, cold, rain and danger.
154.spot: Tan sandstone boxes and towers, some several stories tall, tucked under a huge rock overhang in a canyon wall, with small doorways and round sunken pits (kivas) in front.
154.remember: Mesa Verde is Spanish for “green table”: people farmed on the flat green top and lived in the cliff edges below. Built mostly in the 1200s, empty by about 1300.
compare: No. 161 (§6.9), City of Machu Picchu: Both are settlements built into dramatic terrain with local stone, shaped to fit the land rather than flatten it.
No. 166 (§6.14), Black-on-black ceramic vessel: Maria Martínez’s Pueblo community descends from Ancestral Puebloans like the builders of Mesa Verde.
No. 167 (§7.1), Conical tower and circular wall of Great Zimb…: Both are stone settlements of roughly the same centuries that their people later left, probably partly for environmental reasons.
No. 213 (§10.1), Nan Madol: Both place a community in a hard natural setting, cliff or sea, and build it from local stone.
154.vocab: kiva, sipapu, alcove, mortar, pit house, masonry.

form: Buildings sit inside natural alcoves (shallow caves eroded into the cliff), so the rock overhang acts as a giant roof.
Walls are shaped sandstone blocks set in mortar (a binding paste, here mud, water and ash), with wooden beams for floors and roofs. Many walls were plastered, and some were painted.
Cliff Palace has about 150 rooms and 23 kivas, plus round and square towers up to four stories high.
Rooms are small, with low rectangular or T-shaped doorways; many upper rooms stored corn, beans and squash.
A kiva is a round, partly underground room entered by ladder through the roof, with a fire pit, an air shaft, a bench and a sipapu (a small hole in the floor).
Residents reached the villages by ladders and by hand-and-toe holds cut into the cliff.
function: Housing, food storage and ceremony; Cliff Palace probably housed about 100 people and may have been a social and ritual center for the area.
The south-facing alcoves caught the low winter sun but were shaded from the high summer sun, a form of passive solar design (climate control without machines).
The cliffs gave defense and shelter from rain and snow, while crops grew on the mesa top above.
Kivas were used for ritual, meetings and work such as weaving, as kivas still are in Pueblo communities today.
content: The sipapu stands for the place of emergence, where Pueblo ancestors climbed up into this world from the one below.
Climbing down into a round, sunken kiva and back up a ladder repeated the emergence story.
Building into the living rock rather than on open ground tied the community closely to the land itself.
context: The College Board’s range (450–1300 C.E.) covers the long occupation. People first lived in pit houses (dug-out homes) on the mesa top; the cliff villages were built mostly from about 1190 to 1280.
By about 1300 the area was empty, probably because of a long drought, worn-out soil, crowding and conflict. People moved south to Arizona and New Mexico.
Descendants include the Hopi, Zuni and Rio Grande Pueblos such as San Ildefonso (No. 166). “Anasazi” is a Navajo word, so “Ancestral Puebloan” is preferred today.
Local ranchers Richard Wetherill and Charlie Mason came upon Cliff Palace in 1888; artifacts were dug up and sold, which pushed the government to protect the site.
Mesa Verde became a U.S. National Park in 1906 and a UNESCO World Heritage site in 1978. On the exam.
If asked how architecture responds to the environment → south-facing alcoves for winter sun and summer shade, the overhang for shelter, the cliff for defense.
If asked what a kiva is → a round, semi-underground ceremonial room with a sipapu for ancestral emergence.
Material: sandstone blocks in mud mortar with wood beams, not adobe bricks.
If asked why it was abandoned → drought and resource stress around 1300; conflict probably played a part.
Trap: Mesa Verde is in Colorado, in the United States, not Mexico or Peru.
If asked about continuity → Pueblo peoples still use kivas today, linking Mesa Verde to Maria Martínez’s San Ildefonso Pueblo (No. 166).

155.title: Yaxchilán
155.plain: Yaxchilán is a Maya city on the Usumacinta River, on today’s border between Mexico and Guatemala. Its rulers set carved stone lintels (beams over doorways) into their temples to record rituals and family history in pictures and hieroglyphs. The most famous, Lintel 25 from Structure 23, shows the queen Lady Xook calling up a giant vision serpent after offering her own blood.
155.spot: A limestone relief of a kneeling woman in a tall headdress looking up at a huge rearing serpent with a helmeted warrior coming out of its mouth, framed by blocks of glyphs. Or a hilltop temple with three doorways and an openwork stone crest on its roof.
155.remember: Lady Xook looks UP at the serpent, and visitors looked UP at the lintel. YaxCHEE-lan, Late Classic Maya, 725 C.E.
compare: No. 157 (§6.5), Templo Mayor: Both link blood offerings to rulership and cosmic order, but the Mexica sacrificed captives while Maya royals offered their own blood.
No. 169 (§7.3), Wall plaque, from Oba’s palace: Both use relief to record royal ceremony and rank on the architecture of a palace or temple.
No. 180 (§7.14), Veranda post of enthroned king and senior wife: Both give a royal woman a central role in supporting the ruler’s power.
No. 171 (§7.5), Ndop: Both use art to legitimize a ruler by tying him to his ancestors.
155.vocab: lintel, roof comb, glyph, bloodletting, vision serpent, low relief.

form: Structure 33 sits on a hill above the river: a long temple with three doorways, carved lintels, and a tall roof comb (an openwork stone crest that made the temple taller and once held painted stucco sculpture).
A hieroglyphic stairway leading up to it has carved steps showing the ruler Bird Jaguar IV and his ancestors playing the ballgame.

Lintel 25 is limestone carved in low relief (a shallow raised design), about 1.2 m (4 ft) tall. Lady Xook kneels at lower right holding a bowl of bloodletting tools and gazes at a rearing vision serpent.
From the serpent’s upper jaws a warrior in a Teotihuacan-style helmet emerges with spear and shield; a second head appears at the serpent’s lower end.
Blocks of glyphs (signs of Maya writing) give names and exact dates. Unusually, the text on Lintel 25 is carved in mirror image.
The lintels were carved on their undersides, so a visitor had to look up while passing through the doorway.
function: Temple doorways marked sacred space; the lintels recorded dynastic history (the story of the ruling family) for the elites who entered.
Images of bloodletting (deliberately cutting oneself to offer blood) proved the royal family’s power to reach gods and ancestors, which justified their rule.
Bird Jaguar IV built Structures 33 and 40 to legitimize his reign, since his claim to the throne was disputed after a ten-year gap following his father’s death.
content: A three-part series: Lintel 24 shows Lady Xook pulling a thorn-studded rope through her tongue while her husband holds a torch; Lintel 25 shows the vision that follows; Lintel 26 shows her helping him dress for battle.
Bark paper soaked with royal blood was burned in bowls, and the rising smoke was believed to become the vision serpent, a passage to the spirit world.
The emerging warrior is often identified as the dynasty’s founder, Yat Balam, or as Shield Jaguar himself; scholars disagree.
Lady Xook’s starring role shows that royal women held real ritual and political power.
context: Late Classic Maya (about 600–900 C.E.): rival city-states with full writing, the precise Long Count calendar, and frequent warfare.
Shield Jaguar II (also called Itzamnaaj Bahlam III) ruled for about 60 years and dedicated Structure 23 to his principal wife, Lady Xook, around 723–726 C.E.
His successor, Bird Jaguar IV, was the son of a different wife, Lady Ik’ Skull. He took power in 752 and filled Structures 33 and 40 with images of his parents to stress his lineage.
British explorer Alfred Maudslay removed Lintels 24 and 25 in 1882; they are now in the British Museum in London. Lintel 26 is in Mexico’s National Museum of Anthropology. On the exam.
If asked why Maya royals shed blood → to nourish the gods, contact ancestors and prove their right to rule.
If asked what Lintel 25 shows → Lady Xook’s vision of a serpent from which an ancestorwarrior emerges, after bloodletting.
Who built what: Shield Jaguar II and Lady Xook = Structure 23 and its lintels; Bird Jaguar IV = Structures 33 and 40.
If asked about the role of text → glyphs name people and give exact dates, so Maya art works as historical record.
Material: limestone, carved in relief.
Trap: Yaxchilán is Maya, not Aztec, and about 650 years older than the Templo Mayor (No. 157).
Location trap: two of its lintels are in London, removed in the 1880s.

156.title: Great Serpent Mound
156.artist: Mississippian (Eastern Woodlands); Adams County, southern Ohio
156.plain: Great Serpent Mound is a giant earthen sculpture of a snake, about a quarter mile long, on a ridge in southern Ohio. It holds no burials, so it was a ceremonial monument rather than a tomb. Its head lines up with the sunset on the summer solstice, and scholars still argue about who built it and when.
156.spot: An aerial view of a long, low, grassy ridge of earth winding back and forth like a snake, with a coiled tail at one end and open jaws around an oval at the other, edged by trees.
156.remember: Snake plus Ohio plus solstice. The College Board’s date, c. 1070, is close to Halley’s Comet in 1066: think “comet snake.”
compare: No. 151 (§5.53), Spiral Jetty: Both are coiling earthworks made from the land itself and best seen from above, though Spiral Jetty is 1970s land art.
No. 8 (§2.8), Stonehenge: Both are monuments aligned with the summer solstice that turned the landscape into a ritual calendar.
No. 157 (§6.5), Templo Mayor: Both use serpent imagery with sacred meaning in the Indigenous Americas.
156.vocab: eﬀigy mound, earthwork, solstice, radiocarbon dating.

form: An eﬀigy mound (earth heaped into the shape of an animal), about 411 m (1,348 ft) long following the body and only about 1 m (3 ft) high.
The body makes a series of S-curves, usually counted as seven, ending in a tight coiled tail.
At the head, the open jaws seem to surround or swallow an oval shape, read as an egg, the sun, or an eye.
Made entirely by hand: workers carried basketloads of clay and earth, in places over a base of stones, and shaped them into a smooth, rounded form.
It follows the natural curve of a plateau above Brush Creek, so the land helps shape the art. It is fully visible only from the air or a viewing tower.
function: Ceremonial: no bodies or grave goods were found inside it, unlike burial mounds nearby that date to other periods.
The head points toward the summer solstice sunset; some researchers argue the curves also mark the winter solstice sunrise and the equinoxes, which is debated.
It probably served as a gathering place for rites connected with the seasons, the sky and fertility.
content: In many Eastern Woodlands traditions, serpents are linked to the underworld, water, fertility and powerful spirits.
The oval may be the sun being swallowed (an eclipse) or an egg (new life); scholars disagree.
A date near 1070 has been connected to two bright sky events: the 1054 supernova and Halley’s Comet in 1066, which looked like a fiery serpent.
context: Dating is debated. Radiocarbon dates from the 1990s pointed to about 1070 C.E. (the Fort Ancient culture, contemporary with the Mississippian), while a 2014 study argued for about 300 B.C.E. (the earlier Adena culture). The College Board uses c. 1070 and “Mississippian.”
It sits on the rim of a rare geological feature, the Serpent Mound crater, possibly caused by a meteorite impact some 300 million years ago, which may have made the spot seem special.

Surveyed by Ephraim Squier and Edwin Davis in the 1840s. Harvard archaeologist Frederic Ward Putnam raised money to buy and restore it in 1887–1889, saving it from plowing in one of the first U.S. preservation efforts.
Today it is a protected Ohio state historic site with a small museum and a viewing tower. On the exam.
If asked what an eﬀigy mound is → an earthwork in the shape of an animal; this is the largest known serpent eﬀigy in the world.
If asked about function → ceremonial, not burial: no human remains inside.
If asked about astronomy → the head is aligned with the summer solstice sunset.
If asked about date → c. 1070 C.E. per the College Board, but say that scholars debate it (some argue for about 300 B.C.E., Adena).
If asked about materials → earth and clay shaped by hand; the landscape itself is the medium.
Trap: it is in Ohio (Eastern Woodlands), not the Southwest.
Continuity: Spiral Jetty (No. 151) also makes the land the medium and is best seen from above.

157.title: Templo Mayor (Main Temple)
157.medium: Stone (temple); volcanic stone (Coyolxauhqui Stone); jadeite (Olmec-style mask);
157.plain: The Templo Mayor was the main temple-pyramid at the center of Tenochtitlan, the Aztec (Mexica) capital that is now Mexico City. Two shrines sat on top, one for the war and sun god Huitzilopochtli and one for the rain god Tlaloc. The Spanish destroyed it after 1521, and it was rediscovered in 1978 when electrical workers hit a huge carved stone of the goddess Coyolxauhqui.
157.spot: Excavated ruins of a layered stone pyramid with serpent heads in the middle of a modern city. Or a round stone disk of a naked goddess with her head, arms and legs cut off; a gray stone disk with a face in the center ringed by symbols (the Calendar Stone); or a green stone face mask.
157.remember: Twin temples, twin gods: Huitzilopochtli (war, south, red) and Tlaloc (rain, north, blue). Coyolxauhqui fell down the mountain in pieces, and so did the sacrificed victims.
compare: No. 159 (§6.7), City of Cusco: Both were sacred centers of empires that the Spanish built over, a cathedral city in Mexico and a church on the Qorikancha in Cusco.
No. 155 (§6.3), Yaxchilán: Both tie ritual blood offering to rulership and the order of the cosmos.
No. 153 (§6.1), Chavín de Huántar: Both are temples designed as sacred landscapes where architecture staged myth and religious experience.
No. 158 (§6.6), Ruler’s feather headdress: Both come from the Mexica capital and show how the empire drew precious materials from distant provinces.
157.vocab: twin-temple pyramid, relief, offering, human sacrifice, tribute.

form: A twin-temple pyramid (one pyramid carrying two temples) with two staircases leading to two shrines: Huitzilopochtli on the south side, Tlaloc on the north.
Enlarged about seven times, each new pyramid built over the old one like nesting shells, so the excavated site shows many layers at once.
Serpent heads line the base, and stone frogs and braziers mark Tlaloc’s side.
The Coyolxauhqui Stone (about 1500 C.E., volcanic stone) is a disk about 3.25 m (10.7 ft) across, carved in relief with the moon goddess naked, beheaded and cut apart, with bells on her cheeks.

The Calendar Stone (or Sun Stone) is a basalt disk about 3.6 m (12 ft) across and some 24 tons, with a central face (probably the sun god Tonatiuh, some say the earth deity Tlaltecuhtli) inside rings of day signs and four earlier world-ages.
An Olmec-style jadeite mask, made roughly 2,000 years before the temple, was found buried in one of its offerings.
function: Religious center: priests performed human sacrifice at the shrines to feed the sun and keep the rains and harvests coming.
Political center: it marked the heart of the empire, and each rebuilding celebrated a ruler’s power.
Thousands of buried offerings (shells, coral, jaguar skeletons, ancient masks) brought together goods from across and beyond the empire, mapping its reach.
The Calendar Stone was found in 1790 in the main square (the Zócalo), not on the temple itself; its exact use is debated, perhaps a ceremonial altar or a monument to the sun.
content: The pyramid is a sacred mountain: Huitzilopochtli’s side is Coatepec (Serpent Mountain), where he was born; Tlaloc’s side is a mountain of sustenance holding the rain.

The myth: when the earth goddess Coatlicue became pregnant, her daughter Coyolxauhqui and 400 brothers attacked her. Huitzilopochtli was born fully armed, killed his sister, and threw her down the mountain, where she broke apart.
The Coyolxauhqui Stone lay at the foot of Huitzilopochtli’s stairs, so sacrificed captives thrown down the steps reenacted the myth.
The two gods stand for the two pillars of the Mexica economy: war and tribute (Huitzilopochtli) and farming (Tlaloc).
Burying the older Olmec mask claimed the prestige of ancient peoples for the Mexica.
context: Tenochtitlan was founded in 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco. By 1519 it may have held around 200,000 people, more than most European cities.
Hernán Cortés and thousands of Indigenous allies conquered the city in 1521. The Spanish tore down the temple and built Mexico City and its cathedral on top, partly with its stones.
In 1978 electric company workers found the Coyolxauhqui Stone, which launched the Templo Mayor Project led by archaeologist Eduardo Matos Moctezuma; a site museum opened in 1987.
Excavation continues; in 2006 a huge relief of the earth deity Tlaltecuhtli was found beside the temple. On the exam.
If asked whom the two shrines honored → Huitzilopochtli (sun and war) and Tlaloc (rain and agriculture).
If asked how architecture reenacts myth → the pyramid as Coatepec, with the Coyolxauhqui Stone at the foot of the stairs.
Trap: the Coyolxauhqui Stone is the dismembered goddess; the Calendar Stone is the disk with a central face. Don’t mix them up.
If asked about conquest → the Spanish built Mexico City on top; compare Santo Domingo on the Qorikancha (No. 159).
If asked about the Olmec mask → an heirloom: the Mexica collected and reburied much older objects to link themselves to an ancient past.
Date: 1375–1520 C.E., covering the building phases up to the conquest.

158.title: Ruler’s feather headdress (probably of Motecuhzoma II)
158.plain: This is a huge fan-shaped headdress of green quetzal feathers, smaller blue, pink and brown feathers, and gold plaques, made by Aztec (Mexica) feather-workers before the Spanish conquest. It is one of very few Aztec featherworks to survive. Tradition links it to the emperor Motecuhzoma II, but that is not proven, and it is now in Vienna, where Mexico has asked for its return.
158.spot: A wide semicircle of long, shimmering green feathers over rows of smaller blue, brown and pink feathers, set with rows of small gold disks and plaques, almost as wide as an adult’s arm span.
158.remember: Quetzal feathers in Vienna: an Aztec ruler’s crown ended up with the Austrian Habsburgs. The Mexica valued “Mo”-tecuhzoma’s feathers “mo”re than gold.
compare: No. 215 (§10.3), ‘Ahu ‘ula: Both are royal regalia of thousands of rare bird feathers that signaled sacred rank and were made by elite specialists.
No. 162 (§6.10), All-T’oqapu tunic: Both are royal garments of the Americas whose materials, feathers and fine cloth, were valued above gold.
No. 170 (§7.4), Sika dwa kofi: Both are royal objects bound up with identity that became flashpoints in colonial history.
No. 160 (§6.8), Maize cobs: Together they show Indigenous versus European values: the Spanish melted Inka gold but kept Aztec feathers as curiosities.
158.vocab: regalia, featherwork, amanteca, tribute, repatriation, iridescence.

form: About 116 cm (3.8 ft) high and 175 cm (5.7 ft) wide, with roughly 400 long, iridescent (color-shifting) quetzal tail feathers forming the outer fan.
Inner bands use feathers of the blue cotinga, pink roseate spoonbill and brown squirrel cuckoo, arranged in neat rows.
Small gold plaques and disks are sewn on in bands across the feathers.
Feathers were tied onto a netting backing in overlapping layers so that only the colored tips show.
The feathers shimmer and move with every step, so the wearer would seem alive with light.
A careless restoration in 1878 rearranged parts; a joint Austrian-Mexican conservation project (2010–2012) studied and stabilized it.
function: Ceremonial regalia (special dress that marks rank) for a ruler or high priest; whether it was worn on the head, carried, or displayed is debated.
It made the wearer’s sacred status visible, linking him to the gods.
After the conquest it traveled to Europe as a gift or trophy and sat in princely collections of curiosities.
content: Quetzal feathers were worth more than gold to the Mexica; their green suggested water, young maize, fertility and preciousness.
The quetzal was tied to Quetzalcoatl, the feathered-serpent god, and to rulership.
Feathers from distant tropical birds showed the empire’s control of tribute (goods conquered peoples had to pay) and long-distance trade.
context: Made by amanteca, elite feather-workers of Tenochtitlan who lived in their own district and passed the craft down in families.
Quetzals live in the cloud forests of southern Mexico and Guatemala; some accounts say hunters released the birds after taking their tail feathers, which grow back.
First recorded in a 1596 inventory of Archduke Ferdinand II of Tyrol’s collection at Ambras Castle; now in the Weltmuseum Wien in Vienna.
The link to Motecuhzoma II (ruled 1502–1520) is a later tradition; it may have belonged to a priest instead.

Mexico has asked for its return for decades. Austria, citing the joint study, says vibration during transport would damage it. A replica is shown in Mexico City’s National Museum of Anthropology. On the exam.
If asked about value systems → the Mexica valued quetzal feathers above gold; the Spanish melted down gold but kept this as a curiosity.
If asked who made it → amanteca, specialist feather-workers.
If asked about repatriation → it is in Vienna; Mexico requests it; Austria cites fragility.
Medium: feathers (quetzal and cotinga) and gold.
Attribution wording: “probably” of Motecuhzoma II; the link is not certain.
Classic pair: the Hawaiian ʻahu ʻula feather cape (No. 215), also royal featherwork signaling sacred rank.

159.title: City of Cusco
159.plain: Cusco was the capital of the Inka Empire, rebuilt around 1440 by the ruler Pachacuti as the “navel of the world.” The College Board grouping includes the Qorikancha (the main sun temple), the Spanish church and convent of Santo Domingo built right on top of it, and the giant zigzag walls of Saqsa Waman above the city. Inka stonework here is so precise that blocks fit together without mortar and have outlasted major earthquakes.
159.spot: Gray walls of smooth, tightly fitted stones with no mortar, leaning slightly inward, with trapezoid-shaped doors and niches. Or a curved Inka wall beneath a colonial church, or terraces of enormous many-sided boulders in zigzag lines.
159.remember: Cusco = the Inka “navel.” Spanish church on top, Inka walls underneath, and when earthquakes hit, the top fell while the bottom held.
compare: No. 157 (§6.5), Templo Mayor: Both were sacred imperial centers that the Spanish deliberately built over with Christian architecture.
No. 161 (§6.9), City of Machu Picchu: Both show Inka ashlar masonry and the building program of Pachacuti.
No. 167 (§7.1), Conical tower and circular wall of Great Zimb…: Both use monumental mortarless stone walls to express a state’s power.
No. 160 (§6.8), Maize cobs: The maize cobs probably come from the Qorikancha’s sacred golden garden.
159.vocab: ashlar masonry, battered wall, polygonal masonry, huaca, ceque, mortar.

form: Ashlar masonry (stone cut into precise blocks): each stone was ground to fit its neighbors so closely, without mortar, that a knife blade cannot slide between them.
Walls are battered (they lean inward as they rise), and doors, windows and niches are trapezoidal (narrower at the top), which helps them survive earthquakes.
The Qorikancha’s finest walls are dark gray andesite; a famous curved wall now supports the end of the Santo Domingo church.
Saqsa Waman has three tiers of zigzag terrace walls of huge polygonal (many-sided) stones, some over 100 tons. Many of these giant blocks are a local limestone rather than andesite.
Santo Domingo is a Spanish colonial church and convent with arches, a bell tower and a cloister, built about 1550–1650 on the Inka foundations and rebuilt after the 1650 earthquake.
Inka masons shaped blocks by pounding with harder hammerstones and grinding with sand, and moved them with ramps, ropes and human labor, without iron tools or wheels.
function: Cusco was the political and religious capital of Tawantinsuyu (“the four parts together,” the Inka name for their empire); roads to the four quarters began in its main plaza.
The Qorikancha (“golden enclosure”) was the main temple, for Inti (the sun) and other sky gods (moon, stars, thunder, rainbow); it also housed mummies of past rulers.
Saqsa Waman was a ceremonial and storage complex that could also serve as a fortress; it saw fighting during Manco Inka’s siege of Spanish-held Cusco in 1536.
Santo Domingo housed Dominican friars and still works as a church today, with the Inka rooms open to visitors.
content: By tradition the city plan forms a puma, with Saqsa Waman as the head and the Qorikancha near the tail where two rivers meet; this reading comes from colonial-era accounts and is debated.
The Qorikancha was the hub of the ceque system: about 40 imaginary lines radiating out to hundreds of huacas (sacred places such as springs, rocks and shrines).
Gold sheets covered its walls (gold was the “sweat of the sun”), and a garden of life-size gold and silver plants and animals filled a courtyard (see No. 160).
Building the church directly on the sun temple announced Christian victory over Inka religion; the Inka walls surviving the 1650 and 1950 earthquakes is often read as a symbolic reversal.
context: Pachacuti (ruled about 1438–1471) turned a small kingdom into an empire and rebuilt Cusco as its showpiece.
Francisco Pizarro’s forces reached Cusco in 1533, stripped the gold from the Qorikancha, and gave the site to the Dominican order.
Colonial Cusco was built literally on Inka bases, a visible layering of two cultures that still defines the city.
The Spanish used Saqsa Waman as a quarry, which is partly why mainly the largest, hardestto-move stones remain.
UNESCO listed the City of Cuzco as a World Heritage site in 1983. On the exam.
If asked about Inka masonry → mortarless ashlar, battered walls, trapezoidal openings, earthquake resistance.
If asked about colonial imposition → Santo Domingo built on the Qorikancha; compare Mexico City’s cathedral over the Templo Mayor (No. 157).
If asked about the Qorikancha → main temple to the sun (Inti), once sheathed in gold; center of the ceque system.
Saqsa Waman = huge polygonal stones in zigzag terrace walls above the city.
Date trap: the Inka city is c. 1440; the convent was added 1550–1650.
Medium on the exam: andesite, though Saqsa Waman’s great walls are largely limestone.

160.title: Maize cobs
160.plain: These are life-size ears of corn made from thin hammered sheets of silver and gold alloys by Inka metalworkers. Maize was the Inka staple and was sacred, and objects like this probably stood in the golden garden of the Qorikancha, the sun temple in Cusco. The Spanish melted down almost all Inka gold and silver, so the few survivors are rare.
160.spot: Realistic metal ears of corn, silvery with gold-colored parts, the leafy husks peeled back to show neat rows of kernels.
160.remember: Golden corn for the sun: gold was the “sweat of the sun,” silver the “tears of the moon.” Inka, c. 1440–1533, ending the year Atahualpa was executed.
compare: No. 159 (§6.7), City of Cusco: The maize cobs probably stood in the Qorikancha’s garden in Cusco.
No. 170 (§7.4), Sika dwa kofi: Both use gold as a sacred, power-holding material rather than as money.
No. 153 (§6.1), Chavín de Huántar: Both show Andean skill in hammered sheet gold, nearly 2,000 years apart.
No. 162 (§6.10), All-T’oqapu tunic: Both show what the Inka state truly valued: maize and fine cloth.
160.vocab: repoussé, alloy, sheet metal, naturalism, offering, chicha.

form: Made from thin sheets of gold and silver alloys (mixtures of metals), life-size and naturalistic (close to how real corn looks), with kernels, husks and silk.
Shaped by repoussé (hammering the sheet from the back to push the kernels outward), then trimmed and joined.
Different alloys give different colors, so kernels and husks can contrast, golden against silver.
Thin sheet metal stretched precious material across a large, shining surface.
Inka art usually favors geometric simplification, which makes this close study of a living plant stand out.
function: Probably part of the Qorikancha’s golden garden, described by Spanish chroniclers: a courtyard of life-size gold and silver maize plants, llamas with herders, and other plants and animals.
A sacred offering showing agricultural abundance to the sun god Inti.
Possibly used in state planting and harvest rituals; chroniclers say the Inka ruler opened the planting season in Cusco with a golden digging stick.
content: Maize fed the empire, filled state storehouses, and made chicha (maize beer), drunk at state feasts and poured as offerings.
Gold and silver were sacred materials reserved for the gods and nobility, not money.
A metal plant is a harvest that never ends, a kind of permanent prayer that the real crops would keep growing.
context: Many Inka metalworkers were specialists brought to Cusco from conquered peoples, especially the Chimú of Peru’s north coast, famous for goldwork.
Pizarro captured the Inka ruler Atahualpa in 1532 and demanded a room filled with gold and silver as ransom. It was melted into bars, and Atahualpa was executed in 1533 anyway.
Chroniclers such as Pedro Cieza de León and Garcilaso de la Vega described the golden garden, but nearly all of it went into Spanish furnaces.
Most Inka precious-metal objects that survive were buried in graves or mountaintop shrines rather than displayed, which is how they escaped melting. On the exam.
If asked about technique → repoussé on sheet metal (hammered from the back).
If asked what gold and silver meant → sweat of the sun and tears of the moon: sacred, not currency.
If asked about function → probably the golden garden of the Qorikancha in Cusco (No. 159).
If asked why so few survive → the Spanish melted Inka gold and silver, including Atahualpa’s ransom.
Date: c. 1440–1533 C.E., ending with the Spanish conquest.
Comparison hook: Europeans saw metal as money, while the Inka valued cloth and sacred meaning more.

161.title: City of Machu Picchu
161.plain: Machu Picchu is a royal estate built by the Inka around 1450 on a mountain ridge high above the Urubamba River in Peru, probably for the emperor Pachacuti. It mixes temples, houses, plazas and farming terraces, all shaped to fit and echo the surrounding peaks. The Spanish never found it, so it survived largely intact.
161.spot: Gray stone buildings and green terraces on a narrow ridge with a steep, pointed peak (Huayna Picchu) rising behind. Or a curved stone tower built around a boulder, or a carved stone outcrop with a short post sticking up.
161.remember: Machu Picchu means “old peak.” Pachacuti’s mountain getaway in the clouds, c. 1450, which the Spanish never found.
compare: No. 159 (§6.7), City of Cusco: Both show Inka ashlar and Pachacuti’s patronage, but Cusco was built over by the Spanish and Machu Picchu was not.
No. 154 (§6.2), Mesa Verde cliff dwellings: Both are settlements built into dramatic terrain using local stone.
No. 8 (§2.8), Stonehenge: Both use solar alignment, Machu Picchu’s Torreón with the June solstice and Stonehenge with the midsummer sunrise.
No. 139 (§5.41), Fallingwater: Both fold buildings into the natural setting, even incorporating rock, though Fallingwater is a 20th-century house.
161.vocab: ashlar masonry, terrace, Intihuatana, apu, solstice, fieldstone.

form: About 200 structures on a ridge at roughly 2,430 m (8,000 ft), between Machu Picchu and Huayna Picchu peaks, with the Urubamba River far below.
Built of local granite: sacred buildings in fine ashlar (precisely cut blocks, no mortar), ordinary houses in rougher fieldstone set in clay.
Stepped agricultural terraces hold the soil, prevent landslides, and drain heavy rain through layers of stone and gravel.
The Torreón (Temple of the Sun) is a curved ashlar wall around a natural rock; a window lines up with sunrise on the June solstice (winter in the Southern Hemisphere), lighting a cut in the rock.
The Intiwatana (“hitching post of the sun”) is a granite outcrop carved into angled planes with a short upright post.
The Sacred Rock is a large flat stone whose outline echoes the mountain behind it.
A channeled spring feeds a chain of 16 stone fountains running down through the site.
function: A royal estate for Pachacuti, his family and court, probably used seasonally and run by a staff of servants and farmers.
A religious center for the sun and the mountains; the Torreón and Intiwatana probably tracked solstices and seasons for ritual and farming.
Today it is Peru’s most visited site, a UNESCO World Heritage site since 1983, and a national symbol.
content: Inka religion treated mountains (apus, mountain spirits) as powerful beings; buildings frame views of peaks, and carved rocks copy them, honoring the landscape rather than dominating it.
Building living rock into walls connected architecture to the sacred earth (Pachamama, Mother Earth).
Solar alignments tied the ruler, who claimed descent from the sun, to the cosmic calendar.
context: Built around 1450 and abandoned around the time of the Spanish conquest in the 1530s, probably as the royal system and its estates collapsed.
The Spanish never found it, so it was not looted or built over like Cusco (No. 159).
Local farmers knew it, and some lived there. American explorer Hiram Bingham was guided there in 1911 and made it world famous.
Bingham shipped thousands of artifacts to Yale University; after a long dispute, Yale returned them to Peru in 2011–2012.
Mass tourism and erosion threaten it; in 2000 a crane filming a beer commercial chipped the Intiwatana. On the exam.
If asked about architecture and landscape → buildings and the Sacred Rock echo the mountains; the architecture works with the terrain.
If asked about astronomy → the Torreón window aligns with the June solstice sunrise; the Intiwatana probably tracked the sun.
Function: a royal estate of Pachacuti, not a “lost city” or fortress.
Material: granite, ashlar for sacred buildings and fieldstone for the rest.
If asked why it survived → the Spanish never found it.
Repatriation hook: Yale returned Bingham’s artifacts to Peru.

162.title: All-T’oqapu tunic
162.plain: This is a sleeveless Inka tunic covered completely in small squares of geometric pattern called t’oqapu. Most Inka tunics repeat one standard design, but this one packs in many different ones, which is why scholars think it was made for the emperor himself. To the Inka, fine cloth was more precious than gold.
162.spot: A roughly square, knee-length tunic covered edge to edge in a grid of tiny squares, each with a different bright geometric design in red, yellow, black, white, blue and green.
162.remember: ALL the t’oqapu = ALL the empire = the Sapa Inka. One shirt to rule them all, 1450–1540.
compare: No. 177 (§7.11), Lukasa: Both carry encoded information in abstract patterns that only trained people could fully read.
No. 158 (§6.6), Ruler’s feather headdress: Both are royal regalia of the Americas made of materials valued above gold.
No. 219 (§10.7), Hiapo: Both are textiles that functioned as wealth and gifts, hiapo in Niue and qompi in the Inka empire.
No. 223 (§10.11), Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa cloths t…: In both Fiji and the Inka state, presenting fine cloth was a political act that bound people together.
162.vocab: tapestry, t’oqapu, warp, weft, camelid fiber, khipu, regalia.

form: A T-shaped tunic (unku) woven as one piece, folded at the shoulders and sewn up the sides with a slit for the head; about 91 by 77 cm (3 by 2.5 ft).
Woven in interlocking tapestry (a weave where colored weft threads, the crosswise ones, hook around each other where colors meet, leaving no gaps).
Wefts are dyed camelid fiber (alpaca or vicuña wool) packed tightly over a cotton warp (the lengthwise threads).
The thread count is extremely high, finer than most European tapestry of the time, which meant many months of skilled labor.
The whole surface is a grid of t’oqapu: small squares, each holding a geometric motif such as steps, checkerboards, diagonals or interlocking keys.
The grid looks orderly at first, but the motifs do not follow a strict repeating pattern.
function: Probably worn by the Sapa Inka (the emperor) in state ceremonies; it is unique, with no close match among surviving tunics.
Most Inka tunics were standardized like uniforms; for example, a black-and-white checkerboard tunic with a red yoke marked soldiers or oﬀicials.
The ruler gave fine cloth to nobles, oﬀicials and conquered leaders to win loyalty, and burned it as an offering to the gods.
content: Each t’oqapu probably stood for a group, place, oﬀice or idea; having so many may show the ruler’s authority over all the peoples and parts of the empire.
Some squares are tiny versions of known tunic designs, such as the checkerboard military tunic and the key pattern associated with Inka oﬀicials.
Some scholars argue t’oqapu worked like a writing or record system, comparable to the khipu (knotted-cord records); others see them as heraldic emblems.
context: The Inka had no alphabetic writing; cloth, khipus and stone carried their information and power.
Fine cloth (qompi) was woven by aqllakuna (“chosen women” living in state compounds) and by male specialists (qompikamayuq); households owed plainer cloth as tax.
Cloth filled state warehouses; Spanish observers were amazed by the quantities.
Now at Dumbarton Oaks, Harvard University’s research library and museum in Washington, D.C. On the exam.
If asked what t’oqapu are → small squares of geometric design that probably signified identities, places or oﬀices.
If asked why it belonged to the ruler → its unique all-t’oqapu design suggests authority over the whole empire.
If asked about Inka values → cloth outranked gold.
Technique: interlocking tapestry in camelid fiber and cotton.
Makers: aqllakuna (chosen women) and male specialist weavers.
Comparison hook: abstract visual codes that hold information, like the Luba lukasa (No. 177).

163.title: Bandolier bag
163.plain: A bandolier bag is a large beaded pouch with a wide strap worn diagonally across the chest. This one was made by a Lenape (Delaware) woman around 1850, using glass beads that came through trade with Europeans. Men wore such bags as formal dress and status symbols, often more for show than for carrying things.
163.spot: A flat pouch hanging from a broad strap, both thickly covered in tiny colored glass beads forming curving flowers, leaves and vines or bold geometric shapes, often with tassels or fringe.
163.remember: A bandolier is a soldier’s cartridge belt: same shape, but beads instead of bullets. Lenape, about 1850.
compare: No. 165 (§6.13), Painted elk hide: Both are 19th-century Native objects made under U.S. pressure that adapted tradition to new materials and audiences.
No. 178 (§7.12), Aka elephant mask: Both turn imported glass beads into displays of wealth and status.
No. 166 (§6.14), Black-on-black ceramic vessel: Both are works by Native women that blend tradition with new materials or markets.

form: A pouch and wide strap of leather (other bags of this type use wool or cotton cloth), covered with tiny glass seed beads sewn down in rows.
Designs mix curvilinear (curving) floral motifs of vines and leaves with geometric shapes and strong color contrasts.
Beads were usually stitched down with thread; some straps on similar bags were woven on a loom.
Fringe, tassels or yarn often hang from the bottom of the pouch.
Bright imported colors replaced the earlier natural dyes and porcupine quills.
The shape echoes European military ammunition pouches and shoulder belts.
function: Prestige dress worn by men at gatherings, councils and dances; some men wore several at once.
The pouch is often small or even sealed, so display mattered more than storage.
Bags were given as gifts and traded; a fine one could be worth as much as a pony.
content: The floral style may echo embroidery taught by European missionaries and nuns, but Native women made it their own, often with plants tied to medicine and the natural world.
Wearing a bag displayed the family’s wealth, the maker’s skill and the wearer’s standing.
Combining European materials with Indigenous forms shows adaptation and cultural resilience (keeping identity alive through change).
context: Made by women, who controlled beadwork; beading largely replaced earlier porcupinequillwork (embroidery with flattened, dyed quills) once glass beads were plentiful.
The Lenape homeland covered the Delaware River valley: New Jersey and parts of New York, Pennsylvania and Delaware.

From the 1700s on, colonial land seizures and U.S. removal policy, including the Indian Removal Act of 1830, pushed the Lenape west to Ohio, Indiana, Missouri, Kansas and finally Oklahoma; some went to Wisconsin and Ontario.
Bandolier bags were popular in the 1800s among many Woodlands and Great Lakes peoples, such as the Ojibwe and Potawatomi. On the exam.
If asked about cultural exchange → European glass beads and floral embroidery reworked in a Native style.
If asked who made it → Lenape women made it; men wore it.
If asked about function → status display and ceremonial dress, not practical storage.
Context hook: made during forced removal, so it asserts identity under pressure.
Trap: the medium is beadwork on leather, not quillwork or painted hide.
Region and date: Eastern Woodlands, c. 1850 C.E.

164.title: Transformation mask
164.plain: This carved and painted wooden mask opens up during a dance: the dancer pulls strings, and an animal or bird face splits apart to reveal a human face inside. Made by the Kwakwaka’wakw of British Columbia, Canada, in the late 1800s, it dramatized a family’s story of an ancestor who changed between animal and human. Its history is tied to Canada’s 1884–1951 ban on the potlatch.
164.spot: Two views of one wooden mask: closed, a bird or animal head with a long beak or snout; open, the outer panels swung out like doors to show a human face, all painted with black, red, white and blue-green ovals and U-shapes.
164.remember: Snap, it transforms, like a Transformer toy. Kwakwaka’wakw (KWAK-wak-yawakw), Canada, late 1800s.
compare: No. 153 (§6.1), Chavín de Huántar: Both show human-animal transformation tied to ritual specialists.
No. 218 (§10.6), Buk: Both are performance masks that merge human and animal features.
No. 173 (§7.7), Female: Both are masks whose meaning comes alive only in dance.
No. 165 (§6.13), Painted elk hide: Both relate to Native ceremonies banned by North American governments in the 1880s.
164.vocab: transformation mask, potlatch, formline, ovoid, repatriation.

form: Carved wood (usually red or yellow cedar) in hinged sections joined by strings that the dancer pulls to open and close it.
Closed, it shows an animal, bird or sea creature; open, the outer pieces fan out to reveal a human face, so both beings appear at once.
Painted in formline style (bold, swelling lines that outline every shape), built from ovoids (rounded rectangles) and U-forms, in black, red, white and blue-green.
Often trimmed with shredded cedar bark, feathers or hair; a costume and blanket hid the dancer’s body.
Carved by master artists commissioned by a family, though collectors rarely recorded 19thcentury carvers’ names.
function: Danced at potlatches and winter ceremonies by firelight, with songs and drumming; the sudden opening was the dramatic high point.
A potlatch is a feast where the host gives away wealth to mark events such as namings, marriages, deaths or new chiefs; guests act as witnesses who confirm the host’s claims.
The right to show a mask, its dance and its story is a hereditary privilege owned by a family and displayed at potlatches.
content: It shows an ancestor’s transformation between animal and human, part of the family’s origin story; beings were believed able to shift form.
The mask both hides and reveals: the outer animal and inner human are two sides of one being.
Performing it confirmed a family’s history, rank and rights before the community.
context: The Kwakwaka’wakw (“those who speak Kwak’wala”) live on northern Vancouver Island and the nearby mainland coast of British Columbia.
Canada banned the potlatch from 1884 to 1951 to force assimilation. After Chief Dan Cranmer’s large potlatch in 1921, oﬀicials arrested participants and seized hundreds of masks and regalia.
Seized objects went to museums in Canada and the United States; many have since been returned to the U’mista Cultural Centre in Alert Bay and the Nuyumbalees Cultural Centre on Quadra Island.
Kwakwaka’wakw carving and dance continue today, and artists still make transformation masks. On the exam.
If asked about performance → it was meant to be seen moving and opening by firelight, not sitting in a museum case.
If asked about function → the potlatch, displaying hereditary privileges and family origin stories.
If asked about colonial suppression → potlatch ban 1884–1951, seizures in 1921, later repatriation.
Style: formline ovoids and U-forms; wood, paint and string.
Trap: the Kwakwaka’wakw are from Canada’s Northwest Coast, not the Plains or Southwest.
Theme: transformation, as in Chavín’s jaguar tenon heads (No. 153).

165.title: Painted elk hide
165.artist: Attributed to Cotsiogo (Cadzi Cody), Eastern Shoshone; Wind River Reserva-
165.plain: This is an elk hide painted around 1890–1900 by Cotsiogo (Cadzi Cody), an Eastern Shoshone artist on the Wind River Reservation in Wyoming. The center shows a ceremonial dance around a buffalo head between two poles, and the edges show a buffalo hunt. By then the buffalo were nearly gone and the Sun Dance was outlawed, and Cotsiogo sold hides like this to tourists.
165.spot: An irregular, light tan animal skin filled with small, flat painted figures: a ring of dancers in feathered headdresses and bustles in the center, and riders chasing buffalo around the edges, with tipis.
165.remember: Cotsiogo sounds like “costs a lot”: a souvenir sold to tourists on a Wyoming reservation. Sun Dance in the middle, buffalo hunt around the edge, 1890s.
compare: No. 163 (§6.11), Bandolier bag: Both are 19th-century Native objects made under U.S. pressure that asserted identity in changing conditions.
No. 166 (§6.14), Black-on-black ceramic vessel: Both are Native works made for outside buyers, showing tradition adapting to a tourist market.
No. 164 (§6.12), Transformation mask: Both relate to Native ceremonies that governments banned in the 1880s.
No. 233 (§11.10), Trade: Both deal with Native culture sold to outsiders; Smith’s Trade criticizes that tourist market a century later.
165.vocab: hide painting, stencil, Sun Dance, reservation, pictograph.

form: A whole elk hide, cleaned and softened, used as a canvas; the uneven outline of the animal is kept.
Figures are flat and outlined, shown in profile, with little shading, continuing the Plains tradition of hide painting.
In the center, men in feather bustles (feathered dance ornaments worn at the back) and headdresses dance around a buffalo head set between two poles, with an eagle above.
Around the edges: mounted hunters chasing buffalo, butchered buffalo, warriors returning to camp between tipis, and women resting by a fire.
