Cotsiogo used commercial paints as well as earth pigments, and some figures were probably made with stencils (cut-out templates), which sped up production for sale.
Figures float across the surface with no single ground line or perspective.
function: Made for sale to tourists and collectors visiting the reservation, providing income in the hard reservation economy.
Also a record of Shoshone life and ceremony at a time when both were under attack.
Earlier Plains painted hides were worn as robes or used as tipi covers and recorded a man’s deeds in war and the hunt.
content: The Sun Dance was the most important Plains religious ceremony, a time of prayer, sacrifice and renewal; the buffalo head on the pole honored the buffalo.
Scholars note the center also includes features of the Wolf Dance (a version of the Grass Dance), which the government tolerated; blending the two may have helped the artist avoid trouble.
The buffalo hunt shows a vanished way of life: by the 1880s buffalo had been hunted almost to extinction.
Hunters use bows and arrows rather than rifles, idealizing the hunt as it was in earlier times.
context: Cotsiogo (about 1866–1912) lived on the Wind River Reservation, set aside for the Eastern Shoshone by the Fort Bridger Treaty of 1868.
The U.S. government’s 1883 rules for Courts of Indian Offenses banned the Sun Dance and other ceremonies to force assimilation; the ban lasted into the 1930s.
The mass slaughter of the buffalo, encouraged by the U.S. Army, destroyed the Plains economy and pushed nations onto reservations.
Narrative hide painting was traditionally men’s work; Cotsiogo adapted it for a new tourist market. One of his hides is in the Brooklyn Museum. On the exam.
If asked about content → a Sun Dance (banned) in the center and a buffalo hunt (buffalo nearly gone) around the edges.
If asked about function → made for sale to tourists, but also a way to preserve cultural memory.
If asked about context → reservation era, U.S. suppression of Native religion, destruction of the buffalo.
Artist: Cotsiogo (Cadzi Cody), Eastern Shoshone, Wind River Reservation, Wyoming, c. 1890–1900.
Trap: the medium is painted elk hide, not buffalo hide.
Continuity and change: an old Plains painting tradition adapted to a new market and new paints.

166.title: Black-on-black ceramic vessel
166.artist: Maria Martínez and Julian Martínez, Tewa, Puebloan; San Ildefonso Pueblo,
166.plain: This is a hand-built clay pot from San Ildefonso Pueblo in New Mexico, shaped and polished by Maria Martínez and painted by her husband Julian. Its design shows only as dull black on shiny black, the result of polishing and a smoky firing that turns the clay black. The Martínezes revived ancient Pueblo pottery methods and turned them into signed, collectible art that supported their community.
166.spot: A round, smooth black jar with a mirror-like shine, decorated with dull black bands of feathers, geometric shapes or a serpent, so the design appears only when light hits it.
166.remember: Two blacks, two Martínezes: Maria shapes and shines, Julian paints the dull parts. San Ildefonso, first half of the 1900s.
compare: No. 154 (§6.2), Mesa Verde cliff dwellings: Maria Martínez’s Pueblo community descends from Ancestral Puebloans like the builders of Mesa Verde.
No. 180 (§7.14), Veranda post of enthroned king and senior wife: Both are by named Indigenous artists who worked for outside patrons as well as their own communities.
No. 165 (§6.13), Painted elk hide: Both were made for non-Native buyers, showing tradition adapting to a market.
166.vocab: coiling, burnishing, slip, reduction firing, matte, sherd. 7 Africa Content area 6 · 1100–1980 C.E. · works 167–180 · about 6% of the multiple-choice section. African art from about 1100 to 1980. Most of these objects were made to be used: worn in performance, kept in shrines, used to judge disputes or remember rulers. That means the exam asks about function and performance at least as much as appearance. Many were taken to Europe during colonial conquest, so museum ownership and repatriation also come up.

form: Hand-built by coiling (stacking ropes of clay and smoothing them together), with no potter’s wheel.
Covered with a slip (a thin liquid clay) and burnished (rubbed with a smooth stone) to a high gloss before firing.
Julian painted designs on the polished surface with more slip; those areas stay matte (dull).
Reduction firing: after an outdoor firing, the pots were smothered with powdered manure, cutting off oxygen so that carbon turned the whole pot black.
The design shows only through the contrast of sheen, glossy black against matte black.
Motifs include the avanyu (a horned water serpent), feathers and stepped geometric patterns drawn from older Pueblo pottery.
function: Pueblo pots were once everyday storage and cooking wares; Martínez blackware was made mainly for collectors, museums and tourists.
Sales supported the Martínez family and, as relatives and neighbors learned the method, much of the pueblo.
Today such pots are treated as fine art and shown in museums.
content: Motifs like the avanyu and feathers relate to water, rain and life, central concerns in the dry Southwest.
The work joins ancient tradition (shapes and designs from ancestral sherds) with modern innovation (the black-on-black finish).
Signing pots made them works by known artists, challenging the idea that Native craft is anonymous.
context: Maria Martínez (about 1887–1980) was Tewa, from San Ildefonso Pueblo; Julian Martínez painted her pots until his death in 1943.
In 1908 archaeologist Edgar Lee Hewett asked Maria to recreate pots from ancient sherds (broken pottery pieces) excavated on the nearby Pajarito Plateau.
Around 1918–1920 the couple perfected black-on-black; Santa Fe dealers, world’s fairs and railroad tourism made it famous.
Maria began signing pots in the 1920s at dealers’ urging; after Julian’s death, her son Popovi Da and other relatives painted for her.
Pots with both names date before 1943, so the College Board’s “mid-20th century” is approximate. On the exam.
If asked about technique → coil-built, burnished, painted with slip, reduction-fired.
If asked about collaboration → Maria formed and polished; Julian painted.
If asked about the art market → signing made the pots collectible art and revived the pueblo’s economy.
If asked about tradition and innovation → a revival from ancestral sherds plus a new blackon-black finish.
Trap: no potter’s wheel; it is hand-built.
Named Native artists, like Olowe of Ise (No. 180), challenge the myth of anonymous Indigenous art.

167.title: Conical tower and circular wall of Great Zimbabwe
167.plain: Great Zimbabwe is the stone capital of a Shona kingdom in southeastern Zimbabwe, at its peak around 1300–1450. Its Great Enclosure is a huge oval wall of granite blocks laid without mortar, with a solid cone-shaped tower inside. The city grew rich on cattle and on gold and ivory traded to the Indian Ocean, and the modern country of Zimbabwe is named after it.
167.spot: A tall, curving wall of neat gray stone layers with no mortar and a zigzag (chevron) band near the top; inside, a solid, cone-shaped stone tower, wider at the base, standing beside the wall.
167.remember: Zimbabwe = “houses of stone” in Shona. A granary you can’t open stands for a king who never runs out. c. 1000–1400 C.E.
compare: No. 159 (§6.7), City of Cusco: Both use monumental mortarless stone walls to express a state’s power.
No. 213 (§10.1), Nan Madol: Both are monumental stone complexes built by a ruling elite without mortar to display authority.
No. 8 (§2.8), Stonehenge: Both are monumental stone sites that outsiders once credited to foreign builders instead of local people.
No. 168 (§7.2), Great Mosque of Djenné: Both are major African architecture made possible by long-distance trade networks.
167.vocab: dry-stone masonry, coursed masonry, chevron pattern, enclosure, granary.

form: Three main zones: the Hill Complex (the oldest, on a granite hill), the Valley ruins, and the Great Enclosure.
The Great Enclosure’s outer wall is about 250 m (820 ft) around, up to about 11 m (36 ft) high and about 5 m (17 ft) thick at the base.
Coursed masonry (stones laid in even horizontal rows) of granite blocks split from natural rock sheets, built as dry-stone walls (no mortar).
A chevron (zigzag) band runs along the top of part of the outer wall.
Walls curve instead of turning sharp corners and taper (get thinner) as they rise, which keeps them stable.
The Conical Tower is about 9 m (30 ft) high and 5.5 m (18 ft) across at the base, solid stone with no door or room inside.
Narrow passages wind between parallel walls inside the enclosure.
function: Capital of a powerful state; the Great Enclosure was probably a royal residence, ritual center or initiation site, and scholars debate which.
The walls displayed prestige and separated the elite from commoners; they were not built for defense.
Most people lived in daga (mud-and-pole) houses around the stone walls, perhaps 10,000 to 18,000 at the city’s height.
content: The Conical Tower is most often read as a symbolic granary: Shona rulers collected and handed out grain, so a giant granary stood for royal generosity and control of tribute.
It may also be a fertility symbol or ritual object; being solid, it was made to be seen, not used.
Carved soapstone Zimbabwe birds from the Hill Complex probably honored royal ancestors; one now appears on the national flag.
context: Wealth came from cattle and from gold and ivory traded through Swahili coastal cities such as Kilwa to the Indian Ocean world; Chinese porcelain, Persian pottery and Syrian glass have been found on site.
The city declined around 1450, probably from overpopulation, worn-out land and shifting trade routes.

European colonists, including agents of Cecil Rhodes, refused to believe Africans built it and credited Phoenicians or the Queen of Sheba. Archaeologists David Randall-MacIver (1905) and Gertrude Caton-Thompson (1929) proved it was African.
White-minority Rhodesian governments suppressed that finding into the 1970s; at independence in 1980 the country took the name Zimbabwe.
Several soapstone birds were taken abroad; South Africa returned some in 1981, and Germany returned part of one in 2003. UNESCO listed the site in 1986. On the exam.
If asked about technique → dry-stone, coursed granite without mortar.
If asked about the tower → a symbolic granary showing royal generosity and wealth; it is solid.
If asked about trade → gold and ivory to the Swahili coast and the Indian Ocean; Chinese porcelain found on site.
If asked about reception → colonial denial of African authorship, a racist myth disproved by archaeology.
Political legacy: the nation’s name and the bird on its flag come from the site.
Trap: despite the title’s “circular wall,” the enclosure is an irregular ellipse (oval).

168.title: Great Mosque of Djenné
168.plain: The Great Mosque of Djenné in Mali is the largest mud-brick (adobe) building in the world. A mosque was first founded on the site around 1200 when a local ruler converted to Islam, but the present building dates from 1906–1907. Because rain wears mud away, the whole town re-plasters it every year in a festival, so the building survives only through community labor.
168.spot: A huge, smooth, sand-colored mud building on a raised platform, with three tall towerminarets on the front, rows of pointed pinnacles, and wooden sticks poking out of the walls in neat rows, often with a market in front.
168.remember: Djenné is a mud mosque that needs a yearly “mud spa day.” The sticks sticking out are toron, a built-in ladder.
compare: No. 56 (§4.9), Great Mosque: Both are Friday mosques with hypostyle prayer halls, but Córdoba uses stone arches and Djenné uses mud-brick pillars.
No. 167 (§7.1), Conical tower and circular wall of Great Zimb…: Both are monumental African architecture tied to long-distance trade.
No. 222 (§10.10), Malagan display and mask: Both depend on communal ritual: Djenné is re-plastered every year, and malagan carvings are made for a ceremony and then left to decay.
168.vocab: adobe, toron, qibla, minaret, hypostyle hall, buttress, Sudano-Sahelian.

form: Built of sun-dried mud bricks (adobe, locally called ferey) set in mud mortar and coated with mud plaster (banco) mixed with rice husks and other additives.
Bundles of palm-wood sticks called toron project from the walls as permanent scaffolding for re-plastering; they also help the walls cope with cracking from heat and humidity.
Stands on a raised platform that protects it from seasonal floods of the Bani River; the town itself sits on a floodplain island.
The east-facing qibla wall (the wall facing Mecca, which Muslims face in prayer) has three large tower-minarets and faces the market square.
Vertical buttresses (thick supporting ribs) end in cone-shaped pinnacles, some topped with ostrich eggs.
Inside, a hypostyle prayer hall (a hall filled with columns) has about 90 massive mud-brick pillars holding a flat roof of palm wood and mud; roof vents with removable lids let in air and light.
The style is called Sudano-Sahelian, the mud-brick architecture of the West African savanna.
function: Djenné’s Friday mosque (congregational mosque), where the whole community gathers for weekly prayer.
A center of Islamic learning; Djenné was known for its many Qur’anic schools.
The Monday market in front of it joins religion and commerce at the heart of town.
content: Ostrich eggs on the pinnacles stand for fertility and purity.
Because it needs yearly repair, the building is a symbol of shared faith and civic identity.
Its size and towers express the town’s devotion and the prestige of its Muslim leaders.
context: Tradition says the ruler Koi Konboro converted to Islam in the 1200s and turned his palace into the first mosque.
In the 1830s the reformer Seku Amadu, who thought the old mosque too lavish, let it fall into ruin and built a plainer one nearby.
The present mosque was rebuilt in 1906–1907, when Mali was a French colony, under the masons’ guild leader Ismaila Traoré; scholars debate how much French oﬀicials shaped its design.
Djenné grew rich as a trade city linking West African gold and goods with the trans-Saharan caravan routes, alongside Timbuktu.
Each spring, before the rains, the Crépissage (re-plastering) festival brings everyone together: masons lead, young men haul and spread mud, women carry water, elders supervise.
Part of the UNESCO site Old Towns of Djenné since 1988, listed as endangered since 2016 because of insecurity in the region. On the exam.
If asked about material → adobe (mud brick) with toron of palm wood.
If asked what the toron are for → permanent scaffolding for the yearly re-plastering.
If asked about community → the annual festival; the building is maintained collectively.
Dates: founded c. 1200; rebuilt 1906–1907 under French colonial rule.
Islamic features: qibla wall facing Mecca, minarets, hypostyle prayer hall.
If asked how Islam reached West Africa → through trans-Saharan trade; Djenné was a trade and learning center.
Trap: the building standing today dates from the early 1900s, not the 1200s.

169.title: Wall plaque, from Oba’s palace
169.plain: This rectangular brass plaque was cast in the 1500s by royal guild artists in Benin City, in today’s Nigeria, to decorate the palace of the Oba (king). It shows the Oba or a high chief in the center, larger than his attendants and dressed in coral-bead regalia. Hundreds of such plaques once covered the palace pillars like a picture archive of court life, until British troops looted them in 1897.
169.spot: A flat metal rectangle with figures in high relief: a large, frontal central figure in a beaded collar and cap holding a ceremonial sword or spear, smaller attendants beside him, small European heads in the upper corners, and a background of four-petaled leaf patterns.
169.remember: “Benin Bronzes” are really brass. Big Oba in the middle = hieratic scale. Portuguese heads in the corners = trade partners of the 1500s.
compare: No. 180 (§7.14), Veranda post of enthroned king and senior wife: Both are Nigerian royal palace art about hierarchy, but the plaque is cast brass relief and Olowe’s post is carved wood that stresses the queen’s support.
No. 155 (§6.3), Yaxchilán: Both record royal ritual and rank in relief on palace or temple architecture.
No. 158 (§6.6), Ruler’s feather headdress: Both were taken to Europe and now sit at the center of repatriation debates.
No. 13 (§3.2), Palette of King Narmer: Both use hieratic scale and frontal figures to show the ruler’s supreme rank.
169.vocab: lost-wax casting, hierarchical scale, high relief, frontal, regalia, restitution.

form: Cast brass made by the lost-wax process: a wax model is coated in clay, heated so the wax melts out, and the hollow mold is filled with molten metal.
Figures stand out in high relief (deeply raised) from a flat rectangular background with nail holes at the edges.
Hieratic scale (size shows importance): the Oba or chief is largest and central; attendants who shade him with shields or hold his arms are smaller.
The central figure is frontal and symmetrical, with an oversized head and calm face, wearing a coral-bead collar and cap.
The background is filled with quatrefoil (four-lobed) river-leaf patterns, and small heads of Portuguese men with long hair and hats appear in the corners.
Details such as beads, weapons and textures were worked into the wax before casting.
function: Nailed to the wooden pillars of the Oba’s palace courtyards; a 1668 Dutch account describes pillars covered with cast metal plaques.
A visual record of court ritual, war, rank and history, which could be consulted to recall how ceremonies were done.
Brass was a royal monopoly: only the Oba could commission it, and the casters’ guild, the Igun Eronmwon, worked only for him.
content: The Oba was a divine king; his large, still, frontal figure shows timeless authority.
Coral beads link the Oba to Olokun, god of the sea and wealth; the river-leaf background also refers to Olokun.
The oversized head stresses the head as the seat of judgment and destiny.
The Portuguese heads acknowledge the foreign traders who brought brass and wealth to the court.
context: Portuguese traders arrived in the 1480s. Under Oba Esigie (early 1500s), Benin traded ivory, pepper, cloth and enslaved captives for brass manillas (bracelet-shaped currency), which were melted for casting.
Plaques were made mainly from the mid-1500s into the 1600s; later they were taken down and stored.
In 1897 a British “punitive expedition” burned and looted Benin City and exiled Oba Ovonramwen; thousands of objects, the so-called Benin Bronzes, were sold to Western museums and collectors.
The British Museum holds hundreds. Since 2021 Germany, the Smithsonian, the Horniman Museum and others have returned objects or ownership to Nigeria.
The Edo brass-casters’ guild still works in Benin City, and an Oba still reigns. On the exam.
If asked about technique → lost-wax cast brass.
If asked about hierarchy → hieratic scale, frontality, symmetry.
If asked about function → palace pillar decoration and a visual record of court history.
If asked about global trade → Portuguese figures and brass from melted manillas.
If asked about restitution → looted in 1897; returns and debates are ongoing.
Trap: they are called “bronzes,” but the medium is brass.
Place trap: Edo peoples of Benin City, Nigeria, not the modern country of Benin.

170.title: Sika dwa kofi (Golden Stool)
170.medium: Gold over wood and cast-gold attachments
170.plain: The Golden Stool is the sacred throne of the Asante (Ashanti) kingdom in Ghana, said to have come down from the sky around 1700. It is believed to hold the soul of the whole Asante nation, so no one, not even the king, ever sits on it. When a British governor demanded to sit on it in 1900, the Asante went to war.
170.spot: A small curved stool covered in gold, resting on its side on its own chair, hung with gold bells and small cast-gold figures, shown next to the Asantehene (king) under a large umbrella.
170.remember: Born on a Friday: Kofi is the Akan name for a boy born on Friday. Sky stool, soul of the nation, never sat on. c. 1700.
compare: No. 215 (§10.3), ‘Ahu ‘ula: Both are sacred royal objects that carry the spiritual power of rule.
No. 160 (§6.8), Maize cobs: Both use gold as a sacred material rather than as money.
No. 171 (§7.5), Ndop: Both are royal objects believed to hold a spiritual essence that passes legitimacy between rulers.
No. 158 (§6.6), Ruler’s feather headdress: Both are royal objects that became flashpoints in encounters with European powers.
170.vocab: regalia, eﬀigy, enstoolment, sovereignty, sunsum, casting.

form: A stool with a curved seat, a central support and a rectangular base, carved in wood and covered with gold.
Cast-gold bells and small figures hang from it, including eﬀigies (likenesses) of enemy rulers defeated by the Asante.
Displayed lying on its side on its own chair, so no one can sit on it, and never allowed to touch the ground.
Carried in procession by an attendant and shaded by a large ceremonial umbrella, like a king.
Gold was mined locally in great quantity; Europeans called the region the Gold Coast.
function: Embodies the sunsum (soul) of the Asante people and the unity of the state; the nation’s welfare depends on its safety.
A new Asantehene is “enstooled” in rites in its presence, which legitimize his rule; he sits on a separate stool.
Brought out only for the most important state occasions and otherwise kept in the palace at Kumasi.
content: Among the Akan, ordinary stools belong to individuals and hold part of their souls; after a leader dies his stool is blackened and kept as an ancestral shrine.
Origin story: the priest Okomfo Anokye called the stool down from the sky, and it landed on the lap of Osei Tutu, uniting the Asante clans under one king.
The eﬀigies of defeated rulers show conquered power absorbed into the nation.
context: Osei Tutu founded the Asante kingdom around 1700 and defeated the rival state of Denkyira in 1701.
Asante grew rich from gold and trade, including the Atlantic slave trade, and fought several wars with Britain in the 1800s.
In 1896 the British exiled King Prempeh I. In 1900 Governor Frederic Hodgson demanded the Golden Stool so he could sit on it, a grave insult.
Yaa Asantewaa, queen mother of Ejisu, led the resistance in the War of the Golden Stool (1900). Britain won and annexed Asante but never got the stool, which was hidden.
In 1921 road workers found it and stripped some ornaments; an Asante court condemned them, showing its continuing sacredness. It remains central to Asante identity today. On the exam.
If asked about function → it embodies the soul of the Asante nation; no one sits on it.
If asked about origin → Okomfo Anokye and Osei Tutu, c. 1700.
If asked about colonial conflict → Hodgson’s demand, the War of the Golden Stool, Yaa Asantewaa, 1900.
Material: gold over wood with cast-gold attachments.
Key idea: an object can carry political sovereignty and collective identity.
Trap: it is not a seat; the king sits on a different stool beside it.

171.title: Ndop (portrait figure) of King Mishe miShyaang maMbul
171.artist: Kuba peoples; Democratic Republic of the Congo
171.plain: An ndop is a carved wooden figure of a king of the Kuba kingdom in today’s Democratic Republic of the Congo. All ndop look nearly alike, a calm, idealized man sitting crosslegged; each king is identified by a personal emblem, the ibol, carved in front. This one, carved about 1760–1780 and now in the Brooklyn Museum, is traditionally identified by its drum as King Mishe miShyaang maMbul, though the museum now notes it could depict another king.
171.spot: A dark, polished wooden figure seated cross-legged on a decorated block, with a large head, closed or downcast eyes, a flat cap with a projecting brim, a knife in one hand, and a small drum carved in front of his legs.
171.remember: Ndop is “not a photo”: not a real likeness. You find the king by his ibol, like a name tag. Drum in front = Mishe.
compare: No. 220 (§10.8), Tamati Waka Nene: Both portray leaders, but Tamati Waka Nene uses Western realism while the ndop uses idealization and an emblem.
No. 174 (§7.8), Portrait mask: Both are idealized portraits that show character rather than physical likeness.
No. 43 (§3.32), Augustus of Prima Porta: Both idealize a ruler to express the qualities of leadership rather than an exact likeness.
No. 170 (§7.4), Sika dwa kofi: Both are royal objects believed to hold a spirit and pass legitimacy from ruler to ruler.
171.vocab: ibol, idealization, regalia, attribute, cowrie, spiritual double.

form: Carved from one block of hardwood, about 49.5 cm (19.5 in) high, and rubbed with oil and tukula (red camwood powder) to a dark shine.
Seated cross-legged on a rectangular platform carved with interlaced geometric bands.
The head is very large, about a third of the figure, with closed eyes and a smooth, calm face.
Royal regalia: a shody cap with a projecting brim, cowrie-shell belts, armbands, a shoulder ornament, and a ceremonial knife in the left hand.
In front sits his ibol (a personal emblem chosen by each king): here a cylindrical drum decorated with a hand.
The idealized, symmetrical body shows calm and control rather than individual anatomy.
function: A spiritual double of the king. In life it was kept near him; when he traveled it stayed with his wives, and it was said to help women in childbirth.
At his death it held his spirit and helped transfer royal power to his successor, who by some accounts kept it close.
It served as a lasting memorial of the king in the royal line.
content: Not a portrait in the Western sense: the ibol identifies the person, while the body shows the ideal of kingship.
The large head stands for wisdom; the calm face and closed pose show composure, a key Kuba royal virtue.
Cowrie shells signal wealth and refer to Woot, the mythical founder of the Kuba.
Each ibol relates to the king’s reign or achievements, chosen when he takes power.
context: The Kuba kingdom took shape in the 1600s; tradition credits King Shyaam aMbul aNgoong with starting ndop sculpture. His ibol is a game board.
The Brooklyn Museum dates Mishe miShyaang maMbul’s reign to about 1710, so this figure, carved about 1760–1780, was probably made after his reign as a commemoration or replacement.
Its history is well documented: in 1909 King Kot aPe gave it to a Belgian colonial minister, and the Brooklyn Museum bought it in 1961.
The museum now cautiously labels it as one of three possible kings, since some ibol identifications are debated. On the exam.
If asked how to identify the king → the ibol in front, not the face.
If asked about idealization → all ndop share an ideal body and calm face to represent kingship itself.
If asked about function → spiritual double, transfer of power, commemoration.
Regalia: shody cap, cowrie belts, knife, seated on a platform.
Trap: ndop are portraits by attribute (an identifying object), not by likeness.
Attribution note: the museum now hedges on which king it shows; the College Board title names Mishe miShyaang maMbul.

172.title: Power figure (Nkisi n’kondi)
172.artist: Kongo peoples; Democratic Republic of the Congo
172.plain: A nkisi n’kondi is a wooden figure from the Kongo peoples of Central Africa, bristling with nails and blades. A ritual specialist loaded it with medicines to make it powerful, and people drove in a nail each time they swore an oath, settled a dispute, or asked it to punish a wrongdoer. It worked like a court, a contract and a police force rolled into one.
172.spot: A standing wooden figure with hands on hips or one arm raised, wide staring eyes, an open mouth, and a body covered in hundreds of iron nails, blades and metal pieces, with a box or mirror on its belly.
172.remember: N’kondi means “hunter”: it hunts down people who break their promises. Every nail is a signed contract.
compare: No. 176 (§7.10), Ikenga: Both are shrine figures with spiritual power, but the ikenga serves one man and the nkisi a whole community.
No. 216 (§10.4), Staff god: Both are figures holding sacred power inside them that missionaries seized or destroyed.
No. 177 (§7.11), Lukasa: Both record community knowledge in material form, the nkisi through nails and the lukasa through beads.
172.vocab: power figure, nganga, bilongo, divination, nkisi.

form: A carved wooden human figure, often about 1 m (3 ft) tall, in an alert stance: hands on hips (pakalala, a pose of readiness) or one arm raised to strike.
The body is covered with iron nails, blades and wedges hammered in over time.
A cavity in the belly, and sometimes the head, holds bilongo (medicines: earth, plants, animal parts and other charged substances).
The cavity is sealed with resin and a mirror or glass, often European trade glass.
Eyes may be inset with glass or shell, and the mouth is open as if speaking or about to attack.
Its look kept changing as more nails were added; it was never finished.
function: A nganga (ritual specialist) made and activated the figure by inserting the bilongo.
People came to it to seal oaths and agreements, settle disputes, heal illness, or punish thieves and witches.
For each case a nail or blade was driven in to rouse the spirit and record the matter; parties sometimes licked the nail first to seal the oath.
It served a whole community, and one figure could hold hundreds of cases.
content: Nkisi means a container for spiritual forces (plural minkisi); n’kondi means “hunter,” because it tracked down wrongdoers.
The mirror let the nganga see into the spirit world and reflected evil back on its source.
The aggressive stance shows readiness to strike at oath-breakers.
Each nail records an agreement or dispute, making the figure an archive of community history.
context: The Kongo kingdom had contact with Portugal from 1483 and adopted Christianity; some scholars link nail figures to images of martyrs pierced by arrows, which is debated.
In the late 1800s and early 1900s, oﬀicials of King Leopold II’s Congo Free State and missionaries condemned minkisi as “fetishes” and seized or burned many.
Many went to European museums, where they are inactive and shown without the rituals that gave them meaning.
Their bold forms impressed modern artists, and they remain among the best-known African sculptures.
Kongo ideas about minkisi crossed the Atlantic with enslaved Central Africans and shaped religious practice in the Americas, for example in Cuban Palo and Haitian Vodou. On the exam.
If asked about function → oaths, contracts, dispute settlement, healing and punishment.
If asked about the nails → each records a case or oath and rouses the spirit to act.
If asked about bilongo and the mirror → medicines sealed in the belly; the mirror for divination and protection.
Activation: by a nganga, a ritual specialist.
Context: colonial seizures and missionaries labeling such figures fetishes.
Trap: it is not a voodoo-style curse doll; it upheld law and social order.
Medium and date: wood and metal (iron nails and blades), with resin, glass and medicines; Kongo peoples, c. late 19th century.

173.title: Female (Pwo) mask
173.artist: Chokwe peoples; Democratic Republic of the Congo
173.plain: The Pwo mask is a carved wooden face of an idealized young woman, made by the Chokwe peoples of Angola, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia. It honors the female ancestor who founded the lineage. It is danced by men, dressed in costumes with false breasts, who move gracefully to teach ideals of womanhood.
173.spot: A reddish-brown wooden face with narrow, half-closed eyes in deep sockets, delicate features, filed teeth in a slightly open mouth, carved cross-shaped and tear-shaped scars on the forehead and cheeks, metal earrings and a fiber wig.
173.remember: Pwo means “woman,” but a man wears it. Female ancestor, beauty scars and filed teeth, Chokwe.
compare: No. 175 (§7.9), Bundu mask: Both show ideals of female beauty, but the Pwo is danced by men and the Sande mask by women.
No. 174 (§7.8), Portrait mask: Both are idealized face masks used in dance, but the Mblo portrays a specific living person.
No. 164 (§6.12), Transformation mask: Both are masks that come alive only in performance.

form: A carved wood face mask with a fiber coiffure (hairstyle), metal earrings and a red-brown pigment surface.
Narrow, half-closed eyes set in deep sockets give the face an otherworldly, inward look.
Scarification (decorative scars) is carved in: a cross-shaped mark (cingelyengelye) on the forehead and tear-like marks under the eyes.
Filed teeth show in the slightly open mouth, a former Chokwe beauty practice.
Smooth, symmetrical and refined, with a small nose and mouth; the face is youthful and calm.
Worn with a knitted fiber body suit, a carved chest with breasts, and a skirt or bustle.
function: Danced by men in masquerades (akishi, the Chokwe masked spirits) at celebrations and during the period of boys’ initiation (mukanda).
The dancer moves gracefully, copying women’s movements, to honor women and teach young people ideals of beauty and behavior.
Some performances were also entertainment, and dancers received gifts.
Mukanda is a months-long initiation camp where boys are circumcised and taught adult knowledge; masked akishi represent ancestral spirits who watch over it.
content: Represents a female ancestor, the founding mother of the lineage, and women’s role in fertility and continuity.
Scarification, filed teeth and an elaborate hairstyle were signs of beauty, adulthood and Chokwe identity.
The half-closed eyes link the face to the spirit world and suggest modesty.
Carvers sometimes based a mask on a woman they admired in their community.
context: The Chokwe live mainly in northeastern Angola, with communities in the DRC and Zambia; they were long linked to the Lunda empire.
Chokwe carvers were known for skill, and masks were often commissioned by the dancers who wore them.
Masquerade societies here were men’s institutions, which is why a man performs the female role.
In the 1800s the Chokwe grew powerful by trading ivory, wax and rubber and by hunting, and in the 1880s they overran the Lunda capital, spreading their art across the region.
Colonial-era collecting brought many Pwo masks to European and American museums in the early 1900s. On the exam.
If asked who wore it → men dressed as women; contrast the Sande mask worn by women (No. 175).
If asked about meaning → an idealized female ancestor; women’s role in fertility and community.
Beauty ideals: scarification (the cingelyengelye cross), filed teeth, coiffure, calm face.
Function: masquerade at initiation and celebrations that teaches the young.
Attribution clues: half-closed eyes in deep sockets, carved scars, fiber wig, Chokwe.
Medium and date: wood, fiber, pigment and metal; late 19th to early 20th century.

174.title: Portrait mask (Mblo)
174.plain: A Mblo mask is a carved wooden face that portrays a specific, admired living person among the Baule of Côte d’Ivoire. The likeness is not photographic; calm, refined, idealized features show the person’s good character. It appears in a festive, non-religious dance, and the person honored might even dance alongside it.
174.spot: A small, long wooden face with a high smooth forehead, half-closed downcast eyes, a small closed mouth, fine raised scars near the eyes or temples, and an elaborate carved hairstyle, polished dark.
174.remember: Mblo is a portrait of a real friend, a face-shaped tribute. Baule, Côte d’Ivoire, early 1900s.
compare: No. 173 (§7.7), Female: Both are idealized masks, but the Pwo represents an ancestor and the Mblo a living person.
No. 171 (§7.5), Ndop: Both are idealized portraits that express inner qualities rather than exact appearance.
No. 220 (§10.8), Tamati Waka Nene: Both honor a real individual, but Tamati Waka Nene uses Western realism while the Mblo idealizes.
174.vocab: portrait mask, idealization, scarification, coiffure, masquerade, secular.

form: Carved wood with pigment, about the size of a face, smooth and polished.
A long face with a high forehead, a sign of intelligence.
Downcast, half-closed eyes, a thin nose and a small closed mouth suggest calm and self-control.
Fine scarification marks on the cheeks, temples or forehead, and an elaborate braided coiffure carved on top.
Often includes details from the subject’s real hairstyle or scars, so it is individual within an ideal type.
function: Used in Mblo, a secular (non-religious) entertainment masquerade, called Gbagba in some areas, with music and dance.
Portrait masks come at the end of a sequence of other masks, such as animals and comic characters, as the climax.
The honored person may come out and dance alongside the masked dancer, a rare public tribute.
content: A portrait of a specific respected person, often a woman known for beauty or good conduct, though men were also honored.
Baule call such a mask the subject’s double (ndoma); the two are bound together, and the subject is expected to treat the dancer well.
Beauty here is moral: calm features show inner goodness and composure.
context: The Baule are an Akan-related people of central Côte d’Ivoire; masked dancers are men.
A mask was usually commissioned to honor someone, and carvers sometimes studied the subject in person.
Fieldwork by art historian Susan Vogel recorded names of carvers and subjects for some Baule masks, confirming they portray real individuals.
Early 20th-century European collectors and modernist artists admired Baule carving for its refinement.
Baule carvers also made “spirit spouse” figures (blolo bla and blolo bian) in the same calm, polished, idealized style, a useful clue for attribution. On the exam.
If asked what kind of portrait → an idealized portrait of a real living person: character over likeness.
If asked about function → secular entertainment masquerade; the honored person may dance with it.
Visual clues: high forehead, downcast eyes, scarification, elaborate coiffure.
Key contrast: the Pwo (No. 173) is an ancestral ideal; the Mblo is a specific living person.
Medium and date: wood and pigment, early 20th century, Baule, Côte d’Ivoire.
Trap: the Mblo portrays a living person; it is neither a funeral portrait of the dead nor a sacred mask of a god.

175.title: Bundu mask
175.artist: Sande Society, Mende peoples; Sierra Leone and Liberia
175.plain: The Bundu (or Sowei) mask is a glossy black wooden helmet mask of the Sande Society, a women’s association among the Mende of Sierra Leone and Liberia. It is one of very few African masks danced by women. It represents a water spirit and the ideals of womanhood, and appears when girls finish initiation and return to the community as women.
175.spot: A shiny black wooden helmet covering the whole head, with ringed folds around the neck, a high forehead, small downcast eyes, a tiny mouth, and an elaborate carved braided hairstyle, sometimes topped by a small figure.
175.remember: Sande women, water spirit: shiny black like wet skin rising from water, neck rings like ripples. Women wear this one.
compare: No. 173 (§7.7), Female: Both express ideals of female beauty, but the Pwo is danced by men and the Sowei by women.
No. 174 (§7.8), Portrait mask: Both use calm, idealized features to express moral qualities.
No. 178 (§7.12), Aka elephant mask: Both are masquerade costumes of exclusive associations that cover the dancer completely.
175.vocab: helmet mask, initiation, coiffure, masquerade, raﬀia, idealization.

form: A helmet mask (one that fits over the whole head like a helmet) carved from a hollowed section of log.
Blackened with dye and oil to a glossy black finish.
Neck rings (folds) at the base, a high broad forehead, small downcast eyes, a small nose and a closed mouth.
An elaborate carved coiffure with braids or crests, sometimes topped with small birds, horns or figures.
Worn with a full costume of black-dyed raﬀia (palm fiber) and cloth that hides the dancer’s body completely.
Carved by men but commissioned, owned and danced by women.
The stacked neck rings and the rows of carved hair create strong horizontal rhythms that set off the small, smooth face.
function: Worn by senior women of the Sande Society, which prepares girls for adulthood: marriage, motherhood, farming and social conduct.
Appears at the end of initiation, when the new women return to town, and at other Sande ceremonies.
The masked dancer, called Sowei, is treated as a spirit; no one touches her or speaks to her directly.
content: Represents Sowo (Sowei), the Sande water spirit; the shiny black surface suggests a spirit emerging from water.
Neck rings stand for ripples as the spirit rises, and also for healthy, well-fed beauty and prosperity.
Downcast eyes and a small closed mouth show composure, modesty and wisdom; the high forehead shows intelligence.
The braided hairstyle shows care, social order, and women helping one another.
context: Sande is found among the Mende, Vai, Gola, Temne and neighboring peoples; men belong to the separate Poro society.
“Bundu” is the Temne and Krio term; “Sowei” is the Mende word for the mask and for senior Sande leaders.
Sande initiation has traditionally included female genital cutting, a practice now strongly debated and opposed by many in the region.
Sande remains active and politically important, and leadership in it gives women real public authority.
Sande also teaches healing and herbal knowledge, songs and dances; its leaders, also called sowei, are respected judges of women’s affairs. On the exam.
If asked who wears it → women of the Sande Society; one of the few African masks danced by women.
If asked about meaning → the water spirit Sowo and ideals of female beauty and conduct.
Visual clues: glossy black, neck rings, helmet form, elaborate coiffure.
Function: initiation of girls into womanhood.
Pair it with the Chokwe Pwo mask (No. 173), which is danced by men.
Medium and date: wood, cloth and fiber, 19th to 20th century, Mende, Sierra Leone and Liberia.

176.title: Ikenga (shrine figure)
176.plain: An ikenga is a carved wooden personal shrine owned by an Igbo man in southeastern Nigeria. It shows a horned figure, often holding a knife and a trophy, and stands for the strength of its owner’s right hand: his drive, skill and success. He made offerings to it before major efforts and thanked it afterward, and it was destroyed when he died.
176.spot: A wooden figure, often seated, with two large curling ram’s horns rising from its head, holding a knife in the right hand and a tusk or severed head in the left.
176.remember: Ram’s horns say “I butt my way to success.” Right hand = how you make it. Igbo, Nigeria.
compare: No. 172 (§7.6), Power figure: Both are shrine figures with spiritual power, but the ikenga serves one man and the nkisi a whole community.
No. 179 (§7.13), Reliquary figure: Both are wooden sculptures used in private ritual and tied to personal or family identity.
No. 180 (§7.14), Veranda post of enthroned king and senior wife: Both are Nigerian wood sculpture, but the ikenga is personal and portable while the veranda post is royal and architectural.

form: Carved from one piece of wood, from a few inches to over a meter tall.
Large curved ram’s horns on the head are the one essential feature.
Fuller figures sit on a stool, holding a knife in the right hand and a tusk or trophy head (a carved enemy head showing victory) in the left.
Some are simple (horns on a base), while elaborate ones have scarification, headdresses and detailed bodies.
The surface is often darkened by years of offerings and handling.
In most versions the horns sweep back and curl into a crescent, so the figure is recognizable even in its simplest, most abstract form.
function: A personal shrine for one man, usually acquired when he became an adult or head of a household.
He made offerings (kola nuts, palm wine, yams, sometimes animal blood) before farming, trading, fighting or travel, and thanked it after success.
At his death it was split, then buried with him or thrown away, because it belonged to him alone.
Larger ikenga also existed for groups such as age grades.
content: Ikenga is linked to the right hand, the hand of action, and so to success through personal effort.
Ram’s horns stand for aggression, determination and persistence, since rams charge headon.
The knife and trophy head show success through courage, including in war; a tusk shows wealth.
It expresses Igbo values of individual achievement and enterprise.
context: Many Igbo communities were decentralized, without kings, and honored titles men earned through achievement rather than inherited rank.
Versions for women existed in some areas but were rare.
Christian missionaries in the colonial period discouraged ikenga, and many entered museums during the 20th century.
Ikenga remains a symbol of Igbo identity today, used in names and as a cultural emblem.
Men gained status by earning titles such as ozo, which required wealth and generosity; the ikenga celebrated the hand that won them. On the exam.
If asked about meaning → personal achievement and the power of the right hand.
If asked about the horns → ram’s horns = determination and aggression.
If asked about function → personal shrine with offerings; destroyed at the owner’s death.
Pair with the nkisi n’kondi (No. 172): a personal shrine versus a community legal tool.
Medium and date: wood, Igbo, Nigeria, 19th to 20th century.
Trap: the ikenga honors one living man’s drive, not an ancestor, so it does not outlive him.

177.title: Lukasa (memory board)
177.artist: Mbudye Society, Luba peoples; Democratic Republic of the Congo
177.plain: A lukasa is a small, hand-held wooden board studded with beads, shells and metal pins, made by the Luba peoples of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Experts of the Mbudye society, called “men of memory,” ran their fingers over it while reciting the history of Luba kings, migrations and sacred places. It prompts memory rather than holding a fixed text, so the story it tells changes with the reader and the occasion.
177.spot: A small wooden board roughly shaped like an hourglass or a turtle, its front covered with clusters and lines of colored beads and shells, its back carved with geometric patterns.
177.remember: Lukasa sounds like “look, a saga”: a history board you read with your fingers. Luba, DRC, 19th to 20th century.
compare: No. 221 (§10.9), Navigation chart: Both encode specialist knowledge in abstract objects meant to be studied and memorized rather than read like text.
No. 162 (§6.10), All-T’oqapu tunic: Both use abstract signs to carry information about a state and its power.
No. 172 (§7.6), Power figure: Both record community history in material form, the lukasa through beads and the nkisi through nails.
177.vocab: mnemonic device, lukasa, genealogy, abstract, oral history.

form: A wood board small enough to hold in one hand, roughly hourglass-shaped, read as a tortoise, a royal compound, or a woman’s body.
The front is studded with beads, shells and metal pins of different sizes and colors, arranged in clusters and lines.
The back is carved with incised geometric patterns, sometimes like a tortoise shell.
Some boards include small carved faces standing for important people or spirits.
Made to be touched and read with the fingers as much as seen.
Bead color and size can help separate kings from oﬀicials or sacred places from ordinary ones, though experts read them differently.
function: A mnemonic device (a tool that prompts memory) for members of the Mbudye society, the royal historians and advisors of Luba kings.
At events such as a king’s installation, the reader traced the beads while reciting king lists, genealogies, migrations and the founding myth of Luba kingship.
Used to train new Mbudye members and to advise rulers and support their right to rule.
content: Large beads often stand for important people such as kings and chiefs; clusters for places like royal courts; lines for roads or migrations.
A board can also map the layout of a royal compound and its sacred spaces.
The founding story features the hunter-hero Mbidi Kiluwe and his son Kalala Ilunga, who overthrew the cruel king Nkongolo and founded sacred Luba kingship.
Readings vary: different experts give different versions, so history is performed and shaped by politics.
context: The Luba kingdom flourished in southeastern DRC from roughly the 1500s to the late 1800s.
Mbudye members were known as “men of memory”; women also held important roles in the society and at court.
Art historians Mary Nooter Roberts and Allen F. Roberts studied lukasa readings in the late 20th century, showing how flexible and political they are.
Like many Central African objects, lukasa were collected during the colonial period and many are now in Western museums. On the exam.
If asked about function → a memory aid for royal history, read by touch.
If asked who used it → Mbudye society specialists, the “men of memory.”
If asked about variability → not a fixed text; the reading changes with reader and context.
Classic pair: the Marshall Islands navigation chart (No. 221), another abstract object holding specialist knowledge.
Medium: wood, beads and metal.
Key idea: knowledge is power; the Mbudye both supported and checked kings.

178.title: Aka elephant mask
178.medium: Wood, woven raﬀia, cloth, and beads
178.plain: The Aka mask is a cloth hood covered in imported glass beads, shaped like an elephant with huge round ears and a long trunk-like panel, from the Bamileke kingdoms of western Cameroon. Elite members of the Kuosi society wore it at royal festivals and funerals. Elephants and leopards stood for the king’s power, and the beads displayed enormous wealth.
178.spot: A colorful hood covered in small glass beads in red, blue, black and white triangles and diamonds, with two large round flat ears, a humanlike face, and long rectangular panels hanging down the front and back like a trunk.
178.remember: Big ears, long trunk, lots of beads: big power and big money. Bamileke, Cameroon grassfields, worn by the Kuosi society.
compare: No. 163 (§6.11), Bandolier bag: Both turn imported glass beads into objects of status and identity.
No. 215 (§10.3), ‘Ahu ‘ula: Both use costly, hard-to-get materials to signal rank and royal power.
No. 175 (§7.9), Bundu mask: Both are masquerade costumes of exclusive associations that cover the dancer completely.
178.vocab: hood mask, beadwork, masquerade, regalia, glass bead.

form: A hood mask of cloth over a raﬀia frame, fully covered in small imported glass beads sewn on in patterns.
Two large, round, flat ears on the sides; a humanlike face with round eyes and mouth; long beaded panels hanging front and back like a trunk.
Bold geometric designs, especially triangles that suggest leopard spots, in red, blue, white and black.
Worn with a feathered headdress, an indigo-dyed cloth costume, and a leopard pelt down the back.
The materials (wood, woven raﬀia, cloth and beads) were costly to gather and slow to assemble.
function: Worn by members of the Kuosi society, an elite association of warriors and wealthy titleholders close to the fon (king).
Danced at royal funerals, at the king’s festivals, and at other major ceremonies.
Displayed the strength and wealth of the kingdom to its people and to visitors.
Several masked dancers performed together with drums and rattles, so a group of glittering beaded elephants made a large public spectacle.
content: The elephant and leopard were royal animals; the king was believed able to transform into them.
Imported glass beads were expensive, and their use was controlled by the king, so a beaded mask showed royal favor and wealth.
Combining a human face with elephant features suggests the power to transform.
context: The Bamileke live in many small kingdoms in the western grassfields (high grassland) of Cameroon, each ruled by a fon.
Glass beads arrived through long-distance trade from Europe; older beads came through African and Indian Ocean networks.
The Kuosi began as a warriors’ society and later admitted wealthy men who could afford membership.
Beadwork was a leading royal art across the grassfields: kings also owned beaded thrones, stools, figures and calabashes as treasures of state.
Germany colonized Cameroon from 1884 until World War I, after which France and Britain divided it; many such masks entered Western museums in this period. On the exam.
If asked about materials → imported glass beads = wealth and royal privilege.
If asked about symbolism → elephant and leopard = the king’s power.
If asked who wore it → Kuosi society members, an elite men’s association.
Occasions: royal funerals and festivals.
Attribution clues: beaded hood, round ears, trunk panels, triangle patterns.
Trap: it is a cloth hood mask, not a carved wooden face mask.
Medium and date: wood, woven raﬀia, cloth and beads, 19th to 20th century; Bamileke, western grassfields of Cameroon.

179.title: Reliquary figure (byeri)
179.plain: A byeri is a carved wooden figure that the Fang peoples of Gabon, Equatorial Guinea and southern Cameroon set on top of a bark box holding the skulls and bones of important ancestors. It guarded the relics and stood for the ancestors’ power. Its rounded, balanced forms later fascinated European modernists such as Picasso and Matisse.
179.spot: A dark, glossy wooden figure with a large head and bulging forehead, a long torso, short bent legs, and hands meeting in front of the body, symmetrical and compact.
179.remember: Byeri sounds like “buried”: it guards ancestors’ bones. Big baby head on a grown-up body. Fang, 19th to 20th century.
compare: No. 126 (§5.28), Les Demoiselles d’Avignon: Picasso’s Demoiselles drew on African sculpture of the kind he and his circle saw and collected in Paris, including Fang figures.
No. 214 (§10.2), Moai on platform: Both represent and watch over ancestors, the moai on a coastal platform and the byeri on a reliquary box.
No. 58 (§4.11), Church of Sainte-Foy: Both are tied to sacred relics, one guarding Fang ancestors’ bones and the other holding a Christian saint’s remains.

form: Carved in wood, often seated, with a calm face, a large head and bulging forehead, a long torso, and short, bent limbs.
The proportions are like an infant’s, while the muscles and pronounced navel show an adult body.
Symmetrical and compact, built of swelling, rounded masses balanced against each other.
Rubbed with palm oil, which seeps out over time and keeps the surface dark and glossy.
A peg or stand at the bottom fixed it to the rim of the bark reliquary box.
Some byeri are heads only, but the full seated figure is the type on the exam.
function: Guarded the relics (physical remains of revered people) kept in a bark box: skulls and bones of lineage founders and leaders.
Kept the relics from the eyes of women and uninitiated boys, who were not allowed to see them.
Families consulted the ancestors through the byeri before major decisions, hunts or journeys, and took the box with them when they moved.
Used in initiation rites for young men, when the relics were revealed to them.
content: Expresses the Fang ideal of balance of opposites: infant and adult, life and death, calm and energy.
The babylike proportions link the ancestors with new life and the future of the family line.
The oily shine signals health and spiritual vitality.
context: The Fang moved into the forests of Gabon, Cameroon and Equatorial Guinea over several centuries; portable reliquaries suited a mobile people.
French and German colonial rule and Christian missionaries suppressed the byeri ancestor cult in the early 1900s; many figures were sold or seized and separated from their bones.
Fang sculpture was admired in Paris by Picasso, Matisse, Derain and others, influencing Cubism and so-called primitivism (Western artists borrowing from art they saw as “primitive”).
That admiration prized form while ignoring religious meaning, a central critique of modernist collecting. On the exam.
If asked about function → guardian of ancestral relics on a bark box.
If asked about form → infant proportions on an adult body: a balance of opposites.
If asked about the surface → palm oil gloss as a sign of vitality.
If asked about influence → early modernists and Cubism; compare Les Demoiselles d’Avignon (No. 126).
Medium and date: wood, Fang, southern Cameroon (also Gabon), 19th to 20th century.
Trap: the byeri guarded the relics but is not itself a relic, and it is not a mask; Fang ngil masks are a different object.

180.title: Veranda post of enthroned king and senior wife (Opo Ogoga)
180.plain: This tall wooden post, carved around 1910–1914 by the Yoruba master Olowe of Ise, held up the roof of a courtyard veranda in the palace of the Ogoga (king) of Ikere in Nigeria. It shows the king seated on his throne with his senior wife standing behind him, much taller than he is. Olowe is one of the few African artists of his time known by name, famous for bold, open carving.
180.spot: A tall carved wooden post in which a small seated king in a high conical crown topped with a bird sits in front of a much larger standing woman whose body frames him, with smaller figures around the base and traces of bright paint.
180.remember: Olowe of Ise carved the queen who props up the king: behind every Ogoga stands a great wife. Yoruba, 1910s.
compare: No. 169 (§7.3), Wall plaque, from Oba’s palace: Both are Nigerian royal palace art about hierarchy, but Benin plaques are cast brass relief while this is carved wood in the round.
No. 155 (§6.3), Yaxchilán: Both give a royal woman a central role in supporting a ruler’s power.
No. 18 (§3.7), King Menkaura and queen: Both pair a king with his queen, but Menkaura’s queen stands about his size, while Olowe makes the wife far taller.
No. 166 (§6.14), Black-on-black ceramic vessel: Both are by named Indigenous artists working within and beyond tradition.
180.vocab: veranda post, undercutting, elongation, hierarchy, architectural sculpture, in the round. 8 West and Central Asia Content area 7 · 500 B.C.E.–1980 C.E. · works 181–191 · about 4% of the multiple-choice section. From ancient Persia through the Islamic world: palaces, mosques, tombs, carpets, metalwork and manuscripts. Islamic religious art generally avoids images of people and uses calligraphy and geometric pattern instead, so knowing why that is (and where the exceptions are) is a common exam point. Trade routes such as the Silk Road also matter.

form: Carved from a single tree trunk in wood with pigment (blue, red and white traces), roughly human height.
The king sits on a throne wearing a tall, conical beaded crown topped by a large bird; his body looks small beneath it.
Behind him stands the senior wife, far taller than the king, her breasts and arms framing him; she supports both the composition and the roof beam.
Smaller figures surround the base, including a kneeling woman and attendants.
Olowe carved the figures almost free of the post, with deep undercutting (carving behind forms so they stand away from the block) and open space between them.
Figures are elongated, with long necks and heads tilted at angles, giving a sense of movement.
function: One of several veranda posts holding up the roof of a palace courtyard: both architecture and sculpture.
Displayed royal power and the order of the court to visitors and residents.
Showed off the king’s wealth and taste by employing the most famous carver of the region.
content: Kingship depends on women’s power: the senior wife, who placed the crown on the king’s head at his installation, literally holds him up.
The bird on the crown refers to the spiritual power of women, often called “our mothers” and associated with birds.
Hierarchy is clear: the king at center, attendants smaller, and the senior wife’s height marking her importance.
The poses express àṣẹ (the Yoruba idea of life force and authority to make things happen).
context: Olowe of Ise (about 1873–1938) was court carver to the king of Ise and worked for many Yoruba rulers in the Ekiti region of southwestern Nigeria.
He was famous in his lifetime; Yoruba praise poetry celebrated him as a master carver.
A pair of doors he carved for the Ikere palace was shown at the British Empire Exhibition in London in 1924 and is now in the British Museum.
He worked during British colonial rule, when Yoruba kings still held cultural authority.
The post is now in the Art Institute of Chicago. On the exam.
If asked about named African artists → Olowe of Ise, who challenges the myth that African art is anonymous.
If asked about meaning → the senior wife’s support shows women’s role in sustaining kingship.
If asked about style → elongated figures carved almost free of the post, open space, dynamic angles.
Function: an architectural veranda post in a palace courtyard.
Bird on the crown = the power of “our mothers.”
Date and culture: c. 1910–1914, Yoruba, Nigeria.

181.title: Petra, Jordan: Treasury and Great Temple
181.plain: Petra was the capital of the Nabataeans, Arab traders who grew rich moving incense and spices across the desert between Arabia and the Mediterranean. Its most famous monument, the so-called Treasury, is a two-story temple front carved straight into a sandstone cliff, and it was probably a royal tomb, not a bank. The nearby Great Temple was a huge freestanding complex built of cut blocks. Together they show a local Arab kingdom speaking the Greek and Roman language of architecture with its own accent.
181.spot: A tall, salmon-pink façade cut into a cliff, often photographed through the dark slot of a narrow gorge. Columns below; above, a gable split in two around a small round pavilion topped by an urn, with weathered statues between the columns.
181.remember: Petra means ‘rock’ in Greek, and the Treasury holds zero treasure: the Nabataeans carved a fake bank into a real rock. Date it by its Greco-Roman look, roughly the turn of the millennium.
compare: No. 21 (§3.10), Mortuary temple of Hatshepsut: Both use a dramatic cliff as the backdrop for a ruler’s funerary monument, but Hatshepsut’s temple is built up in terraces while the Treasury is carved out of the rock itself.
No. 46 (§3.35), Pantheon: Both use a classical temple front of columns and pediment to impress, but the Pantheon is built of concrete and brick while the Treasury is cut from living sandstone.
No. 182 (§8.2), Buddha: Both are monuments carved directly into cliffs along major trade routes, showing how long-distance commerce carried artistic styles across Asia.
181.vocab: rock-cut architecture, facade, pediment, broken pediment, tholos, capital, subtractive.

form: The Treasury is rock-cut architecture (carved out of solid stone, like sculpture, rather than built up from blocks), about 40 m (roughly 128 feet) tall and 25 m wide.
Stonecutters worked from the top down, so the uncut cliff below served as their platform and no scaffolding was needed. Mistakes could not be fixed, since stone removed is gone for good.
The lower story has six columns with Nabataean versions of Corinthian capitals (column tops carved with leaves) holding up a triangular pediment (the gable on the front of a classical temple).

The upper story has a broken pediment (a gable split open in the middle) wrapped around a tholos (a small round temple-like pavilion), crowned by a solid stone urn pocked with bullet holes from treasure hunters.

Weathered figures fill the spaces: probably the twins Castor and Pollux with horses below, axe-swinging Amazons above, and a goddess holding a cornucopia in the tholos. Many faces were later chiseled off.
The Great Temple was built of masonry: a broad stairway, a courtyard of columns with elephant-head capitals, and a raised temple containing a small theater-like seating area for roughly 600 people.
function: The Treasury was most likely a royal tomb, often linked to King Aretas IV (ruled 9 B.C.E. to 40 C.E.). Excavations in 2003 found burials beneath its forecourt, though some scholars think it also worked as a memorial temple.
Its placement is theatrical: it is the first thing visitors see at the end of the Siq (a winding gorge about 1.2 km, or three-quarters of a mile, long), like a monumental welcome sign for the city.
The Great Temple’s purpose is debated: a temple to a major Nabataean god, or a civic hall where the little theater seated a council. Scholars disagree.
content: The deities mix Greek, Egyptian and Arabian traditions. The goddess in the tholos is probably Isis-Tyche, a goddess of fortune popular across the Hellenistic world, or possibly the Nabataean goddess al-Uzza.
Castor and Pollux were linked with death and the afterlife, which fits a tomb, and Amazons and Victories were common on Greco-Roman funerary monuments.
Copying Greek and Roman forms announced that Petra’s rulers belonged to the wealthy, cosmopolitan Mediterranean world, much as a company today might hire a famous architect to look important.
context: The Nabataeans controlled caravan routes carrying frankincense (a fragrant tree resin burned in temples) and myrrh from southern Arabia, plus spices and other luxury goods, to Mediterranean ports. Petra was their capital and warehouse.

The style draws heavily on Ptolemaic Alexandria (Egypt ruled by Greek kings), which is why the College Board labels it ‘Nabataean Ptolemaic and Roman.’ Similar broken pediments and tholoi appear in Roman wall painting at Pompeii.

In a desert with flash floods, the Nabataeans built dams, cisterns, clay pipes and channels, including a dam and tunnel that diverted floodwater away from the Siq. A garden-and-pool complex beside the Great Temple showed off this mastery.
Rome annexed the kingdom in 106 C.E. as the province of Arabia. Trade later shifted to sea routes, and a major earthquake in 363 C.E. badly damaged the city.

Dating: the oﬀicial range (c. 400 B.C.E. to 100 C.E.) covers the whole city. The Treasury itself is usually dated to the first century B.C.E. or early first century C.E., and the Great Temple to roughly the same era. On the exam.
If asked who made it → the Nabataeans, Arab caravan traders. The Romans only took over in 106 C.E.
If asked about process → subtractive carving: the Treasury was cut into the cliff from the top down. The Great Temple, by contrast, was built from blocks.
Trap: the ‘Treasury’ never held treasure. It was most likely a royal tomb, perhaps of Aretas IV.
If asked about artistic traditions → Hellenistic and Roman forms (columns, pediments, tholos) adapted by a local Arab culture, with strong Alexandrian influence.
Unit trap: it belongs to West and Central Asia (Unit 7), not the Ancient Mediterranean unit, even though it looks Roman.

182.title: Buddha
182.medium: Cut rock with plaster and polychrome paint
182.plain: Two giant standing Buddhas were carved into a cliff in the Bamiyan Valley of central Afghanistan, a rest stop on the Silk Road, and for well over a thousand years they were among the largest statues on Earth. Their bodies were roughed out in rock, then finished with mud plaster and bright paint. In March 2001 the Taliban government blew them up as ‘idols,’ and the empty niches are now a famous symbol of deliberate destruction of cultural heritage.
182.spot: A tall arched niche cut into a tan cliff face, either holding a huge standing figure with rippling drapery and no face, or (after 2001) standing empty and rubble-filled. Small cave openings dot the cliff around it.
182.remember: Bamiyan = ‘Bam!’ in 2001: two Buddhas, one big bang. Built roughly 400–800 C.E. (radiocarbon puts them in the 500s–600s), destroyed 2001.
compare: No. 195 (§9.4), Longmen caves: Both are colossal Buddhas carved into cliffs, but the Longmen Vairocana is seated and carved entirely in limestone, while Bamiyan’s figures stood and were finished in plaster.
No. 197 (§9.6), Todai-ji: Both use colossal size to express the Buddha’s greatness, but Todaiji’s Buddha is cast bronze housed in a giant wooden hall.
No. 192 (§9.1), Great Stupa at Sanchi: Sanchi shows the Buddha only through symbols, while Bamiyan shows him in huge human form, a clear change in Buddhist art over time.
182.vocab: rock-cut architecture, colossal, Gandharan, circumambulation, niche, iconoclasm, monastery.

form: There were two figures: the larger western Buddha, about 53–55 m (roughly 175–180 feet) tall, and the smaller eastern Buddha, about 35–38 m (roughly 115–125 feet). Published measurements vary by a few meters.
The basic body shapes were carved from the soft conglomerate rock of the cliff, making them rock-cut (carved from the living rock rather than assembled).
The robes were then built up in mud mixed with straw over wooden pegs and ropes set into the rock, creating thick, rope-like folds, and the surface was painted.

Accounts suggest the larger figure was painted red and the smaller one in several colors, and the faces and hands may once have been finished in wood or metal. The upper faces had been cut away long before 2001.

The drapery’s clinging, regular folds echo Gandharan style (Buddhist art of what is now Pakistan and Afghanistan, shaped by Greco-Roman sculpture), mixed with Indian Gupta and Persian Sasanian elements.
Each niche was lined with paintings of Buddhas and donors, and hundreds of caves around them held further murals, some of which scientists found used early oil-based paints.
function: Devotion and pilgrimage: monks and visitors walked around the figures in circumambulation (walking around a sacred object, clockwise), using passageways cut into the cliff at different heights.
The cliff was a monastery (a community of monks). Monks lived and prayed in the surrounding caves, supported by donations from traders and local rulers.
The size itself was the message: travelers on the Silk Road saw the Buddha’s presence from far across the valley.
content: Both statues show the Buddha standing, a figural approach very different from early Buddhist art, which showed him only through symbols.
Colossal scale expressed the Buddha’s spiritual greatness and, for some scholars, the idea of a cosmic, universal Buddha.
Their destruction gave them a second meaning: a symbol of cultural loss and of the clash between religious ideology and shared heritage.
context: Bamiyan sat where trade routes linking China, India, Persia and the Mediterranean crossed the Hindu Kush mountains. Buddhism, goods and artistic styles traveled together along these roads.
The College Board dates them c. 400–800 C.E. Radiocarbon tests on organic material from the plaster point to roughly 544–595 C.E. for the smaller Buddha and 591–644 C.E. for the larger.
The Chinese monk Xuanzang passed through around 630 C.E. and described the figures glittering with gold and jewel-like decoration, along with thriving monasteries.
Islam gradually replaced Buddhism in the region after the ninth century, and the figures were damaged at various times but stood for centuries.

In March 2001 the Taliban dynamited them after declaring them idols, ignoring international appeals. UNESCO listed the valley as World Heritage in Danger in 2003, and fragments have been collected and studied since. On the exam.
If asked about materials → rock-cut bodies finished with mud-and-straw plaster and paint, not solid carved stone all the way through.
If asked about style → Gandharan, meaning Buddhist imagery combined with Greco-Romanstyle drapery, plus Indian and Persian elements.
If asked about context → the Silk Road (the network of trade routes across Asia) carried Buddhism and these styles to Afghanistan.
Key date: destroyed by the Taliban in 2001. This makes it a go-to example for questions about iconoclasm and cultural heritage.
Trap: Bamiyan is in Afghanistan (Unit 7, West and Central Asia), not India or China, even though the subject is the Buddha.
If asked about function → monastery and pilgrimage site where worshippers circumambulated the colossal figures.

183.title: The Kaaba
183.medium: Granite masonry, covered with silk curtain and calligraphy in gold and silver-
183.plain: The Kaaba is a roughly cube-shaped stone building in the center of the Great Mosque (Masjid al-Haram) in Mecca, and it is the holiest place in Islam. Wherever they are in the world, Muslims face toward it when they pray, and pilgrims walk around it seven times during the hajj. It is not an image of God and is not worshipped itself; it is the focal point that unites believers in one direction.
183.spot: A plain, boxy building draped in black cloth with a band of gold calligraphy near the top, surrounded by a huge open courtyard packed with white-robed pilgrims circling it.
183.remember: Kaaba = ‘cube.’ Muhammad cleared out the idols after taking Mecca in 630 C.E.; the College Board’s 631–632 matches the first Muslim pilgrimages, including his Farewell Pilgrimage in 632.
compare: No. 192 (§9.1), Great Stupa at Sanchi: Both are sacred centers that worshippers walk around, clockwise at Sanchi and counterclockwise at the Kaaba.
No. 185 (§8.5), Dome of the Rock: Both are early, central Islamic holy sites tied to Abraham, but the Dome of the Rock is lavishly decorated while the Kaaba is a plain cloth-draped cube.
No. 186 (§8.6), Great Mosque: The Isfahan mosque’s mihrab and prayer hall are oriented toward the Kaaba, showing how this one building organizes mosque design worldwide.
183.vocab: qibla, hajj, tawaf, kiswa, mihrab, aniconism, circumambulation, calligraphy.

form: A nearly cubic building of local granite blocks, roughly 13 m (about 43 feet) tall with sides of about 11 by 13 m. The current structure largely dates from an Ottoman rebuilding of 1629 after a flood.
It is covered by the kiswa (a black silk cloth that drapes the whole building), woven and embroidered in a dedicated workshop in Mecca and replaced every year.
A wide embroidered band about two-thirds of the way up carries Qur’anic calligraphy (artistic handwriting) in gold- and silver-wrapped thread, and an embroidered curtain covers the raised door.
The Black Stone, a dark stone fragment framed in silver, is set into the eastern corner at about chest height. Pilgrims try to touch or kiss it, or gesture toward it.
Inside is a simple room with pillars and hanging lamps. The power of the building comes from its plainness, its position and its ritual, not from carving or images.
function: It sets the qibla (the direction Muslims face in prayer). Every mosque has a mihrab (a niche in the wall facing the qibla), so mosques worldwide are oriented toward this one building.
During the hajj (the pilgrimage to Mecca every able Muslim should make once), pilgrims perform tawaf (walking around the Kaaba seven times counterclockwise).
It is called the House of God in the sense of a sacred place dedicated to God, not a place where God physically lives.
content: Muslim tradition holds that Abraham (Ibrahim) and his son Ishmael (Ismail) built it as a house of worship of the one God, linking Islam to the earlier Abrahamic faiths.
The empty, imageless form expresses aniconism (avoiding pictures of God or holy figures in religious settings). The focus is the one God, who cannot be pictured.
The Qur’anic verses on the kiswa, including declarations of faith, make the cloth itself a carrier of sacred text.
Pilgrims circling it in white garments, rich and poor dressed alike, express the equality and unity of believers before God.
context: In pre-Islamic times the Kaaba held many idols of tribal gods. When Muhammad and his followers took Mecca in 630 C.E., he removed and destroyed the idols and rededicated the building to the one God.
Muhammad’s Farewell Pilgrimage in 632 C.E., shortly before his death, set the pattern for the hajj rituals that continue today.
The building has been damaged and rebuilt several times, including in 683 and 692 C.E. during civil wars, and in 1629 after floodwaters undermined it.

For centuries Egypt produced and sent the kiswa in a grand procession; since the twentieth century it has been made in Mecca, using about 670 kg of black silk plus gold and silver thread. On the exam.
If asked about function → it is the qibla, the direction of Muslim prayer, and the center of the hajj.
If asked about ritual → pilgrims perform tawaf, circling it seven times counterclockwise.
Trap: Muslims do not worship the Kaaba or the Black Stone. It is a focal point for worship of God.
If asked about the date → a pre-Islamic shrine, rededicated by Muhammad after the conquest of Mecca (630 C.E.; the College Board lists 631–632).
If asked about materials → granite masonry covered by the black silk kiswa embroidered with gold and silver-wrapped thread, replaced every year.
Comparison hook: circumambulation also happens at Buddhist stupas, but Buddhists walk clockwise and Muslims counterclockwise.

184.title: Jowo Rinpoche, enshrined in the Jokhang Temple
184.date: Believed brought to Tibet in 641 C.E.
184.medium: Gilt metals with semiprecious stones, pearls, and paint; various offerings
184.plain: The Jowo Rinpoche is the most sacred statue in Tibet, a gilded image of the Buddha as a young prince housed in the Jokhang Temple in Lhasa. Tradition says it was brought from China in 641 C.E. by Princess Wencheng when she married the Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo. What makes it unusual is that you can barely see the statue itself: centuries of gifts of gold, jewels, crowns and silk cover it, so the object keeps growing as people honor it.
184.spot: A seated golden Buddha wearing an enormous jeweled crown and heavy layers of necklaces, pearls and ornaments, framed by an ornate gilded shrine with butter lamps and silk scarves in front.
184.remember: Jowo = ‘Lord,’ Rinpoche = ‘precious.’ Picture a wedding gift (641 C.E.) that guests have been decorating for almost 1,400 years.
compare: No. 58 (§4.11), Church of Sainte-Foy: Both are pilgrimage images covered over centuries in donated gold and jewels, so the accumulated gifts show how much the holy object is valued.
No. 54 (§4.7), Virgin: Both are devotional images believed to have miraculous or holy origins, which makes them sacred presences rather than just pictures.
No. 197 (§9.6), Todai-ji: Both are Buddha images tied to royal patronage that marked the establishment of Buddhism in a new country.
184.vocab: mudra, bhumisparsha mudra, shrine, merit, pilgrimage, offering, gilding.

form: The core is a gilded metal statue of the Buddha Shakyamuni, said to be about 1.5 m (5 feet) tall, seated cross-legged on a lotus throne.
His right hand reaches down in the bhumisparsha mudra (earth-touching gesture, calling the earth to witness his enlightenment) and his left rests in his lap holding a begging bowl.
Unlike most Buddha images, he wears a crown and jewelry, showing him as a prince. Tradition says the image shows him at about age 12, before he gave up royal life.
Over the centuries donors added a large jeweled crown, necklaces of turquoise, coral and pearls, and silk robes. Pilgrims also pay to have fresh gold painted on the face.
The surrounding shrine (a sacred setting built to house a holy object) includes a gilded canopy, guardian figures and rows of flickering butter lamps that blacken the space with soot.
function: It is the focus of Tibetan pilgrimage. Many pilgrims travel hundreds of miles, some by repeated full-body prostrations, to see it once.
Devotees offer butter for lamps, money, and white silk scarves called khata (ceremonial scarves given as a sign of respect).
Pilgrims walk clockwise around the Jokhang on three circuits: an inner path inside the temple, the Barkhor around it, and the Lingkor around old Lhasa.
