Giving to the statue earns merit (spiritual credit from good deeds that improves future rebirths), so each gift adds to both the object and the giver’s spiritual standing.
content: Legend says the statue was made during the Buddha’s lifetime by the divine craftsman Vishvakarman and blessed by the Buddha himself, so it is treated almost as the Buddha in person.
The princely costume and crown point to the Buddha’s royal birth and to the idea of the Buddha as a spiritual king.
The pile of offerings is itself the meaning: the statue records generations of devotion. Its appearance is never finished.
context: Songtsen Gampo (died c. 650) of the Yarlung Dynasty united Tibet into an empire and married two foreign princesses: Bhrikuti from Nepal and Wencheng from Tang China. Each reportedly brought a Buddha image.

Wencheng’s Jowo was first kept in the Ramoche Temple and later moved to the Jokhang, which was founded in the 640s C.E. for Bhrikuti’s image. Accounts differ on exactly when and why the images were swapped.
In 1409 the reformer Tsongkhapa offered a crown to the Jowo at the first Great Prayer Festival, starting a tradition of adorning the image.

During the Cultural Revolution (1966–1976) Red Guards ransacked the Jokhang and reportedly used parts of it as barracks and a pig sty. Reports differ on how much the Jowo was damaged; it has since been restored.
The Jokhang became part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000. A fire struck the temple in 2018, and the Chinese government said the Jowo was unharmed. On the exam.
If asked about form and function together → an image whose appearance is constantly changed by worshippers’ gifts, so devotion is part of the artwork.
If asked who brought it → tradition says Princess Wencheng of Tang China, as part of her marriage to King Songtsen Gampo in 641 C.E.
If asked about iconography → Shakyamuni as a crowned young prince in the earth-touching gesture.
Trap: the original statue is almost invisible under offerings, so describe both the core image and the additions.
If asked about pilgrimage practice → prostrations, butter-lamp offerings, khata scarves and clockwise circuits around the Jokhang.

185.title: Dome of the Rock
185.medium: Stone masonry and wooden roof decorated with glazed ceramic tile, mosaics, and
185.plain: The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem is the oldest surviving major Islamic building, an eight-sided shrine with a gleaming golden dome built over a large rock. The rock is sacred to Jews, Christians and Muslims, and Muslims associate it with Muhammad’s Night Journey to heaven. It was built by the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik in 691–692 C.E., partly as a religious shrine and partly as a very visible statement that Islam had arrived in a city full of churches.
185.spot: An octagonal building covered in blue and white tile, topped by a tall drum and a shining gold dome, standing on a broad raised platform above Jerusalem’s old city.
185.remember: Dome of the Rock, Abd al-Malik, 691: ‘Abd’s eight-sided ROCK concert.’ Remember that it is a shrine, not a mosque.
compare: No. 51 (§4.4), San Vitale: Both are octagonal, centrally planned domed buildings with mosaic interiors, showing how Islamic builders adapted Byzantine forms.
No. 183 (§8.3), The Kaaba: Both are early Islamic holy sites tied to Abraham where pilgrims circle a sacred center, but the Kaaba is a plain cube and this is a richly decorated shrine.
No. 209 (§9.18), Taj Mahal: Both use a commanding dome on a raised platform to make an Islamic monument visible from afar, about a thousand years apart.
185.vocab: central plan, ambulatory, drum, mosaic, calligraphy, shrine, circumambulation.

form: It is a central plan building (arranged around a central point rather than along a long axis): an octagon about 20 m per side, with a dome about 20 m across raised on a high drum (a cylindrical wall supporting a dome).
Inside, two rings of supports (an octagonal arcade and an inner circle of piers and columns) create two ambulatories (walkways that circle a central space).
The interior is covered in marble and gold-ground glass mosaics (pictures made of small pieces of colored glass or stone) showing vines, trees, vases, jewels and crowns, but no people or animals.
A long Arabic inscription in angular script, about 240 m in total, runs around the arcade in gold mosaic, quoting the Qur’an.

The outside originally had mosaics too. Ottoman Sultan Suleiman the Magnificent replaced them with glazed ceramic tile in the mid-1500s, and those tiles were replaced again in twentieth-century restorations.
The dome is a double wooden shell. In the 1960s it was covered with gold-colored anodized aluminum; in 1993 it was regilded with real gold leaf, funded by King Hussein of Jordan.
function: It is a shrine over the rock, often called the Foundation Stone, where pilgrims circle and pray. It is not a congregational mosque; the al-Aqsa Mosque stands nearby on the same platform.
It marked Islam’s claim to Jerusalem: built on the Temple Mount, called the Haram al-Sharif (Noble Sanctuary) in Arabic, where the Jewish Temple once stood.
Under Crusader rule (1099–1187) it became a church called the Templum Domini; Saladin restored it as an Islamic shrine in 1187.
content: In Jewish tradition the rock is where Abraham prepared to sacrifice his son and where the Temple’s Holy of Holies stood. In Islamic tradition it is linked to Muhammad’s Night Journey and Ascension to heaven.
The Night Journey link is now central, but the original inscriptions do not mention it, so scholars debate what Abd al-Malik primarily intended.
The mosaic crowns and jewels look like Byzantine and Persian royal regalia, often read as trophies of the empires Islam had defeated.
The inscriptions stress God’s oneness and describe Jesus as a prophet and messenger of God, not God’s son, an argument aimed at Jerusalem’s Christian majority.
context: Abd al-Malik ruled the Umayyad caliphate (the first hereditary Islamic dynasty, based in Damascus) and built the shrine in 691–692 C.E., the date given in its inscription.
Its form borrows from Byzantine Christian buildings, especially the round Church of the Holy Sepulchre nearby, whose dome is almost the same size. Byzantine-trained craftsmen likely did the mosaics.
Later, the Abbasid caliph al-Mamun replaced Abd al-Malik’s name in the inscription with his own but forgot to change the date, which gives the trick away.
Jerusalem was and remains sacred to three faiths, and the site is still one of the most politically contested places in the world. On the exam.
If asked about plan → octagonal central plan with a dome and two ambulatories for circling the rock.
Trap: it is a shrine, not a mosque, and has no prayer-hall orientation toward Mecca as its main idea.
If asked about patron and dynasty → Abd al-Malik, Umayyad caliph, 691–692 C.E.
If asked about traditions → it adapts the Byzantine central-plan martyrium and mosaic techniques for Islamic purposes.
If asked about decoration → vegetal mosaics, jewels and crowns, plus Qur’anic inscriptions, with no human figures.
If asked about later changes → Ottoman tiles (1500s, later replaced), Crusader use as a church, and a dome regilded with gold in 1993.

186.title: Great Mosque (Masjid-e Jameh)
186.artist: Islamic/Persian (Seljuk, Il-Khanid, Timurid, Safavid); Isfahan, Iran
186.date: c. 700 C.E.; additions and restorations 14th, 18th, 20th centuries
186.medium: Stone, brick, wood, plaster, and glazed ceramic tile
186.plain: The Great Mosque of Isfahan in Iran is the city’s main Friday mosque, built and rebuilt on the same site for over a thousand years. Almost every dynasty that ruled Iran added something, so the building works like a timeline of Persian Islamic architecture. Its most important feature is the four-iwan plan, a courtyard with a huge vaulted hall in the middle of each side, which became the standard design for mosques across Iran and Central Asia.
186.spot: A large rectangular courtyard with a tall, tiled arched hall opening onto it at the center of each side, the arches filled with honeycomb-like vaulting and covered in blue, turquoise and white tile.
186.remember: Isfahan has FOUR iwans and spans FOUR dynasties (Seljuk, Il-Khanid, Timurid, Safavid). ‘Isfahan is half the world,’ and this mosque is half of Iranian history.
compare: No. 56 (§4.9), Great Mosque: Córdoba keeps the early hypostyle plan of endless columns, while Isfahan reorganizes the mosque around a courtyard with four iwans.
No. 84 (§4.37), Mosque of Selim II : Sinan’s mosque puts a single vast dome at the center, an Ottoman solution very different from Isfahan’s courtyard-and-iwan layout.
No. 65 (§4.18), Alhambra: Both use muqarnas vaulting and dense ornament to make heavy architecture seem to dissolve into light and pattern.
186.vocab: iwan, four-iwan plan, muqarnas, hypostyle hall, mihrab, qibla, congregational mosque, glazed tile.

form: Its core is the four-iwan plan: a courtyard roughly 60 by 70 m, with an iwan (a tall vaulted hall closed on three sides and open on the fourth) at the middle of each side.
Between the iwans run hypostyle (many-columned) prayer halls roofed with hundreds of small brick domes, each built in a different pattern.
The iwans are filled with muqarnas (honeycomb-like vaulting made of many small stacked niches), which makes the transition from wall to vault look like it is dissolving.

Two Seljuk brick domes from the 1080s survive: the large south dome over the area in front of the mihrab (the niche showing the direction of Mecca), and the smaller north dome, admired for its precise geometry.
Much of the surface is covered in glazed tile, from mosaic tile to painted square tiles, mostly added from the 1400s through the Safavid period.
The Il-Khanid stucco mihrab of Oljeitu (1310) is carved with dense layers of plants and Qur’anic calligraphy.
function: A congregational mosque (Friday mosque, big enough for the whole community’s main weekly prayer). The south iwan and dome point the faithful toward the qibla, the direction of Mecca.
The courtyard served as an open-air extension of the prayer space and as a place for washing before prayer.
Rulers sponsored additions to show piety and power, so the mosque also functioned as a public billboard for whichever dynasty was in charge.
content: There is no figural imagery. Meaning is carried by geometry, plant-based ornament and calligraphy (artistic writing), especially Qur’anic verses and dedication inscriptions naming patrons.
The muqarnas and domes are often read as images of the heavens, turning heavy brick into something that seems weightless and infinite.
Inscriptions record who built what, so the walls double as a historical document of patrons over centuries.
context: A mosque stood here by the eighth century under the Abbasids (the College Board rounds this to c. 700 C.E.); it was a hypostyle mosque, like early Arab mosques.

Under the Seljuks (Turkish rulers of Iran, eleventh and twelfth centuries), the vizier Nizam al-Mulk built the south dome around 1086–1087 and his rival Taj al-Mulk built the north dome around 1088–1089.
After a fire in the early 1120s, the four-iwan courtyard was created, setting a model copied for centuries in Iran and Central Asia.
Later Il-Khanid (Mongol), Timurid, Turkmen and Safavid rulers added the Oljeitu mihrab, prayer halls and tilework, and restorations continued in the eighteenth and twentieth centuries. On the exam.
If asked about plan → four-iwan courtyard plan, introduced here in the Seljuk period and widely copied.
If asked about change over time → one site, many dynasties: Seljuk domes, Il-Khanid mihrab, Timurid and Safavid tile, modern restorations.
If asked about muqarnas → honeycomb vaulting that makes structure look weightless and suggests the heavens.
Trap: Isfahan’s mosque is in Iran (Persian), not the Ottoman or Spanish Islamic world, and its plan is iwan-based, not purely hypostyle like Córdoba.
If asked about materials → brick, stone, wood, carved stucco and glazed ceramic tile.
If asked about function → congregational Friday mosque oriented toward Mecca, with the main dome before the mihrab.

187.title: Folio from a Qur’an
187.artist: Abbasid; Arab, North Africa, or Near East
187.date: c. eighth to ninth century C.E.
187.medium: Ink, color, and gold on parchment
187.plain: This is a single page from an early handwritten Qur’an, the holy book of Islam, made in the Abbasid period (roughly the 700s–800s C.E.). It is written on parchment in Kufic, a bold, angular style of Arabic script, with only a few lines per page and gold ornaments marking the ends of verses. It matters because in Islam the Qur’an is God’s exact words, so writing it beautifully became the most respected art form of all.
187.spot: A wide, landscape-format page with just three to five lines of thick, dark, blocky Arabic letters stretched by long horizontal strokes, sprinkled with small red dots and a few small gold rosettes or clusters.
187.remember: Kufic looks like it was written with a ruler: ‘Kufic = cubic.’ Wide page, few lines, Abbasid, 700s–800s.
compare: No. 55 (§4.8), Lindisfarne Gospels: Both are lavish sacred books in which ornament and beautiful writing honor scripture, but the Lindisfarne Gospels also include figural images of the evangelists.
No. 229 (§11.6), A Book from the Sky: Xu Bing’s invented, unreadable characters play on the authority of sacred writing, the opposite of a text valued because every word is holy.
No. 185 (§8.5), Dome of the Rock: Both use Qur’anic calligraphy as a main decorative and religious element, one on a manuscript page and one in mosaic on a building.
187.vocab: calligraphy, kufic, parchment, illuminated manuscript, folio, aniconism, codex.

form: The page is parchment (specially prepared animal skin, usually sheep or goat), in a horizontal, landscape format that is wider than it is tall.
The script is Kufic (an early angular Arabic script with strong horizontals and squared-off letters), traditionally named after the city of Kufa in Iraq.

There are only about three to five lines per page, with letters stretched far apart. Legibility for a beginner was not the point; the text was usually memorized and the page was meant to be beautiful and stately.
Red dots show the vowels, which early Arabic writing did not mark; small strokes help tell apart letters with the same shape.

Gold illumination (decoration in gold and color added to a manuscript) marks verse endings with small rosettes or clusters, and chapter headings often have a gold band ending in a palmleaf ornament in the margin.
function: It came from a complete, multi-volume Qur’an used for recitation, study and display, perhaps donated to a mosque.
Because most Muslims learned the Qur’an by heart, a page like this worked as an aid to recitation and an object of honor, not a casual reading text.
A copy this lavish was also a pious gift: commissioning it earned spiritual merit and showed the patron’s wealth.
Today such Qur’ans survive mostly as scattered single pages, because many were broken up and sold; the College Board’s page is in the Morgan Library in New York.
content: The content is the Qur’an itself, believed by Muslims to be God’s word revealed to Muhammad in Arabic. Writing it out was an act of devotion.
Islamic religious art practices aniconism (avoiding images of living beings in sacred settings), so beautiful writing and abstract ornament carry the sacred meaning instead of pictures.
The slow, stately rhythm of the stretched letters can be read as a visual echo of the slow, careful rhythm of Qur’anic recitation.
The horizontal format may have helped set Qur’ans apart from the vertical books of Jews and Christians, though scholars debate this.
context: The Abbasid caliphate (750–1258 C.E.) moved the capital to Baghdad in 762 and ruled an empire from North Africa to Central Asia, so a page like this could have been made in many places.
That is why the attribution is so broad: ‘Arab, North Africa, or Near East.’ Early Kufic Qur’ans are rarely signed or dated.
Parchment was expensive: a large multi-volume Qur’an could require the skins of hundreds of animals. Paper, introduced from China, gradually replaced parchment from the tenth century on.
Kufic was gradually replaced for Qur’ans by rounder, more readable scripts such as naskh, but it remained in use as a decorative script on buildings and objects. On the exam.
If asked why calligraphy matters in Islam → the Qur’an is God’s literal word, so writing it beautifully was the highest art form.
If asked about script → Kufic: angular, horizontal, few lines per page.
If asked about materials → ink, color and gold on parchment (not paper).
If asked about format → horizontal (landscape) pages, unlike most Christian and Jewish codices.
Trap: the red dots are vowel markers, and the gold ornaments mark verse divisions; they are not decoration only.
If asked about aniconism → no figures; meaning is carried by the text and abstract ornament.

188.title: Basin (Baptistère de St. Louis)
188.medium: Brass inlaid with gold and silver
188.plain: This is a large brass bowl from the Mamluk sultanate of Egypt and Syria, covered with figures of courtiers, hunters and animals made of inlaid silver and gold. Its maker, Muhammad ibn al-Zain, signed it six times, which was unusually proud for the period. The bowl later traveled to France, became a French royal treasure, and was used to baptize royal babies, so a luxury object from an Islamic court ended up in Christian ritual.
188.spot: A wide, deep metal basin with a dark background and bright silver figures in horizontal bands and roundels: men in turbans and robes carrying weapons and objects, riders on horseback, and running animals.
188.remember: Saint Louis died in 1270, decades before this basin was made, so the name is a misnomer: Saint Louis never touched it, but Louis XIII was baptized with it.
compare: No. 57 (§4.10), Pyxis of al-Mughira: Both are luxury Islamic court objects covered in figural scenes of princely life, one in ivory and one in inlaid brass.
No. 189 (§8.9), Bahram Gur Fights the Karg: Both show the courtly, hunting world of fourteenth-century Islamic elites, with visual links to the Mongols.
No. 58 (§4.11), Church of Sainte-Foy: Both are objects whose meaning was transformed by later owners and reused in Christian religious practice.
188.vocab: inlay, brass, roundel, frieze, font, secular, provenance.

form: A hammered brass (copper and zinc alloy) basin about 50 cm (20 inches) across and 22 cm (about 9 inches) tall.

It uses inlay (cutting grooves into a surface and hammering in a different material): thin silver and gold sheet and wire were set into the brass, and the background was filled with a black paste to make the figures stand out.

The outside has a wide band of standing figures, probably Mamluk oﬀicials, carrying the objects of their oﬀices (weapons, a cup, a bow), interrupted by four roundels (circular frames) showing horsemen.
The inside has hunting and battle scenes, and the bottom of the interior shows fish, eels and other water creatures, which would appear to swim when the basin was filled.
Bands of running animals (deer, hares, dogs, mythical beasts) border the main scenes.
The maker’s name appears six times, including one prominent signature, while there is no inscription naming an owner, which is very unusual for Mamluk metalwork.
function: Its original use is not certain. It was probably made for a Mamluk court and used for washing hands at banquets or ceremonies.
By the 1600s it was in the French royal collection, stored at the Sainte-Chapelle of Vincennes, and was used as a baptismal font.
Louis XIII was baptized with it in 1606, and in 1856 it was used again for the baptism of Napoleon III’s son, the Prince Imperial.
Today it is in the Louvre in Paris.
content: The scenes celebrate courtly life: oﬀicials, hunts and warriors that reflect the military, horseriding elite of the Mamluks (former slave-soldiers who took power and ruled Egypt and Syria from 1250 to 1517).
Some figures wear Mongol-style hats and dress, so the basin may refer to Mamluk wars and contacts with the Mongols.
Figural imagery is normal in secular Islamic art; the avoidance of figures applies mainly to religious settings like mosques and Qur’ans.
French owners later added French coats of arms over original blank shields, literally rebranding the object as French royal property.
context: The College Board dates it c. 1320–1340, though some scholars place it earlier, around 1290– 1310. Most agree it was made in Egypt or Syria.
How it reached France is unknown; luxury goods traveled through trade, diplomacy and crusades.
The name ‘Baptistère de Saint Louis’ was attached by about the eighteenth century, linking it to the famous Crusader king Louis IX, who died in 1270, before it was made.
Its story shows how an object’s meaning changes as it moves: a Mamluk courtly basin became a sacred Christian vessel and a symbol of the French monarchy. On the exam.
If asked about technique → brass with inlaid silver and gold, with the background filled with dark paste to make the figures pop.
If asked about artist → Muhammad ibn al-Zain, who signed it six times, unusually assertive for an artisan.
Trap: the name is a misnomer; Saint Louis (Louis IX) died before it was made.
If asked about function over time → probably a courtly washing basin in the Mamluk world, then a French royal baptismal font.
Trap: Islamic art does include human figures; aniconism applies mainly in religious contexts.
If asked about cross-cultural exchange → an Islamic luxury object adopted for Christian royal ritual in France.

189.title: Bahram Gur Fights the Karg
189.medium: Ink and opaque watercolor, gold, and silver on paper
189.plain: This painting is a page from a huge illustrated copy of the Shahnama (Book of Kings), Iran’s national epic poem, made in the 1330s for the Il-Khanids, the Mongol dynasty then ruling Iran. It shows the legendary hunter-king Bahram Gur killing a fierce horned monster called the karg. By paying for grand illustrated copies of Persia’s own heroic stories, the Mongol rulers presented themselves as rightful heirs to the old Persian kings.
189.spot: A rider on a horse attacking a large dark horned beast, set in a landscape of gnarled trees and rocks, with blocks of Persian text above and below and the action pushing past the picture’s frame.
189.remember: Bahram Gur = ‘Bahram GRRR’ versus the Karg. Mongols (Il-Khanids), 1330s, reading Persia’s Book of Kings to look Persian.
compare: No. 190 (§8.10), The Court of Gayumars: Both illustrate the Shahnama for a royal court, but the Safavid page is calmer, more densely detailed and more jewel-like than this energetic Il-Khanid scene.
No. 203 (§9.12), Night Attack on the Sanjô Palace: Both are dramatic narrative paintings of violent action on paper made in the 1200s–1300s, one Japanese handscroll and one Persian manuscript.
No. 201 (§9.10), Travelers among Mountains and Streams: The gnarled trees and layered rocks in this page come from the Chinese landscape tradition seen in Fan Kuan’s painting.
189.vocab: manuscript, folio, opaque watercolor, illuminated manuscript, epic, legitimacy, narrative.

form: Ink, opaque watercolor, gold and silver on paper. The silver has darkened over time, which is why some areas look grayish or black.
The page combines blocks of text written in Persian in columns with a large painted scene, so text and picture share the page.
Bahram Gur, on horseback, attacks the karg (a monstrous horned beast, sometimes described as a horned wolf or rhinoceros-like animal); the monster is shown wounded and split, with blood.
The landscape shows Chinese influence: twisted, knotted tree trunks, layered rocks and wispy clouds drawn with lively, calligraphic brush lines.
Figures and the beast press against or extend beyond the frame, making the scene feel energetic and crowded.
function: A page from a lavish, multi-volume court manuscript (a handwritten book), meant to be read, admired and shown off by the Il-Khanid elite.
Small books like this were held in the hands and enjoyed up close by a few people, not displayed on walls.
The epic’s stories of just and heroic kings modeled ideal behavior for rulers and their courts.
Today the pages are scattered in museums around the world after the manuscript was broken up; this folio is in the Harvard Art Museums.
content: The Shahnama (Book of Kings) is an epic of about 50,000 couplets completed by the poet Ferdowsi around 1010 C.E., telling Iran’s history from mythical first kings to the Arab conquest.
Bahram Gur is based on a real Sasanian king, Bahram V (ruled about 420–438 C.E.), famous in legend as a great hunter and lover.
Killing the monster shows the king’s courage and his duty to protect his land from chaos.
For the Mongols, illustrating these tales was legitimization (using art to make a ruler’s claim to power look natural and rightful).
context: The Il-Khanids were a branch of Genghis Khan’s Mongol empire that ruled Iran from about 1256 to 1335. They converted to Islam and adopted Persian culture.
Because they were related to the Mongol rulers of China, Chinese silks, paintings and porcelain flowed into Iran, explaining the Chinese landscape motifs.
The manuscript was probably made in Tabriz in the 1330s, perhaps for the vizier Ghiyath al-Din during the reign of Abu Said; the exact patron is uncertain.
In the early twentieth century the art dealer Georges Demotte broke the manuscript apart and sold pages separately. Fewer than 60 paintings survive from what may once have been around 200.
It is considered one of the earliest and most ambitious illustrated Shahnamas and set the stage for later Persian painting. On the exam.
If asked about source text → the Shahnama by Ferdowsi (completed c. 1010), Iran’s national epic.
If asked about patron/dynasty → the Mongol Il-Khanids, who used Persian epic to claim legitimacy as Persian kings.
If asked about style → Persian painting with clear Chinese influence in trees, rocks and clouds, due to Mongol links with China.
If asked about materials → ink, opaque watercolor, gold and silver on paper.
Trap: the Great Il-Khanid Shahnama is also called the Great Mongol or Demotte Shahnama; do not confuse it with Shah Tahmasp’s Safavid Shahnama (No. 190).
If asked about later history → the manuscript was dismembered by a dealer and its pages scattered.

190.title: The Court of Gayumars
190.artist: Sultan Muhammad, from Shah Tahmasp’s Shahnama
190.medium: Ink, opaque watercolor, and gold on paper
190.plain: This page comes from the most lavish illustrated copy of Iran’s national epic ever made, produced for the Safavid prince Tahmasp in the 1520s. It shows Gayumars, the legendary first king of the world, holding court on a mountaintop with his people dressed in leopard skins, back when humans lived simply in nature. The painter, Sultan Muhammad, packed it with so much tiny, shimmering detail that a historian of the time said it outshone every other painting.
190.spot: A tall, crowded page of swirling, brightly colored rocks in pinks, greens, blues and lavenders, filled with dozens of small figures in leopard-skin clothes and animals, with a king seated on a high rocky throne near the top center. Very little text.
190.remember: Gayumars = ‘Guy who was first.’ Sultan Muhammad for Shah Tahmasp, Safavid, 1520s: sixteenth century, so it is much more jewel-like than the rough 1330s Bahram Gur.
compare: No. 189 (§8.9), Bahram Gur Fights the Karg: Both illustrate the Shahnama to support royal legitimacy, showing how Persian manuscript painting changed from the bold Il-Khanid style to refined Safavid detail.

No. 208 (§9.17), Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings: Mughal painting grew directly out of Persian court traditions like this one, and both use luxurious detail and symbolism to flatter a ruler.
No. 191 (§8.11), The Ardabil Carpet: Both are Safavid court luxury works of the same era that use dense, intricate pattern and fine materials to display royal taste.
190.vocab: manuscript, folio, opaque watercolor, atelier, court art, illuminated manuscript, patron.

form: Ink, opaque watercolor (paint thick enough to hide what is underneath, made from ground minerals) and gold on paper, painted with brushes so fine some were said to have a single hair.
The page is about 47 by 32 cm (roughly 18.5 by 12.5 inches), and the painting fills nearly all of it; the text is reduced to a small panel.
The composition rises in tiers of fantastic, multicolored rocks up to Gayumars, enthroned at the top center against a gold sky.
Hundreds of details reward close looking: faces and animal heads hidden in the rocks, peaceful animals mixing with people, and individualized courtiers.
The style blends the bold, fantastic Turkmen painting of Tabriz with the delicate, balanced painting of Herat associated with the master Bihzad.
function: A page from the Shahnama of Shah Tahmasp, a manuscript (handwritten book) of 258 paintings meant to be studied up close in the hand by the ruler and his inner circle.
Making it trained and showcased the royal atelier (a workshop of artists working together under a master), which included the leading calligraphers and painters of Iran.
The manuscript also served as a diplomatic gift: in 1568 Tahmasp sent it to the Ottoman sultan Selim II on his accession.
Today this page belongs to the Aga Khan Museum in Toronto.
content: Gayumars, from Ferdowsi’s Shahnama, is the first king, who lived in the mountains in an age before cooking, clothing or cities; he and his court wear leopard skins.
His son Siyamak and grandson Hushang appear near him. The story foreshadows tragedy, since Siyamak will soon be killed by a demon.
Animals living peacefully with people suggest a golden age of harmony between the king, his subjects and nature.
A painting about the first ideal king, made for a young future shah, works as a lesson in good kingship and a claim that the Safavids inherited Iran’s ancient royal line.
context: The Safavids ruled Iran from 1501 to 1736 and made Shi’a Islam the state religion. The manuscript was probably begun under Shah Ismail I for his young son Tahmasp, around 1522.
Sultan Muhammad was the leading painter of the Tabriz court workshop. The historian Dust Muhammad wrote in 1544 that even the boldest artists hung their heads in shame before this page.
As an adult, Shah Tahmasp lost interest in painting, partly for religious reasons, and gave the manuscript away.
In the twentieth century it was owned by the Rothschild family and then by the American collector Arthur Houghton, who broke it up and sold or donated individual pages.
In 1994 Iran traded a Willem de Kooning painting (Woman III) to get back over 100 of the pages. The rest are scattered among museums and private collections. On the exam.
If asked about artist → Sultan Muhammad, the head painter at the Safavid court.
If asked about patron → made for Shah Tahmasp (probably commissioned under his father Ismail I), early Safavid period, c. 1522–1525.
If asked about subject → Gayumars, the mythical first king, in a golden age before civilization, wearing leopard skins.
If asked about style → dense, jewel-like color, hidden faces in rocks, tiny detail, and a fusion of Tabriz and Herat traditions.
Trap: do not confuse this with the Il-Khanid Bahram Gur page (No. 189); this is Safavid, about 190 years later.

191.title: The Ardabil Carpet
191.plain: The Ardabil Carpet is one of the oldest dated carpets in the world and among the largest and finest, woven in Safavid Iran in 1539–1540 for the shrine of the dynasty’s ancestor at Ardabil. It is about 34.5 by 17.5 feet, with roughly 26 million hand-tied knots, and its design centers on a golden starburst medallion on a deep blue field. A woven inscription even names its maker, Maqsud of Kashan, which is rare for a carpet.
191.spot: A huge dark-blue carpet with a big yellow-gold, many-pointed central medallion surrounded by small pointed ovals, two hanging lamps of different sizes at either end, quarter medallions in the corners, and dense swirling vines and flowers.
191.remember: Ardabil: two lamps, two carpets, one Maqsud. Woven in the Islamic year 946, which is 1539–1540 C.E.
compare: No. 186 (§8.6), Great Mosque: The carpet’s medallion is often read as a dome seen from below, linking it to the tiled domes and patterns of Persian mosques.
No. 55 (§4.8), Lindisfarne Gospels: The Lindisfarne carpet page imitates a textile on parchment, while the Ardabil Carpet is an actual textile with an equally dense, devotional pattern.
No. 162 (§6.10), All-T’oqapu tunic: Both are luxury textiles made in elite court workshops that use pattern and fine materials to express power and status.
191.vocab: pile carpet, knot, warp, weft, medallion, shrine, court art. 9 South, East, and Southeast Asia Content area 8 · 300 B.C.E.–1980 C.E. · works 192–212 · about 8% of the multiple-choice section. India, China, Korea, Japan and Southeast Asia: Buddhist and Hindu temples and sculpture, Chinese scrolls and porcelain, Japanese prints and screens, Mughal paintings. Learn the basics of Buddhism and Hinduism (they explain most of the symbols), how art moved along trade and pilgrimage routes, and how rulers used art to look legitimate.

form: It is a pile carpet (a rug made by tying short tufts of yarn onto a base so they stand up as a soft surface): wool pile knotted onto a silk foundation of warps and wefts.
The silk base allowed very fine knotting, about 340 knots per square inch, which let the weavers draw curving, detailed lines almost like a painting.
The center has a yellow sunburst medallion (a large decorative central motif) ringed by 16 pointed oval pendants, against a deep blue field covered in scrolling vines and blossoms.
Two mosque lamps hang from the medallion toward the ends, and they are deliberately different in size.
Each corner holds a quarter of the central medallion, as if the design continued beyond the edges, and wide borders frame the whole.
At one end, a small panel holds a woven inscription giving a line of poetry, the maker’s name and the date.
function: It is one of a pair said to have been made for the shrine (a holy place built around a tomb) of Shaykh Safi al-Din at Ardabil, the Sufi mystic from whom the Safavid dynasty traced its descent.
Paying for such costly gifts honored the dynasty’s spiritual ancestor and showed Safavid wealth and piety.
Since 1893 it has been in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, displayed flat and under low light to protect it.
content: The inscription begins with a couplet by the poet Hafez: ‘I have no refuge in the world other than thy threshold; my head has no protection other than this porch-way.’

It ends: ‘the work of the slave of the threshold, Maqsud of Kashan, 946.’ The ‘threshold’ may refer to the shrine or the royal court, and scholars debate whether Maqsud was the weaver, designer or supervising oﬀicial.
The medallion and lamps are often read as the view up into a dome, with lamps hanging inside, bringing sacred architecture down onto the floor.
context: Under the Safavids, especially Shah Tahmasp, carpet weaving became a court art: designs were drawn by court artists and woven in large workshops.
The unequal lamps are often explained by perspective: seen from one end of the carpet, the nearer, smaller lamp and the farther, larger lamp appear about the same size. Not all scholars accept this.
In the 1880s a British firm bought the two damaged carpets, reportedly from the shrine after an earthquake, and used parts of one to repair the other.

The museum bought the repaired one in 1893 after a public appeal supported by designer William Morris. The smaller, borderless twin later went to J. Paul Getty, who gave it to the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. On the exam.
If asked about materials → wool pile knotted on a silk foundation, with about 26 million knots.
If asked about artist → Maqsud of Kashan, named in a woven inscription, unusual for a carpet.
If asked about date → 946 AH, which is 1539–1540 C.E., in the reign of Shah Tahmasp.
If asked about function → made for the Safavid dynastic shrine at Ardabil.
If asked about design → central sunburst medallion with 16 pendants, two unequal mosque lamps, and quarter medallions in the corners.
Trap: the two lamps are different sizes on purpose, probably to correct for perspective from the viewer’s end.

192.title: Great Stupa at Sanchi
192.artist: Buddhist/Maurya, late Sunga Dynasty; Madhya Pradesh, India
192.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
192.plain: The Great Stupa at Sanchi in central India is one of the oldest surviving Buddhist monuments: a solid, dome-shaped mound built to hold sacred relics, surrounded by a stone fence with four elaborately carved gateways. You do not go inside; you walk around it. Its gateway carvings tell stories about the Buddha without ever showing him as a person, using symbols like a tree, a wheel or footprints instead.
192.spot: A large, smooth hemispherical dome on a low round base, crowned by a small square railing and a stacked umbrella, surrounded by a stone fence with tall gateways made of two posts and three curving crossbars covered in carving.
192.remember: Sanchi = ‘Stupa Starts here.’ Started by Emperor Ashoka (200s B.C.E.), enlarged later; gateways around the turn of the millennium. Walk clockwise, and the Buddha is never shown as a man.
compare: No. 198 (§9.7), Borobudur Temple: Borobudur turns the stupa idea into a climbable mountain of terraces, while Sanchi is a solid dome you walk around at ground level.
No. 183 (§8.3), The Kaaba: Both are sacred centers experienced by circumambulation rather than by entering, clockwise at Sanchi and counterclockwise at the Kaaba.
No. 182 (§8.2), Buddha: Sanchi represents the Buddha only through symbols, while the later Bamiyan Buddhas show him in colossal human form.
192.vocab: stupa, relic, circumambulation, torana, harmika, chattra, yakshi, aniconic.

form: A stupa (a solid dome-shaped mound built over relics) about 36 m (120 feet) across and 16.5 m (54 feet) high, with a core of earth and rubble faced in stone.
The dome, called the anda (egg), is topped by the harmika (a small square railing) and a chattra (a stacked, triple stone umbrella) on a central pole.
A stone railing called the vedika encircles a ground-level walkway, and a second walkway runs around the base on a raised terrace reached by double stairs.
Four toranas (gateways) stand at the cardinal points, each roughly 8.5 to 10 m (28 to 34 feet) high, with two square posts and three curved crossbars packed with relief carving.
The stone railings and gates imitate wood construction, such as posts and crossbars that look pegged together.
Brackets on the gates hold yakshi figures (female nature spirits), with full, curving bodies, leaning out from mango trees.
function: It was built to house relics, traditionally of the Buddha; nineteenth-century diggers found nothing in Stupa 1, but nearby Stupa 3 held relics of two of his chief disciples.
Pilgrims perform circumambulation (walking around a sacred object), here called pradakshina, moving clockwise around the dome, keeping the sacred center on their right.
Sanchi was also a monastery complex, with temples, smaller stupas and monks’ living quarters on the same hill.
content: The dome is often read as the world mountain or the dome of heaven, and the central pole as the axis mundi (the axis connecting earth and heaven).
The three umbrellas are commonly interpreted as the Three Jewels of Buddhism: the Buddha, his teaching (dharma), and the monastic community (sangha).

The torana reliefs show Jataka tales (stories of the Buddha’s past lives) and scenes from his last life, with the Buddha represented only by symbols: empty throne, footprints, Bodhi tree, wheel, parasol.
This aniconic approach (representing a holy figure without showing his body) reflects the idea that the enlightened Buddha had passed beyond physical form.
The yakshis, fertility spirits from older Indian religion, bring abundance and good luck, showing how Buddhism absorbed earlier local beliefs.
context: The Mauryan emperor Ashoka (ruled about 268–232 B.C.E.) built the first, smaller brick stupa here after converting to Buddhism, and erected a polished stone pillar nearby.
In the Sunga period (second century B.C.E.) the stupa was doubled in size and faced with stone, and the railing was added.
The four gateways were carved in the first century B.C.E. to early first century C.E., during the Satavahana period. An inscription on the south gate credits ivory carvers from nearby Vidisha.
Hundreds of donor inscriptions show the carvings were funded by many people, including monks, nuns, merchants and townsfolk, not just kings.
Rediscovered by a British oﬀicer in 1818 and damaged by treasure hunters, it was restored under John Marshall in 1912–1919 and is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. On the exam.
If asked about function → a reliquary mound for veneration, experienced by walking around it clockwise (pradakshina).
If asked about iconography → the Buddha is shown aniconically through symbols (wheel, tree, footprints, empty throne), not in human form.
If asked about the parts → anda (dome), harmika (railing on top), chattra (umbrellas), vedika (fence), toranas (gateways).
If asked about patron → begun by Emperor Ashoka (Maurya), enlarged under the Sungas, gateways carved later with many individual donors.
Trap: the toranas date about 200 years after Ashoka; the College Board’s range of c. 300 B.C.E.–100 C.E. covers several building phases.
If asked about yakshis → pre-Buddhist fertility spirits absorbed into Buddhist art.

193.title: Terra cotta warriors
193.artist: Qin Dynasty; mausoleum of the first Qin emperor, China
193.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
193.plain: The terra cotta warriors are an army of life-size clay soldiers, horses and chariots buried in pits near the tomb of Qin Shi Huangdi, the first emperor of a unified China, who died in 210 B.C.E. Estimates put the total at roughly 8,000 figures, though only part has been excavated. They were made with an early assembly-line system of standard parts, then finished by hand so each looks like an individual, and they were meant to guard the emperor forever in the afterlife.
193.spot: Rows and rows of life-size, gray-brown clay soldiers standing in long trenches, in armor or tunics, with topknots and varied faces, some next to horses; often photographed as a vast field of figures.
193.remember: Qin (pronounced ‘chin’) = China’s first emperor, 221 B.C.E. Think ‘an army made in a factory, each with his own face.’ Found by farmers digging a well in 1974.
compare: No. 194 (§9.3), Funeral banner of Lady Dai: Both come from early Chinese tombs and supply the dead for the afterlife, one with an army and one with a painted guide for the soul.
No. 23 (§3.12), Tutankhamun’s tomb, innermost coﬀin: Both are royal burials stocked with costly objects to secure the ruler’s eternal life, Egyptian gold versus Chinese clay soldiers.
No. 250 (§11.27), Kui Hua Zi: Ai Weiwei’s 100 million handmade porcelain seeds also explore mass production and the individual in China, over two thousand years later.
No. 17 (§3.6), Great Pyramids: Both are enormous royal tomb projects that required organizing huge labor forces and show a ruler’s absolute power.
193.vocab: terracotta, modular, mass production, mausoleum, afterlife, funerary.

form: Life-size figures made of terra cotta (fired clay; Italian for ‘baked earth’), mostly about 175–200 cm (5 feet 9 inches to 6 feet 6 inches) tall, with higher-ranking oﬀicers usually taller.
They were built with modular production (assembling standard, interchangeable parts): legs, torsos, arms and hands were made from molds or coiled clay, then joined together.
Heads came from a limited number of basic molds, then were personalized by hand with added clay for mustaches, hairstyles, ears and expressions, so no two look exactly alike.
Bodies show rank and role: armored infantry, kneeling and standing archers, cavalrymen with horses, charioteers and generals with distinctive headgear.
They were originally painted in bright colors over a base coat of lacquer, including a synthetic pigment now called Han purple. Most of the paint flakes off within minutes of exposure to air.
They held real bronze weapons (swords, spears, crossbows, halberds), many of which survive, though wooden parts and some weapons were taken by looters.
function: To protect the emperor in the afterlife. The pits sit east of his tomb mound, facing outward toward the direction of his old enemies.
They are part of a vast mausoleum (a large, grand tomb) complex modeled on an imperial capital, with oﬀices, stables, acrobats, musicians and oﬀicials made in clay or bronze.
The figures also displayed the emperor’s power: only a ruler commanding enormous labor and resources could make an underground army.
content: The army is arranged by real military formations: Pit 1 holds the main infantry, Pit 2 a mixed force of archers, cavalry and chariots, and Pit 3 appears to be a command post.
The individual faces suggest a real army with real people, though scholars debate whether they are true portraits or variations on standard types.

Clay soldiers were a substitute for real ones. Earlier Chinese rulers, including Qin dukes, had been buried with sacrificed humans; however, ancient historian Sima Qian says some of the First Emperor’s concubines and workers were still killed and buried with him.
context: Qin Shi Huangdi became king of Qin at 13 in 246 B.C.E., conquered the other warring states, and declared himself First Emperor in 221 B.C.E.

He standardized writing, coins, weights and measures, and axle widths, and linked earlier walls into an early version of the Great Wall. The same top-down control shows in the figures’ standard parts.
Many figures carry stamped or inscribed names of workshop foremen, a form of quality control so poor work could be traced and punished.
Work on the tomb began when he took the throne. Sima Qian, writing about a century later, said it contained rivers of mercury; soil tests over the mound show unusually high mercury.
The pits were found in 1974 by farmers digging a well near Xi’an. The emperor’s own burial mound has never been opened, partly to protect what is inside. On the exam.
If asked about process → mass production with standard molded parts, then hand-finishing for individuality.
If asked about function → guardians for the First Emperor in the afterlife, part of a vast tomb complex.
If asked about date and patron → Qin Shi Huangdi, c. 221–209 B.C.E.; he died in 210 B.C.E.
Trap: the figures were originally brightly painted and held real bronze weapons; they were never meant to look gray.
Trap: the number is an estimate (around 8,000); thousands remain unexcavated.
If asked about context → unification of China and standardization; workshop names stamped on the figures for accountability.

194.title: Funeral banner of Lady Dai (Xin Zhui)
194.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
194.plain: This T-shaped silk painting was found draped over the coﬀin of Lady Dai, a noblewoman of the early Han dynasty who died around 168 B.C.E., in a tomb at Mawangdui in southern China. It shows the universe in layers, from the watery underworld through her funeral and her own portrait up to heaven, guiding her soul on its journey. It survived because her tomb was sealed so well that even her body was preserved, with skin that was still soft when it was found in 1972.
194.spot: A tall silk banner shaped like a capital T, with a dark background and scenes stacked in layers: a red sun with a black bird at top right, a crescent moon with a toad at top left, twisting dragons, a small woman with a cane in the middle, and a figure holding up a platform at the bottom.
194.remember: Lady Dai rides a T up to the sky: read the T from bottom to top, underworld → funeral → Lady Dai → heaven. Han dynasty, about 180–168 B.C.E.
compare: No. 24 (§3.13), Last judgment of Hu-Nefer, from his tomb: Both are funerary images that guide a named individual through the afterlife, Egyptian judgment scene versus Chinese cosmic map.
No. 193 (§9.2), Terra cotta warriors: Both come from early imperial Chinese tombs and show how the dead were equipped for the next world, one with a painted guide and one with a clay army.
No. 29 (§3.18), Sarcophagus of the Spouses: Both present an elite individual in a funerary setting, emphasizing status and an active, comfortable afterlife.
194.vocab: funerary, silk, register, cosmology, underworld, bi, afterlife.

form: Ink and mineral pigments painted on silk, about 205 cm (6 feet 8 inches) long, and shaped like a T: wide at the top, narrower below.
Flowing, rhythmic outlines and flat areas of red, blue, white and black against a dark brown background create a strongly patterned surface.
The composition is organized in horizontal zones stacked vertically, framed on both sides by long, curling dragons whose bodies loop through a jade bi disc (a flat ring, a symbol of heaven).
The top section spreads wide: on the right a red sun with a crow; on the left a crescent moon with a toad and a hare; at the center a figure with a human head and serpent body.
The figure of Lady Dai is shown in profile, leaning on a cane, in a richly patterned robe, with attendants behind her and two kneeling figures in front.
function: It was laid face down over the innermost of four nested coﬀins, likely after being carried in the funeral procession.

It may have served to guide and summon her soul to the afterlife, and possibly to identify her to the spirits. Its exact ancient name and use are debated; some scholars call it a feiyi (flying garment).
It belongs to a tomb full of goods for the next life: lacquerware, food, clothing, musical instruments, and figurines of servants.
It is now in the Hunan Provincial Museum in Changsha.
content: Bottom zone: the underworld, where a strong figure stands on two large fish and holds up the platform of the earth, surrounded by water creatures and snakes.
Lower middle: a funeral rite or offering scene, with ritual bronze vessels and mourners, probably her family making offerings to her spirit.
Upper middle: Lady Dai herself, as an elderly woman with a cane, receiving homage as her soul begins its ascent.
Top: heaven, with the sun (crow) and moon (toad, hare), dragons, and a gate guarded by two figures. The central serpent-bodied figure may be a creator deity; scholars disagree on who it is.
The banner reflects Han ideas of two souls: one (the hun) rising to heaven, the other (the po) staying with the body, which is why both the journey upward and the well-stocked tomb mattered.
context: Lady Dai, personal name Xin Zhui, was the wife of Li Cang, the Marquis of Dai and chancellor of the kingdom of Changsha under the Han dynasty (206 B.C.E.–220 C.E.).
Her tomb (Tomb 1 at Mawangdui, near Changsha in Hunan) was excavated in 1972. Layers of charcoal and white clay sealed it, keeping out air and water.
Her body was astonishingly well preserved; an autopsy found melon seeds in her stomach and showed that she probably died of a heart attack soon after eating.
The banner is one of the earliest and most important surviving Chinese paintings on silk, offering a rare look at Han cosmology before Buddhism reached China.
Her son’s tomb nearby (Tomb 3) produced important texts on silk, including early copies of the Daoist classic Daodejing. On the exam.
If asked about form → a T-shaped painted silk banner arranged in stacked zones read from bottom to top.
If asked about function → funerary: placed over her coﬀin to guide her soul and supply her for the afterlife.
If asked about content → underworld, funeral offerings, portrait of Lady Dai, and heaven with sun (crow) and moon (toad).
If asked about context → early Han dynasty, Mawangdui Tomb 1, near Changsha, found in 1972.
Trap: it is painted silk, not embroidery or a woven tapestry.

195.title: Longmen caves
195.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
195.plain: The Longmen caves are a huge complex of Buddhist cave shrines carved into limestone cliffs along the Yi River, near the city of Luoyang in China, over roughly 400 years of major work. The site holds about 2,300 caves and niches and more than 100,000 statues, from finger-sized to colossal. Its best-known group is the Fengxian Temple, where a 17-meter seated Vairocana Buddha, paid for in part by Empress Wu Zetian, looks out over the river with attendant figures on each side.
195.spot: A huge seated Buddha with a calm, full face and long earlobes, carved into an open cliff niche, flanked by standing monks, crowned bodhisattvas and fierce armored guardians; the cliff around is honeycombed with small niches.
195.remember: Longmen = ‘Dragon Gate.’ Empress Wu paid for the giant Vairocana (672–675 C.E.), so remember ‘Wu’s view’: the Buddha’s face is said to look like hers.
compare: No. 182 (§8.2), Buddha: Both are colossal Buddhas carved into cliffs along trade and pilgrimage routes, but Bamiyan’s stood and were finished in plaster, while Longmen’s Vairocana is seated limestone.
No. 197 (§9.6), Todai-ji: Both center on a colossal Vairocana Buddha sponsored by the ruling court to tie the state to Buddhism, one carved in rock and one cast in bronze.
No. 192 (§9.1), Great Stupa at Sanchi: Sanchi shows the Buddha only through symbols, while Longmen shows him as a huge human figure, a clear change in Buddhist image-making over time.
195.vocab: rock-cut architecture, Vairocana, bodhisattva, hierarchical scale, merit, patron, colossal.

form: The site consists of rock-cut caves and niches (carved directly from the cliff) along about 1 km of limestone cliffs on both banks of the Yi River.
In the Fengxian Temple, the seated Vairocana Buddha (the cosmic Buddha of light) is about 17 m (roughly 56 feet) tall, with a head about 4 m high.

He is flanked symmetrically by two disciples (the elderly Kashyapa and young Ananda), two crowned bodhisattvas (beings who delay their own enlightenment to help others), two heavenly kings in armor and two muscular guardians.
The figures show hierarchical scale (more important figures are larger): the Buddha is largest, the guardians smallest, and the figures grow more agitated as they move outward.
The Tang-era style is full and rounded, with smooth volumes, simple drapery and a calm, inward-looking face, unlike the thinner, flatter Northern Wei figures in older caves at the site.
Holes in the cliff suggest the Fengxian group was once sheltered by a wooden roof or hall.
function: Buddhist devotion and pilgrimage: worshippers came to pray, make offerings and view the images.
Sponsoring a cave or statue earned merit (spiritual credit for good deeds), often dedicated to family members or ancestors; about 2,800 inscriptions record donors.
Imperial sponsorship also served politics, linking the ruler to the Buddha’s authority.
content: Vairocana is the universal or cosmic Buddha, from whom all other Buddhas emanate, a fitting image for an empire that claimed universal rule.
The arrangement acts as a diagram of the Buddhist world, moving from the calm enlightened center to the fierce protectors at the edges.
The guardians stomp on demons, showing Buddhism’s protective power, while the Buddha’s calm expresses enlightenment.
Tradition says the Buddha’s face was modeled on Empress Wu, merging imperial and divine imagery; this is legend rather than proven fact.
context: Carving began around 493 C.E., when the Northern Wei dynasty moved its capital to Luoyang. Work continued under several dynasties, peaking in the Tang dynasty (618–907), and tailed off by the Song.
The Fengxian group was carved in 672–675 under Emperor Gaozong. His wife, the future Empress Wu, donated 20,000 strings of cash from her cosmetics allowance toward it.
Wu Zetian later ruled in her own name (690–705), the only woman in Chinese history to hold the title of emperor, and she used Buddhism to justify her rule.
Buddhism suffered a major state persecution in 845, and the site later faded as a religious center.

In the early twentieth century many heads and reliefs were chiseled off and sold abroad. Large reliefs of an emperor and empress in procession from the Binyang Central Cave are now in the Metropolitan Museum and the Nelson-Atkins Museum. On the exam.
If asked about patron → Empress Wu Zetian helped fund the Vairocana Buddha of the Fengxian Temple.
If asked about iconography → Vairocana, the cosmic Buddha, with disciples, bodhisattvas, heavenly kings and guardians in hierarchical order.
If asked about function → devotion, pilgrimage and merit-making by donors from emperors to ordinary people.
Trap: the site spans 493–1127 C.E. and several dynasties; the Tang dynasty is when the famous Fengxian group was carved.
If asked about style change → slender Northern Wei figures versus fuller, more threedimensional Tang figures.
If asked about later history → heads and reliefs removed and sold to Western collectors in the early twentieth century.

196.title: Gold and jade crown
196.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
196.plain: This gold crown comes from a royal tomb of the Silla kingdom in Gyeongju, Korea, made in the fifth or sixth century C.E. It is a gold headband with tall branch- and antlershaped uprights, hung with comma-shaped jade jewels and dozens of tiny gold disks that would have shimmered and trembled. It was probably too thin and fragile for everyday wear, so it was most likely made for ceremonies or for burial, and its shapes connect Silla royalty to the shamanic traditions of northeast Asia.
196.spot: A thin gold band with three upright pieces shaped like stylized trees with stacked branches and two antler-like pieces, covered in small dangling gold disks and green comma-shaped jade pendants.
196.remember: Silla = ‘shiny and silly fragile.’ Gold trees and antlers plus jade commas: Korea, Three Kingdoms period, fifth to sixth century.
compare: No. 53 (§4.6), Merovingian looped fibulae: Both are early medieval gold status objects showing links to the steppe and buried with elites, Merovingian fibulae versus a Silla crown.
No. 158 (§6.6), Ruler’s feather headdress: Both are royal headdresses made of rare, shimmering materials that move with the wearer and project the ruler’s sacred authority.
No. 170 (§7.4), Sika dwa kofi: Both are gold royal regalia that embody the spiritual as well as political power of a ruler.
196.vocab: metalwork, regalia, gogok, spangle, tumulus, shaman, funerary.

form: Made from thin sheets of gold cut into shape, decorated with punched dotted lines, and joined with gold rivets and wire. The crown in the College Board image is about 27.3 cm (about 11 inches) tall.
Three front uprights look like stylized trees, with branches often compared to the Chinese character 出 (chu); two uprights at the sides resemble antlers.
Dozens of small gold spangles (thin disks hung on wire so they move) cover the surface, catching the light with every movement.
Comma-shaped jade pieces called gogok (curved jewels, shaped a bit like a claw or a comma) hang from the uprights and band.
Long pendants of gold chains and leaves often hung from the sides, dangling near the wearer’s face.
The metalwork (shaping and decorating metal by cutting, hammering and joining) is light and delicate, relying on shimmer and movement rather than solid weight.
function: Found in a royal tumulus (a large burial mound), it signaled the high rank of the person buried there.
Because the gold is so thin, scholars think it was made for ceremonies or specifically for the burial, not daily use.
Some Silla crowns were found on the heads of the dead in their coﬀins, so this kind of crown could serve the deceased in the afterlife.
Today it is in the National Museum of Korea in Seoul and is designated a national treasure.
content: Trees are often read as the sacred world tree linking earth and heaven, a key idea in shamanism (a religion in which a spiritual expert travels between the human and spirit worlds).
Antlers recall the deer-antler headdresses worn by shamans in Siberia and the steppes, suggesting the ruler was also a spiritual intermediary.
The jade gogok may represent life, fertility or animal claws and teeth used as amulets; their exact meaning is debated.
Taken together, the crown presents the king or queen as both a political and a spiritual leader.
context: Korea’s Three Kingdoms period (traditionally 57 B.C.E.–668 C.E.) saw rivalry between Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla, which eventually unified most of the peninsula in 668.

The College Board crown comes from the north mound of Hwangnam Daechong, a huge double tomb in Gyeongju dug in 1973–1975 and usually dated to the later fifth century. The north mound probably held a queen.
Silla tombs had wooden burial chambers buried under piles of river stones and earth, which made them very hard to loot, so many gold objects survived.
Silla adopted Buddhism oﬀicially in the early sixth century; the crowns reflect older, preBuddhist beliefs and links to the nomadic cultures of the Eurasian steppe. On the exam.
If asked about culture → Silla kingdom, Korea, Three Kingdoms period, fifth to sixth century C.E.
If asked about materials → thin gold sheet with jade gogok and gold spangles.
If asked about iconography → tree and antler forms linked to shamanism and Siberian or steppe traditions.
If asked about function → status symbol found in a royal tomb, likely ceremonial or funerary because it is too fragile for daily wear.
Trap: the medium is listed only as ‘metalwork’ by the College Board, but you should name gold and jade.
If asked about context → Silla’s stone-mound tombs protected treasures from looters.
Attribution clue: gold tree-and-antler uprights with dangling jade commas point to Silla Korea.

197.title: Todai-ji
197.artist: Various artists, including sculptors Unkei and Kaikei (Kei School); Nara, Japan
197.medium: Bronze and wood (sculpture); wood with ceramic-tile roofing (architecture)
197.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
197.plain: Todai-ji is a huge Buddhist temple in Nara, Japan, founded by Emperor Shomu in the 740s to protect the nation through Buddhism. It houses one of the largest bronze Buddhas in the world, about 15 m (49 feet) tall, inside one of the largest wooden buildings in the world. At its Great South Gate stand two giant, ferocious wooden guardian figures carved in 1203 by the sculptors Unkei and Kaikei and their workshop.
197.spot: A massive wooden hall with a sweeping dark tile roof and golden ornaments on the ridge, or two towering, muscular wooden guardians in fluttering drapery, one with mouth open and one with mouth closed, framed by a gate.
197.remember: Todai-ji = ‘Today, Gee, that’s big.’ Shomu, 743 C.E.; guardians by Unkei and Kaikei, 1203 (Kamakura).
compare: No. 195 (§9.4), Longmen caves: Both center on a colossal Vairocana Buddha sponsored by the imperial court to link state power with Buddhism.
No. 25 (§3.14), Lamassu from the citadel of Sargon II, Dur Sh…: Both place huge, intimidating guardian figures at a gateway to protect a sacred or royal space.
No. 182 (§8.2), Buddha: Both use colossal Buddha images to impress pilgrims, but Bamiyan’s were carved into a cliff while Todai-ji’s is cast bronze inside a building.
197.vocab: Vairocana, Nio, joined-block construction, post-and-lintel, bracket system, colossal, consecration.

form: The Daibutsuden (Great Buddha Hall) is a timber building about 57 m wide, 50 m deep and 49 m tall, with a heavy ceramic tile roof; the current hall, completed in 1709, is only about two-thirds as wide as the original.
It is built with wooden post-and-lintel construction (vertical posts carrying horizontal beams) and complex bracket sets that carry the weight of the deep eaves.
Inside sits the bronze Vairocana Buddha (Birushana or Rushana in Japanese), about 15 m (49 feet) tall, seated on a lotus throne with the right hand raised in a gesture of reassurance.
Original eighth-century bronze survives only in a few parts, such as some lotus petals; the head was recast in the 1690s after earlier fires.
The Nandaimon (Great South Gate) holds two Nio guardians (paired fierce protector figures), each about 8.4 m (about 28 feet) tall.
The Nio use joined-block construction (assembling a figure from many separately carved wooden pieces), with thousands of pieces each, allowing huge size and dramatic, lifelike musculature.
function: Todai-ji was the head of a nationwide network of state-sponsored provincial temples (kokubunji), with Buddhism used to protect the country and unify it under the emperor.
The Great Buddha was the focus of worship and of grand state ceremonies, starting with the eye-opening ceremony of 752, which consecrated the statue.
The Nio guard the temple gate, keeping evil out and frightening the unworthy, like bouncers at the door of sacred space.
Todai-ji is still an active temple and part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site (1998).
content: Vairocana is the cosmic Buddha who presides over the entire universe; the image paralleled the emperor ruling the whole country.

The Nio form a pair: Agyo, with mouth open, says ‘a,’ and Ungyo, with mouth closed, says ‘un.’ These are the first and last sounds of the Sanskrit alphabet, standing for beginning and end of all things.
Their bulging muscles, tense poses and fierce faces turn spiritual protection into physical power.
context: Emperor Shomu ordered the Great Buddha in 743 after a period of smallpox epidemics, famine and rebellion. Casting used hundreds of tons of copper plus tin and gold, straining national resources.
The monk Gyoki helped raise support from ordinary people, and the Indian monk Bodhisena performed the eye-opening in 752.
In 1180, during civil war, Taira forces burned the temple. The monk Chogen led the rebuilding with support from the Minamoto shogunate, and the Nandaimon was rebuilt in 1199.
Unkei and Kaikei of the Kei school of sculptors carved the Nio in 1203 in about 70 days, an achievement of workshop organization. Their style marks the naturalism of the Kamakura period (1185–1333).
The hall burned again in 1567; the present hall and the Buddha’s head date from the Edo period rebuilding around 1700. On the exam.
If asked about patron → Emperor Shomu, 743 C.E., state-sponsored Buddhism to protect the nation.
If asked about the Buddha → colossal bronze Vairocana, consecrated in 752, much repaired and recast.
If asked about the guardians → Nio by Unkei and Kaikei, 1203, Kamakura period, joinedblock wood.
Trap: the College Board list spells the second sculptor ‘Keikei’; the correct name is Kaikei.
Trap: the current Daibutsuden (c. 1700) is smaller than the eighth-century original.
If asked about continuity and change → rebuilt after fires in 1180 and 1567, so the complex combines eighth-, twelfth-thirteenth- and seventeenth- to eighteenth-century work.

198.title: Borobudur Temple
198.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
198.plain: Borobudur, in central Java, Indonesia, is the largest Buddhist monument in the world: a stepped stone mountain built around a natural hill around 750–842 C.E. under the Sailendra dynasty. It has no interior rooms. Pilgrims climb it by walking clockwise around each level, passing miles of carved stories on the way up, until they reach open circular terraces with bell-shaped stupas at the top, a journey meant to mirror the path from worldly desire to enlightenment.
198.spot: A wide, gray stone stepped platform seen from above or at an angle, with square, relief-lined terraces at the bottom and three round terraces on top covered in rows of bell-shaped, latticework stupas around one large central stupa.
198.remember: Borobudur = ‘Buddhist Burrito of levels’: square layers then round layers, wrapped around a hill. Sailendra = ‘Lord of the Mountain,’ so the dynasty built a mountain.
compare: No. 192 (§9.1), Great Stupa at Sanchi: Both are stupas experienced by clockwise circumambulation, but Borobudur stacks the walk into a climbing journey of many levels.
No. 199 (§9.8), Angkor: Both are Southeast Asian temple-mountains representing Mount Meru, Buddhist Borobudur versus originally Hindu Angkor Wat.
No. 12 (§3.1), White Temple and its ziggurat: Both are artificial sacred mountains that lift worshippers toward the divine, a Sumerian ziggurat versus a Javanese Buddhist mandala.
198.vocab: stupa, mandala, relief, circumambulation, andesite, terrace, sacred mountain.

form: Built of about 55,000 cubic meters of andesite (a gray volcanic stone) blocks fitted without mortar around a natural hill; the base is about 123 m (403 feet) square.
Six square terraces form the lower levels, topped by three circular terraces and a large central stupa (a dome-shaped Buddhist monument holding relics or symbolizing the Buddha).

The square galleries are lined with 2,672 carved relief panels (images that project from a flat background), 1,460 of them narrative, making it one of the largest collections of Buddhist relief carving anywhere.
There are 504 statues of the Buddha in niches along the galleries and inside the stupas on the top terraces.
The circular terraces hold 72 perforated stupas (32, 24 and 16 per ring), with diamond- or square-shaped openings through which you can glimpse the seated Buddha inside.
From above, the plan forms a mandala (a diagram of the Buddhist cosmos built of squares and circles).
function: A pilgrimage monument for Mahayana Buddhists. Pilgrims performed circumambulation (walking around a sacred center), going clockwise around each level before climbing to the next.
The full walk past all the reliefs covers several kilometers, turning the building into a teaching tool you read with your feet.
There is no hall for gathering inside; the experience is the climb itself, from enclosed galleries with high walls to the open sky at the top.
content: The levels represent three realms of Buddhist cosmology: desire (kamadhatu), form (rupadhatu) and formlessness (arupadhatu).

The base originally showed 160 reliefs of karma, cause and effect in the realm of desire; it was soon covered by an added stone foot, perhaps for structural support. Some are now visible at one corner.
The square galleries show the realm of form: the life of the Buddha, Jataka tales (stories of his past lives) and the quest of the pilgrim Sudhana for wisdom.
The bare circular terraces stand for formlessness: plain surfaces, Buddhas half-hidden in lattice stupas, and an empty central stupa suggest enlightenment beyond images.
Overall it is a model of Mount Meru (the sacred mountain at the center of the universe in Hindu and Buddhist cosmology).
context: The Sailendra dynasty ruled central Java and was closely connected to maritime trade networks linking India, China and Southeast Asia.
Construction took several generations; the College Board dates it c. 750–842 C.E. based partly on inscriptions and style.

After the center of Javanese power shifted east in the tenth century, possibly after volcanic eruptions, and Islam later spread through Java, Borobudur was neglected and covered by volcanic ash and jungle.

In 1814 the British lieutenant governor Thomas Stamford Raffles had it investigated. It was restored by Theodoor van Erp in 1907–1911 and in a major Indonesian-UNESCO project from 1975 to 1982. On the exam.
If asked about form → a stepped stone mandala and cosmic mountain: square terraces below, circular terraces with 72 perforated stupas above.
If asked about function → pilgrimage by clockwise circumambulation and ascent from desire through form to formlessness.
If asked about content → narrative reliefs of karma, the Buddha’s life, Jataka tales and Sudhana’s quest.
If asked about patron → the Sailendra dynasty of Java.
Trap: Borobudur has no interior rooms; it is a solid monument built over a hill, not a temple you enter.
If asked about later history → abandoned, buried, rediscovered in 1814, and restored in the twentieth century with UNESCO help.

199.title: Angkor (temple of Angkor Wat and city of Angkor Thom)
199.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
199.plain: Angkor was the capital of the Khmer Empire in Cambodia, which ruled much of mainland Southeast Asia from about 800 to 1400 C.E. Its two big exam pieces are Angkor Wat, a huge 12th-century Hindu temple to Vishnu, and Angkor Thom, a walled Buddhist royal city built a few decades later. Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument in the world, and both show how kings used architecture to present themselves as god-like.
199.spot: Angkor Wat: five corncob-shaped stone towers in a quincunx (four corners plus a taller center) rising behind long galleries, usually photographed across a moat or reflecting pond. Angkor Thom: gate towers and temple towers carved with giant calm smiling faces, and causeways lined with rows of figures hauling a stone serpent.
199.remember: “Wat” sounds like “what” — what faces west? Angkor Wat, Suryavarman II’s Vishnu temple-mountain of the 1100s. Then “Thom” for “Tom with the faces”: Jayavarman VII’s Buddhist city around 1200.
compare: No. 198 (§9.7), Borobudur Temple: Both are Southeast Asian cosmic mountains built in stone; Borobudur is a Buddhist path walked upward, Angkor Wat a Hindu god-king temple.
No. 200 (§9.9), Lakshmana Temple: Both Hindu temples model Mount Meru with stacked towers and are covered in relief sculpture.
No. 17 (§3.6), Great Pyramids: Both are colossal royal funerary monuments that tie a ruler to the divine and the cosmos.
No. 21 (§3.10), Mortuary temple of Hatshepsut: Both are royal temples whose reliefs insert the ruler into sacred history and cover long processional walls.
199.vocab: temple mountain, quincunx, Mount Meru, bas-relief, naga, corbel, apsara, devaraja.

form: Angkor Wat is a temple-mountain (a stepped temple built as an artificial sacred mountain): three rising, nested rectangular galleries step up to five towers set in a quincunx (four at the corners, one in the middle).
The central tower rises about 65 meters (213 feet). The whole site, moat included, covers roughly 1.5 by 1.3 kilometers; the moat alone is about 190 meters wide.

It is built of sandstone blocks laid without mortar over a core of laterite (a rusty, porous local stone). The sandstone came from Phnom Kulen, about 40 kilometers away, probably floated in on canals.
The towers are corncob or lotus-bud shaped, built with corbelled construction (each course of stone stepping slightly inward) rather than true arches.

The walls of the outer gallery carry roughly 600 meters (about 2,000 feet) of bas-relief (shallow carving), one of the longest continuous relief programs anywhere, plus about 1,800 carved apsaras (celestial dancers).

Angkor Thom is a square walled city about 3 kilometers on a side with five gates. At its exact center sits the Bayon, a crowded temple whose towers (about 37 survive of perhaps 49 or more) carry over 200 huge carved faces.
Style clues: dense, crisp, low relief; rhythmic repetition of figures; elongated towers; strict symmetry and axial planning.
function: Angkor Wat was a state temple dedicated to Vishnu, built for King Suryavarman II (reigned 1113 to about 1150). Most scholars think it was also meant as his funerary temple, where he would be honored as one with Vishnu after death.
Angkor Thom was the capital city of Jayavarman VII (reigned 1181 to about 1218), who rebuilt Angkor after it was sacked by the Cham in 1177. The Bayon was his Buddhist state temple.
Ordinary people did not worship inside. The galleries and inner sanctuaries were for the king, priests and elite; the scale and the moat were meant to impress everyone outside.
Angkor Wat was never fully abandoned. By the 1500s it had been turned into a Theravada Buddhist site, and monks still use it today.
content: The plan models the universe: the central tower is Mount Meru (home of the gods, center of the cosmos), the four outer towers its surrounding peaks, the walls the mountain ranges at the world’s edge, and the moat the cosmic ocean.

The famous Churning of the Ocean of Milk relief (about 49 meters long) shows gods and demons pulling the serpent Vasuki back and forth to churn out amrita (the elixir of immortality). Vishnu stands at the center; his tortoise form supports the churning mountain.
Other reliefs show the Hindu epics (Ramayana, Mahabharata), heavens and hells, and Suryavarman II himself holding court and leading armies, putting the king into sacred history.

At Angkor Thom, causeways to the gates are lined with 54 gods and 54 demons hauling a naga (sacred serpent), echoing the churning myth. The giant faces are usually read as Avalokiteshvara (Bodhisattva of compassion), probably merged with Jayavarman VII himself.
The portrait sculpture Jayavarman VII as Buddha (c. 1200, sandstone, now in Phnom Penh) shows the king seated, eyes lowered, in calm meditation: the ruler as a Buddhist sage.
context: The Khmer kings practiced devaraja (god-king) ideas going back to Jayavarman II, who founded the kingdom around 802 C.E. That is why the source dates the site c. 800 to 1400.

Angkor Wat faces west, which is unusual. West is Vishnu’s direction and also the direction of death and sunset; the reliefs are meant to be read counterclockwise, a direction linked with funeral rites. Both clues support the funerary reading, though scholars still debate it.
Angkor was a huge city, possibly the largest pre-industrial urban area in the world, supported by an enormous network of reservoirs (barays) and canals for rice farming.

Under Jayavarman VII the state religion shifted from Hinduism to Mahayana Buddhism; after his death there was a Hindu backlash in which many Buddha images were defaced. Later the region became Theravada Buddhist.

The Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya sacked Angkor in 1431, and the capital moved south. French explorer Henri Mouhot popularized the ruins in Europe in the 1860s. Angkor Wat appears on Cambodia’s flag and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992. On the exam.
If asked who built Angkor Wat → Suryavarman II, Khmer Empire, first half of the 12th century, for Vishnu.
If asked who built Angkor Thom and the Bayon → Jayavarman VII, late 12th to early 13th century, Buddhist.
If asked why Angkor Wat faces west → Vishnu’s direction and the direction of death, suggesting a funerary temple.
If asked about cosmic symbolism → five towers equal the peaks of Mount Meru; moat equals the cosmic ocean. Same idea as Borobudur (No. 198) and Lakshmana (No. 200).
If shown gods and demons pulling a serpent → Churning of the Ocean of Milk, Angkor Wat east gallery.
Trap: Angkor Wat started Hindu; Angkor Thom is Buddhist. Do not mix up which king built which.
Trap: the giant faces belong to the Bayon at Angkor Thom, not to Angkor Wat.

200.title: Lakshmana Temple
200.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
200.plain: The Lakshmana Temple is a sandstone Hindu temple to Vishnu at Khajuraho in central India, built around 930 to 950 C.E. by the Chandella dynasty. It is the classic example of a north Indian temple: a series of towers that climb like a mountain range to the tallest one over a tiny dark shrine. It is also famous, and slightly notorious, for the hundreds of carved figures on its outside walls, including erotic couples.
200.spot: A tan sandstone temple on a tall platform with a cluster of rounded, ribbed towers that rise left to right in steps to one highest peak; small shrines at the four corners of the platform; every outside surface crowded with horizontal bands of carved figures.
