200.remember: Lakshmana sounds like “Lakshmi” — Vishnu’s wife — and it is a Vishnu temple. “Chandella in Khajuraho, 930 to 950”: think “candle in the cave” for the dark garbhagriha.
compare: No. 199 (§9.8), Angkor: Both Hindu temples turn Mount Meru into architecture, with stacked towers and dense relief carving.
No. 192 (§9.1), Great Stupa at Sanchi: Both are Indian sacred buildings for circumambulation, but Sanchi is a solid Buddhist relic mound and Lakshmana encloses a god’s image.
No. 60 (§4.13), Chartres Cathedral: Both cover a sacred building’s exterior with sculpture that teaches and protects, leading the faithful from the world toward the divine.
No. 202 (§9.11), Shiva as Lord of Dance: Both are Hindu objects of devotion meant for darshan of a god, one in stone architecture, one in portable bronze.
200.vocab: shikhara, garbhagriha, mandapa, mithuna, Nagara style, darshan, mandala, circumambulation.

form: It is built in the Nagara style (the north Indian temple type) from buff sandstone blocks fitted together, largely without mortar, using post-and-lintel and corbelled roofing inside.
It stands on a high jagati (raised platform) with four small subsidiary shrines at its corners, a layout called panchayatana (five shrines). Worshippers climb steep steps on the east to reach it.

The roofline rises in a crescendo of towers. The smaller ones over the porch and halls lead to the main shikhara (curved, beehive-shaped tower) over the sanctum, which is clustered with miniature copies of itself.

The plan runs east to west in sequence: entrance porch, assembly halls (mandapa), a vestibule, then the garbhagriha (‘womb chamber’, the small dark sanctum holding the god’s image). An inner corridor lets worshippers walk around the sanctum.

The exterior is wrapped in bands of high-relief sculpture: gods and goddesses, apsaras (celestial women) with twisting, curvy bodies, animals, soldiers, hunting and procession scenes, and mithuna (loving couples), some explicitly erotic.
Figures have rounded, full bodies, deep tribhanga poses (body bent at neck, waist and knee) and crisp ornament: a hallmark of Chandella sculpture.
function: A working Hindu temple dedicated to Vishnu. The main image inside is Vishnu as Vaikuntha, with three heads: human, boar and lion.

Hindu worship is darshan (seeing and being seen by the god), not congregational preaching. A devotee moves from the bright entrance into darkness, ending at the sanctum where the priest tends the image.
Worshippers also perform pradakshina (walking clockwise around the sanctum), inside the corridor or around the platform outside.
It also showed off the power and piety of the Chandella kings, a newly rising dynasty.
content: The whole building is Mount Meru or Mount Kailasa: the towers are mountain peaks, and the garbhagriha is the cave in the mountain’s heart where the divine dwells.
The plan is laid out on a mandala (sacred grid diagram of the cosmos), so the temple is a small model of the ordered universe.

The erotic sculptures have several readings: they are auspicious (fertility and abundance protect the building); they symbolize the soul’s union with the divine; they relate to Tantric practice; or they show worldly life (kama) left behind on the way inward.
The erotic panels are concentrated on the outer walls, especially where the halls meet the sanctum, not inside it. Inside, the focus is purely on the god.
context: Built by the Chandella (Chandela) dynasty at its capital Khajuraho, Madhya Pradesh. An inscription dated 954 C.E. says King Yashovarman built it and his son Dhanga completed it. The name comes from Yashovarman’s other name, Lakshavarman, not from Rama’s brother Lakshmana.
Khajuraho once had around 85 temples, built roughly 950 to 1050; about 25 survive, Hindu and Jain. It is one of the earliest of the large group.
The site’s remoteness probably saved it from destruction in later centuries. British surveyors publicized it in the 1800s, and Victorian visitors were shocked by the sculpture.
Khajuraho became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986 and is still an active place of worship and pilgrimage. On the exam.
If asked which Indian temple style → Nagara (north Indian), with curved shikhara towers. The south Indian type, Dravida, has stepped pyramid towers instead.
If asked what the towers mean → a mountain range rising to Mount Meru; the sanctum is the sacred cave.
If asked about function → darshan of Vishnu in the garbhagriha plus circumambulation; not a congregational space like a mosque or church.
If asked about the erotic figures → give multiple scholarly readings (auspicious, divine union, Tantric, worldly life outside); avoid calling it simply decoration.
Key ID: Chandella dynasty, Khajuraho, India, c. 930 to 950 C.E., sandstone.
Trap: it is a Hindu temple to Vishnu, not Buddhist, and not dedicated to Lakshmana.

201.title: Travelers among Mountains and Streams
201.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
201.plain: Travelers among Mountains and Streams is a huge Chinese landscape painting on silk made around 1000 C.E. by Fan Kuan in the Northern Song dynasty. A gigantic mountain fills the picture, and you have to hunt to find the tiny men and pack mules on the road below. It is the model of the “monumental landscape” style and one of the most important paintings in Chinese history.
201.spot: A tall, narrow, brownish silk hanging scroll dominated by one enormous dark cliff face in the upper two-thirds, a thin white waterfall to its right, a band of pale mist below it, and a tiny mule train crossing the lower right.
201.remember: “Fan” of nature, around the year 1000: the mountain is a giant fan standing up. Tiny travelers, huge mountain, Northern Song.
compare: No. 109 (§5.11), The Oxbow: Both are landscapes with tiny human presence, but Cole’s sublime stresses man taming nature while Fan Kuan shows harmony within it.
No. 83 (§4.36), Hunters in the Snow: Both use small figures in a vast landscape seen from above, one from Northern Song China, one from 16th-century Flanders.
No. 227 (§11.4), Summer Trees: Song Su-nam’s ink paintings continue the East Asian ink tradition in an abstract modern form.
No. 210 (§9.19), White and Red Plum Blossoms: Both are East Asian nature paintings, but Kōrin’s flat decorative gold screen is the opposite of Fan Kuan’s monumental, illusionistic ink.
201.vocab: hanging scroll, monumental landscape, texture stroke, shifting perspective, shanshui, Neo-Confucianism, Daoism.

form: A hanging scroll in ink and light color on silk, about 2.06 meters tall by 1.03 meters wide (roughly 6 feet 9 inches by 3 feet 4 inches).
The composition stacks three zones: a foreground of boulders, a middle ground with trees, a road, the travelers and a temple roof poking out of the woods, and a towering background mountain.
A band of mist (blank silk) separates the middle ground from the mountain, so the peak seems to float and loom; you cannot measure the distance, which makes it feel enormous.
The rock surfaces are built from thousands of tiny dabs called cun (texture strokes), here the “raindrop” type, giving a gritty, stone-like texture.
There is no single vanishing point. The painting uses shifting perspective (several viewpoints combined), so you look up at the mountain and straight at the road at the same time.
The palette is mostly ink tones on silk that has darkened with age, with very little color; the mood is solemn and still.
function: A painting for private contemplation by educated viewers, unrolled and hung to be studied up close and from a distance.
It works as a kind of imaginary journey: the viewer “travels” through the mountains mentally, an experience later Song writers praised.
Later it became an imperial treasure, stamped with collectors’ seals, and is now in the National Palace Museum in Taipei, Taiwan.
content: Humans are tiny within a vast, ordered nature. The point is not that people are worthless, but that they belong to a larger cosmic order.
Many scholars read the central mountain as an emblem of the emperor or of cosmic order, with lesser hills ranked around it like the social hierarchy, a Neo-Confucian idea.
The landscape reflects Daoist ideas too: harmony with nature, and the flow of qi (life energy) through mountains and water.
The Chinese word for landscape painting, shanshui, literally means “mountain-water”: the mountain (solid, yang) and stream (flowing, yin) balance each other.
Fan Kuan’s signature is hidden in the leaves above the mule train at lower right; it was only noticed in 1958. A later title inscription at the top was added by the Ming painter-critic Dong Qichang.
context: Northern Song dynasty (960 to 1127). After years of war, landscape replaced figure painting as the most prestigious subject, associated with scholar-oﬀicials.

Fan Kuan (active about 990 to 1030) reportedly started by copying the master Li Cheng, then decided nature itself was the better teacher and lived as a near-hermit in the mountains of Shaanxi, studying them directly.
Paintings like this were made for the educated elite and became models that later painters copied and responded to for centuries.
It is so fragile that the National Palace Museum displays it only rarely and for short periods. On the exam.
If asked the ID → Fan Kuan, Northern Song, c. 1000 C.E., ink and colors on silk, hanging scroll.
If asked what makes it “monumental landscape” → the central massive peak, front-facing and filling the frame, dwarfing the people.
If asked about technique → cun “raindrop” texture strokes and shifting perspective with mist creating depth.
If asked the philosophy → humans in harmony with an ordered cosmos (Daoist and NeoConfucian), not a Western-style “sublime” of terror.
Fact to remember: the hidden signature in the foliage, found in 1958.
Trap: it is a hanging scroll read top to bottom, not a handscroll like the Night Attack (No. 203).

202.title: Shiva as Lord of Dance (Nataraja)
202.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
202.plain: This is a Chola-dynasty bronze statue from south India, around the 11th century, showing the Hindu god Shiva as Nataraja, “Lord of the Dance.” Inside a ring of fire, the four-armed god dances the dance that creates and destroys the universe. These statues were made to be carried through the streets in festivals, and they are the best-known Hindu sculpture type in the world.
202.spot: A dark bronze figure inside a circular hoop of flames, with four arms, one leg raised across the body, long locks of hair flying out sideways, standing on a small crouching figure, all on a lotus base with holes or lugs for poles.
202.remember: Nataraja = “Natya” (dance) + “raja” (king). Chola rhymes with “rolla”: Shiva rolls the universe through a dance in a ring of fire, about the year 1000.
compare: No. 41 (§3.30), Seated boxer: Both are bronzes cast by lost-wax, but the Seated Boxer shows human exhaustion while Nataraja shows divine cosmic energy.
No. 200 (§9.9), Lakshmana Temple: Both are Hindu objects for darshan; the temple is a fixed home for a god while Nataraja moves through the community.
No. 184 (§8.4), Jowo Rinpoche, enshrined in the Jokhang Temple: Both are sacred images that are dressed, adorned and worshipped as living presences.
No. 216 (§10.4), Staff god: Both are sacred figures whose wrappings or adornment were part of worship, so museum displays show them stripped.
202.vocab: lost-wax casting, mudra, abhaya mudra, darshan, puja, Nataraja.

form: Cast bronze (really a copper alloy) made by the lost-wax method: a wax model was coated in clay, heated so the wax ran out, and filled with molten metal. Each mold was broken, so every statue is unique. Chola bronzes are usually solid cast.
Typical height is between about 2 and 3 feet; the Metropolitan Museum’s example is about 27 inches tall.
Shiva’s body forms dynamic diagonals inside a stable circle: the prabhamandala (ring of fire), meaning the movement feels both energetic and balanced.
He has four arms, a slim waist, broad shoulders and a calm face even in motion. His long locks fly out horizontally to show how fast he spins.
Details in the hair include a crescent moon, a skull, a cobra and a tiny figure of the river goddess Ganga.
The base has lugs or holes for carrying poles; the figure was designed to be seen in the round, from all sides.
function: A processional image: on festival days priests dressed it in silk, flowers and jewels and carried it through town so the whole community could receive darshan (sight of the god).
Between festivals it stayed in the temple and received daily worship (puja): bathing, anointing and offerings.
Because it was dressed, much of the body was hidden during worship; the nude bronze we see in museums is not how devotees usually saw it.
Today many Natarajas are museum objects; some have been the subject of theft and repatriation cases, returned to temples in India.
content: Upper right hand: the damaru (hourglass drum), whose beat is the rhythm of creation.
Upper left hand: fire, the force of destruction. Together the two hands show the endless cycle of creation and destruction.

Lower right hand: the abhaya mudra (“fear not” gesture of protection). Lower left arm: stretched across the body like an elephant trunk, pointing to the raised left foot, which offers release (moksha) from the cycle of rebirth.

His right foot crushes Apasmara, the dwarf of ignorance or forgetfulness. The ring of fire is the cosmos itself, and the dance is the ananda tandava (dance of bliss), associated with the temple at Chidambaram.
context: Chola dynasty (about 850 to 1279 C.E.), a powerful Tamil kingdom in south India (Tamil Nadu) that also controlled sea trade to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
The Chola rulers, especially Rajaraja I and his family, were devotees of Shiva and sponsored temples and bronze workshops; the queen Sembiyan Mahadevi was a major patron of bronzes.
Bronze casting reached its peak under the Cholas; the Nataraja type became standard in this period.
Bhakti (devotional) hymns in Tamil praising Shiva’s dance at Chidambaram give the textual background for the image. On the exam.
If asked the ID → Shiva as Nataraja, Chola dynasty, Tamil Nadu, India, c. 11th century C.E., cast bronze by lost-wax.
If asked about iconography → drum = creation, fire = destruction, abhaya mudra = protection, pointing hand and raised foot = release, dwarf Apasmara = ignorance.
If asked about function → processional image carried on poles, dressed and adorned; daily puja in the temple.
If asked about form → movement balanced by the circle; diagonal limbs inside a ring.
Trap: it is Hindu (Shiva), not Buddhist; the hand gesture abhaya mudra appears in both religions.
Process fact: lost-wax means each mold is destroyed, so every Chola bronze is one of a kind.

203.title: Night Attack on the Sanjô Palace
203.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
203.plain: Night Attack on the Sanjō Palace is a long Japanese painted handscroll from the Kamakura period (about 1250 to 1300 C.E.) showing a real coup that happened in 1159. Rebel samurai storm the palace in Kyoto, set it on fire, kill guards and courtiers, and kidnap the retired emperor. You read it like a film strip, unrolling it right to left, and it is the classic exam comparison with the Alexander Mosaic.
203.spot: A long horizontal strip of paper crowded with tiny warriors on horseback, ox-drawn carriages, and a huge burst of red-orange flames and black smoke in the middle, all seen from a high angle with buildings drawn in diagonals.
203.remember: “Heiji, the palace is ablaze, 1159.” Night Attack = fire at night, read right to left like flipping manga backward. Painted about a century later, in the Kamakura period.
compare: No. 40 (§3.29), Alexander Mosaic, from the House of the Faun,…: The standard pair: both are chaotic battle scenes, one a single frozen moment in floor mosaic, the other a scroll read over time.
No. 59 (§4.12), Bayeux Tapestry: Both are long continuous narratives of real political violence made to tell the winners’ story.
No. 16 (§3.5), Standard of Ur, from the Royal Tombs at Ur: Both use sequential registers or scenes to tell war stories for elite viewers.
No. 111 (§5.13), Slave Ship: Both use violent fire-like reds and chaos to show catastrophe and human cruelty.
203.vocab: handscroll, continuous narrative, yamato-e, bird’s-eye view, samurai, emaki.

form: A handscroll (emaki, a long horizontal painted scroll) in ink and color on paper, about 41 centimeters tall and roughly 7 meters (about 23 feet) long. It is now in the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.
It is read right to left, unrolled about an arm’s length at a time, so the story unfolds in continuous narrative (the same figures reappearing as time passes).
The viewpoint is high and diagonal (bird’s-eye), with buildings drawn at angles; roofs are sometimes left off so you can see inside, a Yamato-e convention called the “blown-off roof.”
The scroll builds tension: it opens with a calm crowd of ox-carts and figures, crescendos at the burning palace in the center, then thins out to warriors riding off at the end.
Fire is painted with bright red and orange pigments and black ink for smoke; tiny figures have detailed armor, weapons and expressive faces.
The figures are small but numerous; violence is shown frankly, including beheadings and trampled bodies.
function: It illustrates the Heiji Monogatari (Tale of Heiji), a war tale told and recited about the conflict.
It was part of a set of scrolls telling the full story; only three of the scrolls survive, in Boston and in Japanese collections.
Handscrolls were viewed privately by one or two people at a table, rolling the scene along, so the viewer controls the pace like a reader.
For a samurai-era audience it recalled and glorified the dramatic events that led to warrior rule.
content: The subject is the Heiji Disturbance (Heiji Rebellion) of 1159: Fujiwara no Nobuyori and Minamoto no Yoshitomo attacked the Sanjō Palace in Kyoto and abducted the retired emperor Go-Shirakawa.
The emperor’s carriage, surrounded by soldiers, is the key moment; the burning palace marks the collapse of the old court order.
Courtiers, guards and women are killed or flee; the work shows the chaos and cruelty of war rather than glorifying one hero.
The rebels won only briefly: the rival Taira clan crushed them within weeks. Decades later the Minamoto won the Genpei War (1180 to 1185) and founded the first shogunate.
context: Painted in the Kamakura period (1185 to 1333), about a century after the event, when Japan was ruled by a shogun and the samurai class, not by the imperial court.
It looks back at the end of the elegant Heian court period and the rise of the warriors, so it is history painting with a political edge.
Its artist is unknown; it was likely made for an elite patron in court or warrior circles.

The American scholar Ernest Fenollosa acquired it in Japan in the 1880s, and it entered the Boston museum in 1911. It is considered one of the finest Japanese paintings outside Japan, raising questions about how Japanese treasures left the country in the Meiji era. On the exam.
If asked the ID → Night Attack on the Sanjō Palace, Kamakura period, Japan, c. 1250 to 1300 C.E., handscroll, ink and color on paper.
If asked how it is viewed → unrolled right to left, section by section, as a continuous narrative.
If asked about the event → Heiji Rebellion of 1159; Minamoto-backed rebels seize retired emperor Go-Shirakawa; painted a century later.

If asked to compare with the Alexander Mosaic (No. 40) → both show chaotic battles with crowds and diagonals; the mosaic freezes one climactic moment in stone tesserae for a Roman house, the scroll unfolds over time on portable paper.
Trap: it is a handscroll, not a hanging scroll, and it is Japanese, not Chinese.
Style terms: Yamato-e (Japanese-style painting), blown-off roof, high diagonal viewpoint.

204.title: The David Vases
204.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
204.plain: The David Vases are a matched pair of tall blue-and-white porcelain vases made in China in 1351, during the Yuan dynasty under Mongol rule. Their painted inscriptions name the donor, the temple and the exact date, which makes them the earliest securely dated blue-and-white porcelain known. Every other early piece of blue-and-white is dated by comparing it to these.
204.spot: Two tall, slender white vases about two feet high, painted in dark blue with a long scaly dragon among clouds around the body, many decorative bands, and two elephant-head handles on the neck, with a column of Chinese characters on the neck.
204.remember: David’s two vases, 1351 — “one-three-five-one, blue-and-white has begun.” Mongol Yuan dynasty, Persian blue on Chinese white.
compare: No. 250 (§11.27), Kui Hua Zi: Both are Jingdezhen porcelain; Ai Weiwei’s seeds use the same industry to comment on mass production and Mao-era China.
No. 188 (§8.8), Basin: Both are luxury objects shaped by trade between the Islamic world and other cultures.
No. 191 (§8.11), The Ardabil Carpet: Both are dated by an inscription naming the maker or donor and the year, with a pious purpose.
No. 7 (§2.7), Jade cong: Both are Chinese ritual objects in prestigious materials, jade and porcelain, made for communicating with the divine.
204.vocab: porcelain, underglaze, cobalt, votive, inscription, kaolin.

form: A pair of porcelain vases, each about 63.5 centimeters (25 inches) tall, with elephant-head handles on the neck that originally held loose porcelain rings, now lost.
Porcelain is made from kaolin (white clay) and petuntse (china stone), fired at around 1,300 °C so it becomes hard, white and slightly translucent.
The decoration is cobalt-blue underglaze: cobalt oxide was painted on the unfired clay, covered in clear glaze, and fired once, so the blue lies under a glassy surface.
The main band on each body shows a four-clawed dragon twisting among clouds; one dragon’s mouth is open, the other’s closed, so they are a deliberate pair.
Other horizontal bands carry lotus scrolls, flying phoenixes, plantain leaves, chrysanthemum and peony scrolls and petal panels, an orderly stack of registers.
Some blurring and darker spots in the blue come from the high-iron imported cobalt, a typical sign of Yuan blue-and-white.
function: They were votive offerings: an altar set (two vases and an incense burner) given to a temple to earn divine protection.
They stood on an altar, probably holding flowers, flanking the incense burner in front of an image of the temple’s deity.
Today they are evidence used by scholars as the dating benchmark for early blue-and-white porcelain.
content: The neck inscription says that Zhang Wenjin, a devotee from Yushan county in Jiangxi, donated the incense burner and vases to pray for his family’s protection and his descendants’ peace and prosperity.

The offering was made to the temple of a deified general, Generalissimo Hu Jingyi, at Xingyuan (in today’s Wuyuan county), usually described as a Daoist temple. It is dated the fourth month of the 11th year of the Zhizheng reign, which is 1351.
The dragon is a symbol of power, good fortune and the emperor; the phoenix symbolizes virtue and harmony, often paired with the dragon.
Flowers and lotus scrolls are auspicious motifs wishing for purity, long life and prosperity.
context: Yuan dynasty (1271 to 1368), founded by Kublai Khan, when China was part of the Mongol world empire that linked East Asia, Central Asia and Persia.
The cobalt was imported from Persia (Iran), and much Yuan blue-and-white was exported to the Islamic world, so these vases are products of global trade networks.
They are generally associated with the porcelain center at Jingdezhen in Jiangxi, although some researchers have suggested a kiln closer to the temple.

Sir Percival David, a British collector, bought the two vases separately (one in the 1920s, the other at a 1935 auction) and reunited them. They came to the Percival David Foundation in London and since 2009 have been on permanent display at the British Museum.
Blue-and-white became one of China’s most famous exports and was imitated around the world, from Iran to Delft in the Netherlands. On the exam.
If asked why they matter → they are the earliest dated blue-and-white porcelain (1351), the benchmark for dating others.
If asked about materials → white porcelain with cobalt underglaze; the cobalt was imported from Persia.
If asked about function → votive altar vases for a temple, donated by Zhang Wenjin for family protection.
If asked about context → Yuan (Mongol) dynasty, Silk Road and sea trade.
Trap: they are named after their modern collector, Sir Percival David, not the donor or the biblical David.
Trap: Ming is famous for blue-and-white, but these are Yuan, before Ming began in 1368.

205.title: Portrait of Sin Sukju (1417–1475)
205.medium: Hanging scroll (ink and color on silk)
205.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
205.plain: This is a Korean portrait on silk of Sin Sukju (1417–1475), a powerful scholaroﬀicial of the Joseon dynasty who helped King Sejong create the Korean alphabet, hangul. It was painted by court artists to honor him as a “meritorious subject” of the king, probably around 1455. It shows how Confucian Korea used portraits to record loyalty and to let families honor their ancestors.
205.spot: A full-length man seated on a folding chair, facing slightly to one side, in a green oﬀicial robe with a square embroidered badge on the chest, a black winged gauze hat, hands hidden in his sleeves, feet on a carved footstool, against a blank background.
205.remember: Sin Sukju: “Sin” sounds like “sign” — he helped design the signs of hangul. Joseon, 1400s, portrait for the ancestor shrine.
compare: No. 208 (§9.17), Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings: Both are court portraits showing rank and loyalty, but Jahangir’s is an allegory full of symbols while Sin Sukju’s is sober and documentary.
No. 42 (§3.31), Head of a Roman patrician: Both use carefully observed faces to honor an ancestor and express virtue within a family cult of ancestors.
No. 171 (§7.5), Ndop: Both are oﬀicial portraits of a leader whose identity is carried by symbols of rank as much as by likeness.
No. 99 (§5.1), Portrait of Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz: Both are portraits of learned figures that display intellect and status through attributes.
205.vocab: meritorious subject portrait, rank badge, ancestor veneration, Neo-Confucianism, hanging scroll, three-quarter view.

form: A hanging scroll in ink and color on silk, about 167 by 109.5 centimeters (about 5.5 by 3.6 feet), close to life size.
Sin Sukju sits full-length on a folding chair in three-quarter view (head and body turned slightly to one side), hands folded inside his sleeves, feet on a carved footstool.
He wears a green oﬀicial robe (the source data’s “red robe” is wrong), a black silk gauze hat with side wings, and a rank belt.

On his chest is a square rank badge embroidered in gold showing a pair of birds among clouds and plants. Smarthistory calls them peacocks; Korean heritage records describe them differently (as wild geese or silver pheasants), so the exact bird and rank are debated.
The robe is outlined in crisp, angular lines and filled with flat color, while the face is closely observed with fine shading and small details such as wrinkles, giving likeness.
The background is plain, focusing all attention on the sitter and his status.
function: An oﬀicial meritorious subject portrait: the king rewarded loyal oﬀicials with titles, land and a court-painted portrait. Sin Sukju was named a meritorious subject four times.
After his death the portrait hung in a family shrine for ancestor veneration, where descendants made offerings and bowed before it.

It is still kept by his descendants, the Goryeong Sin clan, at a family shrine near Cheongju; it was designated Treasure number 613 in 1977, and in 2024 the Korean government moved to upgrade it to National Treasure status.
content: In Neo-Confucian thought a portrait must be accurate down to a single hair, because a wrong likeness meant honoring someone else during ancestral rites; hence the careful face.
The robe, hat, belt and badge are a visual résumé of rank and loyalty to the king, values at the heart of Confucian government.
The calm, dignified pose expresses ideal virtues: self-control, moral seriousness and devotion to duty.
Sin Sukju was a linguist and scholar who worked on hangul (the Korean alphabet, announced 1446) and served six kings, rising to chief state councillor (prime minister).
context: Joseon dynasty (1392 to 1910), which made Neo-Confucianism the state ideology, replacing Buddhism’s political influence.
Painted by artists of the Royal (Imperial) Bureau of Painting, the court painting oﬀice; the individual painter is not recorded.

It was probably made in 1455, when Sin Sukju was rewarded after supporting King Sejo’s seizure of the throne. Records indicate it was redone or retouched in 1475 and touched up later, so not every surface is 15th century.
Sin Sukju’s career is controversial in Korea: he sided with Sejo, who forced out his young nephew, while other scholars refused and were executed, so he is seen as both brilliant and opportunistic.
It is among the oldest surviving Korean meritorious subject portraits, which makes it an anchor for studying Joseon portraiture. On the exam.
If asked the ID → Portrait of Sin Sukju, Imperial (Royal) Bureau of Painting, Joseon dynasty Korea, c. 15th century C.E., ink and color on silk, hanging scroll.
If asked about function → honoring a meritorious subject and later ancestor veneration in a family shrine.
If asked why the face is so detailed → Neo-Confucian belief that an accurate likeness is a moral and ritual necessity.
If asked about status symbols → rank badge, oﬀicial robe, gauze hat, belt, chair and footstool.
Fact: Sin Sukju helped King Sejong create hangul.
Trap: it is Korean, not Chinese or Japanese; Joseon dynasty.

206.title: Forbidden City
206.medium: Stone masonry, marble, brick, wood, and ceramic tile
206.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
206.plain: The Forbidden City is the enormous walled palace complex in the center of Beijing where Chinese emperors lived and ruled from 1420 to 1912. Built for the Ming dynasty’s Yongle emperor and expanded later, it has roughly 980 surviving buildings laid out on a strict north-south line. Every gate, courtyard and roof color is arranged to show that the emperor sat at the center of the world.
206.spot: Vast paved courtyards and long rows of red-walled halls with sweeping golden-yellow tiled roofs, set on white marble terraces with carved balustrades, all symmetrical along a central axis; the biggest hall sits on a three-tiered white marble platform.
206.remember: Ming built it, Qing kept it, Yongle started it (1406 to 1420). Yellow roofs = emperor only; everything faces south toward the people.
compare: No. 93 (§4.46), The Palace at Versailles: Both are royal palaces planned on axes to express absolute monarchy and control access to the ruler.
No. 30 (§3.19), Audience Hall: Both use raised platforms, vast halls and processional approaches to stage imperial audiences.
No. 65 (§4.18), Alhambra: Both are palace complexes of nested courtyards that grow more private toward the ruler’s quarters.
No. 159 (§6.7), City of Cusco: Both are capitals planned to put the ruler at the symbolic center of the cosmos and empire.
206.vocab: axial plan, post-and-lintel, bracket system, hierarchical scale, courtyard, feng shui, terrace.

form: A rectangular walled city of about 72 hectares (roughly 180 acres), surrounded by a moat about 52 meters wide and walls about 8 meters (26 feet) high, with a watchtower at each corner.

The buildings mainly use post-and-lintel timber frames: wooden columns hold up beams, and interlocking wooden bracket sets (dougong) carry the heavy overhanging roofs. Walls do not carry the roof load.
Materials: wood (prized nanmu timber from southwest China), brick, stone and white marble terraces, and ceramic roof tiles glazed yellow, a color reserved for the emperor.
Strict axial symmetry: the main halls line up on a north-south axis, and side buildings mirror each other on either side.

The Hall of Supreme Harmony (Taihedian) is the largest hall, on a three-tier marble platform; it has a double-eaved hip roof (the highest-ranking roof type) and ten small guardian figures on each roof ridge, more than any other building.
Courtyards get smaller and more private as you move north, from huge ceremonial plazas to intimate residential courts.
function: The imperial palace and the center of government for 24 emperors of the Ming and Qing dynasties, from 1420 until the last emperor, Puyi, abdicated in 1912.
The Outer Court (south) held the three great ceremonial halls for coronations, imperial birthdays, New Year rites and state ceremonies.
The Inner Court (north) was the residence of the emperor, empress, concubines and eunuchs. Access was tightly controlled: rank decided how far inside you could go.
It became the Palace Museum in 1925 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987; today it receives millions of visitors a year.
content: The emperor was the Son of Heaven, the link between heaven and earth. The palace at the center of Beijing, center of the empire, mirrors the Pole Star at the center of the heavens; the “purple” in its Chinese name refers to that star.
The palace faces south, as the emperor did on his throne; south was the direction of warmth and authority, and oﬀicials approached from the south.

Numbers and colors carry meaning: yellow (the color of the center and the emperor), red walls (good fortune), and the repeated use of nine (the highest odd, or yang, number) in door-nail grids and roof figures.
The sequence of gates and courtyards turns politics into space: walking north through evernarrowing gates performs hierarchy.
Later additions such as the Palace of Tranquility and Longevity, built 1771 to 1776 for the Qing Qianlong emperor’s retirement, show how later rulers extended the complex.
context: Built under the third Ming emperor, Yongle, between 1406 and 1420, when he moved the capital from Nanjing to Beijing. Tradition says about 100,000 craftsmen and up to a million laborers worked on it.
Its plan draws on old Chinese city ideals from ritual texts and on feng shui principles: an artificial hill (Jingshan) protects it to the north and water flows on the south side.
Many halls burned and were rebuilt, so much of what stands is Qing work; the current Hall of Supreme Harmony dates largely from 1695.

Puyi was allowed to live in the inner court until he was expelled in 1924. During the Chinese Civil War the Nationalists moved many treasures to Taiwan, which is why Taipei’s National Palace Museum holds imperial collections (including No. 201). On the exam.
If asked the ID → Forbidden City, Ming dynasty, Beijing, 15th century C.E. and later; stone, marble, brick, wood and ceramic tile.
If asked how architecture shows power → axial symmetry, hierarchical courtyard sequence, controlled access, yellow imperial roofs, buildings raised on marble terraces.
If asked about cosmology → emperor as Son of Heaven at the center of the world, facing south.
If asked about construction → timber post-and-lintel with bracket sets supporting heavy tiled roofs.
Trap: built by the Ming (Yongle emperor), but also used and heavily rebuilt by the Qing; it is not a Qing creation.
Fact: imperial palace for about 500 years (1420 to 1912), now the Palace Museum.

207.title: Ryoan-ji
207.date: c. 1480 C.E.; current design most likely 18th century
207.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
207.plain: Ryōan-ji is a Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan, famous for its dry rock garden: a rectangle of raked white gravel with 15 rocks set in small clusters, enclosed by a low earthen wall. The temple was founded in 1450 and rebuilt about 1488 (the source’s c. 1480), but the garden as we see it most likely dates from the 18th century. It is meant to be looked at quietly from a wooden veranda, not walked through.
207.spot: A flat rectangle of white gravel raked into straight parallel lines with circular ripples around a few low, dark rocks sitting on small patches of moss, viewed from a wooden veranda, backed by a low tan-and-brown stained clay wall with a tile roof and trees beyond.
207.remember: Ryōan-ji = “Ryo” rhymes with “no”: no water, no plants, no walking in. 15 rocks, but you can only ever see 14.
compare: No. 65 (§4.18), Alhambra: Both are gardens tied to sacred ideas, but the Alhambra’s lush water courts picture paradise while Ryōan-ji uses absence for meditation.
No. 139 (§5.41), Fallingwater: Both use natural materials and site to create calm harmony between architecture and nature; Wright admired Japanese design.
No. 151 (§5.53), Spiral Jetty: Both are earthworks of rock and ground shaped into a landscape to be contemplated, raising questions about permanence and change.
No. 209 (§9.18), Taj Mahal: Both are gardens with religious meaning: the Taj’s charbagh is a symmetrical paradise, Ryōan-ji an asymmetrical void.
207.vocab: karesansui, Zen, borrowed scenery, asymmetry, wabi-sabi, meditation.

form: A karesansui (dry landscape garden) about 25 by 10 meters (roughly 82 by 33 feet), covered in white gravel raked into lines and ripples.
Fifteen rocks are arranged in five groups (counted as 5, 2, 3, 2, 3), each set into a small island of moss.
From any single seat on the veranda at least one rock is always hidden behind another, so the full set can never be seen at once.
The garden is bounded on two sides by a low wall of clay mixed with oil; over time the oil has seeped out, staining the wall in soft brown patterns that are now part of the effect.
There are no flowers or water; the only plant is moss. The trees beyond the wall serve as borrowed scenery (shakkei, using the landscape outside as part of the view).
The design is asymmetrical and spare, with large areas of empty space, a key Zen aesthetic.
function: A contemplative garden of a Rinzai Zen temple, viewed seated from the veranda of the hōjō (abbot’s quarters).
It supports meditation (zazen): the viewer is meant to empty the mind and see clearly, not to interpret one fixed meaning.
Monks rake the gravel as a disciplined practice of mindfulness; maintaining the garden is itself a spiritual exercise.
Today it is a major pilgrimage and tourist site, part of the UNESCO World Heritage listing of Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (1994).
content: The gravel is usually read as water (sea, river or clouds) and the rocks as islands or mountain peaks, a whole landscape in miniature.
Other traditional readings: a tigress carrying her cubs across a river, or mountain tops rising above clouds. Zen intentionally leaves the meaning open.
The hidden fifteenth rock is often explained as a lesson about incompleteness: full understanding (enlightenment) cannot be seen with ordinary eyes.
A stone water basin nearby is carved with characters read as “I only know contentment,” a Zen teaching about desire.
context: The temple was founded in 1450 by the warlord Hosokawa Katsumoto in the Muromachi period (1336 to 1573); it burned in the Ōnin War and was rebuilt in 1488 by his son.

The garden’s designer and date are uncertain. Later legends credited the painter Sōami, but this is doubted. Two names carved on a rock, Kotarō and Hikojirō, may be those of the laborers (kawaramono) who set the stones.
The current layout is probably from the Edo period (18th century); the abbot’s hall burned in 1797, and a guidebook of 1799 shows the garden.
Zen Buddhism, favored by the samurai class, valued simplicity, discipline and direct perception; related aesthetic ideas include wabi-sabi (beauty in the plain, imperfect and impermanent).
Since the 20th century it has become a symbol of Japanese minimalism and has influenced modern Western designers and artists. On the exam.
If asked the ID → Ryōan-ji, Kyoto, Japan, Muromachi period, c. 1480 C.E.; current design most likely 18th century; rock garden.
If asked about function → Zen meditation, viewed from the abbot’s veranda, not entered.
If asked what the elements represent → gravel as water or sea, rocks as islands or peaks; meaning deliberately open.
If asked about the trick → 15 rocks, but only 14 visible from any one viewpoint.
If asked about dating problems → temple founded 1450 and rebuilt 1488, but the garden in its current form is likely Edo period.
Trap: it is a dry garden (karesansui); there is no real water in the famous rock garden.

208.title: Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings
208.medium: Watercolor, gold, and ink on paper
208.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
208.plain: This small, jewel-like Mughal album painting by the court artist Bichitr, made around 1615 to 1620, shows Emperor Jahangir on an hourglass throne choosing to give a book to a Muslim holy man instead of paying attention to the kings waiting to see him, one of them King James I of England. It is political flattery in picture form: Jahangir is shown as more spiritual and more powerful than any other ruler on earth.
208.spot: A small vertical page: a haloed Mughal ruler in a turban seated on a tall golden hourglass at upper left, chubby European-style cherubs flying at the top and writing at the bottom, and four men lined up at lower left including a white-bearded holy man and a pale European king in a lace collar.
208.remember: Jahangir picks a Sufi over kings, by Bichitr (“bitter” for the kings). Hourglass throne, sun-and-moon halo, James I in the corner, about 1620.
compare: No. 190 (§8.10), The Court of Gayumars: Both are Persianate court paintings with tiny detail, gold and jewel colors; Mughal painting grew out of the Safavid tradition.
No. 86 (§4.39), Henri IV Receives the Portrait of Marie de’ M…: Both are political allegories flattering a ruler with mythological or symbolic figures borrowed from other traditions.
No. 205 (§9.14), Portrait of Sin Sukju: Both are court portraits about rank and loyalty: symbolic and boastful versus sober and documentary.
No. 94 (§4.47), Screen with the Siege of Belgrade and hunting…: Both are hybrid works showing how European and Asian visual cultures mixed through global trade and diplomacy.
208.vocab: album page, allegory, halo, putto, naturalism, muraqqa, Sufism.

form: Opaque watercolor, gold and ink on paper, about 25 by 18 centimeters (10 by 7 inches); it was mounted with decorative borders as an album page.
Jahangir sits on an hourglass throne, framed by an enormous halo that combines a golden sun and a silver crescent moon.
Below him, four figures in a column: a Sufi shaikh receiving a book, an Ottoman sultan, King James I of England, and the painter Bichitr himself.
Faces are highly naturalistic portraits in profile or three-quarter view, a Mughal specialty. James I is shown in three-quarter view because he was copied from an English painting.
European elements: winged putti (cherubs), modeling with light and shadow, and the James I portrait. Persian and Indian elements: flat patterned carpet, bright jewel colors, gold, and calligraphy.
Bichitr signed the work on the footstool beneath Jahangir’s feet, a clever, modest placement.
function: A page for an imperial muraqqa (album) of paintings and calligraphy, looked at privately by the emperor and his close circle.
A political allegory: it flatters Jahangir’s piety and his superiority over rival rulers.
It also served the artist’s career, since Bichitr includes himself, showing what he hoped to gain from royal favor.
It is now in the Freer Gallery of Art, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C.
content: Jahangir hands a book to the shaikh, generally identified as Shaikh Husain of the Chishti Sufi shrine at Ajmer, a family linked to the Mughals. The message: spiritual wisdom matters more to him than worldly power.

The sultan and James I are ranked below the holy man; Jahangir ignores them. In reality England’s ambassador, Sir Thomas Roe (at court 1615 to 1619), struggled to win trade terms, so the painting puts England in its place.

The hourglass suggests time running out, but the putti write on it in Persian a wish that the emperor’s reign last a thousand years. At the top, other putti turn away, one covering its eyes as if dazzled.
The sun-and-moon halo plays on Jahangir’s title Nur al-Din (“Light of the Faith”) and on his wife Nur Jahan (“Light of the World”).
Bichitr holds a small painting showing himself bowing, with an elephant and horses: a reminder of the rewards he hopes the emperor will give.
context: Mughal dynasty, India. Jahangir ruled 1605 to 1627; he loved painting, natural science and portraiture, and kept a large court workshop.
European prints, paintings and Bibles arrived through Jesuit missionaries and English and Portuguese diplomats and traders; Mughal artists copied and reworked them.
The James I portrait was probably based on a painting by John de Critz brought by Roe. The Ottoman sultan is probably a generic type, not a real likeness.
Some Persian verses on the page praise the emperor as one who, though kings stand before him, fixes his gaze on holy men. The Freer dates it c. 1615 to 1618; the College Board says c. 1620.
Jahangir’s power was real but complicated: Nur Jahan held great influence, and he struggled with alcohol and opium, which adds irony to the claims of eternal reign. On the exam.
If asked the ID → Bichitr, Jahangir Preferring a Sufi Shaikh to Kings, Mughal India, c. 1620 C.E., watercolor, gold and ink on paper.
If asked about meaning → an allegory: Jahangir prefers spiritual authority (Sufi shaikh) to worldly kings, and outranks everyone.
If asked about cross-cultural influence → European putti, modeling and the copied portrait of James I blended with Persian and Indian painting.
If asked about the hourglass → time and mortality, countered by the inscribed wish for a thousand-year reign.
Trap: the artist painted himself at lower left, holding a painting, and signed the footstool.
Trap: an album page for private viewing, not a manuscript illustration of a story or a wall painting.

209.title: Taj Mahal
209.artist: Supervising architect Ustad Ahmad Lahori; Agra, Uttar Pradesh, India
209.medium: Stone masonry and marble with inlay of precious and semiprecious stones; gar-
209.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
209.plain: The Taj Mahal in Agra, India, is a white marble tomb built from 1632 to 1653 by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan for his wife Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631 giving birth to their fourteenth child. It sits at the end of a huge walled garden meant to represent paradise. Its perfect symmetry, inlaid stone flowers and Qur’anic inscriptions make it the summit of Mughal architecture.
209.spot: A gleaming white marble domed building on a square platform with four tall slender minarets at the corners, a big onion-shaped dome over a tall arched entrance, reflected in a long straight water channel lined with trees.
209.remember: Shah Jahan + Mumtaz Mahal: “Taj” means crown, “Mumtaz” crowned in marble. Built 1632 to 1653, the year after she died, finished about two decades later.
compare: No. 17 (§3.6), Great Pyramids: Both are colossal royal tombs that use pure geometry and expensive materials to proclaim eternal power.
No. 65 (§4.18), Alhambra: Both use water channels and gardens to evoke the Islamic paradise.
No. 84 (§4.37), Mosque of Selim II : Both are Islamic imperial buildings with large domes, slender minarets and Qur’anic inscriptions.
No. 183 (§8.3), The Kaaba: Both are Islamic sacred sites built around a central focus, one a pilgrimage shrine, the other a tomb modeled on paradise.
209.vocab: mausoleum, pietra dura, charbagh, iwan, minaret, cenotaph, onion dome, symmetry.

form: A mausoleum of white Makrana marble over a brick core, on a square raised plinth, with four freestanding minarets that lean very slightly outward, probably so they would fall away from the tomb in an earthquake.
The tomb has chamfered corners (an octagonal plan within a square) and an iwan (tall arched portal set in a rectangular frame) on each side.
A double dome: a tall bulbous outer onion dome (about 73 meters, roughly 240 feet, to the top of its finial) over a lower inner dome, so the inside room keeps human proportions.
Decoration uses pietra dura (Mughal parchin kari): semiprecious stones such as jasper, carnelian and lapis lazuli inlaid in marble to form flowers and vines, plus carved low-relief flowers.

Qur’anic calligraphy in black marble frames the arches; the letters get larger toward the top so they appear the same size from the ground, an optical correction attributed to the calligrapher Amanat Khan.

The complex is perfectly symmetrical: a red sandstone mosque on one side is balanced by an identical guest hall (jawab, “answer”) on the other, and a monumental gateway faces the tomb across the garden.
function: A tomb for Mumtaz Mahal; Shah Jahan was later buried beside her in 1666. Their real graves are in a lower crypt; marble cenotaphs (empty symbolic tombs) sit in the main hall behind a pierced marble screen.
Shah Jahan’s cenotaph, added off-center beside hers, is the only asymmetrical element in the whole complex.
A place of commemoration, prayer and pilgrimage, with an annual memorial (urs); the mosque was used for Friday prayers.
A statement of dynastic power and piety, meant to impress visitors and posterity.
content: The charbagh (four-part garden divided by water channels) represents the gardens of paradise described in the Qur’an, with its four rivers.

Unusually, the tomb sits at the end of the garden, on the riverbank, not in its center. One influential theory (by Wayne Begley) reads the whole site as a model of the Throne of God above paradise on the Day of Judgment.
Inscriptions include Qur’anic passages about judgment, mercy and paradise, which supports the paradise reading.
The pietra dura flowers make the building a permanent garden in stone, echoing paradise imagery inside and out.
context: Mughal dynasty, mixing Persian (Timurid) plans, Indian building crafts and Islamic religious forms; Humayun’s Tomb in Delhi is an earlier model.
Supervising architect usually named as Ustad Ahmad Lahori; around 20,000 workers and craftsmen from across the empire and beyond worked on it. Materials came from all over Asia.
Shah Jahan (ruled 1628 to 1658) was deposed by his son Aurangzeb and spent his last years confined in Agra Fort, within sight of the Taj.
Across the Yamuna River lies the Mahtab Bagh (Moonlight Garden), aligned with the Taj; the legend of a planned “black Taj” there is not supported by evidence.
It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983. Air pollution yellows the marble, so India restricts nearby industry and the marble is periodically cleaned with clay packs. On the exam.
If asked the ID → Taj Mahal, Agra, India, Ustad Ahmad Lahori (supervising architect), 1632 to 1653 C.E., stone masonry and marble with inlay of precious and semiprecious stones; gardens.
If asked about function → tomb of Mumtaz Mahal, built by Shah Jahan; both are buried there.
If asked about the garden → charbagh representing paradise; tomb at the end, not the center.
If asked about technique → pietra dura inlay and scaled calligraphy that reads evenly from below.
If asked about symmetry → perfect bilateral symmetry, mosque balanced by the jawab; the only exception is Shah Jahan’s cenotaph.
Trap: it is a tomb, not a palace or a mosque, though a mosque stands beside it.

210.title: White and Red Plum Blossoms
210.medium: Ink, watercolor, and gold leaf on paper
210.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
210.plain: White and Red Plum Blossoms is a pair of Japanese folding screens painted by Ogata Kōrin around 1710 to 1716 in the Edo period. A white-flowered plum tree on the left screen and a red-flowered one on the right lean toward a wide, swirling stream, all set on a gold background. It is the signature work of the Rinpa school, which turned nature into bold, flat, luxurious design.
210.spot: Two gold screens side by side with a dark, stylized river swelling down the middle in rhythmic swirling patterns; a gnarled tree with white blossoms at far left and a tree with red blossoms at right, their trunks mottled with blurry green and black patches.
210.remember: Kōrin’s plums: “Kō-rin” sounds like “coral” — red plum on the right, white on the left, a curly river in between, about 1710. Rinpa is named after Kōrin.
compare: No. 94 (§4.47), Screen with the Siege of Belgrade and hunting…: The Mexican biombo adapts the Japanese byōbu folding screen, showing how the format traveled through trade.
No. 211 (§9.20), Under the Wave off Kanagawa: Both are Edo-period Japanese works that flatten nature into strong decorative design.
No. 201 (§9.10), Travelers among Mountains and Streams: Both are East Asian nature paintings: Fan Kuan’s illusionistic ink depth versus Kōrin’s flat gold surface.
No. 128 (§5.30), The Kiss: Klimt’s gold-leaf patterning and flat decoration were influenced by Japanese art like Rinpa.
210.vocab: byōbu, folding screen, tarashikomi, gold leaf, Rinpa, asymmetry.

form: A pair of two-panel folding screens (byōbu), each about 156 by 172 centimeters (about 5 by 5.6 feet); the source data’s “a two-panel screen” should be a pair. They are painted in ink, color and gold leaf on paper.
The flat gold background gives no sense of real space; the river and trees float on it as patterned shapes.
The trunks use tarashikomi (dropping ink or color into still-wet paint so it pools and blurs), producing soft mottled patches like moss and bark.

The central stream is painted with dark pigment over what was silver, now tarnished; its curling wave lines are drawn so rhythmically they look like a textile pattern. Scientists and historians still debate exactly how the gold and stream surfaces were made.
The blossoms are drawn with crisp small dots and outlines, more naturalistic than the stylized stream: Kōrin mixes observation with design.
The composition is asymmetrical: the white plum mostly cropped by the left edge, the red plum fuller on the right, with the stream’s widening shape filling the gap.
function: Folding screens were portable furniture: they divided rooms, blocked drafts, gave privacy and created backdrops in wooden Japanese houses, while the gold reflected dim light.
Screens were often brought out for particular seasons or occasions; plum screens suit late winter and early spring.

Luxury screens displayed the wealth and taste of their owners. These screens were long owned by the Tsugaru family, a daimyō (lord) clan, and are now a National Treasure at the MOA Museum of Art in Atami.
content: The plum blooms in late winter, often while snow is still on the ground, so it symbolizes the arrival of spring, renewal, endurance and perseverance.
The pairing of white and red, old and young, left and right, sets up a balance of contrasts, sometimes read in terms of yin and yang.
The stream suggests flowing time and change between the two trees; its decorative curls turn water into ornament.
The plum also had literary associations in classical Japanese and Chinese poetry, which Rinpa artists liked to revive.
context: Ogata Kōrin (1658 to 1716) came from a wealthy Kyoto family that ran the Kariganeya, a textile business supplying elite women; his feel for pattern comes from that background. His brother was the potter Ogata Kenzan.
He made this late in life, near the end of the Edo period’s Genroku cultural boom, when merchants were growing rich despite ranking low in the oﬀicial social order.
Rinpa (“Rin school”) is named after Kōrin; it looked back to earlier artists Hon’ami Kōetsu and Tawaraya Sōtatsu and favored bold design, gold and silver, and classical themes.
Rinpa was not a workshop or guild but a style revived by admirers across generations; it later influenced Art Nouveau designers and Gustav Klimt (No. 128). On the exam.
If asked the ID → Ogata Kōrin, White and Red Plum Blossoms, Edo period Japan, c. 1710 to 1716 C.E., ink, watercolor and gold leaf on paper; pair of folding screens.
If asked the school → Rinpa: bold, flat, decorative, gold backgrounds.
If asked about technique → tarashikomi on the trunks; gold leaf; stylized stream pattern.
If asked about meaning → plum blossoms = late winter and spring, endurance.
If asked about function → byōbu, folding screens for interior decoration and dividing space.
Trap: Kōrin’s family background is textiles, which explains the patterned stream; do not call him a woodblock printmaker.

211.title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa (Great Wave)
211.artist: Katsushika Hokusai, from Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji
211.medium: Polychrome woodblock print; ink and color on paper
211.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
211.plain: The Great Wave is a Japanese color woodblock print by Katsushika Hokusai, published around 1830 to 1833 as part of his series Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji. A huge clawed wave is about to crash over three boats of rowers, while Mount Fuji sits small in the distance. It was cheap popular art in Edo Japan and became one of the most widely reproduced images in the world.
211.spot: A rectangular print with a towering dark-blue wave curling from the left, its white foam breaking into claw-like fingers, three long narrow boats with crouching rowers, and a small snow-capped Mount Fuji low in the center background.
211.remember: Hokusai’s wave: “Ho! Kusai, a wave!” Around 1830, 36 Views of Fuji, Prussian blue. The tiny mountain is the real subject.
compare: No. 121 (§5.23), The Coiffure: Cassatt’s color prints borrow ukiyo-e flat color, outlines and cropping, a direct case of Japonisme.
No. 111 (§5.13), Slave Ship: Both show the sea as a destructive force, but Turner paints a moral catastrophe in loose oil while Hokusai designs a crisp print.
No. 120 (§5.22), The Starry Night: Van Gogh collected Japanese prints; his swirling sky and bold outlines owe something to ukiyo-e.
No. 210 (§9.19), White and Red Plum Blossoms: Both are Edo-period works that stylize water into rhythmic decorative pattern.
211.vocab: woodblock print, ukiyo-e, Prussian blue, Japonisme, key block.

form: A polychrome woodblock print (ukiyo-e) in ink and color on paper, about 25 by 37 centimeters (10 by 15 inches), a standard horizontal format.
It was made with several carved woodblocks, one for the black outlines (the key block) and others for each color, printed one after another in exact register.
Hokusai used Prussian blue, a synthetic blue pigment recently imported into Japan, for the deep intense blues of the wave and sky.
The wave’s curve forms a strong diagonal and frame; its foam splits into claw-like tendrils, while a small foreground wave echoes Fuji’s triangle.
Space uses a low horizon and a Western-influenced sense of linear perspective, yet the shapes stay flat and outlined, a mix of Japanese and European conventions.
Japanese viewers read right to left, so the boats appear to be rowing into the wave from their point of view.
function: A commercial print sold cheaply to a broad urban public in Edo (Tokyo), roughly the price of a double serving of noodles.

Part of a series, Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, that grew to 46 prints because it sold so well. It is often listed first, but the series’ original order is not certain (the source says it was “the first print,” which is not established).
It also catered to a craze for travel and for pilgrimages to sacred Mount Fuji.
Thousands of impressions were pulled; surviving early impressions now sit in major museums worldwide.
content: Nature’s overwhelming force against fragile human beings, who survive by working together and keeping low in their boats.
Mount Fuji, Japan’s sacred volcano, stands calm and permanent at the center, linked with immortality (one reading of the name is “without equal” or “deathless”).
The scale trick: the near wave dwarfs the distant mountain, a playful reversal that makes viewers look twice.
The boats are oshiokuri-bune, fast boats carrying fresh fish to the Edo market, so this is everyday working life within a dramatic landscape.
context: Katsushika Hokusai (1760 to 1849) was a hugely prolific artist who changed his name many times; this print is signed “from the brush of Hokusai, changing his name to Iitsu.” He was about 70 when he made it.
Prints were made in a publisher system: the designer (Hokusai), a carver and a printer worked for a publisher, here Nishimuraya Yohachi (Eijudō), who financed and sold them.
Ukiyo-e means “pictures of the floating world,” originally the pleasure districts and theater of Edo; Hokusai pushed the genre into landscape.

Edo Japan restricted foreign contact, but Dutch traders brought Western prints and goods. After Japan opened in the 1850s, prints flowed to Europe and fueled Japonisme, influencing Monet, van Gogh, Cassatt (No. 121) and Debussy, whose La Mer score used the wave. On the exam.
If asked the ID → Katsushika Hokusai, Under the Wave off Kanagawa (Great Wave), from Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, Edo period, 1830 to 1833 C.E., polychrome woodblock print.
If asked about technique → woodblock printing, multiple blocks, imported Prussian blue, collaboration of designer, carver, printer and publisher.
If asked about audience → mass-produced, affordable, popular art for townspeople, not elite court art.
If asked about global influence → Japonisme: cropping, flat color and bold outlines influenced European Impressionists and Post-Impressionists.
If asked about cross-cultural exchange → Western perspective and pigment absorbed into a Japanese print, then sent back to the West.
Trap: it is a print (many copies), not a painting; and Hokusai designed it but did not carve or print it himself.

212.title: Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan
212.artist: Based on painting by Liu Chunhua
212.content: CA8, South, East, and Southeast Asia
212.plain: This is a mass-printed color lithograph of a 1967 oil painting by Liu Chunhua showing the young Mao Zedong striding across hills on his way to organize coal miners at Anyuan in the early 1920s. Made during China’s Cultural Revolution, it turned Mao into a heroic, almost holy figure and quietly erased a rival from history. Reportedly reproduced around 900 million times, it may be the most reproduced image of the 20th century.
212.spot: A young long-haired man in a long, pale traditional Chinese robe walking straight toward the viewer, a rolled oil-paper umbrella under his arm and a clenched fist, on a high mountain path with swirling clouds behind him and a bright sky around his head.
212.remember: Mao “on route” with an umbrella: the umbrella is “the rain he’ll bring” to the miners. Painted 1967, printed by the hundreds of millions around 1968 to 1969: Cultural Revolution propaganda.
compare: No. 137 (§5.39), Illustration from The Results of the First Fi…: Both are Communist propaganda in poster form using bold imagery to glorify the state and its leader.
No. 43 (§3.32), Augustus of Prima Porta: Both are idealized images of a leader spread widely to build a political cult.
No. 250 (§11.27), Kui Hua Zi: Ai Weiwei’s sunflower seeds refer to Mao-era imagery of the people as seeds turning toward Mao as the sun.
No. 147 (§5.49), Marilyn Diptych: Both are mass-reproduced images of a celebrity whose repetition turns the person into an icon.
212.vocab: lithograph, Socialist Realism, propaganda, cult of personality, mass production. 10 The Pacific Content area 9 · 700–1980 C.E. · works 213–223 · about 4% of the multiple-choice section. Art of the Pacific Islands (Polynesia, Micronesia and Melanesia): carved ancestor figures, feather capes, navigation charts, tattoo designs, ceremonial houses and barkcloth. Two ideas show up everywhere: mana (spiritual power) and tapu (sacred restriction). Many works were meant to be performed, exchanged or allowed to decay, not kept forever in a museum.

form: A color lithograph (a print made from a flat stone or plate where greasy ink sticks only to the drawn areas) reproducing an oil painting by Liu Chunhua, about 2.2 by 1.8 meters in the original.
The style is Socialist Realism (the oﬀicial Communist style: realistic, clear, and idealized to inspire), with smooth modeling and dramatic lighting.
Mao is placed in the exact center, close to the viewer, alone, and slightly above the horizon, so we look up at him.
Light falls on his face as if he himself were the source of brightness; clouds part behind him like a halo, and wind lifts his robe.
His details are carefully chosen: a long traditional gown (not Western clothes), an oil-paper umbrella, a clenched fist and a firm, forward gaze.
Liu said he studied old photographs and interviewed Anyuan workers, and some scholars note borrowings from Western religious painting, giving Mao a saint-like aura.
function: Propaganda for the Cultural Revolution (1966 to 1976), promoting the cult of Mao.

It was published in color in 1968 in major Communist Party publications and then printed as posters, on badges, on stamps and even woven and sculpted; families hung it at home almost like a religious icon.
Displaying Mao’s image was a sign of loyalty; failing to respect it could be dangerous.
It also rewrote history for political purposes (see below).
content: It shows Mao’s trip to the Anyuan coal mines in Jiangxi province in 1921, which helped lead to the major Anyuan miners’ strike of 1922.
Mao is the lone hero of the revolution; the umbrella suggests he is ready for any storm, and the fist shows determination.
It follows Cultural Revolution rules for depicting Mao: “red, bright and shining” and the “three prominences” (make the hero the most prominent figure of all).
Its political point is what is left out: Liu Shaoqi and Li Lisan actually led much of the Anyuan strike, but Liu had been purged as a traitor in 1966 to 1968, so the image gives Mao all the credit.
context: Liu Chunhua (born 1944) was a young art student in Beijing when he painted it in 1967 for a student-organized exhibition on Mao’s thought and the Anyuan workers’ movement.
At first the work was presented as a collective effort by Beijing students and only later credited to Liu; the student group planned the exhibition together.
During the Cultural Revolution most artistic freedom was suppressed; artists had to serve politics, and individual style was distrusted.

After Mao died, Liu Shaoqi was rehabilitated (1980) and the image lost its role. In 1995 Liu Chunhua auctioned the original canvas for about 6 million yuan, and the museum that had held it sued him over ownership (not authorship, as the source data says).
Today the image survives in kitsch Mao memorabilia and in Chinese contemporary art that reuses it critically. On the exam.
If asked the ID → Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan, based on a painting by Liu Chunhua, c. 1969 C.E., color lithograph.
If asked about function → propaganda and personality cult during the Cultural Revolution, printed about 900 million times.
If asked about style → Socialist Realism: idealized, heroic, centrally placed, illuminated leader.
If asked about medium → lithography allowed cheap, mass reproduction of a painting.
If asked about political rewriting → omits Liu Shaoqi, who led the strike but had been purged.
Trap: the lithograph is by unknown printmakers after Liu’s oil painting; Liu did not make the print himself.

213.title: Nan Madol
213.plain: Nan Madol is a ruined city of nearly one hundred human-made islands built on a coral reef off the island of Pohnpei in Micronesia, walled with naturally many-sided basalt columns stacked like a log cabin. It was the political, religious and burial center of the Saudeleur dynasty, the first rulers to unite all of Pohnpei. It matters because it shows architecture used to gather, display and control power, built with no metal tools, no wheel and no draft animals.
213.spot: Dark gray-black stone ‘logs’ laid in crisscrossing layers, like a giant Lincoln Log cabin, rising from shallow water and mangroves. The big Nandauwas enclosure has thick walls with corners that tilt slightly upward.
213.remember: Nan Madol: the Saudeleur kept rival chiefs close enough to drive them MAD. Stone logs on a reef, Pohnpei, Micronesia, roughly 700 to 1600 C.E.
compare: No. 167 (§7.1), Conical tower and circular wall of Great Zimb…: Both are mortarless stone royal centers whose massive walls displayed and protected elite power.
No. 8 (§2.8), Stonehenge: Both needed huge organized labor to move multi-ton stones long distances without wheels or metal tools.
No. 214 (§10.2), Moai on platform: Both are Pacific megalithic projects tied to ancestors and chiefly power, one architecture and one sculpture.
213.vocab: megalith, basalt, header-and-stretcher, islet, mortuary temple, tribute.

form: Built of basalt (dark volcanic rock) that cooled into long, naturally five- or six-sided columns, so builders could use them like logs without cutting them into shape. Some weigh several tons.

Walls use a header-and-stretcher pattern (one layer laid crosswise, the next lengthwise), like a log cabin. The cores are filled with coral rubble and smaller basalt boulders. No mortar holds anything together.
About 92 islets (small artificial islands) were raised on the reef along Pohnpei’s southeast coast, spread over roughly 1.5 km, each a platform of coral rubble held in by basalt retaining walls.

Shallow canals run between the islets, so at high tide canoes could pass among them, the reason for the nickname ‘Venice of the Pacific.’ Seawalls and breakwaters on the ocean side protected the complex.
The biggest enclosure, Nandauwas (the royal mortuary), has outer walls up to about 7.5 m (25 ft) high, an inner walled courtyard, and a central tomb chamber roofed with basalt columns.
It is megalithic architecture (built from very large stones), raised by human muscle, ropes, levers and probably rafts. Upturned corners, like a canoe’s prow, make the walls look even taller.
function: The complex had two zones: Madol Powe (the ‘upper town,’ northeast), with royal tombs and priests’ islets, and Madol Pah (the ‘lower town,’ southwest), with the rulers’ residence and administrative islets.

The Saudeleur required lesser chiefs from around Pohnpei to live at Nan Madol, where they could be watched and kept from plotting. Food and goods flowed in from the main island as tribute (required payments to a ruler).
Individual islets had specific jobs, such as food preparation, priests’ housing and ritual; oral tradition tells of priests on the islet of Idehd feeding turtle innards to a sacred eel.
After the Saudeleur fell, the site was largely abandoned as a capital, though later chiefs still visited it for ceremonies and burials.
content: There are no carved images; the meaning is in scale, isolation and hierarchy. Water physically separates the rulers from everyone else on the main island.

The sheer labor is itself the message: only rulers who could command thousands of workers over generations could build this. The mortuary islets made dead rulers permanently present, showing that royal status continued after death.
Moving inward through Nandauwas, from outer wall to courtyard to tomb, mirrors moving up a social ladder toward the most sacred and restricted space.
context: Pohnpei is in the Caroline Islands, now part of the Federated States of Micronesia; people settled it roughly 2,000 years ago.

The College Board date (c. 700 to 1600 C.E.) covers the site’s whole life. Most scholars think the big basalt construction came later, mainly after about 1180 to 1200 C.E., under the Saudeleur; exact dates are debated.
The basalt probably came from quarries elsewhere on Pohnpei; how it was moved is unknown. Local legend says two sorcerer brothers, Olisihpa and Olosohpa, flew the stones there by magic.

Tradition says the Saudeleur became tyrants and were overthrown by Isokelekel, a warrior hero from Kosrae, probably in the early 1600s. He set up the Nahnmwarki system of chiefs, which still exists on Pohnpei.
Named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016 and put straight onto the ‘in Danger’ list, because silt and mangroves are clogging the canals and walls are collapsing. On the exam.
If asked who built it → the Saudeleur dynasty, on Pohnpei, in Micronesia (not Polynesia).
If asked about the material → naturally formed prismatic basalt columns, stacked log-cabin style, not cut blocks.
If asked about function → royal residence, administrative center, ritual center and royal mortuary (Nandauwas).
If asked how architecture expresses power → forced residence of rival chiefs, tribute, huge labor, and separation by water.
Trap: it is a city of islets built on a reef, not a hilltop or cliff city like Machu Picchu (No. 161) or Mesa Verde (No. 154).
If asked for a cross-cultural pair on power in stone → Great Zimbabwe (No. 167): another mortarless royal center.

214.title: Moai on platform (ahu)
214.medium: Volcanic tuff figures on basalt base
214.plain: The moai are giant stone figures carved by the Polynesian people of Rapa Nui (Easter Island), one of the most remote inhabited islands on Earth. Close to 900 were carved, and many were set up in rows on stone platforms called ahu, most with their backs to the sea, watching over the villages. They stood for important ancestors whose spiritual power protected the living.
214.spot: A row of tall, stiff stone figures with oversized rectangular heads, heavy brows, long noses, long ears and tight pursed lips on a long stone platform. Arms hug the sides, long fingers meet over the belly, and some wear reddish cylinders on top.
214.remember: Moai look MOAI-nland: they turn their backs on the ocean to watch their families. Rapa Nui, about 1100 to 1600 C.E.
compare: No. 8 (§2.8), Stonehenge: Both are monumental stone works whose transport and setting required massive communal labor and planning.
No. 179 (§7.13), Reliquary figure: Both are ancestor figures that guard and channel the power of the dead for their descendants.
No. 213 (§10.1), Nan Madol: Both are Pacific megalithic projects linked to chiefly authority, one sculpture and one architecture.
214.vocab: moai, ahu, tuff, mana, pukao, monolith, tapu.

form: Carved from tuff (compressed volcanic ash, soft enough to carve with basalt stone tools called toki) at the Rano Raraku quarry, an extinct volcanic crater. About 95 percent of all moai come from there.
The average moai is about 4 m tall and weighs roughly 12 tons. The tallest ever erected, called Paro, is about 10 m; an unfinished one still lying in the quarry would have been about 21 m.

Highly stylized (simplified into a standard pattern): long rectangular face, deep eye sockets under a heavy brow, long nose, thin lips, long earlobes, arms tight to the body and hands meeting near the navel.
Some wear pukao, cylinders of red scoria (a lighter, reddish volcanic rock) from the Puna Pau quarry. They probably represent a topknot of hair, not a hat.
Eyes of white coral with obsidian or red scoria pupils were sometimes set into the sockets; one was found at Anakena in 1978. Inserting eyes may have ‘activated’ the figure.
The ahu (ceremonial stone platforms) are built of basalt; some, like Ahu Vinapu, have tightly fitted stone facing.
function: Each moai represented an important ancestor, usually a dead chief, and held his mana (spiritual power and prestige) for the lineage that made it.
Most moai on ahu face inland, toward the village, so their protective gaze fell on their descendants. The seven moai of Ahu Akivi, which face toward the sea, are a famous exception.
Ahu were ceremonial centers and often held burials, joining the dead, the ancestor image and the living. Rival lineages may have competed to raise ever bigger moai.
content: These are not portraits of individuals. A standard ancestor type signals rank and sacred status rather than personal likeness.
The huge head reflects the Polynesian belief that the head is the most tapu (sacred, restricted) part of the body.
Hands framing the belly may refer to birth and descent, though scholars are not sure.
Later, many moai were pulled down face-first, which broke their necks or hid their eyes, a way of cancelling their mana.
context: Rapa Nui lies about 3,500 km west of Chile, at the eastern corner of the Polynesian triangle.
Settlement dates are debated. Recent radiocarbon studies point to about 1150 to 1280 C.E.; older estimates were as early as 800 C.E. So the College Board start date of 1100 sits at the early edge.
Rapa Nui oral tradition says the moai ‘walked’ to their ahu by mana. In 2012 experiments, teams with ropes rocked an upright replica forward so it seemed to walk.

By the mid-1800s nearly all moai had been toppled, and religion shifted to the Birdman cult at Orongo. The old story of self-inflicted ecological collapse is now debated; rats ate palm seeds, and the worst population crash followed European contact.
Dutch sailors arrived on Easter Sunday 1722, hence the name. Peruvian slave raids (1862 to 1863) and smallpox cut the population to about 111 people by 1877. Chile annexed the island in 1888.
The basalt moai Hoa Hakananai’a was taken by a British ship’s crew in 1868 and is in the British Museum. Rapa Nui leaders formally asked for its return in 2018. On the exam.
If asked about material → volcanic tuff from Rano Raraku, on basalt bases (College Board: ‘volcanic tuff figures on basalt base’).
If asked which way they face → mostly inland, toward the villages, backs to the sea.
If asked about function → deified ancestors holding mana that protected the living community.
Trap: Rapa Nui is in Polynesia, unlike Nan Madol (No. 213) in Micronesia.
Trap: the ‘heads’ have full torsos; the famous heads at the quarry are buried up to the shoulders.
If asked about change over time → toppling of moai and the rise of the Birdman cult at Orongo.

215.title: ‘Ahu ‘ula (feather cape)
215.plain: An ʻahu ʻula (Hawaiian for ‘red garment’) is a cape or cloak covered in tens of thousands, and for the largest hundreds of thousands, of tiny red and yellow bird feathers tied onto a fiber net. Only aliʻi (high chiefs) could wear them, in battle and ceremony, and they were the most valuable objects in old Hawaiʻi. The cape displayed and protected the wearer’s mana, and chiefs gave them as top-level gifts, famously to Captain James Cook in 1779.
215.spot: A semicircular or trapezoid cape in vivid red and yellow, sometimes with black, with bold crescents, triangles or diamonds and a smooth, velvety feather surface.
215.remember: ‘Ahu ‘ula means ‘red garment,’ but yellow was worth more. Hawaiʻi, late 1700s: red for the gods, yellow for rarity, both for the chief.
compare: No. 158 (§6.6), Ruler’s feather headdress: Both use rare tropical feathers, gathered as tribute, to make wearable symbols of a ruler’s sacred power.
No. 162 (§6.10), All-T’oqapu tunic: Both are prestige garments whose labor-intensive materials and patterns announced the wearer’s royal status.
No. 223 (§10.11), Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa cloths t…: Both are Pacific textiles presented to British visitors to create diplomatic and reciprocal relationships.
215.vocab: featherwork, mana, tapu, aliʻi, tribute, regalia.

form: The base is a knotted net called nae, made from olonā fiber, a native plant with some of the strongest fiber known. The netting was made while reciting prayers.
Small bundles of feathers were tied onto the net in overlapping rows, like shingles, so the netting is completely hidden.
Red feathers came mostly from the ʻiʻiwi (and ʻapapane) honeycreepers; yellow from the ʻōʻō (a mostly black bird with small yellow tufts) and the mamo; black also from the ʻōʻō.
