Each ʻōʻō had only a few yellow feathers, so a big cloak needed thousands of birds. Kamehameha I’s all-yellow mamo cloak is said to hold about 450,000 feathers and took generations to finish.
Short capes covered the shoulders; full-length cloaks reached the ankles. Longer, more yellow garments marked higher rank.
Designs are bold, flat geometric shapes with sharp color contrast, readable from far away.
function: Worn by male aliʻi in battle and on ceremonial occasions. It identified the chief on the battlefield and was believed to protect him spiritually.
Used in high-level diplomacy: in January 1779 at Kealakekua Bay, Kalaniʻōpuʻu, ruler of Hawaiʻi Island, placed his own cape and feathered helmet (mahiole) on Cook.
Kept as heirlooms, passing mana, genealogy and prestige from one generation of chiefs to the next.
content: Red was the sacred color of the gods across Polynesia. Yellow, rarer, became the most prestigious color by the late 1700s.
Feathers were linked to the gods. Feathered images of the war god Kūkāʻilimoku were made with the same netting-and-feather method.
Wearing the cape wrapped the chief in mana and tapu (sacred restriction), so the garment worked as spiritual armor.
Specific motifs may have belonged to particular chiefs or lineages, but the meaning of individual designs is not fully known.
context: Made by skilled men. Feathers reached chiefs as tribute (required payments) collected by bird catchers called kia manu, who used sticky sap on branches; by tradition some birds were plucked and released.
Cook reached Hawaiʻi in 1778, and contact quickly changed island politics; Kamehameha I united the islands by 1810, partly with Western guns.
Kalaniʻōpuʻu’s cape went to England, then in 1912 to New Zealand’s national museum (now Te Papa). It returned to Hawaiʻi in 2016 and is at the Bishop Museum in Honolulu.
Several feather-source birds are now extinct, such as the Hawaiʻi mamo (around 1900) and the Kauaʻi ʻōʻō (last heard 1987), mainly from habitat loss and introduced diseases.
Many capes sit in Western museums because of contact-period gifts and collecting. On the exam.
If asked about material → feathers on olonā fiber netting, red and yellow.
If asked who wore it → only aliʻi, high-ranking male chiefs.
If asked about function → rank, battle, ceremony and protection of mana; also diplomatic gifts.
Trap: red is sacred, but yellow was the rarest and most valuable.
Context → contact with Captain Cook, 1778 to 1779.
Classic pair → Motecuhzoma’s feather headdress (No. 158): rare feathers as sacred, elite material.
Labor and tribute as wealth → All-Tʻoqapu tunic (No. 162).

216.title: Staff god
216.plain: A staff god is a long wooden pole carved with a large god head at the top and small figures below, then wrapped in a thick roll of barkcloth (tapa) that hid sacred materials inside. For the people of Rarotonga in the Cook Islands it made a god’s power present. Most were stripped, cut up or burned after Christian missionaries arrived in the 1820s, and some survivors went to London as trophies of conversion, so the object also records a religious and colonial encounter.
216.spot: A tall wooden pole with a big carved head at the top and a column of small stacked figures below, with a fat, cylindrical bundle of pale barkcloth wound around the middle. Many museum pieces are only the carved upper section, without the wrap.
216.remember: Staff god = a god with STUFF wrapped around it. Rarotonga, Cook Islands, around 1800; unwrapped by missionaries in the 1820s.
compare: No. 172 (§7.6), Power figure: Both hold sacred power in hidden materials inside, and both were taken by Europeans as symbols of defeated ‘paganism.’
No. 217 (§10.5), Female deity: Both are Pacific deity images; one hides power in wrapping, the other reduces the god to smooth abstraction.
No. 58 (§4.11), Church of Sainte-Foy: Both are sacred objects whose real power lay in hidden contents, relics in one and feathers and shell in the other.
216.vocab: tapa, barkcloth, mana, tapu, genealogy, iconoclasm.

form: A hardwood shaft, the most complete examples up to about 4 m long, carved at the top end with a large head with big eyes and a projecting profile.
Below the head, a row of small figures alternates between frontal and profile views. The profile figures had phalluses, and the bottom end of the staff was often carved as a phallus.
The middle was wrapped in a huge roll of tapa (barkcloth made by beating tree bark into sheets), turning the staff into a thick cylinder.
Inside the wrapping were sacred materials such as red feathers and polished pearl shell, considered the god’s hidden core.
Fiber cords bound the wrap; the result looks plain outside and holds its most important parts out of sight.
function: A god image carried in procession and set up during rituals, making the god’s power present among the people.
The barkcloth protected people from the god’s dangerous sacred power, and also protected that power from contamination.
After conversion, islanders surrendered their staff gods to missionaries as public proof that they had accepted Christianity.
content: Which god it represents is debated. It is often linked to Tangaroa, a creator and sea god, but scholars disagree.
The column of figures is usually read as genealogy: descent from the god through ancestors to living chiefs, which made chiefly authority sacred.
Phallic forms stress fertility and the god’s power to create and reproduce.
Concealment is the key idea: in Polynesian belief the most sacred things are wrapped and hidden, not displayed.
context: Rarotonga is the largest of the southern Cook Islands, in central Polynesia. The islands are named after Captain Cook, but he never landed on Rarotonga.
The London Missionary Society came in the 1820s: the Tahitian convert-teacher Papeiha landed in 1823, followed by John Williams and other missionaries. Most Rarotongans converted within a few years.
Missionaries stripped off the tapa, cut off the phalluses, burned many staffs and sent some to London, where they were shown in the Society’s museum as ‘idols’ given up.
John Williams’s 1837 book about his missionary work published an engraving of surrendered Rarotongan gods, spreading the image of conversion in Britain.
Most survivors are in the British Museum. Their damaged, unwrapped state is itself evidence of the colonial encounter, and Cook Islanders today treat them as ancestral heritage. On the exam.
If asked about material → wood, tapa, fiber and feathers.
If asked about the main idea → concealed sacred power wrapped inside barkcloth.
If asked about context → London Missionary Society in the 1820s; staffs given up, destroyed or shipped to London as trophies of conversion.
If asked about content → a god plus a chain of figures read as genealogy, with phallic fertility imagery.
Trap: the Cook Islands are culturally Polynesian; the staff gods have nothing to do with Captain Cook.
Pair → Nkisi n’kondi (No. 172): power stored inside, and seized by missionaries or colonial oﬀicers as ‘fetishes.’
Pair → Nukuoro female deity (No. 217): two very different Pacific ways of making a god visible.

217.title: Female deity
217.plain: This is a carved wooden figure of a goddess from Nukuoro, a tiny atoll in Micronesia whose people speak a Polynesian language. It is stripped down to smooth, simple shapes: an egg-shaped head with no face, sloping shoulders, a narrow torso and slightly bent legs. It was kept in the island’s temple and dressed with garlands during festivals. Its extreme simplicity later fascinated Western modern artists, but its makers meant it as the home of a god, not as abstract art.
217.spot: A smooth wooden figure with a completely featureless egg-shaped head, sloping shoulders, arms merged into the sides, small hints of breasts and navel, and slightly bent knees that make it lean forward a little.
217.remember: NO face from NUkuoro: no eyes, no nose, no mouth. Micronesia, 1700s to 1800s, Polynesian outlier.
compare: No. 10 (§2.10), Tlatilco female figurine: Both are small-scale female figures, one smooth and geometric, the other exaggerated in hips and thighs.
No. 216 (§10.4), Staff god: Both are Pacific deity images; the staff god hides its power in wrappings, while this one reduces the god to bare form.
No. 179 (§7.13), Reliquary figure: Both were made as sacred figures but later admired by Western modernists for their simplified forms.

form: Carved from breadfruit wood, smoothed and polished to an even surface.
Extreme stylization (simplification into geometric shapes): an ovoid head, a straight shoulder line, slim arms that blend into the torso, small breasts, a navel and a pubic area.
The head has no facial features at all; some figures have a slight ridge suggesting the brow or hair.
Strict symmetry and smooth curves make it calm and balanced, while the bent knees and forward tilt suggest readiness to move.
Sizes range from small figures about 15 cm high to some more than 2 m tall.
function: Kept in the amalau (the community cult house or temple). Each figure was associated with a particular deity, and some with particular families.
During religious festivals the figures were dressed in cloth, decorated with flower garlands and given food offerings.
Priests mediated between the community and the gods, asking for good harvests, fertility and well-being.
content: It shows a goddess as pure form. The missing face may emphasize that she is a god, not a particular human being.
The figure was not ‘finished’ as a bare object: dressing and garlanding in ritual completed it.
Its smooth, sealed surfaces suggest wholeness and perfection, which fit a divine being.
Female features point to fertility and the continuation of the community, though the specific myths connected to each figure are mostly lost.
context: Nukuoro is a small atoll in the Caroline Islands, now part of the Federated States of Micronesia, home to only a few hundred people.
It is a Polynesian outlier: a community in Micronesia whose language and religion are Polynesian, the result of voyagers settling there centuries ago.
Only about three dozen figures survive. Many were collected in the late 1800s, several for German collections such as the Godeffroy Museum in Hamburg, before the islanders converted to Christianity.
In the twentieth century European modernists admired them for their simplicity, and Western museums began showing them as sculpture rather than ethnographic specimens. On the exam.
If asked to attribute → smooth, faceless egg-shaped head plus geometric body → Nukuoro.
If asked where → Micronesia, but a Polynesian outlier in language and religion.
If asked about function → temple deity figure, dressed and given offerings in ceremonies.
If asked about material → wood (breadfruit).
Trap: its abstraction is local and older than Western modernism; it was not made to look ‘modern.’
Reception → later admired by modernists, like the Fang byeri (No. 179).
Pair → Tlatilco female figurine (No. 10): another female figure with very different, exaggerated proportions.

218.title: Buk (mask)
218.medium: Turtle shell, wood, fiber, feathers, and shell
218.plain: This buk is a ceremonial mask built from plates of heated, shaped turtle shell, combining a human face with a bird on top (usually identified as a frigate bird), decorated with feathers, shells and fiber. It comes from the Torres Strait islands between Australia and New Guinea, the only place where masks were made of turtle shell. Dancers wore it with full-body costumes in funeral and increase ceremonies that linked clans to their animal totems and to the dead. Missionaries suppressed these ceremonies after 1871.
218.spot: A face built from thin, curved brown and amber plates of turtle shell sewn together like panels, with cut-out patterns, crowned by a bird shape, and trimmed with fiber fringes and feathers. It looks assembled, not carved from a block.
218.remember: No big trees? Use TURTLES. Torres Strait, mid- to late 1800s; the ‘Coming of the Light’ in 1871 ended the masked dances.
compare: No. 164 (§6.12), Transformation mask: Both are performed masks that combine human and animal identities to show transformation.
No. 222 (§10.10), Malagan display and mask: Both are Pacific funerary arts that come fully alive only in ceremonial performance.
No. 175 (§7.9), Bundu mask: Both are masks worn with full-body costumes that hide the performer, who then embodies a spirit.
218.vocab: composite mask, totem, openwork, performance art, increase ceremony.

form: Made of turtle shell, mostly from the hawksbill turtle, heated to soften it, then cut, bent into shape, pierced and sewn together with fiber.
A composite mask (made of many separate parts joined together): a human face plus an animal element. Other Torres Strait masks join faces to crocodiles, sharks or fish.
Surfaces are incised and cut into openwork (patterns cut all the way through), sometimes with lines filled with white lime and red or black paint.
Added materials include feathers, shells and seeds that rattle, and fiber or grass fringes for hair and beard.
Light and thin, the shell glows in firelight; the mask was worn with a full costume of grass and leaves covering the dancer’s body.
function: Worn in funerary ceremonies that ended mourning and helped send the spirit of the dead to the land of the dead in the west.
Also used in increase ceremonies (rituals asking for plentiful food, such as turtles, dugong and garden crops) and in initiations.
Performed with dancing, singing and drumming on the warup (an hourglass-shaped drum). Masks were kept at men’s sacred ceremonial grounds.
Inside the mask and costume, the dancer’s own identity disappeared and he embodied a spirit or ancestor.
content: The human-animal combination expresses totemism: each clan is tied to particular animals, its totems, which are ancestors and protectors.
The bird on top may be a clan totem; frigate birds are also linked to the sea and weather in island life.
The fusion of person and creature shows transformation: the performer becomes more than human.
context: The Torres Strait lies between Cape York in Australia and Papua New Guinea. Its islanders are Melanesian and culturally distinct from Aboriginal Australians; the islands became part of Queensland in 1879.
Many islands are small and lack large trees, so islanders used turtle shell, a material from the sea at the center of their economy.
The London Missionary Society landed on Erub (Darnley Island) on 1 July 1871. Islanders still celebrate this ‘Coming of the Light’ each year, though it ended many older ceremonies.
Missionaries and collectors, including the Cambridge Anthropological Expedition of 1898 led by A. C. Haddon, removed many masks, which are now in Western museums.
Contemporary Torres Strait artists, such as Ken Thaiday Sr., revive these traditions in new dance headdresses. On the exam.
If asked about material → turtle shell, the material that instantly identifies Torres Strait masks.
If asked why turtle shell → environment: small islands with few large trees and a sea-centered economy.
If asked about function → funerary, increase and initiation ceremonies with dance, music and full costume.
If asked about content → human plus totem animal.
Context → London Missionary Society, 1871.
Trap: politically part of Australia, but culturally Melanesian, not Aboriginal Australian.
Pair → Transformation mask (No. 164): another performance mask that turns a human into an animal or spirit.

219.title: Hiapo (tapa)
219.medium: Tapa or bark cloth, freehand painting
219.plain: Hiapo is the Niuean word for tapa, cloth made by beating the inner bark of the paper mulberry tree into thin sheets. Niuean hiapo from the late 1800s stands out because its designs were painted freehand, in very fine, dense geometric patterns, sometimes with small plants, human figures and even written words. Made by women, it was used for clothing, gifts and exchange, and its new style reflects contact with Samoan missionary teachers and Christianity.
219.spot: A large, thin beige cloth covered in very fine dark-brown lines forming grids, circles, triangles and radiating shapes inside framed sections, sometimes with tiny leaves or human figures. It looks drawn by hand like a pen drawing, not stamped.
219.remember: Hi, Apo! Niuean women painted me freehand, around 1850 to 1900, after Samoan teachers came to visit.
compare: No. 11 (§2.11), Terra cotta fragment: Both use geometric patterning that runs through Pacific art from Lapita ancestors to the 1800s.
No. 223 (§10.11), Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa cloths t…: Both treat barkcloth as women’s wealth presented in exchange to build relationships.
No. 162 (§6.10), All-T’oqapu tunic: Both are textiles whose dense geometric patterns carried social meaning and high value.
219.vocab: tapa, barkcloth, paper mulberry, freehand painting, motif, gift exchange.

form: Made from the inner bark of the paper mulberry tree, soaked and beaten with wooden beaters on a wooden anvil, then joined into large sheets.
Painted freehand with a dark brown plant-based dye. Other islands mostly decorated tapa with stencils (Fiji) or rubbing boards (Tonga).
Extremely fine lines create grids, concentric circles, triangles, zigzags, stars and radiating shapes, often arranged in repeated square or circular units with borders.
Some sheets add naturalistic motifs, such as leaves, flowers and small human figures, plus written words such as names and dates.
The overall effect is precise and dense, like a complex diagram, with balanced, symmetrical compositions.
function: Worn as clothing and used as covers and wraps.
Given as gifts and exchanged at important events like marriages and funerals. Barkcloth is a classic form of women’s wealth in Polynesia.
From the late 1800s, also traded or given to missionaries and visitors, which is how many examples reached Western museums.
content: Geometric patterns continue a very old Polynesian design tradition, going back to the stamped patterns on Lapita pottery (No. 11).
Naturalistic plants and people, plus writing, show new ideas and new literacy brought by missionaries.
The exact meanings of many motifs are lost, but the skill and density signaled the maker’s ability and the family’s status.
context: Niue is a single raised coral island east of Tonga. Today it is self-governing in free association with New Zealand.

Samoan teachers of the London Missionary Society worked on Niue from 1849. Some scholars think they introduced or reshaped barkcloth making there, which would explain hiapo’s Samoan-style freehand painting.
Christian ideas about modesty increased demand for cloth to cover the body.
Making hiapo died out in the early 20th century as imported cotton cloth replaced it. Only a few dozen examples survive, mostly in museums.
The Niuean-born artist John Pule has drawn on hiapo in his own paintings and co-wrote a 2005 book on the subject, part of a renewed interest in it. On the exam.
If asked about material and technique → tapa (barkcloth) from paper mulberry, decorated by freehand painting.
If asked who made it → women; barkcloth is women’s wealth.
If asked about context → missionaries, especially Samoan teachers, and Christianity in the later 1800s.
If asked what’s distinctive → very fine freehand geometric patterns, sometimes with plants, figures and writing.
Trap: Niuean hiapo is painted freehand, unlike stenciled Fijian masi or rubbed Tongan ngatu.
Continuity pair → Lapita fragment (No. 11): geometric Pacific design over 2,500 years.
Exchange pair → Fijian mats and tapa presentation (No. 223).

220.title: Tamati Waka Nene
220.plain: This is an oil portrait of Tāmati Wāka Nene, a powerful Māori chief who sided with the British and helped persuade other chiefs to sign the Treaty of Waitangi in 1840. The Bohemian-born painter Gottfried Lindauer made it in 1890, nearly twenty years after Nene’s death, working from a photograph. It looks like a European portrait, but for Māori it has become a taonga (treasure) that carries the presence of the ancestor.
220.spot: A realistic oil portrait of an elderly Māori man with white hair and a full, curving facial tattoo (moko), wrapped in a fluffy brown kiwi-feather cloak, holding a long carved wooden staff-weapon, against a dark plain background.
220.remember: Tāmati Wāka means Thomas Walker. Lindauer, 1890, painted from a photo after Nene died in 1871: a Treaty of Waitangi backer preserved in oil.
compare: No. 171 (§7.5), Ndop: Both stand in for a leader through symbolic attributes and act as his presence after death.
No. 205 (§9.14), Portrait of Sin Sukju: Both are oﬀicial-style portraits honoring a statesman for loyal service to a ruling power.
No. 99 (§5.1), Portrait of Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz: Both are posthumous portraits that use objects and setting to define the sitter’s identity and status.
220.vocab: tā moko, taonga, rangatira, Realism, posthumous portrait, regalia.

form: Oil on canvas in European academic realism (careful, lifelike detail). Lindauer trained at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna.
A close, half-length view in three-quarter pose against a dark background, with strong light on the face to show the tattoo clearly.
Tā moko (Māori tattoo, cut into the skin with chisels rather than just pricked) covers the face; Lindauer copied its exact curves because each moko is unique.
Nene wears a kahu kiwi (a cloak covered in kiwi feathers), one of the most prestigious Māori garments.
He holds a tewhatewha, a long wooden weapon with a flat, axe-shaped end that chiefs also used to signal and direct warriors, and wears a pounamu (greenstone) hei-tiki.
Smooth brushwork and photographic detail, especially in the skin, the feathers and the white hair.
function: A posthumous (made after death) commemorative portrait of an important rangatira (chief).

Part of Lindauer’s large series of Māori portraits. Many were commissioned by Auckland businessman Henry Partridge, who gave his collection to the city in 1915; this one is in the Auckland Art Gallery Toi o Tāmaki.
For many Pākehā (European settlers), such portraits recorded what they wrongly assumed was a ‘dying race.’
For Māori, portraits of ancestors are greeted, spoken to and wept over, and are often hung in meeting houses.
content: Every item is a status sign: moko for genealogy and rank, the kiwi cloak for prestige, the tewhatewha for leadership, greenstone for heirloom wealth.
Moko worked as personal identity; Māori chiefs sometimes drew part of their moko as their signature on deeds and documents.
His name, Tāmati Wāka, came from Thomas Walker, an Englishman he admired, taken at his Wesleyan (Methodist) baptism, which reflects his Christian conversion.
context: Nene (born perhaps in the 1780s, died 1871) was a chief of Ngāti Hao, a hapū (sub-tribe) of Ngāpuhi in Hokianga, Northland. He fought in the musket wars of the 1820s.
At Waitangi on 6 February 1840 his speech helped persuade chiefs to sign the Treaty of Waitangi. The English and Māori texts differ on sovereignty, and the treaty is still debated.
In the Flagstaff War (1845 to 1846) he fought on the British side against the fellow Ngāpuhi chief Hōne Heke. The government later gave him a pension.
Lindauer (1839 to 1926) was born in Pilsen, Bohemia (now the Czech Republic), and moved to New Zealand in 1874. He painted from life and, as here, from photographs.
His portraits are now valued both as art and as taonga, and descendants visit them as family. On the exam.
If asked about artist and origin → Gottfried Lindauer, a Bohemian (Czech) immigrant, not a Māori artist.
If asked about medium → oil on canvas, a Western medium used for a Māori subject.
If asked who the sitter is → Ngāpuhi chief who supported the Treaty of Waitangi (1840) and fought for the British.
If asked about function for Māori → portrait as taonga, a living presence of the ancestor.
If asked about moko → unique identity marker recording genealogy and rank.
Key fact: painted in 1890 from a photograph, after his death in 1871.
Pair → Ndop of Mishe miShyaang maMbul (No. 171): a ruler identified by attributes rather than likeness.

221.title: Navigation chart
221.plain: This is a stick chart from the Marshall Islands: a lattice of palm-leaf ribs tied together with fiber, with shells marking islands. It does not map coastlines. It maps ocean swells and how they bend and collide when they meet islands. Navigators studied and memorized charts on land and then steered by feeling the swells through their canoes, so the chart itself stayed at home.
221.spot: An open frame of thin, light-colored sticks lashed together at angles, with some sticks curved, and small cowrie shells or bits of coral tied at certain crossings.
221.remember: A stick chart maps WAVES, not land. Marshall Islands, 1800s to early 1900s: study it, memorize it, leave it, then feel it at sea.
compare: No. 177 (§7.11), Lukasa: Both are memory devices that store specialist knowledge and need a trained reader to interpret them.
No. 11 (§2.11), Terra cotta fragment: Both relate to the Pacific voyaging that spread people and design traditions across the ocean.
No. 213 (§10.1), Nan Madol: Both are Micronesian works shaped by life on reefs and atolls surrounded by ocean.
221.vocab: wayfinding, swell, refraction, mnemonic device, abstract.

form: Made of the midribs of coconut palm fronds, lashed with fiber cord made from coconut husk.
Small cowrie shells or pieces of coral mark the locations of islands.
Curved sticks show swells bending, or refracting, as they wrap around an island; crossings show where swells from different directions meet and create a distinctive bump.
Straight sticks hold the frame together or show the main swell directions.
There is no standard scale or orientation. Each chart was made by and for a particular navigator, so they vary a lot.
The look is abstract and diagrammatic: an open grid, light enough to carry but meant for study, not travel.
function: A teaching tool and memory aid, studied on shore and never taken on the canoe.
Three main types: mattang (an abstract teaching chart showing how swells behave around a single island), meddo (a few islands or part of a chain) and rebbelib (a whole island chain).
At sea, navigators read the swells by the motion of the canoe through their bodies, sometimes lying in the hull, together with stars, birds and clouds.
content: These are maps of process, ocean energy and movement, rather than of land shapes.
Islands appear as disturbances in a moving field of water: you find land by noticing how it changes the sea.
The chart records generations of close observation of the environment, encoded in a form only trained navigators could read.
context: The Marshall Islands are 29 coral atolls and 5 single islands in two parallel chains, Ratak (‘sunrise’) and Ralik (‘sunset’).
Navigational knowledge was closely held, passed down within families and controlled by chiefs. It was a source of power and status.
Westerners learned of the charts around 1900, mainly through a German naval oﬀicer’s report during the German colonial period.

Under German, Japanese and then U.S. rule, and after U.S. nuclear tests at Bikini and Enewetak (1946 to 1958) displaced communities, traditional voyaging declined. Marshallese programs have since worked to revive it.
The charts are evidence of the sophisticated wayfinding (navigation without instruments) that allowed people to settle the remote islands of the Pacific. On the exam.
If asked what it maps → ocean swells and how they bend around islands, not coastlines.
If asked how it was used → memorized on land, not carried at sea.
If asked for types → mattang (teaching), meddo (section of a chain), rebbelib (whole chain).
If asked about social context → restricted, family-held knowledge as a source of power.
Attribution clue → lattice of sticks with shells → Marshall Islands, Micronesia.
Classic pair → Lukasa (No. 177): a memory device read only by trained specialists.
Trap: it is a map, but an abstract one, of movement, not of land.

222.title: Malagan display and mask
222.artist: New Ireland Province, Papua New Guinea
222.plain: Malagan (also spelled malanggan) is a set of memorial ceremonies held in northern New Ireland, Papua New Guinea, to honor people who have died, and the word also covers the elaborate carvings and masks made for them. The carvings are painted, openwork wooden sculptures full of interlocking birds, fish, snakes and human figures, shown in a special display house at the climax of the ceremony. When the ceremony ends their job is done, and they are destroyed, left to rot or sold, so the art is really the event, not a permanent object.
222.spot: Lacy, see-through wood carvings painted in red, black, white and yellow, with figures, birds and fish stacked and interlocked; or a tatanua mask with a tall fiber crest running front to back over the head and shiny round shell eyes.
222.remember: Malagan: ‘my last goodbye, then gone.’ New Ireland, Papua New Guinea, 20th century: carved, shown once, discarded.
compare: No. 218 (§10.6), Buk: Both are Pacific funerary arts that come alive in masked performance.
No. 224 (§11.1), The Gates: Both are deliberately temporary works whose meaning includes their own disappearance.
No. 168 (§7.2), Great Mosque of Djenné: Both depend on community ritual and renewal rather than on a single permanent object.
222.vocab: openwork, ephemeral, funerary, operculum, clan, memorial.

form: Carved from soft, lightweight wood into openwork (carving cut all the way through, so the sculpture is full of holes and lattices). Forms include tall poles, horizontal friezes and standing figures.
Painted in red, black, white and yellow from earth pigments, charcoal and lime, with fine repeating lines and dots over the carved surfaces.
Eyes are often the shiny round opercula (the hard ‘trapdoor’ lids) of sea snails, which glint like real eyes.
Creatures interlock and bite each other, such as a bird gripping a snake or a fish swallowing a figure, making the carvings feel crowded and alive.
The tatanua mask has a carved wooden face, a tall crest of plant fiber, and sides of other plant material; the crest is said to recall a mourning hairstyle.
At the ceremony the carvings stand side by side inside a temporary display house with an open front, like a stage set.
function: Malagan ceremonies are funerary and memorial events, held months or years after deaths, often honoring several people at once.
They settle obligations among the living: the sponsoring family pays debts, holds feasts with pigs and shell money, and land rights pass to heirs.
They are believed to release the spirits of the dead so they can leave the world of the living; they can also mark the initiation of young men.
Men wear tatanua masks in dances; unlike most carvings, some tatanua masks are kept and reused.
content: Each design belongs to a clan. What is owned is the right to reproduce a malagan image, which is passed on by payment, not the physical object.
Birds, fish, snakes and pigs are often read as linking sky, sea and land, and as clan totems or ancestral beings.
The carvings are remembered rather than kept: memory, not the object, holds the image until the next ceremony.
context: Carvers are specialists commissioned and paid by the sponsoring family. They often work in a secluded enclosure, and some stages are hidden from women and the uninitiated.
New Ireland is part of the Bismarck Archipelago in Melanesia. It was a German colony from 1884 to 1914, and Germans collected thousands of carvings, now in museums in Berlin, Hamburg and elsewhere.
Collecting was easy because the carvings were meant to be thrown away once the ceremony ended, so families were willing to sell them.
Surrealists such as André Breton collected New Ireland art, and Western museums still show it as permanent sculpture, which reverses its original temporary purpose.
Malagan ceremonies are still held today, adapted alongside Christianity. On the exam.
If asked about function → funerary and memorial ceremonies that honor the dead and settle obligations among the living.
If asked about lifespan → ephemeral: displayed once, then destroyed, left to decay, or sold.
If asked about form → painted openwork carving with sea-snail operculum eyes.
If asked about ownership → clans own the right to the design, not the object.
Trap: New Ireland is in Melanesia (Papua New Guinea), not Micronesia or Polynesia.
Pair → The Gates (No. 224): art meant to exist only for a short time.
Pair → Great Mosque of Djenné (No. 168): art that lives through repeated community ritual.

223.title: Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa cloths to Queen Elizabeth
223.medium: Multimedia performance (costume; cosmetics, including scent; chant; movement;
223.plain: In December 1953, on Queen Elizabeth II’s first tour of the Commonwealth after her coronation, Fijians welcomed her with a formal presentation of masi (barkcloth) and finely woven pandanus mats. The ‘work of art’ on the AP list is the whole event: the cloth and mats, the costumes, the scented coconut oil on the presenters’ bodies, the chant and the movement, plus the photographs and film that record it. It shows Fijians using their own traditions of ceremonial exchange to shape their relationship with the British monarch who ruled them as a colony.
223.spot: A black-and-white photograph or film still of a long procession of Fijians carrying or wrapped in huge lengths of patterned barkcloth and stacks of mats, approaching the young Queen and oﬀicials.
223.remember: 1953, the coronation year: the new Queen came to Fiji and was wrapped in welcome. Cloth plus scent plus chant plus movement = performance.
compare: No. 219 (§10.7), Hiapo: Both treat barkcloth as women’s wealth, shaped by contact with British missionaries or rulers.
No. 170 (§7.4), Sika dwa kofi: Both show a colonized people using ceremonial objects to assert their own authority to the British.
No. 215 (§10.3), ‘Ahu ‘ula: Both involve prestigious Pacific textiles presented to British visitors to establish a relationship.
223.vocab: masi, tapa, pandanus, performance art, reciprocity. 11 Global Contemporary Content area 10 · 1980 C.E. to present · works 224–250 · about 11% of the multiple-choice section. Art made since 1980, all over the world: installations, performance, video, digital work and buildings. The exam focuses on ideas: identity, globalization, politics, the environment and memory. For each work, know what message or question the artist is raising and what materials or methods carry that message.

form: The College Board medium is a multimedia performance: costume, cosmetics including scent, chant, movement, and mats of pandanus and hibiscus fiber, plus photographic documentation.
Masi: Fijian barkcloth made from beaten paper mulberry bark, decorated with black and red-brown geometric patterns, often made with stencils.
Pandanus mats (ibe): woven from dried strips of pandanus leaves, often with colorful fringed borders.
Presenters’ skin was rubbed with coconut oil scented with flowers or sandalwood, making bodies glisten; scent and sheen were part of the work.
The cloth was carried in long lengths or wrapped around the body in great bulk, then unwound and laid down. Volume and length signal wealth.
The event survives only through photographs and newsreel film, so what we study is the documentation.
function: A formal welcome ceremony honoring Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Philip during their 1953 to 1954 Commonwealth tour.
In Fijian custom, formal presentations create reciprocity (a two-way relationship of obligation): accepting the gift binds the receiver to the giver.
The presentation displayed the wealth, skill and rank of the communities and chiefs who gave it.
Fijian welcomes of high-ranking guests usually also involve a sevusevu, a ritual presentation of yaqona (kava) roots.
content: Mats and barkcloth are women’s wealth: made by women, they are the core gifts at births, weddings, funerals and chiefly occasions.
Barkcloth is linked to chiefly rank; lengths of masi can be laid as a path for a chief to walk on.
By giving, Fijians presented themselves not as passive subjects but as partners with their own protocol and expectations of the Crown.
context: Fiji, about 330 islands, was ceded to Britain in 1874 by high chiefs including Ratu Seru Cakobau. It was a British Crown colony until independence on 10 October 1970.

Source correction: the College Board label says ‘Fiji, Polynesia,’ but geographers usually place Fiji in Melanesia. Fiji, especially the eastern Lau islands, does share much culture with Polynesian Tonga and Samoa.
The Queen was crowned in June 1953 and set out on a Commonwealth tour in November 1953; she reached Fiji in mid-December before going on to Tonga, New Zealand and Australia.
The press and newsreels broadcast the ceremony across the empire, so Fijians’ selfpresentation reached a global audience.
AP includes it as an example of art as an event: in the Pacific, performance, exchange and objects work together. On the exam.
If asked what the work is → the whole performance, with textiles, scent, chant and movement, not just the objects.
If asked about materials → masi (barkcloth) and pandanus mats, with hibiscus fiber.
If asked about function → formal welcome and gift exchange creating reciprocal obligations.
If asked about gender → women’s wealth, made by women.
If asked about context → Fiji as a British colony (1874 to 1970), the Queen’s 1953 to 1954 Commonwealth tour.
Trap: the College Board label says Polynesia; Fiji is usually classed as Melanesian.
Pair → Hiapo (No. 219): barkcloth as women’s wealth.

224.title: The Gates
224.plain: The Gates was a temporary artwork by Christo and Jeanne-Claude: 7,503 saffron-colored gates, each 16 feet tall with a hanging fabric panel, set along 23 miles of footpaths in New York’s Central Park. It stood for just 16 days, from February 12 to 27, 2005, then was taken down and recycled. The artists spent 26 years getting permission and paid the roughly 21 million dollar cost themselves, so it was free and open to anyone who walked through.
224.spot: Long lines of bright orange-saffron gates with fabric panels hanging from the top bars, winding along curving paths through bare winter trees, sometimes with the Manhattan skyline behind.
224.remember: After 26 years waiting at the gate, Christo and Jeanne-Claude opened The Gates in 2005: 7,503 gates, 23 miles, 16 days.
compare: No. 151 (§5.53), Spiral Jetty: Both are large works made in a landscape that change how viewers move through and see that place.
No. 222 (§10.10), Malagan display and mask: Both are deliberately ephemeral; their disappearance is part of their meaning.
No. 148 (§5.50), Narcissus Garden: Both are installations in public spaces that question how art is funded and sold.
224.vocab: installation, site-specific, ephemeral, public art, environmental art.

form: Each gate was 16 feet (about 4.9 m) tall, and between about 5.5 and 18 feet wide, to fit the width of each path. Gates stood about 12 feet apart.
Frames were square saffron-colored vinyl posts set on steel base plates resting on the paths, so nothing was drilled into the ground.
Saffron nylon panels hung from the top bar to about 7 feet above the ground and moved in the wind, catching light.
The bright warm color stood out against the gray and brown of the leafless winter park and the snow.
Everything was made industrially and installed by hundreds of paid workers, then removed and recycled.
Seen from above, the gates traced the park’s paths like a moving golden river.
function: A temporary piece of public art, free, with no tickets and no sponsors.
It made people walk the park’s paths and notice the landscape, designed by Olmsted and Vaux in 1858, in a new way.
It drew millions of visits in two weeks and was estimated to bring hundreds of millions of dollars to the city’s economy.
content: The artists insisted it had no hidden symbolism; they called their projects works of joy and beauty.
Gates are thresholds: walking through thousands of them turns an ordinary walk into a kind of procession.
Impermanence was essential. The artists said the urgency of something that will soon be gone makes people look harder.
context: Christo (Christo Vladimirov Javacheff, born in Bulgaria) and Jeanne-Claude (born in Casablanca, Morocco) were both born on 13 June 1935. Jeanne-Claude died in 2009, Christo in 2020.
They proposed the project in 1979. New York’s parks commissioner rejected it in 1981; Mayor Michael Bloomberg’s administration approved it in 2003.
They paid for it entirely by selling Christo’s preparatory drawings, collages and models, never accepting grants, sponsors or commissions.
Other projects include Running Fence (California, 1976), Surrounded Islands (Miami, 1983) and Wrapped Reichstag (Berlin, 1995).
Reactions were mixed: critics called it decorative or a spectacle, while huge crowds treated it as a winter festival. On the exam.
If asked about artists → Christo and Jeanne-Claude, working as a team.
If asked about the date range 1979 to 2005 → it covers 26 years from proposal to the 16-day display.
If asked about function → temporary, site-specific public art, free to all.
If asked about funding → self-funded through sale of drawings and collages; no sponsors.
Trap: it was not commissioned by the city and not permanent.
Pair → Spiral Jetty (No. 151): art made in and about a landscape.
Pair → Malagan (No. 222): art designed to disappear.

225.title: Vietnam Veterans Memorial
225.plain: The Vietnam Veterans Memorial is a long, V-shaped wall of polished black granite set into the ground on the National Mall in Washington, D.C., carrying the names of more than 58,000 Americans who died or went missing in the Vietnam War. Maya Lin designed it at 21 as a Yale undergraduate, winning an open national competition. It rejected the traditional heroic statue in favor of a quiet, reflective surface where visitors see themselves among the names, and it changed how memorials are designed.
225.spot: Two long, low walls of shiny black stone meeting at a wide V, sunk below the level of the lawn and covered in columns of small carved names, with visitors reflected in the surface.
225.remember: V for Vietnam, V for the shape, V for visitors reflected. Maya Lin, 1982: she was 21, and the wall is black.
compare: No. 119 (§5.21), The Burghers of Calais: Both reject heroic memorial conventions and bring the viewer down to the level of loss and suffering.
No. 248 (§11.25), Shibboleth: Both are cuts or crevices in the ground that turn absence into a metaphor for wounds and division.
No. 150 (§5.52), Lipstick: Both respond to the Vietnam War era, one as protest and one as mourning.

form: Two walls, each about 246 feet 9 inches (75 m) long, meet at an angle of about 125 degrees. They rise from ground level at the ends to about 10.1 feet (3.1 m) at the vertex.
Built of black granite quarried near Bangalore, India, polished to a mirror finish. The panels were cut in Vermont and the names grit-blasted in Tennessee.
Names are cut in plain, uniform letters, with no ranks and no hometowns.
Minimalism (art reduced to simple geometric forms with no decoration): no statues, no ornament, no heroic figures.
A sloping path leads visitors down as the wall grows taller above them, then back up as it shrinks.
Lin described it as a cut into the earth with one polished face; it works as a retaining wall for the ground behind.
function: A memorial to U.S. service members who died or remain missing in the Vietnam War. It honors individuals without taking a position on the war itself.
A place of mourning: visitors touch names, make pencil rubbings, and leave letters, medals, photographs and other items, which the National Park Service collects and stores.
Names are still added when deaths are recognized. A diamond symbol marks a confirmed death; a cross marks someone missing.
content: Names are listed by date of death, not alphabetically. They start at the vertex in 1959, run to the east end, continue from the west end, and finish at the vertex in 1975, closing the circle.
The reflective surface puts the living visitor among the dead, joining past and present.
One arm points to the Washington Monument and the other to the Lincoln Memorial, tying the war to the nation’s history.
Lin compared it to a wound in the earth that is healing, a cut that is polished closed.
context: The Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund, founded in 1979 by veteran Jan Scruggs, raised the money privately. Congress gave land on the Mall in 1980.
The 1981 competition received 1,421 entries, judged anonymously. Lin’s design began as a project for a Yale class on funerary architecture.
It was controversial: one veteran called it ‘a black gash of shame,’ critics objected to the black color and the sunken site, and Lin, a Chinese-American woman, faced racist and sexist attacks.
As a compromise a flagpole and Frederick Hart’s realistic statue Three Servicemen (1984) were added nearby; the Vietnam Women’s Memorial followed in 1993.
Dedicated 13 November 1982, it is one of the most visited memorials in Washington and shaped later memorials such as the National September 11 Memorial. On the exam.
If asked about the artist → Maya Lin, a 21-year-old Yale undergraduate who won an open competition.
If asked about material → polished black granite, chosen to reflect.
If asked how names are arranged → chronologically by date of death, starting and ending at the vertex.
If asked about style → minimalist and anti-heroic, with no figures.
If asked about reception → controversial at first; a realistic statue and flag were added as compromise.
Pair → The Burghers of Calais (No. 119): an anti-heroic memorial at the viewer’s level.
Pair → Shibboleth (No. 248): a cut into the ground as an image of division and loss.

226.title: Horn Players
226.medium: Acrylic and oil paintstick on three canvas panels
226.plain: Horn Players is a large three-panel painting by Jean-Michel Basquiat that pays tribute to the bebop jazz pioneers Charlie Parker (alto saxophone) and Dizzy Gillespie (trumpet). Against a black background, rough figures share space with scrawled and crossed-out words, song titles and body-part labels. It shows how Basquiat brought graﬀiti-style energy into the gallery and put Black artists, long sidelined in art history, at the center of a big painting.
226.spot: Three joined canvases, mostly black, with crude figures in white, brown and yellow: a sax player, a trumpet player and a large head with a big ear and open mouth, surrounded by hand-lettered capital words like ORNITHOLOGY and PREE, some crossed out.
226.remember: Basquiat’s Horn Players (1983): Bird and Diz with their horns, three panels for two jazz saints. ‘Ornithology’ is Bird’s tune.
compare: No. 147 (§5.49), Marilyn Diptych: Both use multi-panel formats to turn famous performers into modern icons.
No. 232 (§11.9), Dancing at the Louvre: Both put Black people and Black creativity at the center of a Western art-world setting.
No. 141 (§5.43), The Migration of the Negro, Panel no. 49: Both record Black American history and culture in a flat, bold, simplified style.
226.vocab: triptych, Neo-Expressionism, oil paintstick, graﬀiti, gestural, homage.

form: Acrylic and oil paintstick (oil paint in solid crayon form) on canvas mounted on wood supports, in three panels; about 2.4 by 1.9 m (96 by 75 inches) overall.
A triptych (a work in three panels), with the joins between panels left visible.
Gestural style (visible, energetic marks of the hand): figures are flattened, mask-like and sometimes skeletal, like X-ray views.
Hand-lettered words in capitals are repeated, underlined and crossed out. Basquiat said crossing words out made people want to read them more.
Layers are painted over so earlier marks show through, giving a collage-like, unfinished look.
The look recalls graﬀiti and children’s drawing but is carefully composed, with text and figures balanced across the dark ground.
function: A painting for galleries and collectors at the height of the 1980s art boom. It was acquired by Eli and Edythe Broad and is at The Broad museum in Los Angeles.
A homage (a tribute) to musical heroes; Basquiat made several works about jazz musicians, including Charles the First (1982) about Parker.
content: ‘Ornithology’ is a 1946 Parker tune and a pun on his nickname, ‘Bird.’ ‘Dizzy’ names Gillespie.
‘Pree’ was Parker’s daughter, who died as a small child in 1954.
The ear and open mouth stress listening and sound. Anatomy words recall Gray’s Anatomy, the book Basquiat’s mother gave him after a childhood car accident.
The triptych format echoes Christian altarpieces, which can turn the musicians into a kind of saints.
Basquiat’s repeating and sampling of words has been compared to jazz improvisation and to hip-hop sampling.
context: Basquiat (1960 to 1988) was born in Brooklyn to a Haitian father and a Puerto Rican mother.
In the late 1970s he and Al Diaz spray-painted cryptic phrases signed ‘SAMO’ on walls in lower Manhattan.
By the early 1980s he was a star of Neo-Expressionism (a return to rough, emotional, figurative painting) and later collaborated with Andy Warhol.
He confronted racism in the art world and society, painting Black athletes, musicians and the history of slavery.
He died of a heroin overdose at 27. In 2017 his 1982 painting of a skull sold for 110.5 million dollars. On the exam.
If asked about the artist → Jean-Michel Basquiat, graﬀiti origins, Neo-Expressionism.
If asked about subject → Charlie Parker and Dizzy Gillespie, bebop jazz.
If asked about medium → acrylic and oil paintstick on three canvas panels: a triptych.
If asked about text → words crossed out to draw attention; references to songs, people and anatomy.
If asked about themes → Black heroes, music, race and memory.
Pair → Marilyn Diptych (No. 147): a multi-panel image of a celebrity.
Pair → Dancing at the Louvre (No. 232): Black artists and art history.

227.title: Summer Trees
227.plain: Summer Trees is an ink painting on paper by the South Korean artist Song Su-nam, made of soft vertical bands of gray and black ink that bleed into one another, suggesting a dense grove of trees in summer haze. Song led the Sumukhwa (ink painting) movement of the 1980s, which argued that Korean artists could be fully modern and abstract while using the traditional ink and brush of East Asian scholar-painters instead of Western oil paint.
227.spot: A soft, blurry field of vertical gray and black ink strokes on paper, darker and denser in the middle and paler toward the edges, with no outlines or details.
227.remember: Song of summer in ink: Song Su-nam, Summer Trees, 1983, South Korea. Sumukhwa = ‘some ink.’
compare: No. 201 (§9.10), Travelers among Mountains and Streams: Both use monochrome ink to express nature, one in detailed monumental landscape, the other in near-abstraction.
No. 149 (§5.51), The Bay: Both let fluid paint or ink soak and bleed into the support to create soft fields of tone.
No. 210 (§9.19), White and Red Plum Blossoms: Both reduce natural subjects to bold simplified forms within East Asian painting traditions.

form: Ink on paper: water-based ink soaks into absorbent paper and spreads, so edges feather and blur.
Broad, wet, vertical brushstrokes laid side by side and layered over one another.
Ink wash (ink diluted with different amounts of water) creates gradations from deep black to pale gray.
No outlines or details: the trees are suggested only by vertical rhythm and tone.
Near abstraction (forms not tied to realistic appearance); without the title you might see only stripes.
Ink cannot be corrected once applied, so the loose look depends on tight control of water, ink and brush speed.
function: A painting for exhibition and quiet contemplation, meant to bring the viewer into a meditative experience of nature.
A statement in a national debate about what modern Korean art should look like.
content: Trees are a traditional East Asian subject; summer suggests fullness and lush growth, reduced here to its essence.
Monochrome ink carries the values of literati painting (painting by scholar-oﬀicials), which prized restraint and inner spirit over outward appearance.
The work balances emptiness and presence, ideas linked to Daoist and Buddhist thought.
context: Song Su-nam (1938 to 2013) taught at Hongik University in Seoul and led the Sumukhwa movement with his students in the early 1980s.
After the Korean War, South Korea modernized fast and its art world was dominated by Western styles, from Informel to the monochrome Dansaekhwa painting of the 1970s.
Sumukhwa revived ink to claim modern painting could grow from Korean and East Asian roots, not only from New York or Paris.
Its soft fields of tone parallel Western Abstract Expressionism and Color Field painting, but its sources are East Asian ink traditions.
The movement arose under the military government of Chun Doo-hwan, after the 1980 Gwangju Uprising, a time of fierce debate over national identity. On the exam.
If asked about the artist → Song Su-nam, South Korea, 1983.
If asked about medium → ink on paper.
If asked about the movement → Sumukhwa, the 1980s Korean ink painting movement.
If asked about continuity and change → traditional literati medium used for modern, nearabstract painting.
Trap: it is Korean, not Chinese or Japanese.
Pair → Travelers among Mountains and Streams (No. 201): the ink landscape tradition it builds on.
Pair → The Bay (No. 149): fluid color soaking into the support, Western version.

228.title: Androgyn III
228.plain: Androgyn III is a sculpture by the Polish artist Magdalena Abakanowicz: a hollow, headless and armless human torso made of coarse burlap stiffened with resin, sitting on a rough frame of wooden poles. From the front it reads as a body; from behind it is clearly an empty shell. It belongs to her many works about anonymous, fragile and repeated human bodies, shaped by her experience of World War II and Communist rule in Poland.
228.spot: A rough, brown, wrinkled figure like dried skin or bark, with no head or arms, perched on a low frame of wooden poles joined with nails and string, hollow when seen from behind.
228.remember: ANDROgyn = no gender, no head, no arms, nothing inside. Abakanowicz, Poland, 1985: burlap bodies.
compare: No. 119 (§5.21), The Burghers of Calais: Both present bodies as vulnerable and anti-heroic, reflecting suffering in a time of crisis.
No. 250 (§11.27), Kui Hua Zi: Both use many near-identical handmade units to explore the individual within a mass society.
No. 193 (§9.2), Terra cotta warriors: Both create figures from molds yet make each one slightly different.
228.vocab: fiber art, mold, casting, resin, Socialist Realism.

form: Made of burlap (rough sacking cloth woven from jute) soaked in resin and pressed into molds based on real bodies; once hardened, the shell keeps the body’s shape.
Each cast comes out a little different because the cloth wrinkles and folds in its own way: repeated but never identical.
The support is a low, stretcher-like frame of rough wooden poles held with nails and string.
The surface is wrinkled, fibrous and earthy brown, like skin, bark or something long buried.
The figure is hollow and open at the back, so you see its emptiness.
Roughly life-size, so viewers measure their own bodies against it.
function: A gallery sculpture from the Androgyn series (1985), related to her earlier Backs (late 1970s to early 1980s) and later crowd works.
Meant to make viewers aware of their own bodies and of human vulnerability.
content: ‘Androgyn’ means neither clearly male nor female, so the figure stands for any human being.
Without a head, it has no face and no individual identity: anonymous, like people in a crowd or victims of history.
The empty shell suggests a body drained of its inner life, or what remains after suffering.
The pole frame can suggest a stretcher, a bier or a sacrificial altar.
Burlap is humble sacking material, tied to labor, poverty and survival; she saw fiber as organic, like skin.
context: Abakanowicz (1930 to 2017) was born near Warsaw into an aristocratic family. As a child she lived through the Nazi occupation and saw wartime violence against her own family.
After the war Poland came under a Soviet-backed Communist government that expected socialist realism (oﬀicial, heroic, realistic art). She turned to weaving instead.
In the 1960s she made the Abakans, huge hanging woven sculptures that won a gold medal at the 1965 São Paulo Biennial and helped launch the fiber art movement.
The 1980s figures followed martial law in Poland (1981 to 1983) and the crackdown on the Solidarity movement.
Her best-known later work, Agora (2006), sets 106 headless iron figures in Grant Park, Chicago. On the exam.
If asked about the artist → Magdalena Abakanowicz, Polish, 1985.
If asked about materials → burlap, resin, wood, nails and string.
If asked about form → headless, armless, hollow figure on a wooden frame.
If asked about meaning → anonymity, vulnerability, the individual lost in the mass.
If asked about context → World War II and Communist rule in Poland; her roots in fiber art.
Pair → The Burghers of Calais (No. 119): human vulnerability and suffering in sculpture.
Pair → Kui Hua Zi (No. 250): the individual within a mass of near-identical units.

229.title: A Book from the Sky
229.plain: A Book from the Sky is a room-filling installation by Chinese artist Xu Bing: hand-printed books laid out on the floor, long scrolls hanging from the ceiling and panels on the walls, all covered with about 4,000 characters he invented. Each looks exactly like a real Chinese character, but none can be read by anyone. Xu spent four years carving and printing this nonsense with traditional methods, raising questions about language, authority and the trust people place in the written word.
229.spot: A large room with rows of open, string-bound books on low platforms, long paper scrolls draped in arcs from the ceiling and printed panels on the walls, all densely printed with black, Chinese-looking characters.
229.remember: Xu Bing’s Book from the Sky (Tianshu, which also means ‘gibberish’): about 4,000 fake characters, 1987 to 1991. Looks readable, reads as nothing.
compare: No. 187 (§8.7), Folio from a Qur’an: Both treat script as an object of reverence, one sacred and readable, the other unreadable.
No. 212 (§9.21), Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan: Both come out of Cultural Revolution image and text culture, one as propaganda and one as a critique of it.
No. 235 (§11.12), Rebellious Silence, from the Women of Allah s…: Both use written script as a central visual element to raise questions of identity and power.
229.vocab: installation, movable type, calligraphy, woodblock print, propaganda.

form: About 4,000 invented characters, built from real components (strokes and parts of characters) recombined so they look correct. Roughly 4,000 is about the number of characters an educated reader needs for daily use.
Xu carved each character himself as movable type (separate blocks that can be arranged and reused), a printing technique invented in China around the 1040s.
The characters are in Song-style type, the standard look of printed Chinese books.
Printed on paper with traditional methods and bound with thread into books in old Chinese formats, with help from a traditional printing workshop.
The installation places books on the floor, scrolls overhead and panels on the walls, giving the space the feel of a temple or a library.
function: An immersive installation meant to be walked through and experienced, not read.
It confronts viewers with the gap between how something looks and what it means.
content: ‘Tianshu’ means a heavenly text, but in everyday Chinese it is also slang for writing nobody can understand.
Its original title was Mirror to Analyze the World: The Final Volume of the Century.
It can be read as a response to the flood of slogans and propaganda posters during the Cultural Revolution, when language was used to control people.
Everyone is equally illiterate before it: Chinese readers and non-readers alike are shut out.
It plays on Chinese reverence for books and scholarship, where printed text carries authority.
context: Xu Bing was born in 1955 in Chongqing and grew up in Beijing. During the Cultural Revolution he was sent to the countryside, where he lettered propaganda bulletins.
He studied printmaking at the Central Academy of Fine Arts in Beijing and worked within the experimental ‘85 New Wave art movement.
Part of the work was first shown in 1988 at the National Art Gallery in Beijing to wide attention.
After the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown, oﬀicial critics attacked it as meaningless and suspect. Xu moved to the United States in 1990.
He later won a MacArthur Fellowship (1999) and became a vice president of the Central Academy of Fine Arts in 2008. On the exam.
If asked about the artist → Xu Bing, China.
If asked about medium → mixed-media installation of books, scrolls and panels printed from hand-carved movable type.
If asked about content → about 4,000 invented, unreadable characters.
If asked about meaning → language, power, propaganda and authority of the written word.
If asked about context → after the Cultural Revolution, ‘85 New Wave, Tiananmen 1989.
Pair → Folio from a Qur’an (No. 187): script as sacred authority.
Pair → Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan (No. 212): Cultural Revolution propaganda.

230.title: Pink Panther
230.plain: Pink Panther is a glossy porcelain sculpture by Jeff Koons of a topless blonde woman hugging the cartoon Pink Panther, made in 1988 for his Banality series. It looks like an oversized gift-shop knickknack, and that is the point: Koons takes kitsch (cheap, sentimental, massmarket taste) and turns it into an expensive, carefully crafted art object. It asks who decides what counts as good taste, and how money, celebrity and pop culture shape the art world.
230.spot: A shiny, candy-colored porcelain statue about a meter tall: a blonde pin-up woman with bare breasts clutching a limp, floppy pink panther against her body.
230.remember: Koons + kitsch = cash. Pink Panther, 1988, Banality series: a porcelain pin-up hugs a cartoon cat.
compare: No. 144 (§5.46), Fountain: Both challenge what counts as art by elevating everyday, massproduced things.
No. 147 (§5.49), Marilyn Diptych: Both turn pop-culture celebrity and mass imagery into high-priced art objects.
No. 80 (§4.33), Venus of Urbino: Both present an eroticized female nude for a male-dominated market of buyers.

form: Glazed porcelain (fine, hard white ceramic, fired at very high heat), about 104 cm (41 inches) tall.
Made by skilled Italian porcelain workshops following Koons’s design. He did not make it with his own hands.
Produced in a small edition (a set of identical copies, here three plus an artist’s proof).
Glossy, flawless surfaces, candy colors and smooth, idealized forms imitate collectible figurines at giant scale.
The pyramid-shaped grouping recalls older European decorative porcelain and Baroque sculpture.
Exaggerated cuteness and sexiness are played completely straight, with no visible irony in the making.
function: A gallery sculpture for the art market. The Banality series opened in 1988 at three galleries at once, in New York, Chicago and Cologne.
Koons said he wanted to free viewers from guilt and shame about what they like.
One edition is in the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
content: The woman is a generic blonde bombshell, often compared to 1950s stars like Jayne Mansfield or Marilyn Monroe.
The Pink Panther comes from the 1963 film’s title sequence and later cartoons: childhood, innocence, mass entertainment.
Combining sex appeal and childish cuteness feels unsettling and exposes how consumer culture sells desire.
It parodies the long tradition of the female nude in art (compare Venus of Urbino, No. 80) by rendering it as kitsch.
context: Jeff Koons was born in 1955 in York, Pennsylvania. He worked as a Wall Street commodities broker while starting his art career and runs a large studio with many assistants.
The work belongs to the 1980s art-market boom and to appropriation (borrowing existing images or objects to make new art).
It continues Marcel Duchamp’s readymades (No. 144) and Andy Warhol’s factory-made pop images (No. 147).
Critics called the Banality series cynical and vulgar; supporters saw a sharp look at consumer taste.

Another Banality work, String of Puppies, led to a copyright case, Rogers v. Koons (1992), which Koons lost. In 2019 his Rabbit sold for 91.1 million dollars, then a record for a living artist. On the exam.
If asked about the artist → Jeff Koons, 1988, Banality series.
If asked about material → glazed porcelain, made by hired artisans.
If asked about key idea → kitsch and the boundary between high and low art.
If asked about authorship → idea by Koons, fabrication by others.
If asked about content → pin-up blonde plus cartoon character: sex, celebrity and childhood mixed together.
Pair → Fountain (No. 144): questioning what counts as art.
Pair → Marilyn Diptych (No. 147): celebrity and mass culture.

231.title: Untitled (#228), from the History Portraits series
231.plain: A large color photograph of Cindy Sherman dressed up as Judith, the biblical heroine, holding the severed head of the enemy general Holofernes. Sherman is photographer, model, makeup artist and costume designer at once, but she is playing a character, not making a self-portrait. The deliberately fake props poke fun at how Old Master paintings built up ideas about women, which makes it the textbook example of postmodern photography about identity.
231.spot: A tall, vertical color photo of a woman in a Renaissance-style costume and wig, holding up a rubbery, obviously fake severed head against a dark backdrop. It looks like an old painting at first glance, but the prosthetics, seams and makeup are visible.
231.remember: Sherman the ‘sheriff’ takes the head: Cindy Sherman, Untitled 228, 1990. The History Portraits ran 1988 to 1990, so this one comes at the end of the series.
compare: No. 105 (§5.7), Self-Portrait: Both are women artists using portraiture, but Vigée Le Brun builds a sincere, flattering self-image while Sherman stages an openly fake one.
No. 235 (§11.12), Rebellious Silence, from the Women of Allah s…: Both photographers pose as the subject in costume to examine how women are represented and seen.
No. 87 (§4.40), Self-Portrait with Saskia: Rembrandt also dresses up and plays a role in his own image, here as a character in a story rather than as himself.
No. 241 (§11.18), Pure Land: Mori, like Sherman, casts herself in costume as a figure from an older visual tradition.
231.vocab: photography, postmodernism, appropriation, male gaze, chiaroscuro, iconography.

form: A chromogenic color print (a standard color photographic print), printed large so it hangs at the scale of a painting in a museum, not a snapshot.
Sherman wears prosthetics (fake body parts), a wig, heavy makeup and a homemade costume; the edges and seams are left visible on purpose so the fakery shows.
Dark background and strong side lighting imitate the chiaroscuro (dramatic light-dark contrast) of Baroque Judith paintings by artists such as Caravaggio and Artemisia Gentileschi.
A single figure fills a tall vertical frame, posed like a sitter in a formal portrait, so the format itself borrows the authority of Old Master portraiture.
Staged alone in her studio: Sherman sets the lights, the camera, the costume and the pose herself, using a cable release or timer.
Like nearly all her photographs it has no real title, only Untitled and a catalogue number, so the viewer gets no fixed story.
function: Made as gallery art, one of about 35 photographs in the History Portraits series (1988– 1990), shown and sold through her New York dealer, Metro Pictures.
Not a self-portrait: Sherman insists her pictures show characters and types, and that the person in costume is a tool, not the subject.
Today it works as a standard teaching image for postmodernism (art that questions originality, authorship and ‘grand’ traditions) and for feminist critiques of art history.
content: In the Book of Judith (in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles; Apocrypha for Protestants), a Jewish widow gets the Assyrian general Holofernes drunk and beheads him to save her town, Bethulia.
Renaissance and Baroque artists painted Judith either as virtue defeating vice or as a dangerous seductress; male painters often eroticized her. Sherman’s clumsy version exposes that both are poses.
The fake head and fake body parts make the point that ‘femininity’ and even ‘great art’ are costumes, constructed and performed rather than natural.
The grotesque, slightly comic tone undercuts reverence for Old Masters and the male gaze (images built on the assumption of a male viewer looking at a woman).
context: Cindy Sherman (born 1954, New Jersey) belongs to the ‘Pictures Generation’ of New York artists who used photography to question media images. She became famous for the blackand-white Untitled Film Stills (1977–1980).

Source correction: she began the History Portraits during a stay in Rome in 1988 but has said she worked from reproductions in books, not museum visits, and made most of the series in her New York studio.

Only a few History Portraits copy specific paintings (one follows Caravaggio’s Sick Bacchus); most, including this one, are generic pastiches of a type of painting rather than a copy of a single work.
It belongs to the late-1980s moment of appropriation (borrowing existing images to comment on them) and feminist art that asked who gets to make and look at images of women.
Her photographs now sell for millions of dollars, an irony for work that questions the ‘masterpiece’ idea. On the exam.
If asked the medium → photograph (color print), not a painting. The trap is that it imitates a painting.
If asked who the figure is → Sherman in costume, but it is not a self-portrait; she plays a role.
Series: History Portraits; subject: Judith and Holofernes; date: 1990.
If asked about style or movement → postmodernism, appropriation and parody of Old Masters.
Attribution clues for an unfamiliar Sherman: the artist herself in costume, wigs and prosthetics, staged sets, numbered ‘Untitled’ titles.
Key theme: identity and gender are constructed, not natural; critique of the male gaze in art history.
Good contrast: Vigée Le Brun (No. 105) presents her real self flatteringly; Sherman presents a fake self to expose the conventions.

232.title: Dancing at the Louvre
232.medium: Acrylic on canvas, tie-dyed, pieced fabric border
232.plain: A painted story quilt by Faith Ringgold: a painting on canvas showing a woman and three little girls dancing in front of the Mona Lisa at the Louvre, framed by quilted fabric and handwritten text. The text tells the story of Willia Marie Simone, a made-up Black American woman artist living in 1920s Paris. It combines painting, quilting and storytelling to put Black women into an art history that left them out.
232.spot: A square-ish painted scene of figures dancing in front of a small framed Mona Lisa and other museum paintings, surrounded by a patchwork border of tie-dyed fabric squares, with strips of handwritten text above and below the picture.
232.remember: Faith Ringgold rings in the Louvre with a dance: story quilt, 1991, from The French Collection. ‘Quilt plus Mona Lisa equals Ringgold.’
compare: No. 141 (§5.43), The Migration of the Negro, Panel no. 49: Jacob Lawrence also tells Black American history in a numbered series of panels with written captions.
No. 143 (§5.45), Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda Pa…: Rivera crowds historical figures into one festive scene, while Ringgold invents a character to rewrite who appears in art history.
No. 245 (§11.22), Old Man’s Cloth: Both turn textile traditions associated with African and diaspora identity into large-scale contemporary art.
232.vocab: story quilt, acrylic paint, pieced fabric, tie-dye, narrative, craft.

form: Acrylic on canvas for the central painted scene, sewn into a pieced (patchwork) border of tie-dyed fabric squares, about 6 feet tall and nearly 7 feet wide.
Strips of handwritten text run across the top and bottom of the painting, so the work is read as well as looked at.
Flat, bright, simplified figures with little shading or deep space, closer to folk art and illustration than to academic realism.
The famous paintings on the wall are shown small and slightly cartoonish, while the dancers are large and lively, flipping the usual hierarchy of a museum.
Quilting brings in soft materials, stitching and a grid, techniques traditionally seen as ‘women’s work’ or craft rather than fine art.
function: Gallery art and the first quilt in The French Collection, a series of twelve story quilts (1991–1997) about the fictional Willia Marie Simone.
The text is written in Willia’s voice, as if in letters home, so the quilt works like a page from an illustrated novel.
It gives Black viewers, especially women and girls, an image of themselves at home inside a famous European museum.
content: In the story, Willia takes her friend Marcia and Marcia’s three daughters to the Louvre; the children and mother dance instead of quietly looking at the art.
Dancing in front of the Mona Lisa, the most famous Western painting, shows joy and ownership instead of awe; the figures have their backs to it.
Willia Marie Simone is an invented Black woman artist in 1920s Paris, the era of Josephine Baker and the Harlem Renaissance, when Paris welcomed some Black American artists more than the US did.
The quilt form itself is a message: African American women’s craft and oral storytelling count as art.
context: Faith Ringgold (1930–2024) was born and raised in Harlem. In the 1960s she painted political works about civil rights, and in 1970 she protested the exclusion of Black and women artists from New York museums.
She began making story quilts in the 1980s, first with her mother, the dressmaker and designer Willi Posey; Ringgold traced quilting in her family back to an enslaved ancestor.
Other quilts in The French Collection place Willia among famous figures; in The Sunflower Quilting Bee at Arles, Black American women activists sew a quilt in a field with Van Gogh.
Her children’s book Tar Beach (1991), based on her quilt of the same name, made her widely known beyond the art world.
The work belongs to feminist and Black arts movements that challenged the ‘high art’ versus ‘craft’ hierarchy. On the exam.
If asked the artist → Faith Ringgold; format → story quilt; series → The French Collection.
If asked the main character → Willia Marie Simone, a fictional Black woman artist in 1920s Paris.
Materials: acrylic on canvas with a tie-dyed, pieced fabric border; the text is part of the work.
If asked about tradition → combines European painting with African American quilting and storytelling; elevates craft to fine art.
Theme: who belongs in the museum and in art history; Black women claiming space.
Trap: the dancers are not Willia’s own daughters; the story says the girls are her friend’s children.

233.title: Trade (Gifts for Trading Land with White People)
233.medium: Oil and mixed media on canvas
233.plain: A large painting-plus-objects by Salish and Kootenai artist Jaune Quick-toSee Smith, made in 1992 when the US was marking 500 years since Columbus. A canoe floats across a collaged, paint-dripped canvas, and above it hangs a chain of cheap souvenirs: sports caps with Native mascots, toy tomahawks, plastic beads. The title offers to trade the junk back for the land, mocking the myth that Native people sold their land for trinkets.
233.spot: A wide, three-part canvas covered with newspaper collage and runny drips of red, yellow and green paint, with a big outlined canoe in the middle and a chain of real objects (team caps, toy tomahawks, beads) strung across the top.
233.remember: 1992 equals 500 years after 1492, so Smith ‘trades’ back. Think ‘Trade-mark mascots’: the trade goods are sports logos.
compare: No. 163 (§6.11), Bandolier bag: The Lenape bandolier bag mixes Native forms with European trade beads, the real history of trade goods Smith satirizes.
No. 165 (§6.13), Painted elk hide: The painted elk hide was made for sale to outsiders, another case of Native imagery shaped by a non-Native market.
No. 237 (§11.14), Pisupo Lua Afe: Tuffery also uses cheap mass-produced goods to criticize what colonial trade did to an Indigenous culture.
233.vocab: collage, triptych, mixed media, combine, colonialism.

form: Oil and mixed media on canvas, a triptych (three-panel work) about 5 feet tall and 14 feet wide, with real objects attached above it.
The surface is a collage of newspaper clippings, including pages from the Char-Koosta News, the newspaper of the Flathead Reservation where Smith was born.
Loose, dripping paint in red, yellow and green runs down over the collage, recalling Abstract Expressionism and also suggesting blood.
Source correction: the large canoe is painted and collaged on the canvas itself, in the center; the objects, not the canoe, hang from a chain above.
Hanging items include caps and pennants of teams with Native mascots (such as the Atlanta Braves and the Washington team then called the Redskins), toy tomahawks, plastic beads and ‘Indian’ dolls.
The mix of painting and real objects follows Robert Rauschenberg’s combines (paintings with attached objects), which Smith admired.
function: Made as gallery art in 1992, the Columbus quincentenary, as a direct response to celebrations of 1492.
That year Smith also organized a traveling exhibition of Native artists, The Submuloc Show/Columbus Wohs (‘Columbus Show’ spelled backward), answering the celebrations.
Now in the Chrysler Museum of Art, Norfolk, Virginia, it is used to teach Native perspectives on colonization.
content: The title flips the old story that Native people traded land for beads and trinkets, such as the largely mythical tale of Manhattan being sold for 24 dollars of goods.
The souvenirs are mass-produced stereotypes of Native people sold by non-Native companies, so the ‘gifts’ are Native identity turned into merchandise.
The canoe stands for Native presence, travel and trade before and after contact; it floats over modern news stories about reservation life.
The humor is ironic: no one would accept such junk for a continent, which points to how unfair the original ‘trades’ and treaties were.
context: Jaune Quick-to-See Smith (1940–2025) was an enrolled member of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Nation of the Flathead Reservation, Montana.
She trained in Western modernism and combined it with Native imagery, using maps, canoes and horses to address land, treaties and environment.
Sports mascots were already being protested in 1992; the Washington NFL team dropped its name in 2020, and the Cleveland baseball team changed its name in 2021.
Her painting I See Red: Target became the first painting by a Native American artist bought by the National Gallery of Art (2020), and the Whitney held her retrospective in 2023. On the exam.
If asked the date’s significance → 1992, the 500th anniversary of Columbus’s 1492 voyage.
If asked the artist’s identity → Native American, Salish and Kootenai (Flathead Reservation, Montana).
Technique: painting plus collage plus attached found objects; drips borrowed from Abstract Expressionism.
Theme: colonization, land theft, commercialization of Native imagery, mascots.
Tone: irony and satire, not mourning.
Trap: the canoe is part of the painted canvas; the hanging items are souvenirs.

234.title: Earth’s Creation
