234.plain: A huge four-panel painting by Emily Kame Kngwarreye, an Aboriginal Australian elder who only started painting on canvas in her late seventies. Dense dabs of green, yellow, red and blue cover the surface, showing her country, Alhalkere, bursting into life after the rains. It looks like Western abstract art, but it comes from ceremony and an ancestral connection to land, and it set an auction record when it sold for over a million Australian dollars in 2007.
234.spot: A very wide painting made of thousands of overlapping thick brush dabs in greens, yellows, reds and blues, with no figures and no horizon, like a dense field of flowers seen from very close.
234.remember: ‘Emily’s Earth’ at age 80-something: Kngwarreye, 1994, two years before her death. Earth is created in four panels, one for each of the four letters in ‘land’.
compare: No. 149 (§5.51), The Bay: Frankenthaler’s stained abstraction looks similar but comes from Western modernism, not ancestral knowledge of land.
No. 227 (§11.4), Summer Trees: Song Su-nam also makes nearly abstract images of nature that grow out of a non-Western painting tradition.
No. 151 (§5.53), Spiral Jetty: Both deal with land on a huge scale, but Smithson reshapes the land while Kngwarreye maps her inherited relationship to it.
234.vocab: synthetic polymer paint, Dreaming, all-over composition, batik, Country, abstract.

form: Synthetic polymer paint (acrylic) on canvas, four panels joined to about 9 feet tall and 21 feet wide.
Built from overlapping thick dabs and dots made with a loaded brush, a late, looser style sometimes called ‘dump dot’, layered over earlier colors.
An all-over composition (no single focal point, edge to edge) with no horizon or single viewpoint, so it reads like land seen from above and from within at once.
Bright greens and yellows over darker underlayers suggest new growth over red desert earth.
Painted flat on the ground, as she sat over the canvas, not upright on an easel.
function: Painted in 1994 for sale through a gallery in Alice Springs (Mbantua Gallery), as part of the market for Aboriginal art on canvas.
For Kngwarreye, painting expressed responsibility for her country (ancestral land) and its Dreaming stories, not decoration or self-expression alone.
It sold at auction in 2007 for just over one million Australian dollars, at the time a record for an Australian woman artist.
content: It shows Alhalkere, her ancestral country in the Utopia region of the Northern Territory, during the wet season when rain makes plants and seeds flourish.
The Dreaming (in her language, Altyerre) is the ancestral law and creation stories linking people, land, plants and animals; the title ‘Earth’s Creation’ points to this.
Her personal Dreaming included the pencil yam (her name ‘Kame’ or ‘Kam’ refers to the yam seed), plus emu and grasses; the dense marks evoke seeds, flowers and roots.
Rather than a landscape view, it is a map of knowledge and relationship: the land as a living thing she belongs to.
context: Emily Kame Kngwarreye (about 1910–1996) was an Anmatyerre elder from Utopia, northeast of Alice Springs; recent exhibitions spell her name Emily Kam Kngwarray.
Women’s ceremonies (awelye) involved body painting; from 1977 she made batik (wax-resist dyed fabric) with the Utopia Women’s Batik Group.
She began acrylic painting on canvas in 1988–1989 and made roughly 3,000 works in about eight years, a remarkable late career.
Western critics compared her to Abstract Expressionists such as Pollock, but she had no contact with that tradition; the resemblance is coincidental.
She represented Australia at the 1997 Venice Biennale, after her death, and Tate Modern held a major exhibition of her work in 2025. On the exam.
If asked the culture → Aboriginal Australian (Anmatyerre), from Utopia, Northern Territory.
If asked the subject → her country Alhalkere and the Dreaming, after the wet season.
Medium: synthetic polymer (acrylic) paint on canvas; four panels; 1994.
Trap: it looks like Abstract Expressionism but comes from Indigenous ceremonial and body-painting traditions.
Biography hook: started painting on canvas in her late seventies, after years of batik.
Continuity and change: ancient ideas about land in a new, market-oriented medium.

235.title: Rebellious Silence, from the Women of Allah series
235.plain: A black-and-white photograph from Shirin Neshat’s Women of Allah series: a woman in a black chador holds a rifle upright so its barrel splits her face, and Persian poetry is written in ink over her skin. Neshat, an Iranian artist living in the US, made it after returning to Iran in 1990 and seeing how the 1979 Islamic Revolution had changed women’s lives. It refuses to give Western viewers an easy story about veiled women.
235.spot: A tight, symmetrical black-and-white close-up of a woman’s face framed by a black veil, with a rifle barrel running vertically up the middle and dense handwritten Persian script inked over her face.
235.remember: Shirin Neshat, Rebellious Silence, 1994: a gun down the middle, words all over, and not a sound. ‘Neshat’s net of words’ covers the face.
compare: No. 107 (§5.9), La Grande Odalisque: Ingres’s odalisque is a Western fantasy of a passive Eastern woman; Neshat shows a veiled woman who is armed and unreadable.
No. 231 (§11.8), Untitled: Both women artists pose in costume in photographs to question how women are represented.
No. 229 (§11.6), A Book from the Sky: Xu Bing and Neshat both use script that most viewers cannot read, making language itself a barrier.
235.vocab: calligraphy, chador, gelatin silver print, Orientalism, martyr, symmetry.

form: Black-and-white gelatin silver print (a standard darkroom photograph) with calligraphy in ink added by hand on top of the print.
Neshat is the model, but the photograph was taken by Cynthia Preston under Neshat’s direction.
Strict symmetry: the rifle barrel divides the face into two halves, framed by the black chador (full-body veil).
The text follows the contours of the face like decoration in an Islamic manuscript, turning skin into a page.
High contrast between white skin, black cloth and black ink creates a stark, graphic image.
function: Gallery art, part of the Women of Allah series (1993–1997), shown mostly to Western audiences in the US and Europe.
Made to examine women’s roles in post-revolutionary Iran, especially women as both devout and militant.
The writing is unreadable to most Western viewers, so the work deliberately blocks easy access and makes them aware of their assumptions.
content: The chador can mean modesty, religious faith, state control, or revolutionary pride; Neshat leaves all these readings open.
The rifle links the woman to martyrdom and armed struggle, recalling women in the 1979 revolution and the Iran–Iraq War (1980–1988).
The inked poem, by the Iranian poet Tahereh Saffarzadeh, praises faith and revolutionary commitment, so the ‘voice’ on the face is a woman’s.
The title is a paradox: silence that rebels. She does not speak, but the text and gun speak for her.
context: Shirin Neshat was born in 1957 in Qazvin, Iran, and left for the US in 1974 to study art, before the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
Returning in 1990 after the revolution, she found strict dress codes and a new public image of women; the series came out of that shock.
The work resists Orientalism (Western fantasies of the ‘exotic’ East) by showing veiled women as active and armed, not passive.
Neshat later turned to film and video, including Turbulent (1998) and the feature film Women Without Men (2009), which won the Silver Lion at Venice.
Her work has made it unsafe for her to return to Iran; she lives in New York. On the exam.
If asked the series → Women of Allah; artist → Shirin Neshat, Iranian-born, US-based.
Medium: ink on photograph (black-and-white print with hand-inked Persian calligraphy).
If asked the context → post-1979 Islamic Revolution Iran; women, faith, violence and martyrdom.
The text is poetry by an Iranian woman (Tahereh Saffarzadeh), in Persian (Farsi) written in Arabic script.
Composition: symmetrical, rifle splits the face.
Trap: it is not simply a protest against the veil; it shows contradictions without picking a side.

236.title: En la Barberia no se Llora (No Crying Allowed in the Barbershop)
236.plain: A room-sized installation by Puerto Rican artist Pepón Osorio that recreates a barbershop, packed floor to ceiling with chairs, mirrors, photos, toys and keepsakes, while small video screens in the barber chairs show men crying. The barbershop is where boys learn how to be men, and the title states the rule they learn: men do not cry. It was first set up in an empty storefront in a Puerto Rican neighborhood of Hartford, Connecticut, for the community itself.
236.spot: A crowded, colorful fake barbershop with barber chairs, mirrors and walls and ceiling covered in photos, trophies and trinkets, with small TV screens built into the chairs.
236.remember: Osorio’s ‘barber-ía’ in Hartford, 1994: chairs that cry. The barber says ‘no se llora’, but the TVs are sobbing.
compare: No. 238 (§11.15), Electronic Superhighway: Both are installations that use TV monitors, Paik to map national media culture and Osorio to show private male emotion.
No. 232 (§11.9), Dancing at the Louvre: Ringgold and Osorio both use everyday materials and narratives drawn from their own communities.
No. 243 (§11.20), Darkytown Rebellion: Walker’s room-sized installation also surrounds the viewer and confronts stereotypes tied to race and gender.
236.vocab: installation, site-specific, video art, machismo, mixed media, community-based art.

form: A mixed-media installation (a whole environment the viewer enters) built from barber chairs, mirrors, furniture, photographs, toys and souvenirs.
Video monitors set into the barber chairs play footage of men crying.
A deliberately crowded, ornamented, colorful style; Osorio draws on the ‘more is more’ decorating of Puerto Rican homes, which he sees as a cultural aesthetic.
Walls and ceiling are covered with images of men, sports memorabilia and keepsakes, including mementos of boys’ first haircuts.
It looks like a real working barbershop, so the line between art and everyday space is blurred.
function: Commissioned in 1994 by Real Art Ways, an alternative arts organization, and installed in a vacant storefront on Park Street in Hartford, Connecticut, a largely Puerto Rican neighborhood.
Made for local people, many of whom never go to museums; neighbors and barbers visited and talked about it.
Later shown in galleries and museums, which changed it from a community event into an art-world object.
content: The barbershop is a male social club: a place for talk about sports, politics and women, and where a boy’s first haircut is a rite of passage.
The title, ‘In the barbershop, one doesn’t cry’, states the code of machismo (an exaggerated ideal of tough masculinity).
The videos of crying men contradict the title and show the emotional cost of that code.
Toys, sports images and portraits of male heroes show how masculinity is taught through objects and role models from childhood.
context: Pepón Osorio was born in 1955 in Santurce, Puerto Rico, moved to New York in 1975, and worked for years as a social worker in the Bronx.
That experience shaped his community-based practice: he talks with residents and builds installations around their stories before showing them in a neighborhood setting.
His earlier installations, such as The Scene of the Crime (Whose Crime?) (1993), also used crowded, kitsch-filled rooms to question stereotypes of Latino life.
He received a MacArthur Fellowship in 1999 and later taught at Temple University’s Tyler School of Art in Philadelphia. On the exam.
If asked the artist → Pepón Osorio, Puerto Rican; date 1994.
Format: immersive installation with video, originally site-specific in a Hartford storefront.
Theme: masculinity and machismo in Latino culture; the barbershop as a place where boys learn gender roles.
Key irony: the title forbids crying, while the videos show men crying.
If asked about audience → made for the local Puerto Rican community, not first for museumgoers.
Style clue: excessive, colorful accumulation of objects.

237.title: Pisupo Lua Afe (Corned Beef 2000)
237.plain: A roughly life-size bull made from flattened corned-beef cans riveted together, by New Zealand artist Michel Tuffery, who has Samoan, Tahitian and Cook Islands heritage. Canned corned beef, called pisupo in Samoa, became a staple and a ceremonial gift in the Pacific, pushing out traditional foods and causing health problems. The bull is a funny, shiny animal and a serious critique of what global trade did to Pacific diets and economies.
237.spot: A full-size standing bull whose body is covered with flattened, brightly printed food-can labels joined by rows of rivets, like a patchwork of tin.
237.remember: Pisupo sounds like ‘pea soup’: the first tinned food, now all canned meat. Tuffery’s tin bull, 1994, looks ahead to 2000 (‘lua afe’).
compare: No. 223 (§10.11), Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa cloths t…: Fijian mats and tapa show traditional Pacific ceremonial gift exchange, which canned corned beef has partly replaced.
No. 147 (§5.49), Marilyn Diptych: Warhol celebrates mass-produced consumer imagery, while Tuffery uses it to criticize its effects.
No. 245 (§11.22), Old Man’s Cloth: Both turn discarded consumer packaging into art that comments on trade and colonial history.
237.vocab: found object, mixed media, rivet, globalization, gift exchange, diaspora.

form: Mixed media: flattened corned-beef tins cut and joined with rivets over a structural frame, keeping the printed labels visible.
Roughly life-size, about 2 meters long, standing like a real animal.
The repeating label designs form a patchwork pattern across the body, giving it a bright, commercial surface.
Uses found objects (discarded or everyday manufactured items) instead of carved wood or stone, the traditional sculptural materials of the Pacific.
The rivets and metal seams give it the look of a machine or a mass-produced product.
function: Made as a sculpture for exhibition; it is now in Te Papa Tongarewa, the national museum of New Zealand, in Wellington.
Tuffery made several tin-can bulls and used some in public performances, including bulls on wheels with fireworks staged to charge at each other.
Aimed at Pacific Islander and New Zealand audiences, opening conversations about diet, health and dependence on imports.
content: Pisupo comes from ‘pea soup’, one of the first canned foods traders brought to Samoa; the word came to mean all canned food, especially corned beef.
Corned beef became a key gift in Samoan ceremonial exchanges (faʻalavelave, such as weddings and funerals), partly replacing fish, taro and other local foods.
The bull refers to cattle introduced to the Pacific by Europeans, and to the meat industry in New Zealand and Australia that exports the corned beef.
‘Lua afe’ means ‘two thousand’ in Samoan: the title asks what Pacific life will look like in the year 2000 if the trend continues.
context: Michel Tuffery was born in 1966 in Wellington, New Zealand, of Samoan, Tahitian and Cook Islands (Rarotongan) descent.
He critiques globalization and the colonial trade relationships that made Pacific Islanders dependent on cheap imported food.
Diet-related diabetes and obesity rates in Samoa and other Pacific nations are among the highest in the world, a public health crisis the work points to.
It connects to Pop Art’s use of consumer packaging, but from the point of view of a culture on the receiving end of that consumer economy. On the exam.
If asked the materials → flattened corned-beef cans and rivets.
If asked the culture → Samoan and wider Pacific diaspora, made in New Zealand, 1994.
Meaning of the title: pisupo means canned food (from ‘pea soup’); lua afe means 2000.
Themes: globalization, colonial trade, health, and gift exchange.
Good comparison theme: traditional gift exchange (mats and tapa) versus imported goods.
Trap: it is not a celebration of cattle or a hunting image; it is a critique of consumption.

238.title: Electronic Superhighway: Continental U.S., Alaska, Hawaii
238.plain: A wall-sized map of the United States made from hundreds of television sets, with each state outlined in colored neon and its screens playing video about that state. KoreanAmerican artist Nam June Paik, the founder of video art, coined the phrase ‘electronic superhighway’ in 1974, predicting a networked world. The work shows America as something experienced through screens and media rather than through travel.
238.spot: A huge wall of old boxy TV screens arranged in the shape of the continental US, with glowing neon lines tracing the state borders; Alaska and Hawaii are separate small sections.
238.remember: Paik’s ‘Pack’ of TVs: 1995, the year the internet went mainstream. ‘Super highway’ plus neon map equals Paik.
compare: No. 239 (§11.16), The Crossing: Viola also uses video, but for slow, spiritual contemplation instead of fast media overload.
No. 117 (§5.19), The Horse in Motion: Muybridge’s photographs were an early step toward moving images; Paik shows where moving images led.
No. 246 (§11.23), Stadia II : Mehretu and Paik both map spaces and networks of modern life rather than picturing a single scene.
238.vocab: video art, installation, closed-circuit video, neon, Fluxus, multichannel video.

form: A video installation of about 336 television monitors, around 575 feet of colored neon tubing, steel and electronics, roughly 15 by 40 feet.
Listed as a 49-channel closed-circuit video work: many separate video sources play at once across the screens.
The neon outlines of the states recall roadside motel and diner signs along American highways.
Each state plays clips tied to it, such as The Wizard of Oz for Kansas and the musical Oklahoma! for Oklahoma.
The screens flash fast-edited, colorful footage, creating sensory overload rather than a single image to contemplate.
A live camera feeds the viewer’s own image into the Washington, D.C. screens, making the viewer part of the work.
function: Made in 1995 as a large gallery installation; now at the Smithsonian American Art Museum in Washington, D.C.
Meant to be walked past and taken in all at once, like the experience of channel surfing or driving through billboards.
Its old cathode-ray TVs are now obsolete, so the museum must find replacement parts, an example of the conservation problems of media art.
content: The phrase ‘electronic superhighway’ compares information networks to the Interstate Highway System begun in the 1950s, which reshaped American life and mobility.
America is shown as a patchwork of media stereotypes: each state reduced to its movie or TV image.
The closed-circuit camera shows that viewers are not just watching media; they are also on it, an early idea about surveillance and self-display.
Paik, an immigrant, maps his adopted country through the medium that shaped how Americans saw themselves.
context: Nam June Paik (1932–2006) was born in Seoul, studied in Tokyo and then music in Germany, where he met the composer John Cage and joined the Fluxus movement.
He moved to New York in 1964 and is called the father of video art; he was among the first artists to use the portable Sony Portapak video camera (1965).
He coined ‘electronic super highway’ in a 1974 report for the Rockefeller Foundation, two decades before the term ‘information superhighway’ became popular for the internet.
Earlier works such as TV Buddha (1974) also explored how television changes perception and attention. On the exam.
If asked the artist → Nam June Paik, Korean-American, the ‘father of video art’.
Form: TV monitors arranged as a map of the US, outlined in neon.
If asked the title’s meaning → Paik’s own 1974 phrase, predicting networked communication like the internet.
Detail: closed-circuit camera puts the viewer into the D.C. screens.
Movement: Paik came out of Fluxus, an experimental 1960s movement mixing music, performance and art.
Themes: media saturation, mobility, American identity seen through pop culture.
Date: 1995; location: Smithsonian American Art Museum.

239.title: The Crossing
239.plain: A video installation by Bill Viola in which two huge projections play on the two sides of one screen in a dark room. On both sides a man walks slowly toward you; on one, flames rise from his feet until he is consumed, and on the other, water pours down on him until he vanishes. Shown in extreme slow motion with roaring sound, it is about death, purification and transformation, drawing on Christian, Buddhist and Sufi ideas.
239.spot: A dark room with a giant screen showing a man engulfed by fire on one side and by a torrent of water on the other, the same figure in the same pose on both.
239.remember: Viola crosses over by fire and water, 1996. Two sides, two elements, one man: ‘crossing’ over to the other side, death.
compare: No. 238 (§11.15), Electronic Superhighway: Both are video installations, but Paik’s is fast, fragmented media culture and Viola’s is slow and spiritual.
No. 77 (§4.30), Isenheim altarpiece: The Isenheim altarpiece also uses physical suffering and transformation to move viewers toward spiritual healing.
No. 89 (§4.42), Ecstasy of Saint Teresa: Bernini’s Saint Teresa also stages a mystic’s transcendent experience as theater for the viewer.
239.vocab: video art, installation, diptych, projection, immersive.

form: A video and sound installation: two channels of color video projected onto opposite sides of a large freestanding screen, about 16 feet tall, with loud amplified sound.
Each sequence runs about ten minutes; a man walks from far away toward the viewer and stops, filling the screen.
On one side small flames at his feet grow into a blaze; on the other, drops of water become a crushing downpour. Both end with him gone and the element subsiding.
Filmed at high speed and played back in slow motion, so the destruction becomes slow, almost calm and beautiful.
Viewers cannot see both sides at once; they must walk around the screen, like a sculpture or a two-sided altarpiece.
The darkened room, scale and roaring sound create an immersive experience.
function: A museum installation meant to give viewers a meditative, almost religious experience in a secular space.
It is in the collection of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum, New York.
Viola wanted people to slow down and pay attention to time, a reaction against the speed of television.
content: Fire and water are opposites but both can destroy and purify; in many religions they stand for cleansing, baptism, cremation and spiritual rebirth.
The man’s disappearance suggests death, or the self dissolving into something larger, an idea found in Sufi mysticism, Zen Buddhism and Christian mystics.
‘The Crossing’ suggests crossing from life to death, or from the physical world to the spiritual.
The diptych-like format (two paired images) recalls Christian altarpieces.
context: Bill Viola (1951–2024) was an American pioneer of video art; early on he worked as a technical assistant to video artists, including Nam June Paik.
As a child he nearly drowned in a lake, an experience he said showed him a beautiful world beneath the surface; water recurs throughout his work.
He studied Zen Buddhism, the Sufi poet Rumi and Christian mystics such as St. John of the Cross.
He later made Martyrs (Earth, Air, Fire, Water) (2014), a permanent video installation in St. Paul’s Cathedral, London, showing the spiritual reading continued. On the exam.
If asked the artist → Bill Viola; medium → video and sound installation; date 1996.
Elements: fire on one side, water on the other; the man disappears in both.
Technique: extreme slow motion, large projection, roaring sound, dark room.
Themes: death, purification, transcendence, spirituality.
Traditions: Christian, Buddhist and Sufi mysticism; Renaissance altarpieces and diptychs.
Contrast with Paik: Viola’s video is slow and meditative; Paik’s is fast and overloaded.

240.title: Guggenheim Museum Bilbao
240.plain: A contemporary art museum in Bilbao, Spain, designed by Frank Gehry and opened in 1997, made of swooping curved forms clad in thin, shiny titanium. It was designed with aerospace software that made its irregular shapes buildable. The building drew so many tourists to a declining industrial city that ‘the Bilbao effect’ became a term for cities using a signature building to revive themselves.
240.spot: A cluster of curving, crumpled, silvery metal forms beside a river, combined with blocky limestone sections and glass, with a bridge running past one end.
240.remember: Gehry’s ‘Gleaming Guggenheim’: titanium, 1997, Bilbao. Bilbao effect = build something famous and tourists follow.
compare: No. 249 (§11.26), MAXXI National Museum of XXI Century Arts: Hadid’s MAXXI is another flowing, anti-box contemporary art museum built as a national cultural statement.
No. 88 (§4.41), San Carlo alle Quattro Fontane: Borromini’s San Carlo also uses curving, undulating walls to break with standard, rectangular architecture.
No. 146 (§5.48), Seagram Building: The Seagram Building’s rational glass box is exactly the modernist approach Gehry rejects.
240.vocab: Deconstructivism, titanium, atrium, cladding, computer-aided design, Bilbao effect.

form: Built of titanium, glass and limestone: about 33,000 paper-thin titanium panels cover the curving parts; the more rectangular sections are clad in limestone.
Source correction: the titanium sheets are well under half a millimeter thick (about 0.4 millimeters), thin enough to ripple slightly and change color with weather and light.
Designed with CATIA, three-dimensional modeling software created for French aerospace engineering, which allowed precise, buildable curves.
A tall glass atrium, around 50 meters high, serves as the central hub from which galleries branch out.
The building wraps under and around the La Salve bridge and sits on the Nervión River, linking the museum to the city’s infrastructure.
Galleries range from conventional rectangular rooms to one huge, boat-shaped gallery that holds Richard Serra’s giant steel sculptures.
function: A branch museum of the Solomon R. Guggenheim Foundation for modern and contemporary art, especially large-scale works.
Paid for by the Basque government as part of a plan to revive Bilbao, a city whose shipbuilding and steel industries were declining.
It drew about a million visitors a year in its early years, quickly repaying the investment through tourism.
content: From the river, the curves can resemble a ship or a fish’s scales, recalling Bilbao’s past as an industrial port; fish forms are a recurring Gehry motif.
The irregular forms reject the modernist box and the idea that ‘form follows function’.
The building is itself the advertisement: the architecture became the museum’s main attraction, sometimes more famous than the art inside.
context: Frank Gehry, born in Toronto in 1929 and based in Los Angeles, won the Pritzker Prize in 1989.
Gehry was included in the 1988 Museum of Modern Art exhibition Deconstructivist Architecture, along with Zaha Hadid; Deconstructivism fragments and distorts conventional building forms.
Thomas Krens, director of the Guggenheim Foundation, pushed for global branch museums, a strategy critics called the ‘McGuggenheim’.
Critics argue the building overwhelms the art, and many cities that copied the Bilbao effect did not get the same results.
Outdoor works include Jeff Koons’s flower-covered Puppy at the entrance and Louise Bourgeois’s giant spider Maman. On the exam.
If asked the architect → Frank Gehry; place → Bilbao, Spain; date → 1997.
Materials: titanium, glass and limestone.
Technique: designed with CATIA aerospace software.
Style: Deconstructivism, with curving, fragmented forms.
Key term: the ‘Bilbao effect’, urban regeneration through a landmark building.
Trap: it is a branch of the Guggenheim, not the original Frank Lloyd Wright building in New York.

241.title: Pure Land
241.plain: A huge, glossy digital photograph mounted on glass in which Japanese artist Mariko Mori, dressed as a Buddhist goddess, floats on a lotus above the Dead Sea while small cartoonish beings play music in the sky around her. The title refers to the paradise of Pure Land Buddhism. It fuses ancient Buddhist imagery with anime, pop culture and digital technology, imagining a future where spirituality and technology meet.
241.spot: A wide, pastel, dreamlike landscape of water and pale mountains with a costumed woman floating on a lotus in the center, surrounded by small, cute alien-like figures playing instruments in mid-air.
241.remember: Mori floats over the Dead Sea in a ‘pure’ digital land, 1998. Mori = more tech, more glitter, still Buddhist.
compare: No. 197 (§9.6), Todai-ji: Tōdai-ji is a traditional Japanese Buddhist temple; Mori relocates Buddhist imagery into a digital, global setting.
No. 231 (§11.8), Untitled: Both Mori and Sherman cast themselves in costume as figures from older images.
No. 184 (§8.4), Jowo Rinpoche, enshrined in the Jokhang Temple: The Jowo Rinpoche is an ancient Buddhist icon venerated in a temple, while Mori’s icon is a photograph for a gallery.
241.vocab: digital photography, Pure Land, lotus, iconography, composite image, bodhisattva.

form: A color photograph on glass: a digitally composited and retouched image printed on a photographic layer sealed in glass panels, roughly 10 by 20 feet.
Digital manipulation combines the real landscape with the artist’s figure, the floating beings and glowing effects.
Soft, unreal pastel colors (pinks, blues, lavenders) and a smooth, shiny surface give it the feel of a video game or anime still.
A symmetrical, centered composition with the goddess at the middle, like an icon or a Buddhist painting of a deity.
Mori designed her own costume and headdress and poses herself, so she is both artist and image.
function: Gallery art meant to create a sense of calm and wonder; Mori connected the work to meditation and the hope for spiritual harmony.
Part of a group of works from 1996 to 1998, often called the Esoteric Cosmos series, with a related 3-D video version.
It brings Buddhist imagery to international contemporary-art audiences who may know it only through pop culture.
content: Pure Land Buddhism teaches that faithful devotees can be reborn in the Western Paradise of Amida Buddha, a place of perfect peace.
Mori appears as Kichijōten, a Japanese goddess of beauty and good fortune, who developed from the Hindu goddess Lakshmi.
The lotus is a Buddhist symbol of purity, growing clean out of muddy water.
The small musician beings echo the heavenly musicians that accompany Amida in Japanese paintings of paradise, redrawn as cute sci-fi characters.
The Dead Sea, the lowest land on Earth and a place sacred to several religions, becomes a backdrop for a universal, borderless spirituality.
context: Mariko Mori was born in Tokyo in 1967, worked as a fashion model, studied at Bunka Fashion College and in London, and was based partly in New York.
Her 1990s work mixed fashion, cosplay, manga and anime with high-tech imagery, reflecting Japanese youth culture.
Her later work became more openly spiritual and environmental, drawing on Buddhism, Shinto and prehistoric Japanese culture.
Critics have debated whether her blend of sincere religion and slick commercial style is critical, celebratory, or both.
The cute musicians connect to kawaii, the Japanese pop aesthetic of cuteness found in anime, toys and advertising, here mixed with sacred imagery. On the exam.
If asked the artist → Mariko Mori, Japanese; date → 1998.
Medium: color photograph on glass, digitally manipulated.
Subject: Mori as a Buddhist goddess (Kichijōten) floating over the Dead Sea.
Title meaning: the Pure Land, Amida Buddha’s paradise.
Themes: spirituality plus technology, pop culture, globalism.
Attribution clue: the artist in costume, glossy digital colors, anime-like figures.
Continuity and change: traditional Buddhist symbols (lotus, paradise, heavenly musicians) carried into a new digital medium.

242.title: Lying with the Wolf
242.plain: A very large, delicate drawing in ink and pencil by Kiki Smith of a nude woman lying calmly against a wolf, her arm around its neck. Smith reworks fairy tales like Little Red Riding Hood and stories of saints so that the woman and the predator become companions instead of victim and threat. It is a feminist retelling about women, nature and animals.
242.spot: A wall-sized drawing on crinkled, patched paper of a naked woman reclining against a large dark wolf, both shown in thin lines with some areas darkened and rubbed.
242.remember: Kiki keeps the wolf: Kiki Smith, 2001. Red Riding Hood rewrites the ending: no hunter needed.
compare: No. 247 (§11.24), Preying Mantra: Mutu also builds a female figure merged with animal and nature imagery to question how women are seen.
No. 115 (§5.17), Olympia: Manet’s reclining nude confronts a male viewer; Smith’s reclining nude ignores the viewer and turns to the wolf.
No. 107 (§5.9), La Grande Odalisque: Ingres’s odalisque is an eroticized fantasy for a male patron; Smith’s nude is self-possessed.
242.vocab: drawing, ink, nude, feminism, reclining nude.

form: Ink and pencil on paper, about 7 by 15 feet, much larger than a typical drawing.
The thin paper is made of pieced sheets, visibly creased, torn, patched and pinned directly to the wall, so it feels fragile and handmade.
The wolf’s fur is built up in dark, dense ink, while the woman is drawn mostly in light outline, creating contrast between them.
Sketchy, searching lines with erasures and reworking are left visible, emphasizing process.
Both figures are close to life-size and lie at eye level, as if the viewer is in the room with them.
function: Exhibited as gallery art; it belongs to a group of works from around 2000 to 2001 in which Smith revisited fairy tales and saints’ lives.
Meant to offer a gentle, alternative image to violent or fearful stories about women and wild animals.
Shown alongside related sculptures, such as Rapture (2001), a bronze of a woman stepping out of a wolf’s belly.
content: In Little Red Riding Hood, the wolf devours the girl until a male hunter rescues her; Smith removes the violence and the rescuer.
Smith has linked the image to Saint Genevieve, the patron saint of Paris, said in legend to have calmed a wolf.
The woman’s nudity is not erotic display for a viewer; she is at ease, without shame, and on equal terms with the animal.
The pairing suggests kinship between humans and animals and between women and the natural world.
context: Kiki Smith was born in 1954 in Nuremberg, Germany, the daughter of the American sculptor Tony Smith, and grew up in New Jersey.
In the 1980s and 1990s she was known for sculptures of the body, its fluids and organs, during the AIDS crisis, which took her sister in 1988.
From the late 1990s she turned to fairy tales, myths, saints and animals, often from a feminist angle.
She works across printmaking, sculpture, drawing and textiles, and has a strong interest in craft and fragile materials.
Her animal works belong to a broader interest in ecology and the idea that humans are part of nature, not separate from or above it. On the exam.
If asked the artist → Kiki Smith, American; date → 2001.
Medium: ink and pencil on paper, very large scale.
Content: a nude woman embracing a wolf, calmly.
Sources: Little Red Riding Hood inverted; Saint Genevieve legend.
Themes: feminism, the female body, human–animal relationships.
Trap: it is a drawing, not a print or painting.
Comparison theme: the reclining female nude, long painted by men for male viewers, rethought by a woman artist.

243.title: Darkytown Rebellion
243.medium: Cut paper and projection on wall
243.plain: A room-sized installation by Kara Walker of black cut-paper silhouettes of figures in the clothes of the pre–Civil War South, acting out violent, sexual and humiliating scenes about slavery. Colored light is projected onto the walls, so visitors’ own shadows fall among the figures. Walker uses the polite, old-fashioned craft of the silhouette to show the brutality and racist stereotypes it was never used to depict.
243.spot: Life-size black paper silhouettes pasted directly onto a gallery wall, in nineteenth-century dress, with colored light washing over them and viewers’ shadows mixed in.
243.remember: Kara Walker walks you into the wall: your shadow joins the silhouettes, 2001.
compare: No. 108 (§5.10), Liberty Leading the People: Delacroix’s revolutionary crowd is heroic; Walker’s chaotic ‘rebellion’ is grotesque and unsettling.
No. 111 (§5.13), Slave Ship: Turner’s Slave Ship also confronts the violence of slavery, but through sublime landscape rather than caricature.
No. 244 (§11.21), The Swing: Shonibare also restages the European past with a twist to expose the slavery and colonialism behind it.
No. 141 (§5.43), The Migration of the Negro, Panel no. 49: Lawrence tells Black history through dignified, simplified figures; Walker uses stereotype and shock.

form: Cut paper and projection on wall: black paper silhouettes cut by hand and adhered to the wall, about 14 by 37 feet.
Colored light from overhead projectors washes over the walls in blues, reds and yellows.
Viewers moving through the room cast shadows onto the wall, which merge with the cutpaper figures.
The silhouette reduces figures to black outlines, flattening them into types, the way stereotypes do.
Elegant, decorative outlines contrast sharply with the brutal actions they show.
function: A gallery installation designed to surround the viewer and implicate them in the scene.
Meant to confront the history of slavery and the racist stereotypes that still shape images of Black Americans.
It provokes discomfort and debate on purpose, rather than offering a clear moral.
content: Figures in antebellum dress perform scenes of violence, sexual exploitation and chaos, mixing caricature with nightmare.
The title uses a racist slur on purpose, in the style of nineteenth-century minstrel humor and racist ‘Darktown’ cartoon prints, paired with ‘Rebellion’, recalling real slave revolts.
Source correction: the title does not cite Delacroix; some writers compare the chaotic crowd to revolutionary history paintings such as No. 108, but that is an interpretation.
Viewers’ shadows joining the scene suggest that everyone, today, is caught up in this history and its images.
context: Kara Walker was born in 1969 in Stockton, California, and moved at thirteen to Stone Mountain, Georgia, a place tied to Confederate memory and the Ku Klux Klan.
Silhouettes, popular in the late 1700s and 1800s, were a cheap, genteel portrait craft; some cutters were Black, such as the formerly enslaved Moses Williams.
She won a MacArthur Fellowship in 1997 at age 27; some older Black artists, notably Betye Saar, criticized her for recycling racist imagery.
Later works include A Subtlety (2014), a giant sugar sphinx in a Brooklyn sugar factory, and Fons Americanus (2019) in Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall. On the exam.
If asked the artist → Kara Walker, African American; date → 2001.
Medium: cut-paper silhouettes plus colored light projection.
Key feature: viewers’ shadows become part of the work.
Themes: slavery, racist stereotypes, sexual violence, the antebellum South.
If asked about tradition → appropriates the genteel 18th–19th century craft of the silhouette.
Reception: controversial; praised and criticized for using racist imagery.
Attribution clue: black cut-paper silhouettes of antebellum figures doing shocking things means Kara Walker.

244.title: The Swing (after Fragonard)
244.plain: A three-dimensional version of Fragonard’s famous Rococo painting The Swing, by British-Nigerian artist Yinka Shonibare: a headless mannequin on a swing, kicking off her shoe, wearing an eighteenth-century dress made of brightly patterned ‘African’ wax-print fabric. The missing head points to the French Revolution’s guillotine, and the fabric points to colonial trade. It asks who paid for European aristocrats’ leisure.
244.spot: A life-size headless mannequin in a full eighteenth-century gown of bold, colorful patterned fabric, sitting on a swing hung in mid-air, one shoe flying off, with artificial leaves around it.
244.remember: Shonibare ‘shone’ a light on Fragonard’s swinger, 2001: same pose, no head, African-looking cloth that is really Dutch.
compare: No. 101 (§5.3), The Swing: The original Rococo painting, which Shonibare restages in three dimensions with colonial history added.
No. 243 (§11.20), Darkytown Rebellion: Walker also re-performs eighteenth- and nineteenthcentury imagery to expose slavery and racism.
No. 245 (§11.22), Old Man’s Cloth: El Anatsui also uses materials tied to colonial trade to make cloth-like art about African identity.
No. 232 (§11.9), Dancing at the Louvre: Ringgold also places a figure of color into a famous European artwork’s world.
244.vocab: installation, Dutch wax print, tableau, Rococo, colonialism.

form: A mixed-media installation: a life-size mannequin, a cotton costume, a swing, shoes and artificial foliage.
The dress is made of Dutch wax print fabric, in bright, bold patterns associated with West Africa.
The figure is headless, a signature feature of Shonibare’s mannequins.
The mannequin’s skin is a brown tone, making the figure’s race hard to pin down.
It is a tableau (a staged scene frozen like a painting) seen in the round, so the viewer can walk around a once-flat image.
Only the woman on the swing is shown; the two men from the painting are left out.
function: A gallery installation, now in the Tate, London; made in 2001.
It reenacts a famous painting in the Wallace Collection, also in London, so many viewers know the original.
It works as a critique and also as a playful, attractive object, using beauty to carry a political message.
content: It recreates Fragonard’s The Swing (No. 101), a frivolous, flirtatious scene of aristocratic pleasure painted in 1767.
The missing head refers to the guillotine and the French Revolution, which ended this aristocratic world.
Dutch wax cloth was made by Dutch (and British) factories copying Indonesian batik, then sold in West Africa, where it became a symbol of African identity.
So the fabric is a hybrid of European industry, Asian design and African markets, revealing how ‘authentic’ identity is shaped by colonial trade.
The point: the luxury and leisure of the European elite were funded by colonialism and slavery.
context: Yinka Shonibare was born in London in 1962, grew up in Lagos, Nigeria, and returned to London to study art.
At eighteen he contracted transverse myelitis, which left him partly paralyzed; he works with assistants to make his pieces.
He was made an MBE (2004) and CBE (2019) and uses the honor in his name partly with irony, given its imperial associations.
He buys his wax-print fabric in London’s Brixton market, itself a sign of global diaspora trade.
Other works include Nelson’s Ship in a Bottle (2010) for London’s Trafalgar Square. On the exam.
If asked the source → recreates Fragonard’s The Swing (No. 101).
Artist: Yinka Shonibare, British-Nigerian; date 2001.
Material: Dutch wax print fabric, which is European-made, Indonesian-inspired and African-marketed.
Headless → guillotine and the French Revolution.
Themes: colonialism, hybrid identity, class, global trade.
Trap: the fabric is not traditional African cloth; that is the point.
Attribution clue: headless mannequins in European period costume made of wax-print fabric means Shonibare.

245.title: Old Man’s Cloth
245.plain: A huge, shimmering wall hanging by Ghanaian artist El Anatsui, made from thousands of flattened aluminum caps and seals from liquor bottles, stitched together with copper wire. It drapes and folds like fabric and recalls Ghana’s kente cloth. The bottle caps carry a history: European alcohol was traded for enslaved people in West Africa, and it is still part of local economies.
245.spot: A large, metallic, quilt-like hanging that ripples and folds on the wall, made of small flattened pieces of gold, silver, red and black metal joined into blocks and stripes.
245.remember: El Anatsui’s ‘Old Man’s Cloth’, 2003: an elder’s kente made of liquor caps. ‘Ana-TSUI’ sounds like ‘a new sew’ of trash.
compare: No. 162 (§6.10), All-T’oqapu tunic: The Inka tunic is a textile that signals rank and power, as kente does.
No. 170 (§7.4), Sika dwa kofi: The Asante Golden Stool comes from the same Ghanaian royal culture associated with kente.
No. 237 (§11.14), Pisupo Lua Afe: Tuffery also turns discarded consumer packaging into art criticizing trade and its effects.
No. 232 (§11.9), Dancing at the Louvre: Ringgold’s quilt also brings a textile tradition into fine art to carry history.
245.vocab: kente, found object, recycled materials, textile, assemblage, installation.

form: Aluminum and copper wire: thousands of bottle caps and neck seals flattened, cut and folded, then joined with copper wire.
Very large (around 16 feet tall, depending on how it is hung), it hangs like textile, with folds and creases that catch the light.
Small units are wired into larger blocks and strips, echoing the way kente is woven in narrow strips and sewn together.
The work is flexible: Anatsui lets installers drape and fold it differently each time it is shown, so its shape is never fixed.
The surface mixes gold and darker tones, creating a shimmering, rich effect from cheap materials.
Up close, the brand names and colors printed on individual caps are still visible, so the viewer sees the trash inside the luxury.
function: Made in 2003 as a gallery work; it is now in the Harn Museum of Art at the University of Florida.
Bridges sculpture and textile, and also painting, since it hangs on the wall like a picture.
Produced in a studio with many assistants who flatten and connect caps, while Anatsui designs the arrangement.
content: Kente cloth, made by the Asante and Ewe peoples of Ghana, signals royalty, status and important occasions; Anatsui is Ewe.
The title suggests the cloth an elder would wear, linking it to age, wisdom and respect.
Liquor (rum and gin) was a major European trade good exchanged for enslaved Africans; the caps recall this history and the continuing alcohol trade.
Turning trash into a luxurious cloth suggests transformation, memory and the connection of local and global economies.
context: El Anatsui, born in 1944 in Anyako, Ghana, has lived and taught since 1975 at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka.
He began his bottle-cap works around the late 1990s after finding a bag of caps; the caps come from Nigerian distilleries.
He has said that cloth is to Africans what monuments are to Westerners: a record of history and memory.
He won the Golden Lion for lifetime achievement at the 2015 Venice Biennale and made a large commission for Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall in 2023. On the exam.
If asked materials → aluminum bottle caps and copper wire.
Artist: El Anatsui, Ghanaian, working in Nigeria; date 2003.
Visual reference: kente cloth from Ghana.
History: liquor and the transatlantic slave trade; recycling and consumption.
Form: flexible; installed differently each time.
Trap: it is sculpture that looks like textile, not woven fabric.
Attribution clue: a draped, glittering metal hanging made of thousands of small flattened pieces means El Anatsui.

246.title: Stadia II
246.plain: A large layered painting by Ethiopian-born American artist Julie Mehretu, combining architectural drawings of stadiums with swirling marks, flags and bursts of color. Stadiums are places where crowds, nationalism, sports, spectacle and advertising meet, and the painting maps that energy. It looks abstract but is built on real architectural plans.
246.spot: A big canvas with fine black architectural line drawings of curved stands and arenas, overlaid with colorful flag-like shapes, arcs and tiny marks swirling in a vortex.
246.remember: Mehretu maps the ‘mayhem’ of stadia, 2004. Stadia is the plural of stadium.
compare: No. 44 (§3.33), Colosseum: The Colosseum is the original stadium for mass spectacle and political control of crowds.
No. 238 (§11.15), Electronic Superhighway: Paik also maps social space and information networks across a large field.
No. 132 (§5.34), Improvisation 28: Kandinsky’s abstraction also uses swirling marks and color, but for spiritual expression rather than mapping social space.
246.vocab: abstract, architectural drawing, palimpsest, acrylic paint, globalization.

form: Ink and acrylic on canvas, about 9 by 12 feet.
Built in layers: Mehretu draws in ink, seals it with clear acrylic, sands it smooth, and draws again, so earlier drawings show through like a palimpsest.
Precise architectural drawings of stadium seating and roofs mix with freer gestural marks.
Colored shapes resembling flags, banners and logos float across the surface.
A swirling composition suggests movement, crowds and energy without a single focal point.
A pale ground and fine black linework let a limited set of bright accent colors stand out like banners in a crowd.
function: Gallery work, part of the Stadia series of 2004 (Stadia I, II, III); Stadia II is at the Carnegie Museum of Art, Pittsburgh.
Explores how public spaces shape group behavior and identity.
Shown in an international art context where questions of globalization were central.
content: Stadiums are places of mass spectacle: crowds unite around teams and nations, sometimes peacefully, sometimes aggressively.
Flags and corporate-looking shapes point to nationalism and globalization, including sponsorship of sports.
Mehretu has called her small marks ‘characters’ with social agency, like individuals in a crowd.
Made in 2004, the year of the Athens Olympics and during the Iraq War, when global competition and conflict were in the news.
The layers act like history: older plans remain visible under newer marks, the way cities are built over their own past.
context: Julie Mehretu was born in 1970 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, and moved to Michigan with her family in 1977 during political turmoil.
She studied in Senegal and at the Rhode Island School of Design, and received a MacArthur Fellowship in 2005.
Her work maps cities, architecture, history and power through layered abstraction.
She has described her paintings as ‘story maps of no location’, combining many places and times rather than picturing one real site.
She is one of the most commercially successful living painters; her large commission Mural (2009) fills the lobby of the Goldman Sachs headquarters in New York. On the exam.
If asked the artist → Julie Mehretu, Ethiopian-American; date → 2004.
Medium: ink and acrylic on canvas.
Content: layered architectural plans of stadiums, flags and marks.
Themes: spectacle, crowds, nationalism, globalization.
Technique: layering and sanding; drawing within painting.
Trap: it looks purely abstract but is grounded in real architecture.
Comparison theme: the stadium as a political space, from Rome’s Colosseum to modern global sport.

247.title: Preying Mantra
247.plain: A collage by Kenyan-born artist Wangechi Mutu of a reclining female figure built from magazine clippings, ink and paint on shiny Mylar film. She is part woman, part praying mantis and part snake, seductive and dangerous at once. Mutu uses fashion, pornography, medical and ethnographic images to critique how media and colonial history have pictured Black women’s bodies.
247.spot: A reclining dark-skinned female figure with collaged patches of skin, a snake-like form and pooled ink stains on a pale, glossy background.
247.remember: Mutu’s mantis prays and preys, 2006. ‘Preying Mantra’ is a pun: praying mantis plus repeated chant.
compare: No. 107 (§5.9), La Grande Odalisque: Ingres’s reclining ‘exotic’ woman is the kind of colonial fantasy Mutu deconstructs.
No. 126 (§5.28), Les Demoiselles d’Avignon: Picasso borrowed African masks to make women look threatening; Mutu, an African woman, takes control of that imagery.
No. 242 (§11.19), Lying with the Wolf : Kiki Smith also merges woman and animal, but in calm harmony rather than menace.
247.vocab: collage, Mylar, composite creature, reclining nude, Afrofuturism, mixed media.

form: Mixed media on Mylar: magazine clippings, ink, paint and other materials on a smooth, translucent polyester film.
The figure’s skin is pieced together from cut-out images, so her body looks fragmented and constructed.
Ink pools and bleeds on the nonabsorbent Mylar, creating organic stains and textures.
She reclines on a patterned blanket, a pose drawn from the long tradition of reclining nudes in Western art.
A snake winds near and around her body, blending with plant and animal forms.
Her collage sources include fashion, motorcycle and pornographic magazines and medical illustrations, cut so their origins are only half recognizable.
function: Gallery art; it is in the collection of the Brooklyn Museum.
Meant to question how images of women are made and consumed, especially in fashion and pornography.
Uses beauty and attraction to draw viewers in, then unsettles them.
content: The female praying mantis sometimes eats the male after mating, linking the figure to the idea of the dangerous woman.
The snake recalls Eve and temptation; some writers also link it to Mami Wata, an African water spirit often shown with a snake.
The collaged body from magazines shows how women’s bodies are assembled by the media, from parts and stereotypes.
The title’s pun combines praying, preying and mantra, mixing devotion, danger and repetition.
Her relaxed, confident pose suggests a woman in control of her own image, even though her body is assembled from other people’s pictures.
context: Wangechi Mutu was born in 1972 in Nairobi, Kenya, studied at Cooper Union and Yale, and lived in New York for many years.
She draws on colonial ethnographic photographs, which presented African bodies as exotic specimens.
Her work belongs to Afrofuturism, which imagines African identities through science fiction and hybrid bodies.
In 2019 she made four bronze seated female figures for the facade of the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
Her use of medical diagrams recalls how Western medicine studied, displayed and exploited Black women’s bodies. On the exam.
If asked the artist → Wangechi Mutu, Kenyan-American; date 2006.
Medium: collage and mixed media on Mylar.
Content: a hybrid woman-mantis-snake, reclining.
Themes: representation of Black women’s bodies, media, colonialism, sexuality.
Tradition: subverts the Western reclining nude.
Trap: ‘Preying’, not ‘Praying’; the pun is deliberate.
Attribution clue: a hybrid female body collaged from magazine skin on glossy Mylar means Wangechi Mutu.

248.title: Shibboleth
248.plain: A crack 548 feet (167 meters) long, running the full length of the floor of the Turbine Hall at Tate Modern in London, by Colombian artist Doris Salcedo. It begins as a hairline and widens and deepens, with chain-link fence embedded in its sides. It stands for the divisions that separate rich countries from immigrants and the colonized; when it was filled in afterward, a scar was left on purpose.
248.spot: A jagged crack in a vast, industrial concrete floor, forking and widening across the hall, with people bending down to look into it.
248.remember: Salcedo splits the Tate, 2007–2008: a ‘shibboleth’ is a word that marks outsiders, and the crack marks who is shut out.
compare: No. 250 (§11.27), Kui Hua Zi: Ai Weiwei’s Sunflower Seeds was another Turbine Hall commission that addressed the individual and politics.
No. 225 (§11.2), Vietnam Veterans Memorial: Maya Lin’s memorial also cuts into the ground to create a space for remembering loss.
No. 224 (§11.1), The Gates: Christo and Jeanne-Claude’s Gates was also temporary, but added objects to a public space instead of cutting into one.
248.vocab: installation, negative space, site-specific, shibboleth, ephemeral, commission.

form: An installation made by cutting into the concrete floor and inserting cast concrete sections, with chain-link fencing embedded in the crack’s walls.
The crack is about 548 feet long, zigzagging and forking across the entire Turbine Hall floor.
It starts as a hairline and grows wider and deeper, in places wide enough to catch a foot.
A ‘negative sculpture’ that is a cut into space rather than an object rising up.
Salcedo did not publish exactly how it was built, adding to the effect that the building itself had split.
function: Made for the Unilever Series, the yearly commission for Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, on view October 2007 to April 2008.
Made viewers look down instead of up, at the foundations of the building and, symbolically, of modern society.
After it closed it was filled in, but a visible scar was left in the floor as a reminder.
content: The title comes from Judges 12 in the Bible: Gileadites identified fleeing Ephraimites because they pronounced ‘shibboleth’ wrongly, and killed them.
A shibboleth now means any test that marks insiders and outsiders, like language, accent or skin color.
The crack stands for borders, racism, immigration and colonial exclusion that divide the wealthy West from everyone else.
Salcedo argued that modernity was built on racism and exclusion, so the crack lies in the foundations themselves.
context: Doris Salcedo was born in 1958 in Bogotá, Colombia; her work deals with violence, grief and the disappeared from Colombia’s long conflict.
Other works include Noviembre 6 y 7 (2002), with chairs lowered from the Palace of Justice in Bogotá, and Fragmentos (2018), floors cast from melted guerrilla weapons.
The Turbine Hall was the turbine room of Bankside Power Station before Tate Modern opened in 2000.
Some visitors tripped into the crack, raising public debate about safety and art.
It was the eighth Unilever Series commission; Ai Weiwei’s Sunflower Seeds (No. 250) was the eleventh in the same hall. On the exam.
If asked the artist → Doris Salcedo, Colombian; date 2007–2008.
Location: Turbine Hall, Tate Modern, London.
Form: a 548-foot crack in the floor, with chain-link fencing in its sides.
Title source: Judges 12, a password that marked outsiders for death.
Themes: racism, immigration, borders, colonial exclusion.
Afterlife: filled in, but the scar remains.
Comparison theme: art made by removing or cutting rather than adding, like a monument dug into the ground.

249.title: MAXXI National Museum of XXI Century Arts
249.plain: Italy’s national museum of twenty-first-century art and architecture in Rome, designed by Iraqi-British architect Zaha Hadid. Long, curving bands of concrete gallery bend, cross and stack over each other like streams or highways, with black staircases hanging in the open atrium and a glass roof filtering daylight. It rejects the idea of a museum as a set of neutral boxes and won the Stirling Prize in 2010.
249.spot: Smooth, flowing concrete forms that curve and overlap, with a large cantilevered gallery jutting out over the entrance and black steel stairs crossing a white interior.
249.remember: Zaha’s MAXXI is the ‘maximum’ curve: Rome, 2009, completed and opened in 2010.
compare: No. 240 (§11.17), Guggenheim Museum Bilbao: Gehry’s Guggenheim Bilbao is another curving, anti-box museum using digital design.
No. 146 (§5.48), Seagram Building: The Seagram Building’s rational glass box is the modernist model Hadid rejects.
No. 46 (§3.35), Pantheon: The Pantheon, also in Rome, shows ancient Roman concrete creating dramatic interior space with light from above.
249.vocab: cantilever, atrium, Deconstructivism, parametric design, concrete, circulation.

form: Built of concrete, glass and steel; curving walls of smooth, poured concrete define the galleries.
Long galleries flow, bend, intersect and stack, like ribbons or rivers crossing over each other.
A cantilevered gallery (projecting out with support at only one end) juts out above the entrance plaza.
The roof is glass with concrete fins and louvers that filter natural light into the galleries.
Suspended black steel staircases and bridges cross the tall atrium, emphasizing movement.
There are few right angles; walls curve continuously and floors slope into ramps.
function: Italy’s national museum of 21st-century arts, combining an art museum and an architecture museum.
Commissioned by the Italian Ministry of Culture after an international competition Hadid won in 1998–1999.
Meant to show that contemporary art and architecture belong in Rome, a city dominated by ancient and Baroque landmarks.
Its open, flexible galleries suit changing temporary exhibitions and large installations rather than a fixed display.
content: The building is about flow and circulation: visitors choose their own paths through intersecting spaces.
Hadid compared it to a confluence of lines, like bundled paths or currents, rather than a fixed sequence of rooms.
It suggests that experience of art is open-ended and that the museum itself is part of the art.
The black stairs against white concrete read like drawn lines, a reminder that Hadid began as a painter of abstract architectural visions.
context: Zaha Hadid (1950–2016) was born in Baghdad, studied mathematics in Beirut and architecture at London’s Architectural Association.
In 2004 she became the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize, architecture’s highest honor.
She was included in the 1988 Deconstructivist Architecture exhibition at MoMA; her later fluid style is often called parametricism, digital design driven by variable parameters.
The site was a former military barracks in Rome’s Flaminio district; construction ran from about 2003 to 2009.
MAXXI won the RIBA Stirling Prize in 2010.
Her other major buildings include the London Aquatics Centre for the 2012 Olympics and the Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku, Azerbaijan. On the exam.
If asked the architect → Zaha Hadid, first woman to win the Pritzker Prize (2004).
Name: MAXXI, National Museum of 21st Century Arts, Rome; date 2009.
Materials: concrete, glass and steel.
Style: Deconstructivism and parametric design, fluid curves instead of boxes.
Function: national museum of contemporary art and architecture.
Trap: it is in Rome, Italy, not Spain; do not confuse with Gehry’s Bilbao.

250.title: Kui Hua Zi (Sunflower Seeds)
250.plain: An installation of about 100 million porcelain sunflower seeds, each one sculpted and hand-painted by artisans in Jingdezhen, China, then spread across the floor of the Turbine Hall at Tate Modern. They look mass-produced but are all handmade. Ai Weiwei, a Chinese artist and government critic, links the seeds to Mao-era propaganda, shared snacks in hard times, and the labor behind ‘Made in China’.
250.spot: A vast flat gray carpet of tiny seed-shaped objects covering a huge industrial floor; close up, each seed has painted stripes like a real sunflower seed.
250.remember: Ai Weiwei’s ‘kui hua zi’ = sunflower seeds, 2010–2011: one hundred million seeds, one for every ‘sunflower’ who turned to Mao.
compare: No. 204 (§9.13), The David Vases: The David Vases were also made in Jingdezhen porcelain workshops for an elite market.
No. 193 (§9.2), Terra cotta warriors: The Terra Cotta Warriors also combine mass production with individual variation.
No. 212 (§9.21), Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan: Chairman Mao en Route to Anyuan shows the Mao cult that the sunflower imagery refers to.
No. 248 (§11.25), Shibboleth: Salcedo’s Shibboleth was an earlier Turbine Hall commission with political meaning.
250.vocab: porcelain, installation, mass production, propaganda, commission.

form: About 100 million life-size seeds of porcelain, totaling roughly 150 tons, spread about 10 centimeters deep over about 1,000 square meters.
Each seed was hand-shaped in a mold, fired at about 1,300 °C, hand-painted with a few brushstrokes, and fired again.
About 1,600 artisans in Jingdezhen worked on the seeds for over two years.
From a distance it is a single gray landscape; up close, each seed is slightly different.
Porcelain is a traditional luxury material, used here for a cheap, everyday object.
function: Made for the Unilever Series commission in Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall, on view October 2010 to May 2011.
Visitors were first invited to walk on the seeds, but this was stopped within days because of porcelain dust, a health hazard.
Afterward, seeds were sold and acquired by museums; the Tate later acquired several million of them.
content: During the Cultural Revolution, propaganda showed Mao as the sun and the people as sunflowers turning toward him.
Sunflower seeds were a common snack shared among friends, a small pleasure in hard times; Ai remembers sharing them as a child.
Each seed is unique yet lost in a mass, raising the question of the individual within the collective.
The work comments on ’Made in China’: mass production, cheap labor and global consumption.
context: Ai Weiwei, born in 1957 in Beijing, is the son of the poet Ai Qing, who was sent to labor camps; Ai lived in New York from 1981 to 1993.
He helped design the Beijing National Stadium (‘Bird’s Nest’) for the 2008 Olympics with Herzog and de Meuron, who also converted Tate Modern.
He investigated the deaths of schoolchildren in the 2008 Sichuan earthquake, angering oﬀicials.
In 2011, while the installation was still on view, he was detained by Chinese authorities for 81 days without charge.
Jingdezhen has been China’s porcelain capital for centuries, producing imperial wares. On the exam.
If asked the artist → Ai Weiwei, Chinese; date 2010–2011.
Material: porcelain, hand-sculpted and hand-painted.
Scale: about 100 million seeds, made in Jingdezhen by about 1,600 workers.
Location: Turbine Hall, Tate Modern.
Themes: Mao propaganda, individual versus mass, ‘Made in China’, labor.
Trap: they look mass-produced but are handmade.
Comparison theme: the individual within the mass, as in the Terra Cotta Warriors, and skilled porcelain labor, as in the David Vases.
